This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world's books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright <note>The legal right that grants the creator of an original work exclusive rights to its use and distribution</note> to expire and the book to enter the public domain. A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that's often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other marginalia <note>Handwritten notes or markings in the margins of a book</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file - a reminder of this book's long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying <note>The use of software to automatically search or download data from a system</note>.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ *Refrain from automated querying* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google's system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, optical character recognition <note>OCR; the mechanical or electronic conversion of images of typed or printed text into machine-encoded text</note> or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ *Maintain attribution* The Google "watermark" <note>A faint identifying image or pattern in paper or a digital file</note> you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ *Keep it legal* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can't offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book's appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

## About Google Book Search

Google's mission is to organize the world's information and to make it universally accessible and useful. Google Book Search helps readers discover the world's books while helping authors and publishers reach new audiences. --- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page provides a detailed table of contents or "Synopsis" for the first volume of Kircher’s Egyptian Oedipus. It follows the main title page and outlines the intellectual structure of the book, which Kircher envisions as a "Temple of Isis" through which the reader must pass to understand ancient wisdom.</meta>

# SYNOPSIS OF THE FIRST VOLUME.
->Which is also titled<-
## THE TEMPLE OF ISIS. <note>original: "Templum Isiacum"; Isis was the preeminent Egyptian goddess of magic and wisdom. Kircher uses the metaphor of a temple to describe the structure of his research.</note>

This volume contains the <term>Chorography</term> <note>The geographical description of regions or districts.</note> of Egypt, its Dynasties, Politics, and Theogony—or the Architecture of the Gods. It covers the origin of Egyptian idolatry and its propagation across the entire world, particularly among the Greeks, Hebrews, Romans, Indians, and other nations. It is divided into five Treatises. <note>original: "Syntagmata"; a Greek-derived term for a systematic collection of writings or a formal treatise.</note>

**THE PROPYLAEUM.** <note>original: "Propylæum"; In classical architecture, this is the monumental gateway to a temple. Here, it serves as the book's introduction.</note> In which the goal, cause, and occasion of the entire work are explained; the arguments of those who oppose the restoration of the hieroglyphic science are refuted in several chapters.

**TREATISE I. *The Nile Delta*.** Contains a geographical description of all Egypt, distributed into 30 <term>Nomes</term> <note>original: "Nomos"; the administrative districts of ancient Egypt.</note>; it presents the names of the Gods usually worshiped in each district; it reveals the causes of the rising and falling of the Nile, as well as the origin of the river itself—perhaps unknown until now—finally uncovered by certain and faithful testimony. It demonstrates the Dynasties of the Kings of Egypt from all the monuments of the East, where the deeds of the Kings before and after the Great Flood are treated extensively according to the tradition of the Arabs.

**TREATISE II. *Egyptian Politics*.** Deals with the life and customs of the Kings and their methods for the successful and prosperous administration of the Kingdom; likewise concerning the laws, institutions, and various classes of subjects. It pursues all these matters through political, <term>tropological</term> <note>An interpretive method that seeks moral or figurative meanings behind literal descriptions.</note>, mystical, and hieroglyphic methods.

**TREATISE III. *Theogony, or the Architecture of the Gods*.** In this section, the origin of Egyptian superstition and its spread to the Greeks and Romans is discussed. It covers Osiris, Isis, Apis, Serapis, Canopus, Horus, Harpocrates, Typhon, Mithra, Ammon, and the rest of the Egyptian Divinities. Finally, it deals extensively with the ceremonies and rites established in their honor, and the worship of various animals. Here it is clearly shown that the foundations of Greek and Roman idolatry were received from the Egyptians.

**TREATISE IV. *The Pantheon of the Hebrews*.** This section treats the various idols, sacred groves, altars, and sacrifices of the Hebrews, Syrians, Chaldeans, Persians, Samaritans, and other nations neighboring Egypt. By a parallel comparison, it demonstrates that all the idolatry and rites of these said nations first flowed from the Egyptians.

**TREATISE V. *The Egyptian Ape*.** <note>original: "Simia Ægyptiaca"; The term "ape" or "mimic" refers to how other cultures "aped" or imitated the original Egyptian religious systems.</note> This deals with the idolatry of the Indians, Chinese, Japanese, Tartars, Mughals, and the New World <note>The Americas.</note>, and its affinity to the Egyptian system, where manifest traces of Egyptian superstition will be revealed to the reader.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut tailpiece featuring symmetrical floral scrolls and acanthus leaves, common in 17th-century book design.</image-desc>

<summary>This page outlines the five "Syntagmata" or Treatises of the first volume, framing Egyptian culture as the "source" from which all other global religions and political systems originated. It introduces Kircher’s theory of "Interpretatio Christiana" and diffusionism, suggesting that even the New World and East Asia inherited Egyptian superstitions.</summary>

statically placed upon the pinnacle <note>original: *fastigio*. Kircher uses architectural metaphors to describe the Emperor's status.</note> of such sublimity and the vehemence of their brilliance, you so dazzle my eyes and mind that—just as it is not possible to describe them sufficiently due to the narrowness of the page nor according to their merits (my strength and pen failing)—I consider that they should be celebrated more wisely by silence alone, or certainly only briefly pointed out. 

This will be achieved, unless I am mistaken, even if with far from worthy praise, by this **Oedipus** <note>Kircher refers to his book, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, named after the mythical riddle-solver.</note> of mine, which, having long been promised to the **Republic of Letters** <note>original: *Reipublicæ Literariæ*, the international community of scholars and intellectuals in the 17th century.</note> and now released in full faith, I present to **YOUR** Most August sight. It was indeed fashioned by me with no small amount of careful study by lamplight <note>original: *lucubrationibus*, specifically referring to scholarly work performed late at night.</note>; yet it is destined to triumph in the Literary World by this glory alone: that it was drawn out by the force and efficacy of **YOUR** invincible mind. 

The work is indeed conspicuous for as many symbols as there are mirrors of **YOUR** virtues; for as many mysteries as there are models <note>original: *ectypis*, referring to a copy or an image molded from an original form.</note> of the sublime actions of **YOUR** great Soul: where all the defenses of the inter-chained virtues, which are seen elsewhere scattered and spread thin among others, are perceived here gathered and packed together; so that those qualities which are found divided and, as if channeled through ditches <note>original: *inciles*, irrigation or drainage channels.</note>, brought together <note>original: *corriuata*, the merging of various streams of water.</note> in many different people, are seen in **YOUR** one and the same breast without precedent, finished and made perfect by such a great embrace of things. 

In others, that virtue which polishes character has shone; but that which informs the mind was lacking. In **YOU**, **Greatest Caesar** <note>original: *Maxime Cæsar*, a traditional title for the Holy Roman Emperor.</note>, I see the faith and constancy toward the empire committed to **YOUR** care ad- <note>The page ends with the catchword "ad-", likely leading to "adorned" or "administered" on the following page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the dedication to Emperor Ferdinand III. The previous page ended with "fo-" which completed the word "forent" (they would be). This page describes the Emperor's virtues, specifically his moderation and justice during the turbulent times of the Thirty Years' War.</meta>

->**<-

...all admire; everyone—the highest, the middle, and the lowest—beholds with wonder your love toward the State <note>original: *Remp.*, an abbreviation for *Republicam*, referring here to the Holy Roman Empire.</note>; they look up uniquely to your devotion to religion and your pursuit of peace and harmony. They observe your other truly heroic virtues not merely through obvious signs; rather, everyone—whether sacred or secular, enemy or friend—feels and speaks of your illustrious deeds, your noble counsels, and your words uttered as if from an oracle. Perhaps a distant posterity will perceive the internal and mystical meanings of these words much more fully and with even greater veneration. 

Others have not lacked strength, fortitude, or power; yet they lacked the intellectual ornaments of knowledge. But in **YOU**, who have embraced all things, there is a wonderful integrity of character, a rare and unusual fortitude, and a mind that remains unshaken, equal, and always the same amidst both prosperity and adversity. There is Justice <note>original: *Iustitia*</note> in your judicial inquiries, constancy in times of doubt, prudence in your counsels, and an incredible clemency—the likes of which no one has ever seen, read about, or heard of in any Prince <note>original: *Principe*, used here as a general title for a sovereign ruler.</note>. 

In the perilous state of these times, there has been no lack of provocations for **YOUR** severity, nor seeds of civil unrest, nor the festering wounds of embittered minds encountered everywhere. But **YOU**, guided by the rule <note>original: *amussi*, literally a mason's level or rule, implying exactness or a standard.</note> of justice—that is, by the provident moderation <note>original: *moderatione*</note> of **YOUR** great mind—have healed what was wounded rather than cutting it away. By choosing to overlook certain things and not inquiring too anxiously into every matter, you preferred to seem to have found good men rather than to have forced them to be so. You reject that foul maxim of Tyrants <note>original: *Tyrannorum*.</note>: "*let them hate, as long as...*" <note>This is the beginning of the famous Roman tragic fragment *Oderint dum metuant* ("Let them hate, so long as they fear"), a sentiment Kircher contrasts with the Emperor's clemency.</note>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to Emperor Ferdinand III. The previous page discussed the Emperor's clemency and justice; this page focuses on his intellectual brilliance and his role as a patron of the arts and sciences. The text concludes with the start of the word "authoritate" (authority).</meta>

...[that they should] fear, you reject by your very deeds, while you substitute a pronouncement truly worthy of Caesar: *let them not fear, provided they love; I prefer to be respected than to be feared by my own.* <note>original: "ne metuant, dum diligant; malo vereri, quàm à meis timeri." This is a virtuous reversal of the infamous tyrant’s motto, "let them hate, provided they fear."</note> But what shall I say of the true standard of Wisdom—I mean, of letters and the sciences?

**TO YOU** belongs a mind wonderfully capable of understanding all things; **TO YOU** a tongue that is the interpreter of all justice: as many words as you pour forth, so many laws you establish. In your knowledge of multiple languages, the World looks up to a revived Mithridates <note>Mithridates VI of Pontus was famously said to have mastered the twenty-two languages of the nations he ruled.</note>; in the choir of humane letters and the Muses, it recognizes an Apollo; in your skill in hidden Mathematics, it acknowledges a great Alfonso <note>Likely referring to King Alfonso X of Castile, known as "the Wise," a famous patron of astronomy.</note>; and finally, in secret Philosophy, it admires Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary "thrice-great" Egyptian sage to whom many foundational texts of alchemy and philosophy were attributed.</note>.

Nor do you pave the way toward the laurel of the learned in any other way than by your own example, since already from a tender age you have erected a training ground <note>original: *palæstram*, a wrestling school or place of exercise, used here metaphorically for a place of intellectual development.</note> for all the Muses within **YOUR** breast. Thus, the literary world acknowledges with joy that the heights of the liberal arts are now crowned not only with the poet's Laurel, but also with the Imperial Diadem; it sees that the long-standing conflict between Mars and Pallas <note>Mars represents war, while Pallas Athena represents wisdom and the arts. This suggests that the Emperor has brought peace and intellectual flourishing to his war-torn lands.</note> and her sisters has finally been settled.

Since you are therefore such a man and so great, **O MOST WISE CAESAR**, **YOU** alone were to be chosen as the Patron <note>original: *Tutor*, meaning a protector or legal guardian.</note> of this work. Because of the admirable Wisdom with which you are endowed, you are not only able to judge this new offspring—so unusual in its rarity—but also to defend it against the contentions of detractors by your authori-

<meta>Catchword: rita- [completing the word "auctoritate" or "authoritate," meaning authority]</meta>

<sig>** 2</sig>

...to confirm with **YOUR** authority, and to bring a safe protection to its novelty through the greatness of your power. Perhaps someone will accuse me of rashness and find me lacking in prudence, because I have not feared to disturb **YOU**, the Caesar burdened with the weight of sustaining the World, with my writing. But **YOU**, most lofty and at the same time most humane Caesar, from the august throne of **YOUR** kindness and Majesty, invited my humble person to approach you; you heartened me so that I would not fear; and finally, you urged me so that I would not hesitate. From this it came to pass that this Work, however narrow and unworthy of the eyes of such Majesty, nevertheless seemed august and worthy by this very fact: that the Augustus <note>A play on words: the Emperor's title was "Augustus," but the word also means "majestic."</note> commanded it to go forth; and so that it might easily come into the light of day, a generosity more than Royal was provided. Therefore, **MOST KIND CAESAR**, what you gave to me, I return to **YOU**—a Work not so much mine as **YOURS**. It is **YOURS** because I acknowledge myself entirely as **YOURS**, for as much as I am; it is mine because by **YOUR** far most generous assistance you have made it mine. Shall I not sing here with the Poet? <note>The author is quoting the Roman poet Martial, from his Epigrams (Book 9, 79 or 8, 82), traditionally addressed to the Emperor Domitian.</note>

> ->*Now we are worthy of the ears of our master and the royal dwellings,*<-
> ->*And may our lyre sound out with Augustus as the judge.*<-
> <note>original: "Iam dominas aures, iam regia tecta meremur, / Et chelys Augusta iudice nostra sonet."</note>

But I shall more boldly claim this: that this Work, arranged in the languages of nearly the entire World, [is fit for] Caesar's ap...

He uses classical metaphors and poetry to frame the Emperor as the ultimate judge of intellectual merit.</summary>

# FERDINAND III,
->by favoring clemency <note>original: *favente clementia*; a standard formula referring to divine grace or mercy.</note> elected Emperor of the Romans, ever Augustus, etc.<-

->For a perpetual memorial of the matter.<-

SO GREAT is the force and power of wisdom, that the wise man <note>A reference to King Solomon in the Book of Wisdom.</note> has judged it not only to be preferred to scepters and Kingdoms, but has also considered all riches as nothing in comparison to it. And rightly so: for nothing can be more effective for correctly governing the actions of the human race, or more strong for sustaining the weight of the World—which presses upon the shoulders of Kings—with a certain imperturbable constancy of mind, or finally more powerful for preserving the political body of the World in peace and union. For a multitude of Wise men is the health of the world, and a wise King is the stabilization of his people. This is the norm and the rule <term>rule<note>original: *amussis*; literally a mason’s leveling tool, used here to mean a standard of perfect precision.</note></term> of all Justice; under its guidance even the greatest empires reach the desired harbor of blessedness and happiness. Just as We, therefore, upon whom the supreme care of the Imperial office has been imposed by God's ordinance, have deemed this virtue to be embraced above others worthy of the Empire and always sought with every zeal; so too have we decided it should be promoted in others. 

When, therefore, We have encouraged our sincerely beloved Father Athanasius Kircher, a Priest of the Society of Jesus and a subject of Our Empire, for many years now, both to the study of natural things and Mathematics—which are certain very fertile nurseries <note>original: *seminaria*; literally "seed-beds" or nurseries where plants are grown from seed.</note> of the said wisdom—and especially to unearthing and explaining that more hidden doctrine of hieroglyphic literature, which they call the Wisdom of the Egyptians; and he indeed, according to the talent for interpretation and capacity of mind given to him by Divine Goodness, has long since published those specimens (as We have heard from men distinguished in judgment and knowledge of affairs) which have proved him to be by no means insufficient for worthily completing the task imposed upon him; and thus he may rightly be seen as the first to have opened the gate to the hitherto inaccessible inner sanctums <term>inner sanctums<note>original: *adyta*; the most sacred, private parts of a temple that were forbidden to the uninitiated.</note></term> of primeval Wisdom; and [he seeks] that praise in the present Work (which he calls the *Egyptian Oedipus* <note>In Greek mythology, Oedipus solved the riddle of the Sphinx; Kircher uses this title to suggest he has solved the "riddle" of Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>), a Work composed through the labors of many years, and also, as We understand, eagerly desired <note>The text ends mid-sentence here: "deside-"</note>

<summary>In this formal opening of the Imperial Privilege, Emperor Ferdinand III extols the virtue of wisdom as the essential tool for a ruler. He formally acknowledges his patronage of Athanasius Kircher and validates Kircher’s efforts to decode Egyptian hieroglyphs as a restoration of ancient wisdom.</summary>

<image-desc>Large historiated decorative initial 'S' featuring a figure amidst dense floral and vine-like scrollwork.</image-desc>LORD, you who honor your heavy diadem
With merit more than it honors you with the throne,
You, in whose breast dwell
Honest, virtuous, and holy desires;
You, who are a knower of true good
Amidst so many cares by which you govern a world,
Of sharp wit and profound knowledge,
Are a follower of doctrine and virtue;

<margin>Wherefore</margin> it happens then that with your frequent example
You precede the high laws; and being good and just,
With feelings of piety from your Imperial <note>original: "Augusto"</note> station,
Before ruling others, you rule yourself;
<margin>You</margin> who well know that he who governs on earth
Ought to feed, and not oppress, the flock,
And that he who greedily turns to another style
Strays and wanders from the straight path;
<margin>You,</margin> who finally are devoted to every good study,
And understand the art of every mastery <term>mastery: "Magisteria," referring here to the authoritative expert knowledge of the various sciences and arts.</term>,
Look upon Athanasius's volume part by part,
And you will see therein every branch of knowledge gathered.
<margin>Oedipus</margin> it is, who for the common good
Reveals the most hidden riddles of every Oedipus <note>The "Oedipus" here refers to Kircher himself or his book, functioning as the metaphorical "riddle-solver" of Egyptian mysteries, just as the mythical Oedipus solved the riddle of the Sphinx.</note>,
And offers and unveils to every understanding
The secrets reserved for the wisest.

--- Page 25 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedicatory poem (Canzone) by Pompeo Colonna to Emperor Ferdinand III. While the previous page praised the Emperor's personal virtues and governance, this section shifts focus to the content of Athanasius Kircher’s work: the "Oedipus Aegyptiacus," which claims to decode the hidden wisdom of ancient Egypt, its hieroglyphs, and the secrets of nature.</meta>

After its winding and crooked path
Where, like a Hydra, the Nile spreads its mouths,
Seen until now only as a giant and great,
It finally reveals its cradle, as a small child. <note>The poet compares Kircher's discovery of Egyptian wisdom to finding the long-hidden source of the Nile.</note>

You will see, Lord, in the commended deeds
Of those Kings who bowed to the laws,
A clear and living image expressed
Of what you have done in your own reign.

And so many Gods in the form of animals—
Isis, Anubis, Apis, or Serapis, or Osiris—
And so many other delusions born into the World,
Whose origins only Egypt could know.

But in those Sages there was not such folly
That they did not enclose hidden and rare mysteries
Within those Gods for whom the Altars smoked;
Of which the learned Athanasius now gives an account.

Further ahead then, a School will offer itself to you
To satisfy the most hungry minds,
Since every word written with those dark signs <note>original: "oscuri segni," a reference to Egyptian hieroglyphs which were then considered a mystical, symbolic language.</note>
Contains a science within it.

The Character <term>Character: Refers here to the "Signatura Rerum" or "Signature of Things," the belief that God imprinted a physical mark or "character" on every living thing that reveals its hidden medicinal or spiritual purpose.</term> that its creator impressed
Upon every creature—but which was not seen
By everyone—shall now be known by everyone,
Along with its virtue and its nature;

We cannot believe otherwise
Than that the first Father Adam, with a wise mind,
Assigned then to every thing here below
The name corresponding to its inner virtue.

Common medicine is here held as vain,
Which only drives out illness with its opposites;
And that alone is pursued for the common good
Which, by its own virtue, balances the humors. <term>humors: In pre-modern medicine, the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that had to be kept in balance to maintain health.</term>

Oh, almost like flashes of resplendent light
To track down secrets—now in the beasts,
In the birds, in the stones, now in the forests,
In the silent fish, or in the flowery fields—

Athanasius will send us! Rejoice now,
O sons of Asclepius <note>Esculapio: The ancient Greek god of medicine; here referring to physicians and scientists.</note>, for with such help
You will be able to restore, for the benefit of the sick,
The lost way of healing well.

--- Page 26 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedicatory poem by Pompeo Colonna. While the previous section discussed the primordial knowledge given to Adam and the "signatures" found in nature, this page outlines the specific disciplines Athanasius Kircher masters in his work: Euclidean geometry, Hermetic alchemy, natural magic, astronomy, and the decipherment of Egyptian obelisks.</meta>

Whoever has set foot in the *Elements*
Of the learned Euclid may now well hope—
Despite those "Wise Men"—to also create
Archytas’s bird and Archimedes’s globe. <note>original: "L'augel d' Archita," referring to the wooden dove of Archytas of Tarentum, an early automaton; the "globe of Archimedes" refers to his famous mechanical planetarium.</note>

Whoever by chance set out to wander
Through the rich and vast gardens of Hermes, <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy and Hermetic philosophy.</note>
With a slow, solitary, and steady pace,
Will eventually reach the sight of the golden borders;

But the greedy man, at whom I am accustomed to laugh,
Who expects to raise up mountains of gold,
Will read that his labor promises only
Hunger, cold, stench, toil, and smoke. <note>original: "Fame, freddo, fetor, fatica, e fumo." A biting critique of "puffers" or false alchemists who sought physical gold rather than spiritual or scientific truth.</note>

Whoever desires, out of curiosity for knowledge,
To both flee from and foresee disasters,
Will find here that through <term>Natural Magic: A branch of science in the Renaissance that sought to understand the hidden properties of nature and the influence of the stars without resorting to forbidden demonic rituals.</term>,
He may make the stars—previously etched against him—propitious.

From beasts and birds, from the elements,
And finally from every created thing in the world,
Whoever has a thirsty desire for divination
Might almost be able to recount future events;

Provided he does not foolishly long to know
The truth through the incantations of Hell;
For he shall read here that it is a vain thought
To hope for truth from the King of Lies.

Of the Mysteries of the Creator up above,
And of the spirits stripped of matter, <note>Angels or celestial intelligences.</note>
And how the great Planet that distinguishes the hours <note>The Sun, which in the geocentric model was considered a planet.</note>
Is moved and traverses so much space—

Whoever yearns for such knowledge shall now be satisfied;
For through Athanasius, with double glory,
The Christian and the Magus are sagely joined today
Through paths never before trodden.

The wonders of famous Egypt,
Once hidden among mysteries, are now made manifest,
Along with the obscure and misunderstood characters <note>Hieroglyphs, which Kircher believed were symbolic characters representing divine ideas.</note>
That ancient Memphis wrote upon Obelisks.

Rome, I know not what brings more to your glory:
That such great monuments serve as your ornament,
Or that he who makes their silent meaning
Fully clear to you now dwells within your walls.

<meta>This page concludes the celebratory poem by Pompeo Colonna. It is no longer necessary to make such long journeys
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To know what mysteries are hidden within
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;When a man governs, or when an island is at sea;
Or when the star <term>Canopus: One of the brightest stars in the night sky, historically used as a primary navigational star for travelers in the Southern Hemisphere and Egypt.</term> shines in the heavens.

In vain do you push your steps toward Egypt
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Upon a perilous, long, and bitter road,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;O curious one, for here even the Sphinxes
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Speak in an intelligible tongue.

From their tombs, the preserved corpses <note>A reference to Egyptian mummies, which were a source of great fascination and study for Kircher.</note>
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Rise up themselves to reveal secrets;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Showing that it was no delirium or vain thought
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To be like children, anointed and swaddled. <note>The poet compares the bandaging and embalming of mummies to the way infants were "swaddled" in the 17th century.</note>

O happy genius, who with a clear flight
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Crosses the path of glorious fame,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;You who know how to satisfy those with a burning thirst
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For every kind of knowledge with a single volume.

Pythagoras and Plato visited Egypt
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To acquire a learning beyond the common sort;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But from now on, everyone will stay their feet,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For having seen your *Oedipus* <note>original: "Edipo"; referring to Kircher's *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* (1652–54), his massive study of Egyptian lore. Like the mythical Oedipus who solved the riddle of the Sphinx, Kircher claimed to have solved the riddle of the hieroglyphs.</note> alone is enough.

Through the sea of knowledge, you now welcome us,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;An expert pilot with a sturdy ship;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Since with a calm and gentle breeze
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;We travel through Egypt within your pages.

Once oppressed by the turns of fortune,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Which wrapped its greatness in vile servitude,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Egypt itself shall receive its own memories—
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Once buried in oblivion—as a gift from you.

You, great **FERDINAND**, <note>Emperor Ferdinand III (1608–1657), Kircher's patron and the dedicatee of the work.</note> alone shall know nothing
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;More than what your mind has already grasped,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But these papers will make manifest to others
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;At least one memory of all that you do.

## EULOGY I.
->Or<-
# THE EPIGRAPH.

---

->Augustus Caesar;<-
->More merciful than Caesar, wiser than Augustus;<-
->More fortunate in birth than both;<-
->Under the Horoscope of the Catholic Religion<-
->Born amidst the labors of your Grandfather and Father for the sake of the Church;<-
->You have drawn from Heaven a prosperity that shall rule on earth through adversity.<-
->After an Infancy exercised by Herculean strength,<-
->A Childhood sacred to Virtue and Minerva, <note>Minerva was the Roman goddess of wisdom and strategic warfare.</note><-
->A Youth strengthened by Constancy and Victory;<-
->With the Heavens and Men conspiring together<-
->Elected Emperor of the Romans<-
->You were named in the Roman manner<-
->"Ferdinand," from having vanquished the iron age, <note>The "iron age" refers to the era of the Thirty Years' War, which Ferdinand III helped bring to a close with the Peace of Westphalia.</note><-
->And "the Third," from having extended the Piety of the First and the Second. <note>Referring to his predecessors, Ferdinand I and Ferdinand II.</note><-
->Soon you ruled in the Austrian manner,<-
->By loving and by triumphing:<-
->With the weapons of enemies turned into trophies of benevolence:<-
->Fortune reconciled to Majesty:<-
->Bellona <term>Bellona: The Roman goddess of war; here, the author suggests that military might has been placed at the service of faith.</term> subjected to Religion.<-
->Thus the great weight of affairs stood firm<-
->By the forces of your Power and Wisdom alike.<-
->The Empire flourishes through Power, and rests upon Wisdom.<-
->Finally, having tamed Mars <note>Mars: The god of war.</note> you tamed untamable Death;<-
->While the "Hope of the World," which you had brought forth, was expiring. <note>This likely refers to the tragic and premature death of the Emperor's eldest son, Ferdinand IV, in 1654, who was the "hope" for the succession.</note><-
->Was it so that Posterity might learn from YOU something more than Caesar-like?<-
->It is Caesar-like not to be terrified by enemies; it is more than Caesar-like not to be terrified by the fates.<-
->Foretell from this a greater triumph.<-
->The fates never harm Piety.<-
->Once the West awaited You, now the East also awaits;<-
->To which you restore Wisdom, you shall also restore happiness.<-
->Thus I vow<-

*Ignatius Bomplanus, of the Society of Jesus.*

It specifically highlights his fortitude in the face of personal tragedy—the death of his heir—as a sign of a character that transcends even the greatness of the ancient Caesars.</summary>

# TO THE MOST GLORIOUS
# FERDINAND III,
# EVER AUGUST CAESAR.

### AN ELEGY

### By Ferdinand de Fürstenberg, Canon of Hildesheim and Paderborn,

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'N' decorated with intricate floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>

It is NOT the house of *AUSTRIA* descended from the blood of <margin>the Gods,</margin>
*Nor an empire enclosed only by the world’s borders,*
Nor immortal triumphs that I would dare to recount,
*Nor brave wars worthy of the Maeonian trumpet;* <note>original: "Maeoniâ tubâ"; a reference to the epic style of Homer, who was said to be from Maeonia.</note>
Whether *CAESAR* overthrew citadels with his victorious eagles
*Under the joyful auspices of the Swabians;* <note>Refers to military successes in the Swabian regions during the Thirty Years' War.</note>
Or whether he reclaimed the *Danube*, which poorly obeyed Roman laws;
*Or if he shattered the riches of the North.*
Let others sing of those things, they whose Muse rises 
*Supported by tragic buskins and labors over the epics of heroes.* <note>The "buskin" or "cothurnus" was a high-soled boot worn by ancient Greek tragic actors; here it represents a high, formal style of poetry.</note>
It pleases me to travel more safely by a path that is not so high,
*Sounding peaceful elegies and humble songs,*
And to celebrate the character and the sacred arts of *CAESAR*.
*That subject matter is well-suited to my rhythms.*
He loves pious poets, and the gifts of pious poets
*Are pleasant to him once the cloud is cleared from his brow.*
He, the glory and the guardian of the Sisters of Helicon, <note>The Heliconian Sisters are the Muses, the goddesses of the arts and sciences.</note>
*Adorns the learned Deities with his own riches.*
Who does not know of the high temples of Athenian Minerva 
*That he built? Or the proud roofs for the Clarian God?* <note>Minerva is the goddess of wisdom; the "Clarian God" is Apollo, the god of light, music, and prophecy.</note>
Where the Oder, his grey hair wreathed with reeds,
*Washes the temples dedicated to the Aonian choirs.* <note>The "Aonian choirs" refers again to the Muses; the "Viadrus" is the Latin name for the River Oder.</note>
Where the *Danube*, having marveled at the "Athens" of the South from afar,
*Lingered more slowly with its moved waters;*
And where the royal Prague, with thresholds rising at *CAESAR’S* expense,
*Equals the peaks of Parnassus.* <note>original: "Cyrrhæis iugis"; Cyrrha was a town near the sacred mountain of Parnassus.</note>
There: just as Jupiter, after the wars against the Giant Enceladus,
*Laid down the hands armed with the fire of lightning;*
And just as Atlas, tired by the long weight,
*Placed the high axis of the sky upon his Herculean shoulders;*
So *CAESAR*, weary of the dominant reins of the world,
*Often leans back from the vast burden of Empire,*

<header>EULOGY III.</header>

# G R E E C E.

## TO FERDINAND THE THIRD,
### THE UNCONQUERED,
### C A E S A R,
### EMPEROR APPOINTED BY GOD,
### AND THRICE-GREATEST KING,
### MOST PIOUS,
### FATHER OF THE FATHERLAND,
### GRACIOUS, FORTUNATE, AND BENEFACTOR,
### GLORY, LIFE, AND EVERLASTING HEALTH.

->According to the set-forth Greek address by<-

## FRANCESCO GOZADINO, BISHOP OF ZAKYNTHOS
## AND CEPHALONIA. <note>Zakynthos and Cephalonia are Ionian islands which, at the time, were under the maritime influence of Venice but maintained strong religious and intellectual ties to the broader European courts.</note>

---

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap initial 'P' featuring a central shield with vertical bars (heraldic pales), surrounded by an ornate frame.</image-desc>

PRESENTED AS Octavian Augustus <note>The first Roman Emperor, who brought several obelisks from Egypt to Rome as trophies of his victory over Antony and Cleopatra.</note> was by his love for Caesar, he revealed the ancient wisdom of all Egypt in the obelisks he erected—wisdom that had been overwhelmed and despaired of amidst a wealth of labors and all-encompassing passions. He did this so that the things which hieroglyphic experience—skilled in learning—had produced might be sent to Rome for the divine service of explaining secret things. Yet, only the physical burdens of those obelisks fell to him, for much of the mystical learning of the ancients had been, as it were, flooded and submerged by the streams of Lethe <note>In Greek mythology, the river of forgetfulness.</note>. Ferdinand III, Augustus, you are more fortunate than that Octavian; for all that was hidden then has now, through your zeal and expense, successfully come to light. Another man—none other than Athanasius Kircher, the German <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), the Jesuit polymath and author of the work this eulogy introduces.</note>—has been brought to you. He is a soul-restored **Oedipus** <note>original: "Οἰδίπους παλιμψυχος"; a reference to Kircher's massive work *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*. Just as Oedipus solved the riddle of the Sphinx, Kircher was celebrated for "solving" the riddle of the hieroglyphs.</note> who bears witness to these enigmas. Having been stirred by a Royal decree, he did not allow his brilliant mind to wander away from the dwellings of wisdom, but rather pursued it. He has revealed and excavated treasures that until now were impassable and inaccessible. 

Whether by your virtues, O Ferdinand, in which you trust, or by your African commands <note>Likely a reference to the Emperor's authority extending over lands or interests associated with the southern Mediterranean/North African spheres.</note>, he has opened the secret seals of the mysteries and the depths of the hidden sanctuary—the **Mimetic** <note>original: "Μιμητικὸν"; here referring to the symbolic or "imitative" nature of hieroglyphs as understood in the 17th century.</note> depth of the inner sanctum. By setting forth your Imperial standard, he has unfolded the mysterious letters and inscriptions of the ancient temples, as if displaying the very soul within the body of your greatness. Therefore, we proclaim you a most blessed Caesar, for through the achievements of these gentle brothers <note>A reference to the Jesuit order (the "Society of Jesus"), to which Kircher belonged.</note> and the most illustrious men, these works have been completed. Whoever would wish or be able to practically examine or carry out such a work, it is men like you who possess the thoughts of the mind to do so. In ancient times, Augustus was able to show you the sphere of the world through the beauty of his un-endowed Obelisks. But you, by a power like his, have not only raised stones upon costly bases, but through your patronage and eternal inspiration, you have made the sweet-speaking verses of the obelisks—silent for two thousand years—speak again. You have searched out and resurrected Egyptian wisdom from its long apathy and hidden state. Truly, the wretched world ought justly to be clothed in the light of your wisdom. The whole human race, joining in celebration and triumph, turns to look upon the fame of your progress, for you are the elder messenger and herald for the entire world.

->* * * *<-

# FERDINAND III

## C A E S A R,

### THRICE-GREATEST KING,

### FATHER OF THE FATHERLAND, &c.

->Prosperity.<-

->*Francesco Gozadino, Bishop of Zakynthos and Cephalonia.*<- <note>Zakynthos and Cephalonia were Ionian islands under Venetian rule but culturally significant to the Catholic and Orthodox worlds.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'O' featuring a seated scholar or saintly figure writing at a desk, surrounded by ornate scrollwork.</image-desc>

Octavian Augustus Caesar was driven by a burning desire to acquire the ancient wisdom said to be inscribed upon the obelisks he had erected. To this end, he explored all of Egypt through the work of learned men, hoping that if he found an interpreter skilled in the lore of hieroglyphs, he might summon him to Rome for the duty of interpreting secret matters. However, he was unable to obtain his wish, for by that time, all the mystical learning of the Ancients had been submerged, as if in the river Lethe <note>In Greek mythology, the Lethe is the river of forgetfulness or oblivion; the author suggests the meaning of hieroglyphs was completely lost to time.</note>.

Ferdinand III, Caesar Augustus, is as much more fortunate than Octavian as the omens under which he achieved what the other could not—despite any prayers or expense—are more favorable. By some stroke of fate, he was granted Athanasius Kircher, a "new Interpreter" and an "Oedipus reborn" <note>original: "Oedipus rediuiuus." In mythology, Oedipus was the only one who could solve the riddle of the Sphinx; here, Kircher is praised as the only one who can solve the "riddle" of the Egyptian language.</note>. Spurred by the Emperor's command, Kircher flew toward the regions of Wisdom with a brilliant intellect and uncovered treasures that had been inaccessible until now. He was the first, relying on the commands of Ferdinand, to enter deeply into the hidden recesses of the sanctuaries of Memphis. There, he opened the secret seals of the mysteries and interpreted the enigmatic scrolls of the ancient priests, with Caesar’s generosity acting as the "midwife" to these discoveries.

Therefore, we proclaim You a happy Caesar! While You burn with a great and grand desire to achieve significant things, such a man has been granted to You—one who both wishes and is able to bring the grand concepts of Your mind into reality. Augustus of old placed the scope of his power in the raising of vast, heavy obelisks; but You are more powerful even in this: for You do not merely raise great stones, but it has fallen to You, above all others, that by Your help and labor the mute stones of the obelisks <note>The text ends here, with the catchword "iam" (already/now) implying the sentence continues on the next page to describe how the stones "now speak."</note>

It contrasts the Roman Emperor Augustus, who could only move the physical obelisks, with Ferdinand III, who has "unlocked" their secret meanings through his patronage of Athanasius Kircher.</summary>

## Greek Epigram for the Most August
# FERDINAND III, CAESAR,
### whom Greece has chosen as its King,
### and Emperor.

> The Greek lyre has sung your praises, recounting your glory.
> Hearing these, learned Greece demands you as its Emperor.
> But come now, break the tyranny of the heavy Turkish Wolf, <note>original: "Lupi Turcæ." A common 17th-century metaphor for the Ottoman Empire, which then occupied Greece.</note>

# EULOGY VI.
# FRANCE
### TO THE MAJESTY OF THE EMPEROR
# FERDINAND III.
### On the *Egyptian Oedipus*. <note>Original: *Oedippe Aegyptien*. This refers to Kircher’s massive work attempting to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs, titled *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*.</note>
## S O N N E T
### BY PIERRE SIFFREIN GALTERII.

---

ROME, you owe much to the magnificence
Of those famous Caesars, from whom you hold your beauties,
And who once caused you to surpass in rarities
All the rest of the world, as well as in power.

Those great books of the Nile, <note>A poetic reference to the Egyptian obelisks covered in hieroglyphs.</note> whose rare science
Rising up to Heaven, flew from every side,
Were by their care transported within your walls,
Making the sea groan beneath their immense weight.

But these books were nothing but silent books;
And all their science, useless forever,
Even to the most piercing minds would have remained secret;

If the great FERDINAND, to reveal it to us
Through the fortunate labors of his learned interpreter, <note>Refers to the author of the book, Athanasius Kircher.</note>
Had not found the means to make them speak.

### EULOGY VII.
## P O R T U G A L
# TO FERDINAND III.
## C A E S A R.
### PORTUGUESE EULOGY
#### TO FERDINAND III, King of the Romans, Elected
#### Emperor.

<image-desc>Printer's ornament consisting of stylized foliage and floral scrolls.</image-desc>

<image-desc>Ornate decorative initial 'C' featuring a scene with a seated figure, possibly a king or deity, surrounded by architectural and floral elements.</image-desc>

The Ancients dedicated their obelisks to the Sun; today they are dedicated to FERDINAND the Emperor, a living Sun. He gives the light of example to Kings, and the shade of protection to the Wise. His virtues are higher than the mysteries of the hieroglyphs are deep. His perfections are more extraordinary <note>Original: *peregrinas*, meaning rare, exotic, or remarkably fine.</note> than the figures of the Pyramids are strange. The pyramids were raised as memorials; now they are illuminated by understanding. With a wise choice, a German <note>Referring to the author, Athanasius Kircher, who was German.</note> offers the true <note>A pun on the Portuguese word *germano*, which means both "German" and "genuine" or "pure."</note> meaning of these enigmas to the Elected Emperor of the Romans, who is simultaneously Augustus and Maecenas <note>Gaius Maecenas was a famous Roman patron of the arts; his name became a title for any generous protector of scholars.</note>: Augustus for his Subjects, and Maecenas for Wise Men. The former he enriches with the fortune of Caesar; the latter he encourages with the favor of Maecenas. Let Charles V <note>The great Habsburg Emperor and great-grandfather of Ferdinand III.</note> take the columns with the *Further Beyond* <note>Original: *Plus ultra*, the motto of the Spanish Empire and the House of Habsburg, signifying the expansion of their power across the Atlantic.</note> of his victorious arms. Let FERDINAND III, the strongest column of the Catholic Religion, accept Obelisks with the *Nothing Further Beyond* <note>Original: *non Plus vltra*, meaning the absolute pinnacle or the ultimate limit that cannot be surpassed.</note> of his divine virtues; for obelisks and columns correspond well to one another. Once Greece, the mother of sciences in name and form, yielded obedience to the Empire; now Egypt does so through mysteries and symbols, with Rome as their theater. In the shadow of Caesarean Majesty, the light of wisdom grows. Dead figures are resurrected to life; those that were silent become eloquent <note>Original: *politicas*, meaning civil or refined in speech.</note>; those that seemed like monsters are revealed as beautiful. These are the miracles of Imperial protection, which succeeds in working wonders even upon the wonders of the world.

The sacred <unclear>street</unclear> with the triumphal <unclear>gate</unclear>,
The court, the porch, the pulpit, set a state
Far other, than brick Walls of Babylon,

Speak <term>cathedratick</term> <note>Authoritative, as if speaking from a professor's or bishop's chair (cathedra).</note> language; by thee, fowls
**Pythagorean** prove <note>Likely referring to the Pythagorean belief in the transmigration of souls, suggesting these animal-symbols now possess human-like wisdom.</note>: transformed an Ass is
So reverend, I'd swear it were **Amasis** <note>Amasis II was a famous Pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty known for his wisdom.</note>.
To thee belongs the fame of **Trismegist** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "thrice-great" author of the Hermetic corpus, often conflated with the Egyptian god Thoth.</note>,
A righter *Hermes*; thou hast outgone the list
Of his *triple grandeur*: or if that not please,
Join **Ptolemies**, and stout **Musagetes** <note>Apollo in his role as the leader of the Muses.</note>.
This is the united sense of the Universe,
Though differing tongues it many ways rehearse.

### GERMANY.

### To the Most Powerful and Most Invincible Emperor

## FERDINAND THE THIRD

### Sung in Honor

->**By G. P. H. <note>Georg Philipp Harsdörffer (1607–1658), a celebrated Baroque poet and member of the Fruitbearing Society in Nuremberg.</note> Counselor of Nuremberg.**<-

### I.

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap 'K' decorated with interlacing vines and foliage.</image-desc>**A**RT-PLAYING Sisters <note>A reference to the Muses, the Greek goddesses of inspiration in literature, science, and the arts.</note>, renew the dance,

The strings ring out with artful joy,
The cheering voices now sing along,

Of the whirling flutes,
The sounding and echoing of the striking cornetts <term>Zincke: a Renaissance wind instrument, also known as a cornett, played with a trumpet-like mouthpiece but with finger holes like a recorder</term>.

God, who has hemmed in the surging waves,
So that they do not flow beyond the shore,
He halts the wars, grants the victory;

That **FERDINAND** brings his wisdom forth!

->I V.<-

The arts, favored by the highest Regent <note>Refers to the Emperor as the supreme patron of culture.</note>,
Once banished and plagued, and not knowing themselves,
Begin to rise: they become their own,
They who lay prostrate;
They prove and praise what was once hidden,
With rare concern.

Because **FERDINAND** brings his wisdom forth!

->V.<-

The wisdom and riddles of the ancients discovered,
Awakened from the dead,
Such clever teachings
Delighting the ear;
Because **FERDINAND**'s wisdom now shines forth!

->V I.<-

God, who has given us Germans the peace,
Preserve the founder of peace in life!
May his name endure, remain immortalized,
With golden lines
In dedicated stones to be read with joy,
Without any decay!
We must now hasten
With a singing choir;
That **FERDINAND** brings the arts forth!

# ELEGY X.
# TO FERDINAND III.
->To his Elected and Crowned<-
->K I N G<-
## OF HUNGARY.

*Just as in these Egyptian obelisks, through the interpretation of Oedipus <note>A reference to the author, Athanasius Kircher, who styled himself as a "new Oedipus" for his supposed ability to solve the "riddle" of Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, one reads of the ancient Egyptian ages granted immortality by various means; so too in FERDINAND III—as if in his own obelisk or a crowned pyramid—Hungary hopes she will read the ancient glories of the heroic times of her Kings. Thus she says:*

<image-desc>A decorative typographical ornament featuring symmetrical floral scrolls and leaf motifs.</image-desc>

<margin>1.</margin> As I gazed upon the stone
of ancient Egypt and of Oedipus;
I recalled the fair fame
of my old Kings and my fallen columns;

<margin>2.</margin> But looking upon you, fixing my heart upon you,
I sighed in hope!

<margin>3.</margin> Here I see the writings

## SONG <note>The original title "Duma" refers to a traditional solemn, epic poem or song found in Slavic cultures.</note>
### Croatian. <note>original: "Harvaçki". While labeled Croatian, the poem invokes the geography of the wider Balkan region (Illyria).</note>

Nymphs, mountain princesses,
Who, gathering in a circle,
Sing wonderful songs,
Above clear springs,
To which an eternal name
Orpheus, Prince of the Odrysian <note>The Odrysians were an ancient Thracian tribe; Orpheus was traditionally their legendary singer.</note> singers, gave.
Where the turbid river Maritsa,
And the swirling Strumica,
Taking their neighboring source,
Go their separate, pure ways.
Nymphs, who from the high
Wooded peaks of Rila
Survey with your eyes
The wide city of Serdica <note>Serdica is the ancient name for modern-day Sofia, Bulgaria.</note>
And the grain-bearing fields.
Tell me the truth:
Where is that lute <note>original: "gusle", a traditional Balkan single-stringed instrument, here used to represent Orpheus's lyre.</note>;
With which, from the pits of the dead,
He led his Eurydice
Into the bright world?
With which he made ravenous wolves,
Wild bears, and lynxes
Obedient to himself.
Is it kept with you, or indeed
Do the Gods delightfully
Play their songs with it?
That, that is what I
Greatly need now:
To praise the powerful Emperor;
To commemorate the wise man;
To tell of a wonderful work.

<column-break/>

## PINDARIC ODE
### In modern Illyrian. <note>This column provides a Latin translation of the Slavic poem, here translated into English. Kircher often provided Latin "keys" for his polyglot texts.</note>

**N**ymphs, mountain princesses,
Who, standing in a chorus,
Sing together joyful hymns:
Above clear waters,
To which Orpheus, prince of poets,
Gave an eternal name.
Where the turbid river Hebrus <note>The Maritsa river.</note>,
And the swirling Strymon,
Having taken their source nearby,
Go their opposite ways.
Nymphs, who from the high,
Leafy ridges of Rhodope,
Survey with your eyes
The spacious lands of Serdica
And the fields fertile with crops.
Tell me the truth:
Where is that Lyre;
With which from the caverns of the underworld,
He led his Eurydice
Toward the bright light?
With which he held the tearing wolves,
Wild bears, and lynxes
Obedient.
Is it hidden with you? Or do the
Gods truly sound their songs
Joyfully upon it?
That now, that is for me
A great necessity:
To celebrate the brave Emperor;
To commemorate the wise man;
To narrate the wonderful work.

**Song (Duma):** A traditional epic Slavic poem.

**Orpheus & Eurydice:** The Greek myth of the master musician who descended to Hades to retrieve his wife.
**Maritsa / Hebrus:** A major river in the Balkans.
**Rhodope / Rila:** Mountain ranges in the Balkan peninsula.
**Serdica:** Ancient Sofia.
**Emperor (Cæsar):** Referring to Ferdinand III.

# P. J. S. A. N. Staroslovinski <note>Likely a pseudonym for a contributor writing in the "Old Slavic" style.</note> BETTINIAN IAMBICS <note>A poetic meter named after the Jesuit scholar Mario Bettini.</note> in ancient Slavonic. ~~ancient.~~

<meta>This page continues the polyglot celebratory verses dedicated to Emperor Ferdinand III and the Jesuit scholar Athanasius Kircher. While the previous page featured "Old Slavic" and "Ancient" styles, this page presents a "Davorija" (a Slavic heroic song) followed by an address to the Ottoman Turks in Turkish. ## HEROIC SONG <note>original: "DAVORIJA". A term for a Slavic patriotic or heroic song, likely derived from the name of the Slavic deity Davor.</note> in the Latin style,
It was not enough for your glory, noble Emperor,
That your virtue was celebrated by the voices
Of countless people: now your name also rings on the rocks,
And cold stones give forth words of wisdom.
Which, since the Sun has completed two thousand yearly circuits,
No single wise man was able to explain;
Athanasius <note>Athanasius Kircher</note> alone performs these wonders: by the force of his mind alone
He abundantly strikes sparks of learning from the stone.
But the Emperor's name, on the wings of praise,
Flies high across mountains and seas, and reaches the heavens.
Now my lute falls silent: but my soul will not cease to wish:
Flourish happily for many years, shine, great name,
Endure, conquer, rule, be a terror to your enemies.

<column-break/>

## HEROIC POEM in the Latin Style. <note>This is the Latin translation of the Slavic poem on the left.</note>
It was not enough, O happy Caesar, for your glories,
That your virtue was proclaimed by the voices of innumerable peoples:
Now even the hard rocks sound your names,
And the icy cliffs bring forth words of wisdom.
Which, since the Sun has run through two thousand yearly circuits,
None of the wise men had the power to explain;
Only Athanasius performs these wonders: only by the strength of his talent
Does he strike sparks of doctrines copiously from the stone.
But the Imperial name, upon the wings of praise, flies sublime
Across the mountains, across the seas, and touches the stars.
And now my lyre grows silent: yet my soul shall not cease to pray:
Most auspiciously flourish for many years, become famous, O mighty name,
Endure, triumph, rule, be a thing of dread to your enemies.

->Sung by Juraj Križanić.<- <note>original: "Georgius Criſanius accinuit." Križanić was a Croatian polymath and theologian.</note>

I am the Queen of Cultures, <note>original: "ܡܪ̈ܕܘܬܐ" (mardutha). This term can mean culture, discipline, or education.</note> and the glory against opponents.

### Latin Interpretation:

# TO FERDINAND III,

## EMPEROR.

<image-desc>Small decorative fleuron ornament with symmetrical leaf motifs.</image-desc>

<image-desc>Large ornate decorative initial S featuring scrollwork and foliate patterns.</image-desc>

Rise up, O pen, and [write] of that Eagle which flies on high, <note>A reference to the double-headed eagle, the heraldic symbol of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>
And bears in its two heads the symbols of two Empires,
Write of his virtues in elegant colors, paint them, and 
->celebrate<- 
his triumphs,
And offer him perfect sacrifices and burnt offerings among the Syrians.
How shall I, a weak pen made from a goose's wing, fly
To that place where even great Jupiter <note>Here used as a metaphor for the highest imperial majesty.</note> scarcely reaches?
Especially in this hand which you yourself know; and to whom shall I flee?
For this reason, I am small in comparison to his praise in every way and form.
Descend therefore, and praise his lesser virtues,
And fulfill your vows among the Syrians, lest you be rebuked:
Nor does the Egyptian Oedipus <note>A reference to the scholar Athanasius Kircher, who was nicknamed "the Egyptian Oedipus" for his attempts to "solve" the riddle of Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> permit me this,
Since he has ordered and fashioned all these things in a wondrous manner.
Therefore, you and I, O pen, dare this much:
That through his praiser we might offer him a crown of eulogies,
And touch upon our theme in a single word, daring
To name him in the Egyptian tongue *Zaphenath-Paneah*. <note>original: "Zaphnatfanebb". This is the name Pharaoh gave to Joseph in the Bible (Genesis 41:45), interpreted by scholars of this era to mean "Revealer of Secrets" or "Savior of the World."</note>

->Abraham Ecchellensis sang this in accompaniment.<-

EULOGY XV. ARABIA.

->To Ferdinand Caesar the Third<-

# FERDINAND III.
# EMPEROR.

<image-desc>Decorative typographical ornament with stylized floral and scroll motifs.</image-desc>

Through you, the religion of truth has spread in the robes of victory,
And the creed of infidelity <note>original: "ملة الكفر" (millat al-kufr). In the context of the 17th-century Holy Roman Empire, this refers to the Ottoman Empire or other non-Christian powers.</note> has been turned back on its heels.
The rulers submit to you, whether by force or by choice,
And all servants wait upon your prohibitions and commands.
O King, who rivals the angels in high standing!
In the highest assembly, he has the sweetest remembrance.
May you find joy in what your Lord has given you; for indeed,
These are deeds of glory [that will stand] at the Gathering for Judgment.
For had you not stood truly for God's sake,
Religion would not have gained this victory.
O King, whose fame has filled the whole earth!
Benefit is hoped for from him, and harm is feared.
You have made people forget the rulers of ages past;
Neither their power nor their status is counted anymore.
He saw in you a glory the like of which has never been,
And after the sun’s radiance, the dawn is no longer mentioned.
Even [the ancient] Caesar falls short of your likeness,
And whoever was like him among the greatest kings.
By my life, your praise excels in all of this,
But your greatest pride lies in the victory of religion.
May your memory be radiant in both lands, <note>Referring to the East and the West.</note>
Found by the inhabitants of the earth and the sea.
But today, Athanasius <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), the Jesuit scholar who compiled this work.</note>
Has engraved my truth upon the granite of the Pyramids of Egypt.

### Interpretation.

<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial T containing a detailed landscape scene with a prominent tower, trees, and small figures in the foreground.</image-desc>

Under your authorship, the true religion has been propagated with victorious banners,
And the unfaithful sect has turned its back in defeat;
Princes obey your commands, willing or unwilling,
And mortals serve you as you command and forbid.
O Emperor, to be compared with the celestial Angels!
In their bosom also, the finest throne is prepared for you.
May the Empire which God has granted you turn out happy and auspicious,
And may another, even more blessed, be bestowed upon YOUR Majesty according to your merits.
For unless you had fought strenuously for God,
The Christian religion would by no means have stood so victorious.
O Emperor, whose fame occupies the whole circle of the earth!
Every person hopes for a reward from you, and fears a penalty.
Now the Emperors of past times are given over to oblivion,
Nor is account to be taken any longer of their power, nor of their majesty:
For such a splendor of majesty is present in you,

**N**oble, he received their wealth and the gifts of their souls as tribute.
**N**oted is the Eagle of whom one of the prophets spoke of old.
**D**riving with strength, he provides shade for the lions of Lebanon. <note>Lebanon was the heartland of the Syrian Christian communities who contributed to this volume.</note>
**V**enerated with a pleasant knocking, his appearance is refined and perfected.
**S**urmounting Mount Lebanon, the fragrance of the incense tree was poured out.
**K**indly he plucked the heart, and toward the West his flight was swift.
**S**hining upon the earth, better than the seed of the vineyard's produce.
**R**aising his branches high, and thus his fruits are fully ripened.
**D**elivered to all the tribes, the scent of the desired time has arrived.
**R**evived is the vision of Maron, the cedar which the prophet sheltered. <note>Maron refers to Saint Maron, the 4th-century hermit and patron of the Maronite Church.</note>
**V**ictorious Ferdinand is like an eagle among them, flashing with light.
**M**ighty Lord, let us exalt him, and all the nations shall flow to hear him.
**I**ndeed, we shall exalt him over the ruins, and the lowly people shall be raised.

<meta>This page provides the Latin translation of the Syriac elegy presented on the previous page. While the previous page displayed the Syriac text (likely in an acrostic format), this page serves as the "Interpretatio Latina" (Latin Interpretation) for the benefit of scholars in the Holy Roman Empire. <header>Latin Interpretation of the Syriac Elegy in the Jacobite rhythm.</header> <note>The "Jacobite rhythm" refers to the poetic meter used by the Syrian Orthodox Church, though here it is being translated into Latin by a Maronite scholar.</note>

ABOVE the clouds and the sublime spheres, the **Cheerful Eagle** <note>original: "Hilaris Aquila"; the Eagle is the symbol of the Holy Roman Empire</note> directs his entreatable path; whom the Lord has crowned with a Triple Empire. He loved the heights, lest the foul world should moisten the gifts of his beauty, or toss it about with its waves. He displays the signs of the Egyptians and diminishes the books of the Persians by his own exhaustive study; he took their riches and attributed to himself the goal of their highest honor. <note>This likely refers to the Emperor’s patronage of Oriental studies, "depleting" the secrets of the East to enrich Western knowledge.</note>

The Eagle, of whom one of the Prophets prophesied, directs his way with force toward the Cedar which shades Lebanon. And with a beat of wings, and a colored appearance of elegant brightness, he ascends Mount Lebanon and drew out the balsam oil from its <unclear>defruesti</unclear> wood. He collected the marrow, and raising his flight toward the regions of the West, he placed it in the earth, having followed through with a vineyard of more fruitful seed. He exalted the sprouts, and further ripened the fruits and sows them, so that he has invited and called all nations to his pleasant shade.

The Seer foreshadowed the exaltation of the Church in the chosen region of the West, and in our century the Caesar has revealed and commended it by his faithful Eagle. May the Lord extol him, and invite all peoples to obedience to him; moreover, may He exalt him over heresies and a demented people.

->Stephen of Ehden, a Maronite<- <note>original: "Stephanus Aldobensis Edenensis Maronita." Stephen Douayrhī (1630–1704) was a significant Maronite scholar who later became the Patriarch of the Maronite Church. "Ehden" is a mountainous town in northern Lebanon.</note>

## Thus he drives the mass, and mingles with the great body. <note>original: "Sic agitat molem, & magno se corpore miscet." A quote from Virgil’s Aeneid (6.727) describing the "world-soul" or divine spirit that animates the universe; here applied to the Emperor’s influence.</note>

<header>EULOGY XVII.</header>

<warning>Significant ink bleed-through from the reverse side of the page (ghosting).</warning>

# ARABIC
## FOR FERDINAND III,
### EMPEROR,
### THRICE-GREATEST KING,

->Most Powerful, Most Glorious, Just, Pious, Fortunate,<-

->**Composed**<-

->By Father Filippo Guadagnolo, Minor Clerk <note>The Clerics Regular Minor are a religious order founded in 1588</note>, and at the<-
->Roman Athenaeum <note>The university or center of higher learning in Rome</note>, Pontifical Professor of the Arabic Language.<-

---

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut horizontal divider featuring symmetrical floral and foliage motifs, with a central floral element.</image-desc>

Piety is the pillar of kingdoms; nothing else endures that is not guided by it. Ferdinand III, the Great Sultan <note>The Arabic text uses the word "Sultan" to translate the title of Emperor or Caesar</note>, demonstrated this with the scepter of kingship and with the wood of the Crucified which sits atop his head in the crown, so that the governance of his kingdom by the Wood of Salvation <note>The Cross</note> becomes greater than it is by the scepter of kings. Piety, if it is united with the judgments of kings, constitutes true wisdom; through it, the King of Kings grants them stability, and kingdoms remain safe by its power. For it is not possible for a kingdom to endure forever unless its foundation is based on the worship of God. ✠ Behold our Great Sultan, Ferdinand III: he has acted thus with perfection, and the world is witness to this. Because this wisdom is not truly wise if it is not established in piety and the fear of God, nor is it possible without knowledge, he has therefore always occupied himself with wisdom along with science, until he obtained, as it were, all the fruits. He became a castle for wisdom and knowledge until the world was filled with them. This is because he has realized the truth of the proverb: "A multitude of wise men is the health of the world" <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Wisdom 6:24</note> and the true, sole support of kingdoms, and nothing else. ✠ Therefore, by his power, this book has come forth as a wonderful work in your honor, O Great Sultan Caesar, to increase your wisdom; and as for the kings besides you, it serves to incite them to support the victory of the sciences, the scholars, wisdom, and the wise. —

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap letter 'F' set within a square woodcut border, depicting a landscape with a building (likely a church) and trees.</image-desc>

THE FOUNDATION of kingdoms is Piety: no one has ruled well who has not also lived well. **FERDINAND III** wished to prove this with the rod of the scepter, and the beam of the Crucified, which he carries upon the Imperial globe <note>The *Globus Cruciger*, an orb topped by a cross representing Christ's dominion over the world</note>, so that he might reign not so much by the scepter as by the Life-giving Wood. Piety joined to the scepters of Kings is that true Wisdom through which Kings reign, and through which kingdoms are preserved in their vigor; for no kingdom can endure for long unless it is founded upon the propagation of divine worship. How **FERDINAND III**, the Emperor, has provided this is known to the world. Unless wisdom is founded in piety and the fear of the Lord, it can by no means be sustained without letters <note>Literacy or scholarly study</note>. Hence, for the fulfillment of all honors, he has always cultivated literate Wisdom and promoted it in others by his own example, certain that the "multitude of the Wise is the health of the world," and the sole and true stability of kingdoms. In the strength of this virtue, therefore, this present wonderful work has come forth: for You, O Emperor, for the increase of Wisdom, and for other Kings as an example for the cultivation of the sciences.

<sig>G II</sig>
<meta>catchword: ELO-</meta>

<summary>This page presents a bilingual (Arabic and Latin) eulogy for Emperor Ferdinand III, written by the scholar Filippo Guadagnolo. It argues that the Emperor’s strength and the stability of his realm come from his combination of Christian piety, represented by the cross on his crown, and his patronage of the sciences and wisdom.</summary>

# CHALDEA.

->**Grace to the great King, to whom no equal is found on earth,**<-
->**to the ruler of rulers,**<-

# FERDINAND III.
# CAESAR.

->And I, having seen the praise of this book and of him about whom<-
->it is spoken, I have raised this song and I say:<-
<note>original Chaldaic: "ואנא בר חזית תשבחתא דספרא דא ולמן דאיתאמר / עליה ארימית שירי דא ואומר"</note>

<columns>2</columns>
Who sits upon the throne
Ahasuerus placed it <note>Referring to the legend of Ahasuerus attempting to use Solomon's throne</note>
Over twenty and seven

### Interpretation.

He alludes in this Chaldaic eight-line poem <note>original: "octastycho"</note> to the Throne of Solomon: which, as the Rabbis recount, when it had been brought among other spoils to King Ahasuerus <note>The Persian king from the Book of Esther</note>, the King was so moved by reverence for such a great work that he neither wished to sit upon it himself, nor for anyone else to sit upon it, unless perhaps someone should present himself who equaled Solomon in virtue and Wisdom. And he says this person is **FERDINAND III**, the Caesar, who as he towers over all in wisdom, glory, and the height of virtues, so he alone is deservedly worthy of that Throne, as if he were another Solomon brought back to life.

<header>EULOGY XIX.</header>

### ARMENIA.

->FERDINAND THE THIRD,<-
->August Emperor. To the<-
->Righteous and God-loving, Great and Mighty<-
->King.<-
<note>original Armenian script: "ՖԷՐԴԻԱՆԴՈՍ ԵՐՐՈՐԴ / օգոստափառ կայսերն։ Արդա- / րոյ և ածասեր մեծահզոր / արքայի։"</note>

# FERDINAND III.
## CAESAR,
## GREATEST OF KINGS.

---

<image-desc>ornamental floral and scroll-work divider</image-desc>

<note>The following paragraph is a transliteration of the Armenian language into the Roman alphabet, allowing European readers of the time to "read" the sounds of the Armenian tribute even if they could not read the script.</note>

**S**ince FERDINAND confesses that his Imperial fortune is nothing other than the power of divine arrangement; for that reason, he has established his throne upon the eternal confirmation of the faith. And because he has adorned his purple imperial cloak <note>original Latin: *paludamentum*, a cloak worn by Roman military commanders and later emperors</note> with the love of heavenly things, he has therefore joined steadfast patience to his victorious right hand and to the scepter of his power. He has also inserted his golden prudence, like a glowing carbuncle <note>a deep red gemstone, often associated with light and energy in heraldry</note>, into the crown of his August majesty. For just as iron is expressed in his name <note>The author is making a play on words: "Ferdinand" starts with the same letters as *ferrum*, the Latin word for iron. The metaphor suggests his "iron" name is transformed into "golden" virtue.</note>, so he has converted it into the most splendid gold through the mastery of all virtues. While he has subdued rebels, what else has he done but prostrate the "iron" strength of his enemies through a golden victory? Therefore, FERDINAND is a Golden Caesar, because he possesses a golden mind, and by a golden treasure of virtues, he turns the eyes of all toward himself—and even turns "iron" minds into gold. Thus, by this golden chain of virtues, we Armenians have also been drawn to prostrate ourselves at the feet of Your Majesty, wishing to pay the tribute of praise that is due. We pray to God that Your August Majesty, who always submits yourself to the divine empire through the conformity of your mind, may enjoy the Empire of eternal happiness in heaven after this life—you who shine so greatly on earth through the splendor of your virtues and the magnificence of your earthly Empire.

### I N T E R P R E T A T I O N.
<note>This section in the original was the Latin translation of the Armenian text provided above.</note>

**S**ince FERDINAND confesses that Imperial fortune is nothing other than the power of divine disposition; for that reason, he has established his throne upon the eternal confirmation of the faith... <note>The Latin text follows the same content as the translated Armenian block above, emphasizing the themes of divine right, the transformation of "iron" (war/strength) into "gold" (virtue/peace), and the loyalty of the Armenian people.</note>

->Zacharias Agam of Nakhchivan <note>A city in the South Caucasus, historically part of Armenia</note> at the foot<-
->of Mount Ararat, Armenian Priest.<-

#### EULOGY 20.
### PERSIA
# FERDINAND III.
## EMPEROR
### DEDICATED TO HIS HONOR.

<image-desc>decorative floral scroll ornament</image-desc>

<note>The following section is written in Persian script. It uses high-flown, poetic language typical of Persian courtly literature to praise the Emperor. It concludes with the name of the author, Athanasius Kircher.</note>

The bride of my thought does not raise her head due to her lack of beauty, and the eye of despair does not lift itself from the back of the foot of shame, nor does she appear among the company of the beautiful, unless she is made radiant by being adorned with the jewel of acceptance by Ferdinand, the Great Prince, who is in truth the one chosen in the court of the King, the refuge of the world, the shadow of the Creator, and the ray of the grace of the Nourisher, the pride of the age, the cave of faith, supported by the Heavens, the arm of the conquering state, the lamp of the brilliant nation, the beauty of mankind, the pride of the great prince, the wise, the just, supported and victorious over enemies, the protector of the throne of sovereignty, the counselor of the administration of the kingdom, the cave of the poor, the refuge of strangers, the nourisher of the learned, the lover of the pious, the pride of the family of the faithful, the right hand of the kingdom, the king of the elite, the pride of the state, the pillar of kings and sultans—may God prolong his life, exalt his power, gladden his heart, and double his reward—for he is the one praised by the greatest of the excellent and of noble character. ۞ Athanasius Kircher ۞

---

->Interpretation.<-
<note>original Latin: "Interpretatio." This is Kircher's own translation of the Persian text provided above.</note>

Behold, O Emperor, the "bride of my meditation"—this very book—does not lift its head because of its own unworthiness. <note>The "bride of meditation" is a poetic Persian metaphor for the author's creative work or intellectual output.</note> Nor does it raise its face, lacking all hope, fixed upon the ground in shame. Nor can it show its form and splendor in the company of the beautiful, unless at that time Emperor FERDINAND should deck her with the ornament of his embrace <note>Meaning his royal acceptance or patronage.</note>. Then, however, it will be truly perfect, when it is seen as pleasing and welcome in the Court of the Great King, who is the refuge in this world of mortals, the shadow of the Creator <note>original Latin: "Conditoris umbra." This reflects the Persian title "Zill-Allah," or Shadow of God, a traditional title for a monarch.</note>, the splendor and ray of divine benevolence, the sustenance and support of the age, the refuge of religion, strengthened from heaven, the strong arm of victorious power, the light of an illustrious people, the beauty of mankind, the delight of the Christian Religion, a Prince great, wise, and just, a victor over enemies, the pillar of the Royal throne, a most prudent Leader in administering the Kingdom, the refuge of the poor, a harbor for strangers, the supporter and valuer of Men of Letters, a lover of the pious, and the confidence of Kings and Princes. May God prolong his life, extol his power, enlighten his mind, and double the rewards of eternal life for him. For he is the most praised of the greatest throughout the whole world, a compendium of all virtues and character.

The Author.

It uses rich, Middle Eastern poetic metaphors—such as the "bride of meditation" and the King as the "Shadow of God"—to express the author's humility and the Emperor's supreme virtues.</summary>
