# EULOGY 21

->*In the Samaritan Language and Character,*<-

<image-desc>Three lines of text in Samaritan characters.</image-desc>

->TO THE IMMORTAL<-

# FERDINAND III.

## E M P E R O R

->Oedipus dedicates this to his honor.<- <note>original: "Oedipus" – A reference to Kircher's major work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*. He casts himself as the "Oedipus" who can solve the "riddles" of ancient and exotic languages.</note>

---

<image-desc>A large block of text (thirteen lines) written in Samaritan characters.</image-desc>

### *Interpretation.*

You bear the EAGLE, Emperor FERDINAND, and indeed a double-headed one, with a spirit and insignia shining with Imperial Majesty. For you are a double-headed eagle because, with the rays of your intellect, you embrace both the rising and the setting Sun. An Emperor and Caesar ought to be equipped with four eyes, so that with one he might look toward the North, with another the South, and with the remaining two the East and West; and thus he might embrace the entire Universe within his mind. You rejoice in a great rowing of wings—which is the power of your Wisdom—through which you penetrate even the heavens themselves. By the strength and vigor of your power, you rule over land and sea, the greatest alone in the political world. You bear the Lion, because you possess a certain heavenly efficacy, granted by God to the Caesar alone, by which you subject all things to your power. You represent the Dove, and indeed one without gall <note>The "gall-less dove" was a traditional symbol of purity and gentleness, as the bird was anciently believed to lack a gallbladder.</note>, so that by the sweetness of heavenly gentleness you might turn everyone toward love of you. You represent the Sun, because with the rays of your providence you flow into the ends of the entire political world. You are Anubis, because by the sagacity of your great soul you investigate all things: you embrace all sciences and arts within the vastness of your genius. Since, therefore, you are adorned with this collection of virtues, obelisks are deservedly erected to you, the tips of which touch nothing less than the sky.

<note>original: "Anubis" – In the syncretic traditions of the Renaissance, Anubis was often linked to Hermes/Mercury, the god of wisdom, communication, and the investigation of secrets.</note>

<term>Ferdinand III</term> (Holy Roman Emperor, reigned 1637–1657), <term>Caesar</term> (the title used here for the Emperor), <term>Samaritan</term> (the ancient Hebrew script and dialect), <term>Oedipus</term> (Kircher’s scholarly alias), <term>Eagle</term> (symbol of the Holy Roman Empire), <term>Lion</term> (symbol of strength), <term>Dove</term> (symbol of peace), <term>Sun</term> (symbol of central authority), <term>Anubis</term> (symbol of sagacity), <term>Obelisk</term> (monument of eternal fame), <term>Interpretation</term> (the translation provided).

<meta>This page continues the sequence of linguistic honors for Emperor Ferdinand III. Having previously presented Samaritan, Athanasius Kircher now moves to Eulogy 22, written in Coptic (which he refers to as the "Ancient Egyptian language"). # EULOGY XXII.
## In the ancient Egyptian language, or
# COPTIC
# EGYPT
# TO FERDINAND III.
# EMPEROR
## ERECTS [THIS],
->And Oedipus <note>Kircher's persona as the "riddle-solver" of Egypt.</note> dedicates it to the same.<-

---

<image-desc>Floral divider ornament</image-desc>

Solomon spoke in the world, regarding the stars ☩ 
and those who build the towers <note>original: "ⲛⲓⲡⲩⲣⲅⲟⲥ" (ni-pyrgos) — likely referring to the structures of the heavens or constellations.</note>, and of all the choice creatures of creation ☩ 
concerning the beasts ☩ he spoke regarding the trees ☩ and the 
fruits ☩ and of the sweet-smelling woods of Lebanon ☩ even unto the 
hyssop. God has given at this time our own Solomon, a true 
one ☩ the ruler <note>original: "ⲡⲓⲇⲓⲁⲧⲣⲟⲭⲟⲥ" — Kircher uses a Greek-derived term for "one who steers the wheel."</note>, the victor who prevails ☩ the 
statesman ☩ the famous ☩ the divine ☩ the crowned ☩ the 
champion, the noble ☩ the honeyed one. God has given him the types of 
languages ☩ He has given him truths and physiology ☩ and 
enigmas and hypotheses ☩ God has given him [knowledge] of the beasts ☩ 
and the birds ☩ and the reptiles ☩ and the fish ☩ He is worthy of 
pillars of stone, he is worthy of the obelisk of immortality ☩

->Interpretation.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter S</image-desc>
**SALOMON** is said to have spoken wisely of the mysteries of the whole world, the workmanship of the heavens, and the nature of things; he keenly understood the nature and properties of animals: he debated prudently about herbs, fruits, and flowers, *from the Cedar which is in Lebanon, even to the Hyssop that comes out of the wall* <note>A reference to 1 Kings 4:33 describing Solomon's encyclopedic knowledge.</note>. Divine providence has given us another Solomon at this time. Is this not **FERDINAND III**, an Emperor whose Majesty is crowned with virtue, wisdom, and power? Who can sufficiently explain with his own tongue the languages and sciences that the Emperor possesses? What in the knowledge of natural things is hidden from him? The world admires his deepest knowledge of Politics, by whose very nod laws are established, and whose words are themselves oracles. Of old, Obelisks were erected to the gods. Why then should we not also consecrate this Obelisk of praise to **FERDINAND III**, the Emperor, as if to a certain earthly deity? Let it therefore be consecrated to the Emperor, the shadow of divinity, for the immortality of his name.

<summary>Eulogy 22 presents a tribute in Coptic, comparing Emperor Ferdinand III to King Solomon for his vast knowledge of nature, languages, and statecraft. Kircher uses this to argue that the Emperor deserves a symbolic "obelisk of praise" for his god-like wisdom.</summary>
<keywords>Coptic language, Solomon, Ferdinand III, Natural Philosophy, Obelisk, Immortality, Political Wisdom, Egyptology</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the series of linguistic tributes to Emperor Ferdinand III from Athanasius Kircher's "Oedipus Aegyptiacus." Following the Coptic eulogy, Kircher presents a tribute in the Ethiopic language (Ge’ez). This section is particularly significant as it features a contribution from Antonio d'Andrade, an Ethiopian-born cleric of Portuguese descent, highlighting the presence of the Ethiopian college in Rome during the 17th century.</meta>

# EULOGY XXIII.

## ETHIOPIA
King of Kings and High Power of Powers,
Ferdinand Caesar.

->To the supreme King, the Highest of the High, the Ruler<-

# FERDINAND III

## EMPEROR.

<image-desc>A small ornamental emblem or monogram featuring a cross-like structure with circular finials and three letters or characters below it.</image-desc>

---

<insert>
Behold, High and Mighty King of Kings, Ferdinand Caesar:

We have come to praise your power while kissing your feet, so that we might truly be established in spiritual peace. We, the priests of Ethiopia who are in Rome, celebrate your name so that all might wonder at your marvelous wisdom, by which you draw the hearts of all people; for it has reached the ends of the earth, just as Solomon drew by his kingdom and his wisdom our Queen of Sheba. Truly, without boasting, you were born to revive for our salvation the wisdom of Solomon.
</insert>

---

->*Interpretation.*<-

Behold, most powerful and exalted Emperor FERDINAND Caesar, we the priests of Ethiopia, who are in Rome, approach the praises of Your virtues, kissing Your venerable knees with the kiss of spiritual peace. For we have heard how all admire Your wonderful Wisdom, by which You draw the hearts of all men; just as Solomon by his wonderful Wisdom drew our Queen of Sheba. Truly, without any flattery, You were born that You might revive the very wisdom of Solomon. He indeed obtained it in bed <note>A reference to the biblical account in 1 Kings 3, where God granted Solomon wisdom during a dream while he slept.</note>; You, however, obtained it in labor, and sweat, and great anxiety. He always ruled his people in peace; You, indeed, placed in the midst of such great wars and enemies, guide Your helm <note>original: "gubernaculum" — a nautical metaphor for the steering of the state.</note> so prudently, on account of a singular virtue implanted in You from heaven, that by Your Imperial rod You place all Your adversaries beneath the footstool of Your feet; and may Your Wisdom show the way to those who are ignorant of the true truth of the faith. Therefore, we humbly pray to God that You, together with all Your people, may find profit in heaven and on earth, and that You may live in peace and safety for as long as possible. Amen.

*I, the Bishop-elect of Gallipoli, Antonio d’Andrade, born in the Ethiopian town of Tacussa, of Portuguese descent; who wrote this and translated it from the Ethiopian language into Latin, with my own hand.*

<summary>This page features a eulogy for Emperor Ferdinand III written in Ge'ez (Ethiopic) by priests from the Ethiopian community in Rome, comparing the Emperor's wisdom to that of Solomon and his relationship with his subjects to the Queen of Sheba.</summary>
<keywords>Ethiopia, Ge'ez, Ferdinand III, Solomon, Queen of Sheba, Antonio d'Andrade, Rome, Wisdom, Kingship</keywords>

<header>EULOGY XXV.</header>

# CHINA.
# FERDINAND III.
### TO THE EMPEROR, EVER AUGUST.

->A colossal monument erected in the Chinese language by the Reverend Father<-
->Michał Boym of the Society of Jesus on the occasion of the *Egyptian Oedipus*<-
<note>original: "Oedipi Ægyptiaci"; referring to Athanasius Kircher's massive work attempting to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>

---

Record of the Tablet Explaining the Egyptian <term>Seal Script (zhuan); an ancient style of Chinese calligraphy used for official seals, which the Jesuits compared to hieroglyphs</term>.

Regarding the seal script on the monuments of the country of Egypt <note>original: "厄日多" (E-ri-duo); a phonetic transcription of Aegyptus</note>: people from ancient times to the present have found no one capable of explaining them. 
Your Majesty <note>literally: "The Saintly One"</note> formerly followed his benevolent will and received the grace of being granted <gloss>provisions and food.</gloss> It was a most auspicious time, <gloss>yet I did not dare to compose or write</gloss> <note>a traditional Chinese expression of humility when facing a great task</note>.
The great name of Emperor Ferdinand <note>original: "福爾提安督" (Fu-er-ti-an-du)</note> is praised throughout the generations without end. In Egypt, there stands the stone of the King <note>likely referring to an obelisk or the "vocal" statue of Memnon</note>.
For eighty years, the seal script on the stone pillars was not understood. 
In ancient Rome, there was also an imperial decree issued to read and understand their meaning.

The great virtue of the Son of Heaven <note>The Emperor</note> is such that all regions and all people—every living soul—harbor deep admiration and reverently pour out their hearts. 
The virtue of the Imperial Court harmonizes with Heaven and Earth, opening up resources and sustaining life. 
Material goods follow; Bohemia <note>original: "貝美利" (Bei-mei-li); Ferdinand III was also King of Bohemia</note> is governed to the highest degree of order, and martial power has stilled the clamor.
Across the four seas, the boiling unrest has settled like dust; the six directions of the universe have returned to peace. 
The hundred barbarian tribes now take the Way and Benevolence as their model.

<meta>This page continues the sequence of multilingual panegyrics (poems or speeches of praise) dedicated to Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand III in Athanasius Kircher’s "Oedipus Aegyptiacus". Following a previous Chinese-style introduction, this page provides a Latin prose dedication by the Polish Jesuit Michał Boym, who serves as a bridge between the Emperor’s court and the missions in China.</meta>

# THE COLOSSUS OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

Following the command of Your most August will, and having received favors and most generous funding, Master Kircher—with a successful daring—has tackled, unfolded, and explained the symbolic characters of the monuments of the Egyptian Kingdom, which not a single man among the ancients or moderns had the power to explain. Infinite future ages will proclaim the great name of **FERDINAND**, the most August Emperor. While the fame of the Egyptian Kings stands in the Colossi <note>Kircher often used the term "Colossus" to refer to massive monuments or the "gigantic" nature of his own scholarly undertakings.</note> of rough and unpolished stones, the city of Rome now reads and understands the symbolic figures which men were ignorant of for a thousand years. The peoples of the entire world will eternally preserve, look up to, and revere the heroic deeds of the most August Emperor in their books. 

Your August Majesty has united heaven to earth through your virtues, unlocked the works of salvation through your benefits, and assisted the state with most beautiful growth; you have reconciled the poles of the world with invincible strength, calmed the four seas, and halted the dust of raging wars; you have restored peace to the Universe; you have given laws and precepts to a hundred barbarian peoples; you have joined Liberality and Clemency to Piety and Majesty. 

I, considering that the Society of Jesus <term>Society of Jesus: The Jesuit Order, to which both Kircher and Boym belonged.</term> dwells under the shadow of your most August Majesty and is numbered among the peoples who follow the Imperial chariot, burn incense to the Lord of the Heavens day and night with reverence, praying from the bottom of my heart that He may preserve the person of your most August Majesty, together with the House of the Empire, for ten thousand years <note>original: "in decem millenos annos"; this is a Latinization of the Chinese greeting "Wan Sui," used to wish the Emperor long life.</note>. Because we truly enjoy the many benefits of your most August Majesty, and the land rejoices in the happiness of its father; I, like a most tiny ant, as a sign of a grateful soul, erect this most flourishing monument in the Chinese language among the explained Egyptian Colossi, as a proclamation of everlasting happiness.

->*From the Society of Jesus.*<-

->**Michał Boym.**<-

# EULOGY XXVII.
## THE ANCIENT WISDOM OF EGYPT.

FERDINAND III, EMPEROR, <note>original: "CÆSAR"</note>
an instrument of divine providence,
eye of the political Universe,
the Austrian Osiris, <note>Osiris: The Egyptian god of kingship and order. Kircher frequently identified the Habsburg Emperors with Osiris to suggest their role as divine civilizers.</note>
who surveys all things with the royal eye of the intellect,
so that he may establish all things by governing providence;
a munificent benefactor of all,
distinguished in Wisdom by heart and tongue,

a promoter of the Mercurial arts, <note>Mercurial arts: Referring to the sciences, alchemy, and linguistics associated with the god Mercury/Hermes.</note>
and himself the author of various inventions,
HORUS, <note>Horus: The son of Osiris, representing the active power of the living king.</note> the Imperial Legislator,
uniquely intent on the care of necessary things;

the Austrian Momphta <note>Momphta: A term Kircher used to describe the "generative power" or "divine mind" within the Egyptian pantheon.</note> in fortitude and strength,

<column-break/>

supporting all things,
directing the operations of his own mind
to be in conformity with the Archetypal intellect;
the divine Legislator of the political World,
fertilizing the Imperial Chalice <note>original: "Craterem", referencing the Hermetic "Mixing-Bowl" of the soul or the cosmic life-force.</note> with a vital influx,
an earthly Osiris;
a tireless watchman to the peoples 
of the Three Kingdoms, <note>Three Kingdoms: Likely referring to the core Habsburg territories of Bohemia, Hungary, and Austria.</note> providing for the peoples 
and their benefits with the watchful 
care of the three Kingdoms;
a most vigilant defender of Religion
and of Ecclesiastical power;

devoted to the preservation of the twelve-towered fortress, <note>original: "dodecapyrgi", a term Kircher used to symbolize a perfectly fortified or structured state.</note>
the cutter-down, router, and

# AN AGONISTIC <note>original: "Agonisticum," referring to a formal athletic or rhetorical contest.</note>
## ENTRANCE-WAY <note>original: "Propylæum," the architectural term for a monumental gateway to a temple.</note>
### To Men devoted to the study of Ancient Wisdom, and to the fair evaluators of this present Work;

---

->In which<-

->Some objections that might be raised against the work are resolved, and the Author’s sincerity and integrity in writing, the reasoning behind his style, and the difficulty of the Work are demonstrated.<-

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'Q' featuring a seated figure in a circular frame surrounded by floral ornamentation.</image-desc> **ALTHOUGH**, most learned Men, none of my present work requires a formal defense, as it has been not only approved by the unanimous consensus of the more distinguished scholars, but even extorted from me by the daily solicitation and "armed" entreaties, as it were, of many years; nor do I fear the sharp <term>obelisks</term> <note>An "obelisk" was a symbol († or —) used by ancient critics to mark words or passages they considered incorrect or suspicious.</note> and censures of certain <term>Aristarchuses</term> <note>Referring to Aristarchus of Samothrace, an ancient scholar known for his rigorous and often harsh criticism of poetry.</note>, which no one laboring "in such glorious dust" <note>original: "in tam glorioso pulvere," a metaphor for the arena of intellectual struggle or the "dust" of the gymnasium where athletes trained.</note> has ever been able to avoid: nevertheless, I thought I should do exactly what we know writers of great reputation have practiced. I have judged it not inappropriate that the foreseen arrows of detractors should not only be cautiously evaded by this combative <note>original: "agonisticâ"</note> prelude, but effectively struck down. For indeed, it seems so arranged by nature in human affairs, and implanted as if by a certain fate, that just as shadow follows light, so <term>envy</term> <note>original: "invidia"</note>—the obscurer of things—is the inseparable companion to distinguished achievements and efforts worthy of praise. For as that famous author <note>A reference to the Greek poet Hesiod.</note> rightly said:

> Potter is angry with potter, and craftsman with craftsman.
> And beggar envies beggar, and singer envies singer. <note>original Greek: "Καὶ κεραμεὺς κεραμεῖ κοτέει, καὶ τέκτονι τέκτων. Καὶ πτωχὸς πτωχῷ φθονέει, καὶ ἀοιδὸς ἀοιδῷ." from Hesiod’s *Works and Days*.</note>

# OF THE AGONISTIC ENTRANCE-WAY
<meta>catchword: fis</meta>

If this holds true in the most difficult matters, how much more so in a literary undertaking? Which is surely as much more excellent as it exceeds all other human actions by its nobility. The most fervent battles of the Learned show this, along with the very frequent literary skirmishes in which they attack each other with such great contention that many, possessing calmer natures and imitating **Antigenides** <note>Antigenides was a famous Greek flute player who, according to legend, told his student to play for him and the Muses rather than the fickle public; here, Kircher suggests scholars often prefer private study to public criticism.</note>, prefer to live for themselves within, content with their private Muse, rather than rashly exposing the offspring of their genius to be torn apart by the insults of so many combatants. This I would have done, had I not been compelled and supported by the authority of my Superiors, and forced at last to bring into the public light this Work, brought forth by the labor of many years. Therefore, what things I see can be opposed to my daring efforts or objected to my completed labors by anyone, I shall explain as briefly as possible in the following chapters.

## CHAPTER I.

->*A response is given to arguments by which someone might think the interpretation of hieroglyphs to be impossible <note>original Greek: "αδυνατον" (adynaton).</note>.*<-

<margin>*Objection.*</margin>
FIRST, therefore, what I see can be objected to me is the **impossibility** <note>original Greek: "αδυναμια" (adynamia).</note> of hieroglyphic interpretation. For I seem to hear those arguing: Why have I embraced a study so arduous, not even attempted by the most learned philologists, and treated by the ancient writers of antiquity only in passing and perfunctorily? A subject, I say, difficult, intricate, uncertain, filled with as many mysteries as difficulties, enclosed by no boundaries, but stretched out into the infinite circuits of a triple philosophy <note>Kircher likely refers to his theory that Egyptian wisdom encompassed the Divine, the Natural, and the Human/Political realms.</note> as yet unknown.

<margin>*Solution.*</margin>
To these, I first respond nothing else except what the rooster once said when caught by the cat: this is my nature, this disposition was naturally given to me. Indeed, I am so constituted by nature that I think nothing more worthy of a man than to test his industry and the powers of his mind especially in restoring those things which forgetful and unlearned ages have neglected over the course of time, or in sagaciter investigating those things which nature has removed from the common sight of men and hidden in the concealed inner chambers of secrets. Not that I extol myself above all those of prior centuries through the happiness and sharpness of my wit, like that haughty **Soldier** in Plautus <note>Referring to the character Pyrgopolynices in the play *Miles Gloriosus*, a classic example of a "braggart soldier."</note>, or show myself more perceptive than the bird of Jove <note>The eagle, famous for its keen eyesight.</note> like that boastful **Thraso** in Terence <note>Thraso is the name of another "braggart soldier" character in the comedy *Eunuchus*.</note>—far from it! For that would be proof of a shameful vanity, entirely contrary to the modesty which my holy religion has taught me from childhood, as I well know. But driven by an insatiable desire for seeking the truth alone, I have attempted to bring back to the anvil this arduous Work, begun by many, penetrated by few, and even abandoned, as it were, because of impenetrable difficulties. To this was added the command of the Emperor, and of most eminent men from various...

<meta>This page continues the "Propylæum Agonisticum" (The Agonistic Entrance-way). Having acknowledged that any public work invites criticism, Kircher now begins Chapter I, where he addresses the specific objection that deciphering hieroglyphs is a task beyond human capability.</meta>

### CHAPTER ONE.

The solicitation of scholars writing from various parts of Europe—who, by the great authority they possess, did not merely persuade me but spurred me on as I was already running toward such a laudable study and the breaking through of this isthmus <note>Kircher uses "isthmus" as a metaphor for a narrow, difficult passage of knowledge that separates two seas of understanding.</note>—has been constant. Yet, older and more significant than all these was the great desire for promoting the honor of God and the common good which blazed in my soul; a desire that is all the better and more desirable the further it extends. I confess that great labor and intense mental heat were required; but I was mindful of that most wise Persian, **Musladini Sadi** <note>This refers to Saadi Shirazi (c. 1210–1291), one of the greatest Persian poets of the medieval period, known for his work *The Gulistan*.</note>, who played with Persian elegance in this way:

> -> ❀ *Though no one can grant anything,* ❀ <-
> -> *except the goods granted by God.* <-
> -> ❀ *Yet one should not show laziness* ❀ <-
> -> *in seeking to acquire them.* <-
> -> ❀ *If the diver fears the open jaws of the crocodile,* ❀ <-
> -> *he shall never obtain the precious pearl.* ❀ <-
> -> ❀ *If you wish to have the spoils within your own home,* ❀ <-
> -> ❀ *let your hands and feet be as busy as those of the spider.* ❀ <-

Animated by these thoughts, I have completed the Work I began under the guidance of the Divine Power; which indeed was the sole cause of such an arduous effort. But now to the task at hand.

<margin>2 Objection.</margin>
Indeed, someone might insist that it is a sign of great rashness to approach a matter hitherto unknown to anyone, and a thing altogether <term>ἀδύνατον</term> <note>original Greek: "adynaton," meaning impossible.</note>, so presumptuously. For if in these times a true, full, and absolute knowledge of hieroglyphs could be had, it would either have been propagated down to these times through continuous use and the uninterrupted tradition of the Egyptians; or preserved in the ancient monuments of writers; or, if lost and extinct, it would have been sought out and found anew by the singular study and industry of men. 

But this knowledge could in no way be preserved until now, because of the immense vicissitudes and metamorphoses of the Egyptians, which they incurred under the various rule of Kings. For the Empire of the Egyptians devolved from the **Chaldeans** to the **Persians**, from the Persians to the **Medes**, from these to the **Macedonians** and **Greeks**, from the Greeks to the **Romans**, from the Romans to the **Saracens**, and finally to the **Arabs**; thus, just as it learned various changes, so too it learned various customs, rites, ceremonies, and doctrines altogether contrary to its own rites, and it has utterly forgotten the laws and institutions of the ancient Priests. Nor could it be preserved in books, since so far no book has been found that might show us any traces of the ancient priestly Wisdom. Nor, finally, could it be restored by human industry, since without a living oracle of authority—which we lack—it is considered breathless and dead.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
These arguments, which could be thrust upon me by opponents, seem to possess some strength to those weighing them at first glance; however, to those examining them seriously, they are not found to be so diamond-hard that they cannot be easily pulled apart and dissolved by opposing reasons.

# PREFATORY CONTESTS

## PREFATORY CONTESTS

Regarding the first point; although Egypt was always subject to many changes, it by no means follows that all knowledge of the hidden sciences and arts was suddenly abolished along with the transfer of power. Who does not know the varied fortune of the Greek Empire and its vast revolutions of circumstances? Yet, despite these things, nearly infinite monuments of volumes—which the learned now enjoy everywhere to the great benefit of the **Republic of Letters** <note>The "Republic of Letters" (Respublica Literaria) was the long-distance intellectual community of scholars in the late 17th and 18th centuries.</note>—show that their sciences and disciplines reached our own times uncorrupted. What people underwent a greater metamorphosis than the Hebrews? Yet, nevertheless, many monuments not unworthy of the Republic of Letters have been propagated down to us.

<margin>Pythagoras and Plato knew the hieroglyphs.</margin>
Regarding the second point, I would not easily deny that in such great changes of Kingdoms, the knowledge of hieroglyphs was gradually obscured by the interruption of rituals. But I believe it is far from the truth to say that among so many people who were most devoted to their ancestral rites—and who worshipped those very <term>mysteries<note>In this context, "mysteries" refers to the secret religious knowledge and rituals of the Egyptian priesthood.</note></term> even to the point of superstition—none were found who cared to propagate the symbolic disciplines, or who would commit to letters and books those recondite secrets of nature expressed through mystic marks. Indeed, if we believe Herodotus, it is known from his *Euterpe* <note>The second book of Herodotus's *Histories*, which focuses on Egypt.</note> that interpreters of these things still survived in his time. Iamblichus also testifies that Pythagoras and Plato learned their symbolic philosophy from the columns of Mercury. However, they could by no means have learned from these columns—by which he means <term>obelisks<note>Kircher correctly identifies that ancient writers often used "columns" to refer to the inscribed stone monoliths of Egypt.</note></term>—if they had not understood the symbols carved upon them. Arrian and Strabo, besides the cited Iamblichus, assert that <term>hierogrammata<note>Literally "sacred letters," referring to the priestly script or the hieroglyphs themselves.</note></term> were still known in the time of Alexander of Macedon. Certainly Cornelius Tacitus writes that when Germanicus Caesar came to the city of Thebes and had curiously inspected those prodigious structures, he called for one of the elder Priests to provide an explanation of the figures carved into the obelisks. Unless this man had been imbued with the knowledge of such letters, he would by no means have been summoned. 

<margin>Hermapion.</margin>
I will not speak here of Hermapion, whom Tiberius calls the "Cymbal of the World" and Tertullian calls "Hermoteles." That he possessed a knowledge of hieroglyphs—if not perfect, then at least significant—is made clear to us by the specimen of such an interpretation recorded by Ammianus Marcellinus; although that interpretation was wrongly applied, based solely on Pliny's estimation, to the Sennefertean Obelisk <note>Kircher refers here to the interpretation of the Flaminian Obelisk (now in the Piazza del Popolo), which Ammianus Marcellinus preserved from a lost work by the scholar Hermapion.</note>. 

<margin>Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*.</margin>
Rufinus writes thus concerning the arts of the Egyptians still flourishing in his age: 
> *Indeed, who could count the superstitious crimes of Canopus? There, under the pretext of "sacerdotal letters" (for so the Egyptians call their ancient letters), there was almost a public school of the magical art.* 

From this it is clear that the knowledge of such letters was not so extinct that some of the priests could not always be found who were skilled in them.

As for the books dealing with these matters, it will be shown shortly that such works were still in use in the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus. He was the son of Ptolemy Lagus, the second of that name; a cultivator of arts and intellects, and, what follows from that, of books. Therefore, he assembled a huge library at Alexandria, aided by the instruction and example of Aristotle—indeed, and by the [themselves]...

<summary>Kircher argues that Egyptian hieroglyphic knowledge survived through political upheavals, citing historical figures like Pythagoras, Plato, and Germanicus who sought priestly interpretations. He maintains that this specialized knowledge was preserved in books and priestly traditions into the Roman era.</summary>

> "And behold, in those days King Ptolemy, a very wise and discerning man, a man of letters, took it into his heart to do what no man before him had done. This is to say: *And behold, in the days of King Ptolemy, a wise and very skilled man, a studious man of letters; and behold, it came to his mind to undertake that which no one before him had; and he sent men distinguished in languages and wisdom into every land and city to collect the monuments of the ancients. Thus he gathered as many books as possible of the Babylonians, Persians, and Hebrews; among which were also books of the Egyptians depicted with figures of animals in place of letters, etc.* To this the Greek reading of Flavius Josephus <note>A 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> agrees; for it says: <margin>Flavius Josephus</margin> *Demetrius Phalereus <note>A student of Aristotle and the first overseer of the Library of Alexandria.</note>, who was in charge of the King’s library, made every effort, if it were possible, to collect all the books in the inhabited world. He purchased whatever he might only hear was worthy of study or pleasing to the King’s purpose—for the King was particularly devoted to the elegant collection of books. He once asked Ptolemy how many tens of thousands of books he had already collected; the King replied that he had about two hundred thousand, but in a short time he would gather five hundred thousand, etc.* <note>original Greek: "Δημήτριος ὁ Φαληρεύς, ὃς ἐπὶ τῇ βιβλιοθήκῃ..."</note> Regarding this prodigious accumulation of books, Cedrenus <note>George Kedrenos, an 11th-century Byzantine historian.</note> also says: <margin>Cedrenus, Book 22, last chapter.</margin> *Ptolemy Philadelphus, he says, having sought out sacred, Chaldean, Egyptian, Roman, and multi-lingual books, took care to have them all converted into Greek, totaling a hundred thousand volumes: all of which he stored in his libraries at Alexandria.* This is supported by Aulus Gellius, Ammianus, Eusebius, and Seneca, although they vary in the number of books cited. <margin>Aulus Gellius, Book 6, last chapter; Ammianus, Book 22; Eusebius, Book 8 on the Preparation for the Gospel; Seneca, Chapter 9 on Tranquility of Mind.</margin> Who would say, then, that from this almost infinite heap of books sought from the whole world, the mystical codices of the Egyptian Sages were the only ones excluded from that rarest library? Who would believe that those monuments—which above all others were held in the highest value and esteem not only among the Egyptians but also among foreigners, and which were so greedily sought by all—were neglected? Certainly no one.

But some will say: all these books were destroyed in the unfortunate fire under Caesar the Dictator <note>The fire during Julius Caesar's siege of Alexandria in 48 BCE, which famously damaged the library.</note>, and thus could not reach posterity. I respond: Let us suppose they did burn; since, however, this huge destruction of books did not happen until 224 years after their acquisition, it does not follow that all were so consumed that the teaching of none reached posterity. For what, in such an exquisite multitude of books over the space of two hundred and...

# ATHLETIC ENTRANCE-HALL
<note>original: "PROPYLÆI AGONISTICI." This is likely an introductory section to Kircher's larger work on Egyptian secrets, styled as a "porch" or "entryway" to a competition of knowledge.</note>

...for more than a thousand years, studious men from everywhere flocked together, both to contemplate that most elegant royal work <note>Referring to the Great Library of Alexandria.</note> and to enjoy its inestimable treasures. What, I ask, could not be excerpted and transcribed? How many treasures do we think were transported away—not common ones, which most neglected, but the most recondite books of all? Among these, the first place was undoubtedly held by those they called the **Priestly Books**, which were remarkable for their hieroglyphic signs and symbols. Indeed, weighing these matters a little more deeply, I believe that whatever fragments of ancient wisdom survive today flowed from that source, as if from a rich **Horn of Amalthea** <note>The "Cornucopia" or horn of plenty from Greek mythology.</note>. From here, all the fragments of **Trismegistus**, **Berosus**, **Chaeremon**, **Manetho**, **Phlegon**, **Astrampsychus**, **Pherecydes**, and others—both Arabs and Chaldeans whom we cite throughout—seem to have emerged. From here, it is certain, came that ancient and mystic philosophy of the Egyptians arranged by **Aristotle**, which had lain hidden for many years in the **Library of Damascus**; which **Francesco Rozzi of Ravenna** <note>original: "Franciscus Roseus Rauennas." A 16th-century translator.</note> finally restored to light, having been translated first from Greek into Arabic, and finally from Arabic into Latin.

<margin>In the dedicatory epistle.</margin>
But let us hear his own words; for thus he speaks: *“When I was staying in Damascus three years before this, Most Holy Pontiff, as a constant cultivator of good letters, I earnestly applied all my effort—sparing no expense or labor—to enter the famous Library of the City. I was accompanied by a friend somewhat skilled in the Arabic tongue to read the inscriptions sufficiently, so that I might explore the countless and precious codices arranged there. Among these, one very old one especially stood out, titled: **The Theology or Mystic Philosophy of Aristotle**. Because I had heard that this had been composed by Aristotle and was lamented as lost, I was immediately seized by the urge to possess the work, thinking how great its reputation would be among all philosophers and theologians; and so forth.”* See what we have discussed at length regarding the excellence of this philosophy in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*.

<margin>Book on the 4 kinds of animals.</margin>
The Arab **Elluchasen** <note>Ibn Butlan (d. 1066), a Christian Arab physician and scholar.</note> testifies that books of this kind are also preserved in the Library of the Babylonians; his words in Arabic sound like this:

->The first men were born in Egypt, and they wrote their books in the form of wild animals<-
->and serpents to hide their secrets, and many others like these they preserve even to this time<-
->in the Royal Treasury. ۞<-

*“The natives boast that the first men were born in Egypt; and these wrote their books with figures of quadrupeds, serpents, and other instruments, so that they might hide the secrets and mysteries of their wisdom from the common people. Books of this kind are still preserved to this day in the King’s treasury.”*

**Seduna**, the Archimandrite <note>A superior of a monastery or group of monasteries.</note> of the same place, relates similar things about the **Library of Gaza**. Treating the customs of the Samaritans in a certain report, he says thus in the Samaritan tongue:

# CHAPTER ONE

<note>original Ge'ez: ኀቤ፡ ሰአልከኒ፡ እምኔየ፡ በመጽሐፈ፡ ዘጸሐፍከ፡ ሊተ... This passage translates to: "In the book you wrote to me, you asked me to give you everything you desired and what we have learned from our father; and I give it to you because there are many books in all of Ethiopia, especially in the house of our King, which were written in the signs of living things that are not disturbed—which have no number of breaths—and all the wild animals of the field."</note>

This means: *We have in our Treasury <note>original Latin: "Gaza," a term derived from Persian meaning a royal storehouse or treasury.</note> a Library full of ancient books; among them, many are found written by the Priests of Egypt; their letters are like the likeness of animals, and it is said that these remain from the Library of Ptolemy, the King of Egypt. Furthermore, Ethiopia does not seem to have lacked these Ptolemaic treasures of books; for an Ethiopian, having been consulted by me via letters regarding Ethiopian matters, responded thus to my questions in the Ethiopic language.*

<margin>Muchi, an Abyssinian Ethiopian, in a certain letter given to me.</margin>
<note>The following is a phonetic transliteration of the Ge'ez text above: "Abi saalacha amneia bemach fachạ zazzahha fachạ lita..."</note>

*In the letters sent to me, you ask that I make you more certain of all those things which we have heard from our ancient Fathers, especially concerning the Libraries of Ethiopia. I tell you, therefore, that many books, and those ancient ones, are found here and there throughout all of Ethiopia, especially in the house of our Emperor, from which many are written with the figures of animals <note>A reference to hieroglyphs, which the author believes were preserved in Ethiopian royal collections.</note>, which they say were translated from Egypt in ancient times.*

<margin>The Libraries of Ethiopia.</margin>
An anonymous writer narrates things not unlike this regarding the Libraries of Ethiopia in the works of Nicolaus Codignus <note>Niccolò Godinho (1559–1616), a Jesuit scholar who wrote about the history and religion of Abyssinia.</note>: *On Mount Amara,* he says, *that most celebrated Library is preserved, which is said to have taken its beginning from the Queen of Sheba; many books were deposited there, which Solomon himself gave to the Queen as a gift when she was departing from Jerusalem to her own country, and which he was thereafter accustomed to send to her every year. Among the rest are certain books which that most ancient Enoch, the seventh from Adam, composed concerning the heavens, the elements, and other philosophical matters. There are others in which Noah handed down mathematical things, and many things pertaining to sacred rites and ceremonies. Others were published by Abraham when he was in the valley of Mamre, where he publicly professed philosophy and had those listeners by whose help he defeated those four Kings who had captured Lot. Others were written by Job, by Ezra, and by many Prophets and High Priests of the Jews concerning various matters. There are other books by the Sibyls <note>Prophetic priestesses of the ancient world whose "Sibylline Oracles" were highly valued in the Renaissance.</note> about various subjects, partly in prose and partly in verse. Others were composed by the Queen of Sheba herself and her son Melilech <note>Menelik I, the legendary first Emperor of Ethiopia, son of Solomon and Sheba.</note>.* Although full faith should not be granted to this account—since, upon a diligent examination, I have found it not entirely in conformity with the truth—it should by no means be doubted that many books, and those most rare and unseen by us, are still stored there; to which other Ethiopians give credit, and among others Gregory, the Abbot of Mount Amara <note>Abba Gregorios (1596–1658), the Ethiopian scholar who collaborated with Hiob Ludolf and lived in Rome.</note>, who is residing in Rome while I write these things.

<margin>The Byzantine Library.</margin>
Shall I not speak here of the most celebrated Byzantine Library, which Zonaras and Cedrenus <note>Joannes Zonaras and Georgios Kedrenos, Byzantine chroniclers who recorded the history of the world and the Empire.</note> mention as being distinguished by one hundred and twenty thousand volumes? In which it is read that even a dragon’s intestine, 170 feet long, was preserved—a memorable thing with the entire *Iliad* of Homer written upon it in golden letters? Who does not know the riches of the Attalic or Pergamene Library <note>The Library of Pergamum in modern-day Turkey, the great rival to the Library of Alexandria.</note>, which, furnished with two hundred thousand unique books, was closest in fame to that of Alexandria, according to the testimony of Plutarch?

<header>AGONISTIC PROPYLAEA</header>
<note>The "Agonistic Propylaea" serves as a "combative entrance" or introduction where the author defends his scholarly thesis against potential critics.</note>

From all of these, without doubt, a great utility and benefit has flowed to the Republic of Letters and to all posterity. For no one should doubt that whatever of the sciences and arts or disciplines now remains has arrived to us having been transferred from them—first indeed through the Greeks to the Romans, and then through these to the rest of posterity. If, therefore, the remaining arts and sciences have been propagated through continuous transcription even to these times, who will deny that the hieroglyphic Wisdom of the Egyptians could have been propagated until now in a similar manner? Indeed, that this is true, this *Oedipus* <note>Refers to Kircher’s work *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, where he attempts to "solve the riddle" of the hieroglyphs.</note> demonstrates everywhere throughout the whole work, using fragments of Egyptian doctrine and the monuments of ancient authors inserted dispersedly here and there; since these are obvious to the eyes of all, I did not think they should be detailed more extensively in this place. Therefore, someone will unskillfully argue for the <term>impossibility</term> <note>original: "ἀδυναμίαν" (adynamian)</note> of hieroglyphic interpretation based on the fact that no books remain.

# CHAPTER II.

->The remaining objections, which could be made, are resolved.<-

<margin>Objection I.</margin> Among other things which someone might think hold great power to overturn the reasoning of our undertaking are also those books of Apuleius, which he says were brought forth from the hidden shrines, marked with "unknowable" letters—partly by the figures of animals, and partly by knotty and wheel-like twisted vine-like condensed strokes.

<margin>Solution.</margin> But he who has rightly understood the argument of the Apuleian <term>transformation</term> <note>original: "ὀνομοφώσεως" (onomophoseos), likely referring to the mystical naming or metamorphosis described in Apuleius's work.</note> will easily see that he who wishes to fortify himself with this argument is attempting to establish his cause against us with fictitious and fabulous reasoning. For besides the fact that narrations of this kind were fashioned by Apuleius not so much for the sake of asserting historical truth as for the sake of showing off his rich wit, I certainly do not see why they should be so greatly trusted. Add to this that Apuleius by no means felt letters of this kind to be precisely and entirely <term>unknowable</term> <note>original: "ἀγνώστους" (agnostous)</note> or ignorant, but only saw them as hindered insofar as they were protected from the reading of the profane by a most difficult method of writing; indeed, he even intimates that he himself was initiated in them in the following context of words:

<margin>Apuleius, Book 11.</margin> > *“Then,” he says, “all the profane being removed far away, the Priest, having taken my hand, led me, covered on all sides with a linen garment, into the innermost parts of the sanctuary itself. You will ask perhaps, studious reader, what was said then, what was done? I would tell, if it were permitted to tell; you would know, if it were permitted to hear; but ears and tongues would contract an equal guilt from rash curiosity.”* 

By a similar reasoning, when Ammianus Marcellinus called hieroglyphic letters "unknowable," he did not say they were unknowable to the Greeks, nor to the Arabs, nor to the Egyptians, but to the Latins. Let us hear his words:

<margin>Book 22, Julian.</margin> > *“There are also,” he says, “subterranean <term>Syringes</term> <note>original: "Syringes," the Greek term for the deep, winding galleries and tunnels found in Egyptian tombs.</note> and certain winding retreats, which, as it is said, those skilled in ancient rites—knowing beforehand that a flood was coming and fearing lest the memory of the ceremonies be wiped out—established in various places, thoroughly arranged with laborious excavations; and on the carved walls they sculpted many kinds of birds and wild beasts, and innumerable species of animals, which they called hieroglyphics, unknowable to the Latins.”* 

But if he called them simply unknowable, why did he assert in another place that they were known and explained by Hermapion?

<summary>This page argues that Egyptian hieroglyphic wisdom was preserved through transcription and is not "unknowable," refuting classical objections by clarifying that authors like Apuleius and Ammianus Marcellinus meant they were merely secret or unknown to the uninitiated and the Romans.</summary>

### CHAPTER TWO.

Therefore, he should be considered to have called the letters "unknowable" in the same sense that we, when we wish to imply something is difficult and impenetrable, call it "Arabic," or written in a similar type of character unknown to us. Furthermore, as for what Strabo says—that Chaeremon, the companion of the Leader Aelius Gallus into Egypt, was mocked by everyone everywhere because he boasted of his knowledge of hieroglyphs—this should not be thought to have happened because he was attempting a subject that far transcended the powers of the human mind. Rather, it was because he was utterly ignorant and unequipped with any scholarly preparation, yet he dared to approach a steep and difficult matter quite presumptuously, as is clear from the context of the words. For Strabo writes: <note>original: "Παρηκολούθει δ' αὐτῷ ἐξ Ἀλεξανδρείας ἀναπλέοντι εἰς Αἴγυπτον Αἰλίῳ Γάλλῳ τῷ ἡγεμόνι Χαιρήμων τοὔνομα τερατολόγος, ζηλοῦντά τινα ἐπιστήμην γινώσκειν δὲ μηδέν ὡς ἁπλοῦν καὶ ἰδιώτης."</note> *A certain man named Chaeremon, a teller of tall tales, accompanied the Leader Aelius Gallus as he sailed from Alexandria into Egypt; he claimed to possess such knowledge, but he was greatly laughed at for his ignorance and arrogance—or, as the Greek text has it, he was laughed at as a boaster and an amateur.* <note>Kircher uses "idiota" here in the classical sense of an unskilled or unlearned person.</note> 

Indeed, a little later, Strabo shows in the following words that even at that time, many priests still masterfully possessed the knowledge of hieroglyphs, even though they hid it from everyone: *There were shown there the houses and dwellings of the priests in which Eudoxus and Plato had stayed. For Eudoxus set out there with Plato, and both spent thirteen years with the priests, as some have recorded. Although the priests themselves excelled in the science of celestial matters, they kept it hidden as a secret and were unwilling to communicate it to anyone; nevertheless, conquered by time and submissiveness, they explained some precepts, while the Barbarians* <note>In this context, "Barbarians" refers to the non-Greek Egyptians.</note> *kept most things hidden.* And a little later: *The length of the year was unknown to the Greeks at that time, as were many other things, until later astronomers received them from those who translated the records of the priests into the Greek language; and even now they receive things from them and from the Chaldeans.* These words are surely so clear that they seem to be a <term>recapitulation</term> <note>original: "ἀνακεφαλαίωσις" (anakephalaiosis)</note> or summary of everything that has been said so far.

Truly, those who speak too despondently and despairingly about the hope of restoring this kind of sacred science should not be listened to—such as Michele Mercati, a man otherwise prudent and learned, but more faint-hearted than is right. For in his supplement on Obelisks, after he had proposed many reasons to show the impossibility of investigating them, he finally exclaims in these words, as if in total despair: <note>original: "*E dunque tanto tempo, che la vera notitia delle lettere hieroglifiche fù oscurata e perduta nell' Egitto, doue essendo prima tenuta da' i Sacerdoti solmente (come diffusamente si è dimostrato nell' altro Capitolo) che hora non possiamo hauer più speranza di ritrouarla così nell' Egitto, come in altro paese, &c.*"</note> *It has been such a long time,* he says, *since the knowledge of hieroglyphics was obscured and lost in Egypt, where it was first preserved only among the priests; thereafter* (for I am completing Mercati’s hanging sentence) *it seems to have perished in such a way that now no hope remains for finding it either in Egypt or in other regions.* I marvel that a man here asserts the impossibility of this business so boldly, or rather, so timidly. If you say: "Mercati could not reach it, therefore no one else can," you bring forward an argument of no weight...

->### THE AGONISTIC GATEWAY<-

of consequence. For who is so ignorant of the rules of logic <note>original: "dialecticarum præceptionum"</note> that they do not see that arguments of this kind conclude nothing? For one would reason falsely, not to say foolishly, if he were to say: "America was undiscovered for all centuries; therefore either it never existed, or it is impossible for it to be found." On the contrary, the scholar Arias Montanus <note>Benito Arias Montano (1527–1598) was a Spanish orientalist who suggested that the biblical "Ophir" was actually Peru.</note> shows by no obscure signs that it was known at one time, indeed in the time of Solomon. He even demonstrates from the etymology of the name that that golden land of **Parvaim** <note>original: פַּרְוַיִם. A biblical location mentioned in 2 Chronicles 3:6 as a source of gold.</note> was first brought from there. Furthermore, it is too well known to need repeating that Amerigo Vespucci and Christopher Columbus have recently revealed it once again in these latter times. By the same reasoning, one would construct a false conclusion if he inferred that the Regions subject to both poles <note>the Arctic and Antarctic</note> either do not exist or cannot be found, simply because they have remained undiscovered by mortals until now. Therefore, the argument from a "thing not done" to the "impossibility of doing it" is false. For because no one has yet been found who has demonstrated the genuine science of hieroglyphs, it does not follow that there will be no one in the future who will eventually demonstrate it.

<margin>Various inventions.</margin>
Many things are found daily that previously seemed to exceed all the subtlety of human ingenuity. Indeed, if anyone in this age were to come forward boasting that he had created the glass sphere of Archimedes, the flying doves of Archytas, or the statues of Daedalus that run about of their own accord, most people would undoubtedly laugh at him as one attempting inimitable works. Nevertheless, I remember seeing such works with my own eyes made in Frankfurt, Germany, designed with such genius that I am fully convinced that neither Archimedes, nor Archytas, nor Daedalus ever dared to aspire to such an eminent peak of art. Therefore, let this weak kind of reasoning cease: "it has not been done; therefore it cannot be done." Many things buried here and there by the neglect and carelessness of unlearned ages, or by the antiquity of times and human forgetfulness, are being dug up and restored in these times by the singular providence of God. Many things were also well known in regions unknown to us, which remained hidden from us. Thus the Art of Printing was successfully discovered by Johannes Gutenberg of Strasbourg at Mainz; and the method of making gunpowder, which was hidden from us for so long, was by no means unknown to the people of China. 

But why do we pursue foreign examples? Let us look at the sky, that common mirror of nature, and we will perceive the present face of the heavens to be unknown to all prior centuries. Stars never before seen appear, and those once seen disappear. Even the Sun <note>original: "Phœbus"</note> itself, which by the opinion of everyone was held to be by far the most beautiful of all visible things in the theater of nature, has in this century finally appeared with a smoky face and a countenance infected with spots; you might say that as it grows old, it suffers from smallpox. The Moon also, imitating the shape of the Earth, now appears clothed with swelling seas, mountains, and rugged valleys—features unseen by ancient ages. Venus, like a second "Ape of the Moon," rises with a horned face, appearing on a stage previously undiscovered, now appearing **gibbous** <note>original: "ἀμφίκυρτος"</note>, now **halved** <note>original: "διχότομος"</note>, or as a **full moon** <note>original: "πανσέληνος"</note>, and putting on other forms. Jupiter, who was thought until now to wander solitary in his orbit, is now seen to walk with a long train of attendants <note>the Galilean moons</note>, a retinue worthy of such a royal star.

### CHAPTER TWO

Comets too, not at all content with the narrow space in which a former, unrefined age used to confine them, are seen holding dominion high above the paths of the Sun and the Moon, seeking higher reaches. Those who desire more on this subject should consult the eagle-eyed <note>original: "lynceos", referring to the sharp-sightedness of the lynx, a common metaphor for the members of the Accademia dei Lincei, such as Galileo</note> mathematicians of this century. On the terrestrial globe, you may see no less significant transformations <note>original: "Metamorphoses"</note> of things. The regions subject to both the torrid and frigid zones are inhabited everywhere, though Aristotle used to assert the former was uninhabitable due to the excess of heat, and the latter due to the harshness of the cold. Today we see the <term>Antipodes <note>original: "ἀντίχθονες" (antichthones), meaning those who live on the opposite side of the earth</note></term> living opposite to us, whose existence the great lights of the Church, Augustine and Lactantius, denied in their own time. Today the globe of the entire earthly world is circumnavigated, which antiquity, in its simplicity, believed was an infinite expanse with a cone-like surface <note>original: "turbinata superficie"</note>. Daily, new kingdoms, islands, mountains, and marvels of humans and beasts, about which nothing was previously known for certain, are discovered. For with this change of things, this variety and transformation, the eternal Wisdom of God plays upon the earth with the children of men. Thus the inconstant order of things is continually turned: so everything goes in a circle, until they finally rest, established in the center, which is everywhere without a circumference. For this change is intended by the Author of nature primarily for the beauty of the universe. Things decay so that they may be born; they are born so that they may decay again, and thus, by alternating change, they are preserved in their state and vigor. Nothing suits this world better than this unending decay of things, and the harmonious disagreement of all things, according to that saying of Pindar <note>A quote from the Greek poet Pindar, Nemean Ode 11, which the author provides in both Greek and Latin</note>:

> ->*The black earth does not always yield fruit,*<-
> ->*Nor do the trees wish to bear sweet-smelling,*<-
> ->*Abundant fruit in every cycle of years,*<-
> ->*But by alternating turns: thus also does fortune turn men.*<-

Seneca indeed subscribes excellently to these things: *Nature does not deliver her sacred mysteries all at once; we believe we are initiated, but we linger in her vestibule. Those secrets are not open indiscriminately nor to everyone; they are withdrawn and closed in the inner sanctuary, of which this age will receive one thing, and the age that follows us, another.* Therefore, all actions of human life follow these laws of change: Kingdoms and Empires are changed, to be restored eventually in their own cycles; sciences and arts are lost, so that in their own time and age—specifically when it seems best to God, the Judge of things—they may be restored. What of the fact that this political world could not long consist of one Empire and one Monarchy? The condition of human life is so desirous of variety. So, if mortals were occupied only with one and the same science, and there were always only one knowledge and faculty of things for everyone, talents would grow dull, schools would languish, and all inquiry into the most worthy things would cease. But now, the death of discovered arts and the new discovery of those not yet known stimulates excellent talents wonderfully, both to search for these with persistent study and effort, and

...to bring them forth, rescued from the shadows of oblivion and ignorance. They have been buried, therefore, so that they might rise again more vividly; they remain hidden so that they might appear more clearly; and finally, they perish lest they perish. <note>The author uses a paradox here: knowledge "perishes" (is hidden away) specifically to prevent it from being "lost" (destroyed) by those who would not appreciate it.</note> But to whom, or when, they are to be restored to their proper places is known only to Him who has reserved for Himself the necessities of future times.

I could confirm these and similar points with countless examples, were I not afraid of abusing the Reader’s patience with a tedious narration of things known everywhere. No science is so arduous, sublime, or unknown that the subtlety of human ingenuity cannot penetrate it; nor do I believe any art is so utterly extinct or lost that its traces do not shine, buried in some unknown corner of the World or some foreign Library, under the cover of a foreign tongue—as if under embers and ashes, among the dusty corpses of half-eaten Codices; or scattered and torn into various parts by the injury of time, found here and there among ancient Authors. That they lie buried happens partly through carelessness and negligence, and partly through the envy and ignorance of those who possess such treasures of books. O how many, and how excellent, monuments of books—not to be compared with any wealth—perish in famous Libraries here and there, struggling with moths and beetles in filth and decay! If these were committed to the light by men skilled in languages, immortal God! what an extraordinary increase we would soon see added to the literary storehouse, so uncultivated and unpolished in many areas, especially from the treasures of the Hebrews and the Arabs. 

For the Arabs—as neighbors and borderers of Egypt, rivals in this sacred Philosophy, and people naturally inclined by nature to the investigation of hidden things—it is likely that, just as they did with all other liberal disciplines, they especially made the more recondite teachings of the Egyptians their own above all other nations, having sought them out from everywhere and committed them to writing. The Hebrews, indeed, have such an affinity for the rites, sacrifices, ceremonies, and sacred disciplines of the Egyptians, that I am fully persuaded either the Egyptians were "Hebraizing" or the Hebrews were "Egyptizing." <note>The author suggests that the cultures of the Hebrews and Egyptians were so deeply intertwined that they mirrored one another's practices.</note> For one might rightly doubt whether the former received the foundations of their primary Philosophy from the latter, or vice versa; were it not that the sacred scriptures clearly showed everywhere that the foundations and architectural principles of superstitious Religion were taken from the law of the Hebrews. For so it is read in the books of the Maccabees:

This biblical quote is used to argue that pagan nations looked to Hebrew law to find patterns for their own religious images.</note>
<margin>The Kabbalah of the Hebrews.</margin>

# CHAPTER THREE.

...as we have shown elsewhere. Countless examples confirm these statements, which are found everywhere among the sacred sculptures of the Egyptians, pointing toward something—I know not what—of a Hebrew nature. For what else do those Egyptian Sphinxes seem to represent, which they had engraved in their temples to demonstrate the <term>unutterable and unspoken</term> <note>original: ἄῤῥητα καὶ ἀνεκφώνητα (arrēta kai anekphōnēta)</note>, that is, the ineffable sacraments, if not the bodies of the Cherubim placed above the Ark? <margin>Book 5, Stromata</margin> Truly, the four-faced golden images <term>of the procession</term> <note>original: τῆς κωμασίας (tēs kōmasias)</note>, according to the testimony of Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, an early Christian theologian.</note>, which were usually carried about in public solemnities, seem to reflect nothing other than those four animals in Ezekiel, celebrated in the monuments of so many writers. Add to this that more secret wisdom of the Hebrews concerning God, Angels, and Demons, which they call the <term>Chariot</term> <note>original: מרכבה (Merkabah); referring to the "throne-chariot" of God in Ezekiel’s vision, a cornerstone of Jewish mysticism.</note>; it is almost the same as the dogmas of the Egyptians, as we have shown extensively in our work on the *Cabala*. I could say much here about the rod of Moses, the sacred Tau <note>The T-shaped cross, which Kircher identifies as an ancient symbol shared by Hebrews and Egyptians.</note>, the Serpent raised in the desert, and other sacred instruments which they used everywhere in their sacrifices, as well as the ornaments of the heads and the Priestly dress—the most well-known traces of all of these are found among the hieroglyphs. But since in this entire Work there will be abundant material for speaking of them in various places, we shall defer each to its proper place. Meanwhile, it will suffice to have demonstrated here in passing how much the knowledge of the more esoteric literature of the Hebrews and Arabs contributes to the restoration of hieroglyphic literature, and that such knowledge must be sought from Oriental sources alone. Indeed, I would dare to solemnly affirm that just as the neglect of such languages brings about ignorance of excellent things, of antiquities unheard of until now, and of other arts and sciences condemned to eternal darkness; so too their cultivation and promotion provides enormous benefits and advantages, not only to the Republic of Letters, but to the entire Church and the Christian Commonwealth.

## CHAPTER III.

->*Concerning the good faith, honesty, and other matters pertaining to the style and method of writing which the Author has followed in this Oedipus.*<- <note>Kircher titles his work "Oedipus" because, like the mythical Oedipus who solved the riddle of the Sphinx, he believes he is solving the riddle of the Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>

<margin>Objection.</margin> Among other things, the frequent citation of certain exotic Authors—namely Arabic, Hebrew, Chaldean, Persian, Coptic, and others like them—will provide no small matter of wonder to my Readers. I see that this could be objected against me: Who has seen these Authors? Who knows whether these testimonies and authorities have been drawn out sincerely and candidly? Whether an honest interpretation of the passages has been provided? <margin>Solution.</margin> To forestall such a judgment, I wished those skilled in the said languages to be witnesses of my sincerity; I took care that the authorities drawn out were examined beforehand, with the original manuscript set before their eyes. Nearly all those who contributed their effort in the *Polyglot Triumph* consecrated to the honor of the Emperor <note>A reference to a celebratory scholarly publication involving many languages.</note> examined the texts of the exotic books and compared them with the original: the Maronites <note>Eastern Rite Catholics from Lebanon, famed for their linguistic skills in Rome.</note> for Arabic and Syriac; Giovanni Battista Jona, the Pontifical Professor of the same, for Hebrew and Chaldean; and then Rabbi Isaac and Rabbi Dactylus of Rome, both of whom were hired by me [to examine] the passages from...

# THE AGONISTIC FORECOURT
<note>The term "Agonistic" (from the Greek *agōn*) refers to a contest or a formal defense. In this context, it is the author's "entrance hall" where he defends his work against potential critics.</note>

<meta>catchword: CA-</meta>

A secretary performed the duty of faithfully extracting records from the monuments of the Rabbis; he was succeeded by the typesetter of the present work, Zacharias Dominicus of Kronenfeld, a native of Old Prague, who composed most of it from the original manuscripts themselves so that the work might proceed with greater reliability. Therefore, let no one doubt my good faith and sincerity anymore, unless they are a destroyer of all human trust; to contradict me in this is nothing other than, as the saying goes, <term>to seek a knot in a rush</term> <note>original: nodum in scirpo; a Latin idiom for finding a problem where there is none, as rushes are naturally smooth and knotless.</note> or a hair in an egg. If anyone should do so, let him understand that he is far removed from the truth of the matter, from the openness of the human heart, and from our intention; let him not blame me, but his own mind. Let him beware lest the same thing happen to him as often happens to the tongues and eyes of the jaundiced: things that are white and sweet to all healthy people appear bitter, pale, and infected with various colors to them.

<margin>Style of writing.</margin>
As for the style of writing, I foresee that it will not be equally pleasing to everyone, since I myself am occasionally dissatisfied with it. For while I attempt to touch upon every single point within that abundance of arts, sciences, and exotic languages—and to do so as briefly as possible—I could scarcely escape a "chaos" of material, especially when there was not always leisure to explain what I gathered through experience and reason in a subtle and refined speech for <term>the polished ears of the Athenians</term> <note>A classical metaphor for a highly sophisticated and critical audience.</note>. I often think it shows greater talent to neglect ornamentation in the exposition of the most hidden matters at the proper place and time than to religiously observe it in everything. Therefore, we do not always embrace <term>Ciceronian phrasing</term> <note>original: Tullianam phrasin; referring to Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman standard for perfect Latin prose.</note> or rhythms, but we use a "many-colored" style according to the nature of the material and argument. Due to the lack of existing terms, we have substituted new names with notes and symbols. We also deliberately omit "makeup" <note>original: fucos; refers to rhetorical flourishes or deceptive ornaments.</note>, as the argument we are treating demands this by its own right; to do otherwise would be nothing other than a foolish effort and an unwise plan to try and make the wrinkled face of an old woman beautiful. Thus, we leave those flourishes to those who spend their whole lives refining their writings against the <term>Lydian stone</term> <note>A touchstone used to test the purity of gold; here, a metaphor for the highest standard of eloquence.</note> of Ciceronian eloquence. For me, it shall suffice to have explained a grave, difficult, arduous, subtle, and hidden subject with words that offer clarity rather than elegance.

As for what remains of the *Oedipus* <note>Referring to his work *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, where the author plays the role of the mythical Oedipus by "solving" the riddle of the Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, I have tried to fulfill the role of a good Oedipus, keeping this especially before my eyes: to speak the truth and things hitherto unknown to the <term>Republic of Letters</term> <note>The international community of scholars and intellectuals.</note>. That is, I have followed only the types of facts, not every detail and difficulty, except when the opportunity of the passage required them to be added safely and usefully. For many things have been falsely attributed to many subjects by various biases; even many true discoveries exist, but this age could not bear to explain them down to the last point because they are utterly overgrown with superstition. This is because curious minds are still burning with the fires of doctrine, and the vigor of things long since forbidden clings to men, not so much to incite them as to instruct them by the examples set before them.

You have the reasoning for my undertaking, Kind Reader; if you find anything worthy of praise in it, I would have you attribute it to God, the giver of all good things. If, however, some things displease you, either excuse them or substitute better ones.

# CHAPTER FOUR.
## CHAPTER IV.

->On the difficulty of the Work, and the assistance gathered from various sources for this Work.<-

<margin>The difficulty of the Work.</margin>
<margin>Labors in gathering assistance.</margin>
Those who sail the sea tell of its dangers; those who explore the unknown recesses of hidden things—with how many labors, cares, and vigils they exhaust themselves, how many reefs of difficulty must be overcome, how many wild, pathless, and remote deserts must be entered, and with how many monsters they must struggle—I am convinced that only those know who have either attempted similar things or, terrified by the difficulties and driven off course by despair, have turned away from their intended path. I, certainly, if anyone else has, will not deny that I have experienced every precipice of the aforementioned difficulties in this present Work. To write histories, to illustrate the sweet gardens of Mathematics, to meditate on Philosophical and Theological matters supported only by the disparate opinions of various schools, and to apply oneself to other studies of the liberal arts for the public good; these might not undeservedly be called tranquil, honey-flowing, and full of sweetness when compared to this most difficult argument. Indeed, in this task, while everywhere, as the saying goes, <term>the water sticks</term> <note>original: aqua hæret; a Latin idiom meaning to be at a complete standstill or facing an insurmountable obstacle.</note>, how anxious is the writer's soul? How doubtful and perplexed is the mind? How great are the struggles of mind and body? For one can scarcely advance a cubit without a reef, a foot without a stumbling block, or finally a hand’s breadth without encountering an indomitable monster. But what was I to do in such a horrific solitude, lacking all counsel, and without a guide or director? I will explain in a few words. Here, all the monuments of antiquity had to be inspected; the Museums and Libraries both of the City of Rome and of almost all Europe had to be consulted. Here, the famous original manuscripts of Oriental Books—drawn from the hidden storehouses of the Greeks, Hebrews, Arabs, Syrians, Chaldeans, and Copts—had first to be leafed through with incredible labor, then transcribed, and finally interpreted. To obtain these, a literary exchange had to be established at no small expense in the native language of each person, with famous and learned men not only of Europe, but also of Africa and Asia (without whose instruction and advice it seemed impossible for the Work to reach its desired perfection). Meanwhile, I shall remain silent regarding the exhausted labors spent in drawing, engraving, and explaining—with genuine sincerity—the Egyptian monuments, both those surviving in Rome and elsewhere, as well as those sent to me.

<margin>Collaborators on the Work.</margin>
But what need is there to recount every detail at greater length, when the very inspection of the present Work displays the structures of these linked labors more than enough, as if in a very clear mirror? But I come now to numbering the auxiliary forces of learned men. This Work was first begun at the urging of Nicolas Peiresc, a <gloss>patrician</gloss> and most wise Senator in the Parliament of Aix in the Province of Gallia Narbonensis <note>Modern-day Provence, France. Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc (1580–1637) was a renowned polymath and a central figure in the "Republic of Letters."</note>, a man whose vast merits toward the Republic of Letters are such that they seem impossible to be erased by any forgetfulness of posterity. Let anyone who wishes read his life—full of immortality and the ideas of grand undertakings—learnedly composed by Pierre Gassendi <note>Gassendi was a famous French philosopher and scientist who wrote a celebrated biography of Peiresc.</note>...

well-polished; and he will openly find that, in ardently promoting the cultivation of literary business, he has had no equal until now. I had traveled at that time from Avignon to Aix-en-Provence, intending to visit the cave of Saint Mary Magdalene <note>The cave of Sainte-Baume in Provence, a famous pilgrimage site where Mary Magdalene was believed to have spent her final years.</note> for religious reasons.
