After I had displayed some skill both in mathematics and Oriental languages, but especially in the interpretation of hieroglyphs, it can hardly be said how ardently and studiously he cultivated the pursuit of the correspondence we began. He encouraged me greatly to pursue my project; he took great care that I should not be assigned by my superiors to any studies other than these; and with a prompt and liberal hand, he supplied from his very rich library whatever could be of use for urging forward the "web" I had begun. He even provided me with ancient coins so that I might describe them for future use.

<margin>The Author is called to Rome.</margin>
Because he saw that this business could not be brought to its desired end except in Rome—which is like the unique theater for all hieroglyphic literature—he first acted ardently with the Most Eminent Cardinal Francesco Barberini <note>The nephew of Pope Urban VIII and a major patron of the arts and sciences in Rome.</note> so that, once permission was obtained from our Very Reverend Father General Mutio Vitelleschi <note>The 6th Superior General of the Society of Jesus (Jesuits).</note>, I might be called there. Then, by his own hand, having sent letters to the same Vitelleschi, he most earnestly requested that he should soon call me to Rome, pulling me away from my journey to Vienna, where I was going to serve as the Imperial Mathematician. All of this was done without my knowledge. Cardinal Barberini, as well as other illustrious men in the City who had already been informed by Peiresc of my arrival, were stirred by the novelty of this unusual undertaking. They did everything possible to promote the work I had begun by every available means.

<margin>The occasion for writing the *Oedipus*.</margin>
Since many people were doubtful about the novelty of this unusual subject and seemed hardly able to believe in the things I was to perform, it seemed best to first send forth a *Preliminary Discourse* <note>original: *Prodromus*; referring to his 1636 work *Prodromus Coptus sive Aegyptiacus*.</note> to all the learned world to show the reasons for my proposal more clearly. This was published in the year 1636 at the expense of the said Cardinal Barberini. When this work moved the opinion of the learned even beyond expectation, I was compelled by letters sent to me from all sides to put my shoulders to the burden. I then began to construct the first outline <term>Ichnographia</term> <note>original: *Ichnographiam*; an architectural term for a ground-plan, used here to mean the structural framework of his massive book.</note> of the *Oedipus*. 

Because it seemed that the business could not achieve its desired success without a knowledge of the Egyptian language—which we call Pharaonic or Coptic—it seemed best to follow the *Preliminary Discourse* with a *Treasury of the Egyptian Language* (once the common tongue, which we now call the restored Egyptian language). This was done under the auspicious munificence of Emperor **FERDINAND III.**, so that we might not seem to have omitted anything necessary for so difficult an undertaking. This was accomplished in the year 1642. 

But while I was urgently pressing on with the *Oedipus*, behold, the new storms of encroaching wars in Italy placed such a persistent delay in my way that I almost cast aside all hope of continuing the Work, and instead gave myself over entirely to publishing other works in the meantime. However, it happened that Pope Innocent X, being about to erect the Obelisk in the Piazza Navona <note>original: *Agonali foro*; the site of the ancient Stadium of Domitian, now one of Rome’s most famous squares.</note>, committed the care of its interpretation to me. Once that interpretation was successfully completed and published, and had earned no small reputation among the learned, the Most August Emperor **FERDINAND III.** was himself stirred by the published sample, and concerning the delay...

# CHAPTER FOUR

Having been informed of the *Oedipus* <note>The *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* (1652–54), Kircher’s most famous work, in which he attempted to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, the Emperor judged that it should be brought to completion with equal haste. And lest the work suffer further delay, out of his immense magnificence, he soon supplied as much funding as would suffice for creating the fonts of all the languages necessary for publishing the work—a generosity truly great and worthy of an Emperor. Indeed, he deigned to appoint himself by his own initiative as the Patron of this work. I add these things here so that a grateful posterity might recognize the incomparable virtues of this Imperial and truly invincible spirit, who—though nearly overwhelmed by the immense ferocity of wars and enemies rushing in from all sides <note>A reference to the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which ravaged Europe during Ferdinand III's reign.</note>—nevertheless so devotes himself to Mars <note>The Roman god of war.</note> that he never excludes Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom and the arts.</note> from his threshold. Concerning the wisdom of this most invincible Emperor, and his inclination and truly incredible affection toward the fine arts, much would need to be said, had I not commemorated these things throughout this work—not as much as was fitting, but as much as the scarcity of time allowed. Concerning him, I might not undeservedly quote what Musladinus <note>Saadi Shirazi (c. 1210–1292), the celebrated Persian poet. Therefore, if anything worthy has been achieved for this Emperor, let the Republic of Letters <note>The "Respublica Literaria," the international community of scholars and intellectuals.</note> acknowledge it as received from God. Furthermore, the Electors of the Holy Roman Empire and other Princes, having been informed of the Emperor’s affection for this work, not only urged the work forward in letters sent to me, but also judged that it should be promoted with subsidies worthy of such great Princes. Their immortal favors bestowed upon me have moved me so deeply that, out of a debt of gratitude, I did not hesitate to dedicate one of the thematic sections of the *Oedipus* to each of them, with the Emperor’s voluntary consent.

Finally, there was no lack of most learned men from all sides—not only from Spain, France, England, Holland, and the rest of the Low Countries, Sweden, Denmark, Germany, Poland, Italy, and Sicily—but even from Greece itself, Syria, Armenia, Persia, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, China, and America. With these men, a bond of literary correspondence had already existed for a long time, involving both various monuments of antiquity and exotic books...

Father Gaspar Schott <note>Gaspar Schott (1608–1666) was a German Jesuit scientist and Kircher's most devoted student and assistant. ## CHAPTER V.

### Concerning the method which the Author used in this Work.

As I was preparing to bring the *Egyptian Oedipus* <note>Kircher titles his work after Oedipus, the mythological hero who solved the riddle of the Sphinx, signaling his intent to solve the "riddle" of hieroglyphs.</note> out into the public light of the world amidst the great heat of an agonizing mind, that elegant Hebrew proverb aptly came to mind: *Writing without order is like darkness without labor* <note>original Hebrew: כָּתָב בְּלִי סֵדֶר : חָשׁוּךְ בְּלִי עֲבוֹדָת (*Katav bli seder: chashukh bli avodat*). Kircher provides the Latin gloss: "A book without order and method is a field without cultivation."</note>. I recognized that in a work filled with such a vast variety of exotic things, there was a need for a singular method—without which nothing can be right, nothing beautiful, and nothing properly arranged in an exquisite order. I did this so that I might not run into that hateful *ataxias* <note>original Greek: αταξιας, meaning "disorder" or "confusion."</note> or confusion in the growing field of this vast work, which usually follows large volumes just as a shadow follows the light. I confess I remained stuck and perplexed for a long time, wondering by what means I could bring beautiful order and exquisite method to a work so varied with the multifaceted erudition of the Ancients. I feared that by rashly heaping everything together in confusion, I would only wrap darkness in more darkness while explaining the most hidden matters. While my goal was to perform the duty of Oedipus <note>The riddle-solver.</note>, I feared that through the intervening obscurity of confusion, I might be said to have performed the duty of the Sphinx <note>The riddle-maker.</note>. Since the sole end and scope of this work was the restoration of hieroglyphic wisdom (which has been lost until now) through a complete, faithful, and sincere interpretation, it seemed absolutely necessary to begin the work with the interpretation itself. However, since the reasoning behind the interpretation required suitable authorities drawn from the best monuments of ancient authors, those authorities needed to be added immediately, so that the reasoning for the explained matters might obtain the desired trust and esteem in the minds of the learned. But even then, I clearly saw that I could not avoid confusion; indeed, from such a massive heap of authorities, I will not say the reader would gain any fruit from the provided interpretation...

### CHAPTER FIVE.

...would follow, but rather I clearly saw that I would entirely lose the *Ariadne's* thread <note>Ariadne's thread is a classical metaphor for a guide through a complex maze or labyrinth.</note> of the exposition amidst such a vast heap of subjects and most long-winded discourses.

Moved by these reasons, I devised another order: namely, to present the entire sequence of hieroglyphic reasoning in the preceding Volumes as a sort of preparation. In this way, the process of interpretation to be carried out in the third Volume might proceed without hindrance. I thought it more advisable that the reader, when dealing with the interpretations set forth in the third Volume, should be referred back to the materials in the first two Volumes—organized with the most exquisite method, order, and reason possible—as if to the roots and foundations of hieroglyphic doctrine which have been extensively treated. For in this way I hoped that the reader, progressing with a steady foot, would perceive the power of the expositions made more clearly and with greater satisfaction.

Since this plan of mine, when communicated to most learned men, pleased them not a little, I followed their advice and approval. In the very first book, it seemed right to deal with the origin of Egyptian superstitions and the roots of polytheism <note>original: *polytheias* (πολυθεΐας)</note>, which we have called the *Isiac Temple*; in this book, using a comparative method, it is shown that all the superstitions of the Hebrews, Greeks, Chaldeans, Persians, and Indians had no origin other than from Egypt. And since a large portion of hieroglyphic doctrine rests upon such superstitions, it seemed impossible that within the rites and ceremonies of these various mentioned nations, significant traces of the hieroglyphic discipline should not also shine forth—even if scattered here and there and torn into a thousand pieces. When collected into one, these would provide great light to our *Oedipus* <note>Referring to his own role as the solver of the Egyptian riddle.</note> in restoring that discipline; all of which are presented in this first Volume.

Because the Egyptians, in the construction of their hieroglyphs, drew suitable symbols from the storehouses of all sciences and arts to display the secrets of their wisdom to the world, we have prepared the second Volume under the name of the *Egyptian Phrontistery* <note>term: Phrontistery (from Greek *phrontisterion*)—a place for deep thought, study, or a "thinking-shop."</note>. In this volume, through twelve Classes, we have presented the entire Egyptian Encyclopedia, compared by a parallel deduction to the theosophy of Zoroaster, Orpheus <note>original: *Orphaicam*</note>, the Kabbalah <note>original: *Cabalicam*</note>, Pythagoras, and Plato. In this way we have found the pomegranate, and having broken the skin, we have extracted the kernel of all Egyptian wisdom. Furthermore, we show that all the philosophy of other nations proceeded from no other source than the Egyptians; with the help of divine grace, we have derived this wisdom as if from a single source through streams into twelve garden beds or classes, as is evident from the very broad arguments of the matters discussed.

These things having been established, we began the third Volume of *Oedipus*, in which you have an explanation of whatever hieroglyphic monuments have survived in the City [Rome] and the World. We have used a method where we do not leave the explained diagrams of the hieroglyphs unproven <note>original: Greek *anapodeikta* (ἀναπόδεικτα)</note> or merely asserted. Rather, we strive to confirm and establish each point with suitable authorities drawn from every kind of learning. And lest we overwhelm the reader with the arguments of long discourses, [we refer] the one who desires further knowledge to the sought-after...

# THE AGONISTIC PROPYLAEUM
<note>The term *Propylaeum* refers to a monumental gateway or entrance to a temple. By calling this introduction "Agonistic" (from the Greek *agon*, meaning a struggle or contest), Kircher frames the difficult intellectual labor of decoding hieroglyphs as a strenuous spiritual and mental battle.</note>

<meta>catchword BE-</meta>

...I refer the reader to the subjects explicitly treated in the two preceding volumes <note>original: *Tomis*</note>, as if for the completion of the work already produced. Because the reader will perceive all these things more clearly from the very structure of the **Oedipus** <note>Kircher refers to his work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*. He casts himself as a modern Oedipus, the mythological figure who was the only one capable of solving the riddle of the Sphinx.</note> itself, I did not think it necessary to describe them in more long-winded words.

Thus you have, kind reader, a work of twenty years, born from a continuous passion of the mind. I shall certainly always profess this: if anything in it has been fortunately discovered, if anything diligently explained, that is entirely **God's**; if anything is wrong, or stated with too little consideration, that is **mine**. Just as it is my nature to err and be deceived in many things, so it will be my part not only to recognize and correct my errors, but also to hold immortal gratitude toward anyone who corrects or points them out. I do not deny that the work and labor were great; so great, perhaps, as no one could suspect. This is not surprising, if the weight and magnitude of the undertaking is compared with the weakness of my talent and strength. Finally, I declare that just as I desire all my works to go solely toward the glory of the **Divine Will**, so I would rightly be unjust if I were to seek any other reward besides that which is the "exceedingly great reward" <note>A reference to Genesis 15:1, where God tells Abraham, "I am your shield, your exceedingly great reward."</note> for all who serve Him:

->**God, the Best and Greatest, for whom I live,**<-

# TO THE BENEVOLENT READER

->The Author’s Associate in Literary Matters<-

## FR. GASPAR SCHOTT OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS SENDS GREETINGS:

<margin>The Wisdom of the Egyptians.</margin>
That the wisdom of the **Egyptians** was extraordinary, and greater than the wisdom of all other nations, is testified not only by secular histories but also by sacred ones. Indeed, the Divine Spirit itself says in the *Acts of the Apostles* (Chapter 7, verse 22), commending the wisdom of *Moses* through the most holy first martyr *Stephen*: "*Moses* was educated in all the wisdom of the **Egyptians**." That the wisdom of *Solomon* was also supreme, the same Spirit of God judged could be proven to us in no other way than by placing it above the wisdom of the **Egyptians**. It is also held in the *Book of Kings* (Book 3, Chapter 4 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Kings 4:29-30</note>) that "God gave *Solomon* wisdom and very much prudence, etc. And the wisdom of *Solomon* surpassed the wisdom of all the people of the East and of the **Egyptians**." This wisdom was indeed so famous among all nations, and had stirred up such great admiration and desire for itself, that even the wisest of the Greeks—*Pythagoras*, *Plato*, *Democritus*, *Eudoxus*, and others—did not hesitate to travel to **Egypt** for the sake of learning it; they preferred to be disciples among foreigners rather than masters among their own people.

From this you may conclude that this so-frequently celebrated wisdom of the **Egyptians** was not common, nor was it open and exposed to everyone—such as **Arithmetic**, **Geometry**, **Astronomy**, **Music**, **Mechanics**, **Medicine**, or other similar subjects. For all of these flourished greatly among the Greeks, even at the time when their greatest luminaries were seeking another, more abstruse <note>difficult to understand; obscure</note> wisdom outside their own borders. Therefore, it was greater and more excellent than these, and of such a nature that it was shared only with the Priests and Kings of the **Egyptians**, and a few others aspiring to priestly and royal dignity; and these were bound by an oath not to divulge it. For this very reason, they did not engrave it in corruptible and easily portable books, but upon the hardest stones of immense mass, hidden moreover under various veils of animals, plants, instruments, and other manufactured things, like certain mysteries; hence they are called **hieroglyphic symbols**.

Indeed, these hieroglyphic symbols contained nothing other than the most serious and profound mysteries—not so much of Physics or Politics, but of Theology—concerning God, the divine Ideas, angels, demons, and the other classes and orders of worldly Powers; furthermore, concerning the rites and ceremonies for appeasing God, for drawing in spirits <note>original: *Genios*</note>, for repelling demons, and for attaining thelepsy <note>original: *θεωληψιαν* (theolepsian); a state of being "seized by God" or divine inspiration</note> and deification <note>original: *θειωσιν* (theiosin); the process of becoming like God</note> itself. Although they also used these same symbols to signify other things, to obtain many good things, and to avert evils—as very effective prophylactics and, as they themselves believed, uniquely necessary tools.

Therefore, these *Isiac* <note>Relating to the goddess Isis</note> symbols, found on Pyramids, Obelisks, Stones, and Tables...

<margin>Kircher’s dedication to learning the Wisdom of the Egyptians.</margin>
When the author of this present work, Father Athanasius Kircher, realized that the inscriptions carved into statues, tablets <note>original: *Abacis* — refers to inscribed slabs or architectural tablets</note>, and vases were swelling with so many mysteries, and that he was attempting to unlock a science so hidden, so praised by all, so sought after by the wise, and so commended by God Himself; he left nothing untried so that he might prepare a way for himself toward it, despite the tireless study of many years. This he finally achieved most successfully through the following method, to the great benefit of the Republic of Letters.

<margin>Expertise in various languages.</margin>
In addition to Latin, Greek, and Hebrew, which he had mastered almost from his youth, he was also highly skilled in Arabic, Chaldean, Syriac, Armenian, Samaritan, Coptic (or Egyptian), and others. Consequently, for many years now, he has been able to speak fluently—to my great astonishment and that of others—not only with Greeks in Greek and with the most learned Rabbis of the Hebrews in Hebrew, but also with Arabs and newcomers from other provinces of Asia and Africa, of whom there is always a huge number here in Rome, using each person's native tongue. He knew, moreover, that many books written in the aforementioned languages—whether in print or manuscript—contained here and there many explained mysteries of the Egyptians. He hoped that if he noted the relevant passages of these authors and compared them with the hieroglyphic marks on obelisks and other fragments brought from Egypt, he would, through persistent study and frequent comparison, attain a significant understanding of them. No sooner thought than done.

<margin>Effort in comparing and examining Oriental books.</margin>
He therefore immediately searched through many libraries, both public and private, in Germany, France, Italy, and especially in Rome, as well as in Sicily and Malta. He sought out or transcribed as many books as treated that subject—books that were for the most part half-eaten, covered in dust and moths, and written in the worst and almost illegible characters. Nearly all of those he still keeps in his study and used in the composition of this work are of this kind. He turned over and over the books he had acquired, though most were such that men otherwise very well-practiced in foreign languages could not, I will not say explain, but not even read, due to the exotic style of writing and characters further half-consumed by decay. Furthermore, he visited the markets, workshops, treasuries, and museums of this City—in short, all places where he knew Egyptian monuments survived. He scrutinized each one most diligently, noting and

<margin>In the seeking out of hieroglyphs.</margin>
depicting all the hieroglyphs. Not content with a single inspection, he visited the same places again and again, surveying what he had seen before and re-noting what he himself had recorded or what he had received as noted by others; this was, of course, so that he would not deviate even a tiny bit from the originals, from which he had discovered others before him had deviated so greatly. Not content even with these efforts, he also searched through friends and patrons of literature in the "other Rome," Byzantium <note>Constantinople</note>; indeed, he even ordered visits to Memphis—the nurse of hieroglyphic science (now they call it Cairo)—as well as the Memphitic fields and the islands of the Nile. He took care that whatever hieroglyphs survived in either place were drawn most accurately and brought to him. Moreover, by sending letters, he asked the learned men of all Europe, and those he knew from our Society <note>The Jesuits</note> and other religious orders in Asia, Africa, and America, that whatever hieroglyphic fa- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the thought on the next page; "fa-" is likely the start of "facerent" (they might do/make) or "faveant" (they might favor/support).</note>

...wisdom, they would deign to send such items to him. This request was fulfilled most generously, with even Great Princes contributing their own tokens. On this occasion, he acquired a vast collection of hieroglyphs, idols, statues, gems, amulets, charms, talismans, stones, and similar objects. These are inserted throughout this Work, though he omitted those that did not reflect the true character of Egypt. Meanwhile, he compared the passages he noted in books with other locations, hieroglyphs with other hieroglyphs, entire Obelisks with other Obelisks, and the characters found on statues, vases, and tablets with one another and with those on the Obelisks. He even began a Hieroglyphic Alphabet, a fragment of which I have recently found among the Author’s notebooks <note>original: *adversaria* — refers to a scholar's miscellaneous notes or journals</note>.

<margin>Supreme skill in hieroglyphic literature.</margin>
Through these many years of diligence, combined with a sharp mind, keen judgment, a most tenacious memory, and every kind of erudition, our Author has attained a level of Hermetic or Egyptian Wisdom—so long hidden under the veils of its primary author, Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure described as the author of the *Hermetica*, a series of sacred texts on philosophy and magic</note>, known to so few in antiquity, utterly neglected for so many centuries, and scattered only in the exotic books of Easterners—the likes of which was once desired by Augustus Caesar and, in the previous century, by Pope Sixtus V. He has already demonstrated this knowledge in his *Coptic Forerunner* <note>original: *Prodromo Copto* — Kircher's 1636 work on the Coptic language</note> and his work on the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, and he now presents it to the learned world in this most scholarly, rare, and truly <term>multifaceted</term> <note>original: *πολυμόρφῳ* (polymorphō) — many-formed or diverse</note> Work. What the learned think of this hieroglyphic knowledge and expertise—even before reading this Work—will be shown in its proper time and place, through the most brilliant testimonies brought forward and the applause of scholars. Here, I shall briefly disclose what Rome and the learned Cardinals think of it.

<margin>By order of the Pope, Kircher interprets the Pamphilian Obelisk.</margin>
When Pope Innocent X decided to erect the broken obelisk that lay buried in the Circus of Caracalla <note>The "Hippodromo" mentioned here is the Circus of Maxentius on the Via Appia, mistakenly associated with Caracalla in Kircher's time</note> in the Piazza Navona <note>original: *foro Agonali*</note> as an eternal monument to the Eternal City, he strongly desired that this massive stone, swelling with Isiac mysteries, should not remain "soulless" without an explanation. He appointed Father Athanasius Kircher to lead this difficult task—one deemed hopeless for many centuries—as he knew him to be famous for his skill in hieroglyphic literature and the most fit to complete it with acclaim. Thinking it a sin to refuse the Pope's commands, Kircher soon undertook the care of the business committed to him with the greatest eagerness, encouraged by such high authority. 

And so, when the Obelisk was brought from the aforementioned Circus of Caracalla, it was discovered to have suffered significant decay (that hungry destroyer of time). It was necessary to repair it using fragments of similar stone, of which a great abundance exists here and there. When this had been most successfully completed through the great effort of the Architect, the Obelisk—despite its great variety and abundance of carved elements—showed certain gaps where characters were missing due to the inserted repair fragments. To ensure the entire mass was not defaced by these ugly patches and did not present a deformed appearance to the curious eyes of onlookers, it seemed expedient to the Architect and others weighing the matter with prudent judgment that "Kircher the Oedipus" <note>Oedipus is the Greek mythological figure who solved the riddle of the Sphinx; Kircher was often called "the Oedipus of Egypt" for his attempts to solve the "riddle" of hieroglyphs</note> should, through his own sagacity and skill, supply the missing and mutilated context of the hieroglyphic literature from his own knowledge. This was done very quickly as ordered, with Kircher asserting that this was a genuine restoration of the entire context...

<margin>He most skillfully fills the empty gaps of the Pamphili Obelisk.</margin>
Because this matter left several people frozen in wonder—to the point that they even suspected the Author of some trickery <note>original: *fuco* — literally "dye" or "paint," used here to mean a deception or ruse</note>—it so happened that some Antiquarians were informed by certain conjectures about fragments still remaining in the pit <note>The foundation trench in the Circus of Maxentius where the obelisk was found before being moved to Piazza Navona.</note> from which the Obelisk had been extracted. They decided the site should be examined more deeply in the hope of finding those fragments. Once this was done, every single fragment was found, by a singular blessing of God. This event greatly sharpened the desire of certain people to test Kircher's skill and his faithfulness in filling the aforementioned gaps. Therefore, when the fragments were soon brought to the forum and each had been assigned to its proper place, it was discovered with great wonder that the hieroglyphic diagrams had been restored so sincerely and genuinely, as if they had been drawn from the very original prototype. This matter was soon reported to the Most Eminent Cardinal Capponi, the overseer of this project, who, having examined the sequence of events, found it exactly as he had heard. From this evidence alone, that most wise Prince concluded it was impossible for the Interpreter, Kircher, not to be profoundly well-versed in the secret constitution of hieroglyphic literature, given such great skill in authentically restoring the symbols. 

All of this is confirmed by an ear-and-eye witness of the whole affair, the Most Excellent and Renowned James Gibbes <note>James Alban Gibbes (1611–1677), a prominent English physician and poet living in Rome.</note>, Doctor of Medicine and an exceptional devotee of all Philology. Since I was well aware of this, I approached the man and earnestly requested that he should not find it a burden to provide an authentic testimony of how the matter took place. In this way, the ingenuity, sincerity, and rare skill with which the Author proceeded in interpreting the Pamphili Obelisk could be established for posterity by a most trustworthy attestation. This most kind man agreed and fulfilled my request abundantly; therefore, I have decided to include his handwritten testimony here. Since he possesses the sharpest judgment <note>original: *crisi*</note> and triumphs in the literary choir due to his devotion to all Philosophy and his knowledge of many languages, I hope that this most solemn testimony will remove the doubts <note>original: *scrupuli* — literally "small sharp stones," metaphorically "worries" or "scruples"</note> of those skeptics who, measuring others by their own yardstick, think things they find impossible cannot be achieved by others. In this way, the truth of the work provided by our Author may shine more brightly before the world. Thus, he writes to me:

->To the Very Reverend Father Gaspar Schott, of the Society of Jesus, James Alban Gibbes, Doctor of Medicine, sends fondest greetings.<-

*I cannot but strongly approve of your love, and likewise love the diligence, which I see you bring to bear in defending your countryman and companion, our Athanasius. For why should those uninitiated <note>original: *ἀμυήτοις* — those not initiated into the sacred mysteries</note> critics <note>original: *Momis* — after Momus, the Greek god of mockery and blame</note> be allowed to remain forever talkative? Should those not initiated into the one man of all—since the original Egyptian inventors—the supreme Priest of the Mysteries <note>original: *Mystagogo*</note>, always be allowed to disparage him with impunity? Certainly, you will not permit it. Granted, those wretched men have previously spoken somewhat arrogantly against the* Magnet, *the* Universal Music-Making, *and the* Great Art <note>References to Kircher's major published works: *Magnes* (1641), *Musurgia Universalis* (1650), and *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae* (1646).</note>; *they have babbled whatever came to their mouths, or rather*

...you might twist (if it pleases the Gods) whatever comes to hand. Regarding the etymology of Oriental languages—especially the Coptic books written by him while still a young man—and his other works of Philology published long ago, you act more cautiously and peevishly, like the Sophists. For those earlier works were indeed of a nature where scientists, logicians, or grammarians could rightly clash in debate. 

However, these latest volumes—beginning with that Pamphili work, in which he commented on the Obelisk of Sothis, the most ancient King of Egypt, and the four volumes besides which now come forth under the name of *Oedipus* dedicated to Emperor **FERDINAND**—are of a truly higher nature and breathe something so sweet <note>original: *γλυκύ τι*</note> that neither mocking Vultures can pluck at them, nor biting critics judge them. 

And here I seem to see you, a good temple-warden, watchful at the very entrance and vestibule of this inner sanctuary, guarding it and removing those you have found impure with that ancient cry: "Be far away, you profane ones." Proceed, my Sebostus, as you have begun; and if there were any of such bold face <note>term: *perfrictæ frontis* — literally "rubbed-smooth forehead," a Latin idiom for being shameless or brazen</note> that they feel no religious scruple in attacking even this Palladium <note>The Palladium was a sacred statue of Athena that protected Troy; here it refers to Kircher's work as a sacred, protected treasure of knowledge.</note>, do not yield to evils. Repel the attack of the wicked with the reminder of their own wrongdoing. Finally, cry out with the greatest voice you can: "Be healthy, O you who go among the healthy!" <note>original: *ἴσϑι ὑγιὴς, ὦ καϑ᾿ ὑγιᾶς ἰών* — a Greek greeting or blessing often associated with those entering a sacred space or seeking healing.</note>

As for your request that I provide a testimonial for the Pamphili Obelisk, believing that this will add authority to the *Oedipus*; although this is unnecessary in a matter that is not in doubt, and I might rightly be judged a "lowly witness" <note>original: *χυμαῖος μάρτυς*</note> who wishes to vouch for the beauty of the Venus of Cos <note>The Venus of Cos was a famous masterpiece by the painter Apelles; the author implies that Kircher's work is so obviously perfect that a testimonial is like trying to prove a masterpiece is beautiful.</note>, I have nevertheless decided to comply, even at the risk of my own reputation, rather than fail your will. 

Concerning Cardinal Capponi, whom the Supreme Pontiff placed in charge of the Obelisk project because of his profound literacy and experience in great matters, I can truly affirm this: as a witness and spectator present for the entire affair, and even a participant in some way (for he discussed with me the composition of the inscriptions to be carved into the sides of the base), he spoke these very grave words to the eternal memory and praise of the Author: either the knowledge of hieroglyphs has not perished at all, as most contend; or, if it was lost, no other concept of the theology within such symbols could exist except for the Kircherian one. 

A brilliant statement indeed, and one most worthy of a man who is a leader in both learning and dignity! This class of men, placed beyond the reach of envious tongues, pronounces sincerely and wishes to detract nothing from the fame of others, because nothing can be added to their own celebrity. For just as each man is most fit in himself, so he is least envious of another's good works. 

Therefore, whether you take my opinion or that of Plato (who said "Plato alone is worth all of them to me"), cease at last to seek out more and to aggregate testimonies so anxiously. Stand by the unique judgment of this most wise Father, believe me, and do not cease at any time to urge that marvel of genius, Kircher—using the great authority you have with him—to continue daily performing such admirable works at your encouragement. "May he always and forever produce, and may the altar-fires of others be present," <note>original: *Αἰὲν ἀεὶ οἴσει, καὶ ὑπάρξοι ἔμπυρα ἄλλων*</note> so that the critics like Zoilus <note>Zoilus was an ancient Greek grammarian known for his harsh criticism of Homer; his name became a byword for a spiteful critic.</note> may burst with envy. 

Although there is no lack of votes from the most learned men in this regard, who have sufficiently shown what they think of these magical writings. You will find these in the *Triumph of Twenty Languages* prepared for the Emperor, our most beneficent patron, which I believe was published together with the *Oedipus*. I myself have even dared to make some noise in the British tongue <note>The author, James Alban Gibbes, contributed a poem in English to this celebratory volume.</note> among the melodious swans; not that I was hunting for a "laurel in a honey-cake" <note>term: *laureolam in mustaceo* — a Latin proverb meaning to seek trivial fame for a small achievement</note>, but because I wanted it to be known that his fame, not content with common boundaries but wandering beyond the paths of the sun and the year, has reached the farthest Thule <note>A mythical land in the far north, used here to mean the absolute ends of the earth.</note>. 

Farewell. From Rome, at the palace of the Most Eminent Cardinal Spada. December 13, 1654.

*Ease and readiness in explaining hieroglyphs.*

From these points, and others which I have mentioned above, it is clearly established (unless I am mistaken) with what great ingenuity and sincerity, as well as with what rare knowledge of hieroglyphic mysteries, the Author has proceeded. This is evident both in his work on the Pamphili Obelisk and in his interpretations of the other obelisks of the City of Rome; it shows, likewise, how much knowledge of similar matters he has acquired through the aforementioned diligence. Certainly, as I myself have very often seen, no hieroglyphic subject is shown to him here in Rome, or brought from elsewhere (and they are shown and brought very frequently), no matter how mutilated or cut into fragments, for which he does not immediately offer a meaning and an interpretation, most successfully and learnedly supported by authorities. I remember a certain time when he was looking quite intently at the Bembine Tablet <note>The Bembine Tablet, also known as the Isiac Tablet, is an elaborate bronze tablet featuring Egyptian-style motifs that Kircher believed held the key to the Egyptian language.</note>, which he kept spread out before the table where he sat for studying and writing; he told me that a light so clear and unusual dawned upon him that, in a single, most distinct gaze, he then understood the entire mystery of the Tablet most clearly. He said that he had no reason to doubt that the very same meaning held by the Egyptian Priests was that which he had put forward in his exposition of it.

<margin>
*Skill in explaining exotic characters and writings.*
</margin>

Nor is our Oedipus <note>The author refers to Kircher as "Oedipus," the mythological hero who solved the riddle of the Sphinx, framing Kircher as the ultimate solver of Egyptian mysteries.</note> skilled only in the mysteries of the Egyptians; with equal dexterity and erudition he handles and interprets the secrets of the Greeks, the amulets <note>original: *periammata*</note> of the Gnostics, the hidden things of the Cabalists, the protective charms <note>original: *phylacteria*</note> of the Arabs, the antidotes <note>original: *Alexipharmaca* — literally "medicine against poison," often used for spiritual protection</note> of the Saracens, and finally the characters, signs, trifles, superstitions, and frauds of all imposters. You will discover this yourself, Reader, if you run through what he presents in this whole work, especially in Volume II, Classes 4, 5, 7, and 10, regarding the Cabala of the Hebrews and Saracens, the Arithmetic of the Arabs, and the Astrology and Magic of the Egyptians. There, he brings forward and explains (or refutes) innumerable things that are entirely new and never before published in print. However, he omits many more things found in the books of the Rabbis, Arabs, and Saracens, or sent to him from elsewhere, lest they be a scandal to others or provide an occasion of ruin to the unwary. But so that you may see the high regard for Kircher’s skill in such matters even among those who are not very well-disposed toward him, I will not find it burdensome to relate what happened this very year in my presence. A noble and learned man came from a distant region to our Roman College; having called out one of the Fathers from that same region, he showed him a gem marked with secret signs and Greek characters, which had been dug out of the earth at Assisi while foundations were being laid for a new temple. He asked that it be offered to Master Athanasius Kircher to be interpreted, though his own name was not disclosed. He added that he had shown that gem in all the cities of Italy to the most learned men and those most skilled in the Greek language; all had replied that the characters were indeed Greek, but the words were foreign and unknown to them, and they were completely ignorant of the meaning of the engraved signs—they said one must turn to Kircher. That man confessed frankly that he had refused to turn to Kircher for so long because he did not want to be forced to give him the credit for the interpretation. The gem was brought to Kircher in my presence; he immediately replied that the gem was a Gnostic Amulet, the signs signified the Solar Genius, and the characters were to be read <gloss>backwards</gloss> <note>original: *retrorsum*</note>. <margin>
Kircher’s supreme skill in explaining foreign writings.
</margin>
But what shall I say of that rare skill Kircher possesses in reading and interpreting inscriptions, no matter the language or the type of characters—even those written in an exotic, intricate, or corrupted hand? Ever since the *Coptic Forerunner* <note>original: *Prodromus Coptus* (1636), Kircher’s pioneering work on the Coptic language, which he correctly identified as a descendant of ancient Egyptian.</note> was published, in which he displayed specimens not only of the Egyptian language and hieroglyphic literature but also of various areas of learning and most difficult interpretations through a new and unusual method, it can hardly be said how many inscriptions—sacred, profane, superstitious, magical, and even diabolical—carved or written upon temples, palaces, cemeteries, tombs, stones, books, swords, knives, statues, coins, gems, and amulets, have been brought to him from every part of the whole world for him to interpret. Indeed, there were even those who, doubting the man’s skill or led by some other ill-intent, made characters that were already quite intricate even more so, or falsified them entirely, or wrote them in reverse order. Yet our **Oedipus** <note>A reference to the mythological hero who solved the riddle of the Sphinx; Kircher was often called the "Oedipus of Egypt" for his work on hieroglyphs.</note> satisfied them all by detecting the frauds, untying the tangled knots, demonstrating which characters were false, corrupted, substituted, or inverted, and explaining the legitimate ones. Thus, he is now deservedly heard of everywhere as one knowledgeable in all languages and the **Mithridates** <note>original: *Mithridates*; referring to King Mithridates VI of Pontus, who was said to speak twenty-two languages.</note> of this age. I myself have seen him more than once explaining with great dexterity, and even at first sight, characters regarded by everyone else as unintelligible. Not long ago, a certain noble and most learned man sent a seal impressed in wax, marked with I know not what exotic characters, together with a letter in which he confessed that he had sent the said seal to the most learned men of France, Germany, Belgium, and even Denmark and Sweden for explanation; but they were all at a loss <note>original: *aquam hæsisse*, a Latin idiom meaning to be stuck or unable to proceed.</note>. He therefore earnestly begged Kircher to turn his helping hands to such a desperate task. I was present when Kircher received and read the letter and inspected the seal; I heard him say that he wondered why no one had been able to read the writing, since it was not particularly difficult. Therefore, taking up his pen, he soon wrote back a most kind letter and sent it to the man together with a most learned and extensive explanation of the seal and the writing. I would be going too far if I wished to recount everything of this kind that has happened in these few years during which I have enjoyed Kircher’s company. He himself admits that he has sent out so many interpretations to all parts of the world that, if they were collected together, they would fill an entire volume. It is therefore a matter of regret that no others are to be found in his possession than those he inserted into the *Coptic Forerunner* and the second volume of the *Egyptian Oedipus*.

<margin>
Kircher’s fame and his reputation among all people.
</margin>
These are the things regarding the skill of this work's author in Egyptian matters, his dexterity in explaining foreign characters, and his faithfulness in interpreting hieroglyphs, which I thought should be pointed out rather than merely stated. Although I could have omitted even these, since the man’s fame and his reputation among everyone in the world is too well known to need telling. For how great Kircher is in every kind of learning is attested by the learned monuments of his genius that have been transmitted to posterity thus far. How great his fame and reputation...

<margin>Letters from Princes to Kircher.</margin>
Among all people, the countless letters of Princes and learned men addressed to him speak for themselves; the praises of scholars inserted into books and letters testify to it, as do all those who have known him and visit him daily for the sake of seeing and knowing him. I discovered a massive collection of letters in Kircher’s archive, which most Princes of the Christian World and the highest heads of the Roman Empire have sent to him at all times, and even now transmit almost daily. Among these are the most August and Wise Emperor **FERDINAND III**; the most Serene and Wise Queen of Sweden, **Christina**; many most Eminent Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church; most Serene Electors of the Holy Roman Empire; and most High and Illustrious Dukes, Princes, Counts, Barons, and Nobles of the same Empire and other nations without number. All of these admire and proclaim Kircher’s learning; they give thanks for the books and other fruits of his genius he has sent; they urge and solicit him to forge other monuments of erudition; they offer and bring their assistance, communicate secrets, seek out mysteries, and search for the explanation of those mysteries, the interpretation of foreign languages, strange inscriptions, unknown characters, and the solution to various doubts. I would include here the various and lengthy letters of the Emperor, other Princes, and almost all the learned men of this century—which are indicators of a singular affection and the highest esteem—if the narrowness of space (in someone else’s work) and the Author’s modesty permitted it, and if I had not reserved them for another time and place. I therefore restrain my pen, even against my will, preferring to say nothing at all rather than too little in such a wealth of things to say.

P. S. These few things I have said were already being sent to the press when there came into my hands a most learned as well as most kind letter from the most learned Prelate of Vaison <note>Joseph Maria Suaresius (1599–1677), Bishop of Vaison and a noted scholar/antiquarian.</note> addressed to the Author. Since he has performed no small service in this noble work—both in starting it and in promoting it by all means through his rare learning, his great zeal for literature and men of letters, and his singular knowledge of ancient wisdom, as he himself does not disdain to admit in the said letter—I could not omit it without a clear mark of an ungrateful spirit. Thus he says:

->**To the very Reverend Father Athanasius Kircher, Priest of the Society of JESUS,**<-
->**the most learned <term>polygnosto</term> <note>original Greek: *polygnōstō*, meaning a person of many-sided knowledge or a "universal scholar."</note>, Joseph Maria Suaresius, Bishop**<-

Recently, while you were withdrawing to Tusculum, you wrote a most kind letter to me; I have delayed replying to it longer than was proper because the funeral rites <note>original Latin: *Iusta*, referring to the funeral ceremonies for Pope Innocent X, who died in January 1655.</note> of the deceased Pope and the assembly for his successor <note>The papal conclave of 1655, which eventually elected Alexander VII.</note> kept me occupied. However, not unmindful of my duty, now that those matters are being adjourned—and as that poet used to sing,

here is my reply, though it arrives late; and I pay my debt, in which I congratulate you—or rather the Republic of Letters, and indeed even our own age—on the stones, or rather

...mountains engraved with letters hitherto unknown, which were once admired only for their size. These you have read through so easily and explained so clearly that even the silent and inanimate stones seem to speak and find their voice. The secrets of the sciences, hidden deep within them like sparks trapped in flint, are struck out by your sharp intellect and clearly, openly revealed. 

Ancient ages were struck with wonder, and recent ages have looked up at those "stony pages," marvelling at how those massive, oblong rocks—which they call **Obelisks** from their pointed shape—could be cut and torn away, or by what art they were transported across seas and lands from so far away. Gelenius, Mercati, and others diligently searched for the machines by which they were erected and raised to threaten the stars, attempting to pass this knowledge to posterity. 

Above all, citizens and visitors were held in a daze by the **hieroglyphic characters** <note>original Greek: ἱερογλυφικοὶ</note> engraved and impressed by the Egyptian Priests <note>original: Hierophants</note>. For no one knew them, and no one understood them; no matter how many learned men gazed upon them, they confessed themselves to be ignorant and "illiterate" <note>original Greek: ἀναλφαβήτους, meaning those who do not know the alphabet</note>. No one ever dared to interpret them except for **Hermapion**, who you have demonstrated fell into the foulest error, and who is proven to have deceived and played a trick on a most wise and August Prince. 

You alone, it seems, were reserved by God for this age to unlock and spread these hidden treasures. Having approached these stony volumes and "literate hills" with the greatest learning and truth, you have most successfully completed a work worthy of all ages, to be proclaimed throughout the entire world. You have brought it to perfection in every part. You have extracted and revealed the seeds of the deeper sciences hidden in those rocks. 

It was not enough for you to win the love of the learned by elegantly publishing the powers of the **Magnet** <note>Kircher's book *Magnes* (1641)</note> and drawing them into admiration of you, nor for the fame of your name to resound everywhere with the applause for your *Musurgia* <note>Kircher's *Musurgia Universalis* (1650), a massive work on music theory and acoustics</note> and your epic poetry <note>original Greek: ἐποποιίας</note>. You rescued the dying **Coptic** (or as others call it, Guptic) language from destruction, bringing back to light the perishing elements and an abandoned tongue to its former splendor. With a truly Herculean effort, you dared to restore it to wholeness with most fortunate success, dispersing the darkest shadows of oblivion and the thickest fog of antiquity. 

By illustrating and polishing the mystical carvings and portentous figures of the **Obelisks**, you have made public the entirety of Egyptian wisdom. Good luck to your spirit, man of all-encompassing learning! Proceed on this Royal road to immortality! 

**Nicolas Peiresc** <note>Nicolaus Peyrescius (1580–1637), a famous French astronomer and patron of science</note>, a hero to be remembered forever—who, by managing the literary correspondence of the whole world, was himself a marketplace of the refined arts—had long ago indicated this racecourse for you to run in and win the prize <note>original Greek: βραβεῖον</note>. The most Eminent **Cardinal Francesco Barberini**, a most skillful lover of antiquity <note>original Greek: Φιλαρχαίας</note> and a seeker and honest evaluator of the sharpest and best minds, and a patron <note>term: Mæcenas, a classic term for a wealthy supporter of the arts</note>, saw and approved of your worth. Having called you to the City <note>Rome</note> by his authority, he led you as if by the hand into these inner sanctuaries. 

I, who have performed no ungrateful service for you with both of these men, offer this again, and I do not cease to cry out "wisely" <note>original Greek: σοφῶς</note> and "wisely" again with joy. 

Farewell, most learned man. 

Rome, the Kalends of March <note>March 1st</note>, 1655.

# PREFACE.
## The scope of Volume I is set forth.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter C, containing an illustration of a bird and floral scrollwork.</image-desc>
SINCE from Egypt, as if from a certain perennial spring flowing through the entire world, the nurseries of both primeval idolatry and superstitious arts have produced a varied offspring of false dogmas in every place: we have decided to do the same in this first part of the *Oedipus* <note>Kircher likens himself to Oedipus, the Greek hero who solved the riddle of the Sphinx, signaling his intent to solve the "riddle" of Egyptian hieroglyphs</note> as those who track a source by following its streams. <header>CHAPTER I. THE ISIAIC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS</header>

...leading to their restoration and to unearth those things unknown until now, we believed it would not be difficult for a wise Oedipus <note>original: "Oedipo"; Kircher frames himself as a new Oedipus capable of solving the "riddle" of the Sphinx and the Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>. Since the Greeks, Hebrews, and other nations neighboring Egypt shared many things with the Egyptians in sacred rites and ceremonies (as Clement of Alexandria <note>original: "Clemente Alexandrino"; an early Christian theologian who wrote about the symbolic nature of Egyptian religion.</note> testifies), it follows that great hieroglyphic wisdom, though disguised in various different colors, shines forth in the traces of their own actions. Therefore, in this first volume of the *Oedipus*, which for the stated reasons we have not inappropriately called the **Hieroglyphic Apparatus** <note>original: "apparatum hieroglyphicum"; here meaning a foundational collection of materials and tools for study.</note>, we shall attempt to demonstrate, God willing, the reasoning behind the philosophy hidden within the diverse rites and ceremonies of the ancient nations, each according to its own nature, through a certain comparison of Greek and Hebrew matters parallel to the Egyptian.

Consequently, it is proven that to easily and successfully expedite that arduous restoration of the hieroglyphs, one must visit workshops of this kind. Although perhaps this material could have been more conveniently interspersed into the practical interpretation of the Obelisks, it nevertheless seemed more advisable to treat it separately in this first Volume—both to avoid the confusion that usually occurs in a large mass of collected facts, and to propose the explanation more clearly and lucidly to the reader, just as we have done in this first Volume. In this, we have strived for one thing: to set down exactly the words of individual Authors, in whatever language they may have written, in order to proceed more faithfully and sincerely. And these are the matters about which we thought you, benevolent Reader, should first be warned, lest you think we have aimed wide of the mark in this work.

# THE NILOTIC DELTA
## TREATISE I.
### In which the name, origin, division, and nature of Egypt, the succession of Kings, the glory of their deeds, and chronology are discussed at length.

## CHAPTER I.
### *On the Name and Division of Egypt.*

<margin>Names and division of Egypt.</margin>
As I begin to investigate that hidden wisdom of the Egyptians from all past ages, it seemed appropriate to start immediately with Egypt itself—as if with those first cradles of the Gods, the mystical temple of the universe, the architect of worldly Spirits, the theater of prodigious works, the fertile Mother of portents, the marketplace of arts, the treasury of all kinds of wisdom, the inventor of detestable Idolatry, the monstrous Kingdom of Morpheus <note>Morpheus, the Greek god of dreams, here suggests Egypt is a land of symbolic visions and mysteries.</note>, and finally the workshop of all superstition.

<margin>On the primacy of Egypt.</margin>
As one which, among the other regions of the world, has always held primacy until now—both for its antiquity, in which it excels all, and for the glory of its deeds, in which it is second to no land—as seen not only in sacred monuments, but also in the profane monuments of writers...

# COMPILATION I. THE CHOROGRAPHY OF EGYPT. CHAPTER I.
<center>A 2</center>

...most celebrated for its monuments; therefore, its dignity and primacy, acquired through virtue and glory, should by no means be denied a place in the vestibule of this work.

<margin>The Etymology of Egypt.</margin>
*Egypt*, then—whether it is named after the first King of this name, as it seems to *Strabo*, *Ammianus*, *Diodorus*, and others; or named after the Nile, because "it lies supine under the goat" <note>original: "ἀπὸ τῆς αἰγὸς ὑπτίᾳ κεί"; a Greek wordplay suggesting Egypt’s position under the zodiac sign of Capricorn.</note>, that is, because it lies flat under the sign of Capricorn, as *Goropius Becanus* <note>Johannes Goropius Becanus was a 16th-century physician famous for his creative, if often eccentric, linguistic theories.</note> likes to think—is a region of Africa known to everyone. It is bounded on the North by the Mediterranean Sea and the seven-fold mouths of the Nile; on the East by the belt of the Red Sea, which extends like a chain of mountains all the way into *Ethiopia*; on the South by the rugged precipices of the cataracts; and finally on the West, both by the fabled *Libyan* Ocean and a continuous series of mountains. These mountains run parallel to the Red Sea range, so to speak, and as *Strabo* testifies, they stretch out in the shape of an unrolled band, or better yet, in the shape of an extended arm (whose hand or palm is represented by the Nilotic **Delta**, which, through the various branching of the river, divides like a hand into fingers).
<margin>The Location of Egypt.</margin>
<margin>The Boundaries of Egypt.</margin>
And just as this land has undergone various shifts in its affairs at every period, so too in succeeding ages has it been allotted such a diversity of names that I believe it should be called "of many forms and ten thousand names" <note>original: "ὄνομα Τμορσον καὶ μυριόνυμον"; a phrase Plutarch used to describe the gods Osiris and Isis.</note> with even better right than *Plutarch* once used for *Osiris* and *Isis*. 
<margin>Various names for Egypt.</margin>
Indeed, by *Berosus* it was once called *Oceania* after the Ocean, its inhabitant; by *Xenophon* it is called *Ogygia* after *Ogyges*; by a certain unknown *Honorius* it is called "shining forth" <note>original: "ἐξέλαμ"; likely a fragment of "Exampolis" or a similar descriptor.</note>; by *Herodotus*, after the river Nile, it is called "River-land" <note>original: "ποταμίτις"; Potamitis.</note>; by *Lucian*, from the blackness of its earth, it is called "Black-soiled" <note>original: "μελάμβολος"; Melambolos.</note>; and for the same reason *Apollodorus*, *Stephanus*, and *Eustathius* refer to it as the "Land of the Black-footed" <note>original: "χώρα μελαμπόδων"; Chōra melampodōn.</note>. By *Homer*, it is called "Hephaestia" <note>original: "ἡφαίστια"; meaning "of Vulcan/Hephaestus."</note> after Vulcan; and "Aeria" by *Eusebius* in his Chronicles. By various historians it is called *Ethiopia* or the Land of *Cush*; by the *Turks*, if we believe *Pinetus*, it is called *Elkebitz*, which means "the hidden." By the Arabs it is called <term>مصر</term> *Misr* <note>Kircher transliterates this as "Mefra," but it refers to the common Arabic name for Egypt, Misr.</note>. By the Chaldeans <term>מצראי</term> *Mitzrai*. By the Syrians *Mizri*; by the Ethiopians *Gaza* and *Mesra*; the name *Mesrem* in *Suidas* does not differ much from these words. By the Romans, since the time of *Augustus*, it was called "Augustanica" <note>original: "Αὐγουσταινικῆ".</note>. By the Copts and ancient Egyptians, it was called *Chemia* <note>original: "χηεία"; related to the Egyptian word "Khem," meaning black earth.</note> after *Ham*, the son of *Noah*; those who support the Sacred Scriptures often point to it under the name of the "tents of *Ham*." Finally, by the Hebrews it is called <term>מצרים</term> *Mitzraim*, a name known everywhere, after *Mitzraim* the son of *Ham*, its first possessor. Others, however, would have it called *Mitzraim* from the word <term>צרה</term> *Tzarar*, which denotes "narrowness" or "distress," because it is closed off and, as it were, hemmed in and constricted from the four corners of the world by the shallow flooding of the Mediterranean Sea, the Isthmus of the Red Sea, the Memphite mountains, the Nilotic cataracts, and the Libyan descent, making it difficult and inaccessible to foreigners.

<margin>Lower Egypt was built up by the silting of the river.</margin>
*Herodotus* calls it "the gift of the Nile"; for he, drawing arguments from the shells found in the mountains, from the saltiness of the springs and ditches, from the earth being a different color than the surrounding borders, and from the Nilometer—a sign of the greatest fertility (since in the past, eight cubits promised an abundance of things, whereas in his own time sixteen cubits barely promised it)—and other similar points, he conjectures with no little clarity that the greatest part of Egypt, especially that which extends from the Memphite mountains to the sea and is widely irrigated by the rising of the river, was gradually brought down and piled up as silt from the higher regions. Indeed, almost everyone who came after him followed this opinion...

<summary>This page introduces the geography and various historical names of Egypt, establishing it as a land of "ten thousand names" and exploring the etymological roots of terms like Mitzraim and Chemia. It also presents the classical theory that Lower Egypt was formed by the silt of the Nile.</summary>
<keywords>Egypt, Etymology, Nile, Mitzraim, Ham, Herodotus, Strabo, Geography, Chorography, Delta, Red Sea</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Egypt's geological formation from page 3, specifically citing Aristotle's theory of siltation, before transitioning into Chapter II, which details the administrative and mystical division of the land into "Nomes."</meta>

<center>CHAPTER II. THE ISIAIC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS</center>

<margin>Aristotle, Meteorology, Book 1.</margin>
...both philosophers and historians descend. Aristotle also says that the land dries out more and more every day, and that the whole of it was carried in and piled up by the Nile; for over a long period of time, marshes are filled with silt and finally rendered suitable for habitation, although the beginning of this process is shrouded in oblivion. And for this reason, only *Thebes* is mentioned by *Homer*, as *Memphis* was either not yet "born" or had not yet progressed to the point where it was considered worthy of mention. Another sign of this is that the water has gradually dried up, and that *Sesostris* <note>Sesostris was a legendary king of Egypt said to have led great military expeditions and attempted massive engineering projects.</note> learned that the Red Sea was higher <margin>The error of Sesostris, who thought the bed of the Red Sea was higher than the surface of Egypt.</margin> than Egypt; for that reason, he abandoned the plan he had in mind to build a canal from the Erythraean <note>The "Erythraean Sea" is the classical name for the Red Sea.</note> Sea to the Nile, fearing he would submerge the entire land in a flood. For he convinced himself that the hollow of Egypt was deeper than the bed containing the Erythraean Sea—an error we shall refute in its proper place in the following pages. Having thus summarized these matters, let us now proceed to a specific description of Egypt.

## CHAPTER II.

### On the division of Egypt into Nomes in general.

<margin>The division of Egypt.</margin>
Furthermore, according to *Strabo*, all of Egypt was anciently divided into thirty *Nomes*, or prefectures—exactly as many as its *Labyrinth* (that mystical temple of Egypt) had halls or lodgings. So it was that the upper part of Egypt, called the *Thebaid*, contained ten Nomes; the Middle or Inland part, also called the *Memphite* region, contained just as many; and finally the Lower region—named the **Delta** because of the triangular shape described by the Nile where it splits at *Memphis*, its sides extending to the coastal base—comprised no fewer than the previous parts. Moreover, they dedicated the honor of all these Nomes to thirty Gods and Spirits, whom *Trismegistus* calls "Ephors" <note>Ephors: overseers or guardians.</note> or "Decans" in the Republic of the Gods, and others call <term>Masters of the House<note>original: "Οἰκοδεσπότας" (Oikodespotas), a term used in ancient astrology to denote the ruling planet of a celestial house.</note></term>. Each of these was believed to preside over individual Nomes as protective Spirits, or "Averruncans" <note>Averruncans: ancient Roman deities invoked to avert or "ward off" calamity; here Kircher uses the term to describe Egyptian protective spirits.</note> of evils; indeed, nothing was done among the Egyptians without mysteries. But as for the partitions and meanings of these Nomes as they correspond to individual Gods, in order to cover many things in few words, we have decided to place before your eyes this single Diagram, drawn from *Ptolemy*.

To these, others add from Pliny and Ptolemy the Nomes of Omphilen, Phanturite, Tinite, Phatnite, Neut, Heptanomus, Athribite, Onephite, Butos, and others, which you may see in the works of Ptolemy.

Moreover, there was a need for such a diligent and subtle division of places because of the constant confusion of boundaries, as Strabo well notes. These confusions were caused by the Nile overflowing in its increase, adding to some lands and taking away from others, changing the shapes of the fields, and burying the markers by which one's own property was distinguished from another's; and so, it was necessary to measure them again and again.

<margin>The cause for the division of Egypt.</margin>
Furthermore, this exact distribution of Egypt into its Nomes—first made by Sesostris <note>A legendary king of Egypt, often associated with Ramses II or Senusret.</note>, according to the testimony of Diodorus—lasted for many ages afterward. It continued until the region, having been attacked by various disturbances of wars and having suffered various destructions of its cities and towns, finally fell into the hands of the Mohamedans <note>referring to the Arab conquest of Egypt in the 7th century.</note>; who, from the ancient...

...to the former customs and statutes of the Priests, they substituted their own. For, having soon abolished the division of the Nomes, they divided Egypt into three other parts. The first of these, which extends from Cairo to the Canopic mouth (whose length is bounded by the western arm of the Nile called the *Agathodaemon* <note>original: *Agathodaemon*; Greek for "Good Spirit," a common name for this branch of the Nile</note>, and whose width is divided by the Athribitic river, cutting the Nilotic Delta in two and bordering the side of the sea), they call <margin>Egypt divided into three by the Turks.</margin> *Nahar allerif* <note>Arabic: نهر الاريف; "The River of the Cultivated Bank"</note>, or simply *Erif*. The second part, which runs in a continuous stretch from Cairo between the Erythraean <note>The Red Sea</note> and Libyan mountains all the way to the cataracts, formerly called the Thebaid, they now call *Assaid* <note>Arabic: الصعيد; *Al-Sa’id*, meaning Upper Egypt</note>, which is to say, *The Tent*. Finally, the third part, which is determined by the Athribitic arm of the Nile and the length of the Bubastic river next to Stony Arabia, they call *Allardt Bechria* <note>Arabic: الارض بحرية; *Al-Ard al-Bahriyyah*, meaning "The Maritime Land"</note>, which is to say, *the marshy or marine land*. The first region abounds in rice and every kind of fruit; the second in grain, legumes, livestock, birds, and flax; the third in sugar canes, cotton, myrobalans <note>A type of plum-like fruit used in medicine and tanning</note>, and other fruits unknown to Europe. Truly, so that you may better perceive the location of all these said parts as well as the Nomes, it seemed fit in this place, besides an exact chorography <note>The description or mapping of regions</note>, to also establish a particular description of each of the Nomes along with their modern locations, so that the sequence of things both already said and yet to be said may be more clearly revealed.

# CHAPTER III.
## FIRST DISTRIBUTION,
->*Of Lower Egypt into its Nomes.*<-

<margin>From where does the Egyptian Delta get its name?</margin>
The lower part of Egypt, which is enclosed by the two rivers, the Agathodaemon and the Bubastic, and the shore of the sea, is called the *Delta* by almost all geographers, from the shape of the letter which it expresses. Furthermore, that entire space of land which is contained by the Bubastic and Busiritic branches is called the *Small Delta*; the *Third Delta* is that which is encompassed by the Bubastic and Athribitic branches, concerning which see Ptolemy in this place. I find that this part of Egypt was called *Phium* by the ancients. Moreover, in the Coptic language it is *Phayum* <note>Coptic: فيوم</note>, which according to our Nomenclator <note>A reference to Kircher's own Coptic dictionary/thesaurus</note> is nothing other than the *sea*; from which I suspect this part was called the sea either because at the time of the Nile’s inundation it resembled a sea, or because they believed, by an ancient tradition, that this whole part was once covered by the sea and grew out of the silt of the Nile, as Strabo teaches. The Arabs certainly seem to support this, since <margin>What is Elphium?</margin> they call *Elphium* <note>Arabic: الفيوم; *Al-Fayyum*</note>, that is, the marshy place of Egypt, *Elph phum* <note>Arabic: الف فوم</note>, which you would call <term>chiliostomon</term> <note>Greek: χιλιοστόμον; "thousand-mouthed"</note>, or *thousand mouths*, because in that same place the Nile is distributed into various mouths. Although I find another reason for the etymology assigned, and one more favoring our purpose, in the Arabic historian Gelaldinus <note>Refers to Jalal ad-Din al-Suyuti, a famous medieval Egyptian scholar</note>, in Book 1 of <margin>Gelaldinus, Book 1, on the Kings of Egypt.</margin> *The Kings of Egypt*, where he relates that *Elphium*, which he nevertheless places not in the *Delta* but in the *Saide* <note>Upper Egypt</note>, was founded by Joseph <note>The biblical patriarch Joseph, often associated in Islamic tradition with the engineering of the Fayum</note>, and this name was given to it for the reason which he describes in these words from Ben Abed Hakem: *In this same [place], he says...*

### TREATISE I. CHOROGRAPHY OF EGYPT. CHAPTER III.

...at that time the stagnant water of Egypt was led out into streams, as Hisham ibn Ishaq <note>Hisham ibn Ishaq was an early Islamic-era historian often cited in accounts of Egyptian history.</note> relates.

<note>original Arabic: في ذلك الزمان استنبطت الفيوم وكان سبب كاما حدثنا هشام ابن اسحق</note>
In that time, the Faiyum was drained and developed; the reason for this was as Hisham ibn Ishaq related to us:

He then follows the text with these words, which I append here in English <note>original: "latina", Latin</note> for the sake of brevity: When Joseph ruled over Egypt and had magnified the house and dwellings of Pharaoh, and was now reaching a hundred years of age, the counselors of Pharaoh said: "Behold, Joseph is worn out by old age, and no longer flourishes in wisdom or judgment; therefore, increase the yoke upon his people, and employ them usefully," and they urged the King for two years. The King finally replied: "Come, let us see if he can be of counsel to us in completing El-Faiyum <note>original: "Elphiu"</note>."
<margin>Joseph’s efforts in drying El-Faiyum.</margin>

<note>original Arabic: وكانت الفيوم يومئذ تدعى الجب انما كانت لمصالح ما الصعيد وفصولة واجتمع رايهم على ان تكون هي المحنة التي يمتحنون بها يوسف وقالوا لفرعون هل يوسف ان يصرف لنا ما الجونة عنها وتخرجه منها وتؤديه بلدا الى بلدك وخراجا الى خراجك</note>
And Faiyum at that time was called "the Pit" [Al-Ghubb], as it was used for the needs of Upper Egypt and its seasons. Their consensus was that this should be the trial with which they would test Joseph. They said to Pharaoh: "Can Joseph divert for us the water from this hollow, remove it from there, and turn it into a land for your kingdom and a tax for your treasury?"

<margin>El-Faiyum was formerly called Al-Gubuh, that is, the stagnant ditch.</margin>
Now, at that time El-Faiyum was called Al-Gubuh, that is, a ditch or pond, because the entire region of El-Said <note>The Arabic term for Upper Egypt.</note> was watery, that is, filled with stagnant waters. He gathered his elders to explore their counsel and mind; after considering the proposed task, they said: "Let Joseph be sent to divert the water of Al-Gubuh; and once it is drawn off, let him add the region to your territory, and its revenues to your revenues." And the King called Joseph, saying: "We know this place is abundant and suitable for buildings and cultivating fields."

<note>original Arabic: واوحي الى يوسف ان يحفر ثلاث خليجا من اعلى الصعيد موضع كدا وخليجا شرقيا من موضع كدا وخليجا غربيا من موضع كدا الى موضع كدا ووضع يوسف العامل فحفر خليجا الذي انتهى من اعلى اشمون الى الارض وحفر خليج الفيوم وهو الخليج الشرقي وحفر خليجا بغربي يقال لها قنهوت من قرب الغدوم وهو الخليج الغربي فخرج ماء من الخليج الشرقي وهب في النهو وخرج من الخليج الغربي وصب في فنهو فنهت الى العرب فلم يبق في الهودة ما ثم ادخلها الفعلة وقطع تها كان فيها من الغصب والطرفا واخرجه منها وكان ذلك ابتدأ جري النيل وقد صارت الجودة رقية برية وارتفع ما النيل ودخل في رأس المنهى وجري حتي انتهى الى الاهون فعطفه الى الفيوم ودخل خليجها وساقها لجة من النيل واخرج اليها الملك ووزراءه وكان قد بعين يوما فلما نظر الى الملك قال لوزراءه هذا عمل الفيوم وسميت الفيوم واقامت تزرع كاما هو ايط مصر</note>

<margin>The first diversion of the stagnant waters of the Nile back into the Nile performed by Joseph.</margin>
And it was revealed to Joseph that he should dig three ditches for the leading of rivers: the first from the upper part of El-Said, from this place; and the eastern river from this place; and the western river from this place. And Joseph began the work, and dug the river stretching from upper Ashmun <note>An ancient city in Middle Egypt, also known as Hermopolis Magna.</note> as far as Al-Lahun <note>original: "Alhalun"</note>, and he dug the river of El-Faiyum, and this is the eastern river. And the river prevailed near the town called Qanhant <note>original: "Kanhemt"</note> among the towns of El-Faiyum, and this is the western river. And its water went out from the eastern river and flowed into it, and coming out from the western river, it flowed spread out into the fields of Qanhant towards the west, and no water remained in the plain. Then he brought in laborers, and having removed from the soil whatever was reedy and marshy there, he made the flow of the remaining water free. And this was the beginning of the flow of the Nile; and the plain turned out dry and pure, and the waters of the Nile were raised; and they entered the beginning of the channel and flowed until they came to Al-Lahun, and from there they flowed back into El-Faiyum, and entered its river and its streams, and it became a part of the Nile.
