### CHAPTER III. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

...and he led the King and his counselors out to see the work he had performed; the entire project was completed in 70 days. When the King had seen it, he said to his counselors: *“Behold, this entire thing is not the work of seventy, but of* <note>original Arabic: الف يوم</note> *Elphium—that is, a thousand days.”* Thus, the place of this province is called *Elphium* <note>original Arabic: الفيوم</note> to this day, meaning "of a thousand days," which in its abundance of crops has matched the other provinces of Egypt. So far the account goes. Certainly, that this place was rendered fit for human habitation by Joseph is clearly taught not only by Jalal al-Din <note>Kircher refers to the polymath scholar al-Suyuti</note>, Salamas, and other Arabic authors, but also by Abulfeda <note>Abu al-Fida (1273–1331), a renowned Syrian geographer and historian</note> in his *Geography* with these words:

<margin>Abulfeda the Geographer</margin>
<note>original Arabic: الفيوم كوره في ديار مصر عن الفسطاط بين الغرب والجنوب وهي في وهده وقد سيق اليها نهر من رشح النيل متصوب الى كشف الطريق ومدينة الفيوم قادرة ولاية وبها حمامات واسواق ومدارس شافعية ومالكية وهي راكبة على نهر يوسف من جانبية النهر تخترق مدينة الفيوم المذكورة والفيوم بساتين كثيرة وهي عن مصر على نحو مسيرة ثلاثة ايام وبين الفسطاط والفيوم ثمانية واربعين ميلا</note>

<margin>Fustat, that is, Cairo.</margin>
*The region of Elphium in Egypt is situated between the west and south of Fustat <note>Old Cairo</note> in a valley, and a river has been diverted to it from the overflow of the Nile, created by Joseph the Just; and the city of Elphium is the seat of the principality, or prefecture, equipped with baths, marketplaces, and the colleges of the Shafi'ites and Malikites <note>These are two of the four major legal schools in Sunni Islam</note>; it is situated above the River Joseph, by which the aforementioned city of Elphium is divided on its southern side; furthermore, Elphium has many gardens, and it is nearly a three-day journey from Cairo <note>original: "Meſra", likely referring to Misr/Cairo</note>, and between Fustat and Elphium it is forty-eight miles.*
And in another place where he describes the city of <note>original Arabic: بهنسا</note> Behansa, he says:

<note>original Arabic: ومدينة البهنسا راكبة على بحر يوسف وهو الفيوم وجميع ما بين بحر يوسف والنيل من ارض البهنسا وغيرها شربه من بحر يوسف ومابين بحر يوسف والنيل من البهنسا يشرب من فرع من النهر</note>

*And the city of Behansa is situated above the Sea of Joseph (for so the Egyptians call their rivers) and it is Elphium; and all those who are between the Sea of Joseph and the mountain from the land of Behansa drink from that River Joseph, and what is between the Sea of Joseph and the Nile drink from a branch of the Nile.* Therefore, it is not without reason that this tract has retained the name "Sea of Joseph" even unto this day. For it is probable that Joseph, being endowed not only with the interpretation of dreams but also with a certain divinely implanted wisdom, conferred the greatest benefits upon all of Egypt; among these, the restoration of Elphium to better fertility was the greatest. Wherefore he was deservedly adorned by the Kings of Egypt with so many and such great titles of honor and prerogatives of dignity.

<margin>The Sea of Joseph.</margin>
Furthermore, Benjamin mentions this Elphium in his *Itinerary* <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler</note>, and relates that the greatest monuments were left there by the Hebrews under Joseph in Egypt, in these words:

<note>original Hebrew: מן חלואן עד קיץ אשר היא ראש הראשית מצרים ג' ימות עד פיום דרך ח' ימות ונקראת פיתום פיחון וניראו בה עד היום זכרונות רבות ובנינות רבות גדולם מבני יוסף מזכרות</note>

*From Helwan as far as Qus, which is the head of the beginning of Egypt, it is a journey of three days, and from there to Faiyum it is a journey of eight days; and it is called Pithom and Pishon <note>Biblical names associated by the author with this location</note>, and there are seen in it to this day many memorials and many great buildings from the constructions of Joseph as remembrances.*

### SYNTAGMA I. CHOROGRAPHY OF EGYPT. CHAPTER III.

From here <note>Referring to the distance from Cairo/Fustat mentioned on the previous page</note> is **Phium**, a journey of five days; this city was formerly called **Pithon**, and even to this day, many monuments and massive buildings are seen there, left to posterity by **Joseph**—may his memory be blessed. <margin>From where the city of Pithon was named</margin> It was called **Pithon** after a serpent of immense size which, born from the putrefaction of stagnant waters and Nile mud, brought great slaughter to men and cattle, until it was slain by the Egyptian Hercules, as the mythologists would have it. <margin>When Lower Egypt began to be inhabited.</margin> Therefore, Elphium—or as I should say in Coptic, **ΦΙΟΜ** <note>original Coptic: ΦΙΟΜ, meaning "the sea" or "the lake"</note>—was once covered by the sea or marshes, but finally, through many days of labor in the time of Joseph, it began to be inhabited. At that time, most of Lower Egypt was either entirely or for the most part covered and made foul by the spreading of marshes and stagnant waters, until these waters were diverted into various trenches. Thus the land, finally liberated from the long-standing tyranny of the waters, could serve the use of men and living creatures. From this, it seems, they were led to drain the remaining pools of stagnant water below Elphium by a similar skill of diversion, and so they finally made the entire land habitable and suited to human needs. When the Kings, in the course of time, found the land flourishing with a wonderful fertility of men and cattle, and fruitful through the continuous diversion of the rivers, they divided it into various Prefectures or Courts to settle disputes and contentions. Because of the admirable abundance and plenty of all things, they called it a gift of the immortal Gods, as Diodorus says. <margin>Egypt called the gift of God.</margin> In this, they followed the Copts, who named it **The Gift of Mercury** <note>original Coptic-script phrase: ΠΕΕΠΤΕΕΦ ΕΡΕΠΠΗΒΙC</note> for the same reason. This was inspired by the Ibises that frequently lived there to devour serpents and other reptiles; through the position of their bodies and legs, and their beaks inserted crosswise, they expressed this **monogram A** composed of **A** and **Δ** <note>Alpha and Delta</note>. This provided a sign to be read by the inhabitants (who were otherwise very prone to every kind of superstition) as to whose gift this land was; for nothing else was expressed by this symbol than **Hermanubis, the Good Spirit** <note>original Greek: ΑΓΑΘΟΔΑΙΜΩΝOC ΕΡΜΑΝΗΒΙC (Agathodaimonos Hermanubis)</note>. ### CHAPTER III. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>Egypt as a temple of the universe.</margin>
Among the Egyptians, a great variety of sacred ceremonies flourished in the worship of the gods; so great was the fervor of <term>idol-madness</term> <note>original Greek: εἰδωλομανία (eidōlomania)</note> that there was scarcely a place that did not establish its own particular deity to whom they paid honor. Consequently, it often happened that a deity worshipped by one group was loathed by another. This great diversity of gods produced no small amount of religious discord. To remove these divisions among the people regarding the cult of the gods, the priests—acting under the authority of the High Priests of **Sesostris** <note>A legendary Pharaoh, often identified with Ramses II or Senusret III, credited by ancient Greeks with many administrative reforms</note>—followed the example of the most ancient gods who distributed the lots of the world among themselves (about which we shall speak shortly). They shrewdly divided all of Egypt into thirty **Nomes** <note>From the Greek 'nomos' (νόμος), meaning a district or administrative province</note>, assigning to each Nome its own deity. They did this so that what they had learned through tradition regarding the actions of the primeval gods in the entire universe might be represented concisely in Egypt, as if in a certain sanctuary or "Pantheon" of the whole world. And lest a monstrous face of religion appear from such a disparity of worship, <margin>Temples in the Thebaid and Heliopolis.</margin> they built certain most sumptuous shrines in the metropolitan cities of all Egypt—namely, **Thebes** and **Heliopolis**. In these two "Pantheons," as it were, whatever was encompassed by the wandering worship of all Egypt would again be celebrated by a united multitude of different nations, arranged in an analogous order parallel to the temple of the universe and in a condensed form of worship. This was truly a clever invention, and wonderfully suited to reconciling different religions under a single cult. Strabo, an eyewitness <note>original Greek: αὐτόπτης (autoptes)</note>, mentions these types of shrines; for thus he says in Book 17, where he discusses the Labyrinth:

> "There is," he says, <note>original: ἔστι δὲ τῷ κήτῳ...; Kircher quotes the Greek text of Strabo's Geography before providing the Latin translation</note> "at the first entrance of the canal, for one proceeding about thirty or forty stades, a certain plain in the shape of a table, containing a village and a royal palace made of many palaces, as many as there were formerly prefectures. For there are just as many courtyards surrounded by columns, all continuous with one another in a single row, and against a single wall, having the courtyards situated before them like a small enclosure." And a little later: "At the end of this building, which occupies more than a stade, is the tomb, a certain quadrangular pyramid, each side of which is nearly four hundred feet long and of equal height. <margin>The marvelous construction of the Tomb of Imandes.</margin> The name of the person buried there is **Imandes** <note>Likely a corruption of Osymandyas, another name for Ramses II</note> (more truly **Simandes**); they say that so many courtyards were built there because it was the custom for all the Nomes to gather there. A banquet was held by the sacred men and women for the sake of offering sacrifices to God and for the administration of justice regarding the greatest matters; moreover, each prefecture proceeded into the courtyard designated for it."

Almost the same things are told by <margin>Abenephius.</margin> <term>Abenephius</term> <note>An Arabic author frequently cited by Kircher, believed to be an authority on Egyptian history and magic</note> concerning <term>Ain Shems</term> <note>original Arabic: عين شمس (ʿAyn Šams), meaning "Eye of the Sun," the Arabic name for Heliopolis</note>, that is, Heliopolis; his words are:

-> And there is a structure in Ain Shems consisting of many houses and halls, as many as there are in all Egypt, and each one of them has talismans and an idol which they worshipped for the safety of the land in which that district was located. ❁ <-

# SYNTAGMA I. CHOROGRAPHY OF EGYPT. 13 CAP. III.

After also determining the number of prefectures, he <note>Referring to the author Abenephius mentioned later</note> says:

<note>original Arabic: ولا يوافقك كان غلغين على حساب غلغين الايام وحده من شهور كنت عشر</note>
And there were thirty prefectures according to the number of the days of one month out of the twelve. For as we shall see in the Astronomy of the Egyptians, each individual day of any month was dedicated to one of the thirty Deities; each tribe or court, which had been assigned that Deity for its worship, celebrated that day with great care. **Plato** teaches in his **Critias** that the Egyptians derived this custom from the earliest times, as we shall see shortly. But with these things having been thus introduced, let us now see the tripartite distribution of all Egypt into its <term>Nomes</term> <note>From the Greek 'nomos' (νόμος), an administrative district</note> made first by **Sesostris**, and then by the Ptolemies, who greatly increased them. And since nothing is read about them besides their names and what was done in them: and since there is a great contradiction among authors regarding the <term>etymologies</term> <note>The study of the origins of words</note> of such names, I certainly thought it right that the rule of <note>original Greek: ὀρθότητος καὶ ἐτυμολογίας (orthotētos kai etymologias)</note> **correctness and etymologies** should be taken from foreign languages, and those older than Greek—as Plato correctly advises in his *Critias* and *Cratylus*. While I attempt to restore this ancient language of the Egyptians according to my small measure, I have indeed found many things which, as far as I know, have been discovered by none of the philologists until now; especially those things which pertain to the etymologies of the Gods, animals, plants, stones, cities, instruments, and similar things, all of which are brought to light with the help of our *Egyptian Nomenclator*. From this, I trust I shall find no small favor among those who apply themselves to criticism and philology, while I reveal in the course of this work, with God as my guide, many things that have remained hidden from critics until now. But to return to the point.

<margin>The Division of Egypt into Nomes.</margin>
We read, therefore, that in the time of Sesostris, all Egypt was divided into three parts: Lower, Middle, and Upper. Each of these was again divided into ten courts or prefectures, according to the testimony of Abenephius; in which division they seem to have looked back to that primeval allotment of the Gods over the entire world, which Plato describes in the *Critias* in these words:

<margin>Plato.</margin>
> <note>original Greek: Σόλων ἐπινοῶν εἰς τὴν αὑτῶ ποίησιν... κατενείμαντο γῆν πᾶσαν.</note>
> Solon, intending to use the story for his own poetry, investigated the power of the names and found that those first Egyptians who had written them down had translated them into their own language. And he himself, taking up the meaning of each name in turn, brought them into our own tongue and wrote them down. These writings were with my grandfather and are now with me, having been studied by me since I was a boy. Therefore, if you now hear names such as are found among us, let there be no wonder. For you have the cause of them: this is a long beginning of a speech, just as in those things concerning the lot of the Gods, how they distributed the whole earth among themselves.

But before I relate this, you must be warned not to be surprised if you now hear many foreign names in Greek; for this happened because Solon, when he thought to include them in his poems, searched into the very power of the names, and found that those first Egyptian writers of these matters had translated those names into their own language. Wherefore he himself, again receiving the sense of each name, converted it into our own voice. *And these writings were at my grandfather’s house, and are now at mine, having been pondered by me long ago as a boy. If therefore you hear such names now as are common among us, do not be surprised; for you understand the cause of this matter, but it would require a long speech if I were to relate from the beginning what I said before about the allotment of the Gods—how they distributed the entire earth among themselves, partly into larger portions and partly into narrower ones, and established temples and sacred rites for themselves.*

# THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>CHAPTER III.</margin> Regarding the allotment of the Gods, the previously cited Plato reports the following a little earlier: <note>original Greek: θεοὶ γὰρ ἅπαξ γῆν πᾶσαν... (from Plato’s *Critias* 109b). Kircher provides this text in both Greek and Latin.</note>

<margin>Plato.</margin> *Once the gods allotted the whole circle of the earth among themselves, distributed into individual regions; nor did strife cause this partition. For it would be far from reasonable to suggest that the gods were ignorant of what was appropriate for each of them, or that, knowing what better suited others, they would attempt to seize the rights of another for themselves. Instead, receiving their own through the lots of justice and law according to their wishes, and caring for their friends, they arranged the individual regions for habitation. They nourished us as their own flocks, possessions, and herds—excepting this: they did not wish to compel bodies with bodies, in the manner that shepherds drive cattle and beasts with blows. Rather, as if steering an agile ship from the stern, they guided the whole human race according to their own will, using persuasion as a rudder to reach the soul. Thus Plato writes.*

Therefore, the Egyptians believed that the gods once distributed the entire circle of the earth individually by lot for the preservation of the human race, so that each of the gods would accept that region and province which was more conformed to his own nature, and toward which he would be drawn—as if toward a <term>sympathy</term> <note>original Greek: συμπαθείαν (sympatheian); the Hermetic and Neoplatonic concept that certain earthly things have a natural, mystical connection to specific divine or celestial powers</note>—by the weight of a natural inclination, and which he would undertake to defend from every hostile and enemy force.

Following the logic of this allotment, the ancient priests of Egypt—and especially the High Priests of King Sesostris <note>A legendary Pharaoh, often a composite of several historical rulers like Senusret I or III and Ramses II</note> (relying on his authority)—distributed all of Egypt according to this principle. As indicated above, what occurred in the universe by the ancients was represented in Egypt through a unified cult, as if in a mystic <term>Pantheon</term> <note>A temple or place dedicated to all the gods</note> of the whole world and the most fertile mother of the Gods. 

However, since we shall discuss these and similar matters in various places throughout this *Oedipus*, we do not wish to linger longer here. Therefore, let us return to the actual distribution of Egypt into its prefectures, as if to the courts of the gods. In this, we intend to ensure that the <term>etymologies</term> <note>The origins and meanings of names</note> of names, which until now have been obscure and unknown, may be restored to their genuine meaning from various records of the Egyptian language, like planks salvaged from a shipwreck. Let us therefore begin the work.

# NOME I. RACOTIS

## THAT IS

->The Alexandrian Prefecture; in Coptic, <gloss>The district of Rakoti</gloss> <note>original Coptic: ⲡⲓⲧⲁϣ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉ ⲣⲁⲕⲟϯ</note><-

Deriving from the earliest sources the first distribution of the Nomes or prefectures—established by <term>Sesofiris</term> <note>Commonly known as Sesostris, a legendary king of ancient Egypt often credited with massive conquests and administrative reforms.</note> (commonly called Sesostris) and the ancient Kings—we begin with Racotis. Just as this area was the first part of this Nile Delta to emerge after the drying of the stagnant waters in these regions and their diversion into various reservoirs, such as Lake Moeris and the Mediterranean Sea, so too it has deservedly obtained the first place among the Nomes.

<margin>What is Racotis?</margin>
Racotis, therefore, was that part of Lower Egypt which the Greeks later called <note>original Greek: Ἀλεξανδρείαν</note> Alexandria after its founder, Alexander the Great. Pliny (Book 5, Chapter 10), Stephanus in his work <note>original Greek: περὶ τῶν πόλεων</note> *On Cities* under the entry "Rakotis," Pausanias in his *Description of Greece*, and finally our own *Egyptian Nomenclator* <note>Kircher's own dictionary of Coptic and Egyptian terms.</note> in the chapter on the names of cities, all testify that it was once called <note>original Coptic: ⲣⲁⲕⲟϯ</note> Rakoti; you may consult them. I also read in the works of <term>Cedrenus</term> <note>An 11th-century Byzantine historian.</note> that it was called <note>original Coptic: ⲣⲁⲕⲁϣϯ</note> Rakashti, though this is likely incorrect or corrupt; no one should doubt that this error arose from a misunderstanding of the name Racota. The Egyptians record that this Racota was founded by a certain woman, a Queen of Egypt named <term>Dalucha</term>, after the drowning of the Pharaoh who persecuted the Israelites in the Red Sea. This is related not only by the historians <term>Abenhaid</term> and <term>Aben Hakem</term>, but also by <term>Salamas</term> in his book titled *The Garden of the World's Wonders*. I subjoin his words:
<margin>By whom and when Racotis was founded. Abenhaid, Aben Hakem.</margin>

> <note>original Arabic: ولما فرق الله فرعون وقومه ضعف امر القبط فملکوا عليهم امراه تسمي دلوکا وبنت رقوط هي الاسکندريه</note> 
> "And when God had drowned Pharaoh and his people, the power of the Copts was weakened; so they appointed a woman over them as Queen named Daluka, and she built Raqut, which is Alexandria."

When God had submerged Pharaoh along with his army, the Kingdom of Egypt remained very weak; for which reason they established a woman as Queen, Daluka by name, who built Racuth, which is Alexandria. It is called <note>original Coptic: ⲣⲁⲕⲟϯ</note> Rakoti from the "cuttings" or "fissures," because the ancient Kings, with incredible labor, made this place suitable for human habitation through various cuttings and diversions of the waters and swamps, as will be narrated more fully in the *Chronology of the Kings of Egypt*.

<margin>The figure and meaning of the Ibis.</margin>
<image-desc>A framed woodcut illustration of an Ibis bird standing on a base. Above the bird are the Greek letters A (Alpha) and Δ (Delta). The bird's long beak curves down to its feet, forming the shape of a monogrammatic "A". On the base where the bird stands is the Greek word ΕΡΜΑΝΕΒΙΣ (Hermanubis).</image-desc>
Furthermore, we read that <term>Mercury</term> <note>The Egyptian god Thoth, whom the Greeks identified with Hermes/Mercury.</note> was specifically worshipped in this prefecture. His image was in the form of an Ibis, with its legs spread apart and its beak inserted transversely between them to form this monogram <note>original Greek: A</note> "Alpha." The rest of the body exhibited the shape of a heart. By the first part, they signified Mercury as the <note>original Greek: Ἀγαθοδαίμονα</note> "Agathodaemon" or Good Spirit; by the second, they signified the wise heart of Mercury, through which—according to Diodorus—he handed down various sciences to the world. Indeed, Ptolemy (following Strabo), Marius Niger, and others whom we cite in the following pages, teach that because of this cult, the city itself and the branch of the Nile (which we previously called the <note>original Greek: Ἀγαθοδαίμονα</note> "Good Spirit") near the canal of the River Tabius, were later called <term>Hermopolis</term> <note>Meaning "City of Hermes."</note>.

# NOME II. PHTENUTI,
## THAT IS
### The Prefecture of Phtenuti; in Coptic, <gloss>The district of Phtenechi</gloss> <note>original Coptic: ⲡⲓⲧⲁϣ ⲫⲑⲉⲛⲉϯ</note> ☩

I find that the second prefecture of the Nile Delta was <term>Phtenuti</term>, or Phtenathi. In Coptic, this is pronounced <gloss>The district of the God of Gods</gloss> <note>original Coptic: ⲡⲓⲧⲁϣ ⲙ̀ⲫⲛⲟⲩϯ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉ ⲫϯ</note>. It was neighboring and contiguous with the prefecture of Racotis. According to the *Coptic Nomenclator*, its name is derived from <term>Ph-ti</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲫϯ</note>, meaning *God*, and <term>Nouti</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲟⲩϯ</note> in the plural, which means *Gods* (from the singular *nouti*, "God"). Ptolemy also mentions this Nome in this passage: <note>original Greek: Μεταξὺ τοῦ ποταμοῦ μεγάλου καὶ φαρμουθιακοῦ πελάς ταῦτα, φθένετου νόμος· καὶ μητρόπολις Βουτῶς</note> "Between the great river and the Pharmuthiac [branch], near these lies the Phtenutu Nome and its capital, Butos." It is called Phtenechi—that is, the prefecture of the God of Gods—because sacred rites were performed there for <term>Serapis</term>. According to Diodorus, Apuleius, and Ammianus Marcellinus, the Egyptians called Serapis the greatest of the gods. They worshipped him in his own temple in the form of a bull. That this is so is amply proven by certain <term>bull-shaped</term> <note>original Greek: ταυρόμορφα</note> idols of the figure you see on the side. These are frequently found in the ruins of Rasfith and Deruthi (that is, Canopus and Butos), which once belonged to this prefecture, confirming that Serapis was worshipped here. In the Museum of the most illustrious <term>Pietro della Valle</term> <note>A famous Italian traveler and scholar who brought many Egyptian artifacts to Europe.</note>, there is such an idol made of brick, the image of which we provide here.

Rosetta was once Canopus.
Strabo, book 16.
</margin>
*Rossetta* is a region on the western side of the Nile formerly called *Canub*, and it is distant from Alexandria by a "Margala," which means the space of a one-day journey; although Strabo prescribes the distance from Alexandria as <note>original Greek: ἐν εἴκοσι καὶ ἑκατὸν σταδίοις ἀπ᾽ Ἀλεξανδρείας αὐτῇ ἐστιν</note> 120 stadia <note>Approximately 13.5 miles or 22 kilometers.</note> for those traveling by land. Today they call Butos <margin>Butos.</margin> <term>Deruthi</term>. Strabo teaches us that in both places, idols of Serapis and Latona (or the horned Io) were worshipped: <margin>Strabo.</margin> "Canopus," he says, "is named after Canopus, the pilot of Menelaus who died there. It possesses a temple of Serapis, honored with great holiness and providing healings, so that even the most distinguished men believe in it and sleep there <note>This refers to the practice of 'incubation,' where the sick slept in temples hoping for a divine dream or a cure.</note> on behalf of themselves or others." Canopus is named after Canopus, the pilot of Menelaus who died there...

# TREATISE I. CHOROGRAPHY OF EGYPT. CHAPTER III.

<margin>Who was Canopus?</margin>
...had died; it possesses a temple of Serapis that is so religiously venerated that even the most noble men place their faith in it, seeking prophetic dreams there for themselves or for others. There are those who compile records of the healings performed there, and others who document the powers of the oracles delivered at that place. And a little later, he speaks of <margin>Butos.</margin> Butos in this way: <term>Near Butos lies Hermopolis, situated on an island. In Butos, however, is the oracle of Latona.</term> <note>original Greek: παρὰ δὲ τὴν Βοῦτον ἐν Ἑρμόπολις ἐν νήσῳ κεῖσθαι. ἐν δὲ τῇ Βοῦτῳ Λατοῦς ἐστὶ μαντεῖον.</note> That Latona is indeed conflated with Io at the Bosporus is evident from Phornutus; furthermore, the very etymology of Butos is said to be derived from the "horned worship" <note>referring to the cow-horns of Io/Isis</note>, according to Stephanus in his work *On Cities* <note>original Greek: περὶ τῆς πόλεων</note> under the entry <term>Butos</term> <note>original Greek: Βοῦτος</note>. This corresponds in every respect to the Coptic word; for <term>Boutos</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲃⲟⲩⲧⲟⲥ</note> in the Coptic language signifies nothing other than "the gift of the Cow." Herodotus, in his book *Thalia*, and other mythologists whom you may consult, declare that Latona—or at least the daughter of the "horned" Phoroneus—was of this nature.

### NOME III. PHTEMPHUTI

->THAT IS,<-

->The Prefecture of Phtemphuti; in Coptic, <term>the district of Phenenouti</term><- <note>original Coptic: ⲡⲓⲧⲁϣ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉ ⲫⲉⲛⲉⲛⲟⲩϯ</note>

<margin>What is Phtemphuti?</margin>
The third prefecture of the ancient Egyptians was <term>Phenenouti</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲫⲉⲛⲉⲛⲟⲩϯ</note>, or Thpnemnuti (corrupted to Phtemphuti). This means "The Heaven of the Gods," from the Coptic word <term>Phe</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲫⲉ</note>, meaning *Heaven*, where <term>ne</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲉ</note> is the mark of the genitive [of], and <term>Nouti</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲛⲟⲩϯ</note> is the plural form meaning *Gods*. The capital of this district was <term>Tane Taua</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲧⲁⲛⲉ ⲧⲁⲩⲁ</note>, which in Coptic is the same as "Temple." This prefecture seems to have been called the "Heaven of the Gods" because it flourished between two rivers, the Pharmuthiac and the Athribitic; it easily surpassed all other Nomes in both fertility and pleasantness. It also encompassed Xois and Pachnamunis, which later acquired the names of separate Nomes. Suidas is the authority that the <margin>The form and worship of Canopus.</margin> worship of Canopus flourished in this prefecture, especially at Xois. That idol was shaped like a jar <note>Latin: dolium</note>, full of holes, as appears here to the side. For the cause and origin of this, see what we have written in our *Coptic Prodromus* and in the aforementioned Suidas under the entry "Canopus"; we also treat the Canopic jars extensively below.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a Canopic idol or jar. The figure has a human head wearing a traditional Egyptian headdress and a large, rounded body decorated with patterns resembling rows of scales or feathers. It stands on a rectangular base.</image-desc>

<margin>The city of Xois.</margin>
Xois was the capital in which Canopus was worshipped, who was therefore called "the Xoite." In Coptic it is called <term>Xois</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲝⲟⲓⲥ</note>, and by later Egyptians <term>Schiagha</term> <note>original Coptic: ϣⲓⲁⲅϩⲁ</note>, in which, according to the Geographer Dubianus, great vestiges of antiquity are still found.

<margin>Etymology of Phtemphuti</margin>
Furthermore, Arabic historians affirm another reason for this etymology of Phtemphuti. They say that when Joseph <note>The biblical patriarch Joseph, often associated with Egyptian engineering</note> had drained the Elphium <note>Likely the Fayum</note> and elevated whatever the Delta contains into dry land by depressing the water into channels, he rendered the region not only fertile but also marvelously pleasant. It is said that Pharaoh, called to behold Joseph’s work, broke out into these words: <term>Is this not a portion of the kingdom of the heavens?</term> <note>original Arabic: هذا من ملكوت السموات</note> From this comes the name Schagha...

# CHAPTER III. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

...where these things are said to have occurred, is called the "Kingdom of Heaven" to this day, as recorded by the Arab Gelaldinus <note>Kircher refers to the historian Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti</note> in his history of the *Kings of Egypt*; but I wished to add this here, so that nothing seems lacking for the illustration of antiquity; meanwhile, everyone remains free to think as they wish about these matters.

### NOME IV. MENDESIAN,
#### THAT IS
#### The Mendesian Prefecture; in Coptic, **the district of Mendes** <note>original Coptic: ⲡⲓⲧⲁϣ ⲙⲉⲛⲇⲏⲥ</note>

**T**he fourth prefecture of the ancient Egyptians was Mendes, in Coptic **banes** <note>original Coptic: ⲃⲁⲛⲉⲥ</note>, a word which signifies "Goat." The prefecture was so named either from the multitude of goats usually pastured in this district, or from the worship of the Goat or Pan, who Strabo teaches was worshipped in this Nome with these words: <note>original Greek: Ἐστὶ δὲ καὶ Ἑρμοῦ πόλις καὶ λυκόπολις, καὶ Μένδης...</note> *There is also Hermopolis, and Lycopolis, and Mendes; there they honor Pan, and among animals the goat, and as Pindar says <unclear>they sacrificed hecatombs to goats</unclear>:*
> Mendes, by the farthest cliff of the sea,
> At the edge of the Nile, where the leaping goats
> Mingle with women.

Furthermore, Mendes is where Pan is worshipped, as well as the goat as a sacred animal; and as Pindar says, in this place goats mingle with women:
> Mendes, near the precipice by the sea,
> At the furthest branch of the Nile, where the lustful
> Husband of the she-goat dares to enter a human woman.

Eusebius, in his *Preparation for the Gospel*, reproaches the Heathens because the head of a goat was customarily adored in this prefecture. This is supported by Clement in the 5th book of his *Miscellanies*; as well as Herodotus and Plutarch—the former in his book *Thalia*, the latter in his book *On Osiris and Isis*. Clear evidence of this cult exists on the Bembine Table <note>The Bembine Table, or Mensa Isiaca, is a famous bronze tablet depicting Egyptian religious scenes, which Kircher studied extensively</note>, where a goat's head is depicted on the border above an altar, in the figure that follows.

<margin>Figure of Mendes.</margin>
<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicts the head of a horned goat facing left, resting on a stone pedestal or altar block inscribed with the name "MENDES".</image-desc>

All of this is confirmed by Suidas in these words: <note>original Greek: Μενδέσιος τόπος καλεῖται τὸν παῖδα Αἰγύπτιοι...</note> *The Egyptians call the place Mendes after the child [Horus/Pan], as most fertile, for whom they also call the goat in their own dialect, and they honor him as being dedicated to the generative power. They also honor him so much that they do not eat goats, for the animal is lecherous; there is also a temple of the Egyptians at Mendes, and in it an image with goat-like legs and an erect phallus.* For what this cult was a symbol of will be discussed at length in the "Pantheon of the Hebrews" in the third treatise of this work. The principal city of this Nome is Thmuis—see Herodotus in *Thalia* regarding its etymology—in Coptic **Thmoui** <note>original Coptic: ⲑⲙⲟⲩⲓ</note>, in Arabic **Elmurade** <note>original Arabic: الموردة</note>.

CHOROGRAPHICAL DISSERTATION ON EGYPT 39 CHAP. VII.

# NOME V. ONVPHIS

## THAT IS,

### The Prefecture of Onuphis; in Coptic, *the basket of Onuphion, the serpent* <note>original Coptic: ⲡⲓϯⲃⲓⲣ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲛⲟⲩⲫⲓⲟⲛ ⲡⲓϩⲟϥ</note>

<margin>Balmis the Hebrew in his Dictionary.</margin>
The Prefecture of Onuphis holds the fifth place in the order of the Nomes. In the Coptic language, it is called **Pihof** <note>original: ⲡⲓϩⲟϥ</note> or **Piahof**, which signifies "the serpent." I believe this city to be the same as the Hebrew **Noph** <note>original: נוף</note>, although Memphis is also called by that name. The reason for this can be attributed to the proximity of Memphis to Onuphis, which consequently leads to the confusion of one with the other—just as Pelusium, Sais, and Damietta are often confused for the same reason, as we shall show below. Balmis describes it thus: *Noph is the name of a city in Egypt; in a foreign tongue it is called Noph, or Memphis.* <note>original Hebrew/Latin: נוף שם מדינת מצרים נקרא חית בלעז נוף Noph nomen vrbis in Ægypto barbarè dicta Memphis</note>. It is called **Pihof** <note>original: ⲡⲓϩⲟϥ</note> because they worshipped the asp serpent there, as Pausanias says in his *Description of Corinth*, when speaking of the animal worship common in Boeotia: <unclear>Just as in the Egyptian city of Onuphis, they tend to asps as if they were gods.</unclear> <note>original Greek: Καθάπερ ἐν τῇ πόλει τῇ Αἰγυπτίᾳ Ὀνούφι τὰς ἀσπίδ' ὥστ' ϑεραπεύουσι</unclear>

<margin>The form of Onuphis.</margin>
<image-desc>Woodcut of a cobra serpent rising from an ornate chalice or pedestal. Above the serpent's head is a winged solar disc emblem.</image-desc>

That "Onuphion" is so named from the worship of the serpent, the etymology itself teaches us; no one should doubt that it is derived from *the serpent* <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄφεως</note>. Indeed, our *Nomenclator* interprets **Pinet-hion** <note>original: ⲡⲓⲛⲉⲧϩⲓⲟⲛ</note> as the Basilisk or serpent; Horus <note>Kircher refers to the author Horapollo</note> supports this, asserting that the serpent was called **Uraeus** by the Egyptians. We have shown in the *Prodromus* that this is an error; there we demonstrate it should be read not as "Uraeus," but as **Uphaeus**. Horus says the following: <margin>What is the *Pi-ouraion*?</margin> <unclear>When they wish to represent eternity, they paint a serpent with its tail hidden under the rest of its body. The Egyptians call this "Uraeus," which in Greek is the "Basilisk"; they make it out of gold and place it around the statues of the gods.</unclear> <note>original Greek: Αἰῶνα ἐθέλοντες γράψαι βουλόμενοι ὄφιν ζωγραφοῦσι ἔχοντα τὴν οὐραν ὑπὸ τὸ λοιπὸν σῶμα κρυπτομένην. ὃν καλοῦσι Αἰγύπτιοι οὐραῖον, ὅ ἐστὶ ἑλληνιστὶ βασιλίσκον ὅνπερ χρυσοῦν ποιῆτες Θεοῖς περιτιθέασιν.</unclear> <margin>An error occurring in Horus regarding the name *Pi-ouraion*</margin> Moreover, in another way, to express eternity, they paint a serpent whose tail is coiled and covered by the rest of its body. The Egyptians call this in their own tongue the "Uraeus" (read: **Uphaeus**), while the Greeks call it the "Basilisk," and having cast it in gold, they place it around their gods. I believe the occasion for this veneration <note>original Greek: ἀφιλαργυρίας, literally "lack of greed," though here likely a misuse for "devotion" or "ritual practice"</note> was the multitude of asps or serpents that swarm every year in that district from the rotting slime of the Nile. Since these serpents brought the greatest harm to men and livestock with their lethal bites, it is probable that they worshipped the Asp as a protecting deity <term>Averruncus|a deity who averts calamity or evil</term>. And perhaps the Egyptians also worshipped it after the fashion and example of the Mosaic serpent raised in the desert; we shall say elsewhere how the Egyptians received many things from the Hebrews. We have placed here an image of the idol taken from the **Bembine Tablet** <note>Also known as the Mensa Isiaca, a famous bronze tablet depicting Egyptian-style deities</note>.

<margin>The cause of the worship of Uphaeus.</margin>
<image-desc>Woodcut of a serpent coiled in an S-shape vertically around a staff. At the base of the image is the Greek inscription ΙΕΡΑΚΟΜΟΡΦΟΝ (Hieracomorphon, or "hawk-formed").</image-desc>

CHAPTER III. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

### NOME VI. SAIS,

### THAT IS,

-> The Saitic Prefecture, in Coptic *Pisai* <note>original: ⲡⲓⲥⲁⲓ</note> <-

<margin>
Sais, the Metropolis of Lower Egypt. *Coi* <note>original: ⲥⲁⲓ</note> is the same as a Sheep.
</margin>
The sixth prefecture was Sais, where Strabo teaches that Minerva was worshipped: *And the Saitic city, and Sais the Metropolis; in which region they honor Athena <note>The Greek goddess of wisdom, identified with the Roman Minerva</note>, and in the temple is the tomb of Psammetichus.* From there, he says, is the Sebennytic city. Sais is the metropolis of Lower Egypt; in this place they worship Minerva, especially because the burial place of Psammetichus <note>A famous Pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty</note> is in her temple. Elsewhere he also records that the Saitans worshipped the sheep; certainly the etymology teaches that this is so, since *Sais* in the ancient language is nothing other than a sheep or lamb—in Coptic **Eso** <note>original: ⲉⲥⲱ</note>, and with the article **P-eso** <note>original: ⲡⲉⲥⲱ</note>, as our Egyptian Nomenclator clearly teaches. Moreover, *Sais* and *Esai* are quite close, differing only by a corruption in the letters produced in different ways by different people.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration showing a ram standing in profile, facing left. It is enclosed in a simple rectangular frame.</image-desc>

<margin>
The Sheep dedicated to Minerva. Clement of Alexandria.
</margin>
Furthermore, all Mythologists testify that the sheep was dedicated to Minerva and Pallas. Clement of Alexandria mentions this temple of Pallas in the 4th book of his *Stromata*: 
> In Sais, he says, before the vestibule of the temple of Pallas, symbols of this kind are seen engraved: an Infant, an Old Man, a Hawk, a Fish, and a Hippopotamus,

<margin>
The Idol of Minerva.
</margin>
the interpretation of which symbols may be seen in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, book 3. Regarding the portentous temple of Minerva in Sais which Herodotus recites in *Thalia* <note>The third book of Herodotus's Histories</note>, see what we have discussed above concerning these matters in the Memphite Nome. Moreover, the idol of Minerva was fashioned in exactly that form and figure as Isis, from whom she does not differ; for as Macrobius rightly says, what is Athena (that is, Minerva) to the Greeks, is Isis to the Egyptians. Her figure is placed here at the side. But since we deal with these and similar matters at length in the *Egyptian Mystagogy*, we thought it necessary only to mention them here in passing.

### NOME VII. ATHRIBIS,

### THAT IS,

-> The Athribitic Prefecture, in Coptic *Piatrebe* <note>original: ⲡⲓⲁⲧⲣⲉⲃⲉ</note> <-

<margin>
Strabo.
</margin>
The seventh prefecture is Athribis, which elsewhere they incorrectly call *Aethibis*. According to Ptolemy, it is: *The Nome, and the Metropolis, and the eponymous river; the Athribitic river.* In Coptic it is called **Atrebe** <note>original: ⲁⲧⲣⲉⲃⲉ</note>; the later Arabs call it **Atrib** <note>original Arabic: اتريب</note>. Strabo describes it in these words: *The Nome and Metropolis is Athribis; they honor the Mygale <note>The shrew-mouse</note>.* From where, truly, **Atrebe** takes its origin, or what it properly—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Egyptian Nomes (provinces), concluding the seventh Nome (Athribis) and beginning the eighth (Tanis). The author, Athanasius Kircher, is attempting to reconcile Arabic histories, classical Greek accounts, and Coptic linguistics to identify the sacred symbols of each region.</meta>

SYNTAMGA I. CHOROGRAPHY OF EGYPT. 21 CHAPTER III.

...properly means, I would not have been able to discover even with much sweat, had not the histories or chronicles of the Arabs led me to some knowledge of this etymology. For the Arabs say that Atribis was so named from the founder of the city, Atrib, <margin>From where the city of Atribis was named.</margin> the great-grandson of Mizraim <note>Mizraim is the biblical name for Egypt, the son of Ham</note>; so says Jalal al-Din <note>A 15th-century polymath also known as al-Suyuti</note> in the *History of the Kings of Egypt*, where among the other Kings of Egypt, he also mentions Atribis in these words:

*And when Copt died (so they call Mizraim), his brother Eshman succeeded him, to whom succeeded his brother Atrib, and he is the one who built the city of Atrib.* <margin>What is Atribis?</margin> <note>original: وتوفي قبط فاستخلف اطام اشمن فاستخلف اخوه اتريب وهو الذي بنى مدينة اتريب</note>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration within a square border. It depicts a scarab beetle with large, outstretched feathered wings like those of a bird. The head of the beetle is pointed, resembling a rodent or a shrew, with a small horn-like protrusion.</image-desc>

Furthermore, where others read "shrew-mouse" <note>original: μυγάλην — mygalē</note> (which the Athribites are said to have worshipped), others in the same passage read "mouse-headed beetle" <note>original: κάνθαρον μυοκέφαλον — kantharon muokephalon</note>; thus says Sylburgius <note>Friedrich Sylburg, a German classical scholar</note>, meaning a species of scarab beetle that displays the head of a mouse. It is likely that the Athribites worshipped this, and it is called by Horus <note>Horapollo, the legendary author of a treatise on hieroglyphs</note> "Unicorn and unique in form; let fortune be consecrated to Hermes, just as the Ibis is among birds" <note>original: Μονοκέρως, καὶ ἰδιόμορφος, τῷ Ἑρμῇ δὲ ἀφιερώσθω ἡ τύχη, καθὰ καὶ ὁ Ἶβις τὸ ὄρνεον</note>. It is of a peculiar unicorn form, which they considered to be an animal sacred to Hermes, just as they thought of the Ibis among birds. Certainly, <margin>The Scarab as an image of the Sun.</margin> Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> teaches in his book *On Abstinence from Animal Food* <note>original: περὶ τῆς ἐμψύχων ἀποχῆς</note> that the Egyptians worshipped a scarab of this kind as a living image of the Sun: *The Egyptians worshipped it as a living image of the sun* <note>original: Αἰγύπτιοι δὲ ἐσέφθησαν ὡς εἰκόνα ἡλίου ἔμψυχον</note>. And from this very elegant reading, it is clearly evident that the "shrew-mouse" or *mygalē* is a textual error; for nowhere else is mention made of the worship of a mouse among the Egyptians. For how could the Egyptians have wished to worship an unclean animal, endowed with no memorable gift of quality, and indeed most prone to causing corruption? I do not see it—unless perhaps they did so through propitiatory sacrifices, as happened in the worship of the *Averruncian* gods <note>Deities whose role was to avert calamity or evil</note>. However, since no traces of this are found among the hieroglyphics, I cannot but strongly approve the reading of Sylburgius, who reads "mouse-formed scarab" instead of "shrew-mouse." Regarding this, consult Aldrovandi <note>Ulisse Aldrovandi, a famous Renaissance naturalist</note> in the chapter on scarabs in general. Moreover, while such worship of the Scarab was common to all of Egypt, it was particularly characteristic of the Athribites. But see what we have said about it in the *Prodromus*, and what we shall say more extensively in other places. We have thought it fitting to place here the likeness of this idol, taken from the Bembine Tablet <note>The Tabula Bembina, also known as the Isiac Tablet, a famous bronze plaque depicting Egyptian deities that Kircher studied extensively</note>.

## THAT IS,

I find much dispute among authors regarding this Tanitic prefecture; some confuse it with Pelusium, others with Damietta, and some with Sais. But since this confusion arose from Holy Scripture, which everyone tries to interpret in their own way, it is a wonder...

### CHAPTER III. 22 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS THE ISIAC TEMPLE

...it is not surprising that various opinions have arisen regarding these matters. But so that this controversy may finally be settled, I have thought it necessary to cite the sacred texts here first; so that it may be revealed by what names God designates Tanis, Pelusium, or Sais, and Alexandria. God, therefore, through Ezekiel in chapter 30, threatens Egypt and its principal cities with these following words:

<margin>Ezekiel ch. 30...</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: ואמרת והאבדתי גלולים והשבתי אלולים מנוף ונשיא מארץ מצרים והשמותי את פתרס ונתתי אש בצוען ועשתי שפטים בנא ושפכתי חਮתי על סין ונתתי אש במצרים חול תחול סין ונא תהיה להבקע ונוף צרי יומם בחوري און ופי בסת בחרב יפלו</note>

> *That is: Thus says the Lord: I will destroy the idols, and I will cause the images to cease from Memphis; and there shall no longer be a prince from the land of Egypt, and I will put fear in the land of Egypt. And I will destroy the land of Pathros, and I will set fire in Zoan, and I will execute my judgments in Alexandria. And I will pour out my indignation upon Pelusium, the strength of Egypt, and I will kill the multitude of Alexandria. And I will set fire in Egypt; Pelusium shall suffer like a woman in labor, and Alexandria shall be laid waste, and in Memphis there shall be daily distress. The young men of Heliopolis and Bubastis shall fall by the sword, and they themselves shall be led into captivity.*

<margin>Explanation of the names of the cities of Egypt.</margin>
The sacred text mentions seven cities in this passage. First, **Memphis**, which the Hebrews call נוף *Noph*. Second, פתרס *Phathures* <note>Pathros</note>, which I interpret as Busiris, as we shall see later. Third, **Taphnis** <note>Tahpanhes</note>, which the Hebrews call צואן *Zoan*. Fourth, **Alexandria**, which in Hebrew is called נא *No* <note>Kircher follows a common early modern identification of the biblical "No-Amon" as Alexandria, though modern scholars identify it as Thebes</note>. Fifth, **Sais**, which the text calls סין *Sin*, though interpreters claim it is Pelusium. Sixth, **Heliopolis**, which in Hebrew is called און *Aven* (that is, "iniquity") <note>The Hebrew text uses *Aven* (meaning vanity or trouble) as a derogatory pun on the city's original name, *On*</note>. Seventh, **Bubastis**, which the said Hebrews call by the contemptuous name פי בסת *Pi-Beseth* (that is, "mouth of ignominy") <note>A pun on the Hebrew *bosheth*, meaning shame</note> because of the idolatry practiced in these last two cities above all others. Most of these names are very different among the Septuagint translators <note>The Septuagint is the 3rd-century BCE Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, as is clear from the text itself:

<note>original Greek: Καὶ ἀπολῶ βδελύγματα καὶ καταπαύσω μεγιστᾶνας ἀπὸ Μέμφεως καὶ ἄρχοντα γῆς Αἰγύπτου, καὶ ἀπολῶ γῆν Φαθούρης, καὶ δώσω πῦρ εἰς Τανὶν καὶ ποιήσω ἐκδίκησιν ἐν Διοσπόλει, καὶ ἐκχεῶ τὸν θυμόν μου ἐπὶ Σαῒν ἰσχὺν Αἰγύπτου, καὶ ἀπολῶ τὸ πλῆθος Μέμφεως, καὶ δώσω πῦρ ἐπ᾽ Αἴγυπτον, καὶ ταραχῇ ταραχθήσεται Σαῒς.</note>
"And I will destroy the abominations, and I will cause the princes to cease from Memphis, and the ruler of the land of Egypt; and I will destroy the land of Pathros, and I will set fire to Tanis, and I will execute vengeance in Diospolis, and I will pour out my wrath upon Sais, the strength of Egypt, and I will destroy the multitude of Memphis, and I will set fire to Egypt, and Sais shall be greatly troubled."

Here, the Septuagint translators call the Alexandria (or *No*) of the Hebrews **Diospolis**. **Zoan** is called **Tanis**. **Sin**, which in the Vulgate <note>The late 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> edition is called **Pelusium**, is taken here by the Septuagint for **Sais**; which in the following verse is also taken for Memphis. The Son of Uzziel <note>Jonathan ben Uzziel, to whom the Aramaic translation or 'Targum' of the Prophets is traditionally attributed</note> in the Targum has **Tanis** for Zoan, following the Septuagint, and **Maphes** for Memphis, saying: ואשצי רפלחין לצלמניא מפכס באלכסנדריא *And I will destroy all those who worship idols of Maphes and Alexandria*. The Syriac reading partly follows the Vulgate and partly the Septuagint; I cite the text:

<note>original Syriac: ܘܐܘܒܕ ܨܠܡܐ ܘܐܒܛܠ ܦܬܟܪܐ ܡܢ ܡܦܣ ܘܪܝܫܐ ܡܢ ܐܪܥܐ ܕܡܨܪܝܢ. ܘܐܚܪܒ ܠܦܬܪܘܣ ܘܐܪܡܐ ܢܘܪܐ ܒܨܥܢ ܘܐܥܒܕ ܦܘܪܥܢܐ ܒܐܠܟܢܕܪܝܐ ܘܐܫܘܕ ܚܡܬܝ ܥܠ ܣܝܢ. ܘܐܫܬܪܚ ܒܡܨܪܝܢ ܘܬܬܪܥ ܣܝܢ ܘܐܠܟܢܕܪܝܐ ܬܬܒܙܚ ܘܡܦܣ ܢܗܘܘ ܒܗ̇ ܥܩܬܐ ܐܡܝܢܬܐ.</note>
"And I will destroy the idols and I will abolish the images from Memphis [Maphes] and the prince from the land of Egypt. And I will lay waste to Pathros and I will cast fire into Zoan and I will execute punishment in Alexandria, and I will pour my wrath upon Sin. And I will cause distress in Egypt, and Sin shall be breached, and Alexandria shall be plundered, and Memphis shall have constant distress in it."

### SECTION I. CHOROGRAPHY OF EGYPT. CHAPTER III

> And I will destroy the terror from Memphis, and there shall no longer be a prince in Egypt; and I will destroy the land of Pathros, and I will set fire in Zoan, and I will execute judgment in No <note>No is the biblical name for the city of Thebes</note>, and I will pour out my fury upon Pelusium, the strength of Egypt, and I will destroy the riches of No, and I will set fire in Egypt; and Pelusium shall be troubled, and No shall be scattered, and Memphis shall be for destruction, etc.

<margin>Reconciliation of names.</margin>
From all of these passages, it finally appears that interpreters have a great deal of diversity regarding names of this kind. To reconcile this diversity of names, therefore, I say that Holy Scripture in this place does not always speak of particular cities, but occasionally in a general sense, so that it takes an entire <term>Nomus</term> <note>A "Nome" was an administrative district or province in ancient Egypt.</note> for a city. Since Sais, Tanis, Pelusium, Busiris, and Memphis were neighbors to one another and belonged to almost the same district—that is, they were contained between the two rivers, the Athribitic and the Bubastic—this region was at times called Memphitic, at others Tanitic, now Saitic, and now Pelusiac. It is not surprising that interpreters have occasionally taken one for the other; and I believe this is the cause of the diversity of readings occurring in this place. However, that Sais, Tanis, Pelusium, Memphis, and Busiris are entirely different cities, we have stated partly in the preceding pages and shall reveal further in the following ones. Indeed, the Copts call Tanis <term>TENECINE</term> <note>original Coptic: TENECINE</note> from the island on which it is situated, which is so named. The Arabs describe it thus:

<note>original Arabic: وتنيس هي جزيرة في وسط بحيرة تعرف ببحيرة تنيس المقدمة الذكر والارز بها وقر خرجت وبادت قال في اللباب ومونه عند تنيس قال في العزيزي ومقدار بحيرتها اقلاع يوم في عرض نصف يوم ويكون ما فني هبوب الريح الشمالي.</note>

*Tanis is an island in the middle of a lake, which is commonly called the Lake of Tanis, already mentioned before; it is not subject to winds, and has now perished in destruction. It says in the treatise "Al-Labab": Mune is near Tanis. And it says in the treatise "Al-Azizi": The extent of the length of that lake is one day’s sailing, and the width is half a day’s sailing when the northern winds are blowing.* Balmis describes it in Hebrew thus:
<margin>The Tanitic Hawk.</margin>
**Tanis is a city of Egypt, called Zoan in the Scripture.** <note>original Hebrew: טאניס היא מדינת מצרים נקראת במקרא צואן</note> Stephanus says: *Tanis, a city of Egypt, anciently named Thanis.* <note>original Greek: Τάνις πόλις Αἰγύπτου, παλαιᾶς ὀνομαζομένη Θάνις.</note>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a hawk or falcon (Accipiter Taniticus) standing in profile on a horizontal perch, looking to the left. The bird has detailed, patterned plumage.</image-desc>

Furthermore, Strabo teaches that the Tanites worshipped the Hawk; Pausanias also mentions the Tanitic Hawk. What the Egyptians actually intended by the worship of the Hawk will be discussed at length elsewhere. And let these remarks suffice regarding the Tanitic prefecture.

This name Pharbæthus is derived from the Coptic <term>perboit</term> <note>original Coptic: περϐωιτ</note> which denotes the "place of the Hawk." For according to our Nomenclator <note>Kircher's own dictionary of Egyptian names</note>, <term>peboit</term> means a "place" or "street,"

<margin>Horapollo.</margin>
...a plaza, a street, a path, <term>ⲡⲓⲙⲁⲛϩⲁⲗⲏⲧ</term> <note>Coptic: pi-man-halēt, literally "the place of the bird."</note> the Hawk. That <term>ⲡⲓⲙⲁⲛϩⲁⲗⲏⲧ</term> signifies a Hawk is also testified by Horapollo <note>Kircher refers to "Horus," meaning Horapollo, the author of a 5th-century treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>; his words are as follows: <note>original Greek: "Ἐπισημαίνει γὰρ αὐτῷ ψυχὴν, ἢ ὑπεροχὴν παντί... ᾧ καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ τρέφεται."</note> "For it signifies the soul to them, or a superiority over all things, based on the interpretation of its name. For among the Egyptians, the hawk is called *BAIETH*. This name, when divided, signifies 'soul and heart,' because *bai* is the soul, and *eth* is the heart. The heart, according to the Egyptians, is the enclosure of the soul. Thus, the composition of the name signifies the 'soul in the heart,' which is why the hawk is said to have a natural sympathy with the god because of the soul; for it does not drink water at all, but rather blood, by which the soul itself is also nourished." Indeed, the Hawk is used to represent the soul according to this interpretation of the name; since among the Egyptians the Hawk is called *Baieth*, a name which, if you divide it, signifies *soul and heart*. For *Bai* is *soul*, and *eth* is *heart*. The heart, in the opinion of the Egyptians, is the vessel of the soul; therefore, according to this customary meaning, this name denotes a *spirited soul* <note>Latin: "animam cordatam," literally a "hearted soul," implying courage or vitality.</note>. From this, because of the harmony of nature it shares with the soul, the Hawk does not drink water at all, but blood, by which the soul itself is also fed. From this truly illustrious testimony, it is sufficiently clear that the etymology of this name was not given to this Nome except from the worship and veneration of the Hawk that was customary there. Just as other cities, such as Diospolis <note>City of Zeus/Jupiter</note> and Hermopolis <note>City of Hermes/Mercury</note>, etc., are named after the worship of Jupiter and Mercury, so also this one found its name from the worship of the Hawk, so that it was called <term>ⲡⲓϩⲏⲣⲫⲁⲓϯ</term> <note>Coptic: Pi-her-phaiti</note>
<margin>What does Baieth denote?</margin>
<margin>What is Pihirphait?</margin>
that is, the *Village of the Hawk*. Certainly, I deduce that this prefecture shared the worship of the Hawk with the Tanitic district from the fact that it was very close to it, and there was a very frequent commercial trade back and forth between the people of Tanis and Pharbethus. That a similarity of customs and religion arises from commerce is too clear to need further explanation.

And between Pharbethus and Tanis was that most famous station of the Israelites' captivity, from which Moses, liberating them, led them directly through the Red Sea; but of these things more elsewhere, now to other matters.

# NOME X. BUSIRIS.
->THAT IS,<-
## The Busiritic Prefecture, in Coptic ⲡⲁϣⲓⲣ ⲛ̀ⲃⲟⲩⲥⲓⲣⲓ

The last Nome of the Delta is the Busiritic, and the city of the same name, which in Ezekiel 30 is called <term>פַּתְרֽוֹס</term> <note>Hebrew: Pathros</note> Pathros, so named after Busiris; various authors derive its etymology in various ways. Some from the legendary Busiris, that slayer of guests; others from Osiris; others devise different things concerning it; others from Busir, the son of Ham—so say the Arabs, about which we will speak more in the following pages. We believe it was so named from the cult of Apis, because the Egyptians fabled that Osiris was there transformed into an Ox, as Diodorus testifies, as if you were to say in Coptic <term>ⲃⲟⲩⲥ ⲛ̀ⲉⲩⲣⲏⲓ</term> <note>bous n-eurei</note>, that is, the *Ox of the King*, or <term>ⲃⲟⲩ ⲟⲩⲥⲓⲣⲓ</term> *Busosiri*. The Greeks wrongly confuse this city with Thebes, which is also called the *hundred-gated* city, when these two places are separated by the entire length of Egypt, as is clear from the map.

TREATISE I. CHOROGRAPHY OF EGYPT. CHAPTER III.

...it could be held that the Ox was worshipped in Busiris. For since Osiris first appeared there in the form of an Ox, it is believed that he provided various benefits to mankind under this form. Certainly, nothing was easier for a superstitious people than to introduce bovine worship when the opportunity arose. Furthermore, since Busiris was located near Memphis and Heliopolis—which we identified above as the ancient Rameses, the station of the Israelites—perhaps from here originated that famous <term>calf-worship</term> <note>original Greek: μοσχολάτρια (*moscholatria*), referring to the worship of the golden calf in the wilderness.</note> or cult of the little calf in the desert, about which we will speak extensively in its proper place. Whatever the case may be, the etymology itself and the surrounding locations, which were steeped in this same cult, sufficiently declare what should be thought regarding the religion of the Busirites. 

<margin>The Busirites' hatred of Donkeys.</margin>I read in Plutarch <note>Plutarch was a Greek philosopher whose work "On Isis and Osiris" is a primary source for Egyptian mythology in the Renaissance.</note> that the Busirites held donkeys in hatred and detested every blast of a trumpet because of its resemblance to braying. This was because they considered Typhon <note>Typhon is the Greek name for Set, the god of chaos, who was often depicted as a donkey or a "Typhonian animal."</note> to be of a related nature, and he is said to have torn apart the body of Osiris; but concerning these matters, see what we discuss elsewhere.

And these are the things that we thought should be said regarding this first distribution of Lower Egypt into its Nomes. We have stated that this order was first established by Sesostris <note>A legendary Egyptian king often credited by early historians with organizing the country's administration.</note>, and then redistributed into various new Nomes by the Ptolemies. But contemplate all these things at a single glance in the following Synopsis.

CHAPTER IV.

## DISTRIBUTION II.

### Of Inland Egypt into its Nomes.

### NOME I. MEMPHIS,

### THAT IS

->*The Memphite Prefecture; in Coptic* ⲙⲉⲙϥⲓ ⲙⲉⲙⲫⲓ <note>original Coptic: *Memphi* or *Memphi*</note><-

---

<margin>The antiquity of Memphis.</margin>
That Memphis was one of the oldest cities in the world is evident from the testimonies of almost all historians; for which reason they often call it the seat of the ancient kings, the workshop of the gods, and a mother forever fertile in marvelous works. The Hebrews call it now *Moph*, now *Noph*, sometimes *Migdal* (a Tower), occasionally *Maphes*, and often *Misraim* <note>original Hebrew: מוף (*Moph*), נף (*Noph*), מגדל (*Migdal*), מפת (*Maphes*), מצרים (*Mizraim*)</note>.

<margin>Various names for the same.</margin>
The Greeks, however, call it Babylon <note>Kircher is likely referring to the Roman fortress of Babylon in Egypt, near modern Cairo, which was often confused with or linked to Memphis.</note>; the Copts call it *Memfi* or *Memphi*, or even *On ni Babylon* <note>original Coptic: ⲱⲛ ⲛⲓ ⲃⲁⲃⲩⲗⲱⲛ, meaning "On of Babylon"</note>. The Arabs call it now *Mesra*, now *Monf*; the Armenians, *Messor*; the Chaldeans, *Kabra*; and finally, the moderns call it Cairo and Al-Cairo. Abraham de Pomis <note>A 16th-century Jewish physician and lexicographer.</note> describes it in his Hebrew lexicon with these words:

<margin>Abraham de Pomis.</margin>
> *Moph* is a city of Egypt built by Mizraim the son of Ham, and every Egyptian city is called *Moph* in the Scripture to this day, meaning "impure" in the vernacular <note>original Hebrew: מוף היא מדינת מצרים בנה מצרים בן חם ונקראת עד היום כל עיר מצרי במקרא מופ ר'ל טמא לעז</note>.

*Moph* is a city of Egypt which Mizraim the son of Ham built; it is called *Mizraim* to this day, but in Holy Scripture it is called *Maphes*, that is, "unclean," because of the practices of foreign slavery that were once common there. Benjamin <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a famous 12th-century Jewish traveler.</note> also mentions this city in his itinerary, and says that many monuments of the Patriarch Joseph are found there:

> From New Egypt <note>Likely referring to Cairo.</note> to the Old is three miles; today it is entirely desolate and devastated, yet there are still many monuments of antiquity in it, as well as traces of the storehouses of our father Joseph (may his memory be a blessing); in it is also seen a certain wonderful column made by the help of magicians, the like of which is not in the whole earth <note>original Hebrew: ממצרים החדשה עד הקדמה ג' מילין היום כולח משוממת ובח רבות זכרונות ונראו בח עדים בית אוצר אבינו יוסף זל ובה עמוד נפלא מאד לא כמותר בכל הארץ:</note>.

Now New Mizraim is three miles distant from the old city; today it is entirely desolate and devastated, yet there are still many monuments of antiquity in it, such as the traces of the treasures and granaries of Joseph (may his memory be blessed); in it is also seen a certain wonderful column made by the power of magicians, the like of which does not exist in the whole world. That Memphis is therefore both very ancient and was built by the sons of Ham in the first years after the Deluge is shown not only by the Hebrews, but also by Arab and Greek authors, as we shall see shortly, after we first say something about the etymology of this name.

<margin>Description of Memphis.</margin>
<margin>* Or "God of water."</margin>
Memphis, therefore, is an Egyptian word composed of *Mem* and *phi*, of which the former means "water" and the latter "God." Thus the compound ⲙⲉⲙϥⲓ *Momphaea* denotes the same as "God's water." This word was later corrupted by the Greeks, and instead of *Memphi*, it was heard as *Memphis*. The occasion and origin of the giving of this name is as follows: When the sons of Ham began to cultivate the first colony of this part of Egypt, they fixed the tents of their first habitation in the Memphite hills...

<meta>The text cuts off here with the catchword "fixisse" (fixed), to be continued on the next page.</meta>

Kircher also provides an Egyptian etymology for the name Memphis, translating it as "God's water."</summary>

### TREATISE IV. CHOROGRAPHY OF EGYPT. PAGE 87. CAIRO.

...it is said that [the city] existed while the rest of Egypt, as has been mentioned, was for the most part stagnant with marshes far and wide. In the course of time, as the marshes dried up and the earth offered itself more kindly, the first city was founded on the banks of the Nile by Mizraim, the son of Ham <note>Mizraim is the biblical name for Egypt and its progenitor; Kircher uses the Latin *Misraimus*.</note>, who wished it to be called *Misraim* after his own name. As the land and the city of *Mesra* received greater increases in fertility day by day from the irrigation of the fruitful river, they assert that it was finally called by the Egyptian name *Monph*—that is, "the water of God"—which posterity later called *Memphis* by a corruption of the word. And that this is so, Abenephius <note>Kircher refers to the author Ibn Wahshiyya.</note> first clearly shows with these words:

->He was among the first who inhabited Egypt: Mizraim, son of Ham, son of Noah, and he is the father of the Copts; so he inhabited Memphis, which is called in Coptic *Menphta*, meaning the water of God.<- <note>original Arabic: كان من اولين الذي سكن مصر مصر ابن حام بن نوح وهو ابو القبط فسكن منف وتدعي بالقبطية منفتأ اعني الما الله</note>

Moreover, the first of the inhabitants of Egypt was Mizraim, son of Ham, son of Noah, and he was the father of the Copt; and he dwelt in *Momph*, which in the Coptic language is called *Monphta*, that is, "the water of God." Certainly, it is clear that Memphis is called *Momemphis* by many writers for no other reason than this etymology: <margin>The etymology of Memphis.</margin> because *Momemphis* in Coptic signifies nothing other than "the waters of the city of God." All of these points agree with those things which the Arabic historian Gelaldinus <note>Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti, a prolific 15th-century Egyptian scholar.</note> recites from Ibn Abd al-Hakam, where he also explains the etymology of *Maphe* slightly differently than Abenephius. I provide the words in full:

### CHAPTER IV. 28 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE

<margin>The division of Egypt made by Mizraim among his sons.</margin>
*...[he was] buried in the place where Hermes was, and this was the first burial in the land of Egypt. He was succeeded by his son Mizraim, who divided Egypt among each of his brothers—specifically, a portion of his own land. As the children of Mizraim and their descendants multiplied, Mizraim selected and divided a portion for each of his sons; he took possession of it for himself and his children. For his son Copt, he set aside the portion on this side of the Nile, the place called Coptos, and Copt dwelt there and the place was named after him. Everything above Coptos as far as Aswan, and what lies below as far as Esmun <note>original: "Esmun" — refers to the city of Hermopolis Magna, known in Coptic as Shmun.</note> on both the eastern and western banks, he gave to his daughter Esmun; Esmun dwelt there and it was named Esmun after her. He divided for Atribi all that was between Memphis and Sais; she dwelt in Sais and it was called Sais after her. Thus, all of Egypt was divided into four portions: two portions were contained in Upper Egypt <note>original: "Saide" — a term used for the Sa’id or Upper Egypt.</note> and two in the lower land.*

Regarding these and similar matters, see also Herodotus, who in his book *Euterpe* <note>The second book of Herodotus's *Histories*.</note> treats extensively of Memphis, asserting it was founded by Menes (whom we have shown elsewhere to be the same as Mizraim). See also what he relates concerning the first division of Egypt into the *Calasiries* and *Hermolybies* <note>original: "Calasiries & Hermolybies" — the two traditional classes of the Egyptian warrior caste.</note>; we shall explain the reasoning behind these names elsewhere.

From this account, it is clear that Egypt was divided by the first sons of Ham, such that Mizraim held the first and better part, Copt the second, Esmun the third, and Atrib the fourth. It is also evident from the cited testimonies that Memphis was established as the metropolis of all Egypt. The cited author asserts that this division, made by the original settlers, remained until the time of Joseph <note>The biblical patriarch Joseph, son of Jacob, who became vizier of Egypt.</note>; Joseph then distributed Egypt into smaller divisions to avoid disputes. Finally, he was succeeded by Sesostris <note>A legendary king of Egypt often identified with Ramses II or Senusret III, credited with vast administrative reforms.</note>, who expanded the city after it had been ruined by various calamities, restored the nearly collapsed religion of the ancients, and most wisely divided the entire region into thirty <term>Nomes</term> <note>original: "Nomos" — the administrative provinces of ancient Egypt.</note> or Councils according to a certain mystical plan.

<margin>What is Momphta?</margin>
Having proposed these things, let us now see which Deity the people of Memphis chose to worship above all. Although various colonies of the Gods found a station in that city as the metropolis, I find among the most serious authors that the Apis—whom they also called *Momphta*, that is, "the God of Memphis"—was worshipped there above the rest. Strabo describes the bovine religion of the Memphites in these words:

<margin>Strabo, Book 17.</margin>
> Close by is Memphis itself, the royal residence of the Egyptians; it is three *schoeni* <note>An ancient unit of distance.</note> from the Delta. It contains temples, specifically that of Apis, who is the same as Osiris; there the bull Apis is nourished in a certain enclosure. As I said, he is considered a God, being all white on the forehead and some other parts of the body, but black in the rest. By these signs they always judge who is fit for the succession when the honored bull has died. There is a courtyard lying before the enclosure, and in it is another enclosure for the mother of the bull. They release Apis into this courtyard at a certain hour, especially to show him to strangers. For while people can see him through a window in his enclosure, they wish to see him outside as well; after he has skipped about a little in the courtyard, he is taken back again to his proper stall. The temple of Apis is situated next to the temple of Hephaestus <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Ptah.</note>; and the temple of Hephaestus itself is sumptuously constructed in terms of size and other features. <note>original: "Ἐγγὺς δὲ καὶ ἡ Μέμφις..." — translated from the Greek text provided in the source.</note>

*Memphis is also nearby, the royal seat of the Egyptians, located three schoeni from the Delta; it has the temple of Apis, who is the same as Osiris. There the Bull Apis is fed in a certain pen, and as we have said, he is held among them as a God. He is white on the forehead and certain small parts of the body, but otherwise black; by these signs they indicate who is suitable for the succession when the other has died. In front of that pen is a certain courtyard, and in it...*

# DISTRICT II. HELIOPOLIS,
## THAT IS, THE
### Heliopolitan Prefecture, in Coptic: ⲡⲓⲙⲁ ⲛ̀ⲣⲏ ⲱⲛ. <note>original: "pima n-rē ōn" — literally "the place of the sun, On".</note>

**H**eliopolis, or the City of the Sun, is one of the primary cities of all Egypt, in no way inferior to Memphis in size, religion, and the worship of the Gods. Although there are some who confuse it with the *On* of the Hebrews, and some wish it to be one and the same with Memphis or Mesra <note>Mesra or Misr is the Arabic name for Egypt/Cairo, derived from the biblical Mizraim.</note>, the reason for this seems to be that it is also called Mesra by the Arabs. Whatever the case, the confusion seems to have arisen from the ambiguity of names and the proximity of the locations. To settle the matter, I say there were two Mizraims <margin>Two Mizraims.</margin>—or Mesras—the old and the new. We said in the preceding sections that the old Mizraim was Memphis, across the river. We affirm that the new one, on this side of the river, is Heliopolis. Benjamin <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler.</note> mentions this double Mizraim (the old and the new) in the passage cited a little earlier, as do the Arabic geographers the "Nubian" <note>Referring to Al-Idrisi, the 12th-century geographer often called the "Nubian" in early modern Europe.</note> and Abulfeda <note>A 13th-14th century Syrian geographer and historian.</note>. The latter describes both in these words:

<margin>Abulfeda.</margin>
> *Monf, or Memphis, is the ancient Mesra, situated on the western side of the Nile. In it, there are still the greatest and most astounding remains of antiquity, made of carved stones covered in green and other colors which, up to this day, have not been changed by the sun or the injuries of time throughout this whole interval. Memphis is separated from Mesra by a short stage, or a journey of one day. As for Heliopolis, which the Arabs call Ain Shams* <note>Arabic: عين شمس (*‘Ayn Shams*), meaning "The Eye of the Sun".</note> *—that is, the Eye of the Sun—he describes it in these words:*

<margin>The Nubian Geography.</margin>
> *Ain Shams—that is, Heliopolis, or the Eye of the Sun—is in our times desolate, and has no inhabitants. It is said that it was the city of Pharaoh, and there are astounding ancient remains of great stones, and a square column called the Obelisk of Pharaoh, about thirty cubits long. It is half a stage from Cairo, and near it is a village called Matariya, which is to the north of Cairo, where it shines upon...* <unclear>on</unclear>

...it is broad, and there are no dwellings in it; it is said to have been the city of Pharaoh. There are also noteworthy monuments of antiquity, built from massive rocks and stones. In it is a square column called the **Pharaoh's Needle** <note>An obelisk, specifically the one belonging to Senusret I, which remains the oldest standing obelisk in Egypt.</note>; its length is nearly 30 cubits. There is also a village there called Matharea <note>Matariyyah</note>, located on the left side of Aliacri (the place where Christ is said to have lived). All of these things agree with the *Geography* of al-Idrisi <note>Kircher refers to the 12th-century geographer al-Idrisi as the "Nubian Geographer."</note> which says:

> And the city of Fustat is Egypt [Mesra] itself; it was named so because Mizraim, the son of Ham, the son of Noah (peace be upon him), built it in the beginning. It was originally Heliopolis [Ain Shams], and what lies south of Fustat is where the city of Memphis [Manif] was built. To its north is the city called Heliopolis [Ain Shams]; these two are like twin cities, and it is said they were the pleasure grounds and retreats of Pharaoh. <note>original Arabic: ومدينة الفسطاط هي مصر سميت بذلك لأن مصرايم بن حام بن نوح عليه السلام بناها في الأول وكانت أول عين شمس ومايلي جنوب الفسطاط بنيت مدينة منيف وهيا حيز شمالها المدينة المسماة عين شمس وهما كالقرينتين ويقال انهما كانا متنزهي فرعون.</note>

The city of Phestad <note>Fustat</note> is Mesra itself, so named because Mizraim, the son of Ham, the son of Noah (peace be upon him), built it at the start. The first city was the **Eye of the Sun** [Heliopolis], and it turns south toward Fustat, where the city of Memphis was built. On its left side is the city called **Ainschems**, that is, the eye or fountain of the Sun. These are like two cities, and it is said they were used for the delights and amusements of Pharaoh. It is called **On** by the Hebrews; thus Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, a major medieval commentator.</note> says in the *Great Bible* on the 30th chapter of Ezekiel: *On is a city of Egypt, called in the common tongue Beth-shemesh or Ain-shemesh* <note>original Hebrew: און מדינת מצרים נקרא בלעז ביתשמש או עין שמש</note>, meaning the house or eye of the Sun. Ralbag <note>Rabbi Levi ben Gershon.</note> and Ibn Ezra demonstrate in their commentary on Exodus 14 that this was the same as the **Rameses** of the Hebrews. Indeed, the very etymology of *On* demonstrates that it was Rameses, where the Israelites endured so many labors; for "Aun" <note>original Hebrew: און</note> signifies nothing other than *strength, power, wealth, and honor* <note>original Hebrew: כח ואומץ הון עשר עמל שקר</note>, with which are ordinarily joined labor, vanity, and affliction of spirit. The Hebrews most appropriately called it the city of *On*, where strength, power, infinite riches, and all the outrages of idolatrous religion had established their seat. Consequently, from this pride and arrogance came labor and sorrow upon the innocent, humble Israelites devoted to the worship of the true God.

<margin>
Why is it called the Eye of the Sun?
</margin>
<margin>
A miraculous mirror reflecting the Sun throughout the entire day.
</margin>
It is called **Ain Shams** <note>original Arabic: عين شمس</note>, that is, the Eye of the Sun, because of a certain mirror that was placed in the temple dedicated to the Sun. It was crafted with such skill that it would reflect the radiant face of the Sun the entire day and illuminate the whole temple with its light. 
<margin>
Ibn Zayyat, Ibn Abd al-Hakam.
</margin>
So report the Arabic historians Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Ibn Zayyat, and others. We have curiously investigated the nature of this mechanical device and teach about it in our *Mechanics of the Egyptians*, which the reader may consult. Therefore, this entire District (Nome) was consecrated to the Sun, or Osiris, whom they represented and worshipped in the form of a bull. Thus Strabo says:

<note>The following is a translation of the Greek passage from Strabo's Geography, Book 17.</note>
*Beyond it is the Heliopolitan district, where the City of the Sun stands upon a great mound. It contains the Temple of the Sun and the bull Mnevis, which is kept in a certain enclosure and is regarded as a God by the Heliopolitans, just as Apis is at Memphis. Now the city is entirely deserted; however, it has an ancient temple built in the Egyptian style, which shows by many manifest signs the madness and sacrilege of Cambyses.* <note>The Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE.</note> 

<margin>
Mnevis, the Bull-God of the Heliopolitans.
</margin>
The temple ruins show where he damaged the sacred things with fire or iron, mutilating and burning them, just as he did to the **Obelisks**, two of which were carried to Rome, while those not damaged by fire remain.
