### DISTRICT III. BUBASTUS
-> THAT IS <-
-> The Bubastic Prefecture, in Coptic: <unclear>The Peace of the Two Bulls</unclear> <-

The **Bubastus District** <term>Nomus: a Greek term for the administrative districts of ancient Egypt</term> and its capital city are called *Boubastos* by Ptolemy, as if one were to say "the step of the bull" <note>original Greek: "βούβαστος", interpreted here as "bous" (bull) and "batos" (stepped/trodden).</note>. Others derive this name from "the bull" and "the city," meaning the **City of the Bull** <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τοῦ βοῦ, καὶ ἄστυ"</note>. In Coptic, it is derived from *bou* and *hotp*, meaning "he gave two bulls." For in this place, **Osiris** and **Isis** are said to have appeared in the form of two bulls—one called **Apis** by the people of Memphis, and the other **Mnevis** by those of Heliopolis. It is said that these two first appeared here and led men to the knowledge of agriculture according to prescribed laws; so says **Abenephius** <note>An Arabic author, often identified by Kircher as a source of ancient Egyptian wisdom.</note>:

<margin>Abenephius.</margin>
"Bubastis is one of the districts of Egypt, and its name in the Coptic tongue is correctly rendered as 'The Gift of the Two Bulls'." <note>original Arabic: فبوبست وحده من اجزاءات مصر فبصحة تسميت بلسان القبطي العطية البقرين</note>

Indeed, whoever wishes to examine the etymology more deeply will see the truth of the matter clearer than light. Whether it is called "the step of the bull," "the city of the bull," or finally "the gift of the bulls," we shall see that the facts agree in every case. 

<margin>The etymology of Bubastus.</margin>
<margin>Why is the dog worshipped in this city?</margin>

Although others claim that **Bubastis** is nothing other than **Diana** <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt, equivalent to the Greek Artemis.</note>, as Herodotus says in his book *Euterpe*: "There is a sacred city at Bubastis; this city is Artemis" <note>original Greek: "Ἔστι δὲ πόλις ἱερὴ ἐπὶ Βουβάστι, ἡ δὲ πόλις αὕτη Ἄρτεμις"</note>. In this city is the temple of Bubastis, who in our language is the same as Diana; and elsewhere: "Bubastis is indeed Artemis" <note>original Greek: "Βουβάστις δὲ ἐστὶν; καὶ ἡ Ἄρτεμις Βουβάστις"</note>. Furthermore, Ceres is Isis, and Diana is Bubastis...

<margin>Bubastus is sacred to Diana.</margin>
...and that there were frequent assemblies of the Egyptians at these cities, especially at the city of **Bubastus** in honor of **Diana**, at **Busiris** in honor of **Isis**, at the city of **Sais** in honor of **Minerva**, at **Heliopolis** in honor of the **Sun**, at **Buto** in honor of **Latona**, and at **Papremis** in honor of **Mars** <note>Kircher lists the Egyptian gods by their "Interpretatio Graeca"—the names of Greek and Roman gods used by ancient historians to describe foreign deities.</note>; truly, regarding the ceremonies which they performed in each city, see **Herodotus** in the cited passage.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a dog-headed deity (representing Diana or Anubis) standing in a landscape. The figure wears a kilt and holds a circular disc, possibly representing the moon or a ceremonial mirror, aloft in its right hand.</image-desc>

I recall also that a dog was held in the place of a Divinity in this city, which is not surprising, since **Diana** is a huntress; just as the Greeks did, so too the Egyptians associated dogs with her. Nor do these things disagree with what we said above regarding the worship of the two bulls performed here. For since Diana is the same as the **Moon** <note>original: "Luna"</note>, and the bull **Mnevis** is dedicated to the Moon—as was said above from the writings of **Strabo** and **Suidas**—certainly the Egyptians worshiped Diana under the form of a Bull. The horned statue of Diana herself clearly demonstrates this, and we have shown it at length in the chapter on **Isis** and **Apis**, which you should consult. See also what we said in the same place concerning **Apis** and **Mnevis**, of whom the latter represented the Moon and the former the Sun. Therefore, in Bubastus, both Bulls—namely Apis and Mnevis, or what is the same thing, the Sun and the Moon—were worshiped insofar as they are the causes of sublunary things and generation. We have declared in the cited chapters that **Diana**, **Isis**, and the **Moon** are one and the same. All these things, therefore, agree perfectly with one another.

Furthermore, many scholars believe **Bubastus** to be the modern-day city of **Asyut** <note>original: "Afiuth"</note>; so say the Arabs, who claim it is situated at the Mountain of the Phoenix; so say **Schaar ebn elfaati** in the works of **Abulfeda**, and **Abn Saida** in the same:

> *Asyut is on the side of the Mountain of Birds, and it is told that the birds make a pilgrimage to it every year, and leave there one of the eggs, distinguished by its shell.* <note>original Arabic: اسيوط في جهتها جبل الطير... This passage refers to a local legend about a "Bird Mountain" where birds were said to sacrifice one of their own or leave a sign.</note>

The Hebrews call it <term>Pi-beseth <gloss>Mouth of Shame</gloss></term> <note>original: "פי-بסת"</note>, that is, the "mouth of ignominy," on account of the abominable idolatry practiced there. Many think this was the Village of the Hebrews, or **Goshen** <note>original: "Gessen"</note> itself, just like Rameses and Heliopolis; but we shall speak of these things more extensively elsewhere; now to other matters.

### DISTRICT IV. HERACLEOPOLIS,

->THAT IS<-

->The Heracleopolitan Prefecture.<-

<margin>Ptolemy.</margin>
**Heracleopolis**, both the District <note>original: "Nomus"</note> and the Metropolis, is so named from the worship of **Hercules**, and the entire District is contained within an Island formed by two branches of the Nile. Thus says **Ptolemy**: *The river extends to this region, making the island the Heracleopolitan district. ### TREATISE IV. CHOROGRAPHY OF EGYPT. CHAPTER IV.

We state that the ancient **Elphium** <note>The Al-Fayyum Oasis, a fertile basin in Middle Egypt.</note> was once this place, and in succeeding times it received various names, such that some substitute for it **Fustat** <note>original: "Phestad," referring to Old Cairo, the first capital of Egypt under Muslim rule.</note>, which many of the Arabs confuse now with **Memphis**, and now with **Heliopolis**. It is certain that Fustat is a modern city situated near **Cairo**; the Arabs teach that it is the same as **Nilopolis** <note>Literally "City of the Nile."</note> in these words:

> And Joseph began to build cities, and he established boundaries for them. The first city constructed in Elphium was that city called **Saphe**, which the children of Pharaoh used to inhabit. Then he commanded that a river <note>Refers to a canal, specifically the Bahr Yussef or "Water of Joseph."</note> be dug, and he built a structure for the measurement of the Nile. When these things were finished, he calculated the weight of the earth and the water, and from that day forward **Geometry** <term>Geometry: used here in its literal sense of "earth-measuring" (from Greek *ge* and *metria*), specifically for managing agricultural land and flood levels.</term> emerged. For they did not know it before this; and it is said that **Joseph** was the first who measured the Nile in Egypt, and he placed a **Nilometer** <note>original: "Nilometrium," a structure used to measure the height of the Nile's annual flood.</note> within it.

Furthermore, that famous **Nilometer** <note>original: "Niloscopium," a synonym for Nilometer.</note> is elegantly described by the **Nubian Geographer** <note>Al-Idrisi (1100–1165), a famous Arab geographer who lived at the court of King Roger II of Sicily.</note>—where he first records the entire Island of the Nile <note>Rawdah Island in Cairo.</note> according to its length and width and the location of the bridges—in these words:

<margin>Description of the ancient and modern Nilometer.</margin>

> The Nilometer, or the house for measuring the Nile, is at the head of the Island on the eastern side, sloping toward Fustat. It is a large dwelling which can be walked around on every side within; the circular perimeter sits upon columns. In the middle of the dwelling is a large, deep basin, which one descends into by marble steps around the circumference. In the center of the basin is an upright marble column, upon which are marked the numbers of **cubits** and **fingers** <note>The "cubit" (brachium/cubitus) was the standard unit of measurement, subdivided into "fingers" (digiti).</note>. At the top of the column is another structure skillfully made of stone, decorated with colors and marked with gold, lapis lazuli, and various durable dyes. Water reaches this basin through a wide pipe or canal that connects it to the water of the Nile. The water does not enter these vaults except at the time of the Nile's rising, which happens in the month of August. Furthermore, a rise of 16 cubits irrigates the King's land equally; and when the Nile reaches 18 cubits, it will irrigate all the lands in that region; and if it reaches

For the water of the well rises and increases equally with the Nile, and there are certain marks engraved on the wall of the well, which serve as indicators of the increases and decreases.* Furthermore, who this **Hercules** worshipped here was has been discussed elsewhere. # NOME V. CROCODILOPOLIS,
<term>Nome: a traditional administrative district of ancient Egypt; from the Greek 'nomos'.</term>

->THAT IS,<-

## Prefecture of the City of Crocodiles, in Coptic: The Land of the Crocodile <note>original: "ⲡⲓⲕⲁϩⲓ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲥⲟⲩⲭⲓ"</note>

I find that this place was once called "The Land of the Crocodile" in a fragment of Coptic Geography. **Strabo** <note>A famous Greek geographer from the 1st century BCE.</note> asserts that the worship of crocodiles flourished most especially in this city and district. This city was also called **Arsinoë**, to distinguish it from the city of Arsinoë on the Red Sea, which others believe to be the same as **Baal-zephon** and modern-day **Suez**.

<margin>Why was the crocodile worshipped in this city?</margin>
<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a crocodile, facing left, with detailed scales and a long tail, set within a simple rectangular frame.</image-desc>

I have stated that it is called in Coptic "The Land of the Crocodile" because, since this city was near **Lake Moeris**, where a vast multitude of crocodiles lived (causing great slaughter among both men and cattle), the inhabitants sought to appease them as a **Typhonian Power** <term>Typhonian: relating to Typhon (the Greek name for the Egyptian god Set), a god of chaos and storms often associated with dangerous animals.</term> through specific rites and ceremonies. From this, that beastly worship spread. Strabo himself also records that the crocodile is called *Suchi* <note>original: "ⲥⲟⲩⲭⲓ"</note> in the Coptic language, in these words: "Passing along these things for a hundred stadia, one finds the city of **Arsinoë**. It was formerly called the **City of Crocodiles**, for in this district they worship the crocodile with great intensity. There is a sacred one kept by itself in a lake, which is tame for the priests. It is called *Suchos* <note>original: "σοῦχος"</note>."

> "As one sails past for a hundred stadia, there is the city of Arsinoë, which was once called the City of Crocodiles; for in this prefecture the Crocodile is worshipped in a wondrous manner. There is a sacred one among them, nourished separately in a certain lake, which is gentle toward the priests and is called **Suchus**. It is fed with bread, meat, and wine, which are brought by foreigners who come to see such a spectacle. They worshipped the Crocodile just as their neighbors, the people of **Heracleopolis**, worshipped the **Ichneumon** <term>Ichneumon: the Egyptian mongoose, a small predator famous in antiquity for its ability to kill snakes and destroy crocodile eggs.</term>, the 'opponent of the crocodile.' Since these mongooses are most deadly to crocodiles and vipers—for they destroy their eggs and even kill the beasts themselves by entering their bellies—it is no wonder that, just as other beneficial animals were honored, these Ichneumons were also raised to a kind of deification by the Heracleopolitans. But concerning these matters, see Strabo, who treats them more extensively and with greater curiosity."

# NOME VI. OXYRYNCHITES,

->THAT IS,<-

## Prefecture of Oxyrhynchus, in Coptic: The Land of Pemdje <note>original: "ⲡⲓⲕⲁϩⲓ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲡⲉⲙϫⲏ"</note>

This district was called the **Oxyrhynchite** prefecture after its capital, **Oxyrhynchus**, because the people there pursued the **Oxyrhynchus fish** <note>A species of elephantfish (Mormyrus) found in the Nile.</note> with an altogether unique worship. The Oxyrhynchus is a fish which the Egyptians report devoured the genitals of **Osiris**, which had been cut off by **Typhon** and thrown into the Nile. <margin>Aelian, Book 10, Chapter 46.</margin> It takes its name from the sharpness of its snout, as if you were to say *oxy rhynchos* <note>original: "ὀξύ ῥύγχος"</note>, or "sharp-snout."

<header>CHAPTER IV. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS</header>

<margin>The worship of fish in this city.</margin>
...our [fish]; and it is held in such great veneration and religious awe, according to **Aelian** <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author of the 2nd century CE known for his works on natural history.</note>, that the inhabitants of this Nome refuse to touch any fish caught with a hook. They fear that the hook might have once pierced a fish that is sacred among them and endowed with great religious significance. Furthermore, when fish are caught in nets, they examine them with the utmost care, again and again, to see if they have inadvertently captured one of these fish along with the others. They would rather catch no fish at all than keep a vast number of them if it meant retaining this one. For they say that the Oxyrhynchus <term>Oxyrhynchus: literally "sharp-snout," a species of Nile fish (Mormyrus kanume).</term> was born from the wounds of **Osiris**. They also hold that Osiris is the same as the **Nile**. The nature and appearance of this fish will be discussed in the hieroglyphic description of animals, where we shall show it to be nothing other than the carnivorous Nile Pike <note>original: "Lucium Niloticum Σαρκοφάγον"</note>, the form of which you see here from the side.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of an Oxyrhynchus fish, shown in profile facing left. It has a long snout, a prominent dorsal fin, and detailed scales.</image-desc>

But let us hear **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian (c. 64 BCE – 24 CE).</note>: *On the opposite bank is the city of Oxyrhynchus and a prefecture of the same name. There the Oxyrhynchus is worshipped, and they have a temple to the Oxyrhynchus, although other Egyptians also worship this fish.* <note>original Greek: "Ἐν δὲ τῇ περαίᾳ Ὀξύρυγχος πόλις... κοινῇ τιμώντων τὸν Ὀξύρυγχον."</note> But more will be said on this in the Latopolitan Nome, and regarding the Lapidotus fish.

### NOME VII. CYNOPOLIS,

->THAT IS,<-

->The Prefecture of Cynopolis, in Coptic: ⲡⲓϩⲓⲃ ⲛⲟⲓⲱⲧ<-
<note>Coptic: "Pi-hib n-oiōt," meaning "The Territory of the Dog."</note>

<margin>The nature of dogs is very similar to that of Mercury.</margin>
This region is called the Prefecture of Dogs, as is its capital, the City of Dogs <note>Cynopolis</note>, because they pursued the worship of the dog there with the greatest devotion. This is why it is called in Coptic *The Territory of the Dog*. To understand this, it must be noted that **Anubis**, or **Mercury**, was represented in a "dog-shaped" form <note>original: "κυνόμορφον"</note> and worshipped as the god of the discovery of things. It was believed that he loved the bodies of dogs as being most similar to his own nature. For just as dogs are keen-scented and follow the tracks of wild beasts, so too they say Mercury sagaciously discovered various arts and letters necessary for the human race. Because of these benefits, he earned this divine deification <note>original: "ἀποθέωσιν"</note>. See **Diodorus Siculus** <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note> for more on this Mercury. Hear Strabo: *Next is the Cynopolite Nome, and the City of Dogs, in which Anubis is worshipped, and where a certain honor and sacred food are assigned to the dogs.* <note>original Greek: "Ἔξης δ᾿ ἔστιν ὁ κυνοπολίτης νομός..."</note>

<margin>Dog worship and food in this city.</margin>
<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of the deity Anubis, depicted with a jackal's head and a human body, standing on a small mound with plants. He faces left and wears a tall headdress with two upright feathers. Below the image frame is written: "The Nile" in Arabic [النيل].</image-desc>

The Cynopolite Nome follows, and the City of Dogs, in which Anubis is worshipped; honor is paid to the dogs, and a specific sacred food is established for them. Some now call this place **Manfalut** <note>original Arabic: "منفلوط"</note> or **Asyut** <note>original Arabic: "اسيوط"</note> near Minya. **Abulfeda** <note>A 14th-century Kurdish historian and geographer.</note> describes Manfalut as follows:

*Manfalut is a small town toward Upper Egypt; it is in Middle Upper Egypt, below Asyut at a distance of one stage, and it is on the western bank of the Nile, on the shore.* <note>original Arabic: "منفلوط بليده نحو الصعيد..."</note>

<margin>☩ Manfalut <note>original: منفلوط</note></margin>
<margin>Al-Minya <note>original: المني</note></margin>
Manfalut is a small city toward the sea, located in Middle Egypt <note>original: "Said Media"</note>, about one stage <term>stage: translation of "margala" (marhala), a day's journey of about 25-30 miles.</term> below Asyut; it is situated in the western desert of the Nile, upon the bank of the river. Others believe this city is now called Al-Minya <note>original: "Almonni"</note>; but it is more likely that, as we said, Asyut is the true and ancient Cynopolis <note>Cynopolis: Greek for "City of the Dog," dedicated to the god Anubis.</note>. This is demonstrated by both its longitude and latitude in the works of Abulfeda <note>A 14th-century Arab geographer and prince.</note>, which match those of Ptolemy, as will be seen from the map of Egypt. Furthermore, the Coptic word **ouhor**, which means "Dog" in our Lexicon <note>original: "Onomastico"; ⲟⲩϩⲟⲣ is Coptic for dog.</note>, demonstrates this more clearly than light itself. The figure usually worshiped here was the one previously mentioned, which we also took from the Bembine Table <note>The Bembine Tablet or Mensa Isiaca, a famous Roman-era bronze tablet depicting Egyptian-style religious rites.</note>.

# THE EIGHTH NOME. HERMOPOLIS,

->THAT IS<-

## The Hermopolitan Prefecture, in Coptic: Tabirethon. ☩ <note>original: ⲧⲁⲃⲓⲣⲏⲑⲱⲛ</note>

This prefecture was named after the worship of Mercury, Hermopolis <note>Greek: Ἑρμόπολις, meaning "City of Hermes."</note>. In the Coptic language, it is called the Territory of Thoth; for we have shown elsewhere at length that **Thoth** <note>original: ⲑⲱⲑ</note> refers to Mercury. Mercury was worshiped in this place for exactly the same reason we mentioned for his worship in the Cynopolitan prefecture. The image was also nearly the same; and today its name is Beni Suef <note>original: بنیسویف "Baniſuaif."</note>.

# THE NINTH NOME. ANTINOUS,

->THAT IS,<-

## The Antinoopolitan Prefecture, in Coptic: Tabirikantinou. ☩ <note>original: ⲧⲁⲃⲓⲣⲓⲕⲁⲛⲧⲓⲛⲱⲟⲩ</note>

This city is called Antinous, known by the Arabs as Ansena <note>original: انصنا "Anſena"</note>, or the City of Antinous <note>Greek: Ἀντινόου πόλις</note>. According to Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century author of a geographical dictionary.</note>, it was called Adrianopolis by some. It is named Antinoopolis after Antinous, the armor-bearer of Jove <note>A reference to the favorite of Emperor Hadrian who drowned in the Nile and was subsequently deified.</note>, who was translated into the heavens; many confuse him with Horus. For this reason, they maintain that Horus was usually worshiped here in the form of Sigalion <note>Sigalion: A name for Harpocrates, the god of silence, often shown with a finger to his lips.</note>; so says Pausanias in his *Description of Corinth*. Whatever the case, it is certain that the Greeks wove all their fables into the mythology of the Egyptians through a kind of parallel reasoning. But concerning these matters, consult our *Egyptian Mystagogy*.

# THE TENTH NOME. LATONOPOLIS,

## THAT IS,

->*The Latonopolitan Prefecture, in Coptic:* Tabir n-te Leton<- <note>original Coptic: ⲧⲃⲓⲣ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲗⲏⲧⲱⲛ</note>

<margin>The worship of Latona, or the Goddess who presides over childbirth.</margin>
This city is called by Stephanus <note>Stephanus of Byzantium, a 6th-century grammarian.</note> *the City of Latona* <note>original Greek: τῆς Λητῶς πόλις</note>, and in Coptic, *the City of Latona* <note>original Coptic: ⲃⲁⲕⲓ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉ Ⲗⲁⲧⲱⲛ</note>. Moreover, Latona—or in Greek, *Leto* <note>original Greek: Λητὼ</note>—is nothing other than the goddess of childbirth, whom Strabo teaches us the Egyptians worshiped here. Herodotus also states that Isis gave birth to Horus in this place. Thus, it is no wonder that the Greeks take Isis and Latona to be the same, since Isis is also worshiped among the Egyptians as the goddess of childbirth, according to Diodorus. However, since this goddess is treated at great length in the *Pantheon of the Hebrews*, chapter 16—where we showed that the Moon, Isis, Ilythia, Lilith, Anacitis, Cabar, Lucina, and Latona are one and the same goddess—we refer the reader there. This city is now called *Esna* <note>original Arabic: اسنا</note> by the Arabs, which Abulfeda describes in these words:

> *Esna is a town furnished with baths and marketplaces; it is [situated] in relation to Aswan and Qus on the western bank, though it is closer to the city of Qus; it is most fertile with palms, vines, and grain.* <note>original Arabic: واسنا بلده بها حمامات واسواق وهي من اسوان وتوقن في بر الغرب وهي الي قوص اقرب وانها نخيل وكروم ومزدرع</note>

# CHAPTER V.

## DISTRIBUTION III.

### Of Upper Egypt into its Nomes.

# THE FIRST NOME. THEBES,

## THAT IS

->*The Theban Prefecture, in Coptic:* Tabir n-te Ban<- <note>original Coptic: ⲧⲃⲓⲣ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲃⲁⲛ</note>

Egyptian Thebes, the metropolis of the Thebaid, is one of the most celebrated cities of Egypt, renowned in the monuments of the most ancient writers. Just as it has been distinguished by various titles and names at all times, so too has it produced the greatest confusion among authors. Strabo calls it *Diospolis* <note>original Greek: Διόσπολιν, meaning "City of Zeus" (Amun)</note>; Stephanus calls it *the hundred-gated* <note>original Greek: ἑκατόμπυλον</note>; and Diodorus calls it *Busiris*. Many authors confuse it with Syene <note>Modern Aswan.</note>, which the Ethiopians call *Siris*, and the Arabs call now *Esna*, now *Asyut*, and now *Aswan*. This similarity of names has produced no small amount of difficulty for authors; therefore, let us finally rescue the truth from such great confusion.

<meta>Continuity: Following the description of Esna (Latonopolis), Kircher moves further south to discuss the city of Aswan, which he identifies with the ancient city of Thebes. This marks the transition into the geography of the Upper Thebaid.</meta>

<header>TREATISE I. CHOROGRAPHY OF EGYPT. CHAPTER II.</header>

<margin>Many cities in Egypt were "double."</margin>
It should be noted that in Egypt, almost most of the cities were "doubled," which is seen not only in the works of Ptolemy—who lists two "Cities of Zeus" <note>original: *Diospoles*</note>, two "Cities of Hermes" <note>original: *Hermopoles*</note>, two "Cities of Aphrodite" <note>original: *Aphroditopoles*</note>, and "Cities of Heracles" <note>original: *Heracleopoles*</note>, etc.—but this was also very common among the Arabs. Thus, they recorded two Memphises, two Efmums, two Asyuts, two Esnas, two Aswans, and so on. No small difficulty arises from this, as one is frequently confused with the other, a problem especially prevalent among the Arabs, who are enemies of clear distinctions. Indeed, I have seen that such difficulties can be overcome by no other means than a diligent and parallel comparison of one to the other, based both on the monuments of antiquity and on the longitude and latitude of the same cities. I say, therefore, that there are two cities in Egypt called *Aswan* <note>original Arabic: اسوان</note>. One we have said is the same as Arsinoë; the other is further upstream, which we have said is the same as the most famous city of Thebes, restored from its very ruins. What moves me to assert this is, first, the massive collection of antiquities surviving in Aswan, about which Abulfeda and Salmasius write thus:

->Aswan is a city in Upper Egypt on the eastern bank. In it is the famous *Barba* <note>original: *Berbe*; a term used by Arab authors to refer to ancient Egyptian temples</note>, which is among the greatest monuments of the ancients in Egypt, decorated and carved; the multitude of images found upon it is a marvel to behold.<-

<margin>Monuments of antiquity in Aswan.</margin>
Aswan is a city of the upper Thebaid on the side of the eastern desert, in which is that most famous pyramid <note>Kircher likely refers to a large temple structure or pylon, as Aswan is not known for major pyramids</note>, which is the greatest monument of primeval antiquity because of the size of the carved stones and the multitude of figures seen upon it. Moreover, Strabo, Diodorus, and Herodotus testify that there were many pyramids and obelisks there, some of which survive, while others were shamefully cast down and fell by the madness of Cambyses <note>The Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE, often accused by ancient historians of destroying temples</note>. Strabo calls it the "City of a Hundred Gates," which Homer also praises in these words:

<margin>Homer.</margin>
> There the life-giving earth produces its most abundant fruits;
> A hundred gates enclose the city, and through each,
> two hundred men with horses and chariots drive forth.
<note>original Greek: Τῇ πλᾶσα φέρει ζείδωρος ἄρουρα / Καὶ Αἰθ’ ἑκατόμπυλοί εἰσι διηκόσιοι δ’ ἐκ ἑκάστη / Ἀνέρες ἐξοιχνεῦσι, σὺν ἵπποισιν καὶ ὄχεσφιν. / Kircher also provides a Latin verse translation by the same meaning.</note>

<margin>Strabo.</margin>
Strabo describes this city exactly and with curiosity, as an eyewitness <note>original Greek: ἀυτὸπτης</note> of all the surviving monuments within it.

There are others who place the metropolis of all Egypt here; for traces of its greatness survive, with a length of nearly 80 stadia <note>approximately 9 miles</note>. It has many temples, largely mutilated by Cambyses. It is now inhabited in villages; part of it is in Arabia <note>referring to the Eastern Bank of the Nile</note>, where the city itself is, and part is in the "Further Region" <note>the Western Bank</note>, where the Memnonium is located. <margin>Two Colossi in this city.</margin> Since there were two Colossi here, made of solid stone and standing near each other, one still remains, but the upper parts of the other have fallen from its seat, as the story goes, due to an earthquake. <margin>A sound heard around the Colossus.</margin> It was also believed that once every day, a certain sound, like a small blow, was emitted from the part that remained on the seat and base. I myself, while I was present with Aelius Gallus <note>The Roman prefect of Egypt, c. 25 BCE</note>, along with a great multitude of friends and soldiers who were with him, heard the sound around the first hour. Whether it was emitted from the base, or from the Colossus, or indeed from one of the bystanders, I cannot say for certain; due to the uncertainty of the cause, one might choose to believe anything rather than that a sound is emitted from stones so composed. Above the Memnonium <note>The temple complex associated with the "singing" Colossi of Memnon</note> are the burial places of the Kings in certain caves cut into the stone, about forty in number... <meta>catchword: mi- [likely *miranda*, "wonderful things"]</meta>

<summary>Kircher discusses the duplication of city names in Egypt and identifies Aswan as the site of ancient Thebes, citing its massive ruins, temples, and the "singing" Colossi of Memnon described by Strabo.</summary>
<keywords>Aswan, Thebes, Memnonium, Colossi of Memnon, Strabo, Homer, Cambyses, Egyptian geography, ancient monuments</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Kircher's geographic survey of Upper Egypt, specifically focusing on the identity of the city of Aswan (Syene) and its relationship to ancient Thebes, followed by the description of the Second Nome (Apollopolis).</meta>

<header>CHAPTER V. 40 THE ISIAIC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS</header>

<margin>Double Syene.</margin>
XL <note>Referring to the forty monuments or temples mentioned in the previous page</note> built in a marvelous way, and truly worthy of being seen; next to these, on certain Obelisks, are inscriptions that declare the wealth and power of those Kings. From Strabo’s description, both the size and the fame and magnificence of the city of Thebes are sufficiently clear. All these details fit modern Aswan; indeed, what the Greeks call Thebes, the Copts call *Souan* <note>original Coptic: Ⲥⲟⲩⲁⲛ</note> or Suan, from which the Arabs seem to have borrowed their name, only prefixing an *A* before *Suan*. It follows that Aswan has the same latitude as Thebes, which Ptolemy assigns, and which Syene has; since Syene is exactly the same as *Souan*, from which name, though corrupted, it obtains its own. Thus we infer that the Thebes of the Greeks, the *Souan* of the Copts, and the *Asuan* of the Arabs were formerly exactly the same as Syene—or more correctly *Suane*—whatever other authors may bring forward to the contrary. For I believe this difference arose because, as Strabo testifies, Syene was "double": one on the borders of Ethiopia, and the other below Elephantine Island, which we say is the same as Aswan.

<margin>The size of Thebes.</margin>
For the city of Thebes was once so vast that it easily spanned 80 stadia <note>approximately 9 miles or 15 kilometers</note> in length, according to Strabo. Hence it is no wonder that it extended almost an entire degree of latitude. Moreover, it was called by the Greeks "the City of Zeus" <note>original Greek: Διὸς πόλιν (*Diospolis*)</note> because of the worship of Jupiter <note>the Egyptian god Amun, whom the Greeks identified with Zeus/Jupiter</note>, which was peculiar to this place. I also find in Herodotus that the Bull was sacred to this location. Furthermore, Ammianus Marcellinus testifies that a temple of Serapis existed here; and Strabo teaches that many obelisks were erected there in honor of the Sun. But whoever desires more concerning the magnitude of Thebes should consult Diodorus Siculus, Book 1, Chapter 6.

---

# DISTRICT II. APOLLOPOLIS,
## THAT IS,
### *The Apollopolitan Prefecture.*

<margin>Horus and Apollo are the same.</margin>
The name itself shows that Apollo was worshipped in this prefecture. However, for the Copts, Apollo is the same as Horus, the author of the Harmony of the World, as we declare at length in our *Egyptian Mystagogy*. For this reason, the ancients used to consecrate this part of Egypt to Horus and adore him as a propitious deity and an "opponent of the god" <note>original Greek: ἀντίθεον (*antitheon*)</note> Typhon. For this reason, they also held the Crocodile in the greatest hatred, asserting that Typhon had turned into one; when plotting snares for Horus, he fled from the face of Osiris and Isis who were pursuing him. Let us hear Strabo: "On the opposite side is the City of Hawks <note>original Greek: ἱεράκων πόλις (*Hierakonpolis*)</note> where they worship a hawk; then the City of Apollo <note>original Greek: Ἀπόλλωνος πόλις (*Apollinopolis*)</note>, which is also hostile to crocodiles."

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration framed in a black rectangle depicts a figure in Egyptian-style dress standing in profile, facing left. The figure wears a tall headdress and a patterned garment with a diamond grid. He holds a long staff or scepter topped with a symbol. The image is set into the text block, with lines of text flowing to its right.</image-desc>

In the further region is the City of Hawks, where the Hawk is worshipped; then the City of Apollo, which is also an enemy to the Crocodiles. See the rest in Plutarch’s book *On Osiris and Isis*. Also, the primary city of this District is Phontis, which in Coptic <note>original Coptic: Ⲫⲛⲧ (*Phnt*)</note> means nothing other than "Sublime God," which they said Horus was; today in Arabic it is called *Richmuni* <note>original Arabic: رخموني</note>.

<summary>Kircher argues that the ancient city of Thebes is identical to Syene and modern Aswan, citing its massive size and religious importance. He then begins describing the Second Nome (Apollopolis), identifying Apollo with the Egyptian Horus and explaining the religious rivalry between the hawk (Horus) and the crocodile (Typhon).</summary>
<keywords>Thebes, Aswan, Syene, Strabo, Horus, Apollo, Typhon, Hierakonpolis, Coptic, Egyptian geography, mythology</keywords>

# NOME III. PANOPOLIS,
## THAT IS
### The Panopolitan Prefecture, in Coptic <term>ⲧⲁϣⲓⲣ ⲙ̀ⲡⲁⲛⲟⲥ</term>

<margin>The worship of Pan.</margin>
The very name of this prefecture and its capital teaches us that Pan was worshiped here. It is likely that they practiced the same religion as the inhabitants of Mendes; that is, they worshiped him in the form of a Goat or a Satyr. In Coptic it is called *Panahe* <term>ⲡⲁⲛⲁϩⲉ</term>, and in Arabic *Bana* <term>بنا</term>. However, *Panahe* is the same as "the one who sees," as if you were to say "the city of the all-seeing one"—whom we call Pan, and the Copts call Osiris, the God of the entire universe who fills all things with his fertile rays. See this discussed more extensively in our *Mystagogia*.

---

# NOME IV. COPTOS,
## THAT IS,
### The Coptic Prefecture, in Coptic <term>ⲧⲁϣⲓⲣ ⲛ̀ⲕⲉⲃⲧ</term>

This was one of the first prefectures of all Egypt, founded by Mizraim <note>original: Mesraim</note>, the son of Ham. The Egyptian Arabs generally call him *Kopt* <term>قبط</term>, while the Copts call him *Keft* <term>ⲕⲉⲃⲧ</term>. From this name, all of Egypt was subsequently called *Coptos*, or by the corrupted form *Giptos* <note>the root of the modern word "Egypt"</note>. Regarding this etymology, see what we have recorded in our *Coptic Prodromus*; but let us hear from the Arabic historian Gelaldinus <note>Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti, a 15th-century polymath</note>, who speaks thus in his history of the Kings of Egypt:

<margin>Gelaldinus in the history of the Kings of Egypt.</margin>
> واستخلف لبيصر ابنه مصر وحاز كل واحد من اخوة مصر قطعة من الارض لنفسه 
> سوي ارض مصر التي حازها لولده والعقب فلما كثر ولد مصر واولاد اولادهم قطع 
> مصر لكل واحد من ولده قطيعة حسب ما تقتضيه والي لقبه لهم هذا النيل قطعة لابنه 
> قبط وسكنها وبه سميت وما فوقها الي اسوان وما دونها الي الشرق والغرب

*And Mizraim, his son, succeeded Boiher <note>likely Beisar</note>, and he divided a portion of Egypt among each of his brothers, keeping for himself a small part of the land which he divided among his own sons. When the sons of Mizraim and their grandsons multiplied, he divided it further into single parts for each. That portion which is next to the Nile he gave to his son Copt—namely, the place Copt or Gipt—and he lived there, and the place was named Copt after him. Whatever is above Copt as far as Aswan or Thebes, and below it as far as Ashmunein <note>Efmun</note>, and whatever was contained within the eastern and western regions, was subjected to his rule.* The geographer Abulfeda <note>Abu al-Fida, a 14th-century prince and geographer</note> describes its location in this way:

<margin>The location of the City of Coptos.</margin>
> وقبط تحت قوص من بر الشرق علي بعض مرحلة من قوص والاقصي بليدة من قوص 
> ۞ علي الشرق فهي اقرب الي الجبل الذي

*Coptos is below Qus <note>Kaus</note> on the eastern side of the desert, at a distance of several stages <note>original: *Margalis*, likely the Arabic *marhala*, a day's journey</note> from Qus; its borders extend from Kauphe as far as Ashraff <note>Efchraph</note>, which is near the mountain of the Nile.* Strabo calls it a common marketplace for both Egyptians and Arabs, to which all Indian, Ethiopian, and Arabian goods are brought from the Red Sea.

It is now called <gloss>Qana</gloss> <note>original: Ⲕⲁⲛⲁ</note> by the Arabs, and as in former times, it is today very crowded with merchants gathering from all directions. Plutarch testifies that in Coptos, Osiris and Isis were worshiped together with Horus; he records that their statue represented one of them holding the genitals of Typhon <note>Typhon is the Greek name for Set, the god of chaos and desert storms</note> in one hand. See what we have handed down more extensively regarding Horus and his worship performed at Coptos in Treatise 3, chapter 7.

### NOME V. TENTYRA,
#### THAT IS
##### The Tentyrite Prefecture <gloss>Dandara</gloss> <note>original: تَنْدَرَة</note>, in Coptic <gloss>Tentyre</gloss> <note>original: ⲧⲉⲛⲧⲱⲣⲏ</gloss> or <gloss>Tantorep</gloss> <note>original: Ⲧⲁⲛⲧⲱⲣⲉⲡ</note>

<margin>The hatred of the Tentyrites for Crocodiles.</margin>
This prefecture is called **Tantorep** in Coptic and **Tanushir** <note>original: تندشير</note> in Arabic, which is the same as Tentyra, or Tenosra, or Tenothra. According to Strabo, the inhabitants of this place, unlike other Egyptians, exceedingly loathe the Crocodile and consider it the most hostile of all beasts. For while others may know the malice of this animal and judge it most dangerous to humankind, the Tentyrites track them down and kill them by every means, being imbued with a certain natural incantatory power over them. This was so much the case that when crocodiles were brought to Rome for spectacle, the Tentyrites themselves were in charge of them and controlled them. Furthermore, Strabo is the source for the fact that the Tentyrites also worshiped Venus <note>The goddess Hathor, whose great temple is at Dendera, was identified with Venus by the Greeks and Romans</note>. But let these remarks on this Nome suffice.

### NOME VI. LYCOPOLIS,
#### THAT IS
##### The Lycopolite Prefecture <gloss>Asyut</gloss> <note>original: أسيوط</note> or <gloss>Siout</gloss> <note>original: ⲥⲓⲱⲟⲩⲧ</gloss>.

<margin>Typhon worshiped under the form of a wolf.</margin>
The very etymology <note>"Lyco-polis" literally means "Wolf-city" in Greek</note> teaches that the inhabitants worshiped the Wolf in this prefecture; Strabo mentions this metropolis and Nome. I have been able to find almost nothing among authors regarding the reason and causes for the wolf-worship, unless we say that Typhon (whom Plutarch says was transformed at times into a Wolf, sometimes into a Crocodile, and now into a donkey) was appeased by certain sacrifices as an <term>Averruncus</term> <note>A deity worshiped specifically to avert his own potential malice or bad luck</note> and was worshiped under the lupine form. But these matters must be left to the judgment of the learned; therefore, let us move on to other things.

### NOME VII. APHRODITOPOLIS,
#### THAT IS
##### The Aphrodisian Prefecture.

<margin>The origin of the worship of Venus.</margin>
The etymology teaches that the worship of Venus was established in this prefecture, since Aphrodite is nothing other than Venus; Strabo describes it thus: <note>original Greek: "After Memphis is the city of Akanthos, similarly as in Libya, and the temple of Osiris, and the grove of Akanthos. Then the Thebaic region follows, then Koptos; then the Aphroditopolite nome and its namesake city."</note>

### NOME VIII. LATOPOLIS,
->THAT IS,<-
->*The Latopolitan Prefecture.*<-

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration showing a large fish (a Latus, or Nile Perch) with prominent scales and fins, enclosed within a rectangular border.</image-desc>
This prefecture is called Latopolitan from the worship of the Latus fish, which Plutarch says is <gloss>eared</gloss> <note>original Greek: ὠτύλωτον; likely referring to the large gill covers or opercula of the Nile Perch</note>. It earned this name because, just like the Oxyrhynchus and the Lepidotus, so too this Latus tasted of the genitals of Osiris when they were thrown into the Nile by Typhon <note>Typhon is the Greek name for Set, the god of chaos, who murdered his brother Osiris</note>.
<margin>Strabo.</margin>
Strabo: <gloss>Therefore, there are certain animals that all Egyptians worship in common; among the land animals, the ox, the dog, and the cat; among the birds, two, the hawk and the ibis. Of the aquatic animals, two: the lepidotus fish and the oxyrhynchus. But there are others they honor or despise individually, just as the Saites and Thebans honor the sheep, while the Latopolitans honor the Latus, which is a certain fish in the Nile.</gloss> <note>original Greek: τινὰ μὲν οὖν τῶν ζώων ἅπαντες κοινῇ τιμῶσιν...</note> There are indeed certain animals that all Egyptians worship: of the land creatures, three: the ox, the dog, and the cat; of the winged ones, the hawk and the ibis; of the aquatic ones, the Lepidotus fish and the Oxyrhynchus. There are also those worshiped separately: thus the Saites and Thebans worship the sheep, but the Latopolitans worship the Latus, which is a certain fish in the Nile. Some confuse this Nome with Latonopolis, but they do so incorrectly; for the latter finds its name from the goddess Latona, while the former from the worship of the Latus fish.

Strabo teaches that Abydos was the greatest city in Egypt after Thebes, and the remarkable monuments left in it teach the same, about which authors everywhere report wonders: see Strabo, Diodorus, and Herodotus. This Nome is also the same as the Memnonian Nome: for in this Abydos is the Palace of Memnon (whom some confuse with Ismandes <note>A name sometimes associated with the Pharaoh Amenemhat III</note>), wonderfully constructed from solid stone. There is also a certain admirable spring there, positioned deep in the earth...

# NOME X. ANTAEOPOLITES,
## THAT IS,
### The Antaeopolitan Prefecture.

This prefecture is contained, according to the testimony of Ptolemy, below the island of Elephantine, on the eastern side of which Antaeus is encountered, the city from which the Nome takes its name. This is also called by some **Cnuphis** and in Coptic **Kaneb** <note>original Coptic: ⲕⲁⲛⲉⲃ</note>, by which name they call the idol Canopus; from this I gather that Canopus was perhaps worshiped here somewhere, as in the prefecture of Menelaus. Certainly, Strabo teaches that there was a very famous temple of **Cnubis** <note>A Greek rendering of the Egyptian ram-god Khnum</note> in this city: *Syene*, he says, and Elephantine—one is a city on the borders of Ethiopia and Egypt; the other is an island situated in the Nile half a stadium in front of Syene, and in it is a city which has the temple of Cnuphis and a **Nilometer** <note>term: Nilometrium; a structure used for measuring the clarity and water level of the Nile during the annual flood</note>. And these are the things which I thought should be said briefly concerning the ancient Nomes of the Egyptians, as much as the obscurity of the matter permitted.

In the partition of these Nomes, we have not followed Ptolemy, but rather the primeval partition of the first Kings, extracted from various Coptic and Arabic fragments. For Ptolemy’s partition—restored anew by the Ptolemaic Kings after the Egyptian empire had already been destroyed by Cambyses <note>The Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE</note>—differs much from the earlier one, as will be evident to anyone looking at the maps of the individual partitions placed here. The Egyptians, with deliberate effort and a certain hidden plan for propagating their religion, first mystically divided the whole of Egypt into 30 territories, as was said above; the Ptolemies then divided it again into 40 for the convenience of government. Finally, the Muslims, just as they devised one division after another, were also the first to introduce the corruption of the ancient names, as is clear in the annexed figure 2 of the diagram. But so that everything may be proposed more exactly, in the following table the longitudes and latitudes...

<header>CHAPTER VI. 48 THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE</header>

### C H A P T E R VI.

->On the Nile and its origin.<-

<margin>Various Names of the Nile.</margin>
The **N**ile is the greatest river in all the world. It is called the "Ocean" by Berosus <note>A Babylonian priest and historian</note>, "Egypt" by Xenophon, "Osiris" by Plutarch, "Triton" by Apollonius, "Astraphon" by Pliny, the "Eagle" by Diodorus, "Melas" <note>Meaning "Black"</note> by Eustathius, "Chrysorrhoas" <note>Meaning "Golden-flowing"</note> by Cedrenus, "Syene" by Dionysius, and the Holy Scriptures, along with the Hebrews, call it "Gihon" and "Sihor." To speak with Aristides: *The Nile is, among many other most beautiful things, the greatest and a divine pleasure, far surpassing all things.* <note>original Greek: "Νεῖλος ἐκ πολλῶν μὲν ἄλλων καλλίστων ἡ μεγίστη καὶ θείας ἡδονῆ, καὶ τοῦ πᾶσι πολὺ νικῶν."</note> The Nile, than which no river is better, more beautiful, or larger, far surpasses all others whether you consider its utility or its certain divine loveliness. Drawing its origin from the lakes **Zambri** and **Zaire** <note>Historical names for the Great Lakes of Africa</note> near the Mountains of the Moon, it traverses the entire width of the Torrid Zone <note>The tropics</note> with immense windings. Finally, burdened with a massive weight of waters collected from all sides, it unloads its burden near Memphis, as if distributing it, through seven branches into the sea.

<margin>Properties of the Nile.</margin>
Watering the entire land of Egypt from both banks, as if raining from the earth (as Nazianzenus <note>St. Gregory of Nazianzus</note> says), it brings an abundance of all good things along with the fertile silt of the Nile. It is seen to be endowed by nature with three primary prerogatives above all other rivers.

<margin>Diodorus, Book 1, Chapter 3.</margin>
First, it does not exhale an "aura" <note>Meaning swampy or foul-smelling vapors</note>; as a result, Egypt enjoys healthy air, subject to no rains, clouds, or other thick atmospheric impressions, but rather a continuous countenance of serene sky.

<margin>Fertility of the Nile.</margin>
Furthermore, it is always quiet and tranquil, without any surges or storms of waves, so that it provides a navigation that is not only pleasant but also free from all dangers for those traveling to and fro. Finally, its fertility is found to be such that it renders not only the land, but also the beasts of burden and cattle, and even humans of both sexes, fertile to the point of a miracle. For this reason, it once surpassed almost all nations of the world in the number of its people; nor even now does it yield to other nations in multitude. For **Diodorus** affirms that there were other notable towns—which we have set before your eyes above—totaling more than eighteen thousand in Egypt, and that the sacred books contain this record.

<margin>Book 1, Chap. 3.</margin>
<margin>18,000 cities formerly in Egypt.</margin>
In the time of Ptolemy son of Lagus <note>Ptolemy I, founder of the Ptolemaic Kingdom</note>, more than three thousand cities were counted, which lasted until the age of Diodorus. The aforementioned **Diodorus** says that in ancient times the number of the entire population was seventeen hundred thousand <note>1,700,000</note>; while in his own time, no fewer than thirteen hundred thousand existed.

<margin>Number of the Egyptian people: 1,710,000.</margin>
This prodigious multitude of humans indeed knows no other cause but the continuous use and drinking of the prolific river water which the Egyptians enjoyed. Because of this, women were not content with one, two, or three children, but frequently brought forth six, seven, or eight offspring in a single birth—something which the Hebrew commentators on Exodus also mention.

<margin>Fertility of women.</margin>
Therefore, it should be a wonder to no one that the propagation of the children of Israel was so immense during the span of nearly two hundred years that they inhabited Egypt; nor is it a wonder that the Egyptian Kings were able to build those monuments of unusual magnificence which we marvel at daily, and the proud pyramids of their glory, and other expeditions, which without an immense and nearly infinite abundance of men...

<summary>This page describes the Nile River's numerous names, its geographic origins in Central Africa, and its unique physical properties that foster exceptional health and fertility. Kircher argues that the river's miraculous qualities explain Egypt's massive historical population and its ability to construct monumental architecture like the pyramids.</summary>
<keywords>Nile River, Egyptian geography, Diodorus Siculus, Mountains of the Moon, population of ancient Egypt, fertility, Zambri, Zaire, Memphis</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Nile’s divine status and its unique physical properties. It moves from the river's geographical origins discussed on the previous page to its symbolic and mythological significance, specifically how its unique behavior—watering the land without rainfall—led ancient peoples to view it as a celestial or divine entity.</meta>

<header>TREATISE I. GEOGRAPHY OF EGYPT. CHAPTER VI</header>

<margin>Egypt enjoys perpetual serenity.</margin>
<margin>Egypt is shaped like an arm, whose median vein is represented by the Nile.</margin>
...pious things could least be done, he could have accomplished. But on these matters consult *Diodorus* <note>Diodorus Siculus, a first-century BCE Greek historian</note> who treats them at length. Furthermore, the ancient Egyptian sages, when they looked upon a river endowed with such unusual gifts of nature, thought it possessed divine power and recorded it in the list of the foremost Gods. To the Nile—as *Aristides* <note>Aelius Aristides, a second-century Greek orator</note> drew (I think) from someone <gloss>among the uninitiated</gloss> <note>original Greek: τῷ ἐκ ἀμυήτων</note>—the solemn festivals of the Egyptians, the masks of the *Isiacs* <note>Followers of the goddess Isis</note>, and many other sacrifices were dedicated and consecrated; as will be seen in the course of the work. Indeed, for this single reason, this unique river in all the lands of Egypt seems to have been held in such great honor and veneration by the Gentiles who lacked the light of faith; for they attribute every blessing to it: that they never feel the earth shake, that they are free from the plague, that they enjoy healthy air, and that it never happens that their land is thrown into disorder by celestial floods or overwhelmed by massive rain. In these matters, they even found Greek supporters; for so says *Aristides* in his Egyptian eclogue, from which we also took the previous points: <gloss>How the land is immune to both earthquakes and floods from the sky because this path was hidden from the Greeks.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ὡς δὲ καὶ σεισμοῖς καὶ τοῖς ἐξ οὐρανῦ κατακλυσμοῖς ἀνάλωτος ἡ χώρα διὰ τὸ τὴν ὁδὸν ταύτην παρ’ Ἕλληνας ἔλαθεν.</note> For this reason, they represented it with innumerable symbols and hieroglyphic marks. They called it the "efflux of *Osiris*," according to *Plutarch*, or as *Abenephius* <note>An Arabic author often cited by Kircher for Hermetic lore</note> says, the "arm of *Osiris*," which provides all good things. For when they observed that the whole stretch of Egypt was enclosed by a continuous series of mountains on both sides, they noted that its length resembled the shape of an arm, with the multiple branches of the *Nile* going off like a palm and fingers. They looked upon the *Nile* moreover as nothing less than a certain Median or "basilic" vein <note>In ancient medicine, the "basilic" or "median" vein was a major vessel in the arm thought to have significant therapeutic importance</note> springing from the heart of *Osiris*, permeating all things with its life-giving liquid, moving, fertilizing, and filling them with an abundance of all goods. From this, they seem to have taken the occasion to represent the overflowing abundance of all goods hieroglyphically by placing that arm (than which nothing is more frequent on the Obelisks), which, with its extended form of fingers, indicates a certain profuse liberality. This is supported by the records of the ancient poets, who for the same reason attribute such various titles to the *Nile*. *Homer* surely demonstrates that this river fell from heaven or the lap of *Jove* <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> in the following verse:

> <gloss>For it is not yet your fate to see your friends... until you have come back once more to the water of the Egyptus, the river that falls from Zeus.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Οὐ γὰρ ἔτι πρὶν μοῖρα φίλους ἰδέειν / Πρὶν γ’ ὅταν Αἰγύπτοιο Διιπετέος ποτάμοιο / Αὖθις ὕδωρ ἔλθῃς. From the Odyssey, Book 4.</note>

*Adamus Fumanus* <note>A 16th-century Italian scholar and poet</note> agrees with this, who, in his *Dialogue on the Nile* printed by Herwagen at Basel, disapproves of the opinion of those who thought the *Nile* sprang forth in heaven, using these words:

<gloss>One might marvel at those who thought the river—which Homer called the river Egypt and said was "fallen from Zeus"—was said to be so because its sources were hidden, and that according to the Egyptians, they were in heaven and flowed from heaven.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Θαυμάσειε τις τὸν ποταμὸν οἰηθέντας, ὃν Ὅμηρος Αἴγυπτον ποταμὸν ἔκληζε Διιπετῆ εἰρῆσθαι διὰ τὸ ἀφανεῖς ἔχειν τὰς πηγὰς καὶ τοὺς Αἰγυπτίους ἐν οὐρανῷ καὶ οὐρανόθεν ῥεῖν.</note>

<margin>The Nile is believed by the ancients to have fallen from Jove or from heaven.</margin>
*One might indeed marvel*, he says, at those who thought the river, which *Homer* called *Egypt*, was called <term>Διιπετὴς</term> <note>Diipetes: literally "fallen from Zeus"</note>, that is, "fallen from *Jove*", because it had hidden sources; and that according to the opinion of the Egyptians, it had them in heaven and flowed from heaven.

<margin>Various attributes of the Nile.</margin>
Therefore, not only the Egyptians but also the later Greek philologists believed the *Nile* fell from *Jove* out of heaven; hence some honored it as the "gift of *Jove*," others as the "tear of the Gods," others the "vein of paradise," the "seed of the Gods," the "fishpond of *Proteus*," the "husband of *Isis*," and with innumerable other epithets, which to...

<margin>
What the Ethiopians call the Nile
</margin>
...peoples have also spread; for the Ethiopians, sharing in its fecundity, everywhere call it: *Ankaata marat schamatavvi*, which means, the **Source of celestial waters**. The Arabic poets Ibn al-Farid and al-Busiri <note>Kircher's "Eldebug" likely refers to the famous poet Al-Busiri</note>, in their Arabic verses which I possess, everywhere call the Nile **Life of the Earth** <note>original Arabic: حياة الأرض, gjateallarthim</note>.

<margin>
Epithets used by the Arabic poets:
</margin>

<margin>
Isaiah ch. 23.
</margin>

The ancient Greeks hinted at this mystical fertility in the very name **Neilos** <note>original Greek: Νειλος</note>; for when this is resolved into numbers according to the <term>gematria</term> <note>original: τελωσιαν; a system where letters represent numbers to find hidden meanings</note> or Cabalistic method, it yields the same number as the days of the year, namely 365, as appears in the table placed here. Countless similar things could be said of the Nile here, but since they are explained elsewhere in various places, we deliberately remain silent so as not to seem to be piling everything together in one place in a confused manner.

## CHAPTER VII.
### On the origin and causes of the rise of the Nile.

<margin>
The difficulty of investigating the rise of the Nile.
</margin>
**O**rder now requires that, after we have briefly discussed the names and various properties of the Nile, we should also discuss its rising and its causes, which rightly ought to hold the chief place in this subject. It is unknown to no one how much that impenetrable cataclysm of the Nile has exhausted the greatest minds of philosophers, and what great disputes it has stirred up in the schools at all times; so much so that anyone could more easily find someone to refute his own opinion than someone to follow it. Scarcely has anyone brought an idea forward without the others immediately going in every other direction and testifying that it did not seem right to them. Therefore, we have added a few more points from various authors available to us who wished to leave a record of this matter and this diversity of opinions.

<margin>
Why did the Egyptian Priests represent the flooding of the Nile hieroglyphically with three urns?
</margin>
And first indeed, the Egyptian Priests, since they thought the rising of the Nile happened for three main causes, attributed three urns to the Nile, whereas for other rivers only one was used for each; as in that passage from Virgil <note>original: Maro</note>:

> *And father Inachus pouring forth the river from an engraved urn.*

<margin>
The first cause.
</margin>
Of these three causes, they asserted the first to be this: that the Egyptian earth generated water from itself and produced it most abundantly, being the nurse of its own moisture. For this reason, Timaeus the Mathematician called the source of the Nile the **Vial** <note>original: Phiala, meaning a bowl or vessel</note>; as if it contained within itself that power of water and did not borrow it from elsewhere. There is, however, a place in the Nile of the same name, so called from its shape, which has nothing to do with Timaeus’s "vial."

The source of the Nile, the Vial.

# SYNTAGMA ON THE CHOROGRAPHY OF EGYPT, CHAPTER VII.

...while the flooding of rivers usually occurs around winter, either from increased rains or melting snow, the land of Egypt alone—situated in the middle of the habitable earth like the pupil in an eye—is irrigated in mid-summer by a unique outpouring of waters. <margin>2. The Second Cause.</margin> Others have attributed the cause to the **Ocean**, from which a story says water overflows into Egypt during its time of growth. This was the primary opinion of **Euthymenes** and the Egyptian priests, as **Diodorus** <margin>Diodorus, Book 1</margin> testifies. They provide no other proof for this claim except that their authority is sufficient to be believed; they followed a knowledge of things handed down through successive tradition. They believe the river first flows from the Ocean at **Mount Atlas**, where it is called the **Dyrin**; from there it pools in a place called **Heptabolum**, flows out under the name **Nigrin**, soon forms the **Coloë** marsh, and then forms the **Austrosoban** and **Astaboras** rivers, until it breaks through upon reaching the cataract and, flowing through the plains of Egypt, finally receives the name of the **Nile**.

<margin>3. The Third Cause.</margin> They say the third cause is **rains**, because in the southern regions of Egypt, the waters are poured out most heavily at the time when the fertile Nile abounds with summer water—with **Democritus** testifying that the **Etesian winds** <note>Etesian winds: Periodical winds of the Mediterranean, blowing from the northwest in summer, which the ancients believed pushed clouds toward the Nile's sources.</note> carry the clouds there. And as **Eudoxus** records, the Egyptian priests believe those rains occur there due to **antiperistasis** <term>antiperistasis: a philosophical concept where a quality is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite, such as heat concentrating in the earth during winter</term>; for when it is summer for us, who live in places closer to the Tropic of Cancer, it is then winter for those who live closer to the Tropic of Capricorn. To these things **Thales** adds that the sea is driven back onto the banks by the force of the Etesian winds blowing against the river; about which **Lucretius** writes:

> Either because there are North winds at the river's mouths
> During the summer season, when the Etesian winds are carried forth.
> Blowing against the stream, they hold it back, and by forcing 
> The waves backward, they fill it up and compel them to stay.
> For without a doubt, these blasts are carried by an opposing 
> Wind, which are driven from the icy stars of the pole.
<note>original Latin: "Aut quia sunt aestate Aquilones ostia contra..." from Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura*, Book VI.</note>

The river begins to rise with the **New Moon** that occurs after the **Solstice**, increasing gradually and moderately as the Sun passes through **Cancer**; it floods most abundantly while the Sun proceeds into **Leo**, and soon recedes in **Virgo** by the same degrees it grew. Let these opinions on the three causes of the Nile’s increase suffice.

<margin>Book 1 of History, chapter 17</margin> Others, such as the **Troglodytes** <note>Troglodytes: A name used by ancient geographers for various cave-dwelling tribes south of Egypt, literally meaning "cave-dwellers."</note> as **Theophylacto Simocata** testifies, frequently say that there are cavities in those places; from this, one might reason that the Nile's flow swells as many springs flow together into one. <margin>The opinion of the Meroites concerning the Nile.</margin> Those who inhabit the island of the Nile called **Meroë** call the river the **Astapus**, a word which you might translate into Greek as **water flowing out of darkness** <note>original Greek: ἐκ τοῦ σκότου ὕδωρ, *ek tou skotou hydōr*</note>. For those people maintain that the nature of this river is incomprehensible. <margin>Anaxagoras.</margin> **Anaxagoras**, nicknamed "the Physicist," attributes the cause to melted snow on the **Ethiopian mountains**. <margin>Herodotus, Book 2</margin> **Herodotus** writes that the Nile is only as large as it appears when it is full. He claims that in winter, the Sun—revolving above **Libya**—draws a quantity of moist substance from the shallow waters of the Nile, and therefore the river flows more sparingly through the winter months. But if these things were true, why would the same Sun do to the Nile what it does to the other rivers of Libya? Yet no such thing is observed in them. It is therefore clear...

<margin>Ephorus's fiction regarding the Nile's flooding</margin>
...that historian spoke quite thoughtlessly in this place. Ephorus brings forward a plainly incredible reason: that all of Egypt is filled with subterranean rivers, and is cold, and by nature pumice-like or porous <note>original: "fistulosam," referring to a structure full of small tubes or channels</note>. He also claims it has large and perpetual cracks, through which it receives a great amount of moisture during the winter, and then at the beginning of the summer solstice, it emits this moisture from every part like a kind of sweat, and thus the Nile river overflows. <margin>Oenopides.</margin> Oenopides devises a cause based on the thinning and thickening of waters; he suggests that the latter constricts the waters in winter, while the former expands them in summer. <margin>Moses Bar-Cepha the Syrian, *Book on Paradise*.</margin> Moses Bar-Cepha the Syrian <note>A 9th-century bishop and prominent author of the Syriac Orthodox Church</note>, when treating the origin of the rivers of Paradise, derives the Nile from the Garden of Eden just like the other three rivers—the Pishon, the Tigris, and the Euphrates. He asserts that as soon as the Nile leaves the garden of delight, it sinks beneath the very shallows of the sea, and from there, spreading again through immense passages in the earth, it finally emerges in the lands of the Ethiopians; then, increased by rains and snows, it provides the cause and occasion for its growth and the Egyptian flood. But since his words are worthy of consideration, it seemed right to set them down here, translated from the Syriac manuscript into English:

> *And the river going out of Paradise to water it is immediately divided from there into four heads: The name of the first is Pishon, which runs through the whole land of Havilah, a land filled with gold and precious gems. The name of the second river is Gihon (which is also called the Nile); this runs through the whole land of Cush. For as soon as it leaves Paradise, it sinks below the deep shallows of the sea and the Ocean, and from there it emerges again through hidden passages of the earth in the Ethiopian mountains; increased by rains and snows, it is the cause of its growth and the Nilotic flood. And a little later, he continues his discourse with Syriac words, which we have rendered here in English for the sake of brevity. But someone will insist, he says, how can it be that those rivers, having departed from Paradise, are cast down beneath the shallows of the Ocean and the heart of the sea, and from there finally emerge in this land of ours? To this we first respond that many things we conceive of as impossible* <note>original: "ἀδύνατα" (adynata)</note> *are not at all so, for they are very easy for God. Indeed, that hidden course of the rivers and other things of this kind are a divine work, not a human one. Secondly, we also assert that Paradise is placed in a much loftier region than this earth of ours, and therefore it happens that from there the rivers fall through the immense precipices of subterranean channels, driven with such force and compressed that they are snatched under the bottom of the sea, from where they emerge again and bubble up in this world of ours. For those who labor to lead water to a high place and pour it out from tall, upright pipes like siphons, prepare for themselves a cataract or precipice from a long distance away with a steep and difficult descent; through this, while the waters are thrust down and pressed with great force for some distance, they finally leap upward through those pipes by the great violence with which they are urged from that headlong fall, and they pour out an overflowing abundance of water in every direction.*

And thus far Moses Bar-Cepha. These words, if you except a few, certainly do not disagree at all with the opinions of other philosophers. For after Plutarch, Agatharchides, and others, nearly all the Hebrew <term>Mekubalim</term> <note>original: "מקבלים" (Mekubalim) — literally "those who receive," referring to scholars of the Kabbalah or traditional mystical reception.</note> hold the same opinion, from whom Bar-Cepha seems to have been taught. For these are located nearly 400 miles from the position Ptolemy assigned, tending toward the Northern region.

<margin>Where the Nile originates.</margin>
The indigenous people believe that the Nile arises from the first of these lakes, and having emerged, is absorbed by the earth. However, Duarte Lopes <note>original: "Odoardus"</note> denies this, along with other inhabitants of these places, who unanimously affirm that as soon as the Nile has exited the lake, it is plunged through certain horrible and impenetrable valleys, through precipices inaccessible to men and pathless deserts. innermost bowels of the earth and swallowed by abysses. And from this first lake, located at about the twelfth degree of southern latitude, the Nile is born. Moreover, this lake is surrounded by mountains of impenetrable height, the larger of which, facing the Eastern region, are called the

**Cafates**, being mountains of saltpeter and silver on one side; on the other side are mountains from which the Nile, having tumbled northward for 400 miles, discharges itself into another lake located directly under the equatorial line (which the inhabitants call a "sea" on account of its vastness, for it is 220 miles wide). And migrating from this second lake, having measured a distance of 700 miles, the Nile marks out the island of **Meroë**. From here, indeed, increased by other rivers and carried down between narrow mountain valleys, and driven headlong through cataracts <note>original: "catadupas"</note> into the low plains of Egypt, it finally glides in a manifold whorl into the Mediterranean Sea. And from this account of Duarte Lopes, an eyewitness, and the Chorography of Pigafetta <note>Filippo Pigafetta, who published Lopes's travels</note>, it clearly appears that no other origin of the Nile can be assigned except Lake **Zambri**. He erred in this alone: that he did not show the proper springs of the Nile, which we shall provide further below. These springs, vomiting forth immense masses of water from all sides, especially toward the northern region, soon create another pool (or better, I should say, a sea) located under the equinoctial line, called **Zaire** by the natives, no smaller than its progenitor. The Nile is derived through the middle of this (just as the Rhine is through the middle of Lake Constance <note>original: "Acronii lacus"</note>, or the Rhone through the middle of Lake Geneva <note>original: "Losannæ lacus"</note>), and having exited here and been precipitated through various cataracts, it finally deposits itself in the sea in Egypt. But so that these things may be better understood,

From these, as if from the breasts of the **Megacosm** <note>The "Great World" or Universe, viewed as a living body</note>, the earth is nourished by a perennial bubbling, so that it might more easily carry out the generation of things. ### CHAPTER VII, 56 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS THE ISIAC TEMPLE

<margin>The origin of rivers.</margin>
Born from the peaks of the Alps in Savoy, Dauphiné, the Apennines, the Vosges, and other mountain ranges, while providing most abundant flows of water to each; this is the cause of the greatest lakes and rivers in all of Europe, such as the Rhine, Danube, Elbe, Po, Rhône, Inn, Ticino, Saône, Moselle, Meuse, and others which are well known from maps of rivers. Thus the Pyrenees and the mountains of Auvergne supply all of Spain and France; the Taurus and Imaus (or Caucasus) supply all of Asia, and other mountains supply most abundant rivers to other regions, as we shall demonstrate at length in our *Subterranean World* <note>original: "Mundo nostro subterraneo"; Kircher's 1665 work on the Earth's interior and hydrology</note> (God willing). By a similar reasoning, in Africa, which is most lacking in moisture, provident Nature placed two "storehouses" <term>penuaria|A storage room or larder for provisions, here used metaphorically for massive water reservoirs</term> of water common to all of Africa. One is located directly under the summer tropic of Cancer within the bowels of the Atlas Mountains, which supplies frequent rivers to the lands closer to the equator struggling with heat and dryness. The other she ordained nearly under the circle of Capricorn toward the parts beyond the equinox to revitalize areas withered by the Sun’s heat. Moreover, there are two lakes that serve as these sorts of storage casks of water: Zambre and Zaire <note>Historical names used by early cartographers for the great lakes of the African interior, like Lake Victoria or Lake Malawi</note>, as appears in the preceding map; the latter of these I would not be wrong to call the offspring of the former, Zambre, both of them swelling with such a great abundance of water that they seem to vomit forth not merely rivers, but seas.

<margin>The size and vastness of the lakes.</margin>
Especially Lake Zambre, which, established as if in the center and spreading out into the largest streams, contributes the most abundant flows of water to every part of the world as if from a very rich vein. To the North it gives the Nile; to the East the huge rivers Cuama <note>The Zambezi river</note> and Coavus; to the South the Zeila, Manhice, or Manhenssen; and finally to the West, the Zaire <note>The Congo river</note>. These rivers, irrigating the entire western region of Southern Africa—the kingdoms of Congo, Angola, Monomotapa, Matama, Bagamidri, and Agasymba, all the way to the Cape of Good Hope—rescue them from sterility with their fertile silt. Others water the entire interior region of the Abyssinians <note>Ethiopians</note>, and all those maritime shores bounded from the mouth of the Red Sea to the mouth of the Cuama, which include Malindi, Barnacassus, Kilwa, Mombasa, Mozimba, Mombara, Membaca, Mozambique, and other such monstrous <note>In the 17th-century sense of "vast" or "extraordinary"</note> kingdoms. Since this is the case, surely those people are greatly deceived who believe the Nile originates from some unknown, countless springs of the "Mountains of the Moon" <note>A legendary mountain range mentioned by Ptolemy as the source of the Nile</note> and from innumerable rivers; for to them, that entire part of Africa situated to the south and west was completely unknown, and thus they were ignorant of the true and proper sources, which have only first become known in our times. But so that we may set down such a notable history here, and so that the truth desired for so many centuries may finally be known, I will attempt to reveal what the proper sources of the Nile actually are.

## The true origin of the Nile newly detected.

<margin>The true origin of the Nile.</margin>
We have said in the preceding pages that Duarte Lopes <note>original: "Odoardum Lopez"; a Portuguese explorer whose accounts of Africa were highly influential</note> applied himself more than others to the discovery of the Nile's origin, and made it his sole aim to assign the proper sources of the Nile. However, Duarte was not an eyewitness of the true spring of the Nile, nor is his account sufficiently consistent with the facts; therefore, we must bring forward more accurate information regarding such a distinguished subject. At that very moment...

### CHAPTER VII. CHOROGRAPHY OF EGYPT. TREATISE I.

At the time when this most intricate and deeply perplexing matter occupied me, Father Francisco Carvalho, the procurator of India and Ethiopia, arrived here in Rome. From him, I was taught the truth through the manuscript of Father Pedro Páez <note>Pedro Páez (1564–1622) was a Spanish Jesuit missionary in Ethiopia who is credited as the first European to reach the source of the Blue Nile.</note>; I wished to record that same truth here for posterity, so that the truth might finally be restored to its luster after so many and such great fallacies and futile conjectures by the most serious authors. The matter is as follows: The province where the Nile rises is 
<margin>Description of the springs of the Nile.</margin>
called Agaos, neighboring the kingdom of Gojam; the land in which it rises is called Sagela. At the summit of a mountain, on a plain surrounded on all sides by trees, the diameter of the spring is one and a half feet wide, of unfathomable depth; it does not overflow its banks, but opens an exit for itself at the base of the mountain. As soon as it emerges from the bowels of the mountain, it spreads out into a river, which, being subsequently increased by other rivers, finally discharges itself into a lake 30 leagues long and 14 wide. When it emerges from there again, wandering through long windings of the lands, it returns almost to the same place from which it had come forth—namely, reaching the spring—and having turned its course back, it glides straight down through huge precipices and inaccessible rocks and turns toward the interior of Ethiopia. All these things are confirmed by the eyewitness testimony of Father Pedro Páez, a priest of our Society, who surveyed this true spring of the Nile together with the Emperor of Ethiopia; both of them, spurred by curiosity as well as a love of truth and accompanied by a great army, examined the said spring. Truly, since the said Father Pedro Páez treated this matter with the greatest diligence in his huge manuscript work on Ethiopian affairs, observing everything possible, 
<margin>Father Pedro Páez was the first observer and describer of the Nile with the Emperor of the Abyssinians.</margin>
I shall set down his words here, translated from Portuguese into Latin, so that the truth of the matter may be more clearly revealed. Thus he says:

> *After we have treated the fertility of the lands under the dominion of Prester John* <note>A legendary Christian patriarch and king, long sought by Europeans and often identified by this era with the Emperor of Ethiopia.</note>*, I thought I would do something worthwhile if I reported in this place something about the principal rivers and lakes of the lands subject to his empire. Among these, the first to present itself is that greatest and most famous river in the whole world, the Nile, which was an object of admiration not only among ancient and modern Doctors and the most serious authors, but of which Holy Scripture makes frequent mention in Genesis 2. It is called* 
> <margin>The Nile is called the Gihon.</margin>
> *Gihon* <note>original: "Gehon"</note>*, one of the four rivers watering paradise. Today it is called by the Ethiopians the Abaai* <note>The Blue Nile is still called the Abay in Ethiopia.</note>*; it has its origin in the Kingdom of Gojam in a territory called Sabala, whose inhabitants are called Agaos. They are Christians, although in the course of time, as the Church grew wild* <note>original: "sylvescente Ecclesia"; implying a decline in organized practice or a lapse into "primitive" states</note>*, they were imbued with various superstitions and, being corrupted by neighboring tribes and pagans, they differ little from them. The source of the Nile is situated in the western part of the Kingdom of Gojam at the summit of a valley which resembles a huge field, surrounded on all sides by mountain ridges. In the year 1618, on the 21st day of the month of April, when I was staying in this*
> <margin>The first spring of the Nile seen by Father Pedro Páez.</margin>
> *Kingdom together with the Emperor and his army, I ascended this place and diligently surveyed everything. I first found two round springs there, each about four palms* <term>palmis|A "palm" was a traditional unit of length based on the width of a human hand, roughly 3 to 4 inches.</term> *wide in diameter, and with the greatest pleasure of my soul I saw that which King Cyrus of the Persians, Cambyses, Alexander the Great, and that famous Julius Caesar could never achieve by any vows. The water of the spring is very clear and light, and most pleasing to the taste; it should be known, however, that neither of these two "eyes" of the spring has an exit on the highest plateau of the mountain, but at the foot of the mountain. We also tested the depth of the springs, and into the first we lowered a lance, which, upon entering, seemed to touch at 11 palms certain roots of neighboring trees, as if they were intertwined with one another.*
