### CHAPTER VII. 58 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE

<margin>The cited Father explores the second spring of the Nile.</margin>
<margin>Location and depth of the spring.</margin>
The second spring lies to the east of the first, about a stone's throw away. When we explored its depth, we lowered a spear twelve palms <note>A 'palm' was a traditional unit of length based on the width or length of a human hand, roughly 3 to 9 inches depending on the region.</note> long and found no bottom; tying two spears together to reach twenty palms, we tried again, but even then we could not reach the floor. The inhabitants say that the entire mountain is full of water. As proof of this, they pointed out that the entire plain around the spring was trembling and bubbling—a clear sign of hidden water beneath. For this same reason, the water does not overflow at the spring itself, but instead forces its way out with great power at the base of the mountain. Both the inhabitants and the Emperor <note>Susenyos I (r. 1606–1632), the Ethiopian Emperor who converted to Catholicism and hosted the Jesuits.</note>, who was present with his army, affirmed that in that particular year the ground trembled very little due to a great drought, but in other years it trembles and boils so violently that it is difficult to approach without danger. The circumference of the site is like a round lake, the width of which might be the distance of a sling-shot. Below the peak of this mountain, people live on the slopes about one league <note>A league usually represented the distance a person could walk in an hour, roughly 3 miles.</note> west of the spring; the place is called Guix <note>Modern Gish Abay.</note>, and from there it seems the spring could be hit by a musket shot. In this place is a village of pagans who sacrifice many cows. They come to the spring on a certain day of the year with a petty sacrificer whom they regard as a priest. He would sacrifice a cow there next to the spring and throw the severed head of the cow into the depths of the spring.

<margin>Portuguese text.</margin>
<note>original: "onde facean solenne sacrificio matando muitas vaccas..."</note> There they performed a solemn sacrifice, killing many cows which the pagans brought there. Afterward, the priest would cover himself entirely with their fat and sit in an iron chair placed upon a great pile of dry wood. He would then command the wood to be set on fire without himself being burned, or even the fat melting. Sometimes they failed after the fire was lit; however, he sat before the people in such a way that with these sorceries he deceived them, so that they held him as a great Saint and gave him whatever he desired.

Furthermore, the field of the Nile’s spring is difficult to climb from all sides, except from the northern side, where it is easily ascended. About one league below the mountain, in a very deep valley, another river emerges from the bowels of the earth. It joins the Nile shortly thereafter. They believe it shares the same source as the Nile, but is led through hidden channels beneath the earth to erupt first at this spot. The stream of the spring that breaks out below the mountain turns eastward for the distance of a musket shot; then, suddenly turning, it heads North. After about a quarter of a league, a new stream appears, bubbling out from rocks and crags. Shortly after, two other streams join it, erupting from the eastern region, and thus, with more and more streams being collected one after another, the Nile grows notably. After the space of a day’s journey, it joins a great river called the Iamà. It then turns toward the west for about 25 to 35 leagues from its first source. Afterward, changing its course, it seeks the east again, winding its way into a huge lake <note>Lake Tana.</note> (located in the province called Bed, lying partly in the kingdom of Gojam and partly in the kingdom of Dambia). It passes through this lake in such a way that the waters of the Nile show a notable difference from the waters of the lake; the entire river maintains its own course and flow, unmixed with the marshy waters. As soon as it exits, it winds in various turns toward the south and irrigates a land named Alatà, five leagues distant from the lake's outlet. There, it plunges over rocks 14 cubits <note>A 'brachium' or cubit, roughly 18–22 inches. This refers to the famous Tis Abay Falls.</note> high with an immense roar and watery smoke, which from a distance looked to me like a cloud. Shortly after this plunge, it is swallowed up between two huge rocks so deeply that it can scarcely be seen by the eyes. The summits of these rocks are so close together that the Emperor sometimes, having laid a bridge across them, crossed with his entire army; I myself was present for all of these events. It extensively irrigates the kingdom of **Begemder**, **Gojjam**, and the other intervening kingdoms of **Amhara**, **Wolaka**, **Shewa**, and **Damot**. Soon, in its course, it returns to the kingdom of **Gojjam**, and having watered the territories of **Bizan** and **Gumançanca**, it gradually approaches the kingdom of **Gojjam** again, so that it is found to be only one day’s journey from its own source. From here, twisting its flow toward **Fazolò** and **Ombareà**—a kingdom of pagans which **Ras Sela Christos** <note>original: *Eraz Selachristos*; 'Ras' is an Ethiopian aristocratic title equivalent to Duke or Prince. From there, declining from the east toward the North, it glides through countless other regions and vast precipices into Egypt, and from there it discharges itself into the Mediterranean Sea. And this is the description of the source of the **Nile** and its flow, which the cited **Father Pedro Páez** <note>A Spanish Jesuit missionary who was the first European to reach the source of the Blue Nile.</note> observed with his own eyes alongside the Emperor of the Abyssinians on April 21, 1618. He noted it with the greatest diligence so that, by this remarkable and eyewitness examination, he might free the "Republic of Letters" <note>A phrase referring to the international community of scholars and intellectuals.</note> from many entanglements and doubts. Indeed, I believe we must uniquely stand by this account in the future, since the source of the Nile has now attained infallible certainty through the approved testimony of the Emperor. But lest anything seem missing from this work, I have decided to add the Chorography <note>The description or mapping of a region.</note> here, which you may see in **Diagram II. figure 3.**

Since this history states that two springs appear within a ground that is trembling everywhere, it is likely that in the past a large part of this field we described was an open spring, contained as if in a mountain crater. Over time, as grasses and shrubs grew and mixed with mud, it contracted a kind of "skin," the likes of which I remember seeing in various places in Europe. If this were moved aside, I do not doubt that the entire trembling plain would soon reveal the face of the ancient spring. But let these remarks on the origin of the **Nile** suffice. It remains for us to speak of its rise <note>The annual flooding of the Nile, which was a mystery to the ancient world.</note>, celebrated by the records of so many writers but truly understood by none; we shall try our strength in this arena as well. In this task, it is not so shameful to fail before victory, as every most learned man has toiled in it in vain until this day. If, therefore, we slip, we shall only share the fate common to the most erudite.

<margin>The rise of the Nile is caused by rains.</margin>
Therefore, it must be placed beyond all doubt that the rising of the **Nile** is increased by heavy rains; but because it is unknown by which rains or how, nothing certain could be declared until now. Thus, amidst a nearly infinite variety of opinions, let something certain be established by us.

<margin>What is required for the generation of rain.</margin>
It must first be supposed that for the generation of rain, there is first a need for matter from which vapors—which **Georgius Agricola** <note>A German scholar (1494–1555) known as the "Father of Mineralogy."</note> calls "exhalations"—are produced. This matter consists of the moisture of either the sea, stagnant pools, rivers, or the dampness of the earth. Secondly, an active cause is necessary, one that has enough strength to lift many vapors; this is almost entirely attributed to the Sun. From this, a place must be found where the united vapors may form a cloud. All of Africa provides this for us, especially the regions of **Zambre** and **Zaire** <note>Historical names for the Great Lakes of Africa, such as Lake Victoria or Lake Tana, often confused or conflated in 17th-century geography.</note>, surrounded by towering mountains, as if adorned by nature to produce this effect. They are united for two main reasons: First, because like rejoices in its like, by which it may resist opposites;

...the other through *antiperistasis* <term>antiperistasis: a philosophical concept where a quality, such as cold, is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat</term>, which occurs there where the force of the Sun’s reflected rays is terminated. For in that part of the air, there is the greatest cold, both at other times and especially when high mountains reach up to it, whose peaks are cold both because of their earthy nature and because of the lack of solar reflection. Furthermore, for rain to occur, it is necessary that vapor be reduced to its original nature, which happens when heat is lost through the surrounding cold and the specific temperament of the cloud. Thus, vapor condensed into water creates rain by falling. Therefore, when these causes are strong and all concur generally, heavy rains also occur. But if any cause is missing, the generation is hindered, especially if there is no material. In many places in **Libya** <note>Referring generally to the North African deserts.</note>, everything is fouled with sand, which is why rain cannot even be produced. Sometimes the material is there and is elevated, but it is not united, being either dissipated by heat or dispersed by winds. Occasionally the material is elevated and united, and that indeed in the proper place, but rain does not occur because the surrounding cold is not measured in the proportion required for showers, but rather in that which snow, or hail, or even wind or storms require.

<margin>The land of Ethiopia is hollow.</margin>
**Secondly, it must be assumed** that the land of interior **Ethiopia** is extremely cavernous, and abounds with a vast supply of subterranean waters, stored as if in certain feminine chambers or storehouses, as was said above; it follows that this place, being necessarily lower than the place from which the inundation arises, is subject to flooding. These things being thus assumed, let us now approach more closely the investigation of the flooding of the rivers.

<margin>Causes of the inundation.</margin>
There are, therefore, two causes in total for the overflowing of rivers that are not miraculous: one, if the mouths are blocked so that they pour out less water; the other, if more water than usual is received. This happens in two ways: either by melted snows or by heavy falling rains, both of which concur in the flooding of the **Tiber** in **Rome**. The first cause pleased **Thales**, who said the **Etesian winds** <note>Strong, annual Mediterranean winds</note> suspended the downward flow of the **Nile**, a theory we nevertheless refuted above. **Anaxagoras** held the first part of the second cause, along with many others who believe the increase of the **Nile** comes from liquefied snows. This cause has a place not only in the regions subject to the **North** <note>original: *Boreae*</note>, but also in mountainous regions, however much they may be subject to the **Torrid Zone**, as is evident in the **Andes** of **South America** and in the **Mountains of the Moon** in **Africa**; indeed, this effect of inundation is as much greater as the rains and melted snows are more abundant. These rains, however, occur not from clouds imported from elsewhere by the annual winds (as **Alexander** believed), but from those elevated in **Ethiopia** itself. For then the daily rains, which we said are not a little excited by perpendicular rays, are generated; because the vapors are then attracted and released from the **Arabian Gulf** <note>The Red Sea</note>, and from both Oceans, and from the rivers, and gathered from the high mountains, and the caverns of the mountains, and the lakes...

# TREATISE I. CHOROGRAPHY OF EGYPT. CHAPTER VII.

...supply a massive <note>original: *immenſam*, completing the word from the previous page</note> heap of moist substance; with the Sun sending down its active force through direct rays and promoting its growth. Next, the union of the vapors attracted by these rays occurs through the cold of the middle air, especially where there are high mountain peaks, which, through their own earthy coldness, increase and intensify the cold of the middle air. Thus it happens that what has been attracted by the Sun gradually acquires the immediate principles of dissolution <note>The process of vapor condensing back into liquid water.</note>.

However, these daily rains are unable to increase the Nile, because they are absorbed by the heated earth before they can gather into rivers. Indeed, not even those rains which occur for the Ethiopians at the Tropic during the winter season <note>Kircher is likely referring to the Southern Hemisphere's seasons or the shift in rainfall patterns relative to the sun’s position.</note> increase the river until the Sun has reached the sign of **Cancer** <note>The summer solstice in the Northern Hemisphere, occurring in late June.</note>. To make this clear, one must understand that the loops or spiral lines which the Sun creates each day as it travels through the **Zodiac** <note>The path the sun appears to follow through the stars over a year.</note> are spaced further apart at the equatorial circle than those it describes at the tropics. And the closer the Sun approaches this circle <note>the Tropic of Cancer</note>, the narrower these spirals become; conversely, the closer it is to the equinox, the wider they become again. From this, it follows of necessity that the day becomes longer as the Sun is nearer to the tropic point of **Cancer**.

At the equator, therefore, those daily rains do occur; but because the Sun does not remain over the same part of the earth for long, due to the width of its daily rotations, and because the day is short, the attraction of moisture is not so violent as to produce copious rains. The volume increases gradually with the length of the days and the narrowing of the solar spirals, but without great weight <note>meaning without sufficient volume or pressure to cause a flood</note>, until it reaches the narrowest spaces of the circles and the longest of days. Here, therefore, at the end of **Gemini** <note>The month of June.</note>, the rains become many and abundant. But because the earth is not yet entirely moistened within, the rains are still soaked up, until the earth is so swollen both inside and out with the moisture of the daily rains that it can no longer drink. In **Gemini**, therefore, the material for the river’s increase is prepared by these causes, but the river does not yet overflow because the subterranean caverns are not yet filled with moisture. Afterward, however, in **Cancer** <note>July</note>, the rains fall more violently, because more moisture has been collected in the earth, and because the Sun also pulls more vehemently due to the increase in heat.

At this time, therefore, when the earth can soak up no more, and all the water-beds are full, and all the reservoirs of the subterranean passages are swollen to the brim with continuous rains gathered from every region of **Africa**, they begin to overflow—not only the Nile, but all other rivers that share in these common "storehouses." For at this same time the **Niger**, called the **Senegal** by the locals (according to the testimony of the Ethiopians themselves and other approved writers), being carried through western **Ethiopia** <note>Referring broadly to sub-Saharan Africa.</note> into the Ocean between chains of the greatest mountains, begins to rise along with the Nile. A certain Ethiopian, whom I consulted by letter regarding this matter, replied in the Ethiopian language, and I subjoin his words, now translated into English <note>Kircher translated the original Ethiopian letter into Latin; it is here rendered into English for the reader.</note>.

# CHAPTER VII. THE ISAIC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

...for the sky is covered every day with clouds, which prepare the greatest rains for the dry land; these rains last for nearly twenty weeks—that is, for almost five months—with all the rivers and lakes already overflowing. Once these have passed, for the remaining time we have the Sun without any rain.

<margin>Duarte Lopez, Book 2, Chapter 10, *On the Account of the Kingdom of Congo*</margin>
These words agree perfectly with the account of Duarte Lopez <note>Duarte Lopez was a Portuguese explorer whose travels in Africa were recorded by Filippo Pigafetta in 1591.</note> found in the writings of Filippo Pigafetta; his words, translated from Italian into Latin, sound like this: *The principal cause of the Nile's increase,* he says, *is the immense abundance of rainwaters, which in the springtime—namely at the beginning of April—begins to rain through Ethiopia in every direction, not in drops and beads like the showers of Europe, but as if soaking the earth with actual streams of water. Since the earth cannot absorb the torrents of water poured out with such great force and quantity because of the rocky ground, they slip into the riverbeds with massive force; the rivers, swollen by these, finally overflow the banks of their channels and lakes, spreading far and wide. Such daily rains last for five continuous months: April, May, June, July, and August. It so happens that since the land is filled with towering mountains and consequently teems with innumerable springs, torrents, and standing waters, all those immense copies of water flow together into the riverbeds and the basins of the lakes. By these, the rivers grow and expand in a marvelous way beyond all other rivers of the world, as is clear enough in the Chorographic description <note>A "chorographic description" is a systematic mapping or geographical representation of a particular region.</note> of the kingdoms of Congo and Monomotapa <note>Monomotapa was a major kingdom in Southern Africa, located in modern-day Zimbabwe and Mozambique.</note>. Hence, the River Nile, in the map provided above, is seen to run with great force from one side toward the North to irrigate Egypt. The Zaire <note>Now known as the Congo River.</note> and the Niger flow toward the West, while other huge rivers shown on the map flow toward the East and South. Thus, at certain and determined times of the year indicated a little earlier, they always and infallibly achieve the effect of their increase. This is most apparent in Egypt, where the Nile begins to rise around the end of June, and its increase lasts until the twentieth day of September, as I myself have seen, at which time, its waters having been discharged, it recovers its former appearance.* Thus far Pigafetta. However, although all these things have been quite correctly demonstrated, a very great difficulty still arises; if this is not solved, we must willingly admit that we have provided nothing new or worthy of praise in our investigation of the Nile’s increase. The difficulty is as follows:

<margin>Why the rains flood when the Sun traverses the Northern parts. The reason.</margin>
Why do those daily deluges of rain occur only when the Sun is traversing the Northern signs <note>The "Northern signs" refer to the Zodiac constellations like Cancer, Leo, and Virgo, which the sun enters during the Northern Hemisphere's spring and summer.</note>, and not at any other time of the year? This happens not only in Ethiopia, but also in other parts of America <note>In Kircher’s time, "America" often served as a general term for the New World or tropical lands across the Atlantic.</note> subject to the Torrid Zone outside of Ethiopia. For this specific and rare effect cannot—and should not—be attributed solely to the rays of the vertical Sun, nor to the length of the days or the brevity of the twilights, as Fracastoro <note>Girolamo Fracastoro (1478–1553) was an influential Italian physician and scholar who theorized on astronomy and geography.</note> believes. Therefore, we must approach other inner chambers of nature; another knot must be untied, so that the complete cause of such great rains may become known to us. Before I proceed to this,

It must be noted: A constant and invariable effect can by no means occur without a certain, constant, and immutable cause. Such causes are the Sun and the natural placement of locations. The Sun, entering the Zodiac, by a necessity of nature, always marks out the revolutions of the years with a similar, constant, and infallible motion. When the Sun is positioned in this or that region, it always [produces] this effect...

### VOLUME I. DESCRIPTION OF EGYPT. 63 CHAPTER VII.

<margin>The location of the Ethiopian mountains as the cause of the flood.</margin>
...always, and it is necessary that no other cause comes forward. I maintain, therefore, that beyond the causes already mentioned, the location of the Ethiopian mountains is the principal and most fundamental cause of both the rains and the rising of the rivers. This is so true that if this same mountain arrangement were placed in other parts of the world with a similar relationship to the Sun, the same effects would surely follow. For wise Nature has arranged and coordinated these mountains—especially those located between the Equator and the Winter Tropic <note>original: "Tropicum hybernum," referring to the Tropic of Capricorn</note>, which stretch across southern Ethiopia like a triple chain to the East, South, and West—in such a way that they act like hollow mirrors <note>The author uses the analogy of a concave or "hollow" mirror to describe how mountains focus solar heat.</note> facing the Sun as it enters the northern signs, perfectly capturing its rays. Once received, the sun’s power to lift vapors is wonderfully strengthened by the union of these rays. Consequently, a vast force of vapors and clouds soon gathers; some are lifted from the regions below, while others are driven by the North winds and the Etesian winds <note>The Etesian winds are strong, seasonal Mediterranean winds that blow from the north in the summer.</note> into those vast mountain amphitheaters. It happens that as soon as the Sun, nearing the meridian circle, strikes the hollows of the mountains with its rays in this manner, the clouds—already heavy with water—are lifted by the reflected heat. Tossed about in every direction, they finally meet the cold sitting upon the peaks of the highest mountains. From that struggle between the heat pressing from below and the cold from above, a process of *antiperistasis* <term>Antiperistasis: A concept in pre-modern physics where one quality (like cold) is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite (heat).</term> occurs, which is the sole mother of rains. This resolves into most copious showers, or rather—because the heavy clouds are so close to the earth—into what seem like rivers of rain falling to achieve nature's predetermined goal. From this physical reasoning, it clearly appears that there can be no other reason for the rains and the resulting floods so certain and infallible as the arrangement of the mountains in Ethiopia. Provident Nature placed them like traps for vapors and rain-bearing clouds to bring aid to a land otherwise parched by the Sun’s heat and desperately lacking moisture. I will not say here how much the placement of mountains matters—not only in Ethiopia but in other parts of the world—for the generation of both rain and wind. For while France is for the most part windy, especially <margin>The sky of Avignon is like a rain-collector.</margin> the territory of Avignon (which rivals the Egyptian sky), I have certainly discovered through long experience no other cause for this than the placement of the mountains. Here, aided by the properties of the land and according to which quarter of the sky it faces, the vapors and exhalations drawn from the earth by the Sun's power are usually turned into either rain or wind in various regions.

<margin>Why the flood is unequal in Egypt.</margin>
<margin>The Reason.</margin>
But since a more abundant opportunity to speak on these matters will be given elsewhere, I will shorten my pen here, preparing to resolve another difficulty no less than the first. Someone might rightly wonder why the abundance of rains falling across all of Ethiopia does not result in the same flood across all of Ethiopia—or why Egypt alone participates in it so much that it looks not like land, but like a sea.

We say, therefore, that the riverbed of the Nile is the cause of this. For as the Nile stretches out from its bed in the high-altitude lakes down a sloping floor, it is granted different depths in different places; thus, being enriched with much water, it floods in different ways according to the location. For the more a river’s channel is narrowed between mountain walls and the deeper its bed, the greater the amount of water...

### CHAPTER VII. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

<margin>
Why the rising of the Nile occurs when the Sun passes through the northern signs.
</margin>
...they will contain a large volume of water, with the obstacles of the mountains preventing them from overflowing and slipping away. On the contrary, the shallower the riverbeds are—especially in flat and wide-open fields—the more subject they will be to floods. Therefore, when that huge mass of water, rushing from the narrow mountain passes and the precipices of cataracts into the flat plains, occupies these areas, it is necessary for it to overflow, as the riverbeds are incapable of holding such a vast volume of water. Thus it happens that all flat places in Ethiopia are subject to these overflows, but not the mountainous ones. Since the Nile brings its channel down from steeper places and, falling through various cataracts, finds the Egyptian land to be flat, low-lying, and situated in a humble place—and finds a riverbed that is not deep enough for such volume—it is truly no wonder if, at set times of the year after those huge rainy floods have rushed down from Ethiopia, it finally begins to overflow far and wide. Therefore, the natural site and arrangement of the mountains linked together in a circle (as we have said), which form a sort of "workshop of rains" around the plains they enclose, must be considered the infallible cause of the rains at set times. Just so, the natural constitution of the Nile’s riverbed must be considered the infallible cause of the Egyptian flood. As for the fact that these rains occur while the Sun traverses the North <note>original: "Boream lustrante," meaning when the Sun is in the northern zodiac signs during the Northern Hemisphere's summer</note>, and not while it passes through the South, this is to be ascribed to the Etesian winds <note>The Etesian winds are strong, seasonal Mediterranean winds that blow from the north; Kircher notes they are called "general winds" by Portuguese explorers</note>. For these, according to the testimony of Pigafetta <note>Filippo Pigafetta (1533–1604), an Italian explorer and author who wrote about the Congo and Africa</note>, blowing from the North as the Sun enters Capricorn, drive the clouds gathered in the mountain hollows and turn them into rain. But when the Sun traverses Libra, the said winds blow from the turbulent motions of the Ocean and the snowy regions of Magellan <note>Refers to the Strait of Magellan/Antarctic regions</note>; since these winds are very cold because of the regions they pass through, they do not permit vapors to be raised, or if the Sun does lift them, they do not condense into rain-bearing clouds, and therefore they enjoy perpetual clarity and calm at those times.

<margin>
Different floods occur because of the diversity of the winds.
</margin>
Whoever knows, therefore, why the North wind, which people commonly call the *Tramontana*, brings cold and a very healthy clarity to Europeans as it blows from the snowy North <note>original: "Arcto"</note>; and why the South wind causes storms, rains, and floods—such as those winds they commonly call the *Libeccio* <note>a southwesterly wind</note> and *Scirocco* <note>a southeasterly wind</note>—will also know why Ethiopia abounds in rains and storms when the sun is in the northern signs, but enjoys perpetual clarity in the winter time. For the Divine Majesty ordained the course of the Sun, Moon, and other planets and stars—indeed, the whole army of the heavens—at the beginning of things with such wisdom that each tract of land would participate in their light and influences with the greatest proportion and measure. This was done so that no place would be rendered unfit for human habitation by too much cold and rain, nor another by heat and drought. For if, for example, He did not aid near Ethiopia with moistening rains and further Ethiopia with cold winds, the former would necessarily perish from heat and the latter from drought. For the same reason, if the rains lasted forever throughout the whole year, or if there were always clear skies, the whole of Ethiopia would undoubtedly be submerged by flood in the first case, or dissolved by excessive drought in the second. Therefore, there is a need for a change of state for the preservation of things. And so, by these sorts of reciprocal alterations of this terrestrial globe...

## CHAPTER VIII.

### A PHYSICO-CHRONOLOGICAL QUESTION,

#### Whether Egypt was inhabited before the Deluge, or not? and who were its first Kings.

I find various controversies regarding this question among the Arabs, Latins, and Greeks. Most of the Greeks—among whom Herodotus and Strabo deservedly hold the first place—assert that Egypt was once covered by the sea and was impassable. For this reason, the former calls it the <note>original: "δῶρον τοῦ Νείλου"</note> *gift of the Nile*; the latter, meanwhile, attempts to establish Herodotus's opinion with various arguments, as is clear from his 17th book and his prolegomena. The Arabs, however, assert not only that Egypt was inhabited before the Deluge, but they even present the Kings themselves, their deeds, inventions, and power. But so that the truth of both opinions may finally come to light, I have decided they should be discussed here.

That Egypt was once covered by the sea is the opinion not only of Herodotus, as I said, and Strabo, but of all those who follow them; you may see their reasons in Goropius Becanus <note>Johannes Goropius Becanus (1519–1572), a Flemish physician and linguist known for his eccentric theories on the origins of languages.</note> in his *Niloscopium*. However, weighing these matters more scrupulously, we say that not all of Egypt, but only a certain part, which we previously called <term>Phium</term> <note>Likely referring to the Faiyum region or the low-lying Delta.</note>, was covered by the sea and emerged from the silt of the Nile over the course of time. 

<margin>
The lower part of Egypt was once maritime.
</margin>

For since Egypt is very steep toward the Red Sea, and becomes higher and higher the closer it approaches the cataracts and Ethiopia, it is entirely probable that the whole land was inhabited right up to the borders of Ethiopia, above the point where the Nile divides into branches to form the Delta. Therefore, when authors speak of Egypt being submerged in water, they seem to be "taking a part for the whole"—specifically, Lower Egypt, which they call the Delta. This is confirmed by various testimonies of very serious authors; Proclus, in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, reports from the opinion of the cited Homer, as does Pliny (Book 2, Chapter 35) and Seneca (Natural Questions, Book 3, Chapter 26), that there was once a voyage of a day and a night from the island of Pharos to Egypt, whereas it is now connected to it. For this reason, Hecataeus and others cited in Dio...

Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE who wrote the *Bibliotheca historica*.</note> in Book I, as Pierius Valerianus <note>An Italian Renaissance humanist known for his work on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> also observed. See also Aristotle on this in Book I of his *Meteorology*, and others commenting on him in this passage. <margin>Sesostris’s attempt to cut through the Isthmus.</margin> Furthermore, we read that Sesostris <note>A legendary king of Egypt often identified with Ramses II or Senusret.</note> wished to join the Red Sea with the Mediterranean Sea by cutting through the intervening Isthmus <note>The Isthmus of Suez.</note>. However, this attempt was discouraged by the Priests, because they contended that the Red Sea was higher than Egypt; thus, if the Isthmus were cut through, all of Egypt would necessarily be submerged by the maritime waves. <margin>The false belief of Sesostris.</margin> I would not say, however, that the waters of the Red Sea are higher than those of the Mediterranean, since this openly contradicts <term>hydrostatic principles</term> <note>The physical laws governing the pressure and equilibrium of fluids.</note> and the demonstrations of Archimedes regarding things that float in water. I have shown this extensively in my *Magnetic Art*, and (God willing) I shall deduce it even more extensively in my *Subterranean World*. Rather, we say the error arose because, to those traveling toward the Red Sea, the land mostly appears through sloping and higher parts, making Egypt seem very low; hence, an error and optical illusion could easily creep in for those ignorant of optics and hydrostatics.

The Arabs, therefore—to move to the other side of the controversy—when they say Egypt was inhabited before the Flood, must be understood to mean that part which later generations called the <term>Heptanomis</term> <note>Literally "Seven Nomes," referring to Middle Egypt.</note> and the <term>Thebaid</term> <note>The region around the ancient city of Thebes in Upper Egypt.</note>, namely the mountainous part. But so that all this may be clearer, I shall bring forward the testimonies of the Arab historians; in citing these, however, I would not wish to force anyone to believe them, but I leave them to be discussed by the free judgment of the learned Reader. Thus, Ahmed ben Joseph Eltiphasi <note>An Arabic writer on gems and history.</note> says in Gelaldinus’s <note>Referring to Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti, a prolific Egyptian polymath.</note> book *On the Names of the Nile*, where among other things he says:

<margin>Ahmed Ben Joseph Eltiphasi.</margin>

It is said that Adam (peace be upon him) gave a testament to his son Seth, and prophecy was in him and his children. God sent down twenty-nine scrolls to him. He came to the land of Egypt, which was then called Bablun <note>Original Arabic: *Bablun*. This refers to the ancient Fortress of Babylon in Egypt, near modern Cairo.</note>, and he and his brother’s children settled there. Seth lived on top of the mountain, while the children of Cain <note>Original Arabic: *Cabil*.</note> lived below in the valley.

<margin>Egypt once called Bablun</margin>

Concerning these "Sethian" or "Enochian" books, more will be said extensively in the second volume, in the treatise on Egyptian philology; therefore, I refer the Reader there. Whatever the truth of this narrative may be, it is certainly probable that before the Flood, Egypt—being a neighbor to Palestine, Babylonia, and Mesopotamia (which were the first colonies of mortals, from which they were then propagated into the whole world)—was inhabited. I do not see how such a fertile region as Egypt could have remained hidden from those first propagators of the human race. After Seth, they say that Kainan possessed the dominion of Egypt, after him Mahalalel, and after him finally Jared succeeded. ### CHAPTER IX.
-> On the Dynasties of the Egyptians. <-

<margin>
Manetho of Sebennytos’s history of the Egyptian Dynasties.

Mention of the Egyptian Dynasties is frequent among ancient historians, yet we have no other author for them except Manetho of Sebennytos, an Egyptian priest. I find that he flourished in Egypt before the time of Alexander, regardless of what Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a famous chronologist who doubted Manetho's antiquity.</note> might say. Iochaides <note>Referring to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, to whom the Zohar is traditionally attributed.</note> also mentions him in his *Zohar*, and whenever there is talk of the Kings of Egypt, he concludes with these words: **Manethon in the history of the Kings of Egypt**; or even with these words:

<margin>
Manetho 1.
</margin>

### TREATISE I. CONCERNING THE KINGS OF EGYPT. CHAPTER IX.
<meta>catchword: immen- (short for "immensum," meaning "immense" or "vast")</meta>

<margin>
Manetho of Sebennytos <note>A priest and historian from the 3rd century BCE.</note>, writer of the 32 Dynasties.
</margin>
I have heard that he preserved these records, and he is the one who lived during the times of *Augustus*; hence many have been deceived by the similarity of the name and have confused him with our ancient compiler of the *Egyptian* Dynasties. Therefore, our *Manetho of Sebennytos* <note original="Manethon Sybennita">A Greek-speaking Egyptian priest who wrote the "Aegyptiaca" (History of Egypt).</note> encompassed the history of the *Egyptians* or their Kings in a very brief description and arranged them into 32 Dynasties or periods of rule. Of these, he omitted fifteen as having been wiped out from human memory along with the Great Flood; the remaining seventeen, drawn from the monuments of the *Egyptians*, he described with whatever faith and diligence he could. From this source *Africanus* <note>Sextus Julius Africanus, an early Christian chronographer.</note> drew most of his material, as did *Eusebius Pamphili* and *Josephus in his work Against Apion*. From these, most subsequent chronological authors plucked their own data, and by tearing *Manetho* into various pieces, they interpreted him so differently that many, perplexed by such great confusion, have doubted the truth of the Dynasties or even the reliability of the author.

<margin>
What the 16th Dynasty was like.
</margin>
<margin>
Objection against the 16 Dynasties before the division <note>Referring to the "Division of the Earth" among the sons of Noah.</note>.
</margin>
<margin>
Solution to the objection.
</margin>
Many are convinced that these Dynasties, like countless other things, were introduced by *Manetho* on the occasion of *Egyptian* fables. For if, they say, the sixteenth Dynasty was enacted immediately after the flood, then fifteen had already preceded it; but this is repugnant both to the order of time and to Holy Scripture. For it is clear to anyone who possesses even a little wisdom that the *Egyptians* were by no means older than their prince and founder *Mizraim* <note original="Misraimo">The biblical ancestor of the Egyptians, son of Ham.</note>, the son of *Ham* and grandson of *Noah*; and that he did not set out for *Egypt* before the division of the lands, nor before the confusion of languages, which falls in the year 275 after the flood, and the year 1931 from the creation of the world. Therefore, those fifteen dynasties which *Eusebius* places before *Abraham* must be regarded as fictitious. Since they could reach back even to *Adam* himself, the adversaries argue in this way. Truly, so that this dispute may finally be settled, and so that we may decide what should be thought of the *Egyptian* Dynasties—especially those fifteen omitted ones—time and place now demand that we act, after we have first presupposed certain things that contribute to our discourse.

<margin>
Supposition 1.
</margin>
<margin>
The propagation of doctrines and arts.
</margin>
Therefore, I suppose first: That the first Patriarchs before the flood, instructed orally by the first author of the human race <note>Adam</note>, made great progress not only in all kinds of sciences and arts, but also in the political way of living. Thus *Seth* was instructed by his father *Adam*, who was enlightened by an infused and supernatural knowledge of all things; he taught his son *Cainan*, and he taught his son *Mahalaleel*; he taught *Jared*, and *Jared* finally taught his son *Enoch*; *Enoch* taught *Methuselah*, *Methuselah* taught *Lamech*, and finally *Lamech* taught *Noah*. And since they all lived almost at the same time as their father *Adam*, it is probable that the sciences and arts of things were propagated in a wonderful manner. All these things will be shown more extensively in what follows from the monuments of the *Hebrews*, *Chaldeans*, *Arabs*, and other Eastern peoples.

<margin>
Supposition 2.
</margin>
<margin>
The condition of men before the flood.
</margin>
I suppose secondly: That men before the flood were of very long life, with strong and robust bodies, and moreover were naturally fertile, very lustful, and most prone to passion. From these factors it happened that the world multiplied to an infinite degree in a short time. From this I further infer that such a great multitude of people could by no means stay in that *Damascene* field <note original="campo Damasceno">The "Field of Damascus," traditionally considered the site where Adam was created and where early humanity lived.</note> alone, which was enclosed by *Babylonia*, *Palestine*, and *Syria*; but having multiplied in immen- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "immen-" (immensely).</note>

### CHAPTER IX. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE

<margin>They seek new colonies; thus the whole world was inhabited.</margin>
...forced mortals to seek new colonies across an immense area, occupying not only the neighboring regions bordering Palestine—such as Egypt, Asia, and Arabia—but also more remote lands like Persia, Media, India, and indeed all of Greater Asia, and even Europe and Africa.

<margin>Demonstration.</margin>
<margin>The number of men from the Flood until the construction of the tower.</margin>
I demonstrate this as follows: if an almost innumerable multitude of people issued from only eight humans in the space of two hundred years—specifically from the Flood until the building of the tower—we find that, based on certain assumptions, they could have reached the following number: 1,247,224,717,455 <note>Kircher calculates over 1.2 trillion people born in just two centuries, a common feature of his "mathematical" theology to explain how the Tower of Babel could be built so quickly.</note>. This is the total sum of mortals procreated from the Flood until the Tower of Babel.

This sum is so great that if all those people had stood in a square, so close that each person occupied one square foot, I demonstrate that one side of this square would have occupied more or less 372 astronomical miles, or nearly 25 celestial degrees. Thus, they would have occupied all of Palestine, Babylonia, and Armenia in a single square. These things might rightly seem paradoxical and incredible, had we not shown them extensively in our demonstration regarding the Tower of Babylon. If, therefore, such a great multitude could be born in the span of two hundred years, how many do we think were born before the Flood in the span of 1,656 years? These were men of longer life, as I have said, with sturdier bodies, more prone to lust, and practicing polygamy. <margin>The immense multitude of men before the Flood.</margin> Certainly, if from the birth of Christ until these times, individual men had extended their lives to 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, and 800 years—just as the Holy Scriptures record of the first men—I believe such a great multitude of people could have been born that the world would not have been capable of holding them. All these things can be very easily demonstrated through mathematical reasoning, provided certain premises are assumed first. Therefore, no one should doubt that the multiplication of humanity before the Flood was immense—beyond any comparison to our own centuries—and consequently, no prudent person can doubt that they occupied all the islands and parts of the world.

<margin>Whether there was a political form before the Flood, and of what kind?</margin>
I say that this multitude could by no means have existed without some political head or form of kingdom. Hence, it is certain that in individual colonies there were certain Kings or Leaders elected by common vote, in whose hands resided the power of judging, deciding, and administering all affairs. It is impossible for any Republic or Kingdom to endure long without a head, as Gregory of Toulouse <note original="Gregorius Tholosanus">Pierre Grégoire (1540–1597), a French jurist and author of "De Republica."</note> most learnedly proves in Book 1 of *On the Republic*; as do Plato in *The Laws*, Aristotle in Book 9 of the *Ethics*, and all others who have treated this subject. And if we read that the barbarian nations discovered in various parts of the world in this our century are endowed with this political instinct, how much more so were those first Patriarchs, who were endowed from heaven with a certain divine wisdom?

<margin>Third Assumption.</margin>
<margin>The political state before the Flood.</margin>
I assume thirdly: that the sons of Noah <note original="Noëmi">Noah</note>, together with their father, shared in all knowledge of things from those primeval fathers, whether through tradition or through writings. They learned the political way of living and other things necessary for the preservation of the human race, and they passed everything on to their sons after the Flood just as they had heard and learned it. <margin>The Egyptian Dynasties before the Flood are real.</margin>

And although I am well aware that these things will be regarded by the philologists of our time as being among those things considered <term>apocrypha <note>original: ἀπόκρυφα; referring to "hidden" or non-canonical texts of doubtful authority</note></term>, I nevertheless did not wish to omit them. This is partly because these histories are unknown to Latin readers, and partly because I have discovered a certain spark of truth lurking even under the embers of these types of "barbarian" accounts. Therefore, I do not believe that everything which reeks of fables and fiction should be rejected. The Arabs possess much information unknown to the Latins and Greeks; if the industry of experts were to make these public, I would hope for a great addition to the "Republic of Letters" regarding many matters hitherto disputed among authors. But more on this elsewhere. Now, therefore, having seen the pattern of the government of Kings before the Flood, let us briefly contemplate the same for the period after the Flood. You see, then, that the Arabs place as many Kings or Dynasties before the Flood in their chronology as Manetho <note>An Egyptian priest and historian (c. 3rd century BCE) who organized the history of Egypt into dynasties</note> had omitted—namely, fifteen. Thus, these fifteen dynasties are beautifully connected to the first dynasty after the Flood, which according to Manetho is the 16th, or the Theban dynasty.

TRANSCRIPTION OF SYNTAGMA I. ON THE KINGS OF EGYPT. 75 CHAPTER IX.

## On the Kings of Egypt after the Flood according to the Arabs.

The Arabs agree with the Latin and Greek authors in some matters and differ in others; we shall treat the series of Dynasties according to the mindset of the Greeks in its proper place, after we have first discussed the sequence of these same dynasties a little more fully according to the opinion of the Arabic chronologers. Thus they report, according to Jalal al-Din, Abd al-Hakam, Anbahni, Othman son of Salcha, Lahaia, Ben Gabasch, Al-Katbahni, Abdalla Elsaiana, and Ismael Sciainscia:

<note>original Arabic: "كان اول من سكن مصر بعد الطوفان بيصر بن حام بن نوح وهو ابو القبط..." — The first who inhabited Egypt after the flood was Beithir son of Ham, son of Noah, and he is the father of the Copts. He founded the city of Memphis, which was the first city inhabited after the flood, he and his children, and they were thirty souls who had reached maturity and married; for this reason, it was called Mese-Mata in the Coptic language, which means 'thirty.' Beithir son of Ham was already old and weak, and Mesra was his eldest son; it was he who led his father and all his brothers into Egypt and they settled there. From Beithir son of Beithir, Egypt was named [Misr]; he took for himself and his children what lies between the two trees behind Al-Arish as far as Aswan in length, and from Barka to Aila in breadth.</note>

<margin>I. Beithir, son of Ham, the first King of Egypt after the flood.</margin>
The first who inhabited Egypt after the flood was Beithir (also called Bosiris), the son of Ham, who was the son of Noah; he was the father of the Copt, and he lived in Memphis, which was also the first city inhabited after the <term>Ghorab</term><note>The Great Flood or devastation.</note>; he and his sons numbered thirty souls already joined in marriage, and for that reason, Memphis is called in the Egyptian language <insert>مسا فه</insert> <insert>ماته</insert> <note>original: "Mese Mata"</note>, that is, "Thirty." Now, Beithir son of Ham was already aged and infirm. <margin>What the name "Mese" means in Egyptian Memphis.</margin> Truly, Mesra was his eldest son, and it was he who led his father and all his brothers into Egypt, and they settled there; and from Mesra (or <term>Egyptus</term>) the son of Bosiris, the land was called Mesra or Egypt. He divided for himself and his sons whatever lies between <term>Alschachartin</term><note>The "Two Trees."</note> behind <term>Algharsch</term><note>Al-Arish.</note> as far as Aswan in length, and whatever lies from <term>Barka</term><note>Cyrenaica in Libya.</note> as far as <term>Aila</term><note>Eilat on the Red Sea.</note> in width.

<margin>II. King Mesra.</margin>
Furthermore, upon the death of Beithir, Mesra succeeded him; he divided the land among each of his sons into one part of Egypt. When his sons and his grandsons multiplied, he subdivided the earlier parts again. A certain part was given to his son Copt, who lived there, and from him, he was called Copt (or <term>Egyptus</term>). Whatever lay below and above Copt as far as Esmun, both to the east and the west, fell to his son Esmun, who lived there and the place was named after him. To Athrib fell whatever lay between Memphis and Sai; Athrib lived there, and it was named after him. He also divided Sai, which is between the city of Sai and the sea; Sai lived there and it was named after him.

<margin>Coptus, the builder of pyramids.</margin>
Upon the death of Mesra, Coptus (or <term>Egyptus</term>) succeeded him, from whom the entire land was called Egypt, just as it was called Mesra from Mesraim. He built the pyramids, and when he had administered the kingdom for many years, he died. His brother Esmun succeeded to his place; for thus says Abdalla Ben Gheled:

<note>original Arabic: "فتوفي قبط فاستخلف اخاه اشمن ثم توفي اشمن فاستخلف اخاه اتريب..." — Then Copt died and his brother Esmun became his successor; then Esmun died and his brother Atrib succeeded him; then his brother Sa succeeded him; then Sa died and his son Idris (or Kadaris) succeeded him; others say that in his time Salih (peace be upon him) was sent; then Kadaris died and his son Maliu succeeded him; then he died and his daughter Harita succeeded him; then she died and her son Kalkan succeeded him, and he ruled them for about a hundred years, then died without a child.</note>

<margin>The Queen of Egypt, daughter of Pharaoh, after the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt.</margin>
*After God destroyed Pharaoh and his army in the Red Sea, the Arabs say that all of Egypt was widowed of its illustrious men and those capable of royal dignity. <note>original Arabic: "ثم اغرق الله فرعون وجنوده..."</note> Then God drowned Pharaoh and his soldiers; there were drowned with him more than two million of the nobles of Egypt, their elders, and their leaders. The noble women of the people of Egypt considered it too great a thing that any of the commoners should command them. So, they reached a consensus to appoint a woman from among them called Deluca, daughter of Zabu. She possessed intellect, knowledge, and experience, and she was of high status and position among them. She was at that time one hundred and sixty years old. They made her queen, but she feared that the kings of the earth would snatch her away <note>i.e., seize the weakened kingdom</note>. She gathered the noble women and said to them: "No one used to covet our land or cast an eye toward it, but our elders and nobles have perished, and the sorcerers by whom we were strengthened are gone. ### SECTION 1 ON THE KINGS OF EGYPT. CHAPTER IX.

<note>original Arabic: "واضع عليه المحارس..."</note> I placed guards over it from every side, so that people would not covet us. I built a wall that surrounded the entire land of Egypt—its farms, its cities, and its villages. I placed a canal below it in which water flows, and established bridges and diversions. I placed guards and outposts there, a horseman for every three miles, and provided them with provisions. I commanded them to keep watch; if anyone approached, they were to tell one another by striking bells. Thus, the news would reach them from any direction within a single hour. They oversaw this, and by these means, Egypt was protected from those who desired it.
-> ۞ <-

<margin>The woman Daluka presides over Egypt.</margin>
Afterward, **God drowned Pharaoh** and his army, destroying with him all the Princes and Great Men of Egypt—more than a million in number. After this slaughter, all of Egypt remained deprived of its illustrious men and nobles; none remained except for slaves, freedmen, and the women or wives of the noblemen who had perished. It was ordered that one woman should be placed in charge from among them. Having gathered their elders, they chose one of them as ruler named *Daluka*, daughter of *Zabu*, a woman distinguished for her wisdom and knowledge of affairs, and of illustrious lineage, who was then 160 years old. Having been placed over the kingdom, and having gathered the noblewomen together, she addressed them as follows: *"Since our region is vulnerable to various incursions by enemies, we have decided to deliberate early on the difficulties we face. Therefore, lest anyone hereafter should covet it or cast greedy eyes upon it—especially after our elders and nobles have perished, and our magic, by whose aid such splendid works were once performed, has withdrawn—I now intend to build a fortification that will surround our entire region. I will place guards at all its borders, and thus I do not believe that men will desire us."*

She then built a wall or earthen rampart which surrounded the entire land of Egypt, providing the cities with sufficient supplies and adorning them with ditches or rivers. She also constructed bridges and various outposts in which she placed guards and weapons. She placed a guard post every three miles, and between these, a small guard post every single mile. She stationed men and mercenaries hired with wages and entrusted them with the care and protection of each location. She ordered that when enemies approached, they should give a signal by striking <note>likely a bell or drum</note> from one guard post to another. In this way, within the span of one hour, with the signals continued from one to the next, all guard posts would be informed of the enemy’s arrival. Those seeing these things would learn to keep away from Egypt.

<margin>After the drowning of Pharaoh, the Egyptian Kingdom devolved to women.</margin>
We read elsewhere that women also ruled in Egypt, though different authors assign their dominion to different times. Certainly, after the drowning of Pharaoh and his army in the Red Sea, it is likely that the remaining women ruled for a time, as almost all sacred and secular writers believe that Pharaoh was accompanied by all the magnates and most illustrious Princes in the persecution of the Israelites. Therefore, with them perishing, the kingdom by right devolved to the surviving women. But more on these matters will be seen in the following pages. Concerning the magical works of this Queen, by which she kept enemies away from Egypt, we have spoken more extensively elsewhere. Then *Abdalla Ben Geled* continues with the rest:

<note>original Arabic: "وملكتهم دلوكة..."</note> Daluka daughter of Zaba ruled them for twenty years, managing their affairs in Egypt until a man from the sons of their elders and nobles, called Darkun son of Batlus, reached maturity, and they made him king over them. Then Darkun died and was succeeded by his son Tus. Then he passed away and was succeeded by his brother Luqas. He did not remain but three years until he died and did not leave...

### CHAPTER IX. 78 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISAIC TEMPLE

He left no son as an heir, so his brother Mardia <note>original Arabic: مرذيا; Latin: Marnia</note> succeeded him. Upon his death, his son Estmarres took the throne. He grew arrogant and tyrannical, openly flaunting his vices. The people, outraged by his behavior, conspired to remove him; they deposed and killed him. They then swore allegiance to a man from among their nobles named Bathulus, son of Mankabil. He ruled over them for forty years. After his death, his son Balus succeeded him, and upon his death, his brother Manakiel took his place. He ruled for a long time before he died, and his son Bula succeeded him, reigning for one hundred and twenty years. He was the "Lame One" who took the King of Jerusalem captive and brought him to Egypt—the first to do so since the time of the original Pharaoh. However, he became insolent, and so God killed him: a bear attacked him and broke his neck, and thus he died. ❁

That is to say: *And Daluka, daughter of Zabu, governed for twenty years, until there came from among the Great Men a man named Darkun, son of Batlus, whom they set over themselves. When Darkun died, his son Iudis succeeded him; and when he died, his brother Lakos followed. After thirty years, Lakos died without leaving a son; so his brother Marnia succeeded him. After his death, his son Estmarres succeeded him, who was eventually killed by having his limbs torn apart because of his monstrous crimes. In his place, they appointed a man from the elders named Bathulus, son of Menkiel, who presided over them for forty years. Upon his death, his son Bulus succeeded him; then Bulus was followed by his brother Manakiel, who ruled them until our times. When Manakiel died, his son Bula succeeded him and ruled for 120 years. This was the lame king who led the King of Jerusalem into captivity and made him serve him, just as in the days of Pharaoh. But he swelled with pride and arrogance, so God struck him with leprosy; then a bear set upon him and killed him by crushing his neck.* Thus says the author. I marvel that the Author, in many places of this chronology, uses this word <term>zamena</term> <note>Arabic: زامنا</note> *Zamena*, which means *in our times*. From this, I gather that Jalal al-Din <note>A prominent 15th-century Egyptian scholar often cited by Kircher</note> possessed very ancient historians who lived in those very times and diligently investigated all things. If this is so, we can certainly infer that the author of such records lived during the time of Solomon, when this last King Estmarres was also living; but these are merely conjectures.

<margin>
10. Karkura.
11. Lachis.
12. Phuis.
</margin>
Furthermore, Ibn Abd al-Hakam reports from Ka'b al-Ahbar <note>An early authority on Islamic tradition and history</note> that after the death of Solomon, this Bula invaded Jerusalem and returned to Egypt weighed down with gold. After this Bula died, his son Marnius succeeded him and ruled in our times. When he died, his son Karkura succeeded him, and after he had presided over them for 60 years, he passed away. His brother Lachis (or Lakis) succeeded him in his place. Many exotic things are reported about him concerning incantations—such as a palace where anyone who tried to take anything from it would be rendered impotent or sterile, and so on. Furthermore, after the death of Lachis, his son Phuis succeeded him, and he reigned in Egypt at the very time when Nebuchadnezzar <note>Latin: Nabuchodonosor</note> marched against Jerusalem. And up to this point, the Arabic histories of the ancient Egyptians continue. These times coincide correctly with the years of the Founding of Rome. There follow next the deeds of the Kings of Persia in Egypt, which we intentionally omit, lest we cause the reader weariness with such exotic names. And this Arabic history, if compared with the Greek history, will appear so different that there is not even a trace in which they seem to agree; for the names of the Kings are entirely different, and they disagree greatly in their deeds. Nevertheless, I wished to add the account of the whole history here, so that if anyone had a mind to compare one with the other, the opportunity would not be lacking. These things having been so considered, let us now pass on to a more particular description of the Dynasties themselves.

# CHAPTER X.

## On the Kings of Egypt, their succession, and deeds, according to Manetho, Africanus, Eusebius, and others.

<margin>The greatest difficulty lies in Egyptian Chronology.</margin>
Since I now consider myself able to emerge from the other waves of difficulties, though exhausted by the troublesome flooding of the Nile: behold, new reefs and new precipices present themselves on every side—all the more dangerous as they are steep and rugged. Yet, unless these are overcome, it is as difficult to fully and perfectly reach the goal of our proposal as the attempts to overcome the reefs and precipices of this field are uncertain. These reefs are presented by the Chronology of the Kings of Egypt; I find it so mutilated, and indeed so imperfect and crippled, that I know more easily whom I should cite than whom I should follow. Such is the variety of opinions, such the perplexity of dissenting writers, so varied and manifold the corruption of proper names that has occurred in succeeding times; and furthermore, the system of times and years used by the ancient Egyptians is so unknown. 

To overcome these reefs of difficulty, then, my natural inclination for unearthing such matters gave me wings and courage. Spurred on by this, I have left no stone unturned to break through this "isthmus." However, when I saw that this could by no means be done without the science of time <note>i.e., the study of chronology</note>, I soon applied my mind to examining the ancient chronologies of the Hebrews, Greeks, and Arabs. My goal was to establish a comparison between these and the records of Berosus, Manetho, Herodotus, Diodorus, Philo, Josephus, and Eusebius. By demonstrating the course of years and centuries—when each person lived and what noteworthy deeds they performed—our *Egyptian Oedipus* <note>Kircher refers to himself as the "Oedipus" who will solve the riddles of Egypt</note>, enlightened by these sources, might proceed with greater certainty and connection in unearthing and solving the riddles of griffins and hieroglyphics.

...would occupy. The Princes and Leaders of the families—since the Babylonian regions were unable to hold such a great multitude of men—were forced by a pact to lead the offspring of their sons with them into various parts of the world to establish new colonies.

<margin>Ham, the first settler of Egypt.</margin>
In this first separation of the sons of Noah, just as Asia fell to Shem and Europe to Japheth, so Africa—of which Egypt is the vestibule, as it were—fell to Ham as his portion. In Egypt, therefore, Ham, the first of mortals, pitched his tents, since he found it to be most suitable for human habitation and overflowing with an abundance of resources. Truly, however, when men had multiplied immensely in a short time—whether due to the necessity of that era or the fertile and prolific abundance of the Nile—and the numerous offspring of his sons were spread everywhere, 

<margin>Ham led colonies from Egypt throughout Africa.</margin>
since the narrow boundaries of Egypt (or <term>Mizraim</term> <note>The Hebrew name for Egypt, often personified as the son of Ham</note>) could not contain the force of the people, Ham left Ethiopia to his son Cush, resigned Egypt to Mizraim, Libya to Phut, and Phoenicia to Canaan. He himself, having led a vast crowd of his grandsons into Persia (which at that time included all that shore neighboring Egypt to the east, which we now call Arabia) and then into Media, migrated to establish new colonies; there he founded the city of Bactria, from which both the entire province and he himself later earned their names.

<margin>Ham-Zoroaster, the discoverer of Magic.</margin>
And this is that celebrated and famous King of the Bactrians named Zoroaster, the first author and inventor of Magic and every superstition, the first Saturn and Osiris of the Egyptians, the Oromasdes of the Persians, the "Son of Heaven," <insert>whose</insert> name later remained in Egypt—the root and foundation of all Egyptian idolatry.

<margin>Berosus, Book 3 of Antiquities.</margin>

Therefore, having found an opportunity while his father Noah lay drunk, grabbing his genitals and quietly murmuring a magical song, he mocked his father, and at the same time made him sterile, as if castrated. > when he was publicly corrupting the human race, asserting and practicing the idea that one should copulate—just as before the flood—with mothers, sisters, daughters, males, and beasts, and every other kind.

> Driven out from here by the most pious Janus <note>Kircher, following his sources, identifies the biblical Noah with the Roman god Janus</note>, who was distinguished by chastity and modesty, he received the nickname Chemesenua, that is, "the infamous and shameless Ham, the incubator, the propagator." For among the Aramaic Scythians, *Esen* is the same as "infamous and shameless." *Enun* indeed means both "shameless" and "propagator."

The Egyptians followed him among men in this doctrine, making that Saturn of theirs a youth among the gods, and they established a city for him called *Chem Myn*, from which we call all its citizens Chemmynites to this day. However, posterity neglected this wicked doctrine, though they retained the original custom that marriage could be entered into between brothers and sisters.

<margin>Ham is called Zoroaster and Osiris.</margin>
<margin>II. The Prince of Egypt, Mizraim or Mesres.</margin>
This first governor of Egypt was immediately followed by his son Mizraim; as the saying goes, "a bad egg from a bad crow." <note>A Latin proverb, *mali corvi malum ovum*, suggesting that wicked children follow wicked parents.</note> He was the "Jupiter Zoroaster," or the Egyptian Osiris. This man promoted the foundations of magic and illicit arts laid by his father with the greatest zeal; he was like his father in all things, professing himself a most devoted rival in his father’s actions. For he first discovered magic characters and the method of crafting amulets; he even claimed to draw the stars down from heaven with incantations. For this reason, he attained divine honors from the Egyptians. According to the historian Genebrardus, this is the Osiris of the Egyptians whom they believed had been taken up to rule the heavens, as we have explained at length in our work on the *Pamphilian Obelisk*.

<margin>Genebrardus in Chronology, Book 1</margin>

Here again, impiety occupied the world. For he, the servant and architect of wickedness, discovered Astrology and Magic, whom the Greeks also named Zoroaster.* This is the person to whom the Apostle Peter refers somewhat obscurely when he says that after the flood, mortals fell back into impiety. Homer calls him Osiris; for from his father Ham and his grandfather Noah, in addition to many sciences and arts necessary for sustaining life, he also learned agriculture, as Tibullus <note>A Roman poet of the 1st century BCE</note> testifies:

He was the inventor of letters and hieroglyphic symbols, under which he could shield the more divine meanings of his philosophy and theology from the reading of the profane <note>the uninitiated or common people</note>; after Mizraim, he also obtained the kingdom. See the more extensive treatment of this in my work *The Pamphilian Obelisk*. Truly, concerning Mizraim, his many diverse names, his deeds in Egypt, his arts and disciplines, and why he was called Zoroaster, Jupiter, Ogyges, and Osiris—all this will be discussed at length in Section II of this work, where he is treated specifically. ### THE DYNASTY
## OF THE THEBANS;

->Which was the Kingdom of the Gods, and is the 16th Dynasty according to Manetho and Africanus.<-

<margin>A Dynasty contemporary with Abraham.</margin>
Thus, after the death of Mizraim, the Dynasty of the Thebans, or the sixteenth power among the Egyptians, began. The beginning of this Dynasty coincided with the twenty-second year of the reign of Ninus among the Assyrians, according to Eusebius, and the twenty-third year of Aegialeus when the Sicyonians ruled in Greece. It lasted 190 years; this Dynasty also coincided with the final years of Abraham. Furthermore, it is difficult to assert who these Thebans were, since hardly any traces of them remain in the records of historians.

<margin>The Kingdom of the Gods.</margin>
However, as far as can be understood from a comparison of various authors, this was that celebrated and famous age in which the Egyptians record that the Gods reigned in Egypt. For these "gods" were the sons and grandsons left from the three sons of Noah, primarily the progeny of Ham. Since they possessed an immense knowledge of things—of God, of Angels, of Demons, of the World, and its constitution—

...instruction, concerning the mysteries of nature, and the virtues and properties of stones, herbs, and animals, which they had received from the first fathers through a continuous tradition. Consequently, relying on the support of this knowledge, and having provided inventions for many things necessary for human use, they gained such high esteem among the unlearned populace that the people believed them to be sharers in the divine nature and worshipped them as holy. <margin>All superstition originated from Thebes.</margin> However, because they devoted themselves more than others to the depraved arts introduced into the world by the evil demon through Ham, they used their incantations and magical deceptions to further amplify the preconceived opinion in men's minds regarding their works—performing feats that seemed impossible for human beings to achieve. And these are the men famous throughout the ages, from whom, as if from a certain Trojan horse, <note>A metaphor for a source of hidden and widespread danger or corruption</note> all superstition and the profession of illicit arts emanated into every land; it seems that whatever fables Egypt or Greece ever devised took their origin from them. These are those Gods or Heroes whom the priests falsely claim (according to Diodorus) reigned in Egypt for a little less than eighteen thousand years, and that the last of the Gods to hold the kingdom was Horus, the son of Isis. These figures are Heaven, Saturn, Jupiter, Isis, Typhon, Hercules, Mercury, Osiris, and Horus; to whom the following correspond in order: Noah, Ham, Mizraim and his wife Rhea, Nimrod, Ninus, and others born from the lineage of Ham, whose names have remained unknown due to the antiquity of the times.

# HERMES MERCURY Or FAUNUS
## Son of Picus Jupiter,
### THE SECOND DYNAST of Egypt.

<margin>Mercury called Faunus.</margin>
Mercury, or Faunus, the son of Picus Jupiter and a descendant of the lineage of Ham, succeeded Mizraim in the empire, as the *Alexandrian Chronicle* <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Christian chronicle of the world</note> records; his inauguration occurred in the following manner:

> <margin>He migrates from Italy into Egypt.</margin>
> *After the death of Picus (also known as Jupiter),* says the Chronicle, *his son Faunus, of the lineage of Janus, who was also called Mercury, governed the kingdom of Italy for 35 years. He was a sagacious, clever man and a Mathematician, who was the first to discover the metal gold in the West and the method of smelting it. But when he realized that his brothers (born to his father Jupiter by various concubines) burned with envy toward him—for they had formed a plan to kill him—he packed up a vast weight of gold and departed from Italy. He traveled to Egypt to the lineage descended from his uncle Ham, the son of Noah, by whom he was received with great honor. While he lived there, he looked down upon everyone else, and dressed in a golden cloak, he practiced philosophy among the Egyptians. He predicted many things that would happen, for he was naturally very gifted. The Egyptians, therefore, worshipping him, proclaimed him the God Mercury, as one who foretold the future and brought them oracles and responses from God about the future like a messenger, and supplied them with gold. They called him the "Giver of Wealth" and the "Golden God."* <margin>Mercury, the God of Gold.</margin> *Thus,* says the Chronicle, *did Mercury come into Egypt.*

<note>original Greek: "Ἐβασίλευσε τῆς Αἰγυπτίων ὅτε ἐκ τοῦ γένος τοῦ Χὰμ ὁ Μεζρὶμ..."</note> Mezrim, of the lineage of Ham, ruled the Egyptians; at the <unclear>the</unclear> same <unclear>hour</unclear> he <unclear>passed away</unclear>, the Egyptians appointed Hermes as King, and he ruled the Egyptians for 38 years in <unclear>great pride</unclear>. Mercury reigned, it says, when a certain man from the lineage of Ham, named Mefrem (or Misraim, which is the same), came into Egypt. Upon his death, the Egyptians appointed Mercury as King in his place, who reigned quite proudly for 38 years. They say he was the inventor of various things: he organized language into order, gave names to many things, and was also the discoverer of letters. He established the honors and sacred rites by which each of the Gods should be worshipped, and he discovered the movements of the stars and the method of dividing the year. For these reasons, Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> records that he was held in the highest honor by Osiris (or Misraim) and served as the counselor to Isis (or Rhea, the wife of Misraim) during her husband’s absence.

## VULCAN
->Of Egypt<-
### <term>DYNAST</term> III.
<note>A Dynast refers to a powerful ruler or member of a reigning family in ancient history.</note>

<margin>
Vulcan was the first author of preserving fire.
Diodorus, Book 1, Chapter 2.
</margin>

The <term>Alexandrian Chronicle</term> <note>A 7th-century Byzantine universal chronicle</note> substitutes Vulcan in the place of Mercury. Vulcan, through a certain divine song or prayer, obtained a craftsman’s genius and the skill of a smith from heaven, so that he could forge weapons from iron. For when a tree had been set ablaze by a lightning strike in the mountains, Diodorus recounts that Vulcan was greatly delighted by it; as the fire began to fail, he supplied it with new fuel. In this way, by keeping the fire going, he called other men together to witness it, claiming the use of preserving fire as his own discovery. Relying on this gift of fire brought from heaven, he demonstrated the method of preparing a living through the fabrication of weapons, as well as the means of achieving military valor, victory, and safety; indeed, before him, men fought only with clubs and stones. Because of this, he was numbered among the Gods and earned immortality. But more on this can be found in Diodorus.

## THE SUN
->Of Egypt<-
### <term>DYNAST</term> IV.

<margin>
The Sun, son of Vulcan.
Alexandrian Chronicle.
</margin>

Furthermore, the Chronicle states that after Vulcan had passed away and been numbered among the Gods, his son, the Sun, took his place. He lived for four thousand four hundred and seventy-seven days, which makes 12 years, three months, and four days. For the Egyptians at that time were ignorant of any other method of calculating time; they defined the orbit of all things by the span of a single day. They only described the number of twelve months much later, when common mortals began to be held as taxpayers to kings. Now the Sun, the son of Vulcan, whom others...
