# DYNASTY XVI.
## Of the Shepherds, lasting 103 years.

<margin>
Various opinions on the Dynasty of the Shepherds.
</margin>
<margin>
The Dynasty of the Shepherds as the beginning of the Pharaonic empire.
</margin>
The Dynasty of the Thebans is followed by the Dynasty of the Shepherds, so called either because during its height, the children of Jacob—who were shepherds according to the Sacred Scripture—descended into Egypt and settled there, as <term>Eusebius</term><note>A 4th-century Christian historian and bishop.</note> and Genebrardus believe; or because the wealth of the Kings then powerful in Egypt consisted of livestock, as <term>Manetho</term><note>An Egyptian priest and historian who wrote a history of Egypt in Greek in the 3rd century BCE.</note> maintains. Who these Kings were, and what their names were, is difficult to assert, especially since Eusebius (whom we have determined to follow as much as possible) made no mention of them. Others, although they mention some who ruled in this Dynasty, have written about them in such a confused manner that it is impossible to discern what should be believed. However, it is so certain that the beginning of the Pharaonic empire was from this Dynasty that whoever contradicts it would seem to contradict the Sacred Scriptures which clearly assert it.

<margin>
Diodorus, Book 1, and Part 1, Chapter 1. Menas or Mitras was the first Pharaoh of the Egyptians.
</margin>
For it is more well-known than needs to be said that Pharaoh, the King of Egypt, seized Sarah, the wife of Abraham; and that Pharaoh the King also appointed Joseph as the Lord of Egypt. Since these things are so, let us now see who from this Dynasty first reigned in Egypt after the Gods. The *Alexandrian Chronicle* places Sesostris there, and confuses him with Mercury Trismegistus, but wrongly so: because that is contrary to history and the opinion of all chronologists, as will be seen below—unless we assert that "Sesostris" was written corruptly for *Sesosiri* <note>original: "Sesosiri"</note>, which signifies "the offspring of Osiris." Others established Apis as the first King because he flourished in Egypt around the beginning of this Dynasty and was later recorded among the number of the Gods, whom they called Serapis, about whom we shall speak in his place. Others say Mesrem or Misraim, others Osiris: we, wishing to hold the most secure path, establish Menas, following Herodotus and Diodorus. For he says: *They say that Menas reigned first in Egypt after the Gods, who taught the people to worship the Gods and to make sacrifices to them, and moreover to set tables and prepare beds, accustoming them to luxuries and a more refined life.* However, whether Mitres, Mithras, or Misraim—who, according to Pliny, is said to have been the first to discover the <term>Obelisk</term>—is the same as Menas, the first King and Pharaoh of the Egyptians, I would not easily assert; especially since "Menas" signifies the Moon and "Mitres" the Sun, both of which were Divinities held in great veneration and worship among the Egyptians; one of whom they called Osiris, the other Isis. Certainly, Herodotus and Diodorus never make mention of a King Mithras, as far as I know. Eusebius, however, in the Dynasty of the Pelitanes, assigns him the fourth place, as...

# TREATISE I. ON THE KINGS OF EGYPT.
## CHAPTER X.

In such great obscurity of events and names, nothing remains for us but conjectures. The confusion of names seems to have arisen from this: that while they reigned in Egypt at the same time, only a few names were recorded by writers—and not all the same names by everyone, but some by some and others by others. This depended on which King the priests, who were tasked with recording the deeds, either loved or hated. For this reason, we read in <term>Diodorus</term><note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note> that nineteen generations, or five hundred and seventy years, passed between <term>Uchoreus</term><note>A legendary king often identified as the founder of Memphis.</note> and <term>Sesostris</term><note>A legendary king of Egypt said to have conquered the world, often a composite of several real Pharaohs like Senusret III or Ramesses II.</note>. Yet in that interval, no one who ruled Egypt is named by Diodorus—as has been said—nor by <term>Herodotus</term><note>The 5th-century BCE Greek historian known as the "Father of History."</note>, except for <term>Moeris</term><note>Commonly identified with Amenemhat III, known for his vast irrigation works and Lake Moeris.</note>. Since <term>Eusebius</term><note>A 4th-century Christian bishop and historian who synchronized pagan and biblical history.</note> mentions none of these but does mention others, it is likely that they were passed over in silence by <term>Manetho</term><note>An Egyptian priest who wrote a history of Egypt in Greek; his king-lists are the basis for modern Egyptian chronology.</note>, whom Eusebius followed, just as others were omitted by those whose reliability and writings Herodotus and Diodorus followed.

<margin>
Herodotus in *Thalia* <note>The third book of Herodotus's *Histories*.</note>.
</margin>
It is truly remarkable that we return to where we started: Herodotus writes that it was <term>Menas</term><note>Often identified with Menes, traditionally the first human Pharaoh who unified Upper and Lower Egypt.</note> who founded <term>Memphis</term><note>The ancient capital of Lower Egypt.</note>, while Diodorus testifies it was founded by Uchoreus, specifically 1,035 years after the founding of <term>Thebes</term><note>The great capital of Upper Egypt.</note>. Eusebius, however, records that Memphis was founded by <term>Epaphus</term>, the son of Jove and Io, following the inventions and fables of the Greeks. Nevertheless, among the Greeks, all confess that Epaphus was Egyptian. For they say that <term>Io</term><note>A priestess of Hera whom Zeus/Jove loved; she was turned into a heifer and wandered the world to escape Hera's jealousy.</note>, after many wanderings, arrived in Egypt, and there, restored to her former shape and embraced by Jove, she gave birth to Epaphus, from whom Memphis later took its origin. Furthermore, Herodotus writes that the bull <term>Apis</term><note>A sacred bull worshipped in the Memphis region, seen as an intermediary between humans and the gods.</note> is called "Epaphus" by the Greeks; thus, by a name of this sort, either a specific man is signified, or the beast which is held among the Egyptians. For when <term>Pindar</term><note>A famous Greek lyric poet known for his odes.</note> testifies that many cities were founded in Egypt by Epaphus, he sings thus: 

<margin>
Ode 10 of the *Nemeans*.
</margin>
> And many cities were established in Egypt by the hands of Epaphus. <note>original Greek: Πολλὰ δ' Αἰγύπτῳ κατωκίσθεν ἄστη ⁑ Ἐπάφου παλάμαις.</note>

<margin>
Who Apis, Epaphus, and Serapis were; and whether they were one and the same.
</margin>
Indeed, the transition from <term>Apis</term> to <term>Epaphus</term> is easy, and we read that Memphis was founded by Apis, and that Apis himself was the first to be called a God in Egypt and was surnamed <term>Serapis</term><note>A Greco-Egyptian deity intended to bridge the two cultures.</note>. Thus the bull Apis, the god Apis, and Apis the founder of Memphis are called by the Greeks by the single name "Epaphus." But whether he was Uchoreus or Epaphus, or whether both were one and the same—the one named by the Greeks, the other by the Egyptians—we surely say they are the same person. For it is established from Eusebius that Memphis was founded by him in the year of the world 3700. But so that some certainty may finally be established in such a great difficulty of matters, two things must be proved by us: first, whether Menas, <term>Mithras</term><note>A sun god; the author is attempting to link Egyptian and Persian/Indo-Iranian figures.</note>, <term>Misraim</term><note>The Hebrew name for Egypt, also identifying a son of Ham and grandson of Noah.</note>, <term>Osiris</term>, and Uchoreus—kings mentioned in this Dynasty by various authors—are the same or different? Second, did they stand out as the founders of Memphis or not? Once these are settled, I trust I shall provide at least some light.

<margin>
Menas and Mithras are one and the same.

### CHAPTER X. THE ISIAK TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>Diodorus Siculus, page 2, book 1, chapter 2.</margin>
...Egypt in it. From these words, gather first, that the first King in Egypt was <term>Mitres</term><note>A variation of Mithras or Misraim used by Kircher to bridge Persian and Egyptian history.</note> and that he was <term>Misraim</term><note>The biblical son of Ham, traditionally considered the ancestor of the Egyptians.</note>. It is clear from <term>Diodorus</term><note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note> that these things also apply to Menas, for he writes thus: 

> They say that Menas reigned first in Egypt after the Gods; he taught the people to worship the Gods and to perform sacrifices twice, and moreover to set tables and couches for them. 

Therefore, both Menas and Mithras are established as the first King and the first author of the worship of the Gods and their sacrifices by the cited authors. There is only this difference: that he was called Menas by the Egyptians (perhaps due to the worship of the Moon <note>original: "Menas" likely linked to the Greek *Mene*, meaning Moon.</note>), while this one was called Mithras by the Persians and Arabs due to the worship of the Sun and fire, to whom he traveled from Egypt, according to Diodorus. These things being established, it is no wonder that some have placed <term>Osiris</term> as the first King of Egypt, and others <term>Vexores</term> or <term>Vechores</term>; since Osiris is everywhere confused with Mithras, as we prove at length in our work on the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>Kircher's 1650 study of the obelisk now in Rome's Piazza Navona.</note>. However, <term>Genebrardus</term><note>Gilbert Génébrard, a 16th-century French scholar and chronologist.</note> suspects Vexores or Uchorius to be the same as Osiris, following the historian <term>Sabellicus</term>; for he says thus:

We say, therefore, that Mithras, Menas, or Mitres is the same as Misraim the son of <term>Ham</term><note>In the Bible, Ham was the son of Noah; his descendants were said to have settled Africa.</note>, whose Counselor was <term>Mercury</term><note>The Roman equivalent of Hermes/Thoth.</note>, his wife <term>Isis</term>, and his son <term>Horus Mesramuthisis</term>; see all these things deduced and demonstrated at length in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. Unless someone wishes to confuse Menas with Isis, whom the ancients called the Moon, he may lawfully do so in such a great confusion of names; since it is also clear from Diodorus that Osiris, having entrusted the care of the kingdom to Isis, traveled across the globe; therefore Isis, or the Moon, could easily be accepted by posterity as "Menas" <note>original: "Mena"</note>, for the first King of Egypt, without regard for gender.

Another difficulty remains to be solved regarding the founding of <term>Memphis</term><note>The ancient capital of Lower Egypt.</note>. Because they knew that he flourished at the very same time that <term>Menas</term> was founding Memphis, they called him its founder. In that same place he founded, they later raised a bull in a certain enclosure, into which they believed he had been transformed, and they called it <term>Apis</term>. Furthermore, since at that same time, as we have said, Menas, Mithras, Osiris, and <term>Vexores</term> or <term>Vechorius</term><note>Names used by ancient historians like Justin to refer to early, possibly legendary, Egyptian kings.</note> reigned as different kings joined into one; and since Osiris (as well as the Persian Mithras, whom we have said is the same as Menas) was worshipped under the form of a bull, it should seem a wonder to no one if they called the first King of Egypt and founder of Memphis by many names: now Menas, now Mithras, now Osiris, Vexores, or Vechorius, and now Epaphus or Apis. This follows that common rule of philosophers: <note>original: "quæ sunt eadem vni tertio, eadem sunt inter se"</note> "things that are the same as a third thing are the same as each other." For through the similarity of their deeds, even if they were distinct individuals, they expressed a single identity. Thus, these and similar names are confused everywhere by the authors. But for those who desire more concerning Mithras, <term>Misraim</term><note>The biblical grandson of Noah, traditionally viewed as the progenitor of the Egyptians.</note>, and Osiris, let them consult the *Pamphilian Obelisk*<note>Kircher's own 1650 work deciphering the hieroglyphs on the obelisk in the Piazza Navona.</note>. We thought these matters should be treated at length so that we might demonstrate by these words how much power the ambiguity of names has in properly judging Chronologies. Now to other matters.

## THE 17TH DYNASTY OF THE STATESMEN

### Which lasted 348 years.

After the 16th Dynasty of the <term>Shepherds</term><note>The Hyksos, a Semitic people who ruled northern Egypt before the New Kingdom.</note>, follows the 17th Dynasty of the Statesmen; so called because Egypt obtained a form of government perfected in all its parts and a complete <term>polity</term><note>original: "politiam," referring to a structured civil administration.</note> from the Kings of this Dynasty. <margin>Amasis.</margin>
The first King of this Dynasty, therefore, according to Manetho in Eusebius, is <term>Amasis</term>, Pharaoh of Egypt. Amasis reigned at the very time when <term>Jacob</term>, while a fierce famine was raging, went down into Egypt to his son <term>Joseph</term>, who at that time governed Egypt as the first man after the King.

<margin>Achoris.</margin>
Others call him <note>original: "Mesrem, Mitrem, Mespheem"</note> Mesres, Mitres, or Mesphees; they confound him with the previous Mitres, Menes, and Mesres I, as often happens with names that sound alike. Following Diodorus and Herodotus, we say he is the same as **Myris** <note>Also known as Moeris, a pharaoh credited with massive irrigation projects.</note>, whom Diodorus identifies as the builder of the <term>propylaeum</term><note>A monumental gateway or entrance to a temple complex.</note> at Memphis and of Lake Moeris. This lake he caused to be excavated with the greatest benefit to all of Egypt to receive the stagnant waters in the plains. Some also attribute to this King that sumptuous structure of the **Labyrinth**, although Diodorus asserts its author was Menides or Marus; you may consult him on this. He was, however, the builder of certain pyramids, one of which he erected for himself and another for his wife as an eternal memorial of their deeds. Following Mephres or Myris was **Misphragmuthosis** (or Mephramutosis II), the fifth King of the Thebans <note>The original uses "Politanorum," referring to the Diospolitan or Theban dynasty.</note>, although we more truly and consistently relegate this Mesra and Mesramuthisis to the preceding Dynasty—namely, to the end of the Kingdom of the Gods—from which the kingdom passed to **Thutmoses**. **Genebrard** <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine scholar and chronologist.</note> thinks he is the one who, while pursuing the children of Israel, perished being swallowed by the Red Sea, though we assert more truly that it was **Cenchres**. After a reign of nine years, Thutmoses appointed as successor **Amenophis II**, whom some call **Memnon** or **Menas**. This man is said to have published the edict against the Hebrews, ordering that whatever males were brought into the light by Hebrew women should be killed. To him was dedicated the statue which authors call the **Statue of Memnon**, famous for the miraculous sound it gave when struck by the rays of the rising sun; we have discussed this at length elsewhere. Furthermore, the successor of Amenophis or Memnon was **Horus II**, whom we identify as **Busiris** along with Diodorus; for both are wrongly called the founder of Thebes, and both are said to have lived at the same time. I believe this mixing of names arose because they thought Horus lived at the same time as that Horus who placed the limbs of Osiris (scattered by Typhon) into a wooden ox and founded the city he later called **Busiris**. But since Diodorus says Busiris built the "City of the Sun" called **Thebes**, and identifies Horus (whom some also call Amenophis) as the author of that same city, this error could easily creep in from the ambiguity of the names, leading them to take Horus for Busiris. For those who desire more regarding the magnificence of the city of Thebes, its prodigious structures, and the multitude of its gates, let them consult Diodorus, who describes each detail extensively and exactly. Therefore Horus, or Busiris, after he had governed Egypt for 38 years, handed the scepter to **Acencheres**, after whom it came into the hands of **Achoris**. At this time lived another **Hermes Trismegistus** <note>Kircher believes in multiple "Hermes" figures throughout history; this "thrice-great" sage was the legendary author of the Hermetic corpus.</note>; because he was a contemporary of Moses, many confound him with Moses or Jethro. But just as with the ambiguity of names, so the diversity of the "Mercuries" <note>The Roman name for Hermes.</note> has everywhere given occasion for great altercations in literature regarding this.

<margin>*Danaus*, *Ramesses*</margin>
...of which *Danaus* took possession, whom *Eusebius* also calls *Armenus* <note>original: "Armenum"; Eusebius was a 4th-century historian who attempted to synchronize world history.</note>. His brother *Ramesses*, who was also called *Aegyptus*, succeeded him through tyranny; for once *Danaus* was deprived of the crown, the former gained control of the kingdom. Finally, *Amenophis*, or *Memphta*, closed the line of Pharaohs of this Dynasty. It was he who restored the Kingdom that had been diminished by God's vengeance through *Moses* <note>Kircher refers here to the aftermath of the Biblical Plagues and the Exodus.</note>. While he strove to restore the obelisks and the sacred disciplines, he was overtaken by death and left his plans to be carried out by his son *Sothis*.

# DYNASTY XIX.
## Which is of the Lartes. <note>The "Lartes" or "Lartum" refers to a specific grouping of kings in Kircher's chronological system, likely derived from his reading of ancient lists like those of Manetho.</note>

<margin>*Zethus*. *Ranses*. *Sesostris*.</margin>
This Dynasty is named after the *Lartian* Kings, the first of whom in *Egypt* was *Sothis*, or as *Eusebius* prefers, *Zethus*, the son of *Amenophis*. According to the testimony of *Pliny*, he erected four obelisks and fully restored the sacred disciplines. *Ramesses*, his son and the erector of four obelisks, co-reigned with him for a time and later succeeded him. After *Sothis* met his fate, he was followed by the second *Larthes*, named *Ranses* or *Ramesses*; and after him came *Sesostris*, who surpassed all his predecessors in glory and the greatness of his deeds. When he had reigned for 33 years, his life ended as his eyes failed him. It is difficult to find a name worthy of his valor; he was a man of great spirit, admired not only by the priests but by all *Egyptians*. He met death with the same greatness of soul with which he had performed such outstanding feats. His glory and the memory of his deeds so occupied posterity that many centuries later, when the *Persians* held the empire of *Egypt*, and *Darius* <note>Darius the Great, the Persian King of Kings.</note> (the father of *Xerxes*) attempted to place his own statue before that of *Sesostris* in *Memphis*, <margin>A memorable deed of an *Egyptian* Priest.</margin> the high priest publicly opposed him. The priest asserted that *Darius* had not yet equaled the works of *Sesostris*. The King was by no means offended by this answer, but rather rejoiced greatly at such freedom of speech, saying that he would see to it that he was in no way inferior to the other’s valor, if only he might live as long. Under *Sesostris*, all arts and disciplines flourished at the highest level, especially the doctrine of hieroglyphics, as witnessed by the various obelisks erected by him in different places. You may read of his expeditions to the most remote shores of the earth, his most sumptuous building structures, and his countless other virtues in the works of *Diodorus* <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note>, who describes them all at length. <margin>*Pheron* or *Noncorius*, son of *Sesostris*</margin> *Amenophis*, or *Pheron*—also known by the name *Noncorius*—succeeded *Sesostris* in the empire. Although he assumed his father's name, he in no way imitated his father's glory. Instead, he was afflicted by the same malady as his father, for he was struck blind, whether due to his father's shared nature or (as some fabulists say) because of his impiety toward the *Nile*, at whose current he had hurled a spear. However, once the Gods were appeased, his sight...

It is said that when this Thuoris (or Thules) was returning to Egypt after having already subjugated Africa, he entered the temple with great pride and consulted the Oracle with these words: "Tell me," he said, "O Fire-Powerful, Truth-Speaker, Blessed One, who tempers the course of the heavens: who before me was able to subject all things to himself? Now, **Thuoris** or **Thules** was the last of the <term>Larthian Kings</term> <note>Kircher's term for a specific lineage of rulers</note>, called **Polybus** by Homer. He lived around the time of the destruction of the city of Troy; for Homer says that Menelaus and Helen visited him after the city was destroyed. Eusebius calculates 375 years from the twenty-third year of the life of Moses to the end of this Dynasty; after which Egypt, deprived of Kings for 177 years, was administered by certain noble families.

# DYNASTY XX.
## Of the Diapolitans. <note>Also known as the Theban Dynasty.</note>

<margin>
1 Kings, ch. 11.
</margin>
<margin>
Egypt is administered by the more noble families.
</margin>
<margin>
Cetes or Proteus.
</margin>
Around the same time that the kingdom of the Jews was divided between Rehoboam and Jeroboam, since Egypt lacked Kings, men from only the more distinguished families were taken into the government of the kingdom. Among these, the first place was held by **Cetes**, whom the Greeks call **Proteus**, and who flourished in Egypt during the time of the Trojan War. They record that he was skilled in the arts and accustomed to turning himself into various forms, so that at times he appeared as an animal, sometimes a tree, or fire, or something else.

> *At first he took the appearance of a Lion's sight,*
> *Soon a Boar, then became a Dragon, then a wild Leopard;*
> *He even turned himself into water, and changed his ancient form*
> *Into a tree, high with branches and foliage.*

He attained the knowledge of these things from his constant association with the Priests. However, Diodorus says that the insignia and ornaments of the Kings of Egypt, which consisted of various objects, gave cause for this fabulous <term>metamorphosis</term> <note>a transformation of shape</note>. <margin>Why did Egyptian Kings wear the parts of animals on their heads?</margin> He says that the custom handed down to the Kings provided the Greeks with the occasion for inventing such transformations. For it was the custom for Egyptian Kings to wear the forepart of a Lion, a Bull, or a Dragon on their heads as the insignia of their sovereignty.

## DYNASTY XXIII
### The Tanite Dynasty <note>Referring to the 23rd Dynasty, traditionally associated with the city of Tanis in the Nile Delta.</note>

<margin>Petubastis. Oforthon. Psammus.</margin>
The first King of this Dynasty was Petubastes, or more accurately in Coptic, *Petoubastes*, so named after the city of Bubastos; <note>Bubastos was the center of worship for the cat-goddess Bastet; the name means "He who belongs to Bastet."</note> when he died, he was succeeded by Oforthon, who was also called Hercules. ## DYNASTY XXIV
### The Legal Dynasty

<margin>Bocchorus the lawmaker.</margin>
Bocchorus (better known as *Bocchoris*) acted as the King of this Dynasty; he was one of the Great Lawmakers of the Egyptians. I find nothing in the authors regarding his successors.

## DYNASTY XXV
### The Ethiopian Dynasty

<margin>Sabachus or Sabazius.</margin>
Sabachus, or as others call him, Sabazius, began this Dynasty; he is recorded as having been an Ethiopian. After defeating Bocchorus, he took possession of Egypt. Diodorus speaks of him thus:

<margin>He governs Egypt prudently.</margin>
> Sabacus, an Ethiopian by birth, excelled other Kings in his worship of the Gods and his generosity. The greatest proof of his virtue was his integrity and his useful attention to upholding the laws. For he never punished those condemned to death with the penalty of execution, but instead forced them to perform labor while bound in chains throughout the cities. This practice provided no small amount of revenue, for he acquired much wealth from that service; by their labor, he constructed many embankments and dug useful canals in various places. In this way, he both softened the bitterness of the punishment and turned what would have been a uselessly harsh penalty into a great public benefit.

<margin>The vision of Sabazius.</margin>
Anyone may easily perceive his outstanding piety and the character of his life from the beginning through a vision he had in a dream. The God who is worshipped at Thebes <note>Likely referring to Amun-Ra.</note> appeared to him in sleep and said that his reign over the Egyptians would be neither happy nor long-lasting unless he killed all the Priests of Egypt and passed with his men through the middle of their corpses.

<margin>He abdicates the Kingdom of his own accord.</margin>
After this dream had occurred several times, he summoned all the Priests from everywhere and told them what he had received through the dream. He said that he did not wish to remain in Egypt if it meant plotting the destruction of anyone; rather, he preferred to depart from Egypt pure and free from all crime, returning his life to the fates, than to possess a kingdom through wicked slaughter and iniquity. Thus, having handed the kingdom back to the Egyptians, he returned to Ethiopia. In the place of Sabazius...

Merres the Ethiopian first administered the kingdom; he was followed by Stephinatis, and he by Nechao (also known as Nichepsos). Once these had passed away, the Egyptians were without a King for two years, during which time everything was in turmoil, and matters even broke out into open war.

Herodotus, Book 2.
</margin>
Consequently, twelve leaders from among the nobility were appointed in place of a King, and the entire care of the kingdom was entrusted to them. However, when they had held power together for fifteen years, the Kingdom was reduced to a single ruler for the following reason: At a appointed time, when these twelve governors were sacrificing in the temple of Vulcan <note>The Roman name for the Egyptian creator god Ptah, whose primary temple was in Memphis.</note>, and were about to offer a libation on the final day of the festival, the High Priest brought out the golden vials they were accustomed to use for the offering. However, he made a mistake in the count; for twelve men, he brought out only eleven vials. When Psammeticus, who stood last among them, realized he did not have a vial, he took off his bronze helmet, held it out, and performed the libation. (It should be noted that all the other Kings also wore and were currently carrying helmets). At that moment, Psammeticus did not act with any deceitful intent <note>original: "dolo malo"</note>. Nevertheless, the others, believing Psammeticus had done this on purpose and recalling an oracle's response—which stated that the man who offered a libation from a bronze vial would be the sole King of Egypt—stripped him of the greater part of his power and banished him to the marshlands. Eventually, with the help of Ionians <note>Greek mercenaries</note> who had happened to land in the marshes, he recovered Egypt by force. After he had governed for forty-four years, his son named Apries became the heir to the kingdom, according to Herodotus and Diodorus; although Eusebius places two other Kings, Nechao (or Necephos) and Psammiten, between Psammeticus and Apries. Thus Apries (also known as Vaphres), who after his grandfather Psammeticus was the most fortunate of all kings up to that age, ruled for 25 years. During this time, he brought war against the Sidonians and fought a naval battle with Tyre. Amasis succeeded Apries (or Anamasas, as Eusebius calls him), and Herodotus narrates the reason as follows: When Apries had suffered a great slaughter after sending an army against the Cyrenaeans, the Egyptians rebelled, blaming him and believing they had been sent to certain destruction so that, once they were wiped out, he might rule the remaining Egyptians more securely. Taking this hard, many revolted from him. When Apries learned of this, he sent Amasis to soothe them with words. When Amasis arrived and was arguing against their actions, one of the Egyptians stood behind him and placed a helmet on his head, saying as he did so that he was crowning him for the kingship. This was not done against Amasis's will, as events showed; for as soon as he was declared King by the rebellious Egyptians, he began making preparations to move against Apries. Upon learning this, Apries sent a man named Patarbemin to bring Amasis to...

## DYNASTY XXVII,
### Of the Persians.

Cambyses, King of the Persians.
</margin>
In this Dynasty, the Egyptian empire was transferred from the native-born to foreigners; for King Cambyses of the Persians, having reduced it to his power by arms, seemed to have declared war not only on men, but also on the Gods and their religion. He overturned altars, shattered statues, and consumed the proud masses of the Pyramids and Obelisks and other structures with iron and fire. He held Egypt from the fifth year of his reign until the time of Darius, the son of Xerxes, for 150 years.

## DYNASTY XXVIII.
### Of the Xerxes.

<margin>
Xerxes.
</margin>
Xerxes gained possession of the Egyptian Kingdom after the successors of Cambyses, and many of this name followed him in the empire. At this time flourished all the most famous writers: <term>Hiero of Syracuse</term> <note>Latin: "Hieronymus Syracusanus," referring to the tyrant and patron of poets.</note>, Aeschylus, Pindar, Sophocles, Euripides, Herodotus, Zeuxis, as well as the biblical figures Esther and Ahasuerus, Ezra, and the philosopher Parmenides; also, Plato was born.

## DYNASTY XXIX.
### Egyptian.

<margin>
Amyrtaeus, Nepherites, Nectanebo.
</margin>
In this Dynasty, when the Egyptian empire had already been recovered from the Persians, <term>Amyrtaeus</term> <note>Latin: "Amarthæus."</note> was the first to rule from a new family; after him Nepherites, and finally Achoris reigned.

# DYNASTY XXX.
->Of the Mendesians<-

<margin>Psammutes, Nepherites, Nectabo.</margin>
The first of this Dynasty was Psammutes, in whose time the philosopher Plato flourished. Psammutes was succeeded by Nepherites; after Nepherites came Nectabo, also known as Nectanebo <note>This refers to Nectanebo I, founder of the 30th Dynasty.</note>.

---

# DYNASTY XXXI.
->Of the Sebennytes<- <note>Original: "Euenitarum." This likely refers to the Sebennyte dynasty, though the chronology here blends several historical traditions.</note>

<margin>Theo.</margin>
The first of this Dynasty was Theo <note>Likely Tachos or Teos.</note>, who, having abandoned the kingdom, fled into Arabia; during this time Aristotle, the pupil of Plato, flourished.

---

# DYNASTY XXXII.
->And the last of the Egyptians<-

<margin>
Nectanebo, Magician and greatest sorcerer.
</margin>
Nectanebo <note>Nectanebo II, the last native ruler of ancient Egypt.</note> was the first and the last of this Dynasty; he was a Magician and a most powerful sorcerer. Indeed, through enchantments and magical illusions, he extorted many secrets from demons regarding the future state of affairs. Among other forms of divination and magical incantations, he practiced **Leucanomancy** <note>original: "Leucanomantiam," a method of fortune-telling using a basin of water.</note>—those specifically which are performed in a basin full of water. 

For when Artaxerxes Ochus <note>The Persian King Artaxerxes III.</note> was prepared to occupy Egypt, Nectanebo, having discovered through these magical oracles the impending destruction of the Egyptian empire by Ochus, packed up a vast quantity of gold, precious stones, and whatever else was valuable in the royal treasury. Disguising his appearance so as to remain unknown to everyone, he fled into Macedonia (though others, such as Eusebius, prefer the account that he fled into Ethiopia). 

There, having used his magical arts to fascinate Olympia, the wife of Philip of Macedon, he persuaded her that she was destined to conceive a son by the God Ammon, who would rule the entire world. He himself, <margin>The father of Alexander the Great.</margin> under the form of the aforementioned Ammon—whose likeness he had already presented to Olympia through incantations in her dreams—lay with the Queen and fathered a son, who was later called Alexander the Great because of the glory of his deeds. <margin>Ben Gorion, Book 1, Chapter 4.</margin> Joseph Ben Gorion <note>A reference to the *Josippon*, a popular medieval Hebrew history of the Jews.</note> relates these events. However, we shall say much more in the proper place concerning the Magic of this King and the various arts he inherited from the Egyptians.

<margin>
Ochus, or Artaxerxes, invades the kingdom.
</margin>
And so, under this King, the kingdom of the Egyptians was destroyed; it was transferred from the Persian Kings and joined to the empire of the Greeks. For after Nectanebo was driven out, Ochus (who is also called Artaxerxes), the second Persian King <note>Referring to the second period of Persian rule.</note>, took possession of it. When he passed away, his son Arses was substituted in his place; after him, Darius <margin>Alexander the Great.</margin> succeeded as the son of Arses <note>Historically, Darius III was a distant cousin, not the son of Arses, but the author follows a specific lineage tradition here.</note>. After Darius had administered the realm for six years, Alexander the Great, having killed Darius in Babylon, subjected the entire Persian Kingdom to his own dominion, and with it, all of Egypt. When Alexander died in Babylon in the 34th year of his age, and the empire was divided among many successors...

different rulers reigned. And indeed, Egypt fell to the lot of the Ptolemies <note>The Greek dynasty founded by Ptolemy I Soter, one of Alexander the Great's generals.</note>, by whom it was governed for nearly 300 years, from the first Ptolemies down to Cleopatra. From her, it finally passed to the Romans, and from the Romans to the Mohammedans, until at last it fell from its former glory.

And these are the 32 Dynasties through which the empire of the Egyptians was extended during the stated times. We have described seventeen of these—two of which are from the Greeks—namely, those that take their beginning from the sixteenth; the remaining fifteen were drawn from the monuments of the Arabs <note>Kircher relied heavily on medieval Arabic manuscripts, believing they preserved ancient Egyptian secrets lost to the West.</note>.

Therefore, it seemed fit to divide that whole interval of time in which the dominion of Egypt persisted—from the creation of the world and the flood until the coming of our salvation—into four parts or chronological distinctions. Thus, we shall call that entire space of time from the creation of the world up to the flood the **Primeval Dynasties of Egypt** according to the mind of the Arabs. From the flood until the birth of Abraham, let us call it the **Dynasty of the Gods**, or the **Kingdom of Heroes**. From the birth of Abraham, or Horus, the last of the Gods, until the year in which Ochus, King of the Persians, took possession of Egypt, let us name it the **Pharaonic Kingdom**. Finally, from this point until Christ, let us designate it the **Ptolemaic Kingdom**. 

In this way, by avoiding everything that could bring confusion of dates or other inconveniences, we may proceed with greater light and clarity. You will see in the following **Chronological Table** <note>original: "Pinace Chronologico"</note> each King of Egypt, beginning from Ham <note>The biblical son of Noah, whom Kircher identifies as the progenitor of the Egyptians.</note> and continuing to Julius Caesar, placed in order with the years in which each reigned, corresponding to the years elapsed since the creation of the world and the flood. To these we have also added the illustrious men who were then famous in the world under the dominion of each king, and other things worthy of memory, which will appear in our **Chronography** <note>original: "Chronographia"</note> set out below. For this Chronography will be of great benefit, both for understanding our work in its entirety and for explaining difficult passages that occur here and there concerning the calculation of times. ->TREATISE II. ON EGYPTIAN POLITICS. CHAPTER I<-

# TREATISE II.
<note>original: "Syntagma." A "syntagma" is a systematic arrangement or a formal treatise on a specific subject.</note>

## Concerning the Politics of the Egyptians, and the method and reasoning by which they both expanded and preserved their Empire.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'I' decorated with floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>

AMONG the other nations and peoples of the world, no race was ever found that applied itself with greater care and vigilance than the Egyptian to the proper and blessed establishment of a system of governance <note>original: "Republicæ." While literally "Republic," in this context it refers to the general "body politic" or state.</note>. For just as they had discovered the true methods of ruling, they also provided an absolute model—a perfect "idea" of a complete polity—which, by the testimony of all writers, was offered at all times as an example for the Kings and Princes of the entire earth to imitate.

<margin>Egyptian politics were founded on the worship of God.</margin>
For since they recognized that all empire and dominion were founded upon God, the Best and Greatest, and the providence of the supreme Divinity, they seem to have taken greater care in this one thing above all others: to direct their entire Monarchy according to the standard of the supreme Divinity and the "measure" (as they say) of the immortal Gods. They believed they would fare well only if they could win over those who hold the final judgment over all things through religious worship, honor, and the reverence shown to the Gods. For if these Gods were provoked to indignation—whether through the neglect of ancestral rites or through the unpunished license of dissolute morals—they believed nothing would remain for them but the discord of the people, the dangerous machinations of rebellions, and finally the ultimate ruin and extermination of their kingdoms and empires.

<margin>The Method.</margin>
To prevent these very things, they were accustomed by truly wise counsel to appoint leaders—not men devoted to the disturbances of the soul, nor the ignorant who are inexperienced in affairs and subject to the contagion of vice—but rather priests and philosophers conspicuous for their wisdom. These men were taught by long practice and experience and were well-trained in ancestral rites and divine ceremonies. By their prudence and counsel, all things in the Kingdom were conducted and administered properly. Those who were proven in this "wrestling-ground" <note>The author uses the term "palæstra," a Greek wrestling school, as a metaphor for a place of rigorous training and testing.</note> of virtue and wisdom were eventually designated as successors to the deceased King. They judged those who had not first mastered themselves, or who did not know how to moderate their own disturbances and ruinous passions, to be least fit for the kingdom. Through this care and constant vigilance, it came to pass that the kingdom—in its teeming population, the greatness of its cities, the wisdom of its subjects, and finally in its abundance of all things necessary for the human race—was second to none. From the building of the Tower <note>A reference to the Tower of Babel, which Kircher uses as a chronological starting point for post-flood civilizations.</note> until the invasion of Egypt by Cambyses <note>Cambyses II was the Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE.</note>, a span of 1,582 years, Egypt stood in the highest concord, peace, and tranquility—a feat which is known to have happened to no other Monarchy.

Therefore, having reviewed the affairs of Egypt from ancient times down to Amasis <note>Amasis II (Ahmose II) was one of the last great pharaohs before the Persian conquest.</note>, the requirements of our order now seem to demand that we also discuss something of their morals, institutions, and political life at an equal pace. For many of the acts of the ancient Egyptians were not only highly esteemed by the natives, but were also held in no small amount of admiration among the Greeks. Although even...

<summary>This page introduces the second treatise of the work, arguing that Egyptian political success was rooted in their religious devotion and the selection of philosopher-priests as rulers. It claims that Egypt maintained a stable empire for over 1,500 years by modeling its state on divine order.</summary>

<keywords>Egyptian politics, divine right, philosopher-priests, governance, Cambyses, stability, religious worship, monarchy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the political structure of Egypt. <header>THE ISIAIC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS</header>

<margin>CHAPTER I.</margin>
...the Egyptians [maintained] an inner sanctuary <note>original: "adytum," a sacred space or shrine restricted to priests.</note> difficult for outsiders to enter; nevertheless, many of the most excellent philosophers did not cease to travel thither, as if to a marketplace of all arts and disciplines, to learn integrity of life and morals. By what manner, industry, and art they preserved their kingdom immune from all foreign invasion for so long a time will be explained in this Treatise; so that this may be done as well as possible, we shall begin our chosen theme from the first establishment of the laws.

# CHAPTER I.

->**Concerning the first institution of Politics, or the Egyptian Monarchy.**<-

<margin>The gifts and genius of Hermes Trismegistus.</margin>
About the three-hundredth year after the Great Flood, there came forth from the lineage of the Canaanites a man most highly adorned with all the gifts of nature. It seemed as though Nature itself had formed him to explore the secrets of the arts and sciences, and that God had given him to a world still raw and unpolished for the sake of educating the human race. The Arabs call him *Idris*, which means "The Disputant"; the Phoenicians call him *Tautus*; the Egyptians *Thouth*; and the Greeks *Hermes Trismegistus* <note>Hermes "the Thrice-Greatest."</note>. For he was of a most sharp wit, of admirable subtlety, and an untiring investigator of nature. Having been informed about the state, customs, and disciplines of the primeval world through his constant conversation with both Noah and his sons and grandsons, he made it his sole aim to cultivate the disciplines passed down by the primeval Patriarchs of the world, and to consign those refined skills to posterity.

<margin>His travels.</margin>
To achieve this more exactly, he stayed for some time in Italy with the descendants of Janus <note>original: "Ianigenis." In the historical framework used here, Janus is often identified with the biblical Noah.</note>, where he learned exactly both the political way of life and the institutions of the arts and other disciplines. 

<margin>He employs the help of Misraim, King of Egypt.</margin>
Thereafter, he went to Misraim <note>In the Bible, Misraim is the son of Ham and the progenitor of the Egyptians.</note>, who at that time held power in Egypt. Since the King himself was a most studious seeker of new things, and always kept his mind intent on great and arduous matters, Hermes arrived at a favorable time to support him. Hermes was no less great in spirit than the King, and he surpassed many by far <note>original: "multis parasangis," literally "by many parasangs," an ancient Persian unit of distance.</note> in knowledge and clarity of intellect. Indeed, that prince should rightly be considered fortunate; for while he conceived in his mind great, arduous designs far beyond the common strength of men, such a partner was joined to him—one to whom nature had given both the will and the power to lead those grand concepts into execution through appropriate means. Therefore, Idris was joined to King Misraim as his Scribe and supreme Counselor. Later, while Misraim's son, Mesramuthis, was still a minor following the death of his father, Idris was appointed the supreme Viceroy of the entire Egyptian Monarchy, as the *Alexandrian Chronicle* <note>original: "Chron. Alex."</note> testifies.

Since he saw that the kingdom was not yet established by any firm laws, nor instructed in political discipline, he seriously pondered how he might introduce an exact form of living into a kingdom that was still free and unrestrained. But "here is Rhodes, here is the jump" <note>original: "hic Rhodus, hic saltus." A Latin proverb derived from Aesop, meaning "now is the time to prove your claims with action."</note>; for who could [tame] an unbridled people, spurred on as if by some gadfly by the lust for power, while everyone followed their own will and untamed appetite through right or wrong at their pleasure...

<meta>The catchword "tur" at the bottom of the page indicates the next word in the original Latin was "turbaretur" or a similar verb completion.</meta>

<summary>This page recounts the legendary origins of Egyptian law and order, crediting the figure of Hermes Trismegistus (Idris) with bringing the wisdom of the pre-flood Patriarchs to King Misraim. It establishes Hermes as the primary architect of the Egyptian state's intellectual and political foundations.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Thoth, Idris, Misraim, Egyptian Monarchy, post-diluvian history, Janus, Noah, Alexandrian Chronicle, political philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 226 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the legendary origins of Egyptian law under Hermes Trismegistus (referred to here as Mercury). It details the transition from divine law to a structured political system managed by a specialized priesthood.</meta>

### TREATISE II. ON EGYPTIAN POLITICS. CHAPTER I.

<margin>Why did he engrave the laws into stones?</margin>
Thus, he seemed to have taken a great task upon himself; and as he was very talented, so he maturely weighed all things in advance. Since he recognized that a government, of whatever kind it might be, could by no means stand without religion, he began a certain sacred and utterly mysterious doctrine—which posterity called *hieroglyphic* <note>original: "hieroglyphicam"; from the Greek words for "sacred" and "carving."</note>—because it was painstakingly worked out with the greatest genius and zeal upon the hardest stones, as if intended to last forever against all the ravages of time. By this doctrine, he bound divine law so closely to human laws that whoever corrupted the latter was rightly judged to have corrupted the former. For he knew that the fear of the Gods was most effective in keeping subjects to their duty.

<margin>He communicates the rule of laws to the college of priests.</margin>
Hence, the subjects, spurred on by that new invention of wisdom, willingly surrendered themselves to Mercury. They venerated him as if he were a divine Power fallen from heaven to earth, and they embraced the political doctrine presented to them with "both hands," as the saying goes. They held that it must be observed with such rigor that later writers have confirmed with most clear testimony that the entire posterity of Egypt preserved it. Nevertheless, because he well knew the frailty of the human will in observing laws, and so that his established laws might have perpetual successors, he instituted a College of Priests. These were the most sagacious men, excelling in genius, wisdom, and experience in affairs, to whom alone the path to the succession of the kingdom would be open. To them, he handed down the rule of the arts and the laws he had established, and he bound them by oath not to communicate these to any others besides the men of their own order. Furthermore, he left to them, as a most excellent inheritance, the prescribed laws for sacrifices and the rites for both worshipping and placating the Divine Powers. And because the priests alone were thought insufficient for such a great burden, he substituted various orders of the kingdom as their coadjutors:

<margin>The helpers of the priests: the Singers, their office, and symbol.</margin>
The first order consisted of the **Singers**, who were to resolve doubts arising from the collected laws of Mercury concerning the hymns and praises of the Gods, and who were to teach the principles of the royal life arranged according to the ideas of the supreme minds.

<margin>The symbol and office of the Horoscopes.</margin>
The second order consisted of the **Horoscopes** <note>original: "Horoscopi"; these were not modern astrologers, but "observers of the hours" who monitored the positions of the stars to keep the calendar and ritual timing accurate.</note>, whose symbol was a clock <note>original: "horologium"; likely a water-clock or clepsydra.</note> and a palm branch. It was necessary for them to have deeply absorbed the four books of Mercury concerning Astrology. Their duty was to observe the exact distribution of times to be followed in the worship of the Gods; to read the handed-down laws to the people at certain times of the year and on solemn days; and to preserve the fixed solemnities of the festivals arranged according to the course of the Sun, the Moon, and the stars in a perpetual and constant tenor. For he had learned that the exact partition of time was of the greatest importance in the proper administration of a kingdom.

<margin>The symbol and office of the Hierogrammatists.</margin>
The third order consisted of the **Hierogrammatists** <note>original: "Hierogrammatistæ," meaning "Sacred Scribes."</note>, that is, the Scribes of sacred matters, who were present at the appointed assemblies, conspicuous by the feathers on their heads. They held in their hands both a book and a rule, in which there was ink for writing and the reed which they used in drawing. These men were especially instructed in the knowledge of hieroglyphics, the science of the disposition of the world and the position of lands, and the order of the Sun and Moon, as well as the other five planets. Furthermore, they were trained in the Chorography <note>The description or mapping of a particular region.</note> of Egypt and the description of the Nile—in a word, everything that in any way pertained to the sacred rites and ceremonies, such as the instruments, the ornaments, and the knowledge of the places dedicated to individual Spirits <note>original: "Genijs."</note>.

...and measurements, according to the prescription of the sacred sculptures, it was necessary for them to be exactly skilled. 
<margin>The symbol and duty of the Stolists.</margin>
The fourth order consisted of the **Stolists** <term>Stolists: From the Greek *stolistes*, meaning "one who dresses"; these priests were responsible for the sacred vestments and ritual purifications</term>, who, equipped with the "cubit of justice" <note>A cubit was a standard unit of length; here it symbolizes the "measure" of law and fairness</note> and a cup for pouring libations, were present at the customary assemblies and councils. Their duty was to urge that everything pertaining to the sacred disciplines and institutions be preserved with inviolable rigor and guarded with unimpaired strength. If any had fallen away from their original strictness, the Stolists were to restore them with the greatest zeal, care, and diligence. Furthermore, they were to perform sacrifices at the appropriate time and arrange the sacred *moschosphagistika* <note>original: "μοσχοσφαγιϛικὰ"; Greek for "pertaining to the slaughter of calves," specifically regarding the selection and sacrifice of the sacred Apis bulls</note>—that is, matters concerning the sacred calves or bulls, both in their marking and their ritual slaughter.

<margin>The symbol and duty of the Prophets</margin>
The fifth order consisted of the **Prophets**, whose symbol was a water jar (*hydria*) carried in the hand. Their duty was to judge the outcomes of matters discussed in the assemblies and to discern unfavorable events from prosperous ones through augury <note>divination based on the behavior of birds</note> and other forms of divination. Moreover, they presided over the distribution of taxes.

These are the orders of the priestly dignity, upon whose authority, counsel, and wisdom the entire mass of the Egyptian Monarchy rested as if on a foundation. 
<margin>The Politics of Mercury contained in 42 books</margin>
The entire system of Egyptian political doctrine and philosophy was contained in forty-two books by **Mercury** <note>Kircher identifies the Egyptian god Thoth/Hermes Trismegistus with the Roman Mercury</note>. Of these, thirty-six were to be held in the minds of the men of the five aforementioned orders; ten of these books specifically contained the whole system of priestly doctrine as well as the secret science of hieroglyphics. This was so that, when difficulties or disagreements arose in the Kingdom, they might discern with a ready mind how to meet them quickly according to the traditional laws. The remaining six books were to be mastered by those called *Pastophoroi* <term>Pastophoroi: "Shrine-bearers," a class of priests who carried the small portable shrines of the gods</term>, Healers, or the "Cloaked Ones." These books contained the entire system of medicine to be observed throughout all Egypt, namely: the constitution of bodies, temperament, the anatomy of individual limbs, the variety and affections of diseases, surgical instruments, and the use, quality, and preparation of medicines. I have discussed these at length in my *Hieroglyphic Medicine*. Since all these things are found confirmed by extensive authorities in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>Referring to Kircher’s earlier work, *Obeliscus Pamphilius* (1650)</note>, I have judged it unnecessary to repeat them here. I will only bring forward as a witness to all these things **Clement of Alexandria**, who in the sixth book of his *Stromata* <note>A major work of early Christian philosophy by Clement (c. 150–215 AD)</note> wove together the whole system to be observed in the precepts of the laws and ceremonies; all of which, by his own testimony, were excerpted from the twelve books of Philistius of Syracuse concerning the religion of the Egyptians:

<margin>Clement of Alexandria from Philistius of Syracuse.</margin>

One of these is about the arrangement of the fixed stars; another about the conjunctions and illuminations of the sun and moon; and the rest about the rising of the stars. For the Egyptian philosophers practice a certain and peculiar philosophy of their own. This is most clearly shown by their sacred ceremonies. <margin>The rites of Egyptian ceremonies.</margin> *First, the **Singer** proceeds, carrying one of the symbols of music. They say he must receive two of the books of Hermes, one of which contains the hymns to the gods, and the other the rules for the king’s life. After the Singer, the **Astrologer** <note>original: Horoscopus; one who observes the hours</note> proceeds, holding in his hand a sundial and a palm branch, the symbols of astrology. He knows everything called* παιδευτικά <gloss>educational/disciplinary</gloss> *and* μοσχοσφαγιστικά <gloss>pertaining to the slaughter of calves</gloss>. *There are ten matters pertaining to the honor of the gods among them which comprise Egyptian religion: namely, sacrifices, first-fruits, hymns, prayers, processions, feast days, and similar things. After all these comes the **Prophet**, who openly carries a water-jar in his robes, followed by those who carry the loaves of bread; he, as the prefect of sacred matters, learns the ten books called "sacerdotal," which contain the laws, the gods, and the entire discipline of the priests. For the Prophet among the Egyptians also presides over the distribution of taxes. There are, therefore, forty-two highly necessary books of Hermes; thirty-six of these, containing the whole of Egyptian philosophy, are learned by the aforementioned classes; the remaining six are studied by the* παστοφόροι <gloss>Pastophoroi or Shrine-bearers</gloss>, *as they pertain to medicine—namely, the construction of the body, diseases, instruments, and drugs.*

---

And from these details it is clearly evident that the entire Egyptian polity was constituted first of **Kings**, then of **Priests** (who, as was said above, were divided again into five classes), and finally of the **Commoners**, who were likewise distinguished by a triple class of soldiers, farmers, and artisans. The time and place now seem to demand, as if by right, that we explain the laws and institutions of all these groups.

CHAPTER II. 118 THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

## CHAPTER II.

->*On the life, customs, and institutions of the Egyptians.*<-

Having reviewed the history of Egypt from ancient times up to the reign of Amasis <note>Amasis II was a pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty (570–526 BCE) who was famous for his friendly relations with the Greeks.</note>, the logic of our order now seems to require that we speak briefly regarding their customs, institutions, and political life. For many of the deeds of the ancient Egyptians were not only highly esteemed by the natives themselves, but also held in no small amount of admiration among the Greeks. Although the Egyptians knew that their "inner sanctum" <note>original Latin: *adytum*; refers to the most private or sacred parts of a temple, here used metaphorically for their secret knowledge.</note> was difficult for foreigners to access, nevertheless, as we have said above, many of the most excellent philosophers did not cease to travel there as if to a marketplace of the arts and sciences, in order to learn integrity of life and character. Thus, the entire social structure of the Egyptians consisted of three classes of people: Kings, Priests, and the Commoners <note>original Latin: *Plebaeis*; here referring to the non-noble/non-priestly classes.</note>, who were either soldiers, farmers, or artisans.

The Egyptian Kings, as Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE, whose "Library of History" is a primary source for Kircher's descriptions.</note> records, did not lead their lives in the manner of other rulers for whom their own will is law. Instead, they followed the established institutions of the laws in matters of collecting money and even in their daily diet.

<margin>The best ministers are assigned to the Kings.</margin>
No person of low status, neither a hired servant nor a bondservant nor a slave, was assigned to their personal service or obedience. Instead, the sons of the most noble priests were chosen—those who were over twenty years old and more learned in doctrine than all others. This was so that the King, moved by the sight of these attendants of his body standing by day and night, might commit nothing shameful; for rarely do the powerful turn toward evil when the ministers of their desires are absent.

<margin>What the Egyptian Kings did each day.</margin>
Specific hours of the day and night were established during which it was lawful for the King, by permission of the law, to act. Rising early in the morning, it was necessary for the King first to receive all letters that had been sent, so that once he knew what needed to be done and gave his response, each matter could be handled correctly, in its proper time and order.

<margin>Their individual actions are described.</margin>
After these acts, when he had washed his body in a gathering of excellent men, he would put on magnificent clothing and perform sacred rites to the gods. It was the custom of the High Priest, once the sacrificial victims were brought to the altar and the King was standing by, to pray in a loud voice in the hearing of the people for prosperous health and all good things. He would pray for justice for the King toward his subjects and, moreover, recount the King's virtues one by one: his piety and religion toward the gods, his supreme humanity toward men, describing him as continent, just, great-souled, truthful, generous, and one who restrained all desires. He would further describe him as demanding punishments milder than the crimes of the wanderer required, while returning a favor more greatly than the merits deserved. Praying for many similar things, he would then pronounce a supreme curse upon the wicked.

<margin>Worship of the Gods.</margin>
Then, clearing the King of blame, the priest would cast all the guilt upon the ministers who had persuaded the King to do unjust things. When these things were finished, the priest would exhort the King toward a happy life pleasing to the gods, and simultaneously toward good morals—acting not according to what the wicked might suggest, but toward what pertained most to praise and virtue. Finally, when the King had performed the sacred rites to the gods, the priest would read aloud from the sacred books various counsels and deeds of the most famous men; so that the King, having been advised, might use his power piously and justly following the example of others. He was not, however, only occupied with collecting money or the ancient laws of judging and vacating: but also in walking...

<header>SYNTAGMA II. ON EGYPTIAN POLITICS. CHAPTER II.</header>

<margin>Frugality of the Table.</margin>
<margin>Kings held their life's conduct according to the law.</margin>
The time for bathing, for washing, for sleeping with one's wife, and for every aspect of spending one's life was prescribed by law. They ate simple food; for their tables, nothing was served except veal and goose. A certain measure was established for drinking wine, so that they could neither distend the stomach nor become intoxicated. In short, their lives were maintained with such modesty that they seemed to have been composed not by a legislator, but by a most skilled Physician for the preservation of health. It is truly a wonder that the Egyptians led their private lives not by their own will, but by law; nor was any license permitted to them for judging, for amassing money, or for punishing anyone out of pride, anger, or any other unjust cause, but they were held to laws as if they were private citizens. Nor did they take this poorly, believing that by obeying the laws, they would be happy. For they judged that many things were done by those who indulged their own desires, through which they underwent losses and dangers. For knowing that they frequently sinned, yet conquered either by love, or by hatred, or by some other disease of the soul, they confessed they were led into this. But those who established their lives by wisdom and counsel offended in few things.

<margin>The love of the people for the Kings.</margin>
<margin>Mourning and ceremonies of the people for a deceased King.</margin>
By using such justice toward their subjects, the Kings so gained the goodwill of all that not only the Priests, but every single Egyptian felt a greater care for the safety of the King than for their wives, children, or other princes. When a King died having lived with such character, all mourned in common grief and tore their garments. With the temples closed, they did not frequent the forums; they held no solemn festivals. For seventy-two days, defiling their heads with mud and girded with linen <note>original: *sindone*; a fine linen cloth often used for ceremonial purposes</note> beneath their chests, about two or three hundred men and women walked about together, renewing the mourning twice a day, and commemorating the virtues of the King in song to a rhythm. They abstained from animal foods, cooked items, wine, and all the finery of the table; they used no baths, no ointments, no spread beds, and no sexual pleasures, but for those days they mourned in grief as if for a deceased son. During this time, when the things pertaining to the funeral pomp were prepared, on the final day they placed the body, enclosed in a coffin, before the entrance of the tomb. There, according to custom, they provided a summary of the deeds performed by the King in life; and the opportunity was given to anyone who wished to accuse the deceased. The priests stood by, praising the righteous deeds of the dead man. The crowd surrounding the funeral rites was immense, applauding true praises, but shouting back in a great tumult as if in protest against anything else.

<margin>The revenues and duties of the Priests.</margin>
From this it happened that many Kings, due to the opposition of the multitude, were deprived of the usual honor and magnificence of a tomb; this fear compelled the Kings of Egypt to live justly, fearing the anger of the common people after death and eternal hatred. This was the manner of living of the ancient Kings. All of Egypt was divided into several parts, each of which was called by the Greek word *Nomos* <note>original Greek: *Νὀμῳ*; these were the administrative districts of ancient Egypt</note>. A Governor <note>original Latin: *Prætor*; Kircher uses a Roman term for the local Egyptian official</note> was present in each, who had care over all things. With the revenues of Egypt divided into three parts, the College of Priests—who held great authority among the inhabitants—received the first portion, both because of their care for the Gods and because of the doctrine by which many are instructed. They shared this portion both for the ministry of sacrifices and for the conveniences of their private lives; for they did not think the worship of the Gods should be neglected, nor did they think it fair for the Ministers of public counsel and utility to lack the comforts of life; so...

### CHAPTER II. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

...for they <note>the Priests</note> were always present in serious matters with counsel and labor for the Kings, predicting future events both through their skill in the stars and indeed through sacrifices. Furthermore, they recounted the deeds of ancestors from the sacred books, so that the Kings might learn from those actions what would be profitable to do. For, unlike among the Greeks, where a single man or a single woman presides over sacred matters, many were occupied in the worship and honor of the Gods, and they handed down this same care of sacred things to their sons. All these men were exempt <note>original: "immunes," meaning they did not pay taxes</note>, and they held the place of honor and dignity second only to the Kings.

<margin>Kings.</margin>
The second portion <note>of the land and its wealth</note> went to the Kings, which they spent on wars, the maintenance of their courtly life, and on rewards for courageous men according to their merits. Because of this arrangement, the common people were burdened with no tribute.

<margin>Soldiers.</margin>
The third portion was received by the soldiers and those burdened with the service of war, so that, having received this payment, they might have a mind more ready to undergo the dangers of battles.

<margin>Agriculture.</margin>
The farmers, having purchased their fields for a small fee from the Priests, the King, or the soldiers, spent their entire lives from childhood onward without intermission in rural work. As a result, they surpassed others in agriculture, both because of the training received from their parents and because of their continuous experience.

<margin>Shepherds.</margin>
In the same way, the shepherds, having received the care and art of managing cattle from their fathers, spent their whole lives in that governance.

<margin>Arts.</margin>
The <term>Arts</term><note>Kircher uses "Artes" to refer to skilled trades and crafts</note> also appeared to be highly cultivated among the Egyptians and brought to the highest perfection. For the Egyptian craftsmen alone, setting aside the cares of public affairs, practiced no work except that which was either permitted by the laws or handed down from their fathers. Thus, neither the jealousy of a teacher, nor political hatred, nor anything else could hinder them from their established practice.

<margin>Judgments.</margin>
Their <term>Judgments</term><note>The legal and court system</note> were not conducted by chance, but by reason. For they believed that properly executed trials were of the greatest benefit to mortal life. They thought that punishing the guilty and bringing help to the oppressed was the best way to prevent evil deeds; however, they believed that if the penalty for a crime were removed by money or favor, it would lead to the confusion of communal life.

<margin>Selection of Judges.</margin>
For this reason, they chose the best men from the most famous cities, such as <term>Heliopolis</term><note>The "City of the Sun," a major religious center</note>, <term>Memphis</term>, and <term>Thebes</term>, to preside over the courts. This assembly of judges seemed to yield neither to the <term>Areopagites</term><note>The high court of Athens</note> nor to the Senate of the <term>Lacedaemonians</term><note>The Spartans</note>, which were established long afterward. After thirty judges had convened, they chose from among themselves the best man, whom they appointed as the Chief of Judgment; in his place, his home city substituted another judge. Sustenance was given to all of them by the King, but more abundantly to the Chief. He wore suspended from his neck a golden chain as a sign of his dignity, adorned with various precious stones, which they called <term>Truth</term><note>original: "veritatem," referring to the amulet of the goddess Maat</note>. When the trials began and the "Sign of Truth" was displayed by the Chief of Judges, and all the laws (which were contained in eight books) were placed in their midst, it was the custom for the accuser to write down the things of which he accused the other, the manner of the injury or damage done, and how much he valued it. Time was given to the defendant to write back regarding each point: either that he had not done it, or that he had acted rightly, or to plead for a lesser penalty by devaluing the injury or damage. Again, there was an opportunity for the accuser and defendant to respond to each other in turn. Thus, after these advocates had been heard and the judges had deliberated on the controversy, the Chief Judge—having turned the Sign of Truth toward the side of the truth—would deliver the sentence. This was the custom of their judgments.

### TREATISE II. ON EGYPTIAN POLITICS. 121 CHAPTER II

Since mention has been made of the institution of laws, it would not be out of place for my purpose to also report the ancient laws of the Egyptians, so that it may be known how much they surpassed others in both their order of affairs and their utility. 

<margin>The Laws of the Egyptians.</margin>
First, those who committed perjury <note>original: "periuri," the act of lying under oath</note> were punished by death, as they were held to have committed a double crime: they violated piety toward the Gods and destroyed trust among men, which is the greatest bond of human society. If anyone making a journey encountered a man being killed by bandits or suffering any injury and did not bring help if he were able, he was guilty of death. If he was unable to bring help, he was bound to report the bandits and pursue the injury through accusation; he who neglected this was punished with a specific number of lashes and went without food for three days.

<margin>The punishment of criminals.</margin>
If anyone falsely accused another and was afterward brought to judgment, the slanderer underwent the penalty of retaliation <note>original: "talionis," the principle of "an eye for an eye," where the accuser receives the punishment they intended for the accused</note> established for such crimes. All Egyptians were compelled to report their names in writing to the governors, and simultaneously by what profession each man lived; in this matter, if anyone lied, or if he lived by unjust gain, he fell under the penalty of death. If anyone intentionally killed either a free man or a slave, the laws commanded him to be condemned to death; for the laws, weighing the intent of the deed rather than the status of fortune, deterred men from crimes, and simultaneously, by avenging the death of a slave, the free were made more secure. For fathers who killed their sons, the penalty of death was not ordained, but they were commanded to sit by the body of the deceased for three continuous days and nights while a public guard stood by. For they did not think it just that he should be deprived of life who was the author of life for his sons, but rather that he should be afflicted by continuous grief and repentance for the deed, so that others might be turned away from a similar act.

<margin>Fines and punishments.</margin>
They imposed an exquisite punishment for parricides <note>those who kill their parents</note>; for after being cut limb by limb with very sharp reeds, they commanded them to be burned alive upon a heap of thorns, judging it the greatest crime among mortals to bring death through violence upon the one from whom they had received life. For women destined for death, if they were pregnant, the birth was awaited; they judged it entirely unjust that one who had committed nothing should suffer punishment along with the criminal, or that two should be punished when only one had transgressed. In wars, those who either left their rank or did not obey the Commanders were not punished with death, but with the greatest ignominy of all; if they later wiped this out through courage and right deeds, they might return to their prior status. This law accustomed men to judge that disgrace as the worst evil, more grievous than death itself. For those who revealed secrets to enemies, the law commanded the tongue to be cut out; and for him who clipped the coinage, or struck counterfeit money, or changed weights or seals, or forged writings, or removed something from a document, or brought forward false bonds <note>original: "syngraphas," meaning written contracts or promissory notes</note>, both hands were cut off, so that the part of the body which had sinned should pay the penalty throughout his entire life. Thus others, warned by the calamity of their fellows, might abstain from similar crimes.

<margin>How adultery and fornication are punished.</margin>
Harsh penalties were also established regarding the transgressions of women. For him who violated a free woman, the genitals were cut off, since in one crime he had encompassed three no small evils. He who was caught in consensual adultery was beaten with rods up to a thousand lashes; the woman’s nose was mutilated, so that the face might be stained with disgrace, and she would be punished in that part by which the face is most adorned.

Regarding the laws which pertain to the commerce of men, the Law of Bocchoris... <note>Bocchoris, or Bakenranef, was an Egyptian Pharaoh of the 24th Dynasty known in Greek tradition as a great lawgiver.</note>
