->CHAPTER II. 122 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE<-

They write that [the king] was the legislator. Moreover, they mandate: if money lent without a written contract were denied, the matter stands on the debtor's oath, as they held an oath in great esteem as a religious matter. For while it is certain that those who swear too often lose their credibility, many say that to avoid losing the name of a good man, one should rarely stoop to taking an oath. Furthermore, the lawgiver, placing all trust in virtue, judged that men should be accustomed to uprightness through good character, lest they appear unworthy of trust. He also thought it unjust that those to whom money had been lent without a written oath should not be trusted when swearing regarding their own property. He forbade interest <note>original: "fœnus," the charging of interest on a loan</note> contracted in writing to be collected beyond double the original loan; repayment was made solely from the debtor's goods. The person's body could not be surrendered to the creditor, for he thought it proper that only assets should be subject to debts. He believed that bodies, whose labor was used in both war and peace, belonged to the state. For it did not seem just for soldiers, who underwent dangers for the safety of the fatherland, to be led into prison for the sake of interest; a law which Solon <note>Solon was a famous Athenian statesman and lawmaker</note> seems to have transferred to the Athenians, which they call the "shaking off of burdens" <note>original: "Sisateam," from the Greek "Seisachtheia," a set of laws instituted by Solon to rectify widespread serfdom and debt</note>; he decreed that the bodies of citizens should not be punished on account of interest.

<margin>Law regarding thieves.</margin> Furthermore, the law regarding thieves among the Egyptians alone was this: It commanded those who wished to steal to register their names with the High Priest, and to immediately report the theft to him. Similarly, those from whom property had been stolen were required to write to the same official the time, day, and hour of the theft. In this way, the theft being easily discovered, the one who had lost the property was fined a fourth part, which was given to the thief; the Legislator considered it better—since it was impossible for thefts to be entirely prevented—that men suffer the loss of a portion rather than lose the entire object.

<margin>Marriage.</margin> The custom of marriage was not the same among all Egyptians. Priests were permitted to marry only one wife; the rest had several according to their will and means. None of their children were considered illegitimate <note>original: "spurius," meaning born out of wedlock or of lower status</note>, not even those born from a purchased slave-woman. For they considered only the father to be the author of the lineage; <margin>Education of children.</margin> they believed the mother provided only the nourishment and the place for the infant. They raised their children with such little and easy expense that it can scarcely be believed; for they nourished the children with stalks and other roots, which they cooked under ashes, as well as marsh-reeds, which they provided for food partly cooked, partly roasted by fire, and partly raw. They lived their lives barefoot and naked for the most part on account of the mild climate of the country. The total expense spent by parents on boys until they reached adulthood did not exceed twenty drachmas.

<margin>Instruction.</margin> The Priests instructed their sons in both the letters which are called "sacred" <note>meaning hieroglyphs</note> and in others which pertain to common learning, being most intent on the study of Geometry and Arithmetic. They also devoted time to Music, insofar as it leads to the contemplation of the order of nature and the harmony of things in the World. <margin>Medical Treatment.</margin> They cured diseases either by fasting or by vomiting, and that either daily, or with three or four days intervening; for they claim that all diseases are created from an excess of food, and therefore that the best care for health is that which removes the beginnings of diseases. <margin>Military Service.</margin> Soldiers or foreigners are treated at no personal expense. For the physicians receive their livelihood from the public funds; they treat the sick according to the law, as handed down by ancient physicians and approved authors. If anyone, following the norm of the sacred book, was unable to cure the infirm,

<margin>*Method of healing.*</margin> [If the physician has followed the prescribed laws], he is free from all blame; but if he has treated the patient otherwise than what is contained in the traditional books, he is punished by death. For the Lawgiver believed that a method of healing which had been observed and developed by ancient physicians over a long period of time could hardly be improved upon.

<margin>*Worship of the Gods.*</margin> The Egyptians worshipped certain animals beyond measure, not only living ones but also the dead, such as **cats**, **ichneumons** <note>a mongoose-like animal valued for eating crocodile eggs and snakes</note>, **dogs**, **hawks**, **ibises**, **wolves**, **crocodiles**, and many more of this kind recited above in the introduction. They did not blush to profess the worship of these creatures openly, but rather, as if devoted to the honors of the gods, they considered it a point of pride rather than a disgrace. When they processed through cities and various places with the specific symbols of these animals, displaying from a distance the creatures they tended, individuals would worship them in the manner of suppliants. When one of these animals died, they covered it in fine linen and, wailing and beating their chests, they smeared it with salt, cedar oil, and fragrant ointments so that the body might be preserved longer; they then buried the anointed body in sacred places. If anyone killed one of these animals intentionally, he was condemned to death. The **cat** and the **ibis** were exceptions: if anyone killed these creatures, whether intentionally or otherwise, a crowd would rush in and, without any trial, they would put the killer to death after subjecting him to various tortures. Out of this fear, anyone who happened to see one of these animals dead would stand far off and lament, testifying that the animal had died through no fault of his own.

<margin>*Nourishment of animals.*</margin> These animals were nourished with the greatest care and expense within the temple precincts by men who were by no means of low status. They fed them fine wheat flour and groats, and various feasts seasoned with milk; they provided geese, both boiled and roasted, daily. For those animals that ate raw meat, they provided captured birds. In short, they maintained them all with great care and expense. They mourned their deaths as much as they did the deaths of their own children, and buried them more sumptuously than their own means might allow; <margin>*Splendor of burial.*</margin> so much so that, when Ptolemy Lagus <note>Ptolemy I Soter, the first Greek pharaoh of Egypt</note> held Egypt, an ox died of old age in Memphis, and the man who had taken charge of its feeding spent all the money that had been allocated for it, and additionally spent fifty talents of silver borrowed from Ptolemy on its burial.

<margin>*Funerals.*</margin> Perhaps these things we have mentioned will seem marvelous, but one will be no less amazed if he considers what occurs among the Egyptians during the funeral of the dead. For when someone has died, all the relatives and friends wander through the city mourning with their heads defiled with mud until the deceased is buried; meanwhile, they do not wash, nor do they take wine or any food except that which is very simple, nor do they wear splendid garments. They had three types of tombs: the expensive, the mediocre, and the humble. For the first, they spent a talent of silver; for the second, twenty minas; for the last, fewer expenses were incurred. Those who cared for the funerals of the dead, practicing the craft handed down by their ancestors, would bring a written description of the funeral expenses to the family, asking at what price they wished the funeral to be celebrated. Once an agreement was made, the body was handed over so that the funeral might be handled according to the expense. <margin>*Custom of embalming, or the preparation of corpses.*</margin> First, the **Scribe** <note>original: "Grammaticus," a temple official</note>, once the body was placed on the ground, would mark the flank with a wooden tool to show how much should be cut on the left side. Then the one called the **Cutter** <note>original: "Scissor" or "Paraschistes," the official who made the initial incision</note>, using an **Ethiopian stone** <note>a sharp blade of flint or obsidian used for ritual purposes</note>, opened the side as much as the law allowed, and immediately fled at a quick run, pursued by those standing by, who threw stones with curses...

# OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACI: THE TEMPLE OF ISIS #

<margin>CHAPTER II.</margin>
...throwing [stones] at him, he would flee. For they believed that hatred should be directed toward anyone who violated the body of a friend by inflicting a wound upon it. However, the caretakers of the body—whom they call **Salitores** <term>Salitores: likely a Latinization of a term for embalmers, derived from the act of "salting" the body to preserve it</term>—were held in honor and deemed worthy of high esteem. Indeed, they associated with the Priests and entered the temples just as they did. While these men stood by the corpse, one would draw out the internal organs through the incision in the body, leaving only the kidneys and the heart; then another would wash each of these with palm wine <note>original: "vino Phoeniceo," literally Phoenician wine, often interpreted as date or palm wine in this context</note> and fragrant substances. Afterward, they anointed the entire body first with cedar oil, then with other precious ointments for more than thirty days; finally, they smeared it with myrrh, cinnamon, and other materials that were capable not only of preserving it for a long duration but also of making it fragrant. They then returned the treated corpse to the relatives of the deceased, with every part of it—even the hair of the eyebrows and eyelids—so perfectly preserved that the entire appearance of the body remained intact, as if the person were merely sleeping.

Before the body was buried, the relatives would announce the day of the funeral to the judges and the friends of the deceased, stating that the dead person was about to "cross the marsh" <note>This refers to the ritual crossing of a lake or the Nile, symbolizing the journey to the afterlife</note>. With more than forty judges present and seated in a prepared **Hemicyclium** <term>Hemicyclium: a semicircular seating arrangement, often used for formal assemblies or theaters</term> beyond the pool, a boat specially constructed for this purpose was brought forward by those assigned to the task. Then, before the body was placed in the coffin, the law permitted anyone who wished to bring an accusation against the dead. If it was proved that the person had lived an evil life, the judges would pass a sentence by which the body was to be deprived of its burial. Anyone who was found to have brought a just accusation was rewarded, while those who brought false charges were punished severely. 

When there was no accuser, or if it was established that the accusation was made out of malice, the relatives would end their mourning and turn to the praises of the dead. They did not speak of his lineage, as the Greeks were accustomed to do, for the Egyptians believed that all of them were equally noble; instead, starting from childhood, they recounted his upbringing and education, and then moved to his adulthood, commemorating his piety toward God, his justice, his self-control, and his other virtues. Calling upon the gods of the underworld, they prayed that they might place him among the pious. At these words, the entire multitude responded by extolling the glory of the dead, as if he were to remain forever among the blessed in the afterlife. 

Afterward, each family buried their own; some in private tombs, while those who lacked them kept the body at home, standing the coffin against a sturdy wall. However, those who were prohibited from burial because of some crime or debt were kept at home without a coffin; their descendants, once they became wealthier and paid off the debts or atoned for the crimes, would later bury them with honor. It is a custom among them to give the bodies of their deceased parents as a pledge to a creditor. The greatest infamy followed those who did not redeem them, and they themselves were denied burial. 

One might rightly admire those who established these institutions, for they pursued not only what pertained to the morals of the living, but also what concerned the burial and cult of the dead; they believed that in this way, human life could be shaped toward good morals as much as possible. The Greeks, certainly, who handed down stories through fictions and the exaggerated words of Poets regarding the merits of the pious and the punishment of the wicked, were by no means able to lead men to virtue through their writings. On the contrary, they were rather mocked and held in contempt by the wicked. Among the Egyptians, however, punishment for the impious and praise for the just were imparted not through fables, but through actual practice. Every day, for both groups, those things which were useful for life...

## CHAPTER III.

->*That the entire doctrine of political philosophy was allegorically signified through the history, or fable, of Osiris, Isis, Horus, and Typhon.*<-

<margin>The character and nature of Osiris inclined toward virtue.</margin>
The Egyptians beautifully place before our eyes how Kingdoms and Empires remain in their state of happiness, and how they fall from it, through the lives of Osiris, Typhon, Isis, and Horus. Osiris and Typhon were indeed born of the same very wise father, yet there existed the greatest disparity in the character and conduct of each. This was signified in these Egyptian brothers by certain signs immediately from their birth, and was afterwards most evidently proven in their adulthood, as will appear from the following details drawn mostly from Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher and bishop whose work "On Providence" tells the story of Osiris and Typhon as a political allegory</note>. For of these, the one who was younger was produced and educated by a certain divine fate; even from boyhood he was eager to listen and fond of stories—for stories are the study and discipline of children. As he grew older, he always burned with a desire for that learning which transcends time and age. He did not merely lend his ears to his father, but whatever anyone possessed that was skillful or exquisite, he greedily swallowed it down. At first, he wished to know everything at once and in a rush, in a "dog-like fashion" <note>original: "canino... more." This refers to a "hungry" or "snapping" style of learning where a student eagerly devours information without yet digesting it</note>, which truly happens in those natures that promise something excellent and great for themselves. For they exult and leap forward impatiently before their time, as if they were already promising themselves the desired end in their minds. 

Afterward, however, long before reaching puberty, he showed himself more composed than a virtuous and well-mannered old man, so that he not only listened to everything modestly, but if he wished to say anything—either about what he had heard or whatever occurred to him—one would recognize him as hesitating and covered in a blush. Furthermore, in the street <margin>Obedience toward elders.</margin> and in seating, he easily gave way to the Egyptian elders, even though he was born of a parent who administered the supreme command over his people. Added to this was his reverence for his peers and a care for men naturally implanted in him, so much so that even at that age, scarcely anyone could be found among the Egyptians for whom some good had not been obtained from the father by this youth. But the other brother, who was older and called Typhon <note>Typhon is the Greek name for the Egyptian god Set</note>, was, to put it in a single word, inept at everything and plainly crude. For teachers not only of Egyptian but of any foreign wisdom had been summoned by the King for his son Osiris; but this very thing Typhon...

### CHAPTER IV. 126 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE

<margin>Typhon's unrefined nature and a disposition inclined toward vice.</margin>
His mind was utterly averse to such things, and he held them in mockery, for he believed that by these studies, souls became sluggish and servile. On the other hand, when he noticed his brother Osiris honestly and moderately giving effort to their teacher, and endowed with a natural, noble modesty of mind, Typhon judged this to be the result of fear and dread. He thought this because no one had ever seen Osiris striking others with his fists, leaping upon anyone with flying heels, or driven by unseemly running—especially since Osiris possessed an agile and refined physical habit, which surrounded his soul like a light, effortless weight. Furthermore, Osiris was never one to swallow greedily with a gaping throat, nor to burst into cackling, nor to be shaken by immoderate laughter in his whole body—things that were done daily by Typhon. Indeed, Typhon believed those to be the only acts of free men: to do whatever one wished, or whatever occurred to anyone as the situation arose. Consequently, Typhon’s character was not like his lineage, nor like any man at all; to put it simply, he was not even consistent with himself, but was a varied and multifaceted evil. At certain times he seemed sluggish and dull, a "useless weight upon the earth" <note>original: "telluris inutile pondus," a classical idiom from Homer and Horace describing someone who contributes nothing to society</note>, waking from sleep only long enough to fill and stuff his belly, which was then sufficient for him to return to his slumber. Yet at other times, he would neglect even the basic necessities of nature so that he might dance awkwardly and cause trouble for his peers and elders alike. He held physical strength in high admiration, as if it were the most perfect of all goods, but he used it perversely—either for breaking down doors or for pelting bystanders with clods of earth. If he inflicted a wound or caused some damage, he would exult in it as if it were a testimony to his "virtue." Furthermore, he swelled with untimely lust beyond his years, and there was a strange violence in his assaults upon women. Therefore, he burned with envy toward his brother and with hatred toward the Egyptians, because the people looked up to Osiris and celebrated him in every song and conversation. Not only in private homes but even in public rites, they would pray to the Gods for every good thing for Osiris. Typhon saw that he himself was of a different sort and was seen as such by everyone. Witnessing this, Typhon began to establish a certain "fellowship" or club of companions made of furious men—not indeed with the intention of loving anyone from his heart (for he was not the type to do so), but so that he might acquire henchmen for his faction who were estranged from Osiris. It was easy for anyone to win Typhon’s favor and obtain anything from him that is useful to boys, if only they whispered something insulting about Osiris. Thus, that diversity of nature in the boys promised a total division in their later lives.

<margin>The seeds of discord are sown between the brothers.</margin>
But just as a fork in the road, at first slightly divided, results in a vast distance when the path is drawn out further, so it happened with these boys; even the smallest disparity in their interests dissociated them further as they grew. Indeed, they did not turn toward opposite interests gradually, but suddenly, as if each had attained perfect virtue or perfect vice by some stroke of fate. Therefore, together with the increase of their age, the opposition of their minds grew stronger, which they proved with clearer evidence through their actual deeds and works. Furthermore, Osiris had scarcely passed the age of puberty when he began to act as a colleague in military command with those who had been appointed as Leaders, even though the law did not yet permit arms to those so young...

...satisfied, but he <note>Referring to Osiris</note> ruled with counsel and judgment, since he was like the mind itself, and he used the commanders of the army as his hands; then, as his nature increased in the manner of a plant, he produced riper fruits day by day. Indeed, having been placed in charge of the Pretorian soldiers, and having become the King’s close advisor <note>original: "Regique ab aure," literally "at the King's ear," a high-ranking confidant</note>, and having attained the Prefecture of the city and the leadership of the Senate, he rendered the magistracy far more venerable than he had received it. He was convicted of embezzlement of public money, of sordid greed, and of stupidity in administering the treasury. 
<margin>Typhon, having been admitted to the Magistracies, behaved insolently.</margin>
Then, having been transferred to another magistracy, in case he might perhaps be suitable for undertaking it, he behaved himself much more basely; and that part of the most fortunate kingdom which Typhon had been appointed to govern regarded this whole year as ill-omened and unlucky. As soon as he had moved himself to other offices, every calamity and ruin was transferred along with him. Such was the mind of Typhon in ruling men. In private, he danced in an unseemly and wanton fashion, and with him every most insolent person among the Egyptians or foreigners, whom he forced to join him—those who had no concern for saying or hearing anything, or for suffering or committing any deed; so that their dining room was a workshop of every impurity. Furthermore, while awake, he himself would snore, and he most willingly listened to others snoring, thinking it to be a kind of wonderful Music. Praises and rewards were even bestowed upon him who could draw out this insolent sound longer, and bring it forth louder and more distortedly. Moreover, one or two of these, the most strenuous of them all, had "rubbed their forehead" <note>a classical idiom for becoming shameless or losing the ability to blush</note> against all things; and refusing no kind of baseness, they carried off many rewards for "fortitude," and in addition, there were available to them the rewards of magistracies and commands for their shameful license. Such, therefore, was Typhon at home. But after he had taken up the insignia of conducting public business and had put on the official dress, he then openly declared his true self: that his wickedness was varied and manifold. For this wickedness is as much at odds with itself as it is with virtue, and its parts are mutually opposed to one another. 
<margin>Typhon's audacity grows.</margin>
Indeed, that insolent man, inflated by his own self-opinion, was repeatedly driven into a madness, barking more fiercely than an <term>Epirot dog<note>A Molossian hound from the Epirus region, famous in antiquity for its ferocity and loud barking.</note></term>. He inflicted one harm upon a private citizen, another upon a family, and another upon the entire city; and he exulted all the more, the more agreeably he had struck some loss or calamity, as if he might finally wash away the disgrace forged from his domestic sluggishness with the tears of men. But yet one advantage was available from these evils; for often when he was about to create danger for someone, or was driven sideways, having been snatched up recklessly into absurd and unheard-of suspicions, he seemed to be like those who are frantic and possessed, contending most stubbornly over a <note>original: "Delphica umbra," a variation of the Greek proverb "disputing over the shadow of an ass," meaning a bitter argument over something completely worthless.</note>. Meanwhile, the accused man would escape, about whom not a word was said afterward; or Typhon would languish in a lethargy, and for some time would grow numb with a heaviness of the head, so that the things which were being done fell completely from his mind. And afterward, when he had recovered himself, the memory of things just past had nonetheless entirely flowed away. But he would then obstinately argue with the stewards about these matters: how many grains of wheat a <term>Medimnus<note>A Greek unit of dry measure, roughly 50-55 liters.</note></term> contained, or how many <term>cyathos<note>A small measure for liquids or solids, roughly equivalent to a small cup or ladle.</note></term> it held—bringing a certain superfluous and troublesome ingenuity of mind

### CHAPTER III. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>His drowsiness and ignorance.</margin>
...displaying [insolence], sometimes sleep, opportunely invading **Typhon**, rescued the man from imminent destruction. Indeed, had he not been seized by it, he would have been knocked headlong from his chair, had not one of the attendants supported him after he dropped his lamp. Thus it happened that his tragic all-night vigils more often ended in comedy. Nor did he administer justice during the day, as his nature was an enemy to the Sun and the light, and better suited to the shadows. And since he understood that there was no one, even those endowed with moderate prudence, who did not judge there to be the greatest ignorance in him, he did not blame his own stupidity, but instead professed a general hatred for the wise, as if he had received an injury from them because they excelled in judgment and sagacity; he was a man completely devoid of counsel, yet a most cunning craftsman of snares. There was in him a madness joined with fury, which two destructions of the soul—if they grow strong with mutual resources—there is no other greater evil in the nature of things, nor can there be one more effective for the ruin of the human race. The father <note>The previous King, father of Osiris and Typhon</note> both saw and understood each of these things, and he provided for the benefit of the Egyptians; for the King was at once Priest and Sage, and it is handed down in the monuments of the Egyptians that he even existed as a God. For it is not incredible to the Egyptians that infinite Divine Powers <note>original: "Numina"</note> ruled among them individually before the empire of the lands reached mortal men, and the race of Kings was reckoned from their ancestors, as a *Piromis* from a *Piromis* <note>original: "Piromis à Piromide." This refers to a passage in Herodotus where "Piromis" is translated as "a beautiful and good man," used to describe the lineage of high priests.</note>. Therefore, after he was translated from the Gods of the lesser to the Gods of the greater nations, and the appointed day had arrived, all the families of the Priests and the military order of the natives gathered from all the cities of the Egyptians, as had been previously proclaimed by a herald.

<margin>Election of a new King.</margin>
The necessity of the law called all these together; as for the rest of the common people, while they were free to be absent, the power of attending was granted to everyone—not as voters in creating the King, but as spectators. However, the spectacle was forbidden to the swineherds, and to the soldiers who were either foreigners themselves or born of foreigners serving for pay among the Egyptians. For this reason, the condition of the eldest of the sons <note>Typhon</note> was far inferior, for the faction of **Typhon** consisted of swineherds and foreigners.

<margin>The common people favor Typhon.</margin>
This was a wild and numerous populace, which, following inveterate custom and not daring anything to the contrary, did not consider that disgrace heavy or unworthy, but thought of it as something due to themselves, as if imposed by right and law, and in a certain way natural to their kind.

<margin>The prudence of Isis joined with piety.</margin>
Furthermore, **Osiris** had a wife named **Isis**, whom they interpret as the wise progress of nature <note>A common Renaissance interpretation of Isis as "Nature" or "Divine Wisdom" in action.</note>, a woman in her morals, life, and religion not at all unlike her husband. Following the example of her husband, she busied herself with this one thing: to bind the human race to her through beneficence, the invention of things, and whatever other ways possible. She was no less intent on the good of the Kingdom than **Osiris**. She appeased the Divine Powers with the perpetual cult of Religion and instituted sacred rites; for the safety of her husband and the preservation of the scepter committed to him, she constantly petitioned the ears of the Gods. She strove by every means to return **Typhon** to his senses, having been reconciled to her husband. From them was born a son named **Horus**, who, formed for any height by paternal instruction, stored the healthy counsels and warnings of his most wise father deep in his heart, as if for his own use in his own time...

<margin>The eloquence of Isis.</margin>

Furthermore, Osiris, having traveled the whole world and become famous for the invention of the most useful things—whom the Greeks later called **Dionysus**—was often depicted with a chain leading from his mouth to the ears of his listeners. This was due to his most effective power of persuasion and his faculty of speech, from which Plutarch reports the fable of **Hercules Ogmius** <note>A Celtic version of Hercules described by the writer Lucian, who leads men by golden chains attached from his tongue to their ears, symbolizing the power of eloquence</note> later arose. Moreover, while Osiris was traveling, **Typhon** attempted no uprisings, as **Isis** kept a shrewd watch against his schemes. But upon Osiris’s return, now famous throughout the world for his achievements, Typhon was spurred by envy and tried every means to ensure that, driven by a frenzy for tyranny, he might eliminate and expel Osiris and lead the Egyptian kingdom to ultimate ruin. Indeed, having deceived Osiris by trickery and cunning, he shut him inside a chest and cast him into the Nile. 
<margin>Osiris, shut in a chest, is committed to the Nile.</margin>
Upon learning of this, Isis, though deprived of everything, wandered far and wide; she passed by no one without inquiring about Osiris. She even asked children about the chest, some of whom, having witnessed the deed, revealed what had happened to it. From that time on, it has been suspected that a power of prophecy exists in children, and people observe their divinations; while they play and chatter in the temples without distinction, whatever comes into their minds is noted. Some believe **Anubis** <note>The jackal-headed god, here appearing in the search for Osiris</note> was among them. But Typhon, having learned of the arrival of Isis and fearing the clever woman’s machinations—lest the safety of the released Osiris should mean his own destruction—tore the body into fourteen parts and scattered them. 
<margin>Osiris is proposed to be worshiped as a Deity.</margin>
Isis, joining the found parts back into a whole, substituted a waxen one where the private part was missing, and in this way proposed him to the priests as a Deity <note>original: "Numen"</note> to be worshiped. Thus, after Osiris was extinguished by Typhonic malice, **Horus**, having been instructed by his mother, attacked Typhon in open war. He finally conquered him and handed the prisoner over to his mother; but Isis did not let him go free; rather, continually intent on his schemes, she restrained him with certain barriers. This is the sum of the **opposition of opposites** <note>original Greek: ἀντιστοιχία (antistoechia), referring to the dualistic struggle between order and chaos</note> between Osiris and Typhon. Let us see what the Egyptians signified by it. 

<margin>Which prince Osiris designates.</margin>
Osiris, raised high with a scepter fashioned in the shape of an eye, represents the **Architectonic** <note>The master-designing or structural intellect that builds a society</note> intellect or the reason of a King equipped with every kind of virtue. By his goodness, justice, piety, solicitude, and religion, the kingdom is filled with every happiness. Typhon, on the other hand, 
<margin>Which prince Typhon designates.</margin>
signifies a tyrant King, whose will stands in place of reason. He is a deserter of justice, an iniquitous overturner of the Kingdom, a lover of his own interests, an oppressor of subjects, a **blood-thirster** <note>original: "sanguinum dipsas"</note>, and a workshop of all iniquity. By his ambition, lust, and greed, all things are turned upside down; having finally shattered the foundations of justice and devastated the bulwarks of religion, he leads the empire to ultimate destruction. To this man, **Isis**, the wife of Osiris—that is, **Providence** 
<margin>Isis denotes Providence.</margin>
or the provident will, or a prudent progress in all things—opposes herself with the greatest care, vigilance, and untiring labor, burning with a desire for the common good. By her sharp-sighted dictates, all Royal duties and ministries are rightly arranged, Typhonic schemes are scouted out, and the civil tumults and seditions born from Typhon’s malice are opportunely suppressed and extinguished. With these things so prudently established, it is no wonder that 
<margin>What Horus signifies.</margin>
**Horus** is born: that beautiful harmony of the political world. For he is the discipline of order, the standard of affairs, the basis of human actions, and the [preservation]...

### CHAP. III. 130 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS THE ISIAC TEMPLE

the support of the world; so, while she <note>Isis, representing political wisdom or providence</note> binds clemency to justice, piety to fortitude, and modesty to magnanimity, she seems to provide the same thing in the political World that God, the Author of nature, provides in the preservation of the universe, while He tempers evils with goods, and consonants with dissonants, in the highest proportion. Hence Isis did not release **Typhon**, once captured by her son **Horus**, as entirely free, being very well aware how much the zeal of an adversary sharpens the wit of a prince toward defending himself in every way against the tricks and cunning arts of the opposing side. But let us explain all these things more fully.

->*The long-lasting peace and happiness of any kingdom should always be suspect.*<-

It is so arranged for the human condition that nothing under the Sun is firm, nothing stable, nothing long-lasting; no peace is established by laws so exact that it does not eventually suffer the shipwreck of its own happiness. History records this very thing regarding the kingdom of **Osiris**, the exemplar of total happiness, which was finally subdued by **Typhon** and led down from the highest peak of bliss into ultimate confusion. For where there is the highest peace without fear, there necessarily is security; where there is security, there is a freer license for living; where this exists, prosperity soon arises from the goods growing during a long peace; the companion of prosperity is luxury; luxury follows envy just as a shadow follows the light; envy stirs up quarrels, dissensions, persecutions, and wars; finally, just as wars shake everything with internal seditions and tumults, they also threaten the kingdom with ultimate extermination. 

**Typhon** arises, who leads the body of **Osiris**—that is, the kingdom—into ruin by dividing it into parts through the factions of seditious men; while he dissolves the body's union, it is distracted into a pernicious multitude. This ruin would undoubtedly be incurred unless the providence of **Isis** had timely consulted the storms arising in the kingdom; unless through **Horus**, when things were almost despaired of <note>original: "conclamatis penè rebus" - a Latin idiom for a hopeless situation, literally 'the funeral cry having been raised'</note>, appropriate means were prepared through counsel and prudence, and thus the Kingdom, with a temperate climate introduced, was restored to its own harmony—that is, to **Horus**. In such calamities, hope and fear, love and hatred usually intervene, so that in the most bitter calamity, just as at the bottom of **Pandora’s box**, the most ardent vigor of hope is occasionally present. For just as in the greatest flatteries of fortune and the most fertile state of affairs, there is the greatest fear—sometimes affecting one with greater torture than the pain from the loss of what was possessed—so grief almost always occupies the extremity of joy, and from the sharpest point of grief, the omens of happiness are brought back.

<margin>The Harmony of the Republic consists in the obedience of subjects to the Prince.</margin>
Furthermore, the Republic preserves its harmonic state as long as the members are joined to the head—that is, the subjects to the Prince—in perfect concord and peace. But the entire harmony of the Empire and the Republic is soon destroyed when distrust and discord, when a change of Religion, and factions of minds against the Prince have arisen.
<margin>In what the Disharmony of the Republic consists.</margin>
If, moreover, the Prince also degenerates into a Tyrant, does not seek the good of the subjects, if he does not condescend to the morals and inclination of the subjects, if he overflows with luxury, pride, and avarice; if, with justice set aside, all things are promiscuous, and there is a certain impunity for sinning...

# SYNT AGMA II. ON EGYPTIAN POLITICS 131 CHAP. III.

...the license to sin breeds confusion; where life is not truly lived, where everyone measures the public good by their own profit, where each person plots their own safety only through the destruction of another, where all justice lies dormant, all order and discipline are torn apart, faith is broken, all piety is loosened, and where humanity toward one's neighbor has grown colder than even barbaric ferocity. For while one member of the Commonwealth does not suffer with another, the whole withers and flows away into decay; just as a harmonic body is soon destroyed when a violent <term>imbalance of humors|dyscrasia</term> loosens its reins, so too is a Commonwealth destroyed where the injustice of Kings and the habit of the worst morals has arisen. On the contrary, just as the body is perfected by the soul, so the Commonwealth is perfected by religion—and I speak here of that true and uniquely soul-saving <note>original: "orthodoxâ Catholicâ"</note> orthodox Catholic religion.

<margin>Religion is necessary for preserving the Commonwealth.</margin>
For as the soul is whole in the whole and whole in every part, so to preserve the harmony of the Commonwealth, there must be one religion and one set of articles of faith held and observed by all. Without this religion, neither the Prince performs his duty nor do the subjects; without it, there is no society, because there is no faith; there is no justice, no virtue, but rather fraud, license, insolence, and, in a word, a confusion of all people and things is born. Just as it is between the soul and the body, so between the King and the subjects, between the Prince and the people, there must be the highest <term>concord|conspiratio</term> <note>The author uses "conspiratio" in the classical sense of "breathing together" or harmony, rather than a secret plot.</note>, without which the foundations of the entire city are rightly split apart as if by a dangerous thunderbolt. For what kingdom is safe whose guardian is the fear of the people? What city is secure in which the multitude lives suppressed by force and arms? Therefore, so that the Commonwealth may harmonize perfectly with itself, the <term>tritone|an interval of three whole tones, considered highly discordant in music</term> must be removed; the tritone with the <term>fifth|diapente</term> must be avoided; the <term>fourth|diatessaron</term> with the semitone or <term>major third|ditono</term> must be utterly rooted out; and the <term>octave|diapason</term> with the fourth, and similar monsters of maximum dissonance, must be fled by all means. This means that dissensions, tumults, the vigor of the worst morals, and the splitting of the said religion into various heresies must by no means be permitted; for these have been, at all times, the greatest nurseries of massive calamities and the overthrow of Kingdoms and Empires.

Under hope and fear, many other such "nurseries of change" are often hidden in the alternation of extremes. For supreme repentance follows the gravest sins; pride, insolence, or forgetfulness of oneself usually follows great achievements. Another's envy drives one’s glory; commiseration lightens misfortune. Character and industry favor poverty; restless anxiety favors wealth. The greatest security attends folly; while a manifold danger and a harvest of hardships attend learning or wisdom. And this is why **Isis** did not release **Typhon**—who had been captured by the fortitude of **Horus**—as entirely free, but detained him as a precaution, like an incentive for care and vigilance in administering the Kingdom. For if **Typhon** were utterly extinguished, the kingdom, shaken as if by the sluggishness of its citizens, would necessarily fall of its own weight. The perfection of a kingdom is enough; the hidden machinations of enemies are the spurs to acting providently and vigilantly in all things. Through these, it happens that the kingdom, finally restored to its former vigor, stands firm.

Truly, the Poets, presenting this fable of **Osiris** and **Typhon** under the persona of **Jupiter** and **Typhon**, translate it to political considerations in this way.

### CHAPTER III. 132 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE

...they say. <note>The text likely begins with "dicunt" or "ferunt," meaning "they say" or "it is said."</note> **Juno**, indignant that **Jupiter** had fathered **Pallas** <note>The goddess Athena, known for wisdom and war.</note> from himself without her help, is said to have exhausted all the Gods and Goddesses with her prayers so that she too might bring forth an offspring without Jupiter. Overcome by Juno's persistence, she struck the earth, and from that movement **Typhon** was born—a huge and horrific monster. Soon after, as his beastly character required, he was given to a serpent to be raised and nourished. After he reached adulthood, he stirred up war against Jupiter. In this conflict, Jupiter was defeated and fell into the power of Typhon, who lifted him onto his shoulders and carried him away to a dark and deserted region. There, having cut the **sinews** <note>original: "neruis"; refers to tendons or nerves, symbolizing the "sinews of power."</note> of his hands and feet, he left him mutilated and helpless. 

However, **Mercury** stole the sinews back from Typhon and restored them to Jupiter. Jupiter, his former strength restored, attacked the Beast once more and struck him with a lightning bolt. It is said that serpents were born from his blood. Finally, as Typhon collapsed and fled, Jupiter hurled **Mount Etna** upon him, crushing him beneath the mountain. They quite aptly apply this fable to the varied fortunes and changes of Kings. For Kings are rightly considered to be joined to their kingdoms by the bonds of marriage, just as Jupiter is to Juno.

<margin>Where the uprisings of the people have their origin.</margin>
But it sometimes happens that Kings, corrupted by the habit of commanding and leaning toward **tyranny**, draw all things to themselves. Scorning the consensus of the **Orders** and their **Senate**, they "give birth" from themselves—that is, they administer everything according to their own whim and absolute power. <note>original: "imperio mero"</note> The people, bearing this poorly from then on, labor to create and raise up some leader from among themselves. This matter almost always takes its beginning from the secret solicitation of the nobles and leaders. When these groups meet and the provocation of the common people is attempted, a certain swelling of affairs follows (signified by the infancy of Typhon). This state of affairs is nourished by the innate depravity and malignant nature of the commoners (a serpent most hostile to Kings). Once the defection has gathered strength, the matter finally breaks out into

<margin>The monstrous image of Typhon.</margin>
open rebellion. Because this inflicts infinite evils upon both Kings and peoples, it is represented under the dire image of that **Typhon**, in which there are: **a hundred heads**, representing divided powers; **flaming mouths**, representing fires; **belts of snakes**, representing pestilences (especially during sieges); **iron hands**, representing slaughter; **eagle claws**, representing plunder; and a **body covered in feathers**, representing perpetual rumors, messengers, and panics, and things of this sort. Sometimes these rebellions are so powerful that Kings are forced—as if carried away by the rebels—to abandon the seats of their kingdom and their primary cities, to draw together their forces, and to 

<margin>This fable contains political lessons.</margin>
retreat into some remote and obscure province of their domain. There, the "sinews" of both their money and their **Majesty** are cut. Yet, not long after, by prudently enduring their fortune, they recover their "sinews" through the virtue and industry of **Mercury**. This means that by becoming approachable, and through prudent edicts and kind speeches, they reconcile the minds and wills of their subjects. They then stir up a readiness to contribute to expenses and a new vigor of authority. Nonetheless, wise and cautious rulers generally do not wish to test the **dice of fortune** <note>original: "aleam fortunae"; a classical idiom for the risks of battle.</note> and abstain from combat; instead, they take care to break the reputation of the rebels through some memorable deed. If this succeeds according to their wish, the rebels, conscious of the wound received and trembling for their own affairs, first turn to broken and empty threats, like the hissing of serpents.

### *Political Corollaries.*

<margin>
Princes are exposed to the most unhappy outcomes.
</margin>

From these things it is clear that all states, whatever they may be, are subject to change; for just as they are exposed to the greatest opposition, so they also labor under continuous rancor, rivalry, envy, suspicion, and ambition. They burn with constant hatred, plots, betrayals, wars, and offenses; therein, the destruction of another results in one's own increase and preservation. The instruments from which the foundations of peace are built are so subtle and so delicate that—while they are subjected to various events and connected by hidden chains of causes, standing amidst dangerous and unforeseen occasions—it is impossible for them not to experience the various fates of the human condition. How many changes of Republics, how many overthrows of Kingdoms, destructions of Empires, and ruins of Monarchies have we known to happen? Which Prince is so fortunate as to escape the discords and ruses <note>original: "τεχνίσματα" (technismata), meaning clever schemes or maneuvers</note> of neighboring Princes and the plots of distant ones? Who can show himself immune from the factions of the powerful, from the conspiracies of subjects, from the most pernicious seditions of the people, from the discords of relatives, from the infidelity of the kingdom's governors, from the treachery of military leaders, from the rebellion of the soldiers themselves, or from the invasion and flood of foreign and barbarian nations? If he is fortified by power and strength, he will incite many against him as if in a formed battle-line; if he is inferior, foreign Princes called in as auxiliary hands will, once liberty is removed, soon subject him to their own law; if he is weak, he will be shaken at the first blow and, precipitated by the strength of the more powerful into the ultimate abyss <note>original: "barathrum"</note> of calamity, he will suffer the loss of all his goods. Therefore, only that Prince will be deemed worthy of the title of "blessed" who, relying on the goodness of his cause, armed with justice, and driven by an ardent zeal for religion, has administered with the highest sincerity and rectitude of intention, free and released from every impulse of passion. In this way, and by these means, Isis—otherwise a weak and feeble woman—eluded and prostrated the Gigantic <note>original: "Gygantæam"</note> ferocity of Typhon and the most atrocious machinations of the Titans, and restored the almost extinguished kingdom to its integrity.

CHAPTER IV. 134 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACI THE ISIAC TEMPLE

<margin>God is the most perfect example of a Monarchical state.</margin>
<margin>Through the unity of the Angelic World, the happiness of a political state is designated.</margin>
<margin>Through the mobility of the sensible world, democratic rule is designated.</margin>
<margin>Monarchy is the most perfect state.</margin>
...observing the divine order shining forth through the series established by the four-fold grouping <note>The "quaternion" or four-fold grouping likely refers to the Pythagorean Tetrad, which Kircher often uses to explain the structure of the universe.</note> of all things, they believed it was set before their eyes as the unique and most fitting model for political governance. For the Supreme Deity of all Deities—the Archetypal or Ideal World—while it governs the Universe with such equity of laws, arranges it with such providence, and preserves it with such love and kindness; what else does it show us but a kind of most absolute model of a Monarchical state? What of the Genial or Angelic World, distributed into so many classes, distinguished into such varied duties and ministries, and conspicuous for such an admirable arrangement of orders? In this world, although there are various and disparate levels of dominion and subjection, all nevertheless seem to strive for this one thing: that all, linked by a single will and purpose, might conspire toward the preservation of the whole. What else, I ask, is designated by this very thing but the state of an Aristocratic polity? The entire happiness of such a state is the union and concord of the elite <note>original: "optimatum," referring to the "best" or highest class of citizens or beings</note>, and its stability is the care and love for the common good in every individual. Finally, what does this sensible machine of the World—composed of the orbits of the stars and the mobile, unstable mixture of corruptible elements—propose to us but the condition of a Democratic state, or plebeian rule? We see it is all the more dangerous as it is more liable to great change and the disturbance of factious men. Therefore, the Egyptians, considering these things more attentively, rightly judged that state to be more suitable for preservation which was more similar to the Archetypal Monarchy and less liable to changes. In this Archetype, since the Angelic Spirits obey the nod of the one supreme Monarch and Author of things, and the individual classes of created things in this sensible World are subjected to an absolute and perfect dominion; the Egyptians applied themselves with the greatest zeal so that they might fashion their own Monarchy according to this model of the monarchical state.

<margin>What the mind is in the body, the Monarch is among the people.</margin>
<margin>Political harmony.</margin>
For just as in a single physical body the mind exercises and perfects its harmonious actions through the concord and binding together of the limbs, and binds those same limbs with a single spirit; in no different way does a single empire produce a most beautiful harmony in this political World (entirely analogous to the two worlds described just before). It does this while it rules and commands by the power of one person, or of several united in a Commonwealth <note>original: "Republica"</note>, providing for everyone, pronouncing laws, strengthening concord, carrying out the necessities of human society, facilitating commerce, and preserving actions and friendships inviolate through suitable precepts urged by either nature or necessity. And just as in stringed instruments, pipes, and song itself, a certain harmony must be maintained from distinct sounds—which, if changed or discordant, learned ears cannot endure—and yet this harmony is made concordant and congruent through the moderation of very different voices; so too a city consists of the consensus of very different people through a balanced reasoning of the highest, lowest, middle, and intermediate orders and sounds. And what is called "harmony" by musicians in song is "concord" in a city or Commonwealth—the tightest and best bond of safety in any state, which can in no way exist without justice. Justice, however, cannot achieve its effect unless it depends on the authority of someone who holds supreme power. How many there are...

### TREATISE II. ON EGYPTIAN POLITICS. CHAPTER IV.

In every form of Republic, there must be a supreme power—only one in each—just as in every physical body there is one soul which rules as the moderator of <unclear>all</unclear> vital operations diffused throughout the entire body, not two. In the World, there is one God, who by His ineffable providence moderates and directs all things in a single <margin>Unity must be loved in a Republic.</margin> harmony. It is impossible for there to be two supreme powers in a Republic administering affairs with equal power and command; for a supreme entity in its own order does not admit a superior, unless it is subordinated to something else. If you establish two, the dissonance of the political body is already at the doorstep; for when the civil body is divided, it is necessary that two Republics emerge from one. Nor does it prevent the supreme power from admitting several administrators and distributors; for these do not hold supreme power themselves, but all share a single power, as occurs in an Aristocracy <note>Rule by a small, elite group.</note> or a Democracy <note>Rule by the people.</note>. In a Monarchy, however, the power over all things rests with one person, upon whom the rest depend—those who, under him, moderate the Republic, the principality, or the kingdom through the roles entrusted to them. The King exercises his authority through the ministry of those appointed, not unlike the power of the soul diffused through the whole body and its limbs as if through certain instruments. For harmony consists in this: that a single string or pipe always sounds either deeper or higher, and yet higher <unclear>in tone</unclear> or according to the pitch, from which eventually, through an artistic symphony, a purposeful melody is born.

Hence that supreme Harmonizer of things <note>original: "Harmosta," a term for a regulator or governor who brings things into tune.</note>, as soon as He had established that great harmonic system of the World with an ineffable variety of "stops" <note>original: "registrorum," likely a metaphor comparing the world to a pipe organ.</note>, acted like a Chief Conductor <note>original: "Archichoragus," the leader of a choir.</note> for each and every creature. For the heavens, elements, animals, trees, foliage, and rivers, and the rest of the works He made, He <margin>The political state is the image of the governing God.</margin> appointed specific leaders and conductors of their own kind. We observe the necessity of this in almost all classes of natural things: when a man is born, lest he perish, he needs another to direct him. One man rules all <margin>An example from natural things.</margin> animals. Within man himself, the more divine part—the soul—rules; and within that soul, two parts—the "irascible" <note>The part of the soul associated with courage or anger.</note> and the "concupiscible" <note>The part of the soul associated with desire.</note>—must be subjected to the dictates of reason. Among the members of the body, one is primary, by whose judgment all the rest are moved—whether that be the head, or as others say, the heart, which is related to the brain. In this way, He set a Prince Angel over the Angels, a Spirit over spirits, a star over stars, a Demon over demons, a bird over birds, a beast over beasts, a serpent over serpents, a fish over fishes, and over men He set a Man, who is the Word incarnate, Christ JESUS. Thus, to command, to rule, to be subject, and to be governed are entirely consistent with natural law, and with the divine, human, and civil laws of nations. Certainly, since this wondrous diversity of the World consists of four elements—substances of contrary qualities, both spiritual and corporal—unless they were bound together by a certain harmony and symmetry of subordination, and tempered by certain laws of subjection and governance, the most beautiful harmonic body of the World would necessarily be consumed in a short time. For such diverse parts could not persist within it if each performed its works by itself through a confused and indifferent rule; rather, power clashing with equal power would possess everything in perpetual discord and irreconcilable disagreement, and would usurp foreign things which it knows not how to rule, and which do not suit it, to its own destruction.

### CHAPTER IV. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>
Order is necessary for the World.
</margin>
Order is therefore necessary in all things, as Boniface <note>Likely referring to Pope Boniface, cited in canon law.</note> is beautifully quoted by Gratian <note>The 12th-century author of the *Decretum*, a foundational collection of canon law.</note>: "By this counsel of divine dispensation," he says, "God established that there be distinct levels and orders, so that while the lesser showed reverence to the more powerful, and the powerful bestowed love upon the lesser, a true concord might be made, a weaving together out of diversity, and the administration of each person's duties might be rightly carried out." For the whole universe could not subsist by any other means, unless this great order of difference preserved it. Because every creature cannot be governed or live in one and the same quality, the example of the heavenly hosts instructs us; for while there are Angels, there are also Archangels, who are certainly not equal, but differ one from another in power and rank, as is well known. Just as was said above, a most sweet melody is born from strings of different tones; likewise, in the society of a Republic <note>The "Republic" here refers generally to any organized state or commonwealth.</note>, a beautiful harmony, a laudable and happy concord—almost divine—is produced by those ruling and those obeying: the rich and the poor; the noble and the commoner; the learned and the craftsmen, and all such various ranks, persons, and statuses. For what is lacking in one voice is supplied by another, and what one lacks is shared by another; for a good harmony cannot be born from strings of a single tone, nor from an instrument whose strings are all stretched to the same pitch.

<margin>
The force of Divine providence in the different states of men.
</margin>
Thus a Republic could by no means stand if all were equal; this harmonious equality appears from the various states in which Divine providence has placed men: while we see one reach the highest peak of Wisdom; another filled with every kind of virtue; another endowed with no ornament of the soul; another likewise raised to the highest peak of dignity, and another depressed to the most desperate and lowest poverty; one abounding, another in need; one rich, another poor; one enjoying perpetual delights and an abundance of wealth, and another leading a miserable life of perpetual labor. Why, then, did the goodness of God not make everyone of equal condition? This lot of mortals is thrown at us as an objection by those who, impiously denying all providence, judge that all things happen by chance.

<margin>
The wonderful distribution of things in the World.
</margin>
I ask them in return: Why did the Artisan <note>original: *Opifex*; a term for God as the Great Creator or "Master Craftsman."</note> not make all animals Angels, or all planets Suns, or all limbs eyes? For if all the limbs were eyes, where would be the hands, where the feet, where the mouth, the stomach, and the other members necessary for the body? And if all the planets were the Sun, where would be the Moon, which oversees the birth of stars so that it may bring forth offspring for us? Where would be Mars providing strength, Jupiter bringing balance, Mercury sharpening the mind, Saturn consolidating, or Venus connecting all things with love? And if all animals were Angels, where would be man, the peculiar image of God? Where would be the horses to carry him? Where the oxen and sheep, the providers of human livelihood, or rather, the food itself? Where the animals and beasts of burden which were produced for the adornment of the world and the service of man? Just as there is no consonance if every string of an instrument were the *nete* or the *hypate*, the *mese* or the *paramese* <note>These are technical terms for specific strings on the ancient Greek lyre: the highest, the lowest, the middle, and the next-to-middle.</note>, or some such <term>unison pitch <note>original: ἰσόφωνον (*isophonon*); sounding the same or having the same pitch.</note></term>, since consonance is generated from equal and unequal strings or voices as the harmony of the World requires; for if all were Teachers, Wise Men, Princes, or rich, it would be necessary for the world to perish. ### SYNTAGMA II. ON EGYPTIAN POLITICS. CHAPTER IV.

<margin>The harmony of the political state</margin>
...by the casting of fate, the symphony of the political world primarily consists; and just as in the structure of the human body, various members destined for various duties work together for one good and the healthy preservation of the individual, so also the various members of the political world ought to work together for the safety of the Republic and the preservation of concord. Therefore, the beauty of the entire human race lies in the variety of individuals, which the highest Governor has drawn into the harmony of one mystical body, under Christ the **God-Man** <note>original: "Θεανθρώπω" (Theanthrōpō). This refers to the Christian doctrine of the hypostatic union, where Christ is both fully divine and fully human.</note>. This consonance of the world and of the political body is conducted with such elegance and sweetness that no more perfect arrangement can be found.

To these people, who differ by nature, various gifts have been assigned, to each according to their own virtue and disposition, for which rewards are also returned according to their works, by **geometric proportion** <note>In political philosophy, geometric proportion (as opposed to arithmetic) means that rewards are distributed based on merit and status rather than being divided equally among everyone.</note>. Thus, as the proportion of duties is to duties, and merits to merits, so is the proportion of rewards to rewards; and by this proportion, not only does God return rewards to individuals, but the civil Republic also establishes its governance, being a certain image of the worldly, or rather the archetypal world.

<margin>The Monarchy of the Egyptians shaped according to the pattern of the Universe.</margin>
But now, to return to the Egyptians: it is of the greatest importance in the method of establishing a Monarchy well and blessedly to continually weigh the archetypal pattern placed before one's eyes, and from there to form and elaborate the political body according to the intended analogy. The Egyptians, by no means ignorant of this divine art, immediately from the very cradle of their rising empire, divided the universal Monarchy of Egypt—according to the pattern and idea of the entire universe—into certain **Nomes** <term>Nomes: from the Greek "Nomos," these were the administrative districts or provinces of ancient Egypt.</term> or Curies, or prefectures, by a certain mystical and secret method, as was said in the preceding pages. Over each of these they placed priests from the Nobility, conspicuous in religion and wisdom, who depended on the nod and will of the Monarch King. 

Their duty was to instruct the people over whom they presided in the worship of the Gods; to teach the rites and ceremonies of sacrifices to be kept with inviolable vigor for the appeasement of the **Genii** <note>In this context, Genii are protective spirits or local deities believed to watch over specific regions.</note> who presided over the prefectures, without which the Kingdom could not stand; to punish degenerate morals with the greatest severity; to rouse the soldiers to the defense of the fatherland, the farmers to the cultivation of the fields and lands so necessary for human life, and the craftsmen to the decoration of the cities and temples; and finally to rouse everyone to assist the civil necessity according to the condition of each person's own craft. They were to honor all those who conducted their business more excellently by offering rewards; and finally, every year, they were to give an account to the King of the proper administration of everything subject to their governance. Thus it happened that the kingdom, through the work of the Priests—to whom alone the path to royal succession was open—stood in perpetual vigor, administered with the greatest affection of love and the unanimous cooperation of all. Furthermore, they learned to recognize and explore the presiding Spirit of each Nome; they believed that once this Spirit was known, they could influence it through the types of things, analogies, and the apparatus of sacred sculptures. Thus, while the Spirit spent itself in the care and protection of the Nome committed to it, the kingdom—administered not so much by human providence as by that of the immortal Gods—would stand by itself without any fear of external invasion; and so not private...

...not only the temples of the individual Nomes <note>The "Nomes" (from the Greek *nomos*) were the administrative districts of ancient Egypt.</note>, but all Egypt—through the conspicuous statues of superior minds—would most exactly exhibit a temple of the Archetypal and Generative World, as if it were so many altars. In these, through continuous sacrifices, hymns, and prayers, the Divinities were petitioned for the safety of the fatherland and to turn away the storms of common calamities. Indeed, they held nothing more sacred than religion, and no matter was more ardently impressed upon them in their sacred books than this: that while religion stood, the kingdom stood, and the Genii <note>original: "Genios". In Kircher's Neoplatonic worldview, these are intermediary spirits or guardian angels assigned to protect specific nations or places.</note> would come to its aid to preserve it out of natural love. But when religion wavered through wicked morals, they believed the kingdom could not long stand, and thus the Genii would utterly desert the guardianship and care of the kingdom committed to them; once this happened, what else could a kingdom destitute of the protection of the Genii expect but ultimate extermination?

### *First political corollary.*

<margin>Why do subjects naturally fear their princes?</margin>
<margin>Whence the ruins and transfers of kingdoms and empires.</margin>
<margin>Why do even the fiercest beasts spontaneously submit to man?</margin>
From this, the cause of the horrendous catastrophes occurring at all times in the change of Empires and states is clear. Is not a King a man similar to other men? Yet we see everyone subject themselves to him with the greatest reverence and fear, which could happen by no reason unless God had impressed upon him the **character of His fear** <term>Character of fear: A spiritual mark or aura of authority granted by God that compels natural obedience from subordinates.</term>, by which the Prince is marked and elevated, so that others, compelled by a certain reverential fear and a hidden force, remain subject. This is carried out entirely through that order of those principalities, the supreme Princes [Archangels]. 

But if, through an unworthy life contaminated by crimes, Kings and Princes place an obstacle to the influence of both God and the Principalities, behold, immediately—as if the character of the fear of God in the Prince were erased by public sins—the people turn from harmony to dissonance, rebellions are stirred up, and the rejection of the Prince occurs, as if he were unworthy of the character of the fear of God. Thus, the changes of empires, the transfers of kingdoms, and the extirpation of principalities and republics have no other origin than what we have described. Let the Prince therefore remember to order his life and cultivate justice and piety so that he may always find the Principalities or presiding Archangels favorable to him; for without their perpetual protection and assistance, neither the kingdom nor the ruler can survive. 

For the same cause, God impressed a character of love even upon the fiercest animals, so that they would be subject to and obey man, for whose sake they were created. We see a boy, weaker in strength, lead by the hand, rule, and commandingly drive with lashes—wherever he wishes—a huge Elephant or a most fierce Lion; and the beast obeys him in all things, submitting itself to him in every way. Certainly for no other reason than that the rationale of order prescribes it, and because the **character of the fear of God** <note>original: "character timoris Dei"</note> impressed upon man compels all things to be subject to him. The same is observed in the order of animals: for if one animal fears another, even if it is much inferior to it in strength and size (as the Elephant fears the ram, or the Lion the cock), the cause is that they are under the protection of a higher order and carry a character of principality, which the lower animals revere by natural instinct when they recognize it. Thus you see how all things are joined by a wonderful bond, in harmony...

# SYNTAGMA II. ON EGYPTIAN POLITICS. 139 CHAPTER IV.

<margin>A wondrous event in the election of Pope Paul V.</margin>
...occur. This harmony shines through even in accidental matters (if indeed anything in the nature of things can be called accidental or a matter of chance). For instance, in the time of Pope Paul V, an eagle—having broken its chains—flew off just before the election of the said Pope and perched upon the image of a Dragon, which the heraldic symbols of the Borghese family contain. This signaled the election of a Pope from that same family. As it occurred to some, God wished to indicate the rule of the world through the omen of the "prince of birds" <note>The eagle, often associated with imperial power and the "Angels of Principalities."</note> by the agency of the Angels of the Principalities.

<margin>A portent concerning the election of Urban VIII.</margin>
Does it not also inspire wonder what happened to Urban VIII? For while the Cardinals were treating the election of the Pope in the conclave, a swarm of bees was found upon the roof of Maffeo Barberini’s chamber. These bees are the crest of the Barberini family, appearing as if his ancestral bees had already designated Cardinal Maffeo for the supreme height, whom the purple-clad Fathers <note>The Cardinals, named for their distinctive red robes.</note> would soon adore as Urban.

<margin>What the Virtues influence in men.</margin>
<margin>The influence of the Powers.</margin>
<margin>The influence of the Dominations.</margin>
Because earthly rule is discordant in itself and deformed unless it is harmonious within itself and with others—and through this harmony acquires grace and beauty—the ministry of the higher beings is necessary for a Prince. This is achieved by the Order of the Virtues. By their favor, and through the acquisition of constancy and strength, we are made strong against the lures of vices and pleasures. But so that we may also prevail against those "powers of the air" <note>A reference to demonic spirits or negative influences in the sublunary realm.</note> full of envy and malice, the protection of the super-celestial and divine Powers is necessary for us, lest we be hindered by worldly passions. Instead, by harmoniously subjecting those passions to rational desire, we might rule ourselves; for this, the assistance of the Dominations was necessary. Thus, once dominion over all lower things is obtained, it remains for us to turn toward God and devote ourselves to Him alone. This occurs if we maintain the memory of celestial things through the help of the Thrones and contemplate them with Cherubic illumination, until we are finally united to our kin and supreme parent, the Divine Monad <note>original: "Monadi diuinæ". In Kircher’s Neoplatonic philosophy, the "Monad" is the singular, ultimate source of all existence—God.</note>, through Seraphic ardor. Thus, just as the Creator descends to us through his power via the Angelic ranks, we may return through those same ranks to Him from whom we proceeded. This is like a staircase of virtues: the first step of rational nature joins us to the Angels through the senses; imagination joins us to the Archangels; fear to the Virtues; sorrow for sins to the Powers; and reason to the Principalities. For just as these spirits preside over us, so reason presides over the senses and passions. Love connects us to the Dominations, intellect to the Thrones, intelligence to the Cherubim, and finally, hope unites us to the Seraphim; for these lead most closely to God, who is the hope of all the ends of the earth.

<margin>Angels as the tuners of the celestial Song-hall.</margin>
You see, therefore, how these ministering Orders, the Harmonists standing before the supreme throne, strive to bring all things into consonance with their Prince, so that they may be faithful. Joined with the singers, these members of the divine <unclear>choirs</unclear> act as tuners of the celestial Song-hall <term>Odœi</term><note>From the Greek *odeion*, a building for musical performances; here used to describe the heavenly court.</note>. They adapt all strings and voices to that supreme Monochord <note>A single-stringed instrument used to demonstrate mathematical musical ratios; here, a metaphor for God's singular underlying order.</note> of God, making it harmonious and most sweet. If there are any useless strings or discordant melodies, they cast them out, cut them away, and reject them, so that no dissonance may be found in the mundane, celestial, or human Polychord <note>An instrument with many strings; here, the complex, multi-layered harmony of the universe.</note>. Thus, all things rejoice when the Father moves them, as Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose 'Celestial Hierarchy' defined the nine orders of angels.</note> testifies. For being moved by God, they move the heavens, and they dispose our bodies and other lower things toward that consonance, just as the first Mover of all things commands.
