<margin>Regarding Astrological truth</margin>
From this, the vain presumption of certain people from the "herd of Epicurus's pigs" <note>original: "de grege Epicuri porcorum" — a derogatory classical reference to followers of Epicurus, who prioritized material pleasure and denied divine involvement in the world.</note> is clear. Driven by his destructive dogma as if they were intoxicated and led astray, they busied themselves with reducing the souls of mortals to a certain <term>ataraxia</term> <note>original: "ἀταραξίαν" — a state of being untroubled or tranquil, which the Epicureans sought by removing the fear of gods or death.</note>. For when they noticed that there are two primary tyrants and executioners of this world—namely, hope and fear—they attempted to pacify human minds by shaking off all fear of the Divine (to which, they think, minds cannot be bound and remain quiet). They tried to provide natural explanations for all things seen daily and to demonstrate the necessity of fate from the heavens alone, through intermediate classes of causes. The guardians of a purer philosophy warn us not to rashly agree with them, and Truth itself, the living doctrine of Christ, forewarns us. Nevertheless, from the overflowing heart of that same divine goodness, even those things which are obvious to the senses, yet occur very rarely and outside the common course of nature, bear witness to the truth.

<margin>Another immutable order in the divine mind.</margin>
For through these things, it is shown that God possesses within Himself another order of His providence that is hidden from us. The "characteristic of order" infused into worldly things often agrees with this hidden plan, but often it differs greatly because of human necessity, <margin>From good comes nothing but good.</margin> and so that the majesty of divine glory may be shown to be free, bound by no chains of nature and enclosed by no prisons. Truly, it is not believable that anything except good is done by or flows from the highest Good, since He is a "good circle," perpetually revolving from good <margin>Why many things seem to happen outside of order.</margin> into good. This remains true even if the common people consider those things that often happen to us, according to our merits, to be "evil" or "sad." The Gods do not bring injuries upon us (as Iamblichus says) but rather just punishments which nevertheless look toward an ultimate good. Many sins are hidden from us that are not at all hidden from the Gods; God also often weighs what is just differently—looking at one soul in one way, and at the entire kinship of souls and the good of the Universe in another.

Indeed, from the whole parts of the World (to use his words), a certain multi-faceted action descends through individual members; <margin>The appearance of evil proceeds from matter.</margin> it descends most easily because of the similarity of powers between the "agent" and the "patient." Thus, it happens by the necessity of the body alone that things which were good and healthy in the whole, and consonant with the harmony of the Universe, are often corrupted by a failure in this or that part. <margin>Four impediments regarding matter.</margin> This happens either because they cannot sustain the force of the delegating faculty, or because of a failing that happens further down the line, or because of the weakness natural to the lowest things. It may also be because the human mind, struck by a certain superstition and panic-fear while considering an effect that is unusual and unknown to it, thinks that effect is devoid of any cause. Or finally, it may be because parts are not proportioned to parts, or acting principles to the passive ones.

Thus, those forms which are pure reasons in the divine intellect take on a certain material deformity and <term>ataxia</term> <note>original: "ἀταξίαν" — disorder or confusion.</note> in the nature of the Universe; things that were united in the whole become discordant in the individual parts. From these points, it is established that the "goods" of the Gods are corrupted sometimes by the fault of matter, and sometimes through intermediate leaders or "evil demons"—though they accomplish nothing unless it is divinely permitted, or unless we deserve it. Therefore, the heavens also often have much to contribute through many wonders; and just as wonders decide human affairs, so sometimes the conjunction of the stars, as if of a wondrous...

...of [these] things, and the signs and causes are mentioned by natural philosophers: as seen in Comets, earthquakes, and countless monstrous births. By the same logic through which divine power is falsely viewed as the efficient cause of evil, one might speak similarly of the power of celestial bodies, albeit in a lower sense; for if anything harsh or calamitous seems to stem from them, it is entirely due to the receiving matter <note>Kircher argues that celestial influences are inherently good or neutral, but they produce "bad" results when they interact with "corrupt" or "unprepared" earthly matter.</note>.

<margin>Evils are not sent from heaven, much less from the Divine.</margin>
Hence, nothing in this world can be so subject to chance that it does not lie hidden, tucked away in the secret inner chambers of divine providence. Therefore, neither sudden catastrophes of wondrous events, nor the unforeseen falls of Princes, the extinctions of families, nor the invasions of barbarians should be thought of as subject to some fatal necessity. Instead, as St. Augustine beautifully proves in his book *The City of God*, anyone who glories in the true profession of the Christian name must believe that these things take their origin, for the most part, from the hidden seeds of divine reason. Nor should God, whose nature is goodness itself, be called the cause of so many arising evils, since all these have already been preceded by the madness of a depraved human will, the injustice and atrocity of Princes, and other hidden crimes—all of which gradually arrange a great "Iliad of woes" <note>An "Iliad of woes" is a classical idiom referring to a series of endless troubles or disasters, referencing the many sufferings in Homer's Iliad.</note>. God deserts Princes who have first deserted Him; He inflicts punishments because He is provoked to do so. The Angels who are the Guardians of kingdoms suspend their protective influence because those who rule place an obstacle in the way of that influence. Therefore, let that foolish opinion of fatal necessity, which is implanted too deeply in the minds of many, cease; this will happen if we commit ourselves and all our affairs to the divine will, without any significant disturbance or varied anxiety for the future.

# CHAPTER V.

->*The doctrine of Hieroglyphs largely concerned the perpetual happiness and preservation of the Egyptian Empire; and why did they suppress it with such silence?*<-

Many wonder why the Egyptians filled nearly the whole land of Egypt with countless monuments—here with Obelisks, there with statues of the Gods constructed with admirable art. For we read that on all the borders of Egypt, and especially on the boundaries of foreign lands, images of this kind were placed. To understand this mystery,

<margin>The doctrine contained in Obelisks is for the most part apotelesmatic.</margin>
it must be known that the Hieroglyphic doctrine was not only significant of sublime and most high things concerning God, Angels, and the disposition of the World, but it was furthermore <term>apotelesmatic</term> <note>original: "apotelesmaticam" — refers to the "completion" or "fulfillment" of astrological effects; in this context, it refers to the use of symbols to manifest specific magical or protective outcomes on Earth.</note>. That is, it produced certain wonderful effects in the attraction of <term>Genii</term> <note>original: "Geniorum" — tutelary spirits or guardian deities believed to watch over specific places or people.</note>. For they believed that since these carvings were fabricated with the greatest ingenuity according to the patterns and prototypes of both nature and the "ideal worlds," it was impossible for the Deities and Spirits not to assist their petitioners. They believed these Spirits were drawn in by symbols that were similar, appropriate, and congruent to their nature—especially when sacred sacrifices and expiations were added—to defend the kingdom from adverse powers.

# CHAPTER V. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS
<meta>catchword: for</meta>

...[for] this reason, Obelisks were regarded not only as diagrams of sacred doctrine, but also as practical results, or highly effective **Amulets**; they were believed to possess a warding power against the adversary spirits that oppose the **Good Spirits** <note>original: "Agathodæmonum Antidæmonas." The Agathodæmon was a "Good Spirit," often depicted as a serpent, representing protection and luck; its "Antidæmons" were the rival, malevolent spirits.</note>. They believed the same regarding the hieroglyphic images of the Deities, which were visible in every corner of Egypt; these are discussed most extensively in the third volume.

<margin>Why the Egyptians suppressed their doctrine and sacred rites with such great silence.</margin>
But why did they suppress both the doctrine itself and the rites and ceremonies—usually celebrated only in the subterranean caves of the inner sanctuaries—with such profound silence? Why did they wish these to be known only to the Priests and their successors? The reason is that they feared if they made public the names of the **Guardian Spirits** and the ceremonies used to appease them, foreign nations might easily draw those spirits to their own side using the same rites. Or, by using opposing **Rival Demons** <note>original: "Antitechnos Dæmonas." These were spirits believed to possess "technical" or specific powers used to counteract the guardian spirits of a city.</note> to plot the ruin of the kingdom, they might strip Egypt of its protective Deities and lead it to ultimate destruction. The Greeks and Romans knew this well;

<margin>The Greeks and Romans were the imitators of the Egyptians.</margin>
both of these nations, acting as **imitators** <note>original: "simia" (literally "monkey" or "ape"). In the 17th century, this was a common way to describe a culture that copied the traditions of an older one.</note> of the Egyptians, always took the greatest care to ensure that the name of the tutelary Spirit of both the city of Athens and the city of Rome was known to no one. The only exceptions were those who, by reason of their office, were tasked with offering yearly vows (or whenever a sudden public disaster demanded it), celebrating the solemnities, and silently invoking its name. They were strictly bound by oath to maintain this silence regarding the Spirit’s name; if anyone violated their word through a sacrilegious disclosure, they believed the crime could only be atoned for by the most gruesome death. This was for no other reason than what I have stated. See what we have written copiously on these matters elsewhere throughout this work.
<margin>The name of the tutelary Spirit of Rome was hidden from the common people.</margin>

Thus, in each **Nome** <note>A "Nome" was an administrative district in ancient Egypt.</note>, specific Priests—and no others—were placed in charge of their own particular Spirits appropriate to those places; they cultivated these among the initiates chosen for the Priesthood. In those same places, they performed secret ceremonies for the safety of the people, the fertility of the land, and the security of the kingdom. Everything said thus far is explained so clearly by **Hermes** in the *Asclepius* that nothing more fitting could be brought forward to confirm these statements; for he speaks as follows in the cited book:
<margin>Hermes in the *Asclepius*.</margin>

> *The things said about man are wonderful, though less so than what follows: but the most wonderful of all surpasses admiration—that man was able to discover nature and to bring it into effect. Because our ancestors wandered far from the truth, being unbelieving regarding the nature of the Gods and not paying attention to divine worship and religion, they discovered an art by which they could "make" Gods. To this discovery, they added a power gathered from the nature of the World, mixing it in; and since they could not create souls, they summoned the souls of demons or angels and introduced them into their images through divine mysteries, so that these idols alone might have the power of doing good or evil. For your grandfather, O Asclepius, the first inventor of medicine, has a temple consecrated to him on the mountain of Libya, near the shore of the Crocodiles; in it lies his "worldly man," that is, his body, for the rest of him—or rather the whole of him, if he is a man—returned to heaven in a better sense of life. Even now, he provides all kinds of help to men through his divine power, which he formerly used to provide through the art of Medicine. Hermes, whose name I share from my grandfather, residing in his ancestral namesake city, helps and preserves all mortals coming from every side. As for Isis and Osiris, we know how many good things they provide when favorable, and how much they can harm when angry.*
<margin>A temple erected in honor of Asclepius, the inventor of Medicine.</margin>

<margin>How Man is the author of the Gods.</margin>

The celestial Gods inhabit the highest parts of heaven, each filling and guarding the order they have received. They are configured not only with heads alone, but with all members and the entire body. Thus, humanity, always close to its own nature and origin, persists in that imitation of divinity; just as the Lord and Father made the eternal Gods to be like Himself, so humanity might figure its own Gods after the likeness of its own countenance.

Then this holiest land, the seat of shrines and temples, will be full of tombs and the dead.

# CHAPTER VI.

## Osiris, Isis, Horus, and Typhon are the hieroglyphic expression of moral philosophy.

<margin>
Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book 2.

The three parts of Ethics.
</margin>
Moral philosophy, according to the testimony of Aristotle, can be considered in three ways: for it either regards private individuals and concerns the shaping of character, and thus is called <term>Ethics</term> <note>original Greek: "ἠθικὴ" (ēthikē)</note>; or it prescribes the laws for governing a family, and in this way is called <term>Economy</term> <note>meaning "household management"</note>; or finally, it regards the State or some community, and is called <term>Politics</term>. These three parts of philosophy, when joined together, constitute that complete and political <term>world-order</term> <note>original Greek: "κόσμον" (kosmon)</note>, or a world most perfect in all its parts, as Plato rightly teaches in the first book of *The Republic*.

<margin>
Plato, *On Providence*, Book 2.

Synesius, *On Providence*, Book 1.
</margin>
Hence, Synesius shows with a truly beautiful discourse that this story of Osiris, Isis, Horus, and Typhon is a kind of "Mirror of Moral Discipline" set before everyone, so that we may see in it what we should embrace and what we should flee. For just as in the "Greater World" <note>the Macrocosm or universe</note> all lower things are governed and sustained by the harmonious union and operation of the Sun and Moon, so in the "Political World," according to a certain analogy, there is a kind of Sun and Moon by whose unanimous agreement the rest of the entire political body is cherished and sustained.

<margin>
What are the Sun and Moon in Ethics?
</margin>
We say that this "Sun" and "Moon" in moral philosophy are nothing other than the concord of the intellect and the will, represented by Osiris and Isis. Just as Osiris (or the Sun), by illuminating and warming, makes the rest of the lower world fit for generation, so the intellect, by illuminating the will (or Isis) and inciting it to love through the representation of the "True Good," makes it capable of producing good works.

<margin>
Horus is both concord and peace in the political world.
</margin>
From their mutual concord is born Horus, that true Apollo, the inventor of music and harmonic proportions. When he plays in harmony, the highest things correspond to the lowest, the lowest to the highest, and finally the lowest and highest to the middle, with the greatest proportion responding everywhere. That is to say: when the exterior powers are subject to the interior ones; when the sensory appetite conforms itself to the rational; and when the will subjects itself to the intellect—with the remaining powers consenting, as it were, into one and being unanimously intent on the Good—they are found to give birth to a certain admirable peace of mind. This is shadowed forth, not badly, by the "Horn of Plenty" <note>the cornucopia</note> and the flowers associated with Apollo. 

However, since all things in human affairs are mixed, and good things are tempered with evils—as Homer wrote, there are two jars on the threshold of Jove <note>a reference to the Iliad, where Zeus/Jupiter dispenses both blessings and miseries from two different jars</note>—it is fair to believe that their dispenser and manager is not one, but that they are distributed by two contrary principles and clashing powers. One of these is carried straight to the right, while the other is borne obliquely to the left; thus it happens that the harmony of the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>the "little world," referring to the internal state of a human being</note> is repeatedly...

### SYNTAGMA II. ON EGYPTIAN POLITICS. CHAPTER VI.

<margin>When Osiris is killed.</margin>
...be disturbed, let Osiris be killed by Typhon and thrown scattered into the sea; let Isis mourn, and, having fashioned a likeness of his body, restore him in his limbs through a certain deceptive artifice of a simulated image. This means that the rational power is overcome by the sensitive and brutal appetite—the true symbol of <term>Typhon</term> <note>In Egyptian myth, Typhon (Set) is the god of chaos and storms, representing the destructive forces of nature and the soul.</note>—and is clouded over, with the splendor of its light extinguished in the darkness of brutal passions. For truly Osiris is said to be killed by Typhon when the intellect, enticed by vain lust and conquered by brutal appetite, judges that what is diametrically opposed to the law of nature or the dictates of right reason must be done. Isis is said to mourn and seek Osiris when the will, seeking the good (and that which is true), is unable to find it because the intellect, which should lead and propose the good, is clouded and prostrate. She fashions a false Osiris by a deceptive art, when she thinks she must find rest in a merely apparent and false good.

The thrice-great Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> and Zoroaster formerly expressed this discord aptly through their symbolic fictions. Zoroaster indicated these rational and sensitive appetites, so contrary to one another, under the names of Gods, of whom he called the former the maker of good things and the latter the maker of evil things. He called the better one <term>Horomazes</term> <note>The Persian god Ahura Mazda</note> and the worse one <term>Arimanius</term> <note>The Persian god Ahriman</note>. 
<margin>Horomazes and Arimanius are opposing gods.</margin>
He likened the former to light, and the latter to obscurity and darkness; but between these two he placed <term>Mithras</term> <note>The mediator god in Persian Zoroastrianism</note> in the middle. He decreed that the first should be entreated with prayers and continuous sacrifices, while to the other, averting amulets and mournful sacrifices, along with curses, ought to be offered. Among other things, they even crush a certain herb by the name of <term>Omomi</term> <note>Likely the plant 'haoma' used in Persian rituals</note> in a mortar, invoking <term>Pluto</term> <note>original: "Ditem"</note> and <term>Darkness</term> <note>original Greek: "Scotum" (Skotos)</note>, and mixing in the blood of a wolf, they carry it away to an opaque place and cast it out. 

By this description, he intends to suggest nothing other than the ceremonies by which the Egyptians fended off Osiris and Typhon: the former like a most excellent Genius, with sacrifices, incense, and innumerable other rites; the latter like an unfortunate demon, with curses and the mournful clatter of <term>sistrums</term> <note>An Egyptian percussion instrument used in religious ceremonies</note>. They wished to signify obscurely what ought to be done in the discord of powers, in domestic controversies, and finally in the tumults and seditions of Republics. For since, as we said above, moral philosophy is considered in a threefold way—regarding private persons, regarding a household, or finally regarding the State—it is rightly inferred:

<margin>Parallel comparisons.</margin>
That what that rebellious and treasonous Typhon is in the rational soul between Osiris and Isis, so is mistrust, jealousy, and suspicion in the domestic Republic between a husband and wife. In the political world, however, it is war, tumult, sedition, and contempt for healthy laws between the Magistrate (or Prince) and rebellious subjects and detractors. To begin with the first: if the better part of a man, that is, the superior part, is subjugated by the inferior, Osiris is killed by Typhon, and the harmony of the entire soul perishes. So also, if in any household the spouses are discordant, jealous, or suspicious, having no confidence between them, Osiris is killed by Typhon, and his body is torn into various parts and cast away. That is, those who ought to be as "two in one flesh" are stained by adulteries and a wandering lust for fornication in various and mixed unions, and are pulled apart into many pieces, as it were. Isis mourns; that is, because of fear, suspicions, pains, and other...

Therefore, Typhon must be put to flight by sistra <note>A sacred rattle used in Egyptian ritual to ward off evil</note>, curses, and other means customary to the Egyptians. Finally, if the Magistrate, King, or Prince is out of harmony with his subjects, or if the laws established for the common good are despised, then Osiris is killed by Typhon—that is, the master-designing <note>Latin: *Architeconicus*</note> intellect of the legislator becomes distorted in the minds of the subjects who receive the law. Through various and wicked interpretations of the laws, Osiris is torn apart; from this arise wars, civil seditions, inhuman slaughters, and other "Iliads of woes" <note>A classical idiom referring to a vast series of disasters, like the tragedies of the Trojan War</note> which usually follow this discord like a shadow follows a body. Regarding these matters, see the excellent discussions in Synesius’s *On Providence* and Marsilio Ficino’s *On Laws*. Among others, however, Plutarch has elegantly shown the things spoken of in the fable of the **etiologists** <term>aitiologōn</term> <note>original: "αἰτιολόγων"—those who explain the causes or origins of things</note> of the Gods. For he relates, as we cited above, that there are two spirits, Horomazes and Arimanium <note>Names for the Zoroastrian figures Ahura Mazda (light) and Ahriman (darkness)</note>—the former born from the purest light, the latter from darkness—and both fight against each other. He imagines that from Horomazes six Prefects came forth: the first presiding over benevolence, the second over truth, the third over the best laws; of the remaining, one over wisdom, another over wealth, and the last as the Maker of delights and sweetnesses. Against these, he records that Arimanium produced just as many, equal in number. <margin>The fable of Horomazes and Arimanium.</margin> Thus Horomazes, raising himself up, moved as far above the Sun as the Sun itself is from the earth; soon he fashioned twenty-four other Gods, all of whom he enclosed in an egg. Then Arimanium, from the opposite side, procreated just as many; these, piercing the egg, cast themselves into the same place, and thus evils were mixed with goods, producing antipathy and this discordant harmony of the World. He adds that a fatal time followed afterward, when Arimanium was removed and evils driven away, the earth became level and solid, and one Republic of happy men emerged. All of these things can be applied quite fittingly to what was said before. For when the Arimanian Typhon is driven out, peace returns, the Horimazian Osiris is restored, Horus is called back to immortality, and Isis rejoices over the finally discovered Osiris who was never sought enough; the healthfully enacted laws are received by all with benevolence. Finally, life is lived free from all pain and evils; all at last attain that intent and long-desired tranquility and peace, enjoying it happily and without weariness. But let these things suffice for the moral explanation.

<header>TREATISE II. ON EGYPTIAN POLITICS. 147 CHAPTER VII</header>

...judged piously. Hence the wise men of the Egyptians, subtle in intellect and
<margin>Fabulous narratives transformed into divine mysteries.</margin>
most suited for the scrutiny of sublime things, when they beheld that abominable and plainly ridiculous manner of the superstitious people in the worship of the Gods, and saw that they could not remove the long-standing custom of idolatry nor the deeply ingrained opinion of the stubborn crowd regarding these ridiculous Gods, they attempted to express—as *Iamblichus* <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the Egyptian mysteries</note> testifies—the greatest mysteries concerning God, the World, Angels, and Demons under these fictions of fables, fleeing to **anagogic** <note>original: "anagogicas" — a method of interpretation that finds a spiritual or mystical meaning leading the mind upward to divine things</note> ways of explaining. For they thought it unworthy to attribute the best, most noble, and most excellent thing conceivable by the intellect—namely, the Divinity—to those things which are either imperfect by their nature or composed of diverse species, or which were subject to corruption or even wicked affections of the mind, such as lust, envy, and fear; and especially to those things
<margin>The ancient sages did not believe in **polytheism** <term>polytheian</term>.</margin>
which are far removed from both reason and sense, such as that deceitful **Apis** <note>The sacred bull of Memphis</note>, or the **Mnevis Bull** <note>The sacred bull of Heliopolis</note>, the **Goat of the Mendesians**, the immense **Crocodile**, the senseless and lifeless **Nile**, garden vegetables as garden Deities, the fodder of beasts, and similar monstrous Gods. These things not only turned sacred matters into a cause for laughter and mockery (which was the least part of their wickedness), but they also entangled the minds of some in sheer and intolerable superstition and the various deceptions of demons, while dragging others into beastly and shameful impiety and a desperate license for sinning. For who is so ignorant of philosophical discipline that they would believe the **world-equal** <term>isokosmōn</term>, **dog-headed** <term>kynokephalōn</term>, and similar **many-formed** <term>poly-morpha</term> idols to be Gods? Furthermore, that the Gods (as the common Egyptians thought), fearing the power of **Typhon** <note>The Egyptian god of chaos and destruction</note> and transforming themselves into different shapes, should now put on the bodies of Ibises or Dogs, and now of Hawks and Cows, exceeds all fables and all portents. Therefore, it is by no means to be thought that the wisest Egyptian Priests either attributed anything to these, or, being persuaded by some false opinion, felt that any divinity existed in them; rather, they used these fables only as certain symbols to hide the sacraments of sublime things from the unworthy, thereby indicating a deeper philosophy. For they were so strong in the light of nature that they believed it **impossible** <term>adynaton</term> for that Being whom we call God to be finite, corruptible, changeable, or manifold.
<margin>Zoroaster. Trismegistus.</margin>
And first indeed, they gathered the infinity of God by the natural reasoning of the mind (as appears from **Zoroaster**, **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Hermetic corpus</note>, and others) from the conservation of all things and the essential dependence of created things upon God—something that is impossible to attribute to a finite and changeable being. Hence, **Orpheus** wisely said in his hymn to Saturn:
<margin>God is one.</margin>

### CHAPTER VII [Page] 148 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACI: THE ISIAC TEMPLE

...around all things at once, and through all things; for He is all action and power, and there is nothing in the whole of existence that is not God Himself. Thus, there is no magnitude, nor place, nor quality, nor shape, nor time concerning God, for He is everything.

<margin>A nerve in a living creature, which, when moved, causes everything in the creature to move.</margin>
Following this, Plato, Pythagoras, Plotinus, and other students of Egyptian wisdom reported similar things regarding these matters (to say nothing of Aristotle for the moment). It is found in living creatures that there is a certain nerve near the nape of the neck <note>original: "Nucham" — a term derived from Arabic used in medieval and Renaissance anatomy to refer to the spinal cord or the back of the neck</note>; those who pull this nerve move all the limbs of the animal at once, so that each part is stirred by its own specific motions. In this way, the Egyptians—and after them Aristotle in his book *On the Universe*—taught that the members of the world are moved by God, the "Cause of Causes."

Therefore, since they called the one God the **Necessary Being**, infinite, immovable, that eternal and immense circle whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere, they considered it impossible for a plurality of Gods to exist. For, taught and led by the light of nature, they judged it to be <term>impossible</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀδύνατον" (adynaton)</note> for there to be more than one first principle. They knew that in any category of things, that which is the highest of its kind must be only one; and if there were many Gods, they recognized that one would lack the perfection of the other, and consequently be subject to some defect, which is contrary to the divine nature. They therefore confessed one God as **Nature naturing** <note>original: "Natura naturantem" — a philosophical term meaning nature as an active, creative force (God), rather than the created world</note> or **Essence essencing**, the beginning and the end of all things. Furthermore, the motion and order of such a vast and complex machine, remaining so constant through so many ages, taught them that there was an untiring and thus infinite power in the Governor.

<margin>Aristotle, *Physics*, Book 4.</margin>
For a finite power, as Aristotle rightly teaches, cannot continue a motion without exhaustion, whether for a finite or an infinite time.

<margin>The ancients expressed the Deity through Osiris, Isis, Typhon, and Horus.</margin>
But let us finally come to the point: the Egyptian sages wished to indicate this God, whose virtues and perfections are manifold, somewhat obscurely to us through **Osiris**, **Isis**, and **Horus**. They established Him as the principle and author of all things, while His wisdom was shown through **Isis** (whom we previously cited from Plutarch as signifying nothing other than the "prudent progress of nature"), moderating and disposing all things. Finally, through **Horus**, they intended to hint at that external and sensible fabric of the World, produced by God with the highest wisdom.

<margin>Iamblichus, *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*.</margin>
Iamblichus testifies that this is indeed the case when he treats the mysteries of the Egyptians. For when his disciples asked what he judged the first cause to be—whether it was intellect, or something above intellect? Whether it was only one thing, or one with another without others? Whether corporeal or incorporeal? Whether the same as the Maker of the World, or superior to him?—and asked similar questions about the first principle, Iamblichus is said to have replied with these words:

<margin>Mercury wrote the accounts of the principles in 20,000 discourses. Seleucus. Manetho.</margin>
> "But I," he says, "will first tell you the reason why the sacred and ancient writers of the Egyptians thought various things about these matters, and moreover why the wise men of this age do not speak of them in the same way. For since there are many essences in the Universe, and they differ from one another in many ways, it is rightly handed down that there are many principles for them, having different orders. Other principles, indeed total and universal ones, are reported by other Priests, as **Seleucus** relates. **Mercury** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom many Egyptian-Greek philosophical texts were attributed</note> himself handed them down in 20,000 volumes, or as **Manetho** <note>An Egyptian priest and historian</note> reports, in 30,000; and in these he perfectly demon-"

They were taught this, as I believe, by the Hebrews and Chaldeans, who expressed all the notable effects of God by just as many names. Hence, from the essential four-letter name of God, the Tetragrammaton, which they write as <term>יהוה</term> <note>The Hebrew name Yahweh or Jehovah</note>, they derive twelve other names of God; from this again forty-two, and finally seventy-two.

We say best, therefore, that **Osiris** is that supreme Archetypal Mind of all things. **Isis**, however, is his providence and love, by whose virtue **Horus Apollo** was born—that sensible World, and that admirable concord and harmony of all things. This was mystically indicated by the ancients under the fable in which they imagined **Harmony** to be the daughter of Apollo, born from Mars and Venus. Similarly, they imagined Harmony to be born from Mars and Venus because of the agreement of similar things with dissimilar ones, and because of the consensus and dissent of hidden things, in which alone the beauty and Music of the World consist. Moreover, the name itself shows that **Osiris** is the Archetypal Mind, for it is beautifully handed down that the name signifies <term>many-eyed</term> <note>original Greek: "πολυόφθαλμος" (polyophthalmos)</note>, undoubtedly because of his manifold virtues...

<margin>Osiris, the Archetypal Intellect.</margin>
...and the operations which it performs, and the all-penetrating power of the divine rays; and for this same reason, they said that Osiris himself was the Sun, and Isis the Moon—the image of the Sun—and her co-worker in preserving his influence for the sake of Horus, their offspring. For just as the light of the Sun is a single, continuous whole, and cannot be divided into parts, nor enclosed anywhere, nor properly separated from its source, and even though it is present, it does not mix with the air; so too the light of God is entirely indivisible and is intimately present to the whole world, even if it imparts its power to a specific part that is suited to it. Meanwhile, however, it fills all things in a certain way because of its perfect power and its utterly immense dominion over everything. Thus, it brings all things to perfection and joins the furthest extremes with one another, encompassing all things within itself through the middle stages, and reflecting itself back upon itself as something entirely unified; a duty which the World also imitates by its circular motion, and by the connection and conciliation of its parts into one, as the elements turn into other elements in their turn, and the power of the higher things is sent down to the lower.

<margin>Isis, love and providence.</margin>

# SYNTAGMA II. ON EGYPTIAN POLICY. 153 CHAPTER VII #

These things indeed accord most perfectly with the eternal wisdom of God; moreover, they represent the intellect generating supreme wisdom through a beautiful hieroglyphic <margin>See the diagram of the preceding figure.</margin> in the Bembine Table <term>Bembine Table: Also known as the Mensa Isiaca, this is a famous bronze tablet decorated with Egyptian-style motifs that Renaissance scholars believed contained the core of ancient wisdom.</term>; where, besides the hieroglyphic inscriptions, Osiris or Hemphta <note>Kircher uses "Hemphta" as a name for the supreme generative spirit or divine mind.</note> appears, seated upon a variegated throne, formidable with a hawk-like face, and with other symbols declaring his operations. <margin>Interpretation of the symbols of Horus.</margin>

Therefore, from the preceding inscriptions, all those things which we have said were signified until now regarding the secret theology of the Egyptians through Osiris, Isis, and Horus, are indeed clearly demonstrated. Furthermore, the fact that they feign that Osiris was torn <margin>What does the killing of Osiris signify in the theology of the early Egyptians?</margin> into pieces by Typhon <note>original: "Typhone". Typhon is the Greek name for Set, the god of chaos who murdered his brother Osiris.</note> and enclosed in a chest is by no means lacking in significance, since they wish nothing else to be indicated by these things but the ignorance and darkness of the human intellect. Since the human mind is not strong enough to comprehend that ineffable and most simple essence of God by its own natural powers, it perceives Him through analogies and similarities of created things—which are, so to speak, "particles of divine breath" <note>original: "divinae particulae aurae", a phrase from the Roman poet Horace meaning a fragment of the divine spirit.</note>. By confusing Him with corporeal, corruptible, and imperfect things, the mind seems to pull Him apart into various pieces. For according to the testimony of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on Egyptian and Greek religion.</note>, it was customary for the Egyptians to compare that supreme Deity with whichever animal in which some excellent power or property shone forth. Hence Zoroaster <margin>Zoroaster describes God as having the head of a hawk.</margin> said that God has the head of a hawk, for no other reason than to indicate the infinite power of insight flourishing in God; we see that this symbol survives to this day, having been accepted among the Egyptians, namely the <insert>hawk</insert> man, as is evident in the preceding diagram, by which Osiris or Hemphta...

### CHAPTER VII 154 THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS ###

<margin>What do the multiform Gods of the Egyptians mean?</margin>
They wish to signify that first archetypal intellect <note>The "archetypal intellect" refers to the original, divine pattern from which all things are created.</note>; which we will interpret hieroglyphically elsewhere. Hence arise so many multiform images and statues of the Gods; which indeed denote nothing other than the manifold power of God, shadowed forth by the various properties of animals. Therefore, Osiris is torn into parts when, through ignorance and the darkness of the intellect, humans confuse God with created things. By applying the divine to corporeal objects—attributing to Him that which does not suit Him, and cannot suit Him—they tear Him apart, as it were, from a whole into fragments. For Plato rightly says that plurality in no way suits God, since all things that involve multitude recede from unity; they are more imperfect and worse the further they stand from that oneness. Osiris is shut in an ark by Typhon <note>In Egyptian myth, Typhon (Set) is the spirit of chaos who traps and murders Osiris.</note> when the human intellect is obscured by the desire for earthly and carnal things. When the mind renounces the love and contemplation of heavenly and divine things, it places an obstacle before itself and makes itself incapable of perceiving the divine rays of Osiris.

<margin>How Osiris is to be restored.</margin>
Moreover, the lost Osiris is sought by Isis, and once found mutilated, he is restored to wholeness. This means that through true wisdom and love—and with the use of sistrums <note>The sistrum was a sacred rattle used in Egyptian ritual to ward off evil and celebrate the divine.</note>, which represent frequent songs of praise—he is recollected from where he was dispersed among created things. Once gathered and adored in true faith, he is restored to his unity. When this is achieved, a great joy immediately arises in the mind, which is quite fittingly represented in the Egyptian ceremonies by that celebrated <note>original: "τῇ Oſirid.ⁱˢ εὑρέσει" (tē Osiridis heuresei)</note> *Finding of Osiris*.

And from this discourse, it is clear how harmoniously these things can be adapted to the mysteries of our faith. For what else does Osiris indicate but that eternal Sun, the first Archetypal intellect, the first and most fecund life, that Father of truly immense majesty? By understanding Himself, and by conceiving within Himself both all things and the perfect notion of His own whole and all perfections, He produces an equal, full, perfect, and consubstantial image of Himself—a life and an idea indistinct from His own nature. This is the Word of the Father and Eternal Wisdom, represented by Isis. Furthermore, by the consubstantial power of both, *Horus* is produced—that is, that admirable machine of the World, the absolute exemplar of most eminent beauty and perfection. This is confirmed by the more secret Theologians of the Hebrews in Genesis 1, who assert that [Hebrew: א] through [Hebrew: בּ] <note>Aleph through Beth</note>, the Father through the Son, created the World. <margin>The World made in the image of the Holy Trinity.</margin>

They are a most similar exemplar of the Divine Triad. Toward this triple image, He exhibits three Hierarchies in the Angelic World, with three orders in each. In the Greater World, there are three spaces: the elemental, the sidereal, and the empyrean, distinct by three qualities: form, light, and motion. In any composite mixture...

...and matter, form, the measure of virtues in all things, number, and weight; furthermore, the beginning, the middle, and the end. In the Microcosm <note>literally "the little world," a term used to describe Man as a reflection of the entire universe</note>—that is, within yourself—you find memory, the power of understanding, and the will; in the sciences, you find the natural, rational, and moral faculties. In any series of Triads, the first shows the power of God represented by *Osiris*; the second, wisdom represented by *Isis*; and the third, love—namely, 그 Spirit <note>original Hebrew: מרחפת על פני המים (*merachephet al penei ha-mayim*)</note> hovering over the face of the waters, called *Amun* in the Egyptian tongue. This Spirit, with the fertile breath of His Divinity, makes the world fruitful and adorns the virtue of both, by which *Horus* <note>In Kircher’s view, Horus represents the created world or the restored soul produced by Power and Wisdom</note> is produced. Thus *the invisible things of God are clearly seen through the things that are made* <note>A reference to Romans 1:20</note>. 

Therefore, the Eternal Father, shining with His Eternal Wisdom (the Son) in the ineffable majesty of glory, had introduced Man—the "lesser world" or Microcosm, created in His image and likeness and equipped with every talent of grace and nature—as a sort of ruler over the "greater world" He had produced. But behold Typhon! He had already been cast into the abyss along with his stricken and confederated Titans <note>Kircher equates the Egyptian Typhon and the Greek Titans with the fallen angels of Christian tradition</note> because of his rebellion against God. Deprived of all the splendor of grace and light, and full of envy, rancor, and indignation, Typhon was driven by a stinging desire for revenge. He began to attempt to overturn the glory of Osiris with every possible machination.

<margin>The figure of Typhon.</margin>
*Now (as Apollodorus writes), Typhon was terrifying even to look upon, the very image of horror. At one moment, he appeared in a strange form of human stature, so tall that he seemed higher than the peaks of all the mountains. Often his head even reached the stars, with one of his hands reaching out to the West and the other to the East. From these hands, a hundred dragon heads projected; on his legs, he possessed massive coils of vipers, whose winding lengths extended all the way to his very crown.* Such was Typhon, the enemy of the human race, who marched against Osiris and the supreme Jupiter. Hence he is depicted with the symbols of malevolence, envy, malice, and the highest perversity, hurling glowing stones into the sky with a poisonous hissing and a horrible bellowing, belching a great storm of fire from his mouth. When he challenged the Supreme Deity in vain, through a 

<margin>Allegorical description of Typhon.</margin>
fraudulent and cunning invention, he shut Osiris in an ark and afterward tore him into pieces. Having done this, he exercised his wrath upon the son, *Horus*, as well, and threw him into the sea after he was killed.

But let us see what these things mean. Osiris was "shut in the ark" when our first-formed parents <note>Adam and Eve</note>, led by the persuasion of the malignant Typhon, transgressed the divine law. By this act, as Saint Augustine testifies, they were changed from children of light into children of darkness. The human intellect, which used to sparkle with a wonderful brightness of grace, fell into extreme ignorance, blindness, and a fog of errors. It was as if intoxicated by a Lethean cup <note>The River Lethe in mythology caused forgetfulness; Kircher means humans forgot their divine origin</note>, incurring a forgetfulness of both God and all heavenly things. Furthermore, the cruelty of Typhon did not stop there; he threw the hidden body of Osiris, torn into parts, into the river, and he killed Horus as well. By this, nothing other than idolatry is signified. By the suggestion of the malignant spirit, the human race was infected and turned away from the true knowledge and worship of God. Thus it happened that the most simple entity, nature, or essence of God was attributed to many things and was, as it were, pulled apart into fragments. Hence some worshipped the Sun, the Moon, and the army of the rest of the stars; others worshipped men...

...men conspicuous for virtue and great deeds; others pursued beasts, brute animals, and things unworthy of the name with divine honor. Others, finally, worshipped and sought to appease with sacred rites whatever a malignant Spirit <note>Kircher uses "Genius" here in the sense of a guiding spirit or demon</note> suggested, or whatever a dull fantasy persuaded each person to believe under the name of God. From this source, as if from a Trojan horse, flowed the diverse rites and ceremonies of the nations, abominable sacrifices, and utterly ridiculous superstitions, by which the World was miserably held fast, as if entangled in certain serpentine coils of Typhon, struggling in vain under the powerful tyranny and dominion of the enemy. Hence the Royal Psalmist <note>King David, traditional author of the Psalms</note>, contemplating this catastrophe of old, cried out full of wonder: *God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any that did understand, or seek God. They are all gone aside, they are altogether become useless; there is none that doeth good, no, not one.* <note>Psalm 14:2-3 (Vulgate 13:2-3)</note> And here is that Horus cast into the sea; for then Horus, the son of Osiris and Isis, is cast into the sea when the human World, made in the image and likeness of God, turning away from God through sins, is submerged in the surging Ocean of earthly pleasures. While Typhon thus exercises his tyranny in the stated manner—Osiris having been torn apart, and idolatry disseminated throughout the entire World—

<margin>Isis is the eternal wisdom of God</margin>

And so, with Horus submerged in all iniquity, the eternal wisdom of God, taking pity on human labors—I mean that celestial Isis—leaving the palace of her eternity, came into this World, clothed in the mournful garment of our humanity. Subject to innumerable labors and persecutions, she gathered the parts of Osiris—that is, the nations disagreeing through the worship of diverse Gods—bringing them to the knowledge of the one true God, and adopting them into the distinguished profession of one God, one faith, and one law. By this divine calling, it happened that the dispersed parts coalesced again into a single, as it were, mystical body. She also recalled to immortality the Horus who had been slain by Typhon; that is, recalling the World submerged in sins back to life by the word of her power, she restored it to its original luster, with Typhon being restrained and extinguished. All these things having been performed, she chose twelve Apostles as Priests, prescribing to them certain laws to be observed concerning the worship of the restored Osiris. Then, she returned to the place from whence she had come—into heaven—to reign eternally with Osiris the Eternal Father.

We have woven this entire discourse at some length for this reason: to show how the Egyptians adorned their politics according to these archetypal patterns <note>original: "archetypas rationes"</note> of the one God. For just as the Archetypal intellect of God binds all things through His wisdom and unites them through His love, so it is necessary for a King to adapt all members of his kingdom into a union through the wholesome counsels of wise men and philosophers. This occurs if the practice of religion flourishes, and if the laws of the kingdom, founded upon archetypal patterns, are accepted and kept by a unanimous harmony of minds. Indeed, once this is achieved, the kingdom will persist in its vigor; otherwise, everything will be exposed to ultimate ruin through the division of minds once the union is dissolved. Osiris, torn into pieces by Typhon (that is, by rebellion) will be shut in a chest; from which the destruction of the kingdom must necessarily follow, as will be made clear in the following pages.

# CHAPTER VIII.

## *Hieroglyphic maxims a) by which they alluded to the true method of political governance.*

To ensure that the laws of the Egyptian kingdom, bound as they were to the laws of eternal reason, would be received by all with greater devotion and reverence—and that they might always remain before their eyes like a constant memorial—they placed appropriate symbols carved for this purpose on the gates of temples, the lintels of houses, and in the public spaces of cities. By looking at these, people would be reminded of their duty and stirred to a perfect observance of the laws; they believed they could do nothing more pleasing to the Gods than to conform themselves perfectly to the eternal law in all things. I will present a few of these symbols out of many.

<margin>What do the dogs carved on the gates of temples denote?</margin> First, it was the custom among the Egyptians to carve figures of dogs on the gates of temples. These indicated nothing other than the care and vigilance with which the protectors of the Kingdom ought to be equipped, in order to restrain every external invasion, whether by barking or by biting. This is shown by Horus <note>Refers to Horapollo, the purported author of an ancient treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note> in Book 1, Chapter 37, in these express words:

> Whenever anyone wishes to become a perfect sacred scribe <note>original Greek: Ἐπειδάνπερ τὸν βουλόμενον ἱερογραμματέα τέλειον γίνεσθαι... </note>, he must practice much, bark constantly, and be fierce, showing favor to no one, just like dogs.

Whoever wishes to perform the duty of a most perfect Scribe as is proper (for the Scribes were of the Priestly class and were Counselors to the kingdom), must meditate much, bark assiduously at everyone in the manner of dogs, and be fierce, showing favor to no one. But all these things will be explained more extensively in the interpretation of the Lateran Obelisk <note>Kircher refers to his own work on the obelisk brought to Rome from Egypt</note>. According to Horus in the cited passage, it was the custom of these sacred Dogs to always gaze at the images of the Gods with fixed eyes. By this, nothing else was indicated except that those burdened with the supreme care of the kingdom must keep their minds fixed upon the providence of the Supreme Deity, and by no means permit anything contrary to His honor to occur. This would happen if the worship of religion prescribed by the laws were polluted by the neglect of idle men, or by the fury and madness of foreign nations imbued with contrary rites. For they knew very well that hearts divided by the struggle between kingdom and religion can hardly be reconciled; and just as the safety of a house depends on the vigilance of fierce dogs, so too is religion—upon which the entire structure of the political fabric rightly rests—supported by the watchful care and anxiety of its guardians.

<margin>What they indicate by a scepter adapted into the shape of an eye.</margin> All these things were also beautifully indicated by the Royal scepter, fashioned into the shape of an eye; so that the scepter signified supreme power, while the eye signified the providence and vigilance to be used in the care of both expanding and preserving the kingdom. In the same way, the power of the divine Sun oversees, animates, nourishes, and preserves the mechanism of the entire world with the mere gaze of its eyes.

Among other political maxims usually inscribed on the lintels of the guardians’ houses, there was also this one, according to Caelius Rhodiginus <note>Ludovico Ricchieri, a Renaissance humanist scholar</note>: *The Crocodile fears the Ichneumon* <note>The Ichneumon is a mongoose-like animal famous in antiquity for its ability to kill crocodiles and snakes</note>. By this, they aptly indicated that nothing in human affairs is so firm and robust that danger does not loom over it, even from a weak source.

<margin>What the Egyptians signified by the Crocodile.</margin> By the Crocodile, they understood political government of a Typhonian tyranny <note>Typhon was the Egyptian god of chaos and disorder</note>...

# CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>Description of the Crocodile.</margin>
...subjected to a scenic representation, which anyone who wishes to possess a kingdom with peace and tranquility ought to avoid with "oars and sails" <note>A Latin idiom meaning "with all one's might" or "at full speed."</note>. The Crocodile is a fierce beast, gaping with an insatiable greed for human blood; it is bold against those who flee, yet fearful toward those who pursue it. Finally, when it is given over to sleep, it is destroyed by the cunning of the Ichneumon <note>The Egyptian Mongoose, famously described in antiquity as the natural enemy of the crocodile.</note>, a creature otherwise held in contempt. A King who abandons the paths of justice, piety, and mercy, and lives according to the whims of his soul's disturbances, will—often from a slight occasion, offense, or a scandal of committed imprudence—find the indignation of the people gradually growing, until he eventually brings about the ruin of both himself and his Kingdom. Therefore, by this very symbol, they were suggesting to the King that he must avoid with the greatest zeal every offense, even the slightest, or any act of unjust severity committed against the people. They judged it quite opportune for a man to be harmed by the very ones whose loyalty he needs. And even if remedies of mitigation are sought after an offense has been given, they nonetheless considered it by no means safe to take back into one's bosom a mind nurtured on hatred—even if reconciled by a new favor—just as one would not trust a viper released from drinking milk. They had learned from experience that fire easily catches on torches that were extinguished only a short time before. Things which are thought small at the beginning spread widely as they grow.

->*It is born small, but gathers strength as it goes,*<-
->*Every river that moves along receives many waters,*<-
->*The bull you fear, you once used to stroke as a calf,*<-
->*The tree under which you now rest was once a twig.*<-
<note>These verses are adapted from the Roman poet Ovid, illustrating how small things develop into powerful forces.</note>

<margin>The Omen of the boy Glaucus of Boeotia.</margin>
Plutarch relates that a wall, which is thereafter called "the swallow-wall" <note>original Latin: *chalidonius* (from the Greek *chelidon*, swallow)</note>, was built by swallows against the damage of floods. There is also the story of Glaucus, a Boeotian boy: while he was working in agriculture with his father and had repaired a fallen plowshare using his hand as a hammer, his father inferred from this that he would be strong. He took him to the Olympic Games to compete. When Glaucus was being heavily pressed by his adversary, being less skilled in the contest, his father cried out: "O boy, the one from the plow!" <note>original Greek: ὦ παῖ τὴν ἀπ' ἀρότρ.</note>—meaning, "inflict the strike from the plow." Inflamed by this voice, the youth struck his opponent with a massive blow and won. This is truly a fitting example of not despising small things. Hence, in the royal vestibule, a ram carved together with an elephant was also to be seen.

<margin>The nature of Elephants.</margin>
Although the Elephant is an animal equipped by nature with the greatest strength and a dexterity of intellect, nevertheless, upon seeing a Ram, it immediately turns to flight due to a certain natural discord. By the Elephant, they denoted the King; by the Ram, they denoted stupidity and foolishness.
<margin>What do the Ram and Elephant signify together?</margin>
The aforementioned symbols warned that these qualities must be avoided by a King with the greatest zeal. Horus <note>Refers to Horapollo, the author of an ancient study on hieroglyphs.</note> confirms this in Book 2, Chapter 81, with these words:

> When they wish to signify a King fleeing from folly and imprudence, they paint an elephant and a ram; for the beast flees the ram. <note>original Greek: Ἄνθρωπον Βασιλέα φεύγοντα μωρίαν , καὶ ἀφροσύνην βουλόμενοι σημῆναι , ἐλέφαντα καὶ κριὸν ζωγραφῶσι· ἐπειδὴ τὸ θηρίον τὸν κριὸν φεὐγεῖ .</note>

Indeed, they knew well that even in the smallest things there is a power and a cunning by which they can elude the machinations of the powerful. They were taught by the example of the hydra <note>Likely referring to a water snake or similar predator.</note> and the Nilotic frog, which nature taught no other kind of resistance against a most powerful enemy except to place a stalk of straw transversely in its mouth; for the hydra, terrified by this, soon ceases to pursue it.

### TREATISE II. ON EGYPTIAN POLITICS
### PAGE 159 — CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>The Asp, Lion, and Dog symbolically designated Royal virtues.</margin>
Furthermore, the Kings of the Egyptians, most often in public assemblies or even on military expeditions, wore various figures upon their heads. Sometimes they bore an asp with a high, coiled crest; at other times, a lion’s head terrifying to behold with its fierce eyes; then a dog’s head, and occasionally that of an Ibis. These were worn to inspire reverence, love, and fear among their subjects, and they served as hidden symbols of the political virtues with which a King ought to be imbued. Indeed, the Asp was an indicator of the protection of the divine Power; the Lion, of fortitude; the Dog, of vigilance; and the Ibis, of piety. Consequently, when the kingdom had transgressed through some grave offense, the King would display either the asp or the lion, as if they were the avengers of the crime committed. But if affairs in the kingdom were conducted properly according to the prescribed laws, he showed the Ibis or the dog, as a token of piety, indulgence, vigilance, and love. Indeed, they believed the Kingdom would persist in peace, tranquility, and happiness for only as long as the King was divinely fortified by this fourfold guard of virtues: piety, vigilance, fortitude, and divine protection. For this same reason, according to the testimony of Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher and bishop who wrote on kingship.</note>, Sphinxes were typically placed at the base of the shrines of Isis, so that Princes might learn that prudence must be joined with fortitude. For the Sphinx is <term>the sacred symbol of the union of virtues; its strength is that of a beast, and its wisdom that of a human</term> <note>original Greek: τὸν συνδεσμὸν τῶν ἀγαθῶν σύμβολον, τὴν μὲν ἰσχὺν θήρειον τὴν δὲ φρόνησιν, ἀνθρωπίνην</note>. To this also pertains the symbol of Horus <note>Referring to Horapollo, the author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphs.</note> concerning the crane carrying a pebble: namely, a symbol of vigilance and prudence that sagaciously explores all things and stabilizes the instability of life through the weight of wise counsel.

<margin>A Prince sins twice when he covers his own errors by blaming his Ministers.</margin>
If any public scandal arose in the Kingdom, the King was accustomed to investigate the cause of the emerging evil himself with the greatest solicitude. If he discovered that it had happened through his own fault or a lack of vigilance, he would openly confess his error. He rightly judged that a prince sins twice when he covers his own mistakes by blaming his ministers. Therefore, having been purified by sacred ceremonies, he was moved with great spirit to proceed more cautiously in the future.

<margin>The Ibis in the midst of serpents denotes union.</margin>
<margin>Why the Egyptians excluded foreign nations from the Kingdom.</margin>
Furthermore, the sole concern of the Kings was to preserve—through union, concord, and a unanimous harmony of minds—the kingdom they had acquired with such great labor and established with so many excellent laws. For where dissolution takes root in a kingdom through discord, there the kingdom must inevitably crack and draw near to ruin. The symbol of this was the Ibis in the midst of a heap of serpents. By its nature, this bird is equipped to first terrify with its rattling sound any united serpents hiding nearby, and then to separate those it has frightened from one another and put them to flight. Thus, those whom it did not dare to attack while they were joined in union, it soon kills and devours once they are scattered and pulled apart in different directions. Truly, nothing in human affairs is more destructive than the disunity of minds, from which alone—as if from a Trojan horse—all "Iliads of calamities" <note>A classical metaphor for an infinite series of disasters.</note> have proceeded. When they discovered that this union was being disrupted by different customs and religious institutions, they passed a law forbidding all social intercourse with foreign Kings and nations. For they knew full well that from this mixture of men differing in nature, character, and laws, there is born that uniquely destructive Hydra of discord and disagreement of minds, which throws kingdoms into turmoil. They also knew that...

### CHAPTER VIII. 160 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE

<margin>The counsels of Princes are safe when they are hidden.</margin>
<margin>Of whom was the frog a symbol?</margin>
<margin>What the image of Harpocrates denotes.</margin>
<margin>Silence is the armor of kingdoms.</margin>
It is no less a virtue to maintain agreements than to seek them; for power is not always increased when it is extended, nor does he who embraces too many things always hold them well. With this care and the greatest concern, the kingdom of Egypt maintained its vigor from time immemorial—whether you look at the vastness of its cities, the density of its population, or the abundance of things necessary for the human race. To this success, a law contributed much weight: it forbade any others, besides the leaders of the priestly order, from being conscious of the secrets of the kingdom. This was not without reason, since the counsels of princes are truly safe only when they are kept covered. The symbols of these secrets were the Seriphian frog <note>original: "rana seriphia." In antiquity, the frogs of the island of Seriphos were proverbially said to be mute.</note> (a mute species of frog), together with an image of Harpocrates <note>The Hellenistic god of silence, derived from the Egyptian Child Horus.</note>, who would press his finger to his lips and suggest silence with a nod. These were placed before the doors of the senate: they believed the kingdom was established more firmly to the extent that there was greater silence in concealing its secrets. I will not speak here of the countless other institutions which the Egyptians used to administer the Republic well and blessedly, but since we will bring these up scattered throughout this work, we refer the readers to those sections.

<margin>Admonitions for Princes.</margin>
<margin>Religion is the foundation of Kingdoms.</margin>
<margin>Solon.</margin>
<margin>Poetic allegories on the turning of human affairs.</margin>
<margin>The instability of private life changes chiefly for three reasons.</margin>
Kings and Princes will learn from these things, if I am not mistaken, how and why they are able and ought to preside over public affairs with dignity. They will recognize those virtues with which a prince must especially be equipped to rightly manage the rudders of the kingdom; they will see what must be avoided to prevent ruin, and what must be embraced for preservation. They will also learn that religion is the unique base and foundation of all government; if it totters, everything else must necessarily totter. They will experience the continuous cycles of human affairs, in which nothing is stable and nothing is firm, unless they strive to rest in Him who is the center of all things. When the ancient philosophers perceived this, such as the most wise Solon, they believed no one could be called blessed before their death and final funeral. For how many mortals, whether among the highest or the lowest, do you think would not sometimes experience the marvelous circle of fickle fortune if they lived long enough? What else does the wheel of Ixion <note>In Greek myth, Ixion was bound to a perpetually spinning fiery wheel as punishment.</note> designate among the Poets? What of the receding waters of Tantalus? Or the liver of Prometheus, eaten away and constantly growing back? What of those who, having piled up mountains to tear down heaven, were struck down by lightning and rolled into the deepest abyss? Or those who roll a huge stone or hang bound to the spokes of wheels? Why do we persist so much among these fictions? Let each person return to his own house and observe the fortune of his own private life: is there not the greatest variety everywhere? This stems either from the unstable face of the business itself, or from the mind of the actor who transcends the just limits of the matter, or from the uncertain fluctuation of the recipient, who, quickly sated with present things, gapes assiduously for new things to grasp—easily forgetting the past, always ignorant of the future, and hardly ever content with the "golden mediocrity" <note>The "Aurea Mediocritas" or Golden Mean; the virtue of moderation.</note> of things. Beautifully, therefore, Euripides said: "Many are the forms of the divine." <note>original Greek: "Πολλὰς μορφὰς τῶν Δαιμονίων" (Pollas morphas tōn Daimoniōn). This is a common closing line in Euripides' plays.</note> There are many masks of the spirits. As Plautus wrote at length: in the life of men many such things happen; they take pleasures, and soon again miseries; angers intervene, and then they return again into favor. But if angers happen to occur between them, once they have returned into favor, they are twice as much friends as they were before. Yet when they saw such great [instability] in human affairs...

### ESSAY II. ON EGYPTIAN POLITICS 161 CHAPTER VIII.

...inconsistency, so that almost all things happen to all people indiscriminately in life. Therefore, some have thought that God now plays with man as if with a ball, and now that the fates of all hang as if on a throw of the dice. Indeed, eventually, even the gods and divine providence began to be doubted. For if individual events happen by chance, you must remove providence; but if you establish providence, you will often join discordant things to it—unless, putting aside disputes, you surrender your mind captive to faith and persist in the inviolable authority of a single, ancient consensus. Otherwise, we shall certainly be carried over into the opinion of Epicurus <note>The Greek philosopher who argued that the gods do not intervene in human affairs and that the world is composed of atoms moving by chance.</note>, with first principles removed; and having surveyed the circuit of things, we shall say both that the World is abandoned to our disputes, and with the wise man <note>A reference to King Solomon in Ecclesiastes.</note>, that all human efforts are vain—even in the wisdom of the World, the vainest of vanities. For from error, we are drawn little by little into opinion, and from there into truer knowledge. Finally, as those who know, once we have recognized ourselves, having slipped back again, we understand that we know nothing at all—determining that the most pleasant life is found almost in not knowing, and considering him most happy who has escaped notice both in birth and in death.

<margin>The cycles of Fortune in political affairs, families, kingdoms, and cities.</margin>
<margin>The deluges of the world.</margin>
Let us move indeed from individual men to the collective; first to men and families, then to cities and kingdoms, even to the most absolute Monarchy. For each in turn, a good Genius <note>A guardian spirit or guiding force.</note> breathes; and in turn, from its own insolence, comes a plague and a salutary deluge to purge the dregs. Sometimes this happens through fire and water, sometimes through epidemic diseases, through wars, or mutual seditions. Thus, a joyful peace hardly lasts without struggle; external quiet is accompanied by internal dissensions, and foreign enemies foster domestic peace. Finally, the entire world lives and is governed by contention no less than by friendship.

<margin>The necessity of a worldly deluge.</margin>
Great, therefore, is the providence of God, so that when from excessive abundance either the human race or luxury and insolence have grown too much, conflicts and contentions arise immediately. From this soon comes the highest cost of grain <note>Meaning famine or extreme inflation.</note> and pestilence, which often rages so cruelly that it invades almost the entire dominion of the World. They recall that two such plagues flourished under Marcus Antoninus <note>original: "M. Antonio." This refers to Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and the devastating "Antonine Plague" of the 2nd century AD.</note>, which seemed to threaten the human race with <term>utter destruction</term> <note>original: "πανωλεθρίαν" (panolethrian).</note>. Our ancestors record that such a thing happened in the year of Christ 1450, so that scarcely a third part of mortals escaped as survivors. Yet, for the insatiable greed of men, and for an earth burdened with the most lost children and foster-lings, what greater remedy or purgation could have been given? If ever it was useful, it is certainly necessary now for this age, than which nothing is more wretched. For by this cycle of causes, both morals and studies and all human affairs are most effectively transformed; for when they have fallen and been neglected, all things become vile. But after a total restoration is received through those things that were worn down, individual things grow in value and hasten again to their vigor, destined to collapse once more at some time.

<margin>The greatest causes of vicissitudes arise from tyranny.</margin>
But those shifting tides of fortune especially vex and pursue tyrants and kings. For the life of tyrants has this particular quality: that they always fear those who ought to be trusted, and trust those in whom there is no honest faith. Hence, from this, injuries are inflicted on the undeserving, and benefits are bestowed on the unworthy; they make friends out of enemies and enemies out of citizens. And through ambition, cruelty, luxury, and greed, with the ranks of the state thrown into disorder...

<margin>CHAPTER VIII.</margin>
...kings, are suddenly cast down from the height of their power; and at last they come to the usual end of the story, falling by poison, or the sword, or by even more miserable fates, according to the saying of the Satirist <note>The Roman poet Juvenal, from his Satires (10.112–113).</note>:
> Few kings descend to the son-in-law of Ceres <note>original: "generum Cereris"—a poetic reference to Pluto, the god of the Underworld, who abducted Ceres' daughter Proserpina.</note> without slaughter and wounds,
> and few tyrants die a bloodless <note>original: "siccâ morte," literally "a dry death."</note> death.

<margin>The violence of Nemesis.</margin>
Moreover, we see from the very violence of Nemesis <note>The Greek goddess of divine retribution against those who succumb to hubris (arrogance).</note> that a perverse people are eventually punished by unjust kings. The kings, however, when they have afflicted the common people longer than is right, are in turn stripped of both their lives and the supreme powers of the Kingdom by those same people, who are once again kindled into a frenzy. Read, I beseech you, the most beautiful hymns of David, especially Psalms 17, 33, 37, 73, and 94. How elegantly he speaks, most of all in the 73rd Psalm! *Truly God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart. But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled, etc.* <note>Psalm 73:1-2.</note> Here, he first expresses the pride of the wicked and their apparent prosperity in eloquent words: *They set their mouth against the heavens, etc.* Then he describes the gnawing of his own soul while he contemplates the peace of sinners. But soon he consoles himself by the very "catastrophe" <note>In the classical sense: the final turn or resolution of a plot.</note> of events, where he says: *Surely you set them in slippery places, etc.*

<margin>The marvelous vicissitudes of the Jewish people.</margin>
Indeed, he painted the entire circle of human change most accurately in Psalms 78 and 107. There, when the Jewish nation is full of good things and forgets God, it immediately rushes into every calamity; then, being afflicted, it implores divine help again. Having obtained this help, it once more neglects the worship of the Divine Power, and being struck and healed again—now suppliant, now stubborn, repenting in hard times and becoming insolent in prosperity—it represents perfectly the image of the present age.

<margin>The main points of human transformation.</margin>
We have summarized the main points of this entire cycle <note>original: "conuersionis," referring to the turning or rotation of history.</note> in these few lines:

<margin>The Platonic Circle.</margin>
> Poverty gives peace, peace wealth, and wealth luxury:
> But luxury gives war, and wars give poverty.
> Love is the source of hatreds, death of life, the crowd of rest:
> Things that have fallen stand, and things that stood, fall.
> And the captured capture, and those who subdued are subdued:
> He who was just now victor becomes the suppliant of the vanquished.
> With a fierce king the fierce commoners are punished, and by the commoners the tyrants,
> So fate turns the alternating cycles in the World.

But you will read more on this sentiment in the books of Divine Wisdom and throughout the Psalms of David. The most abundant fruit of all these readings is considered to be this: that we shape our lives and morals, and in those mockeries of both types of fortune <note>Meaning both good and bad luck.</note>, we learn to heal the sick soul, to love every neighbor, and to lead a social life among fellow citizens. We learn to despise things that are too fleeting, and to accustom ourselves to placing God the Creator before all works. We do this not so that we may argue (in the way it is given to philosophers to do regarding the things of nature), nor so that we may drag the World into controversy—as too many look to do in this age. Nor should we read them merely to seem endured among mortals, or so that, with minds hardened against the laws and decrees of our ancestors, we might open a window to every license under the title of "evangelical liberty." <note>A critical reference to the Protestant Reformation; Kircher, a Jesuit, suggests that the "liberty" claimed by reformers leads to social and religious chaos.</note> Truly, a sophistical theology has birthed this chimera <note>A mythical monster; here meaning a grotesque or impossible delusion.</note> for us; by its breath all things suffer, both private and public. With the orders of things turned upside down everywhere, we are cast down again into the ancient chaos of the World.
