<margin>The primary source of that calamitous age.</margin>
Therefore, since today even the highest things flow downwards with great force, and the lowest things creep upwards, striving beyond the mere appearance of honor; it was consistent with divine justice that those things which are established above nature should follow a similar cycle. For light is taken away from mortals, as is the strength of unity, and consequently almost every happiness granted until now; instead, these are bestowed upon those who for a long time, as suppliants in mourning and immersed in deep darkness, were held in contempt. <margin>The transfer of faith, religion, and Monarchy</margin> You will survey here the whole history of the political world: the form of Monarchy is indeed eternal; the kingdom of holy religion and faith is eternal; the Church of Christ is eternal among mortals; but nevertheless, because of the unsuitability of the human material that receives them <note>Kircher uses the philosophical term "materiæ susceptricis," referring to the idea that the quality of a thing depends on the "vessel" or "matter" that holds it—in this case, the people or nations.</note>, these very things change both place and time, as if migrating through the segments of the earth. They draw an obscure likeness of a cycle along with our own customs; you will weigh this in the rise, growth, stability, and decline of perverse opinions, following the stretch of the entire neighboring world into a continuous circle. This occurs through a certain versatile force of its own contagion that never ceases, until profane things are confused with sacred things everywhere, and the highest with the lowest, driving everything completely into a full circle.

<margin>The fruits of Politics.</margin>
Meanwhile, let the most abundant fruits of this political study suffice for us, so that we may learn to know and govern ourselves, as if translated from shadow into light by a certain ascent of the mind. Thus, when we have perceived the manifold circle of human vicissitude <note>term: vicissitudo (vicissitude), meaning the natural change or mutation of fortunes and states over time.</note>, we may constantly reflect on how evil is sown within fleeting good, and how good may arise from evil.

<margin>The production of Man.</margin>
Man, therefore, alone endowed with a face held high and a gaze directed upward toward the heavens, is a divine animal situated on the border of both mortal and immortal nature; like a unique celestial plant set upon the earth (whose root the Creator bound in these lower seats, but whose foliage and perpetually leafy crown He relegated above the path of the year and the Sun, above the furthest circumference of the sky to orbits that will never perish). This man, I say, when he gazed too curiously upon those most brilliant lights of the World, for the contemplation of which—and for the praising of the Creator in them—he had been created, was gradually lured by their beauty. 
<margin>The origin of Idolatry.</margin>
Having abandoned the true and right path of religion, he reached such a point of madness that he believed those things which had been created for his own sake to be, as it were, his own creators, and he venerated them holily. This madness was increased by the forgetting of the healthy traditions regarding the origin of the World passed down by his predecessors; as this forgetfulness grew stronger, he drank in new opinions about God, the World, the production of man, and other things, since that heavenly fire—the principal part of the human mind—flourished...

<margin>The grandsons of Ham were the first inventors of idolatry.</margin>

<margin>The causes of idolatry and various opinions.</margin>
Furthermore, I judge the cause of these fables and empty delusions to be this: because those first men, left to their own judgment, were held by no certain written law before the time of Moses, and because certain accounts of God, the creation of the World, the flood, and similar matters and significant changes were related only among the first Patriarchs of the human race. Thus it happened that the descendants passed these traditions down through the generations, as if received from the first men. To these stories, later ages and men—the further they were removed from the first ancestors—subsequently added one thing after another, not without absurdity, until the events themselves vanished entirely into the inventions of fables. From this, that diversity of opinions took its origin; and from there, a great and nearly inexplicable confusion of accounts arose.

# CAP. I. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>The Egyptians say the first men were born in Egypt.</margin>
...is in their Geography, they attributed this prerogative to the soil of Arabia Felix <note>Arabia Felix, or "Happy Arabia," refers to the fertile southern part of the Arabian Peninsula, modern-day Yemen.</note>. Finally, the Egyptians firmly believed that the first humans were born in Egypt. They assigned the cause of this both to the perfect temperance and goodness of the air in every direction, and to the fertility of the Nile, which naturally and of its own accord produces many things and most kindly preserves those it has produced. This opinion of theirs was increased by that monstrous crop of shrews or field mice

<margin>Strange species of mice.</margin>
in the territory of Thebes, some of which were found—according to the testimony of Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a 1st-century BCE Greek historian.</note>—to be animated in their upper parts, resembling mice, but in their lower parts remained unformed and "earth-born" <note>original: ὁμόχθονες (*homochthones*), referring to the ancient belief in spontaneous generation where living creatures emerge directly from the mud</note>. Herodotus relates that Psammetichus,

<margin>Herodotus, Book 2, *Euterpe*.</margin>
King of the Egyptians, when he was seized by a great desire to know which province of the world had produced the first humans, attempted to investigate it through the following

<margin>Psammetichus’s experiment concerning the first language.</margin>
ingenious method. He entrusted two newborn infants, removed from all custom of human life, to be enclosed in a certain place and nourished by a goat under the care of a certain shepherd. He imposed such a guard on the enclosure that, with every way of approaching them blocked, they could neither see nor hear any mortal speaking with a human voice. He was undoubtedly persuaded that, having reached a suitable age, they would speak the language of that province which had given the first humans to the world. And so, after a certain cycle of years, the infants were taken out of the cave, and soon, stretching out their arms, they repeatedly burst out with these words: *Bec, Bec*. Since none of those standing by understood these sounds, as they were foreign,

<margin>What does "Bec" mean in the language of the Phrygians?</margin>
after an investigation was finally made, it was discovered that *Bec* in the language of the Phrygians signified nothing other than "bread." Thus King Psammetichus concluded that the first humans had been produced in Phrygia. Time would fail me if I were to bring up the delusions of every individual nation concerning this kind of primary origin of man; therefore, let anyone who desires more consult Berosus, Varro, Eusebius, Jerome, Polydore, Aristophanes, Pererius, Postellus, and others. Leaving these things behind, we shall return to those matters which concern the first origin of idolatry.

<margin>All nations of the world have recognized some Deity.</margin>
It is therefore certain and beyond doubt that at no time in this world has there ever existed a people so barbaric, a nation so foreign, a climate so rude and unpolished—in short, any human so wild, forest-dwelling, and irrational <note>original: ἄλογον (*alogon*)</note>—who did not recognize, either by the law of nature or the dictating light of right reason, some one principle of all things, a Deity, I say, holding the universal moderation of things, to be worshiped with a certain and peculiar rite of religion and ceremonies. It must also be established as certain that at no time was there ever a sacrifice without God, or a religion without sacrifice, with all these things coming together into one with the priesthood as if by an inseparable bond. Thus, religion seems to accompany man, sacrifice accompanies religion, and the priesthood accompanies sacrifice inseparably <note>original: ἀδιαχωρίστως (*adiachōristōs*)</note>. This is apparent both from the nearly innumerable multitude of religions brought down from the very beginning of the rising World to our own times, and from the worship of false idols practiced by various nations and peoples at all times. Finally, Egypt itself shows most clearly how it was more addicted to the worship of such false gods than all other nations, as shown by the nearly infinite number of multiform Deities...

# TREATISE III. ON THE ORIGIN OF EGYPTIAN IDOLATRY. CHAPTER I.

...monsters and portents, the description of which we shall exhibit in the sequence of this Treatise <note>original: *Syntagma*; a systematic arrangement or treatise.</note>.

<margin>Lactantius Firmianus, *Divine Institutes*, Book 2, Chapter 3.</margin>
<margin>Ham, the first inventor of idolatry.</margin>
Lactantius Firmianus <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325 AD) who became an advisor to Constantine the Great.</note>, about to show by what means idolatry was introduced into the world—especially into Egypt as if into the fountain of all superstition—says: Ham <note>original: *Cham*; the son of Noah.</note>, the son of Noah, when he had incurred a curse on account of the impudence committed in uncovering his parent’s nakedness, fled into Arabia bordering Egypt. There, he first infected the entire surrounding neighborhood with the construction of idols. But when the narrowness of the locations could not contain the immense multiplication of men, they were dispersed from there into various seats, and gradually filled the islands, the sea, and all parts of the world.

<margin>The Egyptians said to be from Ham.</margin>
Since they were separated from the holy root, each person established new rites, ceremonies, and religions according to his own judgment and will, which flowed down most especially to the Egyptians. However, the *Arabs* relate that idolatry began before the flood. For it is better known than it ought to be said that among other mortals, they were most devoted to this wicked worship, which the delightful constitution of that land seems to have promoted most greatly.

<margin>The cause of idolatry from the inspection of the stars.</margin>
For since they rarely contained themselves within their houses or huts, they spent the whole night under a clear sky, subject to no harmful influences, sleeping in the open. From the frequent sight of the celestial bodies, and the contemplation of the course of the stars proceeding by such a constant law, and the manifold and various movements of the planets, the Sun, and the Moon, they gradually fell into this opinion:

<margin>Eusebius. John of Damascus.</margin>
That the Stars are Gods, and the preservers of the things of the universe; these they worshiped and venerated with various rites and ceremonies. Eusebius also affirms this in his *Chronicle*. St. John of Damascus, however, ascribes the manufacture of idols to Serug <note>original: *Serucho*; the great-grandfather of Abraham.</note>, the descendant of Ham.

<margin>Serug, the first craftsman of idols.</margin>
<margin>The progress of idolatry.</margin>
*Serug*, he says, *first discovered idolatry; for when all had established worship by common consent, the custom of placing images for the human race took its rise. From this, they began first to shadow forth and paint with certain colors men of some name and fame, and afterwards those more celebrated, such as Princes, tyrants, and Kings, who had excelled in this life either by the glory of their deeds or by the fame of their virtues and memorable works, honoring them with statues placed in their likeness.*

And at first, indeed, potters fashioned statues of the deceased from chalk, clay, and similar material; then sculptors, imitating the clay images, formed them out of stones. Finally, metal-founders, deigning them worthy of more eminent worship, cast them from gold, silver, bronze, and other metals; and they set them before the simpler common folk as Divinities to be adored, as the *Alexandrian Chronicle* <note>A 7th-century Byzantine world chronicle.</note> testifies:

<margin>Alexandrian Chronicle.</margin>
<note>original Greek: Ἑλληνισμὸς ἀπὸ τῶν χρόνων τοῦ Σεροὺχ ἐναρξάμενος διὰ τῆς εἰδωλολατρίας... "Hellenism, starting from the times of Serug through idolatry, as everyone was then settling into some superstition, led men’s actions toward a more political way of life, to customs and the ordinances of idols; no longer merely devising by means of colors, outlining at the beginning and representing those long dead who were honored, either tyrants or leaders, or those who did something in life thought worthy of memory, but through the modeling of body-forms etc."</note>

*Hellenism <note>In this context, "Hellenism" refers to paganism or polytheistic Greek culture.</note>, he says, or Gentilism <note>The state of being a Gentile or non-believer in the Judeo-Christian God.</note>, began in the time of Serug through idolatry, when each person, led by a certain superstition of his own, shaped the ages of men toward a primarily political way of living and use, or custom, and the worship of the Gods, whom then, in progress, magistrates, and tyrants, or leaders, or if anything in that age...*

For soon they pursued Saturn, Mars, Jupiter, and Apollo—along with the rest of the crowd of false Gods and Goddesses that followed these—with erected statues and divine honors; with which that which Cicero asserts when reasoning about the nature of the Gods agrees.

Beyond these, each nation and people first pursued with private worship the founder of some City, or a Prince or lord pre-eminent in singular virtue. And so the Egyptians, inhabiting a delightful land, since they were by no means able to comprehend that invisible essence of the great God by the light of natural intellect alone, turned their eyes and minds to the ornaments of the heavens, and their motions, and to the nature of the Universe. When they perceived that all changes of sublunary <note>Referring to the Earthly realm below the moon, which was thought to be subject to change and decay, unlike the perfect heavens.</note> things, the distinctions of seasons, and similar things proceeded from the two principal stars, the Sun and the Moon, they thought these stars were eternal Gods.

Genies of the horoscope.

After this, lifting their eyes to the rest of the army of stars, and to the four elements, and to the genies <note>guardian spirits or deities</note> of the Horoscopes, and their All-Form <note>original: *Pantomorphum*; likely referring to a universal deity or the zodiacal figure that encompasses all shapes.</note>, they established twelve principal ones besides innumerable lesser Gods, according to the number of the signs observed in the Zodiac, which Herodotus confirms:

It would be a long task to review here the opinions of all nations and peoples concerning the Gods, who, having received the origin of their religion from the Egyptians, either failed to retain the ancient Theology and later mocked their teachers, or fell themselves into worse superstitions. 

Therefore, when men first held this notion of the Gods and perceived that the world was governed by providence, yet were unable to understand whose providence it was, they investigated the matter further. Captured by a despair of certain knowledge, they gradually lapsed from true religion into superstitions; and some introduced certain Gods, and others introduced others, as has been said. For it is so arranged by nature that when men are oppressed by an excessive fear of the Gods, they decline toward everything humble and sordid. They think that no act is so small that the Gods will not avenge it with the greatest wrath and punishment. This mindset caused those same Greeks—who had once mocked the superstitions of the Egyptians and other nations—to fall later into much greater errors. For they came to worship as Gods adulterers, thieves, drunkards, and criminal men, who were much more impure than the beasts. Concerning these, we shall speak more extensively in the following sections.

## CHAPTER II.

-> *On the Multitude and Variety of the Egyptian Gods.* <-

<margin>St. Ambrose, Epistle 1 to the Corinthians, chapter 10. Hermes Trismegistus to Asclepius, chapter 13.</margin>
**R**ightly and wisely does the Holy Doctor of the Church, Ambrose <note>St. Ambrose (c. 339–397 AD) was an influential Bishop of Milan and one of the four original Doctors of the Church.</note>, say that human error was the cause of idolatry. This is supported by Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: *Mercurius Trismegistus*; a legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the author of the *Hermetica*, a body of texts exploring philosophy, magic, and religion.</note>, who states that the error and unbelief of their ancestors was the origin of the abominable idolatry of the Egyptians, in which Egypt was at all times submerged and defiled. 

For since they did not apply their minds with due reverence and consideration to the worship of the true God and to divine religion, they were nonetheless held by a desire for some form of religion. They invented the art of manufacturing idols. But because they did not know how to give these idols life, they used evil arts and diabolical incantations to summon demons and bind them within the statues. To give these idols more power and strength, they consecrated various kinds of animals to them, which they called "holy." In these animals, they worshiped the souls of those who had been famous for their virtues or deeds. They even named <margin>The Egyptians animate idols with demons.</margin> cities after them—cities that had either been founded by those to whom the animals were dedicated or had been imbued with their healthy laws and institutions. In honor of these, they also established various sacrifices. Mor Isaac the Maronite <note>A 7th-century Syriac author and bishop known for his ascetic and philosophical writings.</note> describes these rituals and ceremonies most elegantly in his Syrian philosophy; his Syriac words are as follows:
<margin>Mor Isaac the Maronite in his philosophical treatises, chapter 6.</margin>

> The statues which the first men made [were born] of a great and unutterable fear, and the fear of God in the construction of this world. And they bound within them the powers of sorcerers and the constraints of demons, and the measuring powers of the world, so that they might be rulers and teachers to men, according to the testimony of the book of Asclepius regarding the book of Statues and the book of Likenesses.

However, as several five-year periods <note>original: "lustris"</note> passed and Osiris and Isis died, their fame grew continuously. The preconceived opinion of their excellence and illustrious dignity took deeper root in the minds of men, who were naturally prone to every kind of superstition. Persuaded by a certain foolish and ridiculous opinion, they believed that Osiris and Isis had been transformed—he into the Sun and she into the Moon—and had been taken up to govern heaven and earth. <margin>The Hieroglyphic of Osiris.</margin> Hence <term>Macrobius</term> <note>A late Roman writer whose work *Saturnalia* attempted to interpret all gods as aspects of the Sun.</note> says: *The Egyptians, to assert that he is the Sun, whenever they wish to express him in their hieroglyphic letters, depict the likeness of an eye on a scepter, and by this sign they show Osiris, indicating that this God is the Sun, who from his sublime royal power looks down upon all things; for antiquity calls the Sun the "Eye of Jupiter."* To this error was added another factor that held great weight in superstitious minds: a misunderstood reading of the monuments left by the philosophers, wise men, and priests who preceded them. These predecessors had written of the Sun, Moon, stars, and elements, comparing them to God and the immortal children of the gods. ### SYNTHESIS III. ON THE ORIGIN OF EGYPTIAN IDOLATRY. 173 CHAPTER II.

...they attempted to involve the truth in certain coverings of fables, similitudes, and symbols, in order to instill it into the minds of men with greater pleasure. For in order to teach that the supreme Divinity, whom we call God, does not only claim the celestial seats for himself, but also fills all things—whether those we measure with our eyes or perceive with the intellect—diffused throughout this entire universe by his presence and majesty, they assigned innumerable Gods to various things and places. Hence, they placed Jupiter in charge of the ether, Juno in charge of the air, <margin>The multitude of Gods.</margin> Neptune in charge of the sea, and Cybele in charge of the earth. These, in turn, departed into various sects: so that some Gods were believed to be celestial, others terrestrial, and others aquatic; and among the aquatic ones, the care of the sea was committed to some, of the rivers to others, and of the fountains to others, just as it was with the terrestrial ones. Again, some were presidents of the mountains, others of the forests and shepherds, <margin>All things are full of Gods.</margin> and others of the farmers, and these were thought to dwell for the most part in level places. Among the celestials, some presided over the highest of human affairs, others were counselors, others were in charge of storms and specific regions of the sky as if they were <term>Ephors</term> <note>Ephors were overseers or magistrates in ancient Sparta; here used to mean celestial governors.</note>; others were imagined to inhabit only the infernal places and to preside over the punishments of the wicked. In a word, "there is no part [in Homer] void of gods," <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἐστὶν οὐδὲν μέρος Ὁμήρῳ ἄθεον</note> to speak with Maximus Tyrius; thus, no place was found by Homer to be empty of Gods. Trismegistus <margin>Maximus Tyrius.</margin> mentions this polytheism to Asclepius in these words:

> For there are many choirs of spirits <note>original: δαιμόνων (daimonon)</note>, resembling various armies in their groupings; they are neighbors to us and are not far from the immortals. For under him is attached a choir of Daemons—or rather, choirs; for they are many and various, ordered under the points of the stars, equal in number to each of them. To the principal Gods) individual months were attributed, as will be seen in the Astrology of the Egyptians. To these twelve "Consenting Gods" <note>original: "Dijs Consentibus" — the twelve primary deities of the Roman pantheon</note> or "Gods of the Greater Nations," as Cicero and Lactantius preferred to call them, were added the Patricians, who were themselves thought to hold great offices in the administration of the World, such as Janus, Saturn, Genius, Pluto, Bacchus, the Sun, the Moon, and the Earth; these were called the "Select Gods." There were, therefore, twenty of the more distinguished Gods in number: twelve males and eight females; and among them, twelve acted as leaders. They joined all those twenty together in this manner: Jupiter and Juno; Apollo and Diana; Mercury and Minerva; Liber <note>Bacchus</note> and Ceres; Saturn and Earth—all of these because of their shared duties. Then they paired the lovers Mars and Venus; followed by the two fires, Vulcan and Vesta; and the two lights of the World, the Sun and the Moon. However, they left Janus, Neptune, Genius, and Pluto without female partners. These, then, are the Consenting and Select Gods; it will be clearly shown in what follows that all of these were borrowed from the Egyptians. There were, furthermore, certain "Uncertain" and "Unknown" Gods. Those whose divinity was still doubted were called "Uncertain," such as the Panes, the Silvani, and the Nymphs, of whom Ovid speaks at the beginning of the *Metamorphoses*, placing these words in the mouth of Jupiter:

<margin>Ovid, book 1 of the *Metamorphoses*.</margin>

Middle-rank Gods.
Heroes.
Demigods.
Gods of the Offering-Dish.

The "Unknown Gods," however, were not the same as the "Uncertain" ones; for while the divinity of the Uncertain was doubted, their names were known—unlike the Unknown. It is recorded that Epimenides of Crete was the first to erect sacred altars to these Unknown Gods in the Athenian countryside, which are also mentioned in the sacred Acts of the Apostles. I shall not speak here of the <term>Middle-rank Gods</term> <note>original: "Medioximis" — deities occupying a middle status between gods and men</note>, the Heroes, the <term>Semones</term> <note>original: "Semionibus" — minor deities whose name implies they are "half-men"</note>, the <term>Gods of the Offering-Dish</term> <note>original: "Patellarijs" — domestic gods to whom small dishes of food were offered</note>, and other divine powers encountered everywhere in the writings of Authors; for from these examples it is sufficiently clear that there was scarcely any place into which foolish antiquity did not introduce some colony of Gods. Indeed, the wiser men knew that there was but a single Divine Power and God, the Moderator of all things, and therefore they detested <term>the multiplicity of gods</term> <note>Greek: πολυθεότητά</note> as a thing incompatible with divine unity. But as the centuries passed, more ignorant men interpreted the allegorical meanings regarding God literally, and falling into detestable errors, they finally introduced <term>polytheism</term> <note>Greek: πολυθείαν</note>. To this was added a stupor of the mind, by which they were so struck that they judged it impossible for God to be perceivable by the intellect alone, and not by sight. Consequently, they were accustomed to mock the Jews for this reason, as if they worshipped an "uncertain God" (as Lucan calls Him) or as Petronius says, as if they "addressed their prayers to the highest ears of heaven." Even David seems to complain more than once in the Psalms that he was taunted with the question of where his God might be—as if He who did not fall under the sight of the eyes were nowhere at all. <header>CHAPTER III. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS</header>

<margin>Hermaphroditic Gods, or those held by the ancients to be of both sexes.</margin>
From the consideration of manifold power, that great <term>polyonymy</term> <note>original: πολυωνυμία — the practice of addressing a deity by many names to encompass all their attributes</note> of the Gods and the fabrication of Divinities later arose. And since among the Gods of the Greater Nations, the Egyptians assigned the primary place to their Osiris, we shall begin with him. But first, I must advise the reader that the ancients were frequently accustomed to attribute both sexes to the Gods, just as Valerius Soranus testifies in this couplet:

<margin>Jupiter as both father and mother of the Gods.</margin>
-> *Jupiter almighty, progenitor of Kings, of things, and of Gods,* <-
-> *And mother of the Gods, the one and the all-encompassing God.* <-

*And Virgil, as read by Macrobius:*

-> *I depart, and with the God leading, through the flame and the enemies* <-
-> *I am guided . . . . . . .* <-

<margin>Lunus and Luna. Venus as masculine and feminine nourisher.</margin>
As it happens, "God" is used for the Goddess Venus; and the ancient poet Calvus writes, *And Venus the powerful God*; and Levinus says, *Thus adoring Venus the nourishing god* <note>original: "Venerem igitur almum adorans" — using the masculine 'almum' rather than the feminine 'almam'</note>. I also observe "Lunus" and "Luna" <note>the moon as both male and female</note> among various authors. This seems to be taken from the dogma of the Stoics, who said the Divinities were of both sexes—that is, male in acting and female in being acted upon. Hence, I find them called <term>Hermaphrodites</term> by some, as is demonstrated by the countless statues which show women feigning the male sex, and vice versa; these can be seen in the gardens of various people here in Rome. But leaving these common matters aside, let us reach for higher things.

### C H A P T E R III.

-> **On Osiris, the first Divinity of Egypt; on his origin and <term>polyonymy</term>, according to the views of the Egyptians, Greeks, and Latins.** <-

<margin>From where "Osiris" is derived.</margin>
Regarding the etymology of the name Osiris, various thinkers have felt differently. Plutarch, in his book *On Osiris and Isis*, derives it now from the "holy and sacred" <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁσίου καὶ ἱεροῦ</note>, as if you were to say *Hosios* or *OSIOS* <note>original: ὅσιος — Greek for "holy"</note>, that is, "Sacrosanct"; and now from the Egyptian words **os** and **iri**, of which the former means "much" and the latter "eye," as if you were to say "many-eyed" <note>original: πολυόφθαλμον</note>, or one who signifies many eyes; he shares this derivation with Diodorus, Horapollo, Eusebius, Macrobius, and others. For my part, as much as I have been able to gather from the ancient Egyptian language, I truly conjecture that Osiris signifies nothing other than "Holy Lord," or **Pi-Osiris** <note>original: πιοσιρις</note>, as we demonstrated in the Supplement: a fire burning everywhere. 

However, those who seek a Hebrew origin may say that it sounds the same as *Esch Char* <note>original Hebrew: אש חר</note>, that is, "fire," and the Greek *seirion* <note>original: σείριον</note>, which signifies "to glow" or "scorch," as if you were to say *Essires* or *Esires*, a name composed from *Esch* and *Syrin*. I am moved to believe this by the Arab Abenephi, who, having conflated Zoroaster and Osiris into one Ham <note>the biblical son of Noah</note>, calls him Zoroaster—that is, the figure of a star or constellation, or a sign of hidden fire. Of these, the former comes from the Hebrew name *Esch Zohar* <note>original: אש זהר — "fire of splendor"</note> and the Greek *aster* <note>original: ἀστήρ — "star"</note>, and the latter from the Chaldean words *Sether* and *Oria* <note>original: סתר & אוריא</note>, which is the same as "hidden fire,"

<margin>Gregory of Tours.</margin>
Gregory of Tours agrees with this, proving from Clement of Alexandria that Zoroaster signifies nothing other than a "living star," and he is called <term>aserdoutos</term> <note>original: ἀσερδοῦτος</note> by Diogenes Laertius, which is to say, "sacrificer of the stars." Since the Egyptians believe Osiris to be the Sun, and the Sun, like a living star, gives life to all things by its fire, they did not wrongly designate Ham (or Mizraim <note>Mizraim is the biblical name for Egypt, personified as a son of Ham</note>) under the names of Zoroaster and Osiris as the "image of the star" and the "shining fire." But since these names are treated more extensively in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>One of Kircher's most famous works, an attempt to decipher the hieroglyphs on the Agonal Obelisk in Rome</note>, we refer the reader there. 
<margin>Another derivation of Osiris.</margin>
Others also—lest I omit this—will have Osiris so named from the <term>nebris</term> <note>A fawn-skin worn by followers of Dionysus/Bacchus</note> or dappled skin with which he was depicted as being clothed, silently signifying the variety of the stars. Whether, therefore, you call Osiris the figure or form of the stars, or the fire shining everywhere, or the <term>many-eyed</term> <note>original: πολυόφθαλμον (polyophthalmon)</note>, you always indicate the same thing: namely, the Sun. For the Sun, by communicating light to the other stars, can truly be called their "form," insofar as he animates them with light and spirit; most ancient philosophers also believed the Sun to be the fire shining everywhere. Moreover, he is not incongruously called "many-eyed," because by his rays, as if by certain eyes, he sees and surveys whatever is contained in this universe, according to that line of Homer:

> The Sun, who sees all things and hears all things.

<margin>Diodorus, Book 1, Ch. 1</margin>
Furthermore, they assert the same of her—that is, the Moon, his wife; concerning whom Diodorus says: *Thinking these to be Gods, they say they traverse the entire world, nourishing and increasing all things through the three seasons of the year, completing them by continuous motion: spring, summer, and winter; these, though contrary to one another, complete the year in firm harmony. The nature of these Gods contributes most to the generation of all living things. Since one exists as fiery and vital, the other as moist and cold, the air is common to both; from them, therefore, all bodies are generated and nourished, and the nature of things is perfected by the Sun and the Moon.* His virtues and perfections are found expressed by so many names 
<margin>Osiris the "many-eyed"</margin>
that Plutarch not undeservedly called them <term>myriad-named</term> <note>original: μυριώνυμους (myrionymous)</note>. For the same reason, Homer called him the father of all Gods and her the mother; and from this arises an almost inextricable confusion of Divinities, by which some confuse Osiris with Bacchus (or Dionysus), Mercury, Pan, Neptune, Jupiter, Janus, Saturn, and Caelus; 
<margin>Hesychius. Giraldus, Synthesis 1, On the Gods.</margin>
others make him one with Hercules, Apollo, Pluto, and Horus; still others wish him to be the same as the Nile, Apis, Serapis, Ammon, and Oceanus, as Hesychius does. Finally, Giraldus—on the Gods.

# CHAPTER III. 178 THE ISIAIC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

...from others he calls him by his proper name Hysiris, and Arsaphas; behold the Genealogy of all the Gods represented as if in a single head; furthermore, authors differ on where this many-formed heap of names drew its origin. Our Abenephius <note>Athanasius Kircher's name for the author Ibn Wahshiyya, whom he believed to be a primary source for ancient Egyptian and "Nabataean" wisdom.</note> thinks this <term>polyonymy</term> <note>original: polyonomasiam — the practice of applying many names to a single person or concept</note> is derived from the mixing of the Egyptians with the Hebrews, or from the manifold influence of the Sun. For when the Egyptians, mixed with the Hebrews after the dispersion of the nations, had heard here and there many things about the deeds of the first parents—such as Adam, Eve, and the Serpent in the garden of pleasure <note>The Garden of Eden</note>; the discord of Abel and Cain; the Giants; the universal flood; Noah and his vessel; the construction of the Tower of Babel; Enoch wonderfully translated; the tyranny of Nimrod; the holiness of Abraham, and other similar virtues of the first fathers—and since, furthermore, all those who were distinguished by virtue, knowledge, the glory of their deeds, or the invention of things necessary to the human race, were called <term>Osirides</term> in the Egyptian language (as if they were "providers of all good things"), 
<margin>There are many Osirises.</margin>
he judges that it happened that among the Theban Egyptians, Adam and Enoch (about whom they had heard so much from Noah and his sons) were held to be the first Osirises. When another followed them, radiant with the glory of his deeds, Noah—acting as a second propagator of the World—was honored with the same name by later Egyptians and emerged as the second Osiris. Next followed Ham, Mizraim, and other Kings who expressed the illustrious deeds of their predecessors in their own lives; each, distinguished by this name, was called an Osiris. Since the deeds of these men were narrated in different ways by different people—some exaggerating them more than was right, others mixing in fabulous stories, as almost always happens on such occasions—the entire history, receding from the truth, departed entirely into fables and the inventions of poets. Hence Osiris and Isis are aptly represented in Adam and Eve, and likewise in Noah and his wife Niobe <note>Kircher identifies the biblical wife of Noah with the mythological figure Niobe, viewing her as a "mother of nations."</note>, both of whom were propagators of the human race and inventors of things. From this also, the discord of Abel and Cain, and likewise of Ham and Nimrod, are everywhere confused with the opposition of Osiris and Typhon (the latter of whom, relying on the help of the Titans or Giants and driven by the sting of envy, killed his brother). Finally, in Seth, the just and wise son of Adam, and in Japheth or Prometheus, the Sun, and Jove, Horus the son of Osiris is not ungracefully displayed; but these things will appear better in this attached table.

<margin>From where the origin of the Gods arose.</margin>
Furthermore, when the Egyptians perceived these and similar accounts regarding the first parents, and regarded them with awe as if their deeds far exceeded the boundaries of human actions, nothing was easier for a superstitious people than to honor them with a kind of exotic <term>apotheosis</term> <note>The elevation of a human being to the status of a god.</note>. This was especially so because that remarkable wisdom of the first fathers, their knowledge of natural things in which they excelled, and their long lifespans carried great weight in their minds. The miraculous translation <note>The biblical event where Enoch was taken by God without dying.</note> of Enoch from this world, and similar events, could also provide them with the occasion for creating myths. All these things were confirmed by frequent incantations and magical miracles, which the wicked progeny of Ham, striving for divinity for themselves, performed everywhere. By these means, the minds of the Egyptians were so struck that they worshipped them as celestial gods and holily venerated them as the governors of all things. 

And from here came those first foundations of the "Architecture of the Gods"; from here the origin of Jupiter, Hercules, Aesculapius, Bacchus, Neptune, Janus, and the other gods, about whom more will be said at length in the sequence of this Synthesis. From these passages, it is clear that "Sky" [Caelus] was called the father of Saturn, and "Earth" [Vesta] the mother; from which it is likely that the Egyptian fables of Osiris and Isis flowed, as Minucius Felix <note>Marcus Minucius Felix was a 2nd-century Christian apologist who argued that pagan gods were merely divinized humans.</note> well notes. For those who excel in this world by virtue or the glory of their deeds, or those who suddenly emerge into prominence from unknown parents, we are accustomed to say they "fell from the sky." Lactantius Firmianus <note>A 4th-century advisor to Constantine the Great, often called the "Christian Cicero."</note> proves this by the authority of the very ancient Trismegistus, who, when saying that very few existed who possessed perfect doctrine, named among them Sky [Caelus], Saturn, and Mercury.

<margin>Ennius in *Euhemerus*.</margin>
Ennius confirms the same in his *Euhemerus* <note>Ennius (c. 239–169 BC) translated the work of Euhemerus, a Greek mythographer who argued that the gods were originally great kings. For since they were the most powerful kings, they celebrated the memory of their parents with the names of "Sky" and "Earth," even though they were previously called by other names. For since before Sky and Saturn there were no kings due to the scarcity of men, they began to boast of the King himself and all his posterity with the highest praises and new honors, believing them to be Gods for the reasons indicated above. Xenophon seems to demonstrate this most clearly when he says:
> *Those were called Saturns who, as the most ancient of noble kings, founded cities and peoples; and therefore there was not one, but many Saturns, whose fathers were called Skies, while their sons were Jupiters, etc.*

<margin>Jupiter born of Saturn and Rhea.</margin>
These names, therefore, were titles of dignity and a certain Divinity among the unrefined ancients, invented for the sake of the name's celebrity. Next, Xenophon notes that these names are relative, such as "Begetter" and "Begotten." Thus, "Saturn" is he who was born from "Sky" and "Vesta" (or Earth); and who, from "Rhea" (or Ops), who was both his sister and wife, begat "Jupiter" and "Juno." "Jupiter," moreover, is he who, born from Saturn and Rhea, begat "Hercules." Therefore, these names are more analogous than equivocal <note>Kircher is arguing that these names are not used randomly or confusedly, but follow a logical pattern based on their relationship to the original figures.</note>, because they are said of many later people through their relationship to the first "Sky" (the later Skies) and to the first "Vesta" (the later Vestas), and so on for the rest.

*It happened, therefore, that while Sapho <note>A figure from legendary history; in this context, a founder-hero of the Italian people.</note> was once searching for a lost calf, he heard a voice on the side of a mountain that sounded like a cow or a calf. When he had moved the rock, a beast of horrendous appearance immediately appeared in the cave. This beast, which at that very moment was busy devouring an ox, resembled a wild goat in its upper half and a human in its lower half. Sapho engaged it in battle and killed it. When the people of Chittim (that is, the Italians) learned of Sapho's deed, they said: "What shall we do for the man who, by killing a beast so hostile to us, has saved us all from destruction?" They finally agreed unanimously that a day in the year should be consecrated to his name and celebrated in memory of the event, offering him libations and sacrifices. They elected him King after he had freed all of Italy from the attacks of enemies, and they called him Janus. For when the army of the Gundels <note>original: "Gundelorum"; likely referring to early Germanic tribes or the Vandals, appearing here in a legendary context.</note> again broke into Italy and tried to subject the entire region to plunder and spoils, Janus opposed them and turned them all to flight, thus freeing the entire land from enemy insults. # TREATISE ON THE ORIGIN OF EGYPTIAN IDOLATRY 185 CHAPTER III.

<margin>Osiris's army was composed of various attendants.</margin>
[Osiris] assembled an army from the people, and having entrusted the care of all things to his wife Isis, he joined Mercury to her as an assistant and Counselor in governing the kingdom, for he was a man of the greatest wisdom. He also placed Hercules, a man of incomparable strength and courage, in charge of military affairs. Once he had prudently arranged these matters, Osiris set out on an expedition with his brother Apollo (the discoverer of the Laurel) and his two sons Anubis and Macedo—the former of whom bore a dog on his insignia, while the latter bore a wolf. In addition to Pan (who later obtained divine honors in Egypt), he also took with him Maron and Triptolemus; the former was skilled in the cultivation of vines, while the latter 
<margin>The deeds of Osiris.</margin>
understood the method of committing seeds to the earth. Because Osiris took great delight in music, he also took with him nine female singers—whom the Greeks later called the Muses—along with their instructor, Apollo. He also kept Satyrs in his camp who were suited for playing the lute, singing, and providing relaxation for the mind. For Osiris was not warlike or devoted to battles and dangers, but rather to leisure and the well-being of humanity; because of this benefit, all nations regarded him as a God. He showed the Ethiopians the art of agriculture, building distinguished cities there. Through the help of Hercules, he also confined the Nile within its banks when it was flooding far and wide with the great loss of men and cattle. From this arose the fable of the Eagle (for the river was so called because of its speed) devouring the liver of Prometheus; for Prometheus 
<margin>What does the liver of Prometheus eaten by the eagle signify?</margin>
was the King of that territory, which was being so terribly devastated by the overflowing Nile. After completing these tasks, he migrated into Arabia and from there reached as far as the Indians; there, having performed magnificent deeds, he was held in such high esteem that the natives everywhere offered him divine honors. Departing from there through the rest of the provinces of Asia, he penetrated even to the farthest reaches of Europe, teaching all those things which he had invented. Finally, returning to Egypt, he was enrolled among the company of the Gods on account of the greatness of his deeds. And so it happened that in succeeding times, as his fame grew, the imposition of names also grew; for from the cities he founded, he was called
<margin>Osiris is named in various ways according to his effects.</margin>
Saturn; from his supreme dominion over things, Jupiter; from the invention of wine and oil, Bacchus or Dionysus; Hercules from his supreme strength; Neptune from his traveling around the world; Mercury from his inventions; Apollo from his frequent practice of Music; and finally Janus from his cultivation of a more polished life. This provided the occasion for "polyonymia" <note>original: "πολυωνυμίας" — the practice of having many names.</note>; and the testimonies of the ancient Poets show that this is the case, for they conflate Osiris with all the aforementioned names. > *Osiris was the first to fashion plows with a skillful hand,*
> *and stirred the tender soil with iron.*
> *He first committed seeds to the untried earth,*
> *and gathered fruit from unknown trees.*
> *He taught how to join the tender vine to stakes,*
> *and how to prune the green foliage with a hard sickle;*
> *to him first the ripe grape, pressed by unskilled feet,*
> *gave forth its delightful flavors:*
> *That juice taught voices to modulate in song,*
> *and moved untrained limbs to certain rhythms:*
> *Bacchus gave hearts, exhausted by the farmer’s heavy toil,*
> *the means to dissolve their sadness;*
> *Bacchus brings rest to afflicted mortals,*
> *though their legs ring with the heavy shackle,*
> *To you, Osiris, belong no grim cares, no grief,*
> *But dance and song, and light-hearted love.*
> *But various flowers, and a brow wreathed with ivy clusters,*
> *and a yellow robe <note>original: "lutea palla," a saffron-colored garment typical of Dionysian rites</note> flowing down to tender feet. etc.*

<margin>Chenosyris, the plant of Osiris.</margin>
Therefore, Dionysus and Osiris are the same; for this reason, ivy is called *Chenosyris*, which means "the plant of Osiris." Furthermore, Antipater very elegantly associates Hercules and Bacchus in a certain epigram, using this three-couplet poem <note>original: "tristycho," though the poem is six lines</note>.

<margin>Praises of Hercules and Bacchus.</margin>
> Both are from Thebes, and both are warriors
> born of Zeus; but one holds a thyrsus <note>A staff topped with a pine cone, carried by Bacchus</note>, the other a club.

> the fawn-skin for one, the lion-skin for the other.
> Indeed, a harsh Goddess <note>Hera (Juno), who famously persecuted both heroes</note> pursued them both; 
> but they both ascended from the earth to the immortals through fire.

->That is:<-
> *Both are Thebans, sons of Jove, both leaders,*
> *This one rejoices in a club, the other, bearing the Thyrsus, triumphs.*
> *Both are celebrated with various weapons in their triumphs:*
> *This one has the deer's hide, that one has the Lion's.*
> *Bronze cymbals ring for both; Juno is a stern Power to both;*
> *Fire bore both from the earth to the gods above.*

<margin>Osiris as a symbol of the Sun.</margin>
We have said above, and shall say below, that Mercury and other Gods constitute a single Osiris; it is clear, therefore, that this multiformity <note>original: "πολυμορφίαν" (polymorphian)</note> represented in the person of Osiris signifies nothing else but the multiple and varied power of the one Sun.

# CHAPTER IV.
## *Concerning Isis, the wife of Osiris, according to the mind of the Greeks and Latins.*

The opinions of authors regarding Isis are so numerous and so diverse that it can hardly be discerned which one should be believed. The Greeks assert that she was the daughter of Inachus <note>Inachus was the legendary first king of Argos</note>; hence the story of Isis being transformed into a cow by Juno, on account of the debauchery committed upon her by Jupiter. The *Alexandrian Chronicle* <note>original: "Chronicon Alexandrinum," a 7th-century Byzantine universal chronicle also known as the Paschal Chronicle</note> tells the story in Greek words, which we report here translated into Latin:

<margin>Alexandrian Chronicle</margin>
> *Picus, or Jupiter, the King of the West <note>Picus was an ancient Italian king, but here he is identified with the Greek god Zeus/Jupiter</note>, when he had heard of Inachus, seized his most beautiful virgin daughter called Io through emissaries, and having Ravished her, he made her pregnant; she bore a daughter from him named Libya. But Io, taking the insult brought upon her indignantly, and further disdaining to associate with Picus Jupiter, fled secretly from everyone, abandoning her daughter, and sailed as a fugitive to Egypt because of the shame. Having entered the kingdom of Egypt, she fixed her seat there. But when, some time later, she heard that Hermes, or Mercury, the son of Jupiter Picus, presided over Egypt with royal power, she fled in fear of Mercury to Mount Sipylus; there Seleucus Nicanor the Macedonian later founded a city, which he called Great Antioch after his son. Having later set out for Syria, Io died there, as that most wise man Theophilus recorded. Others, on the contrary, handed down that she died in Egypt. Inachus, however, the father of Io, sent his brothers and relatives, as well as Triptolemus with other Argives <note>original: "Archiuis," referring to the people of Argos</note> to search for her; though they tracked her everywhere, they nonetheless did not find her. After the Argives learned she had died in Syria, they frequented that place and stayed for some time, knocking on individual houses and saying: "May the soul of Io be safe." And having received an oracle through a certain vision, they seemed to see a heifer speaking with a human voice to them in this way: "Here I am, Io." Woken from sleep, they remained there in wonder at the power of the dream, and discussing the matter among themselves, they concluded entirely that she was located on Mount Sipylus. Having placed a shrine there, they fixed their seats and founded a city which they called Iopolis, whose citizens today among the Syrians are called Ionites. Therefore, from that time, when the Argives arrived seeking Io, the people of Antioch in Syria—to bear witness to the memory of the event—strike the houses of the Greeks at a certain time every year. And thus far the Chronicle.*

Although this Io, daughter of Inachus, is frequently confused with Isis, we nevertheless assert that she is not that true Egyptian Isis, the wife of Osiris, but rather the "Assyrian Isis" or the "Isis of the Argives." We revealed the cause of this in the first *Syntagma* <note>a "syntagma" is a systematic treatise or section of a larger work</note> when we treated the Kings of Egypt. Therefore, as to who that Isis was—celebrated in the monuments of so many writers—or where she originated, there are great disputes among authors: some affirm she originated from Ethiopia. Xenophon, in his *Equivocals*, asserts that Osiris and Isis were the children of Saturn, as was also shown in the preceding pages. Others deny that Osiris was the brother of Isis, which Xenophon, Diodorus, Eusebius, and others affirm: Dio-

All these things depend on the ambiguity of the names of those who were distinguished in this way, from which alone that nearly inextricable confusion of names we find among writers took its origin, as we have said and will prove more extensively elsewhere.

Whatever the case may be, Isis is said to have been held in such great veneration among the Egyptians that it was like a capital crime to say she had been a human being. Accordingly, in all the temples where statues of Osiris and Isis were placed, a statue of Horus or <term>Harpocrates</term> <note>The Greek interpretation of the Egyptian "Horus-the-Child," often depicted with a finger to his lips</note>, their son, was also placed. Whence Saint Augustine, reporting the authority of Varro on this matter, adds: *Because in all the temples where Osiris and Isis were worshipped, there was a statue that, with a finger pressed to its lips, seemed to warn men to keep silent about the fact that they had been humans.* Plutarch says she is the same as the Moon, along with Macrobius, Eusebius, Lucian, and countless others, with whom <term>Abenephius</term> <note>An Arabic author Kircher frequently cites, likely Ibn Wahshiyya</note> agrees, indicating she was considered the Moon in these words:

<margin>

Since these things are so, Isis is not poorly called by Plutarch <term>pandektes</term> <note>Greek: "all-receiving" or "all-containing"</note>, that is, containing all things; and <term>keratophoros</term> <note>Greek: "horn-bearing"</note>, that is, horned, fashioned in the likeness of the crescent Moon; also <term>melanostolos</term> <note>Greek: "black-robed"</note>, that is, in black garments, to signify her hiding and overshadowing—clothed in which, and seized by love, she seems to continually follow that Osiris, or the Sun. Hence she was also invoked in matters of love, and love charms were said to be provided by her, as Eudoxus reports. This is confirmed by Abenephius, who says the Egyptians especially carried a figure of the Moon or Isis, impressed upon suitable material at a congruent time, to win the love of others; he teaches the method of this superstitious work in the following words:

They write upon parchment when the Sun is at its highest point <note>original: "absidem tenente," referring to the apogee or orbital peak</note> and the Moon is rising in the sign of Cancer, the name of the person whose love they desire. They then imprint upon it, during the appropriate hour of the Moon and when Jupiter is positioned at its peak, the figure of the Moon. Behold the dreams of the Egyptian Astrologers.

<margin>Isis as the motion of the Nile. What is the motion of the Sistrum?</margin>
But let us return to Isis. Servius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note> considers her to be the <term>Spirit of the Nile</term>, who signified the rising of the Nile through the motion of the <term>Sistrum</term> <note>A sacred percussion instrument or rattle used in Egyptian worship</note>, which she was depicted carrying in her right hand. By the bucket <note>original: "situla"</note> which she held in her left hand, she showed the flowing of the irrigation channels. The aforementioned author says that in the language of the Egyptians, her name signifies nothing other than "the earth." <margin>Horapollo book 1, chapter 3.</margin> Horapollo writes about her thus: *When the Egyptians wish to signify the year, they paint Isis with this same sign; they wish her to be understood as a Goddess, for among them, Isis is a Star, called <term>Sothis</term> in the Egyptian language, and <term>Astrokyon</term> in Greek.* <note>original: "Σώθις" (Sothis/Sirius) and "ἄστροκύων" (Star-dog)</note>

<margin>Macrobius: The many-breasted Isis.</margin>
Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial and writer</note>, however, says that Isis is celebrated in every religion as either the earth or the nature of things lying beneath the Sun. From this, he says, it follows that the entire body of the Goddess is thick with a continuous row of breasts, because the universe is nourished by the food of either the earth or the nature of things. There were those who identified the Syrian Goddess as the same as Isis, but these are easily refuted by the writings of Lucian <note>A satirist who wrote "On the Syrian Goddess"</note>. Apuleius, agreeing with Macrobius in his most elegant description of the Triumph of Isis, makes her the "Nature of Things."

<margin>Isis as the nature of things. Apuleius, book 11 of the *Metamorphoses*.</margin>
> I had not yet fully finished [my prayer], he says, and behold, in the middle of the sea, raising a face venerable even to the Gods, a divine countenance emerged; from here I shall gradually endeavor to report her marvelous appearance to you, if the poverty of human speech will grant me the power of description, or if the Divinity herself will supply a bountiful abundance of eloquent speech. First, her hair was most plentiful and long, gently curled and flowing softly, scattered everywhere over her divine neck. A multiform crown of various flowers adorned her high head; in the middle, above her flat forehead, a roundness like a mirror—or rather the white light of the Moon—glowed, held in place on the left and right by the coils of rising vipers, with ears of corn also extending from above. Her robe was of many colors, woven of fine linen, now shining with white brilliance, now yellow with saffron blossoms, now flaming with rosy redness; and that which most dazzled my sight was a jet-black cloak gleaming with dark luster, which, wrapped around her and returning under her right side to her left shoulder, hung down in many folds like a shield-boss, fluttering decoratively with knotted fringes at the furthest edges. Along the woven border and across its surface, scattered stars were sparkling; and in their midst, a half-moon breathed out flaming fires. Wherever the hem of that remarkable cloak flowed, a garland of all types of flowers and fruits was attached in an unbroken chain. Her attributes were quite diverse: for in her right hand she carried a <margin>Sistrum.</margin> bronze rattle; through its narrow plate, curved like a belt, a few small rods were passed through the middle, which, when shaken by her arm, gave off a sharp sound with triple strokes. In her <margin>Bucket.</margin> left hand hung a golden vessel, on the handle of which, where it is most visible, an asp rose up, lifting its head high with its neck widely swollen. Her ambrosial feet were covered by sandals woven from the leaves of the victorious palm. Such a great being, breathing the scents of fertile Arabia, deigned to address me with her divine voice: "Behold, I am here with you, the mother of the nature of things, mistress of all elements, the initial progeny of the ages, the highest of Divinities, Queen of the Dead <note>original: "Manium"</note>, the primary face of the gods and goddesses of heaven; I who govern the luminous heights of heaven, the sea..."

### CHAPTER IV. 188 THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE

<margin>Various names of Isis.</margin>
*...[I govern] the healthful rivers; the lamented silences of the underworld I dispense by my nods; whose unique Divinity the whole world worships in multiform shape, with varied ritual, and under many names. From there the first-born Phrygians call me the Pessinuntian Mother of the Gods <note>original: "Pessinunciam," referring to Cybele, whose cult center was Pessinus</note>; here the earth-born <note>original Greek: Αὐτόχθονες</note> Athenians call me Cecropian Minerva; there the wave-tossed Cyprians call me Paphian Venus; the arrow-bearing Cretans, Dictynnian Diana; the trilingual Sicilians, Stygian Proserpina; the Eleusinians, the ancient Goddess Ceres; others call me Juno, others Bellona, others Hecate, others Rhamnusia <note>An epithet for Nemesis</note>; and the Egyptians, powerful in ancient learning, honoring me with my own proper ceremonies, call me by my true name, Queen Isis.* Thus far Apuleius, who in this passage describes the whole mysterious appearance of Isis so clearly that he seems to have understood all the mysteries contained within her just by looking at her figure. You will behold her figure on the following page.

Isis is distinguished by so many and such diverse names for no other reason than to signify the diversity and variety of effects she performs in the world. Hence, as appears from the image placed here, the ancients called her sometimes Minerva, Proserpina, the Moon, or <term>Thetis</term> <note>A sea goddess, daughter of Nereus</note> (as Ovid and Claudian call her); sometimes the Mother of the Gods, Venus, Diana, Ceres, Cybele, Juno, Rhea, Bellona, Hecate, Rhamnusia, Berinuncia, a <term>multiform spirit</term> <note>original Greek: Πολύμορφον δαίμονα</note>, and by other names, as can be seen from the cited works of Apuleius, Martianus, Eusebius, Plutarch, Diodorus, and Giraldi. Therefore, not without reason is this inscription of Isis read on a certain ancient marble at Capua:

<margin>Inscription of Isis.</margin>
->TO YOU, THE ONE, WHO ARE<-
->ALL THINGS, THE GODDESS ISIS.<-

Father Giovanni Battista Facchini, a priest of our Society <note>The Society of Jesus (Jesuits)</note>, no less distinguished in genius than in learning and a partner in my studies, brought me a transcription of this inscription with the same diligence with which he has always assisted my *Oedipus* <note>Referring to the title of this book, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>, while he was passing through that place. These words certainly harmonize beautifully with that inscription which Diodorus [Siculus] records in Book 1, Chapter 2 near the end; since I have recorded it elsewhere, I have judged it unnecessary to repeat it in this place.

### CHAPTER IV. 190 THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS
#### Interpretation of the Multi-breasted Statue of Isis, or the Grecian Cybele.

Furthermore, the later Egyptians—or more accurately, the Greco-Egyptians—so as not to omit any hidden mystery, adorned the image of the Great Mother of the Gods with another set of hieroglyphic symbols. This type of statue can be seen in various places here in Rome, both in the various museums of Princes and in gardens; an example follows below.

[A woodcut illustration of a "multimammea" (many-breasted) statue representing Isis or Cybele. The female figure stands on a rectangular pedestal. She wears a tall, three-tiered turreted headdress. Her hair and a thin veil fall symmetrically down her shoulders. Her chest features two small standing figures enclosed within a decorative circular frame (corymbus); above this frame are the symbols for the zodiac signs Cancer and Capricorn. Below the frame, her entire torso is covered with numerous breasts. Her arms are extended outward, and her upper arms are decorated with carvings of crouching lions. Her lower body is encased in a tapered, vessel-like sheath divided into horizontal registers: the top band features Egyptian figures and deer heads flanked by bees; the middle band shows dragons and bull heads; and the bottom band displays lion and calf heads with more bees. Her feet emerge from the bottom of the garment. A small letter "M" is visible on the front of the pedestal base.]

<column-break/>

<margin>Description of the statue.</margin>
The figure is a woman with a turreted crown <note>original: "turrito vertice." This "turreted" style represents city walls and fortifications.</note>, like a peaked diadem of a triple crown, notable for her hair and veil spread out in waves. Her breast features two small statues enclosed in a circular frame <note>original: "corymbo." In classical art, this often refers to a cluster of fruit or flowers, but here it describes the decorative medallion on her chest.</note>, both of whom hold a palm branch in one hand and a laurel crown in the other; above their heads, the figures of Cancer and Capricorn stand out. Furthermore, the image has hands extended as if they are pouring out blessings; the arms are weighted with four crouching lions. The belly and breast swell with a manifold protuberance of udders and breasts. The thighs and shins are enclosed in a conical vessel-like garment <note>The "sheath" or *ependytes* typical of Anatolian and Ephesian statues.</note> featuring a triple series of animals. The first series contains two Egyptian idols on each side; then three deer heads flanked by two flowers and bees. The second series of the tapered leg-coverings shows two dragons, between which three bull heads are placed. The third series is made up of two lion heads, between which three calf heads are likewise placed, with two bees joined on each side. Finally, the whole image reveals the nakedness of the feet emerging from the linen garments.

We have presented the symbols; now it remains for us to explain their hidden meaning in a few words.

<margin>What the turreted crown signifies.</margin>

For all things <term>synonymous</term> <note>original: "συνώνυμα" (synonyma), meaning words with the same meaning.</note> with the Great Mother of the Gods, Cybele, can be applied to Isis—the hair denoting light, and the veil denoting their hidden method of operation. For what else do the two images, distinguished by palms and laurel and the signs of Cancer and Capricorn, denote? By their victorious power and the heat of solar warmth, the growth of all vegetable nature is signified, aptly denoted by the <term>corymbus</term> <note>A cluster or garland of fruit and flowers.</note> arranged in a circle. Strength is added to this by the four Mophtaean Lions <note>Kircher refers to "Mophta," an Egyptian genius or deity he associated with the lion and the creative power of the Nile.</note>, by which the operative power of the Great Mother is, as it were, strengthened and supported; hence she is imagined by the ancients to be carried in a four-horse chariot by four lions. And from this comes the abundance of all things and the richness of nourishment, which are indeed aptly explained through the mass of protruding breasts; for as we showed above, the Great Mother Isis fosters, nourishes, and animates all things. With a certain profuse liberality, which is noted by the extension of her hands, she communicates the necessary aids for living to the lower members of the World, as we showed above from Macrobius.

<margin>The three deer heads.</margin>

Through the two prominent Egyptian statues, a "genial" <note>In the sense of *Genius*, a protective spirit of generation and nature.</note> guardianship is indicated over every storehouse of vegetable nature. In this way, she is called Diana (to whom the stag was therefore dedicated by the ancients, as the three deer heads clearly teach, and for which reason she is called "three-headed" and "threefold") and she exerts her dominion over forests, meadows, and gardens through her influence. For, as Homer testifies, Diana, wandering through the mountain ridges, rejoices in arrows and delights in goats and swift stags, which is why she is called <term>of the deer</term> <note>original: "ἐλαφιαῖα" (elaphiaia), an epithet of Artemis/Diana derived from 'elaphos' (deer).</note> by the people of Elis. <margin>3. Bull heads.</margin>
...three bull heads; for indeed, I find that Diana, the Great Mother of the Gods, was called *Taurione* <note>original: "Taurionem"</note>, as they believe she brings aid to bulls. She is called *Tauropolis* <note>original: "Ταυρόπολις" — meaning 'City of Bulls' or 'tamer of bulls'</note> as in the works of Apollodorus, and *Taurokeros* <note>original: "Ταυρόκερως" — meaning 'bull-horned'</note> among the Taurians because of the shape of her horns. She is also called *Tauropolos* <note>original: "Ταυρόπολος" — meaning 'roaming with bulls'</note>, either "because she goes through all things like a bull" <note>original: "ὅτι ὡς ταῦρος περιέϊσι πάντα"</note>, or because she drove a bull, sent by Neptune against Hippolytus, through the whole earth by attaching a gadfly to it. According to the Egyptian mind, we say more truly that this Isis, or Egyptian Diana, was so named because, having transformed into a cow, she taught the human race various benefits under that form, such as agriculture and beekeeping—which the added bees more than sufficiently demonstrate; concerning these, see more in Book 3 of the *Pamphilian Obelisk* in the <term>hierogrammatism</term> <note>A term Kircher uses for "sacred symbolic writing" or "visual code."</note> regarding the Bull. A Dragon is painted on both sides of these three bull heads, a symbol of vigilance over the things committed to its trust; while Isis nourishes the grasses and plants with her vital embrace, she seems to perform the duty of a Dragon.

<margin>What do the Dragons mean?</margin>
I am not unaware that certain others have taken the Dragon, the guardian of gardens, to represent the roots of trees; because they are twisted like Dragons and driven into the earth, just as the serpent kind mostly hides in the bowels of the earth. Thus, this form of the Dragon performs a service for the plants; for if the roots are either cut or dried up, the plants must also perish. Some interpret this from their sight, which Dragons have most acutely according to Pliny; it is dedicated to Isis for the same reason, because she "looks toward all things, sees all, and is everything concerning all things" <note>original: "πρὸς τὰ πάντα ἀθρεῖν, καὶ βλέπειν, καὶ περὶ πάντα πᾶν"</note>, which some tradition says occurred, and they interpret "prudence" from this. For Isis, according to Plutarch, is nothing other than the prudent progress of nature, as one who perceives all things,

<margin>Meaning of the Bull.</margin>
and understands before all others. Finally, three other bull heads follow; these clearly declare the greatest benefits in matters of grain, namely, the plowing done by bulls according to the three-part span of the year. The word comes from "I nourish" <note>original: "βοῶ" (boô). Kircher is using a creative etymology connecting the Greek word for "ox" (*bous*) to a word for feeding.</note>; for the bull prevailed because it continually feeds us by its labor in working the earth. The Greeks call this *bebaios* <note>original: "βέβαιος" — meaning 'firm' or 'stable'</note>, meaning "happy agriculture," for whom "well-being" <note>original: "εὐεξία" (euexia)</note> is agriculture, and it is also an epithet of the bull. This custom passed from the Egyptians and Greeks to the Romans, who used to carve bull heads—with the skin removed and the flesh cleaned—onto their monuments to represent labor and endurance, taking the likeness from the labors of bulls. Because fortitude is necessary for the endurance of labors, a lion's head crowds each side of the three bull heads.

<margin>Recapitulation of what has been said.</margin>
But to embrace the whole <term>hierogrammatism</term> in a few words: the Egyptian <term>Hieromanthae</term> <note>Sacred seers or priests initiated into the mysteries.</note> indicated the Supreme Deity through the image of Isis or the Egyptian Diana, the Great Mother of the Gods. This is the archetypal Isis as she flows into the fourfold World: through her turreted head, the Archetypal World; through the Geniuses impressed upon her breast, the Genial World; through the multitude of breasts, the Sidereal (Starry) World, whose stars are like udders that bestow a fertile influence upon all lower things; through the conical three-zoned garment on her thighs, the Elemental World, distinguished by three zones (as it were) of the inanimate, the vegetative, and the sensitive. To all of these, she confers life, nourishment, and the necessary faculties and aids for self-preservation. Since Isis is the same as the "prudent progress of nature," as Plutarch pleases, by which she walks through all places of the World, this is aptly signified by the nakedness of her exposed feet. <margin>Isis’s benevolence toward humans;</margin>
Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note> asserts that the Egyptians believe Isis was the discoverer of many medicines for warding off diseases and that she greatly favors the medical art. Having attained immortality, she rejoices in the health of human beings and is continually and chiefly occupied in restoring their well-being. This is so much the case that even during sleep, she suggests divine and suitable means and aids for curing diseases, demonstrating both the presence of the Divinity and her beneficence toward humanity. Those who obey her warnings are said to be cured of even incurable diseases, contrary to all expectation. He adds that all those who have suffered in their sight, or in any other part of the body, are restored to their former health by imploring the Power of this Goddess. They also say that she discovered a remedy for attaining immortality; for her son Horus, having been killed by the <term>Titans</term> <note>Kircher uses "Titans" to refer to the enemies of the Egyptian gods, likely meaning Set and his conspirators.</note> and found in the waters, was not only restored to the light of life by her, but was also made immortal. Horus is said to have been the last of the Gods to hold the governance of the Kingdom after his father Osiris was translated among the Gods.

<margin>Horus is conflated with Apollo.</margin>
Some people, not without reason, conflate this Horus with Apollo. For Horus-Apollo, having been taught the art of healing and divination by his mother Isis, brought much benefit to humanity through both oracles and cures. Thus Isis, most celebrated for the glory of her deeds, achieved such fame over the course of time that she was held in greater honor, worship, and veneration by the Egyptians than Osiris himself. Consequently, the Egyptians committed the greatest benefits received from both of them to eternity by inscribing them upon columns; it has pleased me to place these inscriptions, taken from Diodorus, here. The following is the monument of Isis.

<margin>Diodorus, Book 1.</margin>

### CHAPTER V. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS 194

...with the fear of punishment removed, which is why she is called by the ancients "Legifera" <note>original: *Legifera*, the Law-bringer</note> or the Inventress of Laws, a title confirmed by the words of the inscription mentioned earlier. By others, she is also called *tithēnē* <note>Greek: τιθήνη</note>, that is, "Nurse," and *pandocheus* <note>Greek: πανδοχεὺς</note>, that is, "She-who-receives-all," as Plutarch recites from Plato; this is because she was believed to be the receiver of all generation. From this, it seems to have followed that Isis—both because of the discovery of grain and the invention of laws—has been commonly confused with Proserpina <note>Queen of the Underworld</note> and Ceres <note>Goddess of agriculture</note>, according to these lines of the Poet:

> *First Ceres moved the earth with the hooked plow;*
> *First she gave grain and gentle nourishment to the lands,*
> *First she gave laws; all things are the gift of Ceres.*

But to comprehend many things in a few words, one must know that just as the entire genealogy of the Gods is represented in Osiris, so it is with the Goddesses in Isis. We consider Osiris as the active principle, and Isis as the passive principle. Thus, Isis is Minerva in her wisdom and law-giving; she is Venus for the fecundity she bestows; she is Juno for the air over which she rules; she is Proserpina for her dominion in the subterranean regions; she is Ceres for her oversight of the crops; she is Diana for her protection of the forests and the power she holds over all wild beasts; she is Rhea for the influence with which she continually blesses the earth; and she is Bellona <note>Goddess of war</note> for the tempests she rouses and for her power as the tamer of things. Finally, she is called a *polymorphos daimōn* <note>Greek: Πολύμορφος δάιμων, a "multiform spirit"</note>, because she transforms herself into all shapes, and because she bears the titles of all the Gods, she has not undeservedly attained the name "Mother of All Gods." We could say much regarding the deeds of Isis during her reign, the laws she established, her apotheosis <note>her elevation to divine status</note>, and the mystical significance of the fables attributed to her; however, since material for speaking about her will be provided everywhere throughout this work, we have reserved individual details for their proper places.

# CHAPTER V.

->*Concerning Serapis and Apis according to the mind of the Greeks.*<-

Such is the similarity among all the Gods and Goddesses—differing not so much in reality as in the names imposed by their various effects—that when we designate one among the Gods or Goddesses, we seem to have assigned all the others as if linked in a chain. This is something we have already sufficiently shown above, and will show more fully below when we treat the mystical and allegorical meaning of the Gods.

<margin>Serapis is Pluto.</margin>
Since these things are so, Serapis will be nothing other than that subterranean Osiris whom the Poets call Pluto <note>The King of the Underworld</note>. I state this quite freely, since I have no one among the ancients who does not agree with me. For Plutarch everywhere confuses him with Pluto; Archematus of Euboea recognizes no other Pluto besides Serapis, just as he recognizes no Proserpina besides Isis. Porphyry agrees with them, which is why he is placed among those names that the Greeks call *hypagomena* <note>Greek: ὑπαγόμενα, meaning "subordinate" or "underlying" names</note>. His symbol is that three-headed Cerberus, a most destructive demon ruling over earth, water, and air. Tacitus [mentions] him because of...
