### SYNTHESIS III. ON THE ORIGIN OF EGYPTIAN IDOLATRY. CHAPTER V.

...remarkable inventions in the medical art, he also identifies him—not incorrectly—with Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of healing and medicine</note>. For Serapis, whom they also interpret as the subterranean Osiris, or Pluto, or Dis Pater <note>The Roman "Father of Riches" and lord of the underworld</note>, presides over metals, stones, roots, and other subterranean riches by strengthening their inherent powers. Certainly, no one among the ancients doubts that whatever can contribute to the care of human health has been committed to his distribution and care. It was not without reason that his statue was seen to be cast from all minerals, as we shall demonstrate shortly. For this reason, Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, as cited in the works of Eusebius, says—not wrongly—that Serapis is the prince of evil spirits <margin>The statue of Serapis.</margin>. Following the opinion of the same Eusebius, Ioannes Baptista Leo states that Serapis *was the first to issue symbols by which demons might be expelled, and taught the manner in which demons, having assumed the shapes of beasts, might offer insults, but that he primarily appears with ram's horns*. From this, Diodorus seems to indicate that he is the same as Ammon <margin>Jupiter Ammon.</margin>, and the same as Dionysus and the Egyptian Jupiter, who were all represented with ram's horns. Finally, Heraclides Ponticus writes that the oracle of Serapis, which was most famous, belonged to Pluto; for it is said that he replied in this way to a certain King of Egypt who asked who could be more blessed than himself:

> In the beginning is God, then the Word, and with them the Spirit;
> These three are born together, and all tend toward the One.

<margin>The statue of Serapis.</margin> Ruffinus says that others believe Serapis to be Jupiter, because the *modius* <note>A grain-measure used as a crown</note> placed upon his head shows that he governs all things by measure and weight, or provides life to mortals through the abundance of grain. Others think him to be the power of the Nile, by whose riches and fertility Egypt is nourished. Plutarch, again following Diodorus in another place, says that he is the God who is the Author of the movements of the entire Universe. His Greek words are:

-> More authoritative than Typhon <note>The Egyptian god Set, associated with chaos</note>, and he who sets the movements of all things in motion together. <-

He adds, however, that the Priests felt the same way, asserting that Apis <note>The sacred bull of Memphis</note> and Osiris were the same. "We," he says, "teach that Apis is the soul of Osiris." With this agrees the oracle given by Serapis to Nicocreon, the King of the Cypriots, when he spoke thus:

> I am a God such as I tell you for your learning:
> The heavenly universe is my head, and the sea is my belly,
> The Earth provides my feet, and my ears are set in the ether,
> And my far-seeing eye is the bright light of the Sun.

These words can certainly serve as a sort of <term>anakephalaiosis</term> <note>original: ἀνακεφαλαιώσεως; a "recapitulation" or "summing up"</note> of all those things we have said about Serapis until now. Thus, he is easily confused with Pan, since these words most easily explain how such a great imposition of names can fit a single false deity <note>original: *Deastrum*, a term used by Kircher for a constructed or planetary idol</note>: he is Jupiter in his head, Neptune in his belly, Pluto or Dis in the earth, Dionysus and other Stygian <note>Underworld</note> deities in his lower parts, and Mercury in his ears.

### CHAPTER V. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

...clearly reflects Mercury and Apollo with his eyes. It remains for us to say something about the origin of Serapis <margin>The origin of Serapis.</margin>, regarding whose assignment I also find great diversity among authors. Cornelius Tacitus <note>A famous Roman historian</note> says that the image of Serapis was brought from Pontus <note>A region on the southern coast of the Black Sea</note> to Alexandria by Ptolemy Lagus <note>Ptolemy I Soter, the first Greek ruler of Egypt</note>, who was warned in a dream, and placed in a temple most magnificently consecrated to his name. Plutarch, however, seems to vary in his history. Eustathius agrees with Tacitus, writing that Ptolemy was warned by a demonic apparition. This is contrary to Gorionides <note>A reference to Josippon, a history of the Jews attributed to Joseph ben Gorion</note>, who asserts that the idol of Serapis had been in Egypt long before the time of Ptolemy Lagus; for when the King of the Egyptians, Nectanebo <note>Nectanebo II, the last native Pharaoh of Egypt</note>, had escaped by flight, the Egyptians are said to have consulted the oracle of Serapis. The words of Gorionides <margin>Gorionides.</margin> are as follows:

->And the men of Egypt, when they saw that their lord was missing, went to an image of one of their abominable idols named Serapis, and they sacrificed and offered sacrifices before him, and their wise men asked him about their king. <note>original Hebrew: "ואנשי מצרים בראותם, כי נפקד אדוניהם וילכו אל צלם מצלמי תועבותיהם ושמו סאראפיס ויזבחו ויקרבו לפניו קרבנות וישאלוהו חכמיהם במלכם :"</note><-

> But the Egyptian men, when they saw their King appeared nowhere, went to the idol of Serapis, and offered sacrifices and victims, asking about their King Nectanebo, etc. Since Nectanebo, as we showed above, was a contemporary of Darius and Artaxerxes—who were much earlier than Ptolemy Lagus—it is likely that under him Serapis was not first brought into Egypt, but had been worshipped there long before. Furthermore, others wish for the statue of Serapis to have been brought from the city of Seleucia in Syria, not from Pontus; others believe it was placed not in Alexandria, but in Memphis. Nymphodorus contends that the Apis bull, when dead and placed in a *Soros*—which in Latin we call an ark or coffin—was first called *Sorapis*, and then *Serapis*. This corresponds to the Egyptian etymology, for as we showed in the Supplement, *Saran* or *Sar* signifies both a prince and a bull, as is evident from the Treasury of the Egyptian Language. Saint <margin>St. Augustine, Book 18 of The City of God.</margin> Augustine says: "In those times, Apis, the King of the Argives, having been transported by ships into Egypt, when he died there, became Apis, the greatest god of all the Egyptians." From this it is clear that Apis and Serapis are commonly confused, here as among other authors; but why Apis was called Serapis after death, Varro teaches us. Because the ark, he says, in which he was placed is called *Soros* in Greek or Egyptian, whence *Sorapis*, as if "the Ark of Apis," and then by changing one letter he was called *Serapis*. However, that Bull which Egypt raised in his honor with almost stunned veneration was not called Serapis, but Apis, since they worshipped him alive without an ark. Suidas, continuing the history, says that Serapis—whose image was removed by Bishop Theophilus of Alexandria during the time of Theodosius the Great—was said by some to be Jupiter or Osiris, and by others the Nile, according to those lines of Martianus Capella <note>A late antique author of an influential encyclopedia</note> in his work on Philology:
> ->The Nile admires you as Serapis; Memphis as Osiris;<-

He was called the Nile, however, because he had a *modius* <note>A cylindrical grain-measure or basket often shown on the head of Serapis</note> on his head, and a *pechu* <note>Greek for "cubit"</note>, that is, a cubit or measure of water; in which habit he is seen here and there in various Roman museums. Abenephius <note>An Arabic source frequently cited by Kircher</note>, agreeing with Suidas, Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra, and others, says that Joseph, on account of Egypt being freed from famine, or <margin>Some wish Serapis to be Joseph.</margin> because of his interpretation of the dream of the seven cows, was called Apis by posterity. His words in Arabic sound thus:

And he said <note>original Arabic: "وقال"</note>

### SYNTAGMA III. ON THE ORIGIN OF EGYPTIAN IDOLATRY. CHAPTER V.

<warning>A large ink smudge or wax seal remnant obscures several words in the center of the page. </warning>

And Joseph said to the King, "Set me over the storehouses of the land, for I shall be a faithful guardian"; and the King appointed him over all the storehouses of the land, and Joseph became like a King in Egypt, and his name was Api— <note>original Arabic: "وقال يوسف للملك اجعلني على خزائن الارض وأكون حفيظ امين واقامه الملك على كل خزائن الارض ووشק صار الملك في المصر واسمه افي—"</note>

<margin>Who was Apis?</margin>
And Joseph said to Pharaoh, *“Appoint me over the treasury of the land, since I will be a faithful guardian,” and the King appointed him over all the storehouses of the land, and Joseph became like the King of all Egypt, and they called him Apis.* <note>The author is quoting an Arabic tradition and then providing its Latin equivalent to link the biblical Joseph with the Egyptian bull-god Apis.</note> However, others say, on the testimony of Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note>, that Apis was a blessed man and a King in the city of Memphis in Egypt who, during a famine, provided nourishment to the Egyptians from his own resources. When he died, they established a temple in which a Bull was reared, bearing the symbol of agriculture and having certain markings of color; for in the Egyptian language, "Apis" is nothing other than "Bull." All these details are adapted to Joseph by Hebrew and Christian interpreters; Genebrard <note>Gilbert Génébrard, a 16th-century French theologian</note> even suggests that Joseph built those prodigious masses, the pyramids, for the purpose of storing grain. The <unclear>Chaldean</unclear> and Martianus <note>likely Martianus Capella, a late antique writer</note> believe that the name Serapis signifies "merriment" and "joy" in the Egyptian language, and therefore the Egyptians call joyful festivals <term>Sarapis</term>, because they were performed with the common applause and dancing of the cities. Furthermore, <margin>Sarapis in Egyptian signifies "to rejoice."</margin> certain Hebrews attempt to derive "Serapis" from <term>Seraphim</term> <note>original Hebrew: "שרפים"; celestial beings in Jewish theology</note>; for they say the image of Serapis was constructed in the likeness of the Seraphim, which we read that Solomon placed in the Temple. But we leave this to their own conjectures. 

<margin>What were Laban's Teraphim?</margin>
The <term>Teraphim</term> <note>Household idols mentioned in the Book of Genesis</note>, the idols of Laban, will also be demonstrated at length to have been "Serapides" in the *Pantheon of the Hebrews* in the chapter on Teraphim. We are also not displeased by the opinion of Varro, Plutarch, Lucian, and others, who think that Serapis was so named from the ark <note>Latin: *arca*</note> representing a bovine form, into which Osiris (the inventor of agriculture), or <margin>Serapis is the same as the "Ark of the Bull."</margin> Apis (which we said means "bull" in the Egyptian language), was cast after death and first worshipped with divine honors by Isis. This view is more congruent with both history and the traditions of the Egyptians. However, regarding the manner in which Apis, Serapis, Epaphus, Busiris, and Osiris are reconciled among themselves, and at what time the first foundations of bovine worship were laid, we have spoken in the first Syntagma, in the chapter on the Kings of Egypt during the Dynasty of the Shepherds. It now remains for us to say something about the image of Serapis. Macrobius <note>A Roman provincial writer known for his Saturnalia</note> says in his *Saturnalia*: <margin>The figure of Serapis.</margin>
> They attach a grain-measure <note>Latin: *calathum*</note> to his head, and add to the image the sign of a three-headed creature; this expresses, in the middle and largest head, the likeness of a Lion. On the right side, the head of a dog rises with a mild expression, while the left part of the neck ends in the head of a ravenous wolf. A Dragon <note>or serpent</note> connects these animal forms with its coil, its head returning to the right hand of the God, by which the monster is restrained.

Those who interpret this as the sun want the present time to be indicated by the Lion’s head: because its condition, between the past and the future, is strong and fervent in present action. They infer the past from the wolf's head, because that animal is utterly forgetful, and forgetfulness belongs to the past. The future is seen in the likeness of the fawning dog, which is a sign of hope, which always fawns upon us; for hope is always of the future. As for what the serpent signifies, Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria</note> makes it clear:
> They paint the serpent as a sign of Time, because it is stretched out in length and folded in many coils, which are the many successions of days and years, and it creeps along silently, making no sound, according to that line by Maro <note>The poet Virgil</note>:

### SYNOPSIS III. ON THE ORIGIN OF EGYPTIAN IDOLATRY. 199 CH. V.

<warning>Handwritten circular doodle with a humanoid figure obscures parts of the text in the lower half of the page.</warning>

But there may also be this reason for the hidden tail <note>Refers to the serpent's tail mentioned on the previous page, symbolizing the end of time</note>, that time is considered either from the past, the present, or the future; all of which are uncertain to us. Indeed, we can focus on the past very little, nor can we even fully conceive of it in the mind; the future even less so, because it does not yet exist and its end is entirely unknown; as for the present, since it is unstable and passes by most swiftly, it can scarcely be perceived. But this is more likely a fiction of the Greeks than of the Egyptians; therefore, leaving behind this description, let us examine what his image properly was. The Egyptians, interpreting Serapis as the spirit or the harmony of the World, fashioned his likeness from all the materials of the World. Moreover, the statue was so large that it touched both sides of the temple in Alexandria, concerning which Beroaldus <note>Filippo Beroaldo (1453–1505), a famous Italian Renaissance scholar and commentator</note> writes thus in his commentary on Apuleius:

<margin>The statue of Serapis was made with marvelous skill.</margin>
*At Alexandria there was a temple of Serapis constructed with vaulted work and to be seen as a marvel of art: in which there was a vast likeness of the Deity, so that with its right hand it brushed against one wall, and with its left the other: which was said to be composed of all kinds of metals and woods. There was also a small window arranged by trickery and art, aligned with the rising of the Sun, so that a solar ray directed through it would illuminate the mouth and lips of Serapis; so that, to the watching people, he appeared to be greeted by the Sun with a kiss.* Ammianus also mentions this temple of the Serapeum.

<margin>Ammianus Marcellinus, Book 6.</margin>
*To these,* he says, *are added temples supported by high foundations, among which the Serapeum stands out, which, although it may be diminished by the meager-ness of my words, is nonetheless so adorned with colonnaded courtyards, most ample halls, lifelike statues, and a greatness of other works, that the world sees nothing more magnificent after the Capitol, by which venerable Rome raises itself into eternity.* <note>original Latin: "post Capitolium... nihil orbis terrarum ambitiosius cernat." Ammianus (c. 330–391 AD) was a Roman soldier and historian.</note> However, the reason why it was maintained by the Egyptians as a perpetual rule that they should never admit the temples of Saturn or Serapis within the towns was this: so that, like ever-watchful sentinels and guards, they might permit them to have their seats outside the city limits <note>term: <term>pomerium</term>—the sacred boundary of a city</note> and in the suburbs, as if they were protected by the powerful defenses of their divine power and favor; and they would stand guard for the sake of the hearths and homes, the temples of the Gods, and the very soil in which they were born, noting themselves to be safe from hostile incursion and clandestine snares through their ministry and labor.

**B**ut the bull, which the Egyptians call Apis, Pliny describes thus: *The bull,* he says, *worshipped in Egypt as a substitute for a Divinity, is called Apis; it is distinguished by a white spot on its right side, and horns like those of the crescent Moon, and it has a knot under its tongue which they call the Cantharus* <note>meaning "beetle" or "scarab," considered a sacred symbol</note>. *After certain years of its life have passed (beyond which it is forbidden for it to live), the priests drown it in their fountain and kill it; meanwhile, they mourn until they find another to substitute for it, mourning with shaved heads until it is found; once found, it is led by the Priests to Memphis; there are twin shrines for it, which they call "thalami" [bedchambers], which serve as the omens for the people; to have entered one is joyful, but in the other it portends something ominous. It gives responses to private individuals by taking food from the hands of those consulting it; it turned away from the hand of Germanicus Caesar, who was extinguished [died] not long thereafter. Otherwise, when it breaks out in secret into the gatherings, with the noise of the attendants removed, a flock of boys accompanies it, singing a song in its honor; it seems to understand and to wish to be adored; these flocks, suddenly inspired, prophesy future things. ### CHAPTER V. 200 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE.

...[each] year she is shown with her own signs; although others report that she is found and extinguished on the same day. At Memphis, there is a place by the Nile which they call the "vessel" <note>original: *phiala*, referring to a bowl-shaped basin or pool</note> because of its shape. Every year, during the seven days of Apis's birth, they submerge a golden and silver ritual bowl there. It is a marvel that during those seven days, no one is touched by crocodiles; but on the eighth day, after the sixth hour, the ferocity of the beasts returns. We have recounted these things mostly in the words of Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman naturalist whose *Natural History* was a primary source for Renaissance scholars</note>.

<margin>Ceremonies in the search for the Apis bull.</margin>
Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC</note> writes: After the death of an Apis and its magnificent burial, the Egyptians search—through priests appointed for this specific duty—for another calf similar to the previous one. When it is found, the people end their mourning. The priests, who oversee this care, first lead the calf to the "City of the Nile" <note>Nilopolis</note>, where they feed him for forty days. Then, placing him into a covered boat containing a golden dwelling, they lead him to Memphis as a god and place him in the sanctuary of Vulcan <note>The Roman name for the Egyptian god Ptah, the patron deity of Memphis</note>. During these [forty] days, he says, only women may look upon the Bull; at all other times they are forbidden from seeing his face.

<margin>Why Apis is worshipped under the form of a Bull.</margin>
They give as the reason for worshipping a bull with such zeal that the soul of Osiris first migrated into him, and thereafter passed into his successors as a refugee. But others say that after Osiris was killed by Typhon <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Set</note>, Apis gathered his limbs and placed them into a wooden bull covered with white cowhide; thus the city was called Busiris <note>Kircher derives "Busiris" from the Greek *Bous* (bull) and *Osiris*</note>, as we mentioned in the preceding section. Furthermore, according to Herodotus <note>The 5th-century BC Greek "Father of History"</note>, Apis is called Epaphus by the Greeks. Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus (c. 175–235 AD), a Roman author of works on natural history</note> says he is great and powerful, procreated from a cow that conceived after being struck by lightning.

<margin>Another description of Apis.</margin>
This Apis has these marks: his whole body is black, having a white square-shaped mark on his forehead, the image of an eagle on his back, a beetle <term>cantharus</term> <note>original: *cantharum*. This refers to a knot or mark under the tongue supposed to resemble a scarab beetle</note> under his tongue, and double hairs on his tail. Thus says Herodotus in his third book. But the Egyptians, according to Aelian, do not agree with these: for they attribute twenty-nine marks to this sacred bull, corresponding to the twenty-nine days of the periodic lunar month. They represent him everywhere in this way, as is clear from the Bembine Tablet <note>Also known as the *Mensa Isiaca*, a famous bronze altar plate covered in Egyptian-style imagery that Kircher studied extensively</note>.

<image-desc>An illustration of the sacred Apis bull. The bull is shown in profile, walking to the left. It has a solar disk between its horns and a crescent moon mark on its flank. <margin>He is conceived not by mating but by lightning.</margin>
Pomponius Mela <note>A Roman geographer of the 1st century AD</note> states that Apis is the deity of all people, and especially of the Egyptians; he says the **bull is black, marked with specific spots, and conceived divinely by celestial fire.** He is distinct in his tail and tongue; such a bull is rarely born to others, nor is he conceived by the mating of cattle, but by a lightning bolt. Finally, whenever one is born, it is the greatest festival for the nation. Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Salamis known for his writings against heresies</note> recounts that the Persian Kings Cambyses and Ochus paid the penalty for their rashness in either striking or killing the sacred Bull. The one who wounded Apis perished by a disastrous death, injured by his own sword; the other passed away with a not dissimilar end. Both, according to the testimony of Herodotus <note>The "Father of History" (5th century BC)</note>, stood as examples of divine vengeance for the irreverence committed against the Gods.

<margin>Two bulls sacred to the Egyptians.</margin>
Furthermore, it should be noted that there were two bulls sacred to the Egyptians: one at Memphis, of which we have already spoken; the other at Heliopolis, known by the name **Mnevis**, who was raised in a certain enclosure, as Ammianus Marcellinus <note>A 4th-century Roman historian</note> mentions. Among the animals consecrated by the ancients, Mnevis (or <term>Mneuis</term> <note>original: Μνεῦις</note>) and Apis are recorded. Mnevis was dedicated to the Sun, while Apis was dedicated to the Moon. Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus (c. 175–235 AD), a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric</note> agrees with this, saying, *And a sacred cow was kept for Venus Urania in the Hermopolitan Prefecture.* The nature of the astronomical mysteries indicated by the Solar Mnevis and the Lunar Apis has been discussed in my work on the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. One thing I cannot pass over here as worthy of attention is that this bull-worship, or to put it better, this detestable <term>bull-worship</term> <note>original: μοσχολατρεία (moscholatreia)</note>, was so deeply ingrained in the minds of men that even the people chosen by God, infected by the contagion of such brute worship, did not shrink from building altars to them and offering libations. For as Pererius <note>Benito Pereira (1535–1610), a Jesuit theologian and commentator</note> rightly says: *The superstitious Hebrew nation had seen the solemnities of the Egyptians in the worship of the Bull while staying in Egypt and mixing with them; they also saw the cause of such great worship, namely the abundance of earthly goods redounding from it. Therefore, while undergoing hardships in the desert, they suddenly adopted for themselves those Gods who could remedy their want—gods such as they, along with the Egyptians, considered the Apis bulls to be.* But more on this later in the <term>idol-madness</term> <note>original: ειδωλομανία (eidolomania)</note> of the Hebrews. The worship of this stupid God spread not only to the Israelites but was gradually diffused into neighboring regions and persuaded the entire East, as the records of the Persians, Assyrians, and Gymnosophists <note>A term used by Greeks for ancient Indian philosophers who practiced asceticism and went naked</note> testify.

<margin>From where the worship of the calf in the desert arose.</margin>

## CHAPTER VI.

->On Ammon, or the Egyptian Jupiter.<-

The diversity of the names of the Gods arose from various events, as the names of all the other Gods—and indeed Apis and Hammon—show well enough. In reality, these are nothing other than Osiris or Ham <note>The biblical Ham, son of Noah, often identified by early modern scholars with Egyptian deities.</note>, who, affecting divinity, transformed himself through incantations and illusions into various forms of animals, but especially into those of a Bull and a Ram, as we have proved in the preceding sections. By the Egyptians, astonished by the novelty of the thing, he was called Apis or the Bull; but by the Libyans he was called Hammon, from the name of Ham, from which it does not much differ. This is the opinion of Genebrardus, Pererius, and Cornelius <note>Cornelius à Lapide, a famous Jesuit biblical commentator.</note> in their commentaries on Genesis, following Berosus.

<margin>Pliny, book 31.</margin>
The Greeks, however, derive the name of Hammon from "sand," which in Greek is called <term>ammos</term> <note>original Greek: "ἄμμος"</note>, as Pliny also suggests when he writes thus concerning the "Ammoniac" gum:

> Therefore Africa, situated below Ethiopia, drips the tear of the ammoniac plant in its sands; from this it also takes its name from the oracle of Ammon, near which the tree grows.

<margin>Etymology of the name Amun.</margin>
Sextus Pompeius <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note> agrees with this, writing:

> He was surnamed Hammon because he is thought to have been found in the sand; ram's horns are attached to him because of the kind of livestock among which he was found.

Others from the school of the Arabs wish him to be named from the Arabic word <term>the Ram</term> <note>original Arabic: "الحمل" (al-hamal)</note>, as if you were to say, "the ram." But since the Egyptians seem to speak with more certainty, let us also bring forth what they themselves hand down: *Amun*, they say, *is the name of Jupiter*; which Plutarch also notes in his book on Osiris and Isis. Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> also notes that this name *Amun* in the Egyptian language signifies nothing other than a certain power of the Divinity that brings the secret forces of hidden reasons into the light.

<margin>What is the name Amun?</margin>
This is consistent with the assertion of Manetho <note>An Egyptian priest and historian.</note>, who hands down that the name signifies something "secret" or "hidden." Hecataeus <note>Hecataeus of Abdera, an ancient Greek historian.</note>, however, says the word was used by those invoking God; they were accustomed to use it especially when they called upon the unknown and the secret. For this reason, it happened that they called that supreme God, the creator of things, as one hidden and secret, by the voice "Ammon." They expressed this in hieroglyphic letters in the following manner, the interpretation of which follows. Whence the first Egyptians represented him through some unknown figure, a navel, or I know not what circular or spherical shape, as we shall prove at length in the third book.

Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE known for his "Library of History."</note> recorded that Ammon was a King of Libya who married Rhea, the daughter of Sky, and loved Amalthea, by whom he fathered a son, Dionysus; the rest of the accounts concerning him can be read in his works. <margin>Hyginus in the Book of Fables, under the name Aries.</margin> Hyginus, however, tells the story in this way, following Hermippus: *At the time when Liber <note>Another name for Dionysus or Bacchus, the god of wine and ecstasy.</note> was attacking Africa, he arrived with his army at a place called "Ammodes" <note>original: "Ammodes". While they were pondering what to do, a certain ram, wandering by chance, reached their soldiers; when the ram saw them, it sought safety in flight. The soldiers, though oppressed by dust and heat, began to follow the ram until they reached the place where the Temple of Jupiter Ammon was later established. When they arrived there, they could find the ram nowhere, but what was more desirable, they found a great abundance of water in that place. Having restored their bodies, they immediately reported back to Liber, who, rejoicing, led his army to those borders and established the Temple of Jupiter Ammon with a statue made with ram's horns. He placed the figure of the Ram among the stars, so that when the Sun is in that sign, all things being born are restored, which happens in the springtime; this was done chiefly because Liber restored his army by the flight of that ram.* Furthermore, he wished it to be the leader of the twelve signs <note>The first sign of the Zodiac, Aries.</note> because it had been the best leader for his army. <margin>The army of Liber in Libya.</margin> Moreover, Leo <note>Likely Leo of Pella, an author who wrote on Egyptian history.</note>, who wrote about Egyptian matters, says of the statue of Ammon: *When Liber held the kingdom of Egypt and the remaining borders, and was said to be the first to show all things to men, a certain Ammon came from Africa and brought a great number of livestock to Liber, so that he might more easily enjoy his favor and be said to be the first to have discovered something. Therefore, in exchange for this benefit, Liber is thought to have given him the land that is opposite Egyptian Thebes; and those who make statues of Ammon fashion them with a horned head, so that men might remember that he first showed them livestock. However, those who wish to assign the deed to Liber—stating that he did not seek it from Ammon, but that it was brought to him voluntarily—make his statues horned and say that the Ram was fixed among the stars for the sake of memory.* <margin>Herodotus, Book II.</margin> Herodotus, in his second book, says that when Jupiter did not wish to be seen by Hercules, and yet was moved by his prayers, he devised a scheme: he cut off the head of a ram, and having put on the shaggy skin he had stripped from it, he showed himself to Hercules in this way. From this, it happened that the Egyptians fashioned the statue of Jupiter with a ram's face, and it is said the Ammonians <note>A people living in the Libyan desert, famous for the Oracle of Ammon.</note> received this from the Egyptians. By others, it is handed down that in war, Ammon used a helmet...

They say that when Alexander understood that Perseus and Hercules had traveled to the oracle of Ammon, he wished to travel there himself. However, when he was driven back by a strong south wind and had wandered for a long time through the sands, at last, with two crows showing the way, he arrived at the intended place. His mother Olympias is remembered to have taken this quite poorly; there exists a letter from her to her son on this subject, recorded in Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius, a 2nd-century Roman author.</note>, urging him not to persist in making her an object of hatred to Juno <note>The goddess of marriage and wife of Jupiter/Ammon; Olympias feared the divine jealousy of a wife whose husband supposedly fathered her child.</note>. Why Olympias might have taken this address of Alexander so poorly will be easily clear from the words of Ben Gorion cited above; for Alexander was the son of Nectanebus, who had seduced Olympias under the assumed figure of Ammon. For this reason, she rightly feared for herself from Juno, the wife of Jupiter Ammon, under whose form she had been falsely and through malicious trickery violated. Others claim that his image had outstretched hands and was of immense stature, and was placed at the boundaries of shores or on public roads, such as the statues they commonly call Herms <term>Herms: pillars topped with a bust, used as boundary markers or road signs</term>. The author of the *Arabic Geography* mentions such idols in the following words:

<margin>Arabic Geography, p. 1, climate 1.</margin>
This first climate begins from the western side, from the Western Sea which is called the Sea of Obscurity or Darkness <note>The Atlantic Ocean.</note>, and that is the sea of which it is not known what lies beyond it. In it are the Isles of Goodness (understand these as the Fortunate Isles <note>The Canary Islands.</note>), and from these islands Ptolemy begins the measurement of the longitude of cities. They record that in these islands there are certain idols fashioned from stone, and the height of each of them is one hundred cubits. Atop each of these is a figure, or another image made of brass, with hands spread out or turned backward. They say there are six such idols; one of them holds in its hand a certain vessel with pointed edges, and no one knows anything of the dwellings that lie beyond the said islands. This is the account of the Arab.

<margin>A prodigious statue.</margin>
Certainly, Indian history abundantly testifies that such statues of Ammon pervaded not only Libya but the whole of Africa and the islands of the surrounding ocean, for in those records mention of such images is frequently made. Indeed, an Ethiopian man, when consulted by me regarding similar things, confirmed this, writing in the Ethiopian language as follows (I provide the words in Latin letters, as the Ethiopian characters were unavailable):

<margin>Ethiopian words.</margin>
<note>original Ge'ez transliterated: "Asina falacha amneia chama asabe lacha vchutat imlachta achzia..."</note>
Since you have asked me to tell you something about the gods of the Ethiopians, you should know that our fathers (for so it is read in our Annals), when they were mingled everywhere with the gentiles and pagans, began to learn their works. They made for themselves private gods and worshipped them, sculptures perfected by the hand of man. Their idols were in the likeness of animals: the calf, the ram, the dog, and others. I myself have seen many such things still in Ethiopia in Barnagasch <note>Bahr Negus, a northern province of the Ethiopian Empire.</note>; for the most part, they featured the head of a Lion and a Ram. Their name was Amun. It is said by our predecessors that Solomon and Saba <note>The Queen of Sheba.</note> were also led astray by them, and they originated from the ancient Mages of Egypt.

Pigafetta, Hondius, Mercator, and nearly all others who describe Ethiopia agree with this...

SYNT. III. ON THE ORIGIN OF EGYPTIAN IDOLATRY 207 / CHAPTER VII.

<margin>
Ammon's idols are still seen in Ethiopia.
</margin>
Travelers in this century have described in their reports that many monuments of the ancient gods are still to be seen around the regions of Cyrenaica <note>An ancient Greek and Roman province in modern-day eastern Libya.</note>; to these, the Ethiopians would flee as if to oracles in times of necessity, to receive answers about the future outcome of events. These accounts agree excellently with what we have said so far regarding the image of Ammon. For that oracle was one of the greatest, oldest, and most famous that ever existed; Herodotus, handing down its origin, says: *“I heard these things from the priests at Thebes; the overseers of the Dodonaeans <note>Dodona was the oldest oracle in ancient Greece.</note> say that two black doves flew from Egyptian Thebes—each black—one to Libya, the other to them. The one [that came to them], sitting in a beech tree, spoke with a human voice, saying that an oracle of Jupiter <note>original: "Iouis." The Romans identified the Egyptian Ammon with their supreme god, Jupiter.</note> must be established in that place; they interpreted what was announced to them as being from the divine, and for that reason they did so. But the dove that went to the Libyans ordered them to establish the oracle of Ammon, which is also belonging to Jupiter.”*

<margin>
Two doves as founders of the oracles.
</margin>
<margin>
Strabo book 17. The famous Temple of Ammon in the Libyan desert.
</margin>
The location of this celebrated Ammon is described by Strabo. "There was also," he says, "beyond Cyrene in the furthest gulf among the Garamantes <note>A powerful Saharan tribal confederation that controlled trade routes.</note>, a most august and ancient oracle of Jupiter Ammon in vast solitudes and scorched fields, on sterile, dry, and bare soil. Toward this place, with the sun burning and the heat scorching <note>original: "fragrantissimo," likely a variant or error for "flagrantissimo" meaning blazing.</note> through immense masses of sand and a vast plain infested with heat and thirst, the journey was scarcely tolerable for anyone. Indeed, the wind is accustomed to drive the sands like waves now here, now there, and to infest the fields like seas; for it carries clouds of dust and vexes with a foul tempest. After these trials, a grove pleasant with a dense forest, olives, and tall trees, and with springs flowing here and there, provided a pleasant site in the middle of the sands. This site, no more than forty stadia <note>A stadium was roughly 600 feet; forty stadia is about 4.5 miles.</note> wide, enclosed the sanctuary of the oracle; beyond it, however, lay a wide desert region, inaccessible to human footsteps; nearby, however, the Ammonians inhabit various places."

<margin>
Description of the oracle of Ammon.
</margin>
Ammon himself, clothed with a goat-like head <note>original: "hircinô capite." While Ammon is usually ram-headed, Kircher notes the goat-like features often attributed to desert deities.</note> and skin, was worshiped with many ceremonies. When the priests sought answers, they used to carry him in a golden boat and sing a traditional song; once he was propitiated, they would give the answers to those asking. These answers were issued by Ammon not in words, but by a nod and obscure signs. This reached such a peak of majesty that it was considered a miracle that, after the Persian King Cambyses, Alexander the Macedonian <note>Alexander the Great, who famously visited the Siwa Oasis to be declared the son of Ammon.</note> penetrated there through such great heat. I would have many things to say here about the sacrifices, and the mysterious actions and ceremonies with which they worshiped that Ram-like <note>original: "Arietinum."</note> Ammon of theirs; but because I have reserved all those things for other places, let us turn our pen to treat of other matters.

# CHAPTER VII.

## Concerning Canopus, Horus, Harpocrates, Mithras, and other Egyptian Deities.

### CANOPUS.

Canopus, according to Plutarch, was the pilot or steersman of Osiris's ship, which the Greeks call the *Argo*. "They name," he says, "Osiris the commander, and Canopus the pilot, after whom the star has the same name; and the ship, which is called the *Argo* by the Greeks, was placed among the stars in honor of Osiris's ship, carried not far from Orion and the Dog Star." Canopus is, moreover, a star of the first magnitude

...magnitude, the largest and brightest of all fixed stars, according to the testimony of Pliny, where he calls Canopus a "huge and bright star." However, it is unknown to Europeans because of its proximity to the Antarctic Pole. When positioned on the meridian at the island of Rhodes, it seems to just graze the horizon; these are the words of Pliny: *“Italy does not see Canopus. To those looking from Alexandria, Canopus seems to rise nearly a fourth part of one sign <note>A "sign" refers to one of the twelve divisions of the Zodiac.</note> above the earth. From Rhodes, it seems in a certain way to graze the earth itself.”* Others maintain that Canopus was the <term>Navigator (original: nauclerus)</term> of a certain Menelaus, the supreme commander of the Greeks. They say that while he was returning to his ancestral home with Helen after the fall of Troy, he was driven by the force of the winds into one of the branches of the Nile. After landing on a small nearby island full of snakes and other poisonous beasts, Canopus—by some misfortune—was bitten by a venomous <term>Hemorrhoid snake <note>original: "Hemorrhoide." A species of snake whose bite was historically believed to cause fatal bleeding from all orifices.</note></term> and died there shortly after. Because Menelaus held him in the greatest affection and took the man's calamitous fate bitterly, he honored him with the highest distinctions by building a magnificent tomb in that same place. He also built a city named after him near the mouth of the Nile, which was afterwards called the Canopic mouth. Later, Alexander the Great expanded this city so much that it seemed to form a single city with neighboring <term>Pellaea <note>A reference to Alexandria, named "Pellaean" after Pella, the birthplace of Alexander the Great.</note></term>. Strabo also, among other things, makes a specific mention of this place; his words are: *“Canopus is 120 stadia <note>An ancient unit of distance; 120 stadia is roughly 14 miles or 22 kilometers.</note> from Alexandria by land, so named after Canopus, the pilot of Menelaus, who died there of a snake bite.”* Cornelius Tacitus, in recounting the journey of Germanicus Caesar as he went into Egypt to examine its antiquities, says this among other things: *“He sailed up the Nile, starting from the town of Canopus; the Spartans founded it because the pilot Canopus was buried there—at the time when Menelaus, seeking to return to Greece, was driven in a different direction to the sea and the land of Libya.”* Thus, whether this Canopus was the pilot of Osiris or of Menelaus, it is clear that he provided the superstitious people with great material for fables and inventions, as seen in the astonished veneration and the diligent, foolish worship they offered him at all times. This grew to such an extent that after Osiris, Serapis, and Isis, the Navigator Canopus was also counted among the greatest deities of the Egyptians. He was worshipped primarily in that city which Menelaus had built in his honor and which was called Canopus after his name, and in which a magnificent temple dedicated to him was seen. According to Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a Christian theologian who wrote extensively on Egyptian customs.</note>, there was also in this place the most famous school in all Egypt, the fountain and origin of all Egyptian theology. Here they taught the sacred letters, which they call <term>hieroglyphs (original: ἱερογλυφικὰς)</term>; priests were initiated here; the sacred mysteries were delivered nowhere more accurately, and consequently, it was frequented by every kind of person, especially by the Greeks. Indeed, the idols of Canopus which the Egyptians worshipped were sometimes in the shape of a water-jar <note>original: "Hydriæ." Rufinus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 11.</margin> *They say that at one time the Chaldeans <note>Ancient people of Mesopotamia, often associated in early modern texts with fire-worship and astrology.</note>, carrying around the fire which they themselves worshipped as a Deity, held a contest with the Gods of all the provinces; the condition being that whichever god won would be believed by everyone to be the true God. The Gods of the other provinces were made of bronze, gold, silver, wood, or stone, or whatever material they consisted of, which would undoubtedly be destroyed by fire; as a result, fire held the supreme position in all places.* (All of these things are beautifully displayed on a certain gemstone from the Museum of Stephanonius, as follows.)

When the Priest of Canopus heard these things, he devised a clever plan. <margin>The origin of Canopic worship.</margin> *In parts of Egypt, earthenware <term>Hydria <note>A type of water-carrying vessel or jar.</note></term> are typically made, porous with many tiny holes on all sides; through these, murky water filters out and is purified. He took one of these jars, blocked the holes with wax, painted it with various colors on the outside, filled it with water, and set it up as a God. He then carefully attached the head—which had been cut off from an old statue and was said to be that of Menelaus—onto the top. After this, the Chaldeans arrived and the contest began. Fire was placed around the water jar, but as the heat melted the wax, the fire was extinguished by the water leaking out. By the Priest’s trickery, Canopus was shown to be the victor over the Gods of the Chaldeans. For this reason, the image of Canopus itself is formed with very small, barely visible feet, a drawn-in and squeezed neck, and a swollen belly in the shape of a water-jar, with an equally smooth back.* This account is supported by very ancient statues still surviving in the Roman <term>Gazophylacia <note>Treasuries or storehouses for valuable objects.</note></term>, the shapes and mysteries of which will be explained in detail in their proper place. However, the following statue, made of white marble from the <term>Cimeliarchium <note>A cabinet of curiosities or museum of precious things.</note></term> of Lord Gerard Reinst, Senator and Magistrate of Amsterdam, sent to me by the most learned Berthold Nihus, is shown in another form.

For since the Egyptians pursued the waters of the Nile with such honor as seemed fitting for a God bestowing such great benefits;

...also related to that number; for we have said above that three small vessels were a symbol of the Nile. Therefore, once the vessels were obtained, nothing was easier—with the added deception and cunning of the Canopic priests—than to elevate that watery <term>godling</term> <note>Latin: "Deastrum," a somewhat dismissive term for a pagan deity</note> of theirs above the other gods by that clever invention we cited, and to make him the victor over all. Indeed, Abenephius the Arab clearly teaches that the Canopic idols, which they shaped bulging with many breasts, were arranged this way for mystical reasons: so that when water was received inside and poured out through the breasts, they might suggest the one who, as if through certain breasts, nourishes all things. His words in Arabic sound like this:

<margin>Many-breasted Canopi.</margin>

> *And they themselves have a certain idol by the name of Canopus, and it is in the manner of a swollen vessel, and when it is filled with waters, the water is poured back out through the breasts which they fashioned in it, and by that flow is indicated the process of nature nourishing all things.* <note>Kircher provides an Arabic transcription and translates it into Latin; it is translated here into English.</note> Moreover, that Canopi were once fashioned with many breasts is attested by an ancient coin from the treasury of Francesco Menedrio, in which Canopus appears, swollen with breasts and clothed in a latticed garment; keep the image of it before your eyes.

<margin>Breasted Canopus.</margin>
Certainly that many-breasted Isis, whom we explained in the preceding pages and who is seen in many places in Rome, seems to represent nothing else than a similar <term>poly-masthon</term> <note>original Greek: πολύμασθον, meaning many-breasted</note>, or breasted Canopus; since the description of the entire Canopus can be very easily adapted to her. For just as Canopus ends in a cone-shaped surface, swells with breasts, and is adorned on the outside with various hieroglyphic pictures, so Isis in her attire very closely approaches the Canopic mysteries. In the end, they differ in nothing, except that this one was a fiction of the Greeks; the other, I say, the Canopus of the Egyptians. Through her, they signify that great mother of all; through him, they signify that great all-nourishing Ocean, which they also call the Nile. For Canopus is the same deity among the Egyptians as Neptune or Tethys is among the Greeks. Abenephius the Arab asserts the first part in these words:

<margin>Canopus as Neptune.</margin>

> *And they worshipped him (meaning Canopus) as a deity who presides over the sea, the rivers, and the whole of moist nature, and they called him by the name of the river Nile.* That this is the case is shown by many symbols of moisture, such as: bowls, buckets, boxes, water-jars, and other vessels occurring everywhere in the hieroglyphs; these are assigned to no other than Osiris, insofar as he is the Nile. For the Egyptians believed that the essences of all bodily things consist in moisture, an opinion in which Thales of Miletus <note>Thales (c. 624–545 BCE) was a pre-Socratic philosopher famous for proposing that water is the fundamental substance of the universe.</note> is also read to have been; he thought that water was the first principle of things, and that from it all the elements of the world, and the world itself, and those things which are born in it, exist. Thus, it is no wonder that they viewed the Nile as the vein of life, and of every...

...the source of all good, with such great honor. They called idols of this kind "Canopi" after the Pilot of Osiris. Since he, like a second Neptune, ruled the sea and furthermore spent his life upon the waters, he was easily confused after death with Osiris, whom he served. Thus, he earned divine honors from a superstitious people.

### HARPOCRATES.

<margin>Two kinds of Canopi.</margin>
There are, moreover, two kinds of Canopi. Those which reflect the figure we marked above with the letter B were, according to the testimony of Goropius <note>Johannes Goropius Becanus (1519–1572), a Flemish physician and antiquarian known for his idiosyncratic theories on linguistics and Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, placed in the schools of the Egyptians alongside Harpocrates. Through the latter, they suggested that students of letters ought to be observers of silence; through the former, they symbolically indicated everything that a man ought to do from infancy even unto extreme old age. The words of Goropius Becanus are: <margin>Goropius, Book 8, *Hieroglyphics*.</margin> *This Canopus was depicted in the Egyptian schools in the same manner as Harpocrates; and just as this God gradually emerged from human ignorance, so too was Canopus drawn into the material of error, providing various common fables.* From this, I believe that Lorenzo Pignoria <note>An Italian antiquarian (1571–1631) who wrote extensively on the "Isiac Tablet" and Egyptian artifacts.</note>—a man otherwise remarkably well-versed in every kind of antiquity—nevertheless took the opportunity to confuse Canopi of this kind with Harpocrates or Horus, the sons of Isis, for no other reason than being deceived by the similarity of the idols. However, it will be clear from what follows that the Canopi are greatly different from the statues of Harpocrates. For the statues of Harpocrates were depicted in various ways, just like the Canopi; however, all "Harpocrates" figures were distinguished from "Canopi" by the fact that the latter, swollen with thick bellies, ended in a cone-shaped surface, as is clear from their images reported above. The former, however, were fashioned in the likeness of a beardless and naked boy, either sitting upon a lotus—as here—always pressing a finger to his lips, or even wrapped in infant swaddling clothes, as appears from the images placed here. For a model of the Canopic images, see Volume III, where they are shown in all their diversity.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of the Egyptian deity Harpocrates depicted as a nude, seated youth with a shaved head and a sidelock of hair. He sits cross-legged on a lotus flower rising from a body of water. He holds a flail (nekhakha) over his right shoulder and presses the index finger of his left hand to his lips in a gesture of silence.</image-desc>

Harpocrates was the God of silence among the Egyptians, held in the highest veneration, so much so that he was never absent from Osiris and Isis. He was depicted in two ways: first as a beardless, naked boy who marked his mouth with the index finger of his right hand, urging silence with his finger. His left hand, extended downward, supported a Cornucopia <note>The "horn of plenty," a symbol of abundance and nourishment.</note> reaching up to his ears and filled with fruits, among which a pine nut stood out. The head of the God appeared to be bound with a miter, which, standing somewhat high, ended in two things like birds, as you will see in the following figure.

The second method of depiction did not differ from the method of depicting Canopi: namely, a boy dressed in a latticed garment, or rather wrapped in certain swaddling bands, with a <term>lituus</term> <note>An augur’s curved staff used in Roman and, supposedly, Egyptian ritual.</note>, a <term>gnomon</term> <note>A carpenter's square or an instrument used to measure shadows.</note>, and a staff marked with a doll's head, as in the figure...

# TREATISE III. ON THE ORIGIN OF EGYPTIAN IDOLATRY. CHAPTER VII

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration featuring two figures. On the left, a smaller, nude figure stands facing forward. <margin>Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*.</margin>
...appears. Indeed, Harpocrates was the son of Osiris and Isis, whom Plutarch writes was conceived by Isis after the death of Osiris along with Helitomenus <note>Kircher's transcription of a name likely referring to a "premature birth" or a specific epithet of the infant god</note>, and was born weak in his lower limbs. However, elsewhere the same author denies that the boy was imperfect, nor should he be thought of as a type of legume; rather, he is the God, presiding over and moderating youthful, as yet imperfect, and unarticulated speech. For this reason, they depicted him with a finger moved to his mouth, as a symbol of silence and taciturnity. To him, in the month of Mesori (that is, August), the Egyptians were accustomed to offer legumes and sing thus:

->The tongue is fortune, the tongue is a spirit.<-
->That is: *The tongue is fortune, the tongue is a spirit.* <note>original Greek: Γλῶσσα τύχη, Γλῶσσα δαίμων</note><-

Furthermore, Plutarch asserts that Harpocrates was born around the Winter Solstice, and was honored with lentils and the first-fruits of the crops. Moreover, the Persea tree <note>an Egyptian evergreen tree, often associated with the heart and tongue in sacred symbology</note> was dedicated to him, because the leaves of that tree are very similar to a tongue, and the fruit to a heart. Furthermore, Saint Epiphanius relates that the sacred rites which were performed for this boy-God in the city of Buto were truly most ridiculous; for the priests would pretend to nourish him just like nurses. In all the temples where Isis and Serapis were worshipped, as we have said above, there was an image with a finger pressed to its lips, which many interpret as meaning that one must keep silent about the fact that those gods were once mortals. This entire invention, moreover, was Egyptian: that a finger pressed to the lips should signify the silence to be kept concerning the immortal Gods, lest we speak too freely about them—a point on which we are also warned by Plato in his *Laws*. In other places, Pliny records that the seal of Harpocrates was commonly worn on rings by the ancients for this reason: to indicate silence regarding matters to be done. Among the Romans, there was also the image of Angerona <note>the Roman goddess of secrecy and the winter solstice</note> with her mouth bound and sealed, to suggest that the name of the deity in whose protection the city of Rome rested, and what that deity’s proper name was, should be passed over in silence.

<margin>Why it was a crime to reveal the name of Rome's protector.</margin>
This was surely due to the superstition that the protecting Gods might be called away or "devoted" <note>referring to *evocatio*, a ritual where an enemy's gods were summoned to leave their city</note> by certain sacred rites. Hence it is well known that Valerius Soranus was put to death because he dared to reveal this secret. For that reason, Pliny, speaking of Rome, says: *Whose name it is considered a crime to speak to another, according to the secrets of the ceremonies.* See what we have treated more abundantly on these matters elsewhere.

And for this reason, Harpocrates was placed by the Egyptians in all their temples, inner sanctums, shrines, and other places everywhere, indicating silence:

<margin>Ovid, *Metamorphoses*.</margin>
> Who suppresses his voice, and persuading silence with a finger.

I say "silence" regarding those sacred rites which were then being performed, and which were established with various ceremonies, the adjuration of demons, and the summoning of Genii <note>protective spirits or minor deities</note>. Indeed, Martianus says: "While sacrificing,
<margin>Martianus Capella, *The Marriage of Philology and Mercury*.</margin>
the boy stood by, and with a finger pressed to his mouth, he reminded us of a salutary silence." And in Book 7: *But then, that boy, muttering to you as you rose from the earth, was ordered to command a pious silence.*

But concerning Harpocrates and his mysteries—what his silence signifies, what the symbols he is depicted with mean, and what his statues and amulets represent—these things will be discussed extensively elsewhere.

### HORUS.

Horus and Harpocrates are commonly taken to be the same by various authors, since both are found to be gods of silence marked with the same symbols. This error seems to have arisen from the following source:

The Egyptians record that the God [Horus] and Harpocrates were brought forth into the light with a finger pressed to their lips, as if they had grown together that way. However, anyone who carefully considers the intentions of the Egyptians will easily see that Horus cannot and should not be confused with Harpocrates. Horus is not a god of silence; indeed, the two differ greatly in their image, their symbols, and their mystical significance. In fact, they are distinguished by traits that cannot possibly belong to the same person. Writers assert that the former [Horus] is vigorous and healthy, while the latter [Harpocrates] is weak and imperfect in his limbs; the latter is a persuader of silence, while the former is the greatest recommender of the voice and of Music. Who cannot see how much these two differ? I add that Horus is commonly called *Apollo* by the Egyptians, as Plutarch demonstrates in many places in *On Isis and Osiris*. From this, even the Sun was called by that name by the same people, according to the testimony of Macrobius and Censorinus; and from his name, the "Hours" of the day and the "seasons" <term>Horae: the Latin word for hours and the Greek goddesses of the seasons</term> of the year were named. Nevertheless, Plutarch seems to have established two Horuses: the first is an older one, blind due to the darkness, who was called *Arueris* <note>Har-wer, or Horus the Elder</note> and born on the second day when the world was not yet perfected, but was both a likeness of the world and a certain sketch of it. The other Horus, however, was perfect and complete, whose statue they say was in the city of Coptos, holding the genitals of Typhon <note>Typhon is the Greek name for Set, the rival of Horus</note> in one hand.

<margin>Macrobius; Censorinus in the book *On the Natal Day*.</margin>
<margin>Diodorus Siculus, Book 1, Chapter 2.</margin>
Diodorus says that this Horus was the son of Isis, killed through the snares of the Titans, found among the waters, restored to life by his mother, and finally achieved immortality. He also interprets him as Apollo, highly skilled in healing and divination; from this seems to have originated that "Horus Apollo" <note>original Greek: ὁ ῥῶ Apollo</note> of the Hermionians—that is, the "presider over boundaries"—whom they once worshipped according to the testimony of Pausanias.

<margin>Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*.</margin>
Epiphanius writes that the priests of Horus and Harpocrates, with their heads shaved, carry their idols about as they run around; with their faces smeared with porridge, they drop the idols into a boiling cauldron. They shamelessly carry a "slavish and detestable sign of a boy" <note>likely a reference to a phallic amulet or a specific ritual object the Church Father found offensive</note> and other things which the same Holy Writer mocks. But many other things are brought forward concerning this Horus Apollo, which they believed pertained to their hidden interpretation and to nature, which we shall present elsewhere. For here it will suffice to have declared only this: that Horus, the son of Osiris and Isis, when considered allegorically, is nothing other than everything that is generated from the Sun and Moon...

SYNTAGMA III. ON THE ORIGIN OF EGYPTIAN IDOLATRY. CHAPTER VII

is generated in the World; as will be stated throughout this entire work. His images testify to this abundantly; they were always fashioned either in the form of a standing boy, or a nursing infant, or wrapped as if in swaddling clothes with legs joined together <note>original: *indiscretis pedibus*; referring to the mummiform shape where the legs are not carved separately</note>. The Egyptians held these in such high veneration that no house, no crossroads, and no temple could be found without them. They wore these around their necks in place of protective charms <note>original: *phylacteriorum*</note>; they held them in the place of their Household Gods <note>original: *Penates* and *Lares*</note>. They appealed to this Horus as a kind of intercessor and peacemaker with Osiris and Isis through frequent vows and sacrifices; they believed the spirits of the World were drawn to him. Since the images, or idols, of Horus possessed such great power, it is no wonder that the Priests—with rites as foolish and ridiculous as they were—would hold them to their breasts like nurses, refreshing them with a simulated nursing, and devoting themselves to them with other ceremonies that are commonly read about in the works of various authors. Furthermore, the idols were prepared by the Egyptians according to the diversity seen here.

## M I T H R A S

<margin>Mithras is the same as Mizraim</margin>
**M**ithras, or Mytrius to the Persians, is the same as Osiris to the Egyptians, or the Sun, their primary God, as Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer</note> says. This name is not poorly derived from Mizraim <note>original: *Mythraim*; the biblical son of Ham and traditional ancestor of the Egyptians</note>, who was the first King of the Egyptians and Persians; having obtained divine honors through incantations, he was called Zoroaster, as is deduced above. Others, however, derive the name from the word *mydos* <note>original: *μυδός*</note>, which signifies a red-hot stone. Yet this meaning does not differ much from the meanings of the names Osiris and Zoroaster (the former of which signifies a fire burning everywhere, and the latter a living star, both of which suit the Sun perfectly). From this it is clear that Mithras, Osiris, Mizraim, and Zoroaster are the same being. For Mithras—as Osthanes <note>A legendary Persian magus</note> and, following him, Lactantius the Grammarian state—was worshipped in a cave. 

<margin>The figure of Mithras.</margin>
His image was fashioned with the face of a Lion, in Persian dress with a tiara, holding the horns of a struggling bull with both hands. By this, it was signified that the Moon receives light from him when she begins to be separated from his rays; for she herself, indignant at following her brother, meets him and weaves her light beneath him, thus obscuring it. For this reason, he is said to be in a cave,
<margin>Mithras as the Sun with a Lion's face; what does it mean?</margin>
because the Sun—that is, Mithras—suffers an eclipse. He has the face of a Lion because the Sun has Leo as his primary [zodiac] sign; or because, as the Lion excels among animals, so the Sun excels among the stars. The Moon, however, because she clings more closely to Taurus, was represented by a heifer or a bull. All these things are most similar to the Egyptian mysteries concerning Osiris and Isis; indeed, Statius <note>A Roman poet of the 1st century AD</note> shows they are entirely the same when he sings in the first book of the *Thebaid*:

<margin>Statius, Book 1 of the *Thebaid*.</margin>
> *...whether it pleases you to be called the rosy Titan*
> *after the custom of the Achaemenid race <note>original: *Gentis Achemeniæ*; the Persians</note>, or fruitful Osiris,*
> *or Mithras, who beneath the rocks of a Persian cave*
> *twists the horns of the bull that refuses to follow.*

And Claudian <note>A late 4th-century Roman poet</note> also, when he sings thus:

<margin>Claudian.</margin>
> *...and the Persian women, transfixed by their beautiful guest,*
> *sighed with secret passion;*
> *with heaps of fragrant incense and harvests of Sheba <note>original: *messe Sabæa*</note>,*
> *they seek peace at the altars; they carried the sacred fire*
> *from the inner shrines, and according to the rite, the bullocks*
> *the Chaldean Magi have stationed: the King himself [shining...]*

# CHAPTER VIII.
## On Typhon.

<margin>Diodorus Siculus, Book 1, Chapter 2.</margin>
<margin>Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*.</margin>
<margin>The mythical birth of Typhon.</margin>
<margin>The origin of Typhon.</margin>
**S**ince we have discussed Osiris, Isis, and other Egyptian gods up to this point, and have only touched upon Typhon incidentally, I have decided to treat him separately in this place. Diodorus asserts that Typhon was born from the Titans. Plutarch, in his book *On Isis and Osiris*, relates at length that he did not come forth in the manner of others, but leapt out through his mother’s side from a wound he had struck; and that he was the brother of Osiris and Isis. Others confuse him with Nimrod <note>the biblical figure often associated with the Tower of Babel and tyranny</note> because of the similarity of their lives and most perverse characters. Some believe Typhon was a King of Egypt, an inhumane man whose cruelty caused nearly all of Egypt to be devastated and overturned; he was called Typhon, however, because of the most cruel nature of a Dragon, or because he ravaged Egypt in the manner of a Dragon; or even because he was thought to be born from the blood of a Dragon and a Serpent. Others record that Typhon was a notable Dragon, so named for the singular efficacy of his venom, with which he would burn all things and cause them to wither at his touch.

<margin>Typhon named from the Dragon.</margin>
There are those who say that Typhon was procreated by Juno <note>Hera</note> after she struck the earth, and that he fled into Egypt for fear of Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, where, unable to bear the heat, he <unclear>threw himself submerged into a lake</unclear>. <margin>Strabo. The lands of Pozzuoli, Lipari, and Etna have subterranean channels corresponding with Greece.</margin> Many have distorted this whole fable to refer to natural phenomena. For as Strabo records, the entire region from Cumae all the way to Sicily and Etna, as well as the Lipari Islands and the lands of Pozzuoli, Naples, and Baiae, and the Pithecusae Islands <note>Ischia and Procida</note>, has certain deep caverns beneath it that join together and stretch even into Greece, in which a great sulphurous force resides. Therefore, when subterranean winds blew and frequent earthquakes occurred in those places, and floods of flames and boiling waters, as well as exhalations of fire and ash with embers, were violently emitted, the ancients fabulated that that serpent—or the tyrant of Egypt condemned to perpetual punishment—lay beneath those places; whenever he moved, he would vomit up fire and ash. From the shaking of his shoulders, Mount Epomeo <note>a volcanic mountain on the island of Ischia</note> was born. There are some who believe Typhon to be the force of winds—not subterranean ones, but those blowing from a high place—which reached both the regions of the east and west with its hands, its head rising even to the stars themselves. But let us hear Hesiod.
<margin>How Typhon was called a wind.</margin>

This creature was of a double nature, both human and bestial at once; for Typhon surpassed all others whom the earth had produced in the vastness and strength of his body. Down to his legs, he possessed an immense human form, so great that he seemed taller than the peaks of all the mountains; his head also frequently reached the stars. Furthermore, one of his hands reached as far as the West <term>Hesperus</term> <note>The personification of the evening star, representing the West</note> and the other to the East. From these [shoulders], a hundred heads of dragons protruded; on his legs he bore the massive coils of vipers, whose lengths extended even to the very crown of his head, and those vipers raised a mighty hissing. The entire body of Typhon was covered in feathers; moreover, filthy hair from his head and an uncombed, long beard from his chin fanned out in the wind, and his eyes flashed with fire. Such and so great a Typhon, having hurled glowing stones into heaven, was carried along with a hiss and a bellowing; great storms of fire also flowed from his mouth. When the Gods in heaven saw him breaking forth, they were driven into flight and hurried into Egypt; and when they saw him following, each one transformed himself into various animal forms.

### CHAPTER VIII. 222 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS THE ISIAC TEMPLE

<margin>
Natalis Comes, Book 1 of *Mythologiae*. <note>Natalis Comes (Noël Conti) was a 16th-century mythographer whose work was a standard reference for interpreting classical myths in the Renaissance.</note>
The physical interpretation of Typhon.
</margin>
Therefore, the fables of antiquity attributed to Typhon a stature that touched the stars, because the winds wander most widely. They granted him many heads because of the various forces of the winds. His beard was unkempt and his hair was filthy, because the air is disturbed by the force of the winds and filled with malignant impressions. He was fire-vomiting because, through the force of the winds, the thicker air often blazes into flames, whence the air seems to vomit "fiery swords," <note>original: "igneos enses," likely referring to lightning bolts or meteorological phenomena like meteors.</note> fiery darts, and thunderbolts. His body was covered with feathers because of the speed of the winds. Around his legs were many coils of vipers, because of the harmful power of the winds, which corrupts the air and the earth. His eyes were fiery and flames breathed from his mouth because of the "matter" of the winds, which is composed of dry and hot exhalations. He is imagined to have fled to Mount Caucasus because winds mostly dominate on very high mountains.

<margin>
Plutarch.
Typhon as everything harmful.
The physical interpretation of Typhon.
</margin>
Plutarch also says that Typhon is nothing other than that force of the winds by which the water of the Nile is dried up and the sterility of the earth is induced. Others have thought Typhon to be the pestilential nature of air badly affected by excessive heat; for indeed, the hot force of summer is most harmful to human bodies, making them weaker for enduring the remaining changes of the seasons. Soon, when the heat ceases a little as the Sun recedes through the zodiac, a great abundance of rain and thunder occurs. While the rains cannot coalesce because of the heat, frequent thunderbolts fall; for this reason, Jupiter first drove Typhon into Egypt with thunderbolts, into the hotter places toward the south, and then thrust him under Mount Etna. It is said, moreover, that while the Gods were fleeing and transforming themselves into various shapes, Typhon followed Jupiter as far as the Syrian mountain of Caucasus and wounded him with a thunderbolt. By this, nothing else is suggested except that the regions of the heaven or air—which are like certain Gods (and, as Comes says, the dwellings of the Divinities)—take on various impressions through the force of the Typhonic winds and are condensed into various forms and figures. They are then purified by Jupiter, or the Sun, through the power of his rays, the multi-formed air being dissipated, and with Typhon "slain," the air is restored to its original face of serenity.

<margin>
Synesius, *On Providence*. An ethical interpretation of Typhon. <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD) was a philosopher-bishop. His work *On Providence* uses the Egyptian myth of Osiris and Typhon as a political allegory for good and evil governance.</note>
</margin>
Certain authors seem to pull this whole fable toward morality, as Synesius does in two entire books titled *On Providence*. Among other things, he speaks thus: "But Typhon was neither similar to his own race in nature, nor to any human at all, and in short, he was not even similar to himself; rather, he was a certain varied evil. At one moment he seemed to be sluggish, a useless weight upon the earth, withdrawing from sleep only as much as was necessary to serve his belly, and bringing other instruments to a sleeper; yet at another moment, neglecting even the moderate things that are necessary for nature, he would exult unbecomingly and cause trouble both to his equals and to his elders. For he admired the strength of his body as the most perfect good, and used it poorly, breaking down doors and pelted people with clods of earth; and if he had caused a wound to someone or perpetrated some other evil, he rejoiced as if it were a testimony to his virtue."

Under these and similar descriptions, which he pursues at length throughout his two books, Synesius describes nothing other than a vicious, inconsistent, foolish, and reckless man who is a despiser of good things and a seeker of evil, as will be clear to the reader. This is also what those do who say that Typhon was a ferocious and active man, who, having gathered a great band of exiles and envious people, attempted to drive Jupiter from his kingdom—

Mercury stole these back and returned them to Jupiter, because afterward the minds of those who had deserted Jupiter were reconciled by his speech. <margin>Moral interpretation of Typhon.</margin> Although many have also fashioned this fable to recall minds from ambition, since they wish to signify that it [ambition] is the worst of almost all vices, they called her the daughter of Erebus <note>Erebus was the personification of primordial darkness in Greek mythology.</note> and said she breathes fire from her mouth. <margin>The evil of ambition.</margin> This ambition rises up against Jupiter <note>Representing divine order or reason.</note>, because there is no care for religion, no care for humanity, and no care for justice where ambitious fury sprouts; because it has many heads, they signified its many methods, its many anxieties, and its many troubles. Jupiter finally crushes and overthrows this Typhon, or this ambition fleeing here and there; for even if desire resists reason and wisdom for a while, it is ultimately conquered by them. But to summarize much in a few words: whatever is vicious, corrupt, violent, foolish, reckless, and presumptuous in the discipline of morals; or whatever is harmful, violent, stubborn, sinister, scorched, and corrupt in the consideration of nature—everything that threatens the destruction of things—the ancients called by the name of Typhon. For this reason, they also called him a certain demonic force. <margin>Typhonic properties:</margin> Of this sort of "Typhon" were Nimrod, Esau, Ahab, and others mentioned in the Sacred Scriptures—servants of ambition and workshops of all iniquity; there are also Typhons of this kind in the sublunary world <note>The region below the moon, which in ancient science was the realm of change, decay, and the four elements.</note>: harmful atmospheric impressions, violent eruptions of fire, impetuous winds, excessive drought, and six hundred similar portents of the elements. I would have much to say here about the birth of Typhon, the conspiracy made against his brother Osiris, the dismemberment of Osiris's body performed by Typhon, and the death of Typhon; likewise, the reason why the Egyptians applied these things to the nature of reality. But since we will treat these matters both in the following sections and in other places, we refer the reader to consult those.

# CHAPTER IX.

->On the ceremonies and rites of the Egyptians, which they observed both in sacrifices and in other solemnities.<-

Osiris, having been killed by his impious brother Typhon—who was, to use the words of Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene, a Neoplatonist philosopher and bishop.</note>, a "workshop of all wickedness"—seems to have provided the beginning of the detestable sacrifices practiced by the Egyptians. And so Osiris, King of Egypt, since he had governed Egypt most wisely for many years, earned such a reputation among everyone that even while alive he was numbered among the Gods and Divinities. Typhon, however, stirred by a frenzy and the sting of envy against his brother Osiris, burned with an irreconcilable hatred toward the Egyptians, because they—and especially the common people—admired Osiris and sought all good things for him everywhere, in conversations, in songs, at home, and in public sacrifices.
