### CHAPTER IX. 224 THE ISIAIC TEMPLE OF EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

<margin>The discord of Osiris and Typhon.</margin>
Driven by madness, Typhon allied himself with the Titans—who were to be his accomplices in crime—and left no stone unturned in his plots to remove his brother from his path. At last, having deceitfully and treacherously slain him and seized the kingdom, <margin>Osiris is cut into pieces by Typhon.</margin> Typhon cut the body of Osiris into twenty-six (or as others say, fourteen) parts. He distributed these parts among those who had participated in the crime and been conscious of the deed, leaving a single part of the body with each person. However, Isis, his wife—a most prudent woman and one who loved her husband above all others—learned of the crime. With the help of her son Horus <note>The text reads *Osi*, likely a shorthand or error for *Ori* (Horus).</note> and Anubis, she avenged her husband's death. Having killed Typhon and the followers of his crime, she recovered the kingdom. Once these things were finished, Isis was anxious for her husband's body. Since all the parts of Osiris had been intentionally scattered by Typhon, and she had found nothing except the genitals <note>original: *pudenda*</note>, she desired that her husband’s tomb remain uncertain, yet that he be held in honor by the Egyptians and by every individual man. Therefore, out of spices and wax, she fashioned those individual parts into the shape of a man resembling her husband. Then, having summoned the Priests of Egypt, she gave each of them an image of Osiris, asserting that his body had been entrusted to them alone. She made them swear a solemn oath that they would never reveal to anyone that they possessed the tomb of Osiris, but that they would worship it in secret as a God. She commanded them to dedicate whatever animal they preferred to him; they were to worship this animal as if it were the living Osiris, and after its death, they were to observe it with similar ceremonies and rituals. Indeed, to bind them to her with greater goodwill and make them more ready to act, she assigned certain revenues to each of them so they might more promptly carry out the intended worship. The Priests, enticed by the benefit bestowed upon them, strove with everything they had to promote the honor and worship of Osiris; for they immediately turned their minds toward new methods of manufacturing and worshipping idols. From this source, <margin>The origin of impious sacrifices.</margin> those celebrated <term>Phallophoria</term> <note>Festivals where representations of the male generative organ were carried in procession.</note>, <term>Pammelia</term>, <term>Dionysia</term> <note>The Greek festivals of Bacchus, which Kircher identifies as originating from Egyptian Osiris-worship.</note>, and other portentous sacred rites and ceremonies (of which we shall speak soon) emerged as if from a Trojan horse—stupid sacrifices filled with innumerable impieties. These later flourished, disseminated by the works of demons, not only throughout Egypt but throughout the entire world. Indeed, the rituals of this kind are recorded by various authors. On fixed days of the year, the Priests, in the hidden recesses of the temple, would pretend to have the body of Osiris and an idol buried in a place unknown to men. On that very day, they would wail with the greatest expression of sorrow and enormous lamentations. <margin>Rites in the search for the body of Osiris.</margin> As a sign of the highest mourning, they would shave their heads, beat their breasts, and strike their flesh with frequently repeated blows. They would even cut themselves, <margin>The cruelty of the Priests toward themselves.</margin> (O, the blind hearts of mortals!) renewing the scars of old wounds with a sense of the greatest pain—and they did this in memory of Osiris, who was snatched away by such a regrettable death. However, after a certain interval of days had passed in wailing and lamentations, as if the body of Osiris had been found by divine intervention, they would suddenly leap from mourning to extreme dissipation, and from wailing to songs, hymns, joys, and dances <note>original: *tripudiaque*</note>. And this was the ritual observed by the Egyptians in the discovery of the body of Osiris. <margin>Isiac rites.</margin> In the Isiac rites, on the day appointed for performing her sacred duties, the Priests would wander through the city streets. They wailed, recalling the death of Osiris to memory with the greatest groans and shrieks; dressed in a long linen toga, they carried upon their heads a statue of Anubis, who was dog-faced <note>original Greek: *κυνοπρόσωπον* (*kynoprosopon*)</note>, and in their right hand, a branch of wormwood...

### SYNTAGMA III. ON THE ORIGIN OF EGYPTIAN IDOLATRY. CHAPTER IX.

<note>Suetonius</note> reports concerning Domitian that they [the Romans], honoring these rites, stabilized those which had been recalled from the underworld; this is what <term>Lucan</term><note>Marcus Annaeus Lucanus (39–65 AD), a Roman poet.</note> seems to reproach the Romans for when he says:

<margin>Tertullian.</margin>
And <term>Tertullian</term><note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD) known for his critiques of Roman paganism.</note> seems to most especially object to the Romans for that extreme levity and inconstancy in receiving and changing their gods, when he says: *Even regarding your very gods, those things which your fathers had decreed, you yourselves, being most compliant, have rescinded. Father Bacchus with his mysteries—which the Consuls, by the authority of the Senate, banished not only from the City but from all of Italy—as well as <term>Serapis</term>, <term>Isis</term>, and <term>Harpocrates</term> with his <term>Cynocephalus</term><note>A "dog-headed" figure, referring to the god Anubis.</note>, were prohibited from being brought into their Capitol, that is, they were driven from the assembly of the gods; the Consuls Piso and Gabinius, who were certainly not Christians, abolished them and even overturned their altars, restraining the vices of shameful and idle superstitions; yet you, having restored these, have conferred upon them the highest majesty, etc.* <term>Aelius Spartianus</term> and <term>Eutropius</term>, along with <term>Lampridius</term>, also report that <term>Commodus</term> and <term>Antoninus Caracalla</term> were so devoted to these sacred rites that they themselves, with shaved heads and carrying sistrums, did not disdain to mix with the lowest rabble, wandering through the city streets and crossroads in a certain frantic dissolution of spirit.

<margin>Commodus and Caracalla were students of the Isiac rites.</margin>
Furthermore, concerning the <term>Apis</term> and <term>Serapis</term> of the Egyptians, and their ridiculous sacred rites and vain rituals, enough has been said in the preceding chapters; it remains for us to say something concerning the <term>Phallophoria</term>, <term>Pammelia</term>, and <term>Dionysia</term>, though we shall do so only very soberly and sparingly. For it is better to damn to eternal darkness those enormous things—not sacrifices, but crimes; not ceremonies, but iniquities; those most shameful rites, I say, which are true inventions of the Devil for plunging souls into every kind of vice—rather than to offend chaste ears by reciting them.

<margin>What the phallus is. Herodotus, book 2.</margin>
The <term>Phallophoria</term><note>Literally "carrying of the phallus."</note> therefore arose from the discovered genitals of <term>Osiris</term> which were affected by divine worship, as we said a little earlier. For the <term>Phallus</term> is called <term>Priapus</term>, and signifies the male member; wherefore, when <term>Herodotus</term> says that in the sacred rites of Dionysus there were Phalli, we understand them to be Priapuses, that is, the male members which hang from the neck of the Apis bull and above his back, as appears from the figure itself which we displayed above in chapter four.

<margin>Statues of phalli measuring a cubit.</margin>
<term>Diodorus</term>, in discussing Egyptian sacred rites, called the genitals of Osiris the "phallus," and in memory of that thing, statues a cubit long were made and called by the same name; these were carried around preceded by a flute-player. Herodotus explains the ritual of this, and shows that <term>Melampus</term> demonstrated it to the Greeks from Egypt; <term>Lucian</term> writes that there were phalli before the doors of the Syrian Goddess, which he says were placed there for Dionysus by his stepmother Hera. Others say, with <term>Stephanus</term>: *elongated pieces of wood having a leather penis at the end*; <note>original: Ξύλον ἐπίμηκες ἔχον ἐν τῷ ἄκρῳ σκύτινον αἰδοῖον</note> concerning which, see <term>Suidas</term>, and the interpretation of <term>Aristophanes</term> in the *Acharnians*, and others; and hence the <term>Phallagogia</term> (the celebration and procession which was performed for Dionysus) was named from the phalli, according to <term>Hesychius</term>. It was also called <term>Phallologia</term>, as <term>Theodoret</term> and <term>Phornutus</term> say, that is, days and festivals dedicated to Priapus; from which they were also called *phallovitrobuli*, from phalli made of glass, although they were also made of other materials: ivory, gold, and—if it please the gods—of silk and linen cloth, which women used.

...since we shall speak of these things many times throughout this entire work, I have judged it superfluous to say more here; therefore, let us gradually descend to the particulars of the sacrifices.

# CHAPTER X.

->*Concerning the various Sacrifices attributed to the Gods, and their properties.*<-

To make it clear, however, that the virtues of the Elements and of natural things—as well as the powers of those <term>demons</term><note>In this context, "demons" (daemones) refers to intermediary spirits or spiritual intelligences that Athanasius Kircher believed inhabited the natural world, rather than necessarily "evil" spirits.</note> who dwell within them, whom the ignorant multitude considered to be Gods—were called by these names by the wise, it will not be out of place if I briefly explain the reasons for the sacrifices attributed to individual Gods. Indeed, there were many kinds of sacred rites established by the ancients according to the nature of each God, including various victims, various methods of <term>fumigation</term><note>The burning of incense or aromatic herbs as part of a ritual.</note>, and differing appearances of those performing the sacrifice. For <term>salted meal</term><note>original: "molæ". A mixture of grain and salt traditionally sprinkled on sacrificial victims.</note> was not offered to all, nor were lamps lit for all; nor were sacred rites always performed upon high altars, nor always by day. Finally, diverse sacrifices were offered everywhere according to the customs of different nations, the variety of times, and the nature of the supposed Gods; for some were suited to celestial beings, others to terrestrial ones; some to aquatic beings, and others to the gods of the underworld. Of these, some were performed privately, others publicly.

<margin>Terrestrial Gods.</margin>
First of all, therefore, it is fitting to know that the influence of food and the temperament of the air contribute to the strength and goodness of individuals not only in animals or plants, but also in those demons with which the wise have taught this entire visible universe is filled. For those who dwell in caverns are more ungentle, fierce, and wild, and consist of a coarser matter—since it approaches closer to the physical body (as <term>Psellus</term><note>Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine monk and scholar who wrote "De Operatione Daemonum" (On the Operation of Demons).</note> asserts somewhat incautiously in the books he published concerning demons)—than those demons who inhabit the region of fire or air. This happens, as he says, because of the nature of their habitation and the power of the stars. For why is it a wonder, says <term>Natalis Comes</term><note>Natale Conti (1520–1582), an influential Renaissance mythographer.</note>, that the stars have great power in these matters, since they are said to rule over both metals and the hardest stones, and plants? Or who does not know that some metals are attributed to the Sun, others to the Moon, others to Venus, others to Mercury, and others to other stars because of certain properties and similarities, which also happens to other bodies? They believe, therefore, that the entire power of sacred rites, and the method of rightly appeasing all the Gods, consists in knowing the nature of these demons.

<margin>Fiery Gods were worshipped with analogous things.</margin>
Therefore, since they believed the celestial bodies were fiery, they added lights and shapes and many things pertaining to sight in the sacrifices for these; for them, high altars were built, upon which lights were lit and slaughtered victims were sacrificed. Thus, when sacred rites were performed for the Higher Gods, and especially for Jupiter, altars were erected in high places, as <term>Melanthes</term><note>An ancient Greek author whose works are mostly lost; he is often cited in scholia regarding religious rituals.</note> says:

> Every mountain is called the mountain of Jupiter, since it was the custom of the ancients to perform sacrifices in a high place to the God who is most high.
<note>original Greek: "Πᾶν δ' ὄρ@ τῷ Διὸς ὀνομάζε), ἐπεὶ ἔθ@, ἦν τοῖς παλαιοῖς ὑψίστῳ ὄντι τῷ Θεῷ ἐν ὕψει θυσίας ποιεῖσθ)." Kircher provides the Latin translation immediately following: "Omnis, inquit, mons, mons Iouis appellatur, quoniam mos fuit antiquorum, vt altissimo Deo existenti in loco sublimi sacrificarent."</note>

Thus Apollonius...

### SYNTAGMA III. ON THE ORIGIN OF EGYPTIAN IDOLATRY. CHAPTER X.

<margin>Apollonius Rhodius in the *Argonautica*.</margin>
<margin>The etymology of "altar".</margin>
<margin>The reasoning for erecting temples.</margin>
...with a massive altar built and sacred rites placed upon the mountains, because Jupiter himself willed it; and indeed, even where there was no mountain, they built a high altar upon the shore. It is from this practice that the <term>etymology</term><note>The study of the origin of words.</note> of the word "altar" seems to derive, as if one were saying a "high altar" <note>original: "altam aram"</note>. Furthermore, there was a custom among them when constructing the fabrics of temples: they were to be built not only high and spacious, but also in such a way that they might immediately catch the rising Sun (which we recall was the case in the temple of Serapis, as mentioned above). As Plutarch says in his *Life of Numa Pompilius*, they were not to be hindered by any obstruction but were to be open on all sides and completely unencumbered, as Promachides of Heraclea and Dionysius Thrax testify in these words:

<margin>Promachides of Heraclea.</margin>
<margin>Dionysius Thrax.</note>
<note>original Greek: "Οἱ γὰρ ναοὶ τῶν παλαιῶν, καὶ τὸν ἥλιον ὑπερκύψαντα εὐθὺς ὑποδέχεσθαι εἰώθεσαν, καὶ τῷ φωτὶ εὐθὺς ἐμπίπλασθαι τῶν θυρῶν ἀναπεπταμένων, ὅπου καὶ τὰ ἱερὰ ἐῤῥέζετο."</note>
*For the temples of the ancients were accustomed to receive the rising Sun immediately, and to be filled with light as soon as the doors were thrown open, at the very place where the sacrifices were performed.*

<margin>Buildings were founded according to the analogy of the Gods.</margin>
I should certainly not think it right to overlook the fact that the ancients intended the styles of buildings to correspond closely to the nature of those Gods to whom they were dedicated. For Jupiter, Mars, and Hercules, only the **Doric** style was used; for Bacchus, Apollo, and Diana, the **Ionic**; and the **Corinthian** was believed to be especially suited to the virgin Vesta—although sometimes all these styles were used in the same temple. In the shrine of Minerva Alea among the Tegeatans, whose architect was Scopas of Paros, there was a triple order of columns: the first was of Doric work; the second, Corinthian; and the third, which was next to the temple (as Vitruvius testifies), was fashioned with Ionic skill. This occurred when shrines were consecrated to various Gods, or dedicated to those Gods whose power was manifold, relating to both males and females and the elements. Such were the temples of Olympian Jupiter and Juno Triphylia, both crafted by the artisan Oxilus with Doric work and columns, as Pausanias testifies. The Egyptians especially observed this method of constructing temples, as was said regarding the temple of Serapis and other Gods, about whom the Greek Possidippus writes in an epigram:

<margin>Possidippus.</margin>
> *He says the shrines, with doors unlocked, catch*
> *the first rays of Vulcan and Phoebus as the Sun rises.*

<margin>Virgil, Book 12 of the *Aeneid*.</margin>
Virgil also writes of these things with no less elegance than skill:

->*They turned their eyes toward the rising Sun.*<-

<margin>The time of sacrifices.</margin>
Furthermore, it was the custom of the ancients that sacrifices were not made indiscriminately at any time, but for individual Gods at times consistent with their natures. Hence, offerings were made to the celestial gods in the morning at sunrise, and to the gods of the underworld at sunset. For this reason the Egyptians, according to Plutarch, used certain perfumes and <term>incense</term><note>original: "incensis", referring to burnt aromatic offerings.</note> composed of various types of spices every day—at morning, noon, and evening—to attract the Divine powers. The mysteries of this <term>suffumigation</term><note>The ritual act of burning incense or herbs to produce smoke.</note> will be set forth in the *Encyclopedia of the Egyptians*. For the same reason, the Egyptians are said to have attributed different months to different Gods...

### CHAPTER X. 232 THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE TEMPLE OF ISIS

<margin>Different garments for different Gods.</margin>
...they established that each of the Gods should be worshiped at the time most consistent with their natural condition. Furthermore, different garments were assigned to different Gods, as the logic of their attire varied. For the gods of the underworld, black garments were used, as the appearance of the Eumenides <note>The Furies, deities of vengeance.</note> and Pluto sufficiently shows. For the celestial or aerial gods, purple or light blue garments were appropriate, matching the color of the heavens, as Menander observes. For certain others, white was used, such as in the sacrifices to Ceres, according to those lines of Ovid <note>original: "Nasonis", referring to Publius Ovidius Naso.</note>:

> ->White suits Ceres; wear white garments for the Cerealia;<-
> ->now there will be no use for dark-colored wool.<-

I find that the Egyptians especially used white, dark, and blue linen garments in their sacrifices; these will be discussed at length in the explanation of the Bembine Tablet <note>A famous bronze tablet of Isiac provenance that was a central object of study for Kircher.</note>.

<margin>Different fire in different sacrifices of the Gods.</margin>
Furthermore, they also observed a specific logic regarding fire in their sacrifices. One type of fire was celestial, another aerial, and finally, another was terrestrial. They ignited the first, the celestial, from the rays of the sun gathered upon concave and highly polished surfaces. They drew out the second type from the striking of two bodies together, which they called "aerial" because it was generated from the friction of the air. Finally, they lit the third kind of fire from another fire, which they called "terrestrial" because it burned from an impure flame imbued with various earthly mixtures.

<margin>Different woods for different Gods.</margin>
Once the fire was procured and arranged, no small amount of diligence was applied to choosing the woods that were suitable for each kind of sacred rite. Fire was not kindled from just any wood, nor (as the saying goes) "is a Mercury made from any piece of timber" <note>A Latin proverb meaning that not every person has the natural talent to become a scholar or a wise man.</note>; rather, it was made from the woods named in the laws of the sacrifices. Thus, in the rites of Serapis, Pausanias testifies that they used all kinds of wood;
<margin>The statue of Serapis made from every kind of wood and mineral.</margin>
this is abundantly demonstrated by his statue, which was fashioned from every kind of wood and mineral. In the rites of Osiris, they used the Lotus and *Chenosyris* (or ivy); in those of Isis, *Seriphium* (or sea-wormwood), the Reed, and the *Cyllo-cyperus*, which they call <term>κύπειρον</term> <note>galingale or a type of sedge</note>, were employed; regarding these, see the explanation of the Bembine Tablet. Having been taught by these examples, the Greeks in ancient times
<margin>Virgil, Book 2 of the *Georgics*.</margin>
burned no wood in the rites of Bacchus except for the *Oporobasilis*, or the *Phibalean* fig, or the chaste-tree with vine leaves, as Hegemon says. In the rites of Venus, myrtle was burned; but among the Sicyonians, fire was made only from juniper wood, to which
<margin>Pausanias in *Description of Greece: Corinth*.</margin>
leaves of "youth's-love" <note>original: "pæderotis", a plant identified by some as a species of acanthus or chervil</note> were added, as Pausanias says. In the rites of Jupiter, they used holm-oak; in those of Mars, ash; in those of Hercules, white poplar, oak, or cornelian cherry, as written by Ephorus and by Epigenes in *The Heroine*. Supporting this matter are
<margin>Ephorus, Book 2 of *The Weights of Asia*. Epigenes in *The Heroine*.</margin>
the writings of Timaeus Siculus in the second book of his histories, where the virgins of the Locrians, by order of the oracle, were slaughtered by the Trojans and burned with wood from sterile and wild trees. It is also proof of the extreme care they took in choosing wood for sacrifices that, along with the Temple-keepers, Augurs, Heralds, and Interpreters, there were also officials called <term>Lignitores</term> <note>Wood-bearers or fuel-preparers</note> who presided over the sacrifices, whose only task was to ensure that the legally prescribed woods were prepared and properly consumed by the fire. For they believed that unless everything was kept according to the law in sacrifices, public calamities would arise; an example of this is seen when anyone entered the temple of Jupiter Lycaeus, or even the altar...

### PART III. ON THE ORIGIN OF EGYPTIAN IDOLATRY. 233 CHAPTER X.

...precinct, if he had entered without first performing the legitimate purifications <note>original: "lustrationibus", ritual cleansing rituals involving water or fire.</note>, he would surely die within a year, as Hegesander and Pausanias have recorded. Theagenes mentions this in his book *On the Gods*; and Pausanias mentions in his earlier books on Elis and in his Lydian-Persian accounts that, due to a lack of proper purification, two cities <margin>Theagenes, Book *On the Gods*.</margin>—Hypæpa and Hierocæsarea—were swallowed up. He says that in these cities there was a very large temple with inner chambers and altars upon which there were ashes of a color quite different from common ash. Upon entering, a priest wearing a tiara <note>A traditional Persian or priestly head-covering.</note> on his head would place wood on the altar and, speaking in a language unknown to the Greeks, would invoke the surname of an unknown God. When he had recited a chant from a book in a language entirely foreign to the Greeks and finished his prayer, a most pure flame would spontaneously burst forth from the wood without any fire being applied, while all the bystanders watched from a distance. Whether this is a fable or a history, it certainly draws its origin from nowhere else but Ezra. It is said that when the temple had been destroyed by Cyrus and finally restored, and the sacred fire was missing with which to perform sacrifices, Ezra—together with the rest of the assembly—requested the Lord with urgent prayers to provide the sacred fire. While they were praying, Gorionides <note>Referring to the author of the *Josippon*, a medieval history of the Jews popularly attributed to Joseph ben Gorion.</note> says:

<margin>Gorionides, Chapter 5.</margin>
> And it happened while they were praying with these words, there was a certain elder among the sages who remembered the place where Jeremiah the Prophet had hidden the fire. The elder stood up and all the elders followed him, and behold, he saw a pit under the wall with a large stone over it, plastered with lime. They broke through the plaster and rolled the stone away from the mouth of the pit, and they saw in it water like thick oil and honey. Ezra said to the priests: "Go down into the pit and take some of the water." They went down into the pit, carried the water, and went to the Temple. They sprinkled the water upon the altar and upon the wood. As they did this, a fire suddenly blazed up with a terrible and mighty flame, and the flame licked it, and the fire was a consuming fire and very strong.

> *As they were praying to the Lord with these urgent words, one of the elder priests remembered the place where the sacred fire had been hidden by the Prophet Jeremiah; and having gone out with the priests, behold, under a wall was a cistern protected by a large stone and encrusted with lime. When they had opened it by removing the lime and the rock, there soon appeared water like thick fat or honey; and Ezra commanded the priests to go down and draw the water. Once this was done, the priest approached the altar, and when <margin>The fire is lit by a miracle.</margin> he had sprinkled the victims and the wood placed on the altar with the water, the fire soon blazed up into a huge flame.*

From this, it is apparent that the Greeks, with the greatest zeal, attempted to drag sacred histories into their own fables, as we showed just before regarding the rites performed in Lydian-Persia.

Furthermore, there were specific waters believed to be more suitable for individual sacrifices. For instance, in the sacred rites and weddings at Athens, no water was used except from the Callirhoë spring, as <margin>Different waters for different Gods.</margin> was the custom. In Delos, the water of the temple was used for nothing else but sacred rites; nor were the waters of all other rivers thought to be suitable for every sacrifice. Indeed, the water of the Alpheus was pleasing to Olympian Jupiter, as Pausanias testifies in his *Arcadian* writings. But regarding the so-called Spring of Amphiaraus, because it was in the territory of the Oropians near the temple of Amphiaraus and Apollo, they deemed it unlawful to use its water for purification or even for washing hands. In the Egyptian rites, they used the water of the Nile and no other—specifically that which an Ibis <note>A bird sacred to the god Thoth, often associated with wisdom and purity in Egyptian lore.</note> had made turbid with its foot. Such was the industry and diligence, or if you prefer, the superstition, of the ancients in rightly performing sacred matters.

Moreover, during the sacrifices themselves, the victims, the altars, and the men <margin>Different crowns.</margin> were all crowned...

### CHAPTER X. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS 234

...men sacrificing; which are beautifully described in the verses of the Delphic Oracle found in Demosthenes’ oration *Against Meidias*. Indeed, because different trees were consecrated to different Gods, the Priests who were about to sacrifice to various Gods were adorned with various crowns. For example, in the Dionysian <note>Festivals of Dionysus or Bacchus, the god of wine.</note> rites, they used myrtle, as noted by <margin>Timachidas.</margin> Timachidas in his book *On Crowns*, and Aristophanes in *The Branches*:

<margin>Aristophanes.</margin>
->Shaking a crown of myrtles,<-
->heavy with fruit and blooming<-
->about your head.<-
<note>original Greek: "Πολύκαρπον μὲν τινάσσων / ἀμφικεφαλᾶ βρύοντα / στέφανον μυρτῶν"</note>

<margin>In the rites of Ceres.</margin>
But in the rites of Ceres <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture, equivalent to the Greek Demeter.</note>, they were crowned with oak, as a perpetual memorial of the benefit received from that Goddess, according to that passage from Virgil. In which the things said thus far are quite aptly described:

<margin>Virgil, Book 1 of the Georgics.</margin>

->anyone puts the sickle to the ripe grain,<-
->should he, his temples wreathed with twisted oak,<-

<note>original Latin: "neque ante / Falcem maturis quisquam supponat aristis, / Quam Cereri torta redimitus tempora quercu, / Det motus incompositos & carmina dicat."</note>

<margin>In the rites of Hercules.</margin>
In the rites of Hercules, they were crowned with Poplar, according to the passage of Virgil cited before; for the Poplar was a symbol of vigor and strength.
->Their temples are bound with branches of poplar.<-
<note>original: "Populeis adsunt evincti tempora ramis."</note>

<margin>In the rites of Apollo. Apollonius, Book 2 of the Argonautica.</margin>
In the sacrifice to Apollo, they were crowned with laurel, as Apollonius of Rhodes notes. For since Apollo was the Sun, they aptly attributed the solar plant to him.
->And their golden temples are bound with green laurel.<-
<note>original: "Flavaque sunt viridi redimiti tempora lauro."</note>

<margin>What crowns were used in the Egyptian rites.</margin>
In the Egyptian rites, we read that they were crowned with ivy, <term>scryphium</term> <note>A type of floral garland or wreath often associated with festive or sacred adornment in antiquity.</note>, laurel, lotus, <term>persea</term> <note>An Egyptian tree, likely *Mimusops schimperi*, whose fruit and leaves were sacred to Thoth and Isis.</note>, etc. Andreas of Tenedos writes in his *Voyage of the Propontis* that the ancients used a triple order of crowning in sacred rites. The commentator on Apollonius also explained this passage: some placed crowns high upon the head, others pressed them down as far as the temples, and others drew them down to the neck. Truly, not only were the priests or those sacrificing crowned in the rites, but also the vessels they used and the victims that were to be sacrificed; crowns were placed around the necks of the animals, and their horns were gilded.

<margin>Different victims for different Gods.</margin>
Finally, there was no small diligence in choosing victims for the sacrifices of individual Gods, since some were slain for the good Gods so that they might be helpful, and others for the bad Gods so they would not be harmful. For black victims were appropriate for the bad, white for the good; sterile victims for the sterile deities, and pregnant ones for the fertile; males for male gods, and females for female gods. They offered victims of a subtle and celestial nature to the celestial gods; aerial victims to the aerial ones; watery victims to the aquatic; and victims of an earthy nature to the terrestrial. This was often done due to some similarity, such as the horse to the Sun because of its speed, etc. All these things are clearly evident from the Egyptian rites. Of all the Gods, they especially worshipped Osiris, Isis, Horus, the Nile, Canopus, Apis (or Serapis), and Rhea (or Vesta); yet they did not worship them indiscriminately, but each one with certain ritu-

# CHAPTER X. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>
The search for Horus was performed with sistrums.
</margin>
...since it was the highest part of the air, then musical instruments were employed. For this reason, the search for Horus <note>A ritual reenactment of the goddess Isis searching for her son Horus (or her husband Osiris), a central myth in Egyptian religion.</note> was performed with sistrums <note>The sistrum was a sacred metal rattle used in Egyptian liturgy to ward off evil spirits and symbolize the pulsing of the universe.</note> and cymbals. For the same reason, musical instruments are not attributed to Mercury <note>Thoth</note> and Apollo unless they are considered as the power of the Sun dominating the air.

<margin>
Strophe and Antistrophe.
Aristoxenus, *Book on the Holes of Flutes*.
Bito.
</margin>
Therefore, we read in ancient records that in sacrifices of this kind, the melodies of the Strophe and Antistrophe <note>In ancient choral performance, the 'strophe' (turning) and 'antistrophe' (counter-turning) involved moving across the stage to mimic the rotation of the heavens.</note> were sung in imitation of the movement of the stars, as Aristoxenus says in his book *On the Holes of Flutes*, and Bito in the book he wrote to Attalus *On Musical Instruments*. For during those sacred rites, they turned now this way and now that, and through the Strophe, they signified the primary movement of this Universe; through the Antistrophe, they signified the specific motions of the individual planets.

<margin>
What did the song signify mystically?
</margin>
Furthermore, the chants in the sacred rites were nothing other than commemorations of those benefits which the Gods themselves had kindly bestowed upon men, along with the glorification of the power, clemency, and liberality of the Gods themselves. 
<margin>
Philochorus, *On Sacrifices*.
</margin>
They were also accompanied by prayers, so that the Gods might approach those praying with kindness and ease, as Philochorus says.

<margin>
With what the aquatic Gods were delighted.
</margin>
But in truth, because those spirits <note>original: "dæmones," referring here to divine or elemental entities rather than "demons" in the modern sense.</note> who presided over the waters were thought to be thicker in substance due to the nature of their environment, more substantial offerings were presented in their sacrifices than either smells or songs—things that pertained to taste and had a more solid body. Hence the Nile, Canopus, and Oceanus <note>Personifications of the Nile River, its delta, and the world-encircling sea.</note> were expressed in ancient times by the Egyptians with various symbols denoting water; for these were their aquatic spirits. Among the Greeks, however, the blood of slaughtered victims was collected and poured from a shallow bowl into the sea with 
<margin>
Apollonius, Book 4.
</margin>
prayers, according to that passage of Apollonius <note>original: "Apollon. l. 4." referring to the *Argonautica* by Apollonius of Rhodes.</note>:

> ->*He, pouring forth prayers, slaughtered it in the wave of the sea*<-
> ->*Soon he casts it from the stern.*<-

<margin>
Virgil.
</margin>
To which that line of Virgil also corresponds, while he indicates the method of sacrifices:

> ->*Standing far off on the prow he holds the bowl, and proffers the*<-
> ->*entrails into the salt waves, and pours liquid wine.*<-

<margin>
Nymphs.
</margin>
Likewise, since the Nymphs were thought to be Goddesses of the waters, they also required somewhat thicker sacrifices, to whom honey, milk, and mead were offered. However, the sacrifices made to Serapis (or the Egyptian Pluto), Rhea, Proserpina, and other terrestrial and infernal Gods differed greatly—not only in time, but also in the color of the victims and the ritual. For as we have said, these sacrifices were usually performed only at night, as Virgil testifies:

<margin>
Virgil, Book 6.
</margin>
> ->*Then for the Stygian King he begins the nocturnal altars.*<-

> ->*Hither the chaste Sibyl*<-
> ->*Shall drench you with much blood of black cattle.*<-

### TREATISE III. ON THE ORIGIN OF EGYPTIAN IDOLATRY. CHAPTER X. 239

<margin>Cleon in the 1st book of the *Argonautica*. Myrtilus in the 2nd book of *Lesbian Histories*.</margin>
Just as victims sacrificed to the Heavenly gods <note>original: "Superis"</note> were forced to turn their throats upward, so those sacrificed to the Infernal gods <note>original: "inferis," the gods of the underworld</note> held their heads pressed down toward the earth, as Cleon says in the first book of the *Argonautica*, and Myrtilus in the second book of *Lesbian Histories* in these words:

<note>original Greek: Εἰώθασιν οἱ ἱερεῖς τὰ θύματα τοῖς μὲν κατὰ θεοὺς ἀποστρέφειν εἰς τὴν γῆν ἀποτείνοντάς τὰς κεφαλάς· ἔτω δὲ θύουσι τοῖς ὑποχθονίοις, τοῖς δὲ οὐρανίοις ἀεὶ ἀναστρέφουσι τῷ ἱερεῖον τὸν τράχηλον σφάζοντες.</note>
"The priests are accustomed," he says, "to cut the heads of victims sacrificed to the gods below upon the ground—for thus they sacrifice to the subterranean ones—but when sacrificing to the heavenly ones, they slaughter them while turning the necks of the victims upward." The victims of these underworld gods were also slaughtered in dug-out pits, and their blood, mixed with wine, was poured into those pits in the earth destined for that purpose, as noted by Apollonius and Ovid.
<margin>Ovid, Book 3.</margin>

<margin>Sacrifices to Pluto.</margin>
In Egypt, however, when sacred rites were performed for Serapis <note>A syncretic god combining Osiris and Apis, often equated by the Greeks with Pluto or Hades.</note> or the Argive Pluto of the underworld, he was thought to be a divine mind diffused through the entire mass of the earth, penetrating and governing all things just as the Ocean is believed to penetrate the sea. His sacred rites did not shrink entirely from the sacrifices of the Heavenly gods; for fire was employed, and oil instead of wine, according to that passage of Virgil:

> Then he begins the nocturnal altars to the Stygian King,
> And places the solid entrails of bulls upon the flames,
> Pouring rich oil over the smoking vitals.
<note>A quote from Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book VI, describing a sacrifice to Pluto (the Stygian King).</note>

<margin>White victims were sacrificed to beneficial gods, black to malevolent ones.</margin>
Furthermore, white and gentle victims were sacrificed to all the beneficial gods; but to the malevolent ones, so that they might not do harm, both black and fiercer victims were thought appropriate. Similarly, the Egyptians would cast down donkeys and offer red cows to Typhon <note>The Egyptian god Set, associated with chaos and storms, often depicted with red hair or skin.</note>. They also attempted to appease these deities with black garments. The reason why sacrifice was made to the underworld gods was that they were considered the authors of all evils, as Sophocles signifies in *Electra*. Sacred rites were usually performed for them by those who had recovered from some disease, as if the gods had spared them; this type of ritual was called a <term>katharmós</term> <note>original Greek: καθαρμός; a purification or ritual cleansing.</note>, or a lustration.

Truly, which sacrificial rites are appropriate for each kind of Spirit <note>original: "Dæmonum"</note>, which victims were dedicated to each, and nearly everything observed in these rituals, were not only diligently written down in the laws of sacrifices, but the ancients were also compelled to follow them to the letter by the command of the oracle. The laws for all these things are handed down by Apollo as follows:

<margin>The Oracle of Apollo.</margin>
> Do these things, friend, who have entered by the nod of the Gods
> Upon the journey of this life; a beast must be sacrificed by all
> To many Gods: whether those who hold the lands, or the vast sea,
> Or the air; whether those who inhabit the wide atmosphere, or the ether,
> Or those who hold the heights of heaven, or the lowest realms of the abyss.
> I shall tell you in what ways each must be observed;
> Hold my spoken precepts in your mindful soul.
> Indeed, a triple sacrifice to the heavenly Gods, and this
> Must be slaughtered white; triple also to the terrestrial, and
> Likewise black; they rejoice further and are captivated by open...

> Favor the celestial deities with altars, while on the contrary,

<note>This poem acts as a liturgical guide, distinguishing between the "Superi" (celestial gods who receive burnt offerings), the "Inferi" (underworld gods who receive blood in the earth), and the gods of the sea and air.</note>

In these verses, everything that has been said so far is contained as if in a certain summary <note>original: "anacephaleosi," a Greek term for a recapitulation or summary</note>; however, so that it may be known in detail which victims were offered to which God, it seemed best to exhibit them briefly here, beginning with Jupiter.

<margin>The Ox is sacred to Jupiter</margin>
<margin>Plutarch. Seneca.</margin>
**Plutarch** and **Seneca** sufficiently show that the Ox was consecrated to the Egyptian Jupiter:

> *Let the first scepter-bearer bring the high backs*
> *Of a white bull to the thundering gods.*
<note>Jupiter was often associated with the bull, a symbol of strength and sovereignty, particularly in his aspect as the "Thunderer."</note>

<margin>The Bull for Neptune and Apollo. Virgil.</margin>
->**FOR NEPTUNE & APOLLO.** **Virgil** records that bulls were offered:<-

> *A bull for Neptune, a bull for you, fair Apollo.*

These are what **Homer** calls "entirely black bulls" <note>original Greek: ταύρους παμμέλανας</note>; on which passage the interpreters say: Bulls, on account of the violence of the sea; but black, on account of the heat of the water appearing from the depths of the sea.

<margin>Black cattle for Pluto. Tibullus.</margin>
**FOR PLUTO.** They performed sacrifices with black cattle, and poured libations to the same from cups of wine mixed with milk, hence **Tibullus** writes:

> *Meanwhile, promise black cattle to Dis,*
> *And cups of snowy milk mixed with pure wine.*
<note>"Dis" or "Dis Pater" is another name for Pluto, the Roman god of the underworld.</note>

<margin>The Buck was slaughtered for Bacchus. Virgil.</margin>
**FOR DIONYSUS** or **BACCHUS.** A buck or a goat was slaughtered, because this kind of animal especially gnaws at vines, according to that verse of **Virgil**:

> *The goat, having gnawed the vine, is slaughtered at the altars of Bacchus.*

<margin>A Goat for Aesculapius. Plutarch.</margin>
**FOR AESCULAPIUS**, the divine rite was performed with a goat; they assign the reason because a goat is said never to be without a fever, and Aesculapius is the God of health. A rooster was also sacrificed to him; just as it was to Mercury-Anubis and Hermanubis, about which **Plutarch** says: *To him, he says, the lower things, just as to*...
<note>The rooster was associated with vigilance and the dawn, fitting for gods who mediated between the light of the living and the darkness of the underworld.</note>

# TREATISE III. ON THE ORIGIN OF EGYPTIAN IDOLATRY

...to whom the upper realms pertain; therefore, they sacrificed a white cock to him, and a saffron-colored one to the other; but King Pyrrhus also, when healing those suffering from the spleen <note>Ancient medicine often linked the spleen to melancholy; King Pyrrhus of Epirus was said to have a healing touch in his right foot for such ailments</note>, performed the sacred rite with a white cock.

<margin>Sacrifices to Vulcan were consumed by fire.</margin>
When rituals were performed for **VULCAN**, everything was consumed by fire, which they called *protervia* <note>original: "proterviam," a Roman sacrificial term for a feast where all leftovers had to be burned before the next day</note>; for unless the victim and whatever remained were given to the fire, the sacrifice was thought to be polluted.

<margin>To Mars: a Horse, Dog, Wolf, Goat, Cock.</margin>
Apollodorus writes that some offered a Horse and others a Dog to **MARS**; the Latins offered the Wolf and the Woodpecker; the Lusitanians <note>People of ancient Portugal</note> a Goat; and the Gauls a Boar.

<margin>To Hercules: an Ox.</margin>
An Ox was once sacrificed to **HERCULES**, as Livy, Ovid, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and others record.

<margin>To Saturn: a black Ox.</margin>
Among the Romans, a tawny or black Ox was sacrificed to **SATURN**; but it is recorded that the Cyrenians, their temples bound with crowns of fresh fig, established sacrifices to Saturn and sent honeyed cakes to one another.

<margin>Sacrifices to Janus were made from Cake.</margin>
To **JANUS**, sacrifices were made using a cake, which the ancients called *Janual* after him, for it was a type of pastry; sometimes they used incense or wine; perhaps because of the discovery of wine, which is attributed to Janus—otherwise known as Noah <note>The author reflects a common Renaissance belief that the Roman god Janus and the biblical Noah were the same historical figure</note>.
<margin>Ovid.</margin>
> *Janus, to you I first bring incense and pure wine.*

<margin>To Pan: a Goat.</margin>
A fertile goat <note>original: "Hircus coleatus," an uncastrated male goat</note> was sacrificed to the god **PAN**, which goat was driven to the cave where Pan himself was thought to dwell, as the cited Lucian teaches. But to Pan Lycaeus <note>Pan in his aspect as a protector against wolves</note> during the Lupercalia, a dog was sacrificed, as Plutarch says, since the dog is both guardian and friend of the flock; others say a white she-goat; some a male goat, from whose hide the Luperci priests <note>The "Wolf-brothers" of the Roman Lupercalia festival</note> made whips with which they struck women throughout the city.

<margin>To Sylvanus: Milk. To Faunus: a kid, lamb, or wine.</margin>
To **SYLVANUS and FAUNUS**, they performed sacrifices; for the former with milk, and for the latter with a kid, a lamb, or wine.

<margin>To Priapus: a Donkey.</margin>
To **PRIAPUS**, the god of nature and gardens, the Donkey was the victim because of the size of its member, about which Ovid says:
<margin>Ovid.</margin>
> *And the little donkey is slain for the stiff guardian of the countryside.*

<margin>Virgil.</margin>
However, others offered him milk and cake, as Virgil seems to indicate:
> *A bowl of milk and these cakes, Priapus, is enough for you*
> *To expect each year; you are the guardian of a poor garden.*

<margin>To Juno: a Heifer.</margin>
Seneca writes in *Medea* that a sacrifice was made to **JUNO** from a heifer; others offered a peacock and a goose, others a sow or a lamb, others flowers and crowns.

<margin>To Ceres: a sow.</margin>
To **CERES**, the ancients dedicated ears of grain and crowns made from them, but Xenophon testifies that they also performed a sacred rite with a sow; the first fruits of the crops were also offered to her. Hence, in the month of April, priests dressed in white, with lamps and torches lit, performed the ritual after a sow was slaughtered.
<margin>Ovid.</margin>
> *Ceres was the first to rejoice in the blood of a pregnant sow.*

To the goddess **HECATE**, a Dog was offered, as Plutarch witnesses.
To **VENUS** of Argos <note>original: "Archivæ"</note>, white doves, or to the Egyptian Venus.
To **JUNO**, a cow was sacrificed.
To **RHEA** or **CYBELE**, the mother of the Gods, the priests made offerings with their own blood; indeed, to be purer in performing sacrifices of this kind, they would cut off their genitals with a sharp stone; and at Athens and elsewhere they drank hemlock to extinguish the force of lust, and women spread beds for themselves with the leaves of the chaste-tree <note>original: "viticis," the *Vitex agnus-castus*, a shrub believed in antiquity to suppress sexual desire</note> to restrain illicit desires.

Arnobius.

To **VESTA** and **TELLUS** <note>The personification of Mother Earth</note>, a *forda* <note>original: "forda," an ancient Roman term for a cow with calf</note> or pregnant cow was dedicated; there are those who say black victims were offered to Tellus; of which Arnobius says: "A huge pregnant sow is sacrificed to Mother Earth."

<margin>
The rites of Bellona were performed with the blood of the priests.
</margin>
The rites of **BELLONA** <note>Goddess of war</note> were performed not with animal victims, but with the blood of the priests themselves; for with drawn swords, which they held in each hand, they would strike their own shoulders and arms.

<margin>
A Sow for the Moon.
</margin>
Finally, the Egyptians sacrificed a sow only to **THE MOON** and **LIBER** <note>The Roman name for Dionysus, whom Kircher identifies here with Osiris</note>; to the other Gods they sacrificed male oxen, calves, and geese, but in no way a she-goat or a he-goat.

<margin>
Birds for the Stars.
</margin>
To the **PLANETS** and **STARS**, birds were dedicated; a goose to **ISIS**, a cock to the Owl <note>original: "Noctuæ," referring to Minerva’s owl or the goddess of night</note> and to the **LARES** <note>Household protective spirits</note>, and sometimes a pig. Among the people of Tussa in Egypt, a cow was dedicated to the horned Venus <note>likely Hathor</note> because of the resemblance <note>The horns of the cow were seen as a physical representation of the lunar crescent or the goddess’s crown</note>.

And from all these things it appears that the victim dedicated to each of the Gods was that which was most in harmony with their nature.

### CHAPTER XI.

->On the Worship of Animals Peculiar to the Egyptians.<-

Rightly and wisely has the philosopher determined that the cause of human lapses and errors is levity and the inconstancy of the human mind. Driven by this, men have applied their souls to the founding of new sacrificial rites and ceremonies, with each individual instituting that which his own particular nature and "Genius" <note>The "Genius" refers to a person's guiding spirit or inherent natural inclination.</note> suggested to him. I believe all these things came to pass partly through the lack of skill of foolish men, who were ignorant of how much reason and true religion require; and partly through the false snares of priests, who sought to keep their business profitable through a variety of ceremonies. To those looking upon them correctly, these practices might rightly have seemed ridiculous rather than containing any true sanctity. Furthermore, this also happened through the fraud of malignant demons—while the power of darkness still held sway—who strove to keep men in a foreign servitude through these intricacies, binding them perpetually with the chain of false religion and idolatry. They granted those souls, oppressed by such superstitions, no opportunity to breathe freely, so that they might for a moment consider the magnitude of the deceptions surrounding them, and finally recognize how absurd, how vain, how ridiculous, and how contaminated by every kind of crime was the religion they embraced.

<margin>The blindness of the Egyptians in the worship of the Gods.</margin>
Plutarch testifies that among all mortals, the Egyptians labored most especially under this blindness; and therefore it is no wonder that, having fallen into ridiculous and dull-witted superstitions, they gave birth to such loathsome monsters as Gods. For since they (as was said in the preceding chapters) worshipped the principal Gods—the Sun and the Moon, or Osiris and Isis—as the moderators of the entire Universe, they eventually arrived at a point where, beyond the innumerable fables and old wives' tales attached to them, they were everywhere persuaded by a certain dull-witted opinion. They began to regard anything that bore some resemblance to the Sun or the Moon, or which possessed "Phoebian" <note>Solar or light-bearing properties associated with Apollo/Phoebus.</note> properties, as a sacred particle of the solar soul. From this, that manifold worship of "all-shaped" gods <note>original: "pantomorphorum"</note> found its origin. Hence also emerged those ridiculous Gods whom we behold to this day as witnesses of pagan madness: the dog-headed <note>original: "κυνοκεϕάλος" (kynokephalos)</note>, the hawk-headed <note>original: "ἱερακοκεϕάλος" (hierakokephalos)</note>, the cat-headed <note>original: "αἰλουροκεϕάλος" (ailourokephalos)</note>, the snake-headed <note>original: "ὁϕιοκεϕάλος" (ophiokephalos)</note>, the bird-headed <note>original: "ὀρνιθοκεϕάλος" (ornithokephalos)</note>, the bull-headed <note>original: "ταυροκεϕάλος" (taurokephalos)</note>, and six hundred other monsters and portents of this kind. Sedulius <note>Coelius Sedulius, a 5th-century Christian poet.</note> excellently attacks their worship when he sings:

<margin>Sedulius.</margin>
> Alas, wretched ones, who worship rumors, who with a sinister heart
> Carve for themselves religious idols, and flee their own
> Creator; and fear the very things they have made.
> What madness is this? What great insanity mocks their minds,
> That a man should prostrate himself as a suppliant to adore
> A bird, a shameful ox, a coiled dragon, and a half-human dog?

Similarly, Tertullian, attacking a Senator who had turned from the Christian religion to the servitude of idols, rebukes this vain religion thus:

<margin>The disagreement of the Egyptians in worshipping the Gods.</margin>
Furthermore, Diodorus Siculus says that there was the greatest dissension among the Egyptians regarding the worship of brutes. For the people of Lycopolis <note>Lycopolis, the "City of the Wolf."</note> abstained from eating sheep, so as not to deprive the wolf—whom they adored as a Divinity—of its proper food; the Oxyrhynchites worshipped a fish; and the people of Cynopolis <note>Cynopolis, the "City of the Dog."</note> held the dog in the place of a Divinity.

Plutarch relates that in his own time, a cruel war flared up between the Oxyrhynchites and the Cynopolitans, because the latter had devoured the *Oxyrhynchus* <note>original: "Oxyrinchum piscem"; a sharp-snouted fish of the Nile.</note> fish, which the former worshipped with divine honors; in revenge, the Oxyrhynchites captured and sacrificed a dog, to which the Cynopolitans were accustomed to offer victims as a Divinity.

<margin>St. Athanasius, Oration against Julian.</margin>
St. Athanasius also mentions this discord: *Every disagreement,* he says, *and the continuous war seething among the Egyptians, I believe took its origin from the diversity of the animals they adored. For the Crocodile, which was worshipped by some as a God, was hated and held in abomination by others as a supreme evil and an accursed animal (into which they believed Typhon <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, associated with chaos and the desert.</note> had been transformed after committing fratricide). The people of Leopolis adored the Lion, which the people of Collimitatis hunted down as a cruel beast to be destroyed; for Diodorus shows that in different parts, different beasts were worshipped. Indeed, the Ox was worshipped in Memphis; Mnevis <note>The sacred bull of Heliopolis.</note> in Heliopolis; the Goat in Mendes; the Crocodile at Lake Moeris; and the Lion in the district of Leontopolis.* <margin>Lactantius.</margin> Concerning the worship of the Ox, or Apis, much has been said in abundance above; from which worship, according to the testimony of Lactantius, the "Calf-worship" <term>Moscholatria</term> <note>From the Greek 'moschos' (calf) and 'latreia' (worship).</note> of the Israelites in the desert seems to have flowed. <margin>The worship of the golden calf in the desert derived from the Egyptians.</margin> For he says: *The Israelites, having now laid aside their Egyptian servitude, and having been delivered from hunger and thirst, fell into luxury and turned their minds toward the profane rites of the Egyptians. For while Moses was ascending the mountain, they fashioned the golden head of an Ox, whom they call Apis, so that it might lead them as a sign.* <margin>Herodotus. The worship of various animals among the various cities of Egypt.</margin> Herodotus says that the people of Latopolis venerated a fish of the same name; the Hermopolitans a Dog-headed Baboon or Ape; the Babylonians <note>Referring to the Egyptian city of Babylon, located near modern-day Cairo.</note> worshipped onions; the Thebans an Eagle; the Leontopolitans a Lion; the Mendesians a Goat; and the Athribites the mouse and the frog with divine worship, in which St. Athanasius concurs. <margin>St. Athanasius.</margin> So greatly, he says, have some fallen in mind, and with such darkness have they shrouded their souls, that they have even devised things which could not possibly exist by any reason, nor had ever been seen, and made them Divinities: namely, those who, mixing brute and rational animals together and contracting them into a single form, worship them as Gods. <margin>Divinities of a composite nature.</margin> Such as are found among the Egyptians: Dog-headed, Snake-headed, and Donkey-headed figures; and in Libya, Jupiter Ammon <note>The syncretized god of the Greeks and Egyptians, often depicted with ram's horns.</note> configured with a ram’s head. Thus says the Holy Doctor.

<margin>The worship of things lacking sense and life.</margin>
But what is more wondrous is that foolish heathendom held in the place of Divinities not only irrational animals, but even things lacking life and sense, such as the Nile, the earth, the leek, onions, garlic, and other similar things; about which Juvenal <note>The Roman satirist who mocked Egyptian religion in his 15th Satire.</note> surely plays with elegant and festive wit:

The vanity of the Egyptians did not stop here; they even held in the place of a Divinity those things which can hardly be recounted without shame and modesty, as Lactantius <note>An early Christian author and advisor to Constantine I.</note> testifies in these words: <margin>Lactantius.</margin> *Do we destroy religions more than the Egyptian nation? Pelusium was a major Egyptian city on the eastern Nile delta.</note> I find no other cause for this stinking religion than a vain superstition and an observance almost innate to the Egyptians. For while they were struck by a certain "panic" fear of the Gods, they thought nothing in human actions was without an omen; it is no wonder they reached such a point of madness that they thought there was something divine in unseemly noises of this kind. To this was added the frequent trickery of demons, who, through oracles—

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE

### CHAPTER 11.

...insinuating themselves into small statues and images, these spirits would deliver responses to those seeking counsel, not from the mouth, but from the belly. Concerning this, Isaiah seems to complain in chapter 29, when he says: *And the Egyptians shall consult the Idols, and the Magicians, the Pythons <note>In this context, "Pythons" refers to spirits of divination or "familiar spirits."</note>, and the Knowers.* Where, in place of "Pythons and Knowers," the Hebrew text has *Oboth vaidgonim* <note>original: אובות וידעונים (*’ōḇōṯ wə-yiḏ-də-‘ō-nîm*); traditionally translated as "mediums and spiritists."</note>. Now, *Oboth* signifies the same thing as "wineskins," as seen in Job 32: *Behold, my belly is like wine that has no vent; like oboth—that is, new wineskins—it is ready to burst.* 

<margin>What a Python and an *engastrimythos* are.</margin>
From this, some judge by no slight conjecture that these "Pythons" were named after wineskins because those who were inspired by such a spirit would, with their mouths closed, bring forth their responses from the belly, just as if from a wineskin or a small flask. This is not inappropriate; for this reason they were called by the Greeks *engastrimythoi* <note>original: ἐγγαστρίμυθοι; literally "belly-talkers."</note>, as if you were to say "ventriloquists." For it is the specific nature of these most deceitful and unclean spirits to mock the human race through the most impure actions—that is, to give responses from the private parts of the body. Since this seemed like something sacred to a superstitious and unskilled people, it is no wonder that even flatulence <note>original: *crepitus*; Kircher is referring to the historical claim that certain Egyptian sects incorporated bodily sounds into their rituals.</note> was included among the rites of divine worship by the Egyptians with a certain supreme stupidity of mind. But it is better to suppress these filthy matters in deep silence than to cause harm by exciting nausea in tender minds with their abominable stench. 

Anyone who desires more on these and similar matters—especially regarding the extreme care they took in feeding beasts—should consult Diodorus and Plutarch, who describe at length the animals themselves and the methods of feeding, worshipping, and burying them.

<margin>Clement of Alexandria, Book 5 of the *Stromata* <note>A series of miscellaneous observations on Christian life and Greek philosophy by the 2nd-century Church Father.</note></margin>
<image-desc>Historiated ornamental initial 'Q' featuring a figure seated at a desk with an open book, representing a scholar or author.</image-desc>SINCE in the preceding chapters we have treated at length the origin and variety of the Gods, and finally the sacrifices and worship of false deities practiced by the Egyptians, I have judged it a worthwhile endeavor if, at this point, I turn my pen to the ancient idols of the Hebrews and their origin. For since, according to the testimony of Clement, the mysteries, rites, ceremonies, and other sacraments of the Hebrews are very similar to the mysteries of the Egyptians, the Egyptians also borrowed many things from the Hebrews, just as the Hebrews did from the former, making them a matter of reciprocal exchange. Because of this, we hope that from a comparison of these mysteries common to both peoples, our "Oedipus" <note>Kircher uses "Oedipus" as a metaphor for his work or the reader—someone who, like the mythological hero, is able to solve the "riddles" of the Egyptian Sphinx.</note> here, having been enlightened, will capture even greater progress day by day in investigating the secrets of the Egyptians.

<margin>The offspring of Ham and the concubines of Solomon taught Egyptian superstitions to the Hebrews.</margin>
<margin>4 Kings 23 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 23.</note></margin>
It should be noted, therefore, that there were two kinds of people through whose effort and plotting the idolatry of the Egyptians reached the Hebrews. The first kind was that rejected offspring of Ham <note>original: *Cham*; Noah's son, whom Kircher identifies as the progenitor of the Egyptians and the "inventor" of post-flood idolatry.</note>, concerning whom we have spoken in various places in the preceding chapters; as well as the Israelites who lived among the Egyptians and were infected by their superstitious teaching. The second kind consisted of the concubines of Solomon—foreign women, especially Egyptians—by whose charms and deceitful love the Sacred Scriptures say Solomon was ensnared, leading him to build shrines, altars, and groves, and to erect idols to which he might offer incense. Seduced by his wicked example, the rest of his successors, the Kings of Israel (if you except a few), all adhered to this shameful cult, as will be shown in the following sections regarding Jeroboam, Ahab, Manasseh, and others. But we return to the Arch-idolaters.

<margin>Ham was the first inventor of idolatry after the flood.</margin>

# THE ISIACTEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>
CHAPTER I.
</margin>

<margin>
The Israelites infected by the early Egyptian worship.
</margin>
...ened by these habits and imbued with the perverse teachings of the Egyptians, over the course of time, not only the neighboring nations but especially the Hebrews—with whom the Egyptians lived for nearly two hundred years—became followers of their institutions. It was not difficult for a fleshly people, immersed in the pleasures of the senses, to embrace those dogmas by whose help they hoped to reach the height of all happiness. Furthermore, that tranquil, peaceful, and finally most fortunate life of the Egyptians, which they credited to the tireless worship of idols, sacrifices, and other unholy arts as the sole cause, carried great weight in the minds of those idle men. This can be made manifest from this single fact: excited by this Egyptian prosperity and the fame of their memorable deeds, not only the Hebrews, but also the Persians, Arabs, Phoenicians, Syrians, Babylonians, and Greeks traveled to Egypt with the intention of being imbued with that wondrous knowledge of the priestly disciplines; and by their help, having been made participants in the secrets of Isis <note>original: "arcanorum Isiacorum"</note>, they might also attain the same prosperity as the Egyptians.

<margin>
Phylacteries of the Israelites from Egypt.
</margin>
It was the custom in Egypt to use various phylacteries <term>phylacteries: from the Greek *phylaktērion*, meaning a safeguard or amulet. Here, Kircher refers to magical charms rather than the Jewish ritual leather boxes used for prayer.</term> against the incursions of evils. Therefore, when the Hebrews noticed the Egyptians leading a secure life through the power of these objects, they too, in order to attain this security, began to set their minds toward those superstitious engravings of images; these were fashioned from various materials corresponding to the stars, under certain celestial positions, and were worn continually on the neck, hands, and belts. Again, the Egyptians ascribed the abundance of earthly goods they enjoyed to the diligent worship of Apis <note>The sacred bull of Memphis, worshipped by the Egyptians as a symbol of fertility and strength.</note>. Hence the Israelites, dwelling in the dismal desert and suffering from a lack of water, when the onions, garlic, meat-pots <note>A reference to Exodus 16:3, where the Israelites long for the "fleshpots" of Egypt during their wanderings.</note>, and similar delights of carnal men were missing, remembered Egyptian prosperity and themselves erected an Apis bull, hoping that by its constant worship they would obtain the goods of the said land. From here also appear to have emerged those "Portable Gods" which they call *Teraphim* <term>Teraphim: small household idols or statues used for divination and protection in the ancient Near East.</term>, and six hundred other monstrous idols, which we shall treat in the following sections. Indeed, in a short time, these practices made such progress among the "chosen people" that the most enlightened "Teacher of the Perplexed," Rabbi Moses, called Rambam <note>Moses Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note>, when he considered this inclination of his nation toward pagan rites, clearly demonstrated that the Law was given to Moses for no other reason than to abolish the unholy Egyptian customs that the Hebrews had absorbed, replacing them with a healing law.

<margin>
The Hebrews imitated the Egyptians in all things.
</margin>

<margin>
Worship of Apis in the desert.
</margin>

<margin>
The Teraphim of Laban.
</margin>

But since the words of the cited Doctor can bring immense light to hieroglyphic matters, it seemed fit to produce them here at length, though in parts; for they not only confirm those things we have said previously, but they also faithfully and learnedly exhibit, as if in a synopsis, what must be said hereafter. His words are taken from the Hebrew manuscript book which they call *Moreh Nevuchim*, that is, the *Teacher of the Perplexed*. Rambam in *Moreh Nevuchim*, Book 3, Chapter 3.

*The precepts,* he says, *which the second part contains, are all those precepts which respec-*

<meta>catchword: respec- (referring to the Latin "respiciunt," meaning "they respect" or "they regard")</meta>

<summary>Kircher argues that the Israelites adopted Egyptian idolatry, including amulets and the worship of the Apis bull, because they envied Egypt's material prosperity. He cites Maimonides (Rambam) to argue that Mosaic Law was established specifically to counteract these deeply ingrained Egyptian superstitions.</summary>

### TREATISE IV. PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER I.

<margin>Precepts prescribed by Moses against the idolatry of the Egyptians.</margin>
...they regard idolatry. It is well known, moreover, that the logic and cause of all such precepts is to escape the errors of idolatry, and other deceptive opinions and wicked dogmas; among these are contained the precepts regarding augury, divination, the magic arts, and all other similar things.

<margin>The Rambam.</margin>
<note>Rambam is an acronym for Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, known in the West as Maimonides (1138–1204), a preeminent Jewish philosopher whose work *The Guide for the Perplexed* Kircher quotes here.</note>
These things having been prefaced, the Rambam continues his words in this manner:

<note>original Hebrew: וכשקרא כל הספרים... "And when you read all the books which I have mentioned to you..."</note>
When indeed, he says, you have read all the books which I have mentioned to you, they will explain to you that the Magic art of which you have heard—which was practiced by the Zabians <term>Zabians: an ancient group often identified by medieval scholars as the primary practitioners of Chaldean star-worship and magic</term>, the Casdim (or Babylonians), and the Chaldeans—was even more prevalent among the Canaanites and the Egyptians. By these arts they deceived others, being themselves deceived; they believed that by the power of such magic they could perform wonderful works in reality, whether for a single person or for the inhabitants of an entire city.

<margin>The magic art of the Zabians.</margin>
From these things it is first clear that the Zabians—who are of the lineage of Tsaba <note>original: "Tsaba filii Cus," referring to Seba, son of Cush in Genesis 10:7</note>, a people neighboring Egypt—as well as the Chaldeans, Babylonians, and Canaanites, originally drew most of their dogmas from the Egyptians. This is clearly indicated by these words: *more of these works were among the Egyptians, by which they deceived others, and by which they thought themselves able to perform miracles.* Having proposed these points, the Rambam continues his discourse thus:

<margin>The Rambam.</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: ודע שכוונת התורה... "Know that the intention of the whole Torah and the axis upon which it turns..."</note>
Know, therefore, that the intention of the entire Law <note>The Torah</note>, and the pillar upon which it is placed, was to uproot and destroy idolatry. For if it is believed that any of the stars harms or helps in any of these matters found in the lives of individual men, and since that opinion leads men to the service of those stars, it followed necessarily that every sorcerer should be killed. This is because such a person undoubtedly serves Idols, even if his service involves the use of strange and external things outside the common way the nations worshiped idols. 

<margin>Astrology of the Egyptians.</margin>
Furthermore, because women were admitted to perform most of these works more than men, the Law said: *You shall not suffer a sorceress to live* <note>Exodus 22:18</note>. For although mercy is naturally found in human nature so that they do not easily kill women, for this reason, regarding the law of idolatry, it made mention of both man and woman. And again it said, *The man and the woman.* No such specific mention is made regarding the violation of the Sabbath, nor in other prohibitions besides this one. This was intended to overcome the natural mercy people feel toward women. 

And because the sorcerers thought in their folly that they were performing great deeds—thinking that by those actions they could drive away wild beasts from the towns, such as lions, snakes, and the like, and also believing that by their sorceries they could ward off types of damage from the plants of the earth—for there are found among them rituals to kill the worms of the vineyards so they would not destroy the crop. They have already spoken at length about the "riddles of the vineyard-worm"—that is, the Zabians and the "ways of the Amorites" <note>A Talmudic term for superstitious pagan customs</note> mentioned in the book of *Egyptian Agriculture*... <note>original: "Gofthya" / Coptic/Egyptian agriculture. Maimonides likely refers to the "Nabataean Agriculture," which he believed recorded ancient Egyptian and Zabian beliefs.</note>

Sorcerers <note>catchword: Magi</note>

<summary>Athanasius Kircher uses the writings of Maimonides (the Rambam) to argue that Biblical laws against magic and sorcery were specifically designed to uproot the Egyptian and Zabian superstitions that the Israelites had adopted.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Kircher's analysis of the Hebrew Law as a reaction against ancient magic, specifically drawing from the "Guide for the Perplexed" by Maimonides (the Rambam) to explain how specific biblical prohibitions targeted Egyptian and "Amorite" superstitions.</meta>

# CHAPTER I. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS’S ISIAC TEMPLE

<margin>False opinion of the Magi concerning the power of their art.</margin>
The Magi <note>In this context, "Magi" refers to ancient sorcerers or practitioners of hidden arts, particularly those of the East and Egypt.</note> believe that the magic art possesses the power to exterminate harmful animals from cities, such as serpents, scorpions, and other such creatures; they also believe that magical acts can prevent the various types of damage that befall plants. Thus, works are found through which they believe they can repel hail, and other works intended for killing the worms that plague vineyards. Much was said on this by the nations of the Sabians <term>Sabians: A group of star-worshipers from Harran whom medieval scholars, including Maimonides, considered the keepers of ancient Mesopotamian and Egyptian magic</term> and the Egyptians, including the killing of vineyard worms through the "Ways of the Amorite," <note>original: "vias Amorrhæi"; a Talmudic term referring to superstitious or pagan customs that have no rational or medical basis.</note> which are mentioned in the *Book on Egyptian Service*.

<margin>The Book on the Servitude of the Egyptians.</margin>
And similarly, they believe they possess works by which the falling of leaves, nuts, and other fruit from trees can be prevented. Because all these things were well known, the Law stated in the words of its confirmation: <note>Refers to the blessings and curses in Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28.</note> *If you walk in the service of idols, and in those magical works by which you think losses will be removed from you, then for that very reason, disasters and losses will happen to you, as it is written: I will send the beasts of the field among you, and they shall rob you of your children, etc.* The sum of this reasoning, therefore, is that all those things which the idolaters believe they are doing to strengthen their service—and through which they think they can escape damage—will actually lead to the very disasters mentioned in the words of confirmation. By performing such services, they will lose the very benefits they sought.

<margin>The intention of the divine law.</margin>
It has thus been shown to you what the intention of the Law was in proposing the blessings and curses contained in the words of confirmation regarding these specific details and no others. Understand the magnitude of this benefit: in the same way that the Law sought to distance men from every magical work, it prohibited everything pertaining to the magic art—even those things relating to the cultivation of the earth and the science of it. That is, it prohibited everything they claimed was useful in agriculture that does not fall under natural consideration <note>By "natural consideration," Kircher means what we would call "natural science" or "rational cause-and-effect."</note>, but which was used by them according to their customary practices. Therefore it is said in the Law: *You shall not walk in the rites of the nations and their customs,* which the Sages called "the Ways of the Amorite." These are branches of the magic art which are necessarily attributed to Astronomical matters; by a certain circuitous route, they procure honor and service for the Stars.

<margin>Medicinal practices of the Amorites.</margin>
The Sages also openly declared: we shall not hesitate to use anything that is truly medicinal, even if it seems like the "Ways of the Amorite." <note>This means that if a remedy actually works by natural means, it is permitted, even if it was used by pagans.</note> Likewise, all things required by natural consideration are permitted, while others are prohibited. For instance, it was said: *A tree whose fruit falls should be weighed down with stones and smeared with red dye.* The Sage, considering this practice, said: *It is good to weigh it with stones so that its excessive strength might be weakened; but why should it be smeared with dye?* It is clear, then, that if it is dyed with the red pigment called *Almagra* in Arabic <note>original: "Almagra"; red ochre or ruddle</note>, or with something similar for which reason cannot find a cause, it is prohibited as one of the "Ways of the Amorite."

<margin>Magical superstitions.</margin>
Similarly, they spoke concerning a miscarriage, and where it should be buried: they said it shall not be hung in a tree, nor buried at a crossroads, for that is of the "Ways of the Amorite." Let it not seem a contradiction to you that certain things seemed permitted, such as hanging a nail in a secret place; for at that time they believed this was done by way of experiment <note>i.e., empirical evidence</note>, and they understood such things to be medicinal. There is even a certain herb which they hung from the neck of a demented person, called *Femura* <note>Likely referring to a plant used in folk medicine, possibly a corruption of a Hebrew or Arabic name</note>; and they gave dog dung in a drink to those suffering from scrofula <note>A form of tuberculosis affecting the lymph nodes</note>, and they fumigated with vinegar and another medicine called *Martefica* <note>original: "Martefica"; likely from the Arabic "martafak," meaning litharge or lead oxide</note> for severe pain in the knees. They had experienced the utility of all these things, even though reason could not grasp the cause; and therefore, they were permitted under the name of medicine.

---

<margin>Precepts of the Law opposed to the laws of the Egyptians.</margin>
From all of this, it is clear that the entire Law of the Hebrews was, as it were, parallel to the wicked laws of the nations, and opposed to them diametrically.
