# SYNTAGMA IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER I.

...the primary intention of the Law was to destroy idolatry, to erase its very name, and all things pertaining to it; as well as whatever leads to any of their works, such as the <term>Ob<note>Hebrew: אב; a spirit-medium or "pit-spirit" mentioned in Leviticus.</note></term> and the <term>Ideon<note>Hebrew: ידעון; a "knowing one" or wizard/soothsayer.</note></term>, passing children through the fire, sorcery, augury, divination, and consulting the dead. It also prohibited, by a general precept, any imitation of their works—to such an extent that the Israelites were not even to use clothing, food, or colors similar to the garments of the Egyptians. This is testified by the <term>Rambam<note>An acronym for Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, known as Maimonides (1138–1204), the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher.</note></term> in the cited passage, saying:

<margin>Rambam.</margin>
<note>original: "והנה ביארנו..." (Hebrew). Translation: "And behold, we have explained in our great composition that rounding the corners of the head and the corners of the beard is forbidden because it was the grooming habit of the priests of idols. It is also the reason for the prohibition of mixing wool and linen (sha'atnez), for such was the grooming of their priests as well; they would combine plant and animal fibers in a single garment, and wear a ring made of a certain type of metal on their hand—this is found written in their books. This is also the reason for the command: 'A woman shall not wear a man's items, nor shall a man wear a woman's clothing' (Deut. 22:5). You will find it in the book of Qantir (Centir), which commands that a man should wear a dyed woman's garment when he stands before the star called Venus, and a woman should wear armor and weapons of war when she stands before Mars. There is also, in my view, another reason: that such an act excites lust and leads to types of fornication."</note>

<margin>
Why the cutting of the beard is forbidden in Sacred Scripture.
</margin>
*Now therefore, he says, hear our great wonders, for the style of the hair and beard was prohibited because a servant of idols among the Egyptians used to walk in that manner. For the same reason, there was a prohibition against anyone wearing a garment of linen and wool together, or a woven fabric of both, because the elders of the idols used such a garment; they joined plant and animal products in their clothes and made a sign on their hand with some species of metal; and this is written in their books. It is for this reason that the Law says: a woman shall not take up the arms of a man, nor shall a man be dressed in a woman's garment. You will find in the book of the magic art, or of hidden things, composed by Centir <note>Likely a reference to an Arabic Hermetic or magical text attributed to a figure like "Qantir" or " Hermes."</note>, that it is said there that a man should put on a colored woman’s garment when he stands before the star called Venus, and a woman should take up a breastplate and weapons of war when she stands before the star called Mars. There is also another reason here: because that act excites concupiscence and leads to various types of fornication.*

<margin>
Centir, an Arabic author of a book on the magic art.
</margin>
Thus far the Rambam. Abenephius the Arab <note>Kircher frequently cites "Abenephius" as an authority on Egyptian lore; modern scholars often identify these texts with the writings of Ibn Wahshiyya.</note> agrees with him so closely that they seem to have collected these opinions of the ancient Egyptians from a single author. For he himself also shows at length that the sacred disciplines of the Egyptians remained among the Hebrews; and therefore, lest this false Egyptian religion infect the whole nation, the Law was given by God, by which the superstitious minds of the Hebrews might be restrained through the intense rejection of external worship. Indeed, since his observations are worthy of careful consideration, we have chosen to bring them forward here, and at the same time to show how great are the treasures that still lie hidden in the monuments of the Arabs and Hebrews, unknown to the Latins, and how much they contribute to the exploration of any hidden matters. Thus, he says in Arabic:

<margin>
Abeneph. book on the mysteries of the Egyptians.
</margin>
<note>original: "فنبتدي بشرح..." (Arabic). Translation: "We begin by explaining the teaching of the sages of Egypt, the knowledge of which is important for everyone who seeks and desires the wisdom of Egyptian philosophy. Because of the worship of idols, the sages of Egypt forbid us [idolatry], and also all idol worship and [certain styles of] hair, and judgments of the unseen (divination), and all the evil worship that is practiced. In place of those, the Law commands us that we believe in and worship and honor the one God. For that reason, He commands us in the first commandment that we should not prostrate ourselves to any god besides Him; because many of Israel sinned with the obsessed and the unbelievers in Egypt by their prostration to the creation instead of the Creator, and they also sinned with the astrologers and the sorcerers..."</note>

# CHAPTER I. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS’S ISIAC TEMPLE

CA-
<meta>catchword: CA-</meta>

* *Beware of those who worship the Devil as their god.* <note>Original Arabic: حذرون الذين يعبدون الشيطان كالههم. Kircher frequently cites Arabic manuscripts to provide a "pagan" perspective on Egyptian history.</note>

*We now begin the explanation of the doctrine of the Egyptian sages, the knowledge of which is necessary for anyone desiring to understand the wisdom of the Egyptian philosophers. You should know, therefore, that on account of the idolatry of the Egyptian sages, God—through the giving of the Law—prohibited all foreign servitude, magic, and the arts of divination by which hidden things are discerned; in short, He forbade every wicked and illicit cult. In its place, He commanded us to confess and serve Him, and to honor the one true God. For this reason, He commanded us in the first precept not to worship any God besides Him; for many from Israel had sinned and strayed with the Gentiles and the Egyptian Pagans by worshiping the creature instead of the Creator. They also strayed into the exercise of wicked arts with Mages, Soothsayers, and other diviners who serve the Demon as if he were their God. Therefore, the entire Law is set in opposition to the errors of the ancients. For it is well known that the Egyptians used to construct images and arrange idols on high mountains. Turning toward the east, they would worship them, especially the statue of the Sun; therefore, the Law abolishes the "high places" and the turning toward the east—and thus the Sages say, "the Glory [of God] is in the west." <note>A reference to the Jewish tradition that the Divine Presence (Shekhinah) in the Temple was associated with the West, contrary to the Solar cults of the East.</note> Furthermore, the Egyptians used to hold oxen, rams, and goats in the highest veneration, and they considered it a most <margin>The Law of the Hebrews is completely contrary to the law of the Egyptians.</margin> serious sacrilege to kill those animals. Yet, to turn the Hebrews away from this rite, the Law taught the opposite: namely, the sacrifice of oxen, rams, and goats. Moreover, those people worshiped the Sun, Moon, Stars, and planets as Divinities. But the Israelite Law taught them not to be led astray by the sight of the stars and the "host of heaven." Furthermore, in the sacrifices of Egypt, the priests used leaven and honey, but they detested salt, which they called "the foam of <term>Typhon<note>In Egyptian mythology, Typhon (Set) was the god of chaos and the desert; the sea and salt were seen as his remains, hence impure to some cults.</note></term>." In contrast, the Law ignored leaven and honey in sacrifices and instead required the use of salt. Finally, there was a frequent use in Egypt of <term>phylacteries<note>Here meaning amulets or protective charms, not the Jewish ritual items.</note></term> marked with various images, by which they <margin>Portable Egyptian statues.</margin> believed they would become fortunate. To these they added certain small statues, which they called "averters" <note>Probably referring to *apotropaic* figures meant to ward off evil.</note>; these they were accustomed to wear on the neck, chest, or hands, and sometimes placed them in the corners of houses and other places as if they were their guardians. All these customs <margin>Hebrew Frontlets.</margin> were converted by the Law into the <term>Tephillin<note>Phylacteries; small leather boxes containing Torah verses worn during prayer.</note></term>, <term>Mezuzoth<note>Parchment scrolls fixed to doorposts.</note></term>, and <term>Totaphot<note>Another biblical term for Tephillin/frontlets.</note></term>. These were nothing other than leather made from a clean animal, upon which were written the words of God's Law—persuading and commanding a continual memory of its observance—and they were placed upon the forehead, the arms, and the doorposts. You see, therefore, how by the occasion of various Egyptian rites which had then occupied the entire East, the Law refuted them by prohibiting them. And thus far we follow <term>Abbenephi<note>Ahmad ibn Wahshiyya, a 10th-century author whose "Nabataean Agriculture" Kircher believed contained ancient Egyptian secrets.</note></term>, whose accounts come so close to those we brought forward above from <term>Moses the Egyptian<note>Maimonides.</note></term> that you might say they are nearly the same. From this I conclude that these two authors took these facts regarding the ancient customs of the Egyptians from the same Arabic authors, who at that time were held in the highest esteem for their antiquity; for both frequently cite the *Book of Centir* regarding Egyptian Magic, and a certain Moorish Arab regarding Egyptian service, and finally Ezechias regarding their medicines. But we shall discuss these elsewhere with greater care. Whoever desires more on these recently reviewed rites of the Hebrews and Egyptians should consult the Talmudic <term>Tosafot<note>Medieval commentaries on the Talmud.</note></term>, Rabbi Samson, Rabbi Elias Mizrachi, Judah ibn Tibbon, Gedaliah’s *Chain of the Kabbalah*, and other Hebrew commentators whom we shall cite below; for in them he will find all that we have said above confirmed.*

<summary>Kircher argues that Jewish Law was intentionally designed as a "mirror-image" of Egyptian paganism, turning idolatrous symbols like amulets and animal worship into monotheistic rituals like Tefillin and animal sacrifice. He cites both Maimonides and Arabic sources like Ibn Wahshiyya to prove that the Torah's specifics were direct responses to Egyptian "magic."</summary>

SYNT. IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS CH. II.

# CHAPTER II.

## Concerning the specific Idols of the Hebrews, and a comparison of them with the Idols of the Egyptians, from whom they first originated.

### On the worship of Fire.

<margin>Cush and Mizraim were the first worshipers of fire</margin>
Since nothing in this world is more similar to those celestial fires—the Sun, the Moon, and the Stars—than our own earthly fire, the ancients believed that the fire we use was a small particle of the solar fire lying hidden throughout all things. It is truly no wonder, then, that fire was worshiped by all the Eastern peoples with such great zeal, care, and devotion. The first authors of this worship were Mizraim and Cush, the sons of Ham. Cush, through his son Nimrod, brought this worship to the Babylonians, Assyrians, and Phoenicians; Mizraim, through his descendants, first carried it to the Egyptians, Persians, Arabs, and Libyans. Among the other nations after the Egyptians, fire was most highly worshiped by the Chaldeans and Persians; this is attested regarding the Chaldeans by the history of Canopus related earlier from Rufinus and Suidas. Regarding the Persians, <margin>Agathias, *History*, Book 2</margin> Agathias asserts that fire was the greatest God of the Persians. He demonstrates that it was first introduced by Zoroaster—whom we have previously identified as being confused with Mithras, Mizraim, and Osiris—and was later propagated by Perseus. This is supported by George the Monk:

<margin>George the Monk</margin>
> Perseus himself taught the Persians the abominable ceremonies and the magic called that of Medea <note>original Greek: Μηδείας; Kircher’s Latin translation reads "Medusa," but the Greek refers to the sorceress Medea</note>. During his reign, fire descended from heaven into Persia. Lighting another fire from this and building a temple, he placed it within, calling it the "immortal fire." Appointing prudent men to serve and guard the fire, he called them Magians <note>The *Magi* were the priestly caste of ancient Persia, famous for their knowledge of astronomy and fire rituals</note>. The Persians continue to observe these rites with great honor even to this day.

Cedrenus records these events regarding Persia in almost the same words, <margin>Cedrenus. Diodorus, Book 1, Ch. 1</margin> although Diodorus Siculus attributes them to Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire and metalworking</note>. However it may be, it was shown in the preceding volume that Zoroaster (whether he was Ham, Mizraim, or Nimrod, all of whom we have said used this same name) imbued the Persians with magical rites and the worship of fire. Perseus, having been instructed by these people and finding new methods of worshiping fire, established at Iopolis and in all his other domains the worship of fire as a God fallen from heaven, calling the priests of this fire "Magians." <margin>John Tzetzes, *Chiliads* 1, Ch. 67</margin> Hence, the Persians and the Magians prefer fire over the other elements, using it in the ceremonies of Mithras. They do this partly because they consider the Sun (Mithras) to be the Leader of fires and the parent of lights, and partly because, according to Nicetas, they maintained that Mithras himself was, as it were, the very core <note>original Latin: *renem*, literally "kidney," here meaning the essential inner source</note> of fire. Therefore, fire was held in the highest worship among the Persians and Babylonians, and even among the common people themselves. This is evident from that elegant (though false) epigram, where a certain common Persian shows that he would more willingly give up his life than violate the fire:

<sig>Ii 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: πῦρ (fire)</meta>

<summary>Kircher traces the origins of fire worship back to the biblical figures Cush and Mizraim, explaining how it spread through Zoroaster and Perseus to the Persians and Babylonians. He argues that fire was venerated as a terrestrial fragment of the divine celestial bodies, eventually becoming the central element of Mithraic and Magian rituals.</summary>

### CHAPTER II. THE ISIAIC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>Anthology, book 3.</margin>
-> . . . . fire to reveal . . . . <note>original Greek: πῦρ δὲ μῆναι</note> <-
-> To us, the bronze is more bitter than death. <note>original Greek: Ἡμῖν τὸ χαλκοῦ πικρότερον θανάτου</note> <-

<margin>Eustathius on Dionysius’s *Description of the World*.</margin>
Hence they worshiped not only the Sun (which they called a <term>glowing mass</term> <note>original Greek: μύδρον; a term for a red-hot stone or metal</note> or a white-hot stone) and this elemental fire, but also anything that bore the appearance of fire. Eustathius asserts that <note>original Greek: Πάντα ἀνεκδοτῆ σεβασμους Πέρσας</note> the Persians worshiped all things that were unconsumed or inexplicable. For this reason, they also held <term>Pyropus</term> <note>a gold-copper alloy or gemstone known for its fiery red color</note> in honor, as if it were emitting flames, as Strabo notes. It will be proven elsewhere that this material was placed atop obelisks and pyramids by the Egyptians to represent the fiery nature of the Sun. Indeed, they fell into such superstition that nothing was denied to those who had carried fire into a river; if their wishes were not granted, they would threaten to <margin>Plutarch</margin> drown the fire in the water, as Plutarch mentions. Fire was worshiped not only by the common people, but especially by Kings in buildings sacredly prepared for that purpose; <margin>Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 5.</margin> and this was done daily, says Theodoret, who calls it the <term>inextinguishable fire</term> <note>original Greek: πῦρ ἄσβεστον</note>. Likewise, the temples themselves were called <term>fire-temples</term> <note>original Greek: πυρεῖα; pyreia</note>, in which Procopius says they kept the fire for divinations, beginning all their sacred rites from it, just as the Romans did with Vesta and Janus. <margin>Strabo, book 15; Maximus Tyrius, sermon 26.</margin> Strabo says: <note>original Greek: Ὅτω δ’ ἂν θύωσι Θεῷ πρώτῳ τῷ πυρὶ ἔχον</note> "To whichever God they might sacrifice, they first addressed their vows to the fire." Maximus Tyrius also notes that whenever they sacrificed to the fire, they would bring food to the fire and say, *Fire, O Lord, eat*, <note>original Greek: Θυσιαι πέρσα ταὶ πυρὶ ἐπιφέρουσιν αὐτῷ τὴν πυρὸς τροφὴν ἐπιλέγοντες, πῦρ δεσπότα ἔσθε</note>. They treated it with such honor that, according to Strabo and Laërtius, they believed it a crime to be atoned for only by death to stir the fire with a breath, or to pollute it by throwing in corpses or other unclean things.

<margin>Gregory of Tours: Fire worship from Ham.</margin>
Gregory of Tours says that all fire worship flowed from the lineage of Ham, and especially from Cush. These are his words:
> Cush was the firstborn of Ham. He was imbued by the Devil with the whole of the magical arts and was the first inventor of idolatry. He was the first to decree that a statue of fire should be worshiped; through magical arts, he falsely claimed that stars and fire fell from heaven. When he passed over to the Persians, he was called Zoroaster for this reason, which they interpret as "living star."

<margin>Clement of Alexandria.</margin>
This agrees with what Clement records in the fourth book of his *Recognitions*:
> The Persians derive their race from one of the sons of Ham, who was called Mizraim; after his death, they called him Zoroaster, that is, "the living star."

From these accounts, it is clear—as we suggest everywhere throughout this work—that the sons and grandsons of Ham were called "Zoroasters" after the name of their father, due to the similarity of their actions, customs, and the established worship of the stars and fire. If you weigh this equivalence of names well, it will not be difficult to aptly reconcile many discordant passages <margin>Worshipers of fire.</margin> of history. Thus, from these three Magicians—Ham, Mizraim, and Cush—the worship of fire, like that of the stars, was propagated through the entire world. And first, indeed, Mizraim, having been taught by Ham, disseminated it through his sons Ludim, Lehabim, Anamim, and Pathrusim into all the regions neighboring Egypt and the islands of the sea. But Nimrod, the son of Cush, along with Canaan, first introduced it into Babylonia, Assyria, and Phoenicia. Nimrod, a most famous astronomer, when he had vowed and arranged to be struck by fire from heaven, commanded the Persians to gather, preserve, and worship his bones after his burning, promising that the Kingdom would not be taken from the Persians as long as they worshiped his bones. Therefore, when Zoroaster was reduced to ashes by a lightning bolt, the Persians worshiped his remains; when these were neglected, they lost their empire. This history is told in nearly the same

<margin>Constantinus Manasses.</margin>

But his father, seeing the matter was otherwise, heard many insults directed at Nimrod. Abraham was then led to Nimrod, the King of Babel, who commanded him to worship fire.”*

Hence they dedicated everything analogous to it; they erected statues, pyramids, obelisks, and the shapes and types of fire. Finally, from those celestial fires, as if from a certain source, flowed all the idolatry not only of the Hebrews, but of other nations. After the progeny of <term>Ham</term> <note>Chami</note>, the first among the Hebrews to practice this were <term>Nahor</term> and <term>Serug</term> <note>Saruch</note>, who discovered both new methods for manufacturing idols and new ceremonies for fire. These men, relying on diabolical arts, first taught how to animate the statues of the Sun, Moon, and constellations by summoning demons; we shall deal with these matters in the course of this treatise, God willing.

# CHAPTER III.
### Concerning the Teraphim, the First Idols of the Hebrews

<margin>Rupert's commentary on Genesis, chapter 31.</margin>
**Certainly**, that idolatry is most ancient and was introduced into the world by the reprobate stirp of <term>Noah</term> in the very first years after the flood is abundantly attested both by those things of which we spoke shortly before, and by the idols which the Hebrews call <term>Teraphim</term>. The authority of Holy Scripture first mentions the name of these idols, as <term>Rupert</term> <note>Rupert of Deutz, a 12th-century theologian</note> well notes, in the 31st chapter of <term>Genesis</term>, with these words:

-> And Laban went to shear his sheep; and Rachel stole the Teraphim <note>original Hebrew: התרפים</note> which belonged to her father. <-

*Laban,* it says, *departed to shear his sheep, and Rachel stole the Teraphim—that is, the idols of her father.* These are interpreted in various ways by various authors. Others, such as <term>Pererius</term> <note>Benedictus Pererius, a Jesuit commentator</note> in this passage, maintain that <term>Teraphim</term> are nothing other than, generically, images, whether likenesses or figures of any kind, and of any things, whether of men or of gods, which are called idols. I say images and figures of any kind, expressed either through painting, sculpture, or weaving. This is also supported by the Chaldean Paraphrase of Rabbi <term>Onkelos</term> <note>The Targum Onkelos</note>, which in place of <term>Teraphim</term> reads *Tsalmanaia* <note>original Aramaic: צלמניא</note>, that is, "images" or "simulacra." His words are:

<margin>Teraphim, that is, any image whatsoever.</margin>
<margin>Onkelos in the Chaldean Paraphrase.</margin>

### SYNTAGMA IV. PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. PAGE 255. CHAPTER III.

"And Laban went to shear his sheep; and Rachel took the images that belonged to her father." <note>original: "ולבן אזל למיגז ית עניה ונסיבת רחל ית צלמניא די לאבוהא", Genesis 31:19</note>

*And Laban went away to shear the sheep; and Rachel carried off the small images which were her father’s.* The Syriac reading also agrees with this:

"And Laban went to shear his sheep, and Rachel stole the images of her father." <note>original: "ܘܠܒܢ ܐܙܠ ܠܡܓܙ ܥܢܗ ܘܓܢܒܬ ܪܚܝܠ ܨܠܡܘ̈ܗܝ ܕܐܒܘܗ̇"</note>

*And Laban went away to shear the sheep, and Rachel stole the small images of her father.*
The Greek reading uses the word <term>morphōmata</term> <note>original: "μορφώματα", meaning forms, shapes, or figures</note>, as witnessed by Saint Augustine, who in his 113th letter to Marcellus discourses on the word **Teraphim** in these words: <margin>St. Jerome</margin> "Know that 'Teraphim' is interpreted by Aquila as <term>morphōmata</term>, which we can call figures or figurations." For in the first book of Kings, where it is said that Saul sent messengers to capture David, <margin>1 Samuel 19</margin> the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> translated it thus: *And the messengers came, and behold, there were <term>kenotaphia</term> in the bed;* <note>original: "κενόταφια", meaning empty tombs or funerary monuments</note> in place of *kenotaphia*, the Hebrew has **Teraphim**, signifying a pillow sewn from goat skin, which, with its unshorn hair, was wrapped up to imitate the head of a man in the small bed. In the third chapter of Hosea as well, where the Hebrew reading has "without Ephod and without Teraphim," <note>original: "בלי איפד ובלי תרפים"</note> the Seventy translate it: *the children of Israel sat without priesthood and without manifestations.* From these examples it appears that this word **Teraphim** does not always hold the same meaning everywhere, but is transferred to many things <term>catachrestically</term> <note>original: "καταχρηסτικῶς", a rhetorical term for using a word in a strained or non-literal way</note>; a fact which Rabbi Abenezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a renowned 12th-century scholar and biblical commentator</note> also observed in this passage. His words are:

<margin>Rabbi Abenezra</margin>
"And I am not able to explain the nature of those images—which Michal, the daughter of Saul, hid in the bed to mock the visitors so they would believe David was there—as being strictly **Teraphim**. Furthermore, that verse (without Ephod, and without Teraphim) has two explanations: the first explains it as 'no King and no prince in Israel,' because God chose a King only from the family of David; therefore it is said in the second verse, 'and they shall seek the Lord their God and David their King.' It also means 'no sacrifices, nor altar, nor statues of foreign service,' nor an **Ephod** <note>A ceremonial garment worn by high priests</note>, because those who served Baal made their own Ephod in the likeness of the sacred one, but it was not the Ephod made by Moses."

Therefore, this word **Teraphim** is taken in various ways in different places of the Holy Scriptures. <margin>Teraphim have various meanings.</margin> For in Hosea, as we have just heard, it is taken for "manifestations"; in the prophets Ezekiel and Zechariah, it stands for images of divine worship. In the Book of Kings, however, it refers to any image suited to deceiving others—of the sort like that garden-dwelling **Priapus** in the works of Horace, the greatest terror of thieves and birds <note>A reference to the Roman poet Horace’s Satires, where the wooden god Priapus acts as a scarecrow</note>; and the **Cenotaph** of Michal, which was essentially a hollow frightening-object, representing a buried man or one placed on a mound for burial, as Pierius <note>Likely Pierio Valeriano, a Renaissance expert on symbols</note> would have it. But Laban’s **Teraphim**, which the sacred page records Rachel stole from her father, properly signify idols treated with divine honors, or rather the "Gods" themselves, whom Laban (having been instructed by the Egyptians and Babylonians) worshipped. This is apparent from the thirtieth verse of the cited chapter of Genesis, in which Laban, rebuking Jacob for the stolen Teraphim, says: *Why have you stolen my Gods?* These words in the Coptic or Egyptian version carry great force. We have decided to write the Coptic words here...

### CHAPTER III. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>Egyptian Reading</margin>
...we have excerpted from the Egyptian Pentateuch preserved in the Vatican Library, where it is written: "Why have you stolen the greatest of my Gods?" <note>original Coptic: "ⲉⲑⲃⲉ ⲟⲩ ⲁⲕⲕⲱⲡⲉ ⲛⲛⲁⲛⲟⲩϯ"; Kircher is quoting a Coptic translation of Genesis 31:30</note> For in the Coptic or Egyptian language, **Phti** ☩ and **Pnouti** ☩ <note>original: "ⲫϯ & ⲡⲛⲟⲩϯ"</note> are essential names for God, which signify the greatest mysteries, as we indicated in our *Coptic-Egyptian Prodromus*. Therefore, it was not without reason that Laban so harshly rebuked Jacob for the theft of his most mysterious Gods; for he esteemed them so highly that he judged that if they were taken away, all his fortune and happiness would be stripped from him at once. This is testified by his diligent search for the idols, his Isiac-like <note>Referring to the intense ritual mourning associated with the goddess Isis</note> grief, and that insane raving, all of which are signs of a man utterly devoted to idolatry.
<margin>Laban’s idol-mania.</margin>

But having touched upon these things, let us now see what figure these **Theraphim** were, and what kind of images they properly were. **Abenezra** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a prolific medieval Jewish scholar</note>, followed by **Arias Montanus** <margin>Arias Montanus, Commentary on Judges, chapter 17.</margin>, thinks that by the word **Theraphim** are signified images of the heavens and the stars, crafted through certain observation <note>meaning astronomical timing</note> and consecrated by Egyptian rites for the purpose of augury and divination. Or, they might even have been a kind of "averruncus" gods <note>from "averruncare," meaning to ward off or avert evil</note> which they carried everywhere with them to avoid unfortunate encounters. *He says,* says **Abenezra**, *that the Theraphim was a bronze instrument for knowing the parts of the hours; but others say that the Theraphim is nothing else than that force or power in those who have knowledge of the stars, by which at certain times and hours known to them they manufacture figures suitable for divinations, for the figure of the Theraphim spoke; and it was made in the likeness of a man, directed toward drawing out the power of the superior bodies.* <margin>Tostatus or Abulensis, cited on Genesis.</margin> **Tostatus** <note>Alonso Tostado, a Spanish bishop and scholar</note> also agreeing with **Abenezra** in this passage, narrates how images of this kind were made by astronomical and necromantic art to be suitable for giving answers. *They were,* he says, *certain heads made of metal at a certain time and under certain influences of the stars and conjunctions of the planets, so that virtue from heaven might be derived into that head; and it would become capable of responding to those consulting and questioning it. And this was done partly through astrology and partly through necromancy; **Albertus Magnus** <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and polymath</note> of the Order of Preachers made a head of this kind, which his disciple **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> broke one day.* Thus says **Tostatus**. *But these things he says about Albert, etc., are fables.*

### CHAPTER III. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS
<meta>catchword: in.</meta>

<margin>The *Baal Aruch* <note>original: "Baal Aruch"; a famous 11th-century dictionary of the Talmud and Midrash.</note> on the word Teraphim.</margin>
...it gave answers to those seeking them, predicting the future and revealing hidden things. It also disclosed those things which were happening in remote places: even death and the secrets of hearts, as they believed, were revealed. Thus, they deceived many souls, whom they held miserably in their service by the novelty of these things. Regarding these, see further the *Baal Aruch*.

<margin>The worship of Teraphim passed down from the Egyptians to the Hebrews.</margin>
Since these things have been established, it now remains for us to investigate the origin of these Teraphim, about which I find that the Hebrew Doctors have held various opinions. Some derive them from Nahor and Serug; others from Zoroaster-Ham, whom we showed above was the first to construct small statues and propose them for adoration; others from the Babylonians, and finally others from various sources. Be that as it may, it is so certain that this worship of the Teraphim first flowed from the Egyptians to the Hebrews, that to demonstrate it, no other reasons are needed than those we shall bring forward shortly to prove this truth. These points may be easily perceived by anyone.

It should be noted that for the first Egyptians, instructed by Mizraim and his successors, the worship of certain clay images was extremely solemn. These images were first called in the Egyptian language *Apes* and *Serapes*, while later generations called them sometimes *Canopi*, sometimes *Horus*, or *Harpocrates*. These *Serapes* were small statues of a sort, fashioned in the likeness of boys wrapped in swaddling clothes; they were made either to show Osiris 
<margin>What "Serapis" means in Egyptian.</margin>
or Apis enclosed in a chest (for *Serapis*, speaking in the Egyptian tongue, is nothing other than "Apis in a chest," or "the bone of the bull," or "the bound Apis"); or they were made to represent Horus, the son of Osiris, whom we have demonstrated in the preceding pages to be the same as Osiris, and whom we find everywhere on the Bembine Table <term>Bembine Table: A famous bronze tablet of the 1st century AD, decorated with Egyptian-style deities and hieroglyphs, much studied by Kircher.</term> in the form of a swaddled boy, or placed upon a bed or chest; or they might show Osiris as an infant nourished by the gods, still being carried among the heavenly beings. So great an abundance of these idols—constructed from various materials and under certain alignments of the stars—was found everywhere in Egypt that, 
<margin>Innumerable small statues of swaddled boys among the Egyptians.</margin>
besides the temples which swarmed with them, no village, no corner, or path seemed to be without them. These they worshipped and observed not only at home and abroad in place of the *Lares* and *Penates* <term>Lares and Penates: Traditional Roman household gods who protected the family and the home.</term>, and as if they were *averruncous* gods <note>original: "Deos auerruncos"; deities responsible for averting calamity or "shooing away" evil.</note>; but also, so that their worship might be more pleasing to the gods, they wore them suspended from the head, neck, arms, and belts wherever they went, as will be seen throughout this work. They even inserted these into the corpses of mummies, one of which, as I write this, was brought to me from Egypt, made of cedar wood and distinguished by hieroglyphics, which we shall present in its proper place.

Thus, while this "idol-mania" was flourishing in Egypt, it happened that while Abraham (who at that very time had migrated from the land of Canaan due to the high price of grain) 
<margin>The servants of Abraham carry Teraphim with them from Egypt.</margin>
was staying in Egypt, his servants mingled with the Egyptians. They admired and looked up to many of those things, but especially these *Serapides*, whom they saw performing wonders for the Egyptians; for since a demon was animating them, they gave various answers to those consulting and questioning them, and promised prosperity to their worshippers in all their actions. Therefore, incited by curiosity and the desire to share in this prosperity, the Hebrew household servants of Abraham suddenly turned their minds to these Egyptian cults; and when Abraham returned to his homeland, it is said that, having acquired the idols and images mentioned, they returned.

# SYNTAGMA IV. THE HEBREW PANTHEON. CHAPTER III.

Returning to their homeland, they gradually spread the errors conceived in Egypt among the Chaldeans (or Alphaxadeans) and Babylonians, and soon gave birth to a vast progeny of execrable gods. Indeed, for the Chaldeans—who had previously been imbued with that wicked worship by Nahor and Serug <note>Biblical ancestors of Abraham associated with the period before the monotheistic covenant</note> and were quite prone to every kind of superstition—nothing was easier than to submit themselves to this foreign servitude. Adding superstition to superstition, they continually propagated it so that from that time until the Kingdom of David, this worship of *Teraphim* or *Serapis* never ceased among the Hebrew descendants. But lest we seem to have drawn any of these statements merely from our own storehouse, let us hear the words of Abenephius <note>original: "Abenephius"; likely referring to the 10th-century writer Ibn Wahshiyya or a similar Arabic source used by Kircher</note>, confirming these things in almost the same words; for he writes thus in Arabic:

<margin>Abenephius</margin>
> The Egyptians had idols in the form of children, and they were called by their name, *Saraphis*. They used to worship them and ask them about the secrets of nature and the future. They placed them in all the prominent places of the cities, burning incense in their presence, and they carried them with them like talismans against every evil. These idols are like the *Teraphim* which the children of Israel had, which Laban worshipped; and it is said that the household of Abraham brought them with them when they returned from Egypt.

> *That is: Moreover, the Egyptians had certain images in the likeness of a boy, which were called by the Egyptian name Serapis; these they adored, questioning them about future and hidden things. They placed them in all the more celebrated places of the cities, burning incense before them; they were also accustomed to carry them with them against the occurrence of evils. And these idols are similar to the Teraphim, which the Israelites worshipped, and which the Scripture records that Laban adored; and it is said that the members of Abraham's household, while staying in Egypt, brought them back with them upon their return.*

<margin>What are the Teraphim of the Hebrews?</margin>
And from these things it is gathered that these *Teraphim* of the Hebrews were nothing other than the *Serapis* figures of the Egyptians, since these kinds of idols correspond exactly to one another not only in name, but also in form and the rituals by which they were worshipped. But lest any scrap of doubt remain in the mind of the hesitant reader, we confirm these statements with the following.

<margin>The Etymology of Teraphim.</margin>
And first, indeed, it must be known that this word *Teraphim* is by no means Hebrew (even if it seems to affect the form of the Hebrew idiom in some way) but is purely foreign and adopted. This is evident from the fact that this word is never used by Hebrew Doctors outside of the Scripture, nor is it found anywhere in the singular with this meaning. As a witness to this matter I bring forward Oleaster <note>Jerónimo Azambuja, a 16th-century Portuguese Dominican commentator</note>, who greatly approves of this interpretation of the word:

<margin>Oleaster in his commentary on this passage cited from Genesis.</margin>
> *It is not agreed, he says, among the Hebrew Doctors what the word Teraphim signifies, which we translate as idols; however, we have this certainty regarding that word: that it signifies images of men that spoke.*

To which Eliezer <note>Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, to whom the Pirkei De-Rabbi Eliezer is attributed</note> subscribes in this place:

> I have not found among the grammarians what the matter of the *Teraphim* is. <note>original Hebrew: "לא מצאתי במדקדקים . מה ענין תרפים"</note>

<margin>Eliezer on Chapter 31 of Genesis.</margin>
He says: I have not yet found among the Grammarians what this word *Teraphim* means for itself. It is asked, therefore, what kind of word is this? I answer that it is an Egyptian word, and is the same as *Serapis*, which Abenephius hints at not obscurely in the preceding citation, where he compares the *Teraphim* with *Serapis* for this very reason.

<margin>Abenephius, Book 1, on the religion of Egypt.</margin>

### CHAPTER III. 260 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE

"Mitzra" <note>original: מצרא; a name for Egypt</note> is pronounced by some with a natural defect of the tongue; as is well known to those familiar with the Chaldean language.

<margin>Serapis and the Teraphim are the same.</margin>
When the Hebrew-Chaldeans, who had become imbued with the cult of Serapis <note>A Graeco-Egyptian deity associated with the sun, healing, and the afterlife</note> while in Egypt, frequently heard the name of Serapis repeated, they brought these idols along with the name into Chaldea and made them their own. These images, which the Egyptians called Serapes, they called **Theraphis** <note>Teraphim</note> by changing the letter *S* <note>original: צ or ס</note> into *T* <note>original: ת</note>. 
<margin>The Chaldeans pronounce words beginning with S as if they start with T.</margin>
This word later became entirely part of Hebrew usage, with the final *S* changed to an *M* <note>original: ם to מ</note> due to similarity, so that instead of *Theraphis* they were called *Theraphim*, and it was eventually numbered among the other words of the Hebrews. From this, it is manifest that **Serapis** and **Theraphim** are the same name. Another reason we believe the Teraphim and Serapis to be identical is the similarity of the rituals in performing these types of sacrifices. For just as the Teraphim were constructed from various materials under a certain position of the stars, so too was Serapis fashioned from every kind of wood, stone, and metal. The Teraphim were not made without human blood, as we showed previously from Abenezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a renowned 12th-century Spanish Jewish scholar and biblical commentator</note>, nor were the idols of Serapis in the Mithraic mysteries. Again, the Teraphim were commonly worn in place of 
<margin>The Teraphim were worn in place of phylacteries.</margin>
phylacteries <note>protective amulets or religious scrolls worn on the body</note>; which we read was also done with the idols of Serapis. Finally, they practiced divination through the Teraphim and investigated hidden things, which is evident even from the words of Abenezra in the place cited. When he examines the reason why Rachel stole her father’s Teraphim, he finally concludes that it was because Rachel feared her parent, by consulting his idols in his usual manner, would learn from their responses where Jacob had gone and by what way he had fled. But let us hear the words of Abenezra discussing it thus:

<margin>Rabbi Abenezra on Genesis, chapter 31.</margin>
->And behold, the Teraphim—Laban called them his gods. And some say that Rachel stole them to stop her father from practicing idolatry. But if this were so, why did she take them with her? She would have hidden them on the road. It is more likely that Rachel stole them because she knew her father, Laban, was an expert in the stars <note>Astrology</note>, and she feared her father would look at the stars to learn which way they had fled.<-

> "Lo," he says, "*the Teraphim, which Laban called his gods, are said to have been taken by Rachel for the purpose of calling her father away from idolatry. But if this were the case, why did she take them away with her, and not rather hide them on the road near Laban's house? She took them, therefore, because since her parent was skilled in Astrology, Rachel feared lest by consulting them and the stars, he might learn where Jacob had fled.*" 

The Teraphim were therefore idols that gave answers to those who consulted them; we shall prove extensively elsewhere that the statues of Serapis or Isis were of the same kind. Furthermore, it now falls to us to prove that the Teraphim were not dissimilar in form to the images of Serapis. And first, the Teraphim, no less than the Serapes of the Egyptians, represented various figures. For some were adorned with such industry that, besides other uses, they also showed the **divisions of the hours**; and this is what Rabbi Abenezra hinted at above when he says:

->...that it was a bronze instrument made for knowing the divisions of the hours.<-

<margin>The form of the Teraphim.</margin>
*That the Teraphim were like a certain bronze instrument made for discerning the parts of the hours.* A trace of this matter appears in that most ancient hieroglyphic table which Herwart <note>Hans Georg Herwart von Hohenburg, a 17th-century scholar of chronology and hieroglyphs</note> inserted into his hieroglyphic treasury, in which the third hieroglyphic diagram (A) shows a man dressed in a toga, who, extending a rod, points to a certain minute image adapted into the form of a casting...

Thus, the Teraphim of the Hebrews occasionally also provided the means of knowing the hours; which Horus Apollo <note>a supposed Egyptian author of a treatise on hieroglyphs, often cited by Kircher</note> also shows regarding the Serapic Idols of the Egyptians, in whose writings a <term>Cynocephalus</term> <note>A dog-headed baboon, a creature sacred to the god Thoth</note>, by dripping water from its private parts, showed the hours by the increase of water in a vessel placed below. With this Macrobius <note>a 5th-century Roman provincial administrator and author</note> agrees, who describes idols of this kind as being <term>hydrometers</term> <note>original: ὑδρόμετρα; water-clocks</note>, a custom which the Hebrews, taught by the Egyptians, without doubt inserted into their own sacred rites.

<margin>Why the Egyptians constructed their Teraphim without hands and feet.</margin>
Furthermore, the <term>Teraphim</term> idols were almost always prepared in the form of a wrapped child, as has been said, and suited for carrying; hence they appear to have been constructed mostly without hands and feet. For the Egyptians especially feared any defect in their images resulting from some breakage; that the Serapes also had this kind of figure is evidenced by those little statues, partly made of clay, partly of stone and wood, a vast quantity of which are dug up every year by merchants from the ancient monuments of the Egyptians and brought to Europe. 

Moreover, as for Eliezer <note>Rabbi Eliezer ben Hyrcanus, a famous 1st-century Jewish sage to whom various mystical descriptions are attributed</note> saying that the <term>Teraphim</term> was the head of a firstborn son, preserved with salt and spices, which they placed upon a wall and worshiped, seeking responses from it and performing divinations on various matters; that certainly also flowed entirely from the Egyptians, who worshiped the preserved bodies of their Kings as if they were Gods, seeking knowledge of the future from them when they were animated by a demon. We shall show elsewhere that in the <term>Mithraic</term> <note>The mystery cult of the god Mithras</note> rites as well, nothing was done without bloody rituals of this kind. And from all these things alleged thus far, it is gathered that the Hebrew-Chaldeans—just as they did with these portable idols (which they call <term>Teraphim</term>, or in the Egyptian manner, <term>Serapis</term>)—so too they introduced all other kinds of superstitions learned from the Egyptians into their Synagogue...

### CHAPTER IV. THE ISIACT TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>How tenacious the Hebrew people were in the worship of Idols. The proneness of the Hebrews to Egyptian idolatry.</margin>
...introduced, as the Hebrews' habitual and continuous worship of idols shows more than enough. Once this kind of **idolo-mania** <note>original: εἰδωλομανία; a madness or obsession with idols</note> was introduced, it fixed its roots so deeply that it seemed impossible to tear it out from the minds of these blinded men, even by the greatest miracles and various wonders performed by different Patriarchs. From this came the scandalous life of the Hebrews; from this, the calves—the **Apis-bulls** <note>Apis was an Egyptian bull-deity; Kircher suggests the "Golden Calf" of the Exodus was an imitation of this Egyptian god</note>—in the desert; from this, the golden statues of Jeroboam; from this, the construction of "high places" <note>hilltop shrines used for pagan or unauthorized worship</note>; from this, the deeply rooted worship of **Teraphim** in the house of Jacob. Concerning these, Oleaster <note>Jerónimo Azambuja (1500–1563), a Portuguese Dominican scholar who wrote influential commentaries on the Pentateuch</note> aptly notes that the Scripture itself indicates in Genesis 35 that there were idols in the house of Jacob, even after the departure from Laban and the journey out of Mesopotamia, where Jacob warns his household:

> *Cast away the strange gods that are among you, and be cleansed, and change your garments. And they gave to Jacob all the strange gods that were in their hands, and the earrings which were in their ears; and he hid them under the oak which was at Shechem.*

Furthermore, it is not believable that the women, servants, and other companions of Jacob, being accustomed to idols, would have so easily abandoned everything and so quickly forgotten the worship of their gods as to not carry some trace of idolatry with them—especially since the **Teraphim**, those idols, were said to predict the future, for which they were all most greedy. So says Oleaster. But let these remarks on the Teraphim of the Hebrews suffice. Now let us pass to the remaining idols of the Hebrews.

# CHAPTER IV.
## Concerning the Baalim of the Hebrews.

Since authors torment themselves in a strange manner over these monstrous names of the gods—**Baal**, **Bel**, **Baalim**—as to what they properly signify and from whence they drew their origin, I thought I would be doing something worthwhile if, before I proceeded further, I offered a brief prelude concerning the origin of such names. In doing so,

<margin>The Origin of Idolatry.</margin>
<margin>Nimrod called Bel, that is, Lord.</margin>
<margin>בעל or Baal, or Bel, what it signifies.</margin>
it must be known: At that time when, after the Flood of the world, the offspring of the human race was taking on immense growth everywhere, **Mizraim** <note>The biblical ancestor of the Egyptians</note>, who at that time held power in Egypt, frequently sent new colonies elsewhere to relieve the province of people. Among other colonists, he also destined **Nimrod** for Babylonia. Since Nimrod was clever and of a versatile spirit, and was driven by an uncontrollable desire for reigning, he left nothing unturned. By using the malicious arts with which he had already been imbued by his father, and by fascinating the minds of his subjects, he sought to acquire divine honors for himself—just as he knew his father Mizraim had already obtained them in Egypt by a similar way of acting, as was said in the preceding pages. Nor was his crafty spirit <note>original: *versipelle ingenium*; literally "skin-changing," implying a deceptive or versatile nature</note> cheated of its hope; for having invented the art of reigning and commanding, when he first ascended the peak of Monarchy, he obtained such fame for his name among the Assyrians that, with temples and altars built in his honor, they everywhere called him **Bel**. Now, **Bel** in the Babylonian language is nothing other than **Lord**, a patron and one who is powerful in affairs; they were accustomed to call by this name those who, by virtue and the glory of their deeds, had earned divine hon—

### SYNTHESIS IV. PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS CHAPTER IV.

...they had earned honors. Thus, the Babylonian Bel was called Nimrod <note>Nimrod is described in Genesis as a "mighty hunter" and the first king of Babylon</note>, just as Misraim <note>Misraim is the biblical name for Egypt, or the son of Ham who settled there</note> was called the Egyptian Bel; this was because the former held power in Assyria and the latter in Egypt, and through their invention of various things, they earned divine honors among their descendants.

<margin>Diodorus Siculus.</margin>
Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> first demonstrates that this is indeed the case; he says that Osiris, having established many colonies, first brought Bel (the son of Neptune and Libya, who had settled near the Euphrates and established the Chaldean Priests) into Babylonia. Furthermore, we demonstrated in the first chapter of this Synthesis that Osiris is the same as Misraim. Now, because this Bel was powerful in his remarkable knowledge of the stars, he was called by his descendants *Baal shamayim* <note>original: בעל שמים; "Lord of Heaven"</note>, that is, the Lord of Heaven; concerning whom Philo of Byblos <note>A writer who claimed to translate the works of the Phoenician priest Sanchuniathon</note> and Eusebius write that he was named *Beelsemen* by the Phoenicians, which in the Phoenician language signifies the Lord of Heaven. <margin>Saint Jerome.</margin> Saint Jerome also says, in his first book on Hosea, that when Semiramis <note>The legendary queen of Babylon</note> had overcome Zoroaster the Magician and King of the Bactrians in battle, she attained such great glory that she elevated her father Bel into a God, who in Hebrew is called *Beel*; he says the Sidonians and Phoenicians called him **Baal** <note>original: בעל</note>, who is the same as Belus. I find that the Latins, by unanimous consensus, interpreted Baal, Bel, and Belus as **Jupiter** <note>The king of the Roman gods, equivalent to the Greek Zeus</note>, concerning which one may read the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, which treats these types of names most extensively. And not without reason; for it is established from the monuments of the ancients that both were of a most fierce <margin>Bel and the Babylonian Jupiter are the same.</margin> character, both were possessed by an unrestrained lust for ruling, and both were contaminated by every kind of vice, both Jupiter and Bel; yet many were not ashamed to call each of them a "God," calling him "Best and Greatest" <note>original: "optimum, maximum"; the standard title for Jupiter (Iuppiter Optimus Maximus)</note> according to Cicero, though he deserved nothing less. This Bel, or Babylonian Jupiter, was possessed by such ambition as no one else has been found to have, or will be found to have, through all ages; wherefore some, by his own command, and others to court his favor, established altars and temples to him, as well as Priests and their own ritual ceremonies. But what? Is it not the greatest sign of ambition which is written by Lactantius in his book *On False Religion*, that he frequently stayed on Olympus—which he [the author] not wrongly identifies with that Babylonian tower and the lofty city which he first built—just as Jupiter did on the mountains? He invited everyone, by proposing rewards, who could devise some new invention useful to the human race to bring it to him first; he himself was later believed to be the inventor of these things, and for this reason, as with many other inventors of useful things, divine honors were paid to him. The fact that there was a most ample and magnificent temple of Bel among the Babylonians, which Diodorus describes, demonstrates this sufficiently.

<margin>Bel Jupiter.</margin>
The celebrity and reverence of the name of this Bel or Jupiter was so great among all nations that not long afterward he began to hear the prayers of mortals, and, being invited to the banquets of many sacrifices, he was glutted with the steam of smoking platters. What then? If, among an infinite number of prayers, fortune had breathed upon someone so that they obtained their wish, that person, thinking they had secured it from Bel or Jupiter, immediately erected altars and temples, and imposed a surname upon Jupiter or Bel or Baal based on the outcome or the place where it happened. From this, countless monstrous gods soon arose, everywhere [spreading] various...

### CHAPTER IV. 264 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAIC TEMPLE

...idle men have provided material for storytelling, as is clearly shown by Bel, Belus, Baal, Baalim, Balaam, Beelphegor, Beelsephon, Beelteem, Beelzebub, Beelmeon; and those derived from the Hebrew Baal, such as Baalberith, Baalgad, Baalhamon, Baalhasor, Baalhermon, Baalpharasin, Baalthamar, and six hundred others of this kind, which we shall discuss in the following sections.

<margin>What "Baal" signifies.</margin>
Therefore, the Hebrew name **Baal** <note>original: בעל</note>, equivalent to the Babylonian **Bel** <note>original: בעל</note>, signifies nothing other than that than which nothing greater or better can be conceived by man—namely, God, insofar as He is powerful and ready to help men in their needs. The name of **Jupiter** himself also indicates such a nature, which some derive from the word for "helping" <note>original: "à Iuuando"; Kircher refers to the traditional etymology of *Iuppiter* as *Iuvans Pater* or "Helping Father"</note>, and they seem to clearly support our opinion.

Thus, **Belus** was considered to be **Jupiter** by the Babylonians and Assyrians; mention of him is found not only in profane histories but also in sacred ones. For this reason, it seemed appropriate to repeat, from various authors, what I have discovered about him from a somewhat deeper perspective.

<margin>The etymology of Hel and Bel.</margin>
First, **Servius** <note>A 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Virgil</note> wrote that the name of Bel is not without reason; for in the language of the Assyrians, it signifies the **Sun**. From this, with an aspiration added, he was called in Greek **Helios** <note>original: ἥλιος</note>. Others maintain he is called by the Phoenician name **Hel** <note>original: אל (El)</note>, from which **Helius** is derived, and who was soon also called Belus. Furthermore, Servius reports that while *Hal* is the word for God in the Punic language, among the Assyrians he was called *Hel*, being for certain mystical reasons both **Saturn** and the **Sun**. But anyone who is even moderately instructed in Hebrew and Chaldean will easily reject all such far-fetched derivations and etymologies that have nothing to do with the matter. Furthermore, sacred scripture shows in more than one place that there were many **Bels** and **Baals**, which can also be gathered from that passage in the first book of the *Aeneid*:

<margin>Virgil, Aeneid, Book 1.</margin>
->engraved in gold<-
->*The brave deeds of the fathers, a very long series of events*<-
->*Led through so many men, from the ancient origin of the race.*<-

"Through so many men," he says, led from the first Belus of the Assyrians, as in "Cinnamon lasting from ancient **Belus**"; and hence "The Queen calls for a bowl heavy with gems and gold, and filled it with pure wine, which **Belus** and all his descendants were accustomed to use." Therefore, this is the lineage of the race: **Jupiter**, **Epaphus**, **Belus the Elder**, **Agenor**, **Phoenix**, and **Belus the Younger**, who was also called **Metres**. **Sanchuniathon** <note>An ancient Phoenician author whose works survive in fragments</note>, however, in his Phoenician theology, counts Belus among the sons of Saturn and asserts that he was Jupiter, a point which
<margin>Eusebius.</margin>
**Eusebius** <note>The "Father of Church History," writing in the 4th century</note> also supports. We read of another Belus, the grandson of Jupiter and son of King Epaphus of Egypt, who also fathered another Belus. We also suggested above that **Misraim** was called the "Egyptian Bel" by the Assyrians, just as **Nimrod** was the "Babylonian Bel," to whom (as **Pliny** <note>A Roman author and natural philosopher</note> relates) a gemstone was dedicated by the Assyrians and called "the Eye of Bel."

<margin>Cyril.</margin>
**Cyril** <note>Likely St. Cyril of Alexandria</note>, however, in his third book against **Julian the Emperor**, reveals that Belus was also called **Arbelus**, and was the first man to receive the name of God from his subjects, and to whom the Assyrian and neighboring peoples paid sacrifices and worship—something which Eusebius also writes in his *Chronicles*. From this, therefore, that celebrated and frequent Hebrew practice of **Baal-worship** <note>original: "Baalatriæ"</note> took its origin. We shall discuss this now, beginning with the most famous deity, **Beelphegor**.

<header>SYNTAX IV. THE HEBREW PANTHEON. CHAPTER V.</header>

# CHAPTER V.

->*Concerning Beelphegor, who is a minor deity or idol of the Ammonites.*<-

<margin>Theodoret, Basil, and Chrysostom on Genesis.</margin>
<margin>Rhodiginus.</margin>
<margin>Scaliger.</margin>
**B**aalphegor, to the Hebrews **Baal Peor** <note>original: בעל פעור</note> or what amounts to the same thing, "Lord of the gap" or "opening," was an idol of the Moabites. He is mentioned by the prophet Hosea, and also appears in the books of Numbers (chapter 25), Deuteronomy (chapter 4), and Joshua (chapter 22). Frequently, the name "Baal" is omitted, and he is simply called "Phegor" or "Phogor," as in the letter to the Hebrews (chapter 17) <note>Kircher likely refers to a commentary or a specific Vulgate citation here</note>. Regarding what kind of idol this was, opinions vary. Theodoret, Saint Basil, and Chrysostom record that he was called **Saturn** by the Greeks; I find that Apollinaris was also of this opinion. Chrysostom adds that "Baal" is the general name for an idol, while "Phogor" is the name of a place; furthermore, he notes that this particular idol is also called "Bel." Rhodiginus agrees on other points, but along with Jerome, he states that **Bel**, **Beel**, and **Baal** are common names and signify the same idol. This is because Belus, the first King of the Assyrians and son of Ninus (though we call him the father), was the first to receive the name of "God" from his subjects, as was previously related. Whatever the case may be, it is certain that "Baal" is used for a specific idol, and the plural "**Baalim**" for various idols, or for that same Assyrian deity which other nations later fashioned or named in different ways. Thus, Scaliger incorrectly inferred that "Baal" is never found without an adjunct title. This contradicts the sacred text, which often mentions "Baal" alone, with no other name attached.

<margin>What does Beel signify?</margin>
We say, therefore, that the Hebrew name **Baal** <note>original: בעל</note> and the Chaldean **Beel** or **Bel** <note>original: ביל</note>, in a general sense, signify nothing other than any false deity, just as we use the word "idol" or "god," which is common to Jupiter, Saturn, or Mercury. Thus, "Baal" holds the place of the **genus** <note>The broad category</note>, while the attached name represents the **species** <note>The specific type</note>. In this way, Beelphegor is distinguished from Beelzebub, Beelthemar, and the others indicated above.

<margin>What kind of idol was Beelphegor?</margin>
<margin>Beelphegor is the same as Priapus.</margin>
With these things established, it is asked: what exactly was Beelphegor, and what kind of idol was it? To decide this, I would ask the modest reader to forgive me if, perhaps, their chaste ears should be struck by the obscenity of the subject matter; for the investigation of a superstitious origin suggests nothing else. Let all things be pure to the pure, and let the reader know that I shall add nothing of my own words, but shall allege everything word-for-word from Sacred Scripture, the Holy Fathers, and other writers—both as a caution and to reveal the roots of these superstitions. First, there are those who confuse him with the Sun, Saturn, Jupiter, or Bacchus, as is clear from what was said above. We conclude, however, that he was none other than **Priapus** <note>A Greek god of fertility, often depicted with permanent arousal</note>. This is clear first from the etymology of the name; for "Priapus" in Hebrew is nothing other than **Peor-peh** <note>original: פה פעור</note>, that is, "the mouth of nakedness." Thus says the *Baal Aruch* <note>A famous 12th-century dictionary of the Talmud and Midrash</note>: "And the name Beelphegor, its explanation is the mouth of nakedness" <note>original Hebrew: ובעל פעור פירשו פער פה</note>. From this it is clear that Priapus, since it is not a Greek word, surely took its origin from no other than the Hebrew **Peorpè**, to which the word "Priapus" is very similar. Added to this is the fact that *Peorpè* among the Hebrews properly signifies the male member, and specifically that part called the *glans*; Saint Jerome writes that Beelphegor was fashioned in this image—consult him, and...

### SECTION IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. 267 CAP. V.

...impious and most wicked sacrifices offered to Beelphegor, this precept was given to the priests: that at the time of sacrifice they should walk about wearing breeches <note>The Latin 'braccati' refers to trousers or breeches, a garment often associated by Romans with 'barbarians,' but here emphasizing modesty</note>, lest they show any irreverence to God by an appearance of nakedness. I shall provide his words:

<note>original Hebrew: "But you know that the public worship of Peor in those times consisted of the uncovering of nakedness; because of this, He commanded the priests to make breeches to cover the flesh of their nakedness during the time of service, and that they should not go up to the altar by steps, so that their nakedness would not be revealed."</note>

*But you know that the service of the Peor idols in those times was such that they would uncover their <unclear>shameful</unclear> parts before him; and for that reason, the priests were commanded to make breeches and undergarments with which they might cover their shameful flesh at the hour of sacrifice. Therefore, they did not ascend to the altar by steps, lest they be uncovered.*
These are the words of Rambam <note>A common acronym for Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, also known as Maimonides, the preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher</note>.

Therefore, having weighed all those things which the ancient monuments record concerning Baalphegor and his impious rites, let us now return to our purpose. This is to show that this entire "Phegor-worship" and this collection of wicked rituals flowed from nowhere else but the Egyptians. Diodorus teaches us that the Egyptians always held the phallus—the private part of Osiris—in the highest veneration, by the institution and advice of Isis. We have already sufficiently and more than enough insinuated this by showing his entire history above in the chapter on Osiris and Apis, drawing profusely from the authors.

<margin>The Phallus and Phegor are the same.</margin>
Moreover, it is the common opinion of all mythologists that the phallus is the same as Priapus <note>The Greek god of fertility, usually depicted with a permanent and oversized erection</note>. They held these Priapi or phalli in such high honor that it seemed no action could be performed without them.
<margin>Herodotus.</margin>
According to Herodotus, they carried these suspended from their necks during the sacred rites of Dionysus. These were statues a cubit high <note>About 18 inches</note> which, according to Diodorus, were carried about in honor of Osiris during festivals to the sound of a pipe. They were made of various materials: glass, ivory, gold, silk, and cloth. Women used them especially to satisfy the cravings of Venus <note>A euphemism for sexual desire</note>.
<margin>What the Ithyphallum is.</margin>
From this, the Ithyphallia also seem to have taken their origin. Now, an *ithyphallos* <note>original Greek: ἰθύφαλλος</note>—as we have often said in preceding pages and shall say hereafter—is nothing other than a Priapus with an erect phallus.
<margin>Diodorus, Book 1, Ch. 2. Lucian, On the Syrian Goddess. Herodotus in Euterpe.</margin>
According to Diodorus, Lucian, and Herodotus, this was celebrated annually by the Egyptians with the greatest investigation and cult. Its image was *one which held the penis erect*, according to Suidas. Lucian demonstrates that among these, Typhon was also marked with the name of Priapus. *The Egyptians,* he says, *fashioned the likeness of Priapus (whom they called Horus and Typhon) in a human form. In his right hand he held a scepter, because they believed that the earth and sea were brought to light by him. In his left hand he held his own erect penis, because he sends forth the seeds covered by the soil into the open. The wings, however, indicated the swiftness of motion, and the disk signified the circumference of the World (for they thought him to be the same as the Sun).*
<margin>The Phallus as the 'Fascinum.' St. Augustine, City of God, Book 6.</margin>
We also find the word *Fascinum* <note>A phallic charm or amulet intended to ward off the 'evil eye'</note> used by authors to stand for Priapus or the phallus. St. Augustine mentions it among others. *What shall I say of this?* he asks, *since Priapus is there, undoubtedly a male, upon whose immense and most foul phallus a new bride was commanded to sit, according to the most "honorable" and "religious" custom of the Matrons.* Horace also writes of this:

<margin>Horace.</margin>
->*To sit red with a reddening phallus*<-
->*The phallus languishes no less.*<-

<margin>Why the Hebrews, Greeks, and Romans studied phallic worship so intensely.</margin>

It was partly because, through this worship, those evils which might impede generation were turned away as if by a charm; and partly because of that part of the body from which the origin of all things arises. <margin>Why the Hebrews accepted the most shameful rites of Priapus.</margin>
We assert, therefore, that for these same reasons the nation of the Hebrews also embraced these most shameful rites—and did so all the more willingly and greedily as they were more prone to every kind of superstition, luxury, and all-encompassing defilement. Under the mask of religion, they could safely and with impunity indulge themselves, and by following the example of the Egyptians, they might avert that shameful sterility (which was cursed in the Law) through Priapic worship. # SYNTHESIS IV. THE HEBREW PANTHEON. CHAPTER V.

...so that they might do so more easily and willingly, the fertility of the Egyptians moved them, along with the greatest pleasures they perceived from this cult, and the license to sin without punishment. Among the superstitious, there were also those infatuated by this cult who did not attribute all that prodigious fertility of the Hebrew women in Egypt to anything other than their fertile Beelphegor <note>A Latinized form of the Hebrew deity Baal-Peor, associated with the mountains of Moab and often linked to shameful or phallic rituals</note>, and to the worship of the foulest idols in which they were so entangled. It seemed that no miracles, threats, vengeances, or the obstacles of the commandments could lead them away from this mental insolence and madness. This is evident from the fact that even after the unusual and unheard-of miracles performed by God through Moses—infinite benefits performed for the sake of an ungrateful people, which the stiff-necked <note>original: "duræ ceruicis," a biblical idiom for stubbornness</note> and evil-obsessed people enjoyed daily in the desert—they despised the manna. Nauseated by the heavenly and seemingly "lightest" food, they meditated on nothing other than voluptuous Egypt and its onions, garlic, asphodels, and pots of meat <note>A reference to Exodus 16:3</note>. A certain excellent Rabbi interprets these "meat pots" quite aptly as the harlots with whom they sat in insatiable fornication. God, through the Prophet, seems to reproach the ungrateful people more than once for these most serious crimes when He says that they committed every abomination that the Lord hates with their Venus-like <note>original: "Venereis," referring to lustful or sexual deities</note> idols. These brutish desires were greatly increased by mixing with the foreign women of the Moabites, Ammonites, and Midianites, toward whom the sons of Israel were carried away with unbridled lust, as Sacred Scripture testifies.

<margin>
Numbers 25.
</margin>
<margin>
The daughters of Moab brought the rites of worshipping Beelphegor from the Egyptians to the Hebrews.
</margin>
Now Israel, it says, was staying at that time in Shittim <note>Setim in the original text, the final encampment of the Israelites before entering the Promised Land</note>, and the people committed fornication with the daughters of Moab. They called them to their sacrifices, and they ate and worshipped their gods; and Israel was initiated into the rites of Beelphegor. These women were the remnants of the incestuous offspring of Lot <note>According to Genesis 19:30–38, the Moabites and Ammonites descended from Lot's daughters</note>, and because they were neighbors to Egypt, they embraced these carnal rites of Priapus or Phogor <note>Phogor is another variant of Peor</note>. With great zeal, they first transferred these rites to the Israelites, where they soon grew. As Sacred Scripture testifies, many were so devoted to these abominations, occupied with carving phalluses and fashioning such minor deities, that they seemed to have cast aside all memory of the worship of the one true, best, and most beneficent God.

<margin>
R. Solomon, or Rashi, cited on the passage in Numbers.
</margin>
The rite of worshipping such shameful minor gods is aptly described for us by Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud</note>, also known as Rabbi Solomon Iarchi, commenting on the words *and they worshipped their gods* in the cited passage of Numbers: *When the women,* he says, *were stimulated by the itch of Venus <note>lust</note>, they approached the Israelites saying: "I have something to tell you, please listen to me." With these words, they produced a statue of Peor from their bosom and said, "Worship this." Once this was done, they prepared themselves for the work of Venus, believing that they were showing that shameless and wicked god the greatest honor by that very act; and this was that "excellent" rite—if it pleases the gods!* But let us hear the words of the author himself from the Hebrew:

->And when his inclination [lust] overcomes him, he says to her, "Submit to me," and she brings out an image of Peor from her bosom,<-
->and says to him: "Bow down to this."<-

<margin>
The foul custom of the Hebrews.
</margin>
*When,* he says, *anyone was stirred by a more vehement temptation, he would say to a woman, "Listen to me," or "Hear me, for I am in desire of you." And she would suddenly produce the idol of Peor from her bosom and say to him, "Worship this," etc., after which the act followed.* We shall show, God willing, in various places in this work, that these same things were practiced by the Egyptians in the rites of Isis.

### CHAPTER V. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

It is therefore clear that all those impious rituals proceeded from the aforementioned Egyptians; this will become brilliantly apparent not only from what we have said so far, but also from the extreme similarity of the ceremonies common to both nations. However, so that the origin may be better perceived, I have decided that they should be proven by making a comparison between them.

<margin>Priapus, the phallus, and Phegor are the same thing.</margin>
And first, we know from Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> that the Egyptians always worshipped this phallus <note>a representation of the male reproductive organ used as a symbol of generative power</note> of Osiris with the greatest zeal, which we have shown in the preceding pages was also done by the Hebrews. Moreover, this Priapus <note>the Greek god of fertility, often identified with these Egyptian symbols</note> or phallus was a small statue fashioned in the form of a penis, which they placed in public gardens, fields, and other rural locations to ward off sterility. They also carried it around for private benefit on the neck, ears, belt, and thighs in place of a phylactery <note>here used in the sense of a protective amulet or charm</note>. It is clear from the preceding that the Hebrews observed this same practice in the worship of Phegor <note>Baal-Peor</note>. In those passages, we showed from Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, a medieval commentator on the Bible and Talmud</note> that the image of Phegor was "formed in the likeness of the human male organ" <note>original Hebrew: כמין זכרות - k'min zakhrut</note>, and was carried about in the bosoms of harlots and other immodest women.

<margin>Phalli carried in the festivals of Dionysus. Herodotus in his book *Euterpe*. Egyptian Priapic festivals. Maimonides in *The Guide*. Pausanias in his *Description of Phocis*.</margin>
Furthermore, Herodotus testifies that the Egyptians carried phalli of this kind through the crossroads of cities during the Dionysian festivals <note>festivals of Bacchus/Dionysus</note> with a certain insane mental dissolution, shouting, and the blaring of flutes, in the manner of a triumphal procession. We taught above, from Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria</note>, that the Hebrews also observed these ceremonies in the Egyptian manner when we spoke of the effeminate priests of Priapus. According to Plutarch, Diodorus, and Suidas, it was the custom for Egyptian women to approach Apis <note>the sacred bull of Egypt</note> during the Ithyphallic rites <note>festivals featuring the upright phallus</note> (which were celebrated once a year with a solemn procession) and, lifting their garments, to expose their backsides to him. We have passed down from the *Guide for the Perplexed* <note>original: Moreh Nebuchim</note> by Maimonides <note>original: Rambam</note> and others that this was common practice for Hebrew women in the rituals usually celebrated for Beelphegor. Additionally, Pausanias records that the Priapic rites or Pamelia festivals were mostly celebrated in hidden places, thickets, groves, and caves; we have proven from the third book of Kings <note>Known as 1 Kings in modern Bibles</note> that the Hebrews also did this, imitating the Troglodytes <note>cave-dwellers</note>; where it is said of King Asa:

> And he took away the effeminate <note>original: "effœminatos" - referring to male cult prostitutes or those involved in ritual sexual acts</note> from the land, and purged all the filth of the idols which his fathers had made; moreover, he removed his mother Maacah, so that she should not be a princess in the rites of Priapus, and in the grove which she had consecrated; and he overthrew her cave, and broke the most shameful image, and burned it at the brook of Kidron.

<margin>Phalli were amulets against bewitchment. The Hebrew is the Ape of the Egyptian people.</margin>
Finally, the Egyptians used phalli as a kind of phylactery to ward off the evil spells that hinder procreation. It is clear from what has been said that Hebrew women did this to avert the supreme evil of sterility. In short, no one who diligently weighs these comparisons of ours will deny that the Hebrews were the "Apes" <note>meaning "imitators"</note> of the Egyptians. Thus, the Ithyphallic, Pammelian, or Priapic rites, having first arisen in Egypt, first infected their neighbors the Hebrews; then, spreading as far as Greece, they gave birth there to a huge offspring of new superstitions; these were later adapted by the Romans, and with the spread of this notorious superstition, they filled the whole world. Indeed, these grew so much in a short time that even after the coming of Salvation <note>The birth of Christ</note>, there were still those initiated into such abominable rites who enslaved themselves to the most shameful Phegor, as is read concerning the detestable sect of the Gnostics in the writings of Epiphanius, Philastrius, and other heresiologists <note>scholars who cataloged and refuted heresies</note>.

Kircher uses biblical accounts of King Asa and Rabbinic texts to demonstrate how these "shameful" rituals spread from Egypt to the Hebrews, and eventually to the Greeks, Romans, and Gnostic sects.</summary>
