PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. 271 CHAPTER VI.

<margin>All those who are lustful are worshippers of Phegor <note>Phegor refers to Baal-Peor, a deity associated with licentious rites.</note>.</margin>
From this source also seems to have flowed that impious law of Muhammad, or the Quran, which, while it places supreme happiness in the enjoyment of brute pleasures and <term>Epicurean delights</term> <note>A reference to the philosophy of Epicurus, which in this context is used (perhaps unfairly) to mean the pursuit of physical pleasure.</note>, does nothing else than renew these most shameful Phegorian rites and ceremonies. Finally, all those who are struck by the frenzy of lust—who, like irrational beasts, are strangely empty of mind, confused in heart, and utterly fanatical—regard this <term>Beelphegor</term> <note>Baal-Peor</note> as their God. Truly, like the <term>suitors of Penelope</term> <note>The aggressive and gluttonous men from Homer's Odyssey who sought to marry Odysseus's wife.</note>, or better yet, like unclean pigs, they wander about all day wounded by this sweet poison; and whether they drink, eat, or sleep, they defile their minds by being always intent on this idol of Venus <note>Here used to mean an idol of sexual desire.</note>. Indeed, they think of nothing else—not of their own well-being nor of themselves—being tightly bound in the chains of ignorance and shame by a certain fanatical disease. They are true monsters of prodigious lust; detestable slaves of Phegor, whom it is better to suppress in deep silence than to wound chaste ears more dangerously by bringing them forward. Therefore, leaving them behind, let us proceed to what remains to be said about the <term>Baalim</term> <note>The plural form of Baal, referring to the various local manifestations of the deity.</note>, among whom Beelzebub deservedly holds the second place; we read in the Gospel that he is called the prince of demons.

# CHAPTER VI.
### ->*Beelzebub, the Idol of the Ekronites.*<-
<note>The Ekronites were the inhabitants of Ekron, one of the five major cities of the Philistines.</note>

Concerning the name of this being, whether a God or a Demon, I find great controversy among authors. However, I do not believe this arose from any other source than those Gospel passages in which the Jews accused Christ of casting out demons only by Beelzebub, the prince of demons. For in this place, others read *Beelzebul* instead of *Beelzebub*; which reading, as we said a little while ago, has provided an occasion for various opinions as well as fables everywhere—as we shall soon discuss, after we have first presented the various versions of this passage. # CHAPTER VI. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE

<margin>The Greek text.</margin>
"This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebul, the prince of demons." <note>A translation of Matthew 12:24 from the original Greek.</note>

<margin>The Arabic text.</margin>
"This man does not cast out devils except by Beelzebul."
->*This man does not cast out devils except by Beelzebul.*<-

<margin>The Coptic text.</margin>
"And he does not cast out the devils except through Beelzebul."
->*This man does not cast out devils except by Beelzebul.*<-

<margin>The Ethiopic text.</margin>
"Who does not cast out demons except by Beelzebul."
*ZaiWaZaa agananta zaabala baBeel zebul .*
->*This man does not cast out demons except by the God of dung.*<- <note>Kircher provides a literal translation of the Ethiopic sense here, highlighting the derogatory meaning.</note>

<margin>Origen. Chrysostom. Athanasius. Cyril. Prudentius.</margin>
Supported by these sacred authorities are Origen, St. Chrysostom, Athanasius, Cyril, and others of the ancients, who all read "Beelzebul" in this place instead of "Beelzebub." Prudentius also, in his work *On the Crowns* <note>original: *περὶ στεφάνων* (*Peri Stephanon*), a collection of hymns by the late Roman poet Prudentius.</note>, sings thus in the fifth hymn for Vincent the Martyr:

> ->But Christ destroys the clever<-
> ->Inventions of Beelzebul.<-

Indeed, to untie this knot of difficulty, it must be noted that Eastern Christians only devised the name "Beelzebul" in this passage as an insult to <term>idolaters</term> <note>Those who worship idols instead of the Christian God.</note>. For just as in the Hebrew language <term>Baal-Zebub</term> <note>original: בעል זבוב</note>, a name derived from *Baal* and *Zebub*, means the "God or Lord of the Fly"; so "Beelzebul" <note>original: بعل زبول</note> in the Arabic language (which the Christians of those regions commonly used), derived from the names *beel* and *zabul* or *zabel*, means nothing else than a "dung-like Bel," or the "God and Lord of dung and manure." By this name, they called the idol or demon Beelzebub out of contempt. This is also testified by Abraham Ben Kattun, where he explains verse 33 of the 23rd chapter of Exodus in this manner: *You shall not let those who worship foreign or dung-like Gods dwell with you.* I have no doubt that "dung-like" is used here as a term of reproach.
<margin>Rabbi Abraham Ben Kattun.</margin>

That this is the case is shown to us by two things. The first is that this name "Beelzebul" is found nowhere except in the New Testament <note>original: *novo instrumento* ("new instrument"), a common scholarly term for the New Testament.</note>; this clearly indicates that this title was first devised by Christians to bring shame upon idolatry, and for that same reason, it was inserted into the Gospel. The second thing is taught to us by the custom of the Hebrews; various words occurring here and there in their books demonstrate that they once commanded such titles to be used in contempt of false deities. Hence, they began to call that most lying impostor who sold himself as the Messiah under the Emperor Trajan, "Barchoziba" (meaning "son of a lie"), though he was previously called "Barcoceba" (that is, "son of a star"). The Old Testament is not lacking in examples of such names: for the Mount of Olives, after it was defiled by idols, is called *Har Ha-Mashchit* <note>original: הר המשחית</note>, that is, the "Mount of Corruption."
<margin>Who Barcoceba was.</margin> <note>A reference to Simon bar Kokhba, leader of the Jewish rebellion against Rome (132–136 CE).</note>
<margin>The insulting imposition of names.</margin>

### SYNT. IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER VI.

<margin>הר המשחת *har hammischat*</margin> **har hammischat**, which means the "Mount of Olives" or the "Mount of Anointing," but with a letter changed and a *Yod* added so that a pun might be made on the name and reproach would not be lacking <note>In 2 Kings 23:13, the Mount of Olives (*Har ha-Mischah*) is mockingly called the Mount of Corruption (*Har ha-Maschit*) because of the idols placed there</note>. In the same way, those who would blaspheme our most holy law call it <term>און גיליון</term> **Euangilion** <note>The Gospel</note>, that is, the "Volume of Iniquity," from <term>און</term> **auen** and <term>גיליון</term> **gilaion**, the former denoting iniquity, lies, and fraud, and the latter a volume. I could bring forward more examples of this sort here, but since they are well known everywhere even to the unlearned, I will remain silent about them. Furthermore, I am not unaware that Jupiter was also called "stercoreous" <note>meaning: consisting of or smeared with dung</note> or smeared with filth by the Greeks, as can be seen in that song of Orpheus:

<margin>Orpheus.</margin>
->*O most glorious Zeus, greatest of the Gods, enwrapped in dung.*<- <note>original Greek: *Ζεῦ κύδιστε, μέγιστε Θεῶν, ἐλλύμεθε κόπρῳ.*</note>

And St. Gregory of Nazianzus cites this in his first *Invective*. Yet this is by no means to be understood as if they did it out of mockery; for the phrase "enwrapped in dung" no more refers to a dung-covered Jupiter there than that line of Virgil:

> *The Mind, infused through the limbs,*
> *moves the whole mass, and mingles with the great body.* <note>original Latin: *Totamq. infusa per artus / Mens agitat molem, & magno se corpore miscet.* From the Aeneid, Book VI.</note>

For Virgil acts as the interpreter or paraphraser to understand that point of Orpheus; by both, only the secrets of nature are taught, and God was thought to be, as it were, enwrapped within it. By this name, a certain order of Gods is mentioned in Seneca’s *Natural Questions*, drawn from the monuments of the Etruscans. Furthermore, it is difficult to assert for what reason the prince of demons was called **Beelzebub** or **Beelzebul**. Origen confesses he does not know where men learned <term>ἐπὶ</term> <note>concerning</note> that name *about Beelzebul*; but look, if you please, at the responses attributed to Justin Martyr, where that writer (whoever he may have been) thinks that the priests and <term>ἱερατεύεις</term> <note>temple ministers</note> learned this name from the demons themselves. Nor do the records of the Hebrews make him the prince of demons, but rather **Asmodæus**, whom the Chaldean Paraphrast <note>The Aramaic Targum</note> in Ecclesiastes calls <term>אשמדיי מלכא דשידים</term> *Aschmadai, King of the demons*. He is called <term>אשמדיי</term> from <term>שמד</term> <note>shamad</note>, which is "to destroy" or "to exterminate," and it is very consistent with those names for the Angel of the Abyss, namely **Abaddon** and **Apollyon** <note>Hebrew and Greek names for "The Destroyer" mentioned in Revelation 9:11</note>. <margin>Why Beelzebub is called the Prince of demons.</margin> <margin>Jonathan the Paraphrast on Ecclesiastes Chapter 1. <margin>Rambam, Moreh, Book 2, Chapter 31.</margin>

### CHAPTER VI. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>Samael, in the form of a serpent sitting upon a camel, deceives Eve.</margin>
The one who deceived Eve was in the form of a camel, upon which sat Samael <note>In Jewish mystical tradition, Samael is often seen as the Accuser or the Angel of Death. Here, Kircher cites a legend where the Serpent of Eden was a giant, camel-like creature ridden by the demon.</note>, which is a name precisely used for the Devil. You will find them saying in many places that he wished to restrain our father Abraham from sacrificing his son, and Isaac from obeying his father. They say, therefore, for this reason, that Samael came to meet Abraham and said to him: "Why have you come to this place?" And it has already been shown that Samael is the Devil, and that name was imposed upon him for a hidden reason, just like the name <term>נחש</term> **nachash** <note>Hebrew for "serpent"</note> similarly. They also said that Samael, when he came to deceive Eve, sat upon a **camel-shaped** serpent <note>original Greek: *καμηλόμορφον*</note>. But the Creator laughed at the camel and its rider, and so forth, as follows. Hence, in the ancient commemoration of the Saints of the Eastern Church, one reads: *Remember not the accusation of Samael, but remember the defense of Michael.* For Samael is the "path which no bird of prey knows," says the Tishbite <note>Referring to Elijah Levita, a famous 16th-century Hebrew scholar known as "The Tishbite" after his book *Sefer Tishbi*</note>; his words are:

<margin>Rabbi Elias Levita the Ashkenazi in *The Tishbite*.</margin>
> **Samael is the "path no bird of prey knows" (Job 28:7); the Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Bible</note> translates this as "the path not known by Samael, who flies like a bird." And so they say: "Give a bribe to Samael on the Day of Atonement" <note>This refers to the "scapegoat" ritual in Leviticus 16, interpreted by some kabbalists as a gift to keep the Accuser quiet</note>. Others say that Ashmodai <note>Asmodeus, a king of demons</note> is Samael, and that he is called by two names; I have already mentioned him under the root *Ashmodai*.**

->This is: Samael, the path which no bird of prey knows; the Targum translates it as that which<-
->Samael, who flies like a bird, did not know. Hence it is that they say: "Give a<-
->gift to Samael himself on the day of atonement." Others say that Ashmodai is Samael, and<-
->that he has two names, of which he makes mention under that root. So says Elias; but in<-
->another place he says:<-

> **And our Rabbis say that Naamah, the sister of Tubal-Cain, was the mother of Ashmodai, and from her the demons were born.**

And our wise men say that Naamah, the sister of Tubal-Cain <note>A descendant of Cain mentioned in Genesis 4:22; in legend, her beauty was so great it led angels and demons astray</note>, was the mother of Ashmodai, and that from her the demons were procreated. But concerning these and similar matters, a more copious subject for discussion will be given elsewhere.

But to return to where we digressed: who is that Beelzebub? What was his idol? From where did that "god of flies" come to the Hebrews? This remains to be explained.

<margin>From where does the idol of Beelzebub come?</margin>
Certainly, the first chapter of the Fourth Book of Kings <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 1:2-3</note> teaches that he was an idol of the Ekronites. For when King Ahaziah of Israel happened to fall headlong through the lattice work of his upper chamber (for so the Jews wish the word for "grating" to be understood) and was badly injured with a crushed body, he wished to consult the oracle of Beelzebub, the god of the Ekronites, regarding his health. This name is the same as "God of the Fly"; hence Flavius Josephus, speaking of Ahaziah’s fall, calls him **the fly god of Ekron** <note>original Greek: *ἐν Ἀκκάρῳ Θεὸν μυῖαν*</note>.
<margin>Gregory of Nazianzus, *Second Oration on the Resurrection*.</margin>
The seventy elders <note>The translators of the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament</note>, and Gregory of Nazianzus in his second oration, and others who follow the Septuagint version, use this name. Whether this name was invented by the Ekronites, or by the Jews as a reproach against the idol, is debated. There are those who think it was named from the multitude of flies which usually swarm around the flesh of sacrifices. For it is recorded in the *Pirkei Avot* <note>The "Ethics of the Fathers," a collection of rabbinic wisdom and tradition</note> that flies never infested the sacrifices of the True God.

### SYNT. IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Flies did not infest the sacred rites of the Hebrews.</margin>
> *They say ten wonders were shown to our Fathers in the house of the sanctuary. No woman miscarried because of the smell of the sacrifices; the flesh of the burnt offering never emitted a stench or foul odor. Not even the smallest fly was seen in the place where the sacrificial victims were slaughtered, etc.*

<margin>Joseph Scaliger, *Refutation of the Three Sects*, No. 5.</margin>
<note>Joseph Scaliger (1540–1609) was a famous French religious scholar and philologist known for his vast knowledge of ancient languages.</note>
Others claim he was called Beelzebub because idols, soaked in the stench of meat, were infested by flies; there are also those who think that the Scripture used a joking term, calling the "God of the Fly" what was actually *Baal zebahim*—that is, the God of victims, offerings, and sacrifices. As Scaliger says: *That which was called Baal zebahim, the God of victims, offerings, and sacrifices, the Scripture called the God of the fly as a mockery, because in the Temple of Jerusalem flies did not lick the meat of the victims, whereas the temples of the gentiles were infested by flies due to the stench of the sacrifices.* But I am most thoroughly convinced that he was called Beelzebub as a proper name by the Ekronites <note>The inhabitants of Ekron, one of the five great Philistine cities</note> themselves, as we shall later demonstrate with strong arguments. For who <note>original Greek: "ὁ σεβιזόμενον ὑβρίζει?"</note> insults the very thing he worships? For was he not mentioned by Ahaziah as a venerable divinity? *Go,* he said, *and inquire of Beelzebub, the God of Ekron, whether I shall survive this illness?* Would anyone address a divinity they worshiped, and whom they thought to consult regarding the restoration of their health, with a dishonorable and joking name? Furthermore, even among the Europeans, Jupiter and Hercules were worshiped under almost the same name.

<margin>Beelzebub is the same as the God of Flies. Pausanias.</margin>
I say, therefore, that the idol of the Ekronites, Beelzebub, was the same as Myagrus, the "God of Flies" mentioned by Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer</note> in his *Description of Arcadia*. For when he speaks of the festival celebrated for Pallas Triton among the Arcadians, he says: *Ἐνταῦθα τῇ πανηγύρει μυάγρῳ θύουσιν* <note>original Greek: "There, at the festival, they sacrifice to Myagrus"</note>, that is, *In that celebration, they first celebrate or sacrifice to Myagrus, pouring out prayers to the hero during the rites, invoking Myagrus.* And by doing so, the flies cause no further trouble. Mention of Myagrus is also found in the corrected copies of Solinus <note>A 3rd-century Latin grammarian and compiler</note>, in which we read: <margin>Antiquity imagined that dogs and flies were kept away from the Chapel of Hercules. Solinus.</margin> *The Chapel of Hercules,* he says, *is in the Forum Boarium, in which evidence of his grand feast remains; for by divine power, neither dogs nor flies enter it. For it is said that when he gave a feast of meat to the priests, he invoked the God Myagrus; and he left a club in the inner sanctum, from the scent of which the dogs would flee.* Thus far Solinus. Pliny writes the same. However, he does not include the name of the God, which we see is also missing in most manuscripts of Solinus. <margin>Pliny, Book 29, Chapter 6.</margin> Pliny, in Book 29, Chapter 6, while dealing with remedies for baldness, did not call this god Myagrus, but Myodes, speaking thus of flies: *No animal,* he says, *is considered less teachable or of less intellect; which makes it all the more wonderful that at the sacred games of Olympia, clouds of them depart out of the territory after a bull has been sacrificed to the God they call Myodes.* These are the words of Pliny, who nevertheless in Book 8, Chapter 28, also writes that the people of Cyrene used to invoke Achor, the God of Flies, when a multitude of them brought pestilence, and they died immediately after the sacrifice was performed. <margin>Gregory Nazianzen in the first oration against Julian Caesar.</margin> Gregory Nazianzen, in his first oration against Julian Caesar, does not say Achor, but Accaron, which...

### CHAPTER VI. 276 THE ISIAK TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>Jupiter named for his power to drive away flies.</margin>
...I do not know what affinity he has with the city of the Ekronites <note>The city of Accaron in the text refers to Ekron, one of the five great Philistine cities.</note>, whom he seems to call upon. 
> *Flies,* he says, *will no longer seek the God of Ekron, or anything more ridiculous than a fly.*

However, I do not state this as a certainty myself, as I do not currently have access to the Greek manuscripts. Elsewhere, I have mentioned to you that among the Greeks, there is a title for Jupiter, *Apomyios* <note>original Greek: ἀπόμυιος, meaning "Expeller of flies"</note>, whom they worshiped because he was named for driving away flies. Indeed, Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Roman grammarian and geographer.</note> records that when he instituted the sacred rites of the Potitii and Pinarii, he is said to have invoked the god *Myagrus*—that is, the fly-chasing Jupiter. *Myagrus*, or rather *Myiodes*, *Myiagrus*, *Apomyius*, and similar names, specifically include the fly in their meaning, and explain him as a "Lord of the Fly."

<margin>Hercules so named because he gathered locusts and worms from vines.</margin>
Similarly, Hercules was worshiped as *Kornopion* <note>original: κορνωπίων</note> by the Trachinians; he was called this because he drove away the *kornopas* (which in their language meant *parnopas*, or locusts). Among the Erythraeans, the same god was called *Ipoktonos* <note>original: ἰποκτόνος</note>, which means one who kills the little worms that infest vines; and Apollo *Smintheus* <note>A title of Apollo related to his power over mice.</note> was called *Myoktonos* <note>original: μυοκτόνος, mouse-killer</note>, as Eustathius <note>A 12th-century scholar and archbishop of Thessalonica.</note> records in his commentary on the first book of the *Iliad*:

> *Are these titles of the gods any less ridiculous than that of the Ekronites? Should the Ekronites be considered less pious than the Greeks and Romans, or less religious in the titles they gave their idols?*

Certainly, Philastrius <note>A 4th-century bishop and heresiologist.</note> derives a heresy from Beelzebub, 

<margin>The Ekronites worshiped a fly.</margin>
namely that of the "Fly-worshipers," or the "Fly of the Ekronites," who (as his words go) *worship a fly in the city called Ekron*. But having duly considered all these things, let us now prepare ourselves to fulfill what we proposed from the beginning: to thoroughly investigate the origin of this "Fly-worship" <term>Muscilatria</term><note>Kircher's term for the religious veneration of flies.</note>. To do this more soundly,

<margin>The flooding of the Nile is the origin of many animals, especially flies.</margin>
It must be known that such is the nature of Egypt that after the annual flooding of the Nile, from the remains of stagnant waters, both crawling animals of every kind and especially vast swarms of flies, gnats, and similar troublesome little beasts arise, which torment both humans and animals in a piteous manner.

<margin>Among the Egyptians, the fly is a symbol of the greatest evil.</margin>
Indeed, this is so much the case that the Egyptians, when signifying impudence and the highest evil through hieroglyphs, were accustomed to paint a fly, as will be seen shortly. The Prophet Isaiah also, when mentioning the punishments destined for Jewish perfidy, remembered the Egyptian fly among others. <note>original Hebrew: וישרק יי לזבוב, *V'sharak Adonai lazbub*</note>

> *The Lord shall whistle for the fly that is in the farthest part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria, and they shall come and rest, all of them, in the desolate valleys, and in the holes of the rocks, and upon all thorns.*

Or as the Septuagint <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> has it: *in the reed-beds and in every crevice.* Rabbi Solomon <note>Commonly known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud.</note> calls this passage "the war of the flies" <note>original Hebrew: מלחמת הזבובים, *Milchamot ha-zebubim*</note>, the armies of Egyptian flies that invade a rebellious people.

<margin>Among Eastern peoples, flies were repelled by the worship of a fly.</margin>
Therefore, when the Egyptians saw that not only were their idols unworthily defiled by the multitude of flies, but even their sacred animals—dogs, oxen, cows, and goats—were piteously tormented, they consulted an oracle about driving the flies away. The oracle is said to have responded that the flies must be repelled by the worship of a fly; if they did this, the flies would be more respectful in the future. No sooner said than done: the Egyptians immediately placed that "Fly-God" in all places infested by flies. His hieroglyphic symbol was a fly with a Scyllocyprian thyrsus <note>A "thyrsus" is a ritual staff. "Scyllocyprio" likely refers to a type of rod or wand made from specific maritime or Cypriot plants used in purification.</note>,

<margin>An amulet against flies.</margin>
which, besides signifying a "multiform demon" <note>original Greek: πολυμόρφου δαίμονα</note>, also represented the driving away of flies.

<summary>Kircher explains that the Philistine and Greek worship of "Fly-Gods" like Beelzebub or Jupiter Apomyius originated as a superstitious response to real pestilence. He specifically traces this back to Egypt, where the post-flood swarms of the Nile led to the fly becoming a hieroglyph for evil and the creation of fly-shaped amulets to ward off the insects.</summary>

# TREATISE IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS.

<image-desc>A square woodcut illustration depicting a large fly or winged insect next to a stalk of grain or a botanical specimen.</image-desc>

And in this type of hieroglyph, nothing was more frequent on the Obelisks than this animal; they would attach it to figures, or carve it upon Canopic jars, Sphinxes, and other idols. By placing this sign as if by a certain pact, the **summoned Demon**, or "Fly-Spirit," was believed to put flies to flight. But so that I do not seem to assert anything based solely on my own conjectures, let us hear what Abenephius <note>A name used by Kircher to refer to an Arabic author, likely Ibn Wahshiyya or a similar source of Hermetic and occult lore.</note> says regarding these matters:

<margin>Abenephius, *On the Servitude of the Egyptians*, Book 3.</margin>
The flies used to disturb every province of Egypt and all its animals, and they defiled the idols. The Egyptians sought an oracle, and it said to them: "By the worship of the fly, the fly shall be driven away." The Egyptians acted according to the word of the oracle and drove away the flies by the power of a crafted image of a fly, combined with an herb called *al-Sa’ad* <note>original Arabic: السعد (*al-sa'ad*), likely referring to nut-grass or a similar aromatic plant used in ancient medicine and magic.</note> in Arabic. They placed these on the obelisks of Pharaoh, on the banks of rivers, and in every place where flies were numerous.

That is: *And flies used to infest the entire surrounding region and all the animals, and they fouled the idols; the Egyptians consulted an oracle, and it told them that in the worship of the fly, the fly would be driven off. The Egyptians acted according to the word of the oracle, and the flies retreated because of a magic figure or image of a fly which the Egyptians had made, placing it on Obelisks and pyramids, and finally in all places that were infested by flies,* etc., as follows in the text.

Truly, we shall treat these and similar mysteries of the Obelisks more extensively in their proper place; for now, let it suffice to have suggested these points. From this, it appears that the Egyptians—whether prompted by an oracle, or as some Rabbis believe, in imitation of Moses driving away the swarms of gnats <note>Refers to the plague of lice/gnats in Exodus.</note>, or for some other reason—were certainly the first authors and inventors of <term>Musclatria</term> <note>Literally "fly-worship," from the Latin *musca* (fly) and Greek *latreia* (worship).</note>. From them, the Hebrews and Greeks were taught, believing that those huge swarms of flies could be kept away from temples, altars, and other places of sacrifice by no other means than the institution of a similar cult. We have already mentioned this regarding the Arcadic and Cyrenaic rites; for the Hebrews foolishly believed that their Beelzebub would be appeased by this kind of worship, just as the Greeks believed regarding their Jupiter "the Fly-Catcher," or *Myagrus*. Let these remarks on Beelzebub suffice.

## Beelsephon.

<margin>בעל צפון</margin>
Beelzephon or Baalsephon derives its name from *Baal* <note>Lord</note> and *Zephon* <note>North or Hidden</note>, which signifies the "Hidden Lord" or the "Lord of the North." I find various opinions among authors regarding him. Some consider it to be a city, such as Adrichomius in his *Description of the Holy Land*, and Ezekiel the Tragedian <note>A 2nd-century BCE Jewish poet who wrote Greek tragedies on biblical themes.</note>, who in his *Exagoge* <note>original: ἐξαγωγῇ; a play about the Exodus of the Israelites.</note> speaks through the character of an Egyptian Messenger:

> Since we have placed the camp near it,
> A certain city called Beelzephon by mortals.

Others believe it to be the name of a place or a rock, as do most interpreters; finally, others—such as the Rabbis—opine that it was an idol of the Egyptians. Whatever the case, whether Beelzephon was the name of a city or a desert place, certainly...

This was in a narrow passage which is opposite the Red Sea, between Pi-hahiroth and Migdol, names which individually suggest something rocky and precipitous. ### CHAPTER VII OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE

...this was the cause, both because of the wealth of gems and precious stones and other things cast up by the sea which were found scattered there on the desert shore; Jonathan Ben Uziel <note>Also known as Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, an Aramaic translation of the Torah</note> shows in no obscure words that the children of Israel also collected these while camping in that same place, commenting on this passage as follows:

*And they caught them, he says, already encamping by the sea, occupied in collecting gems and precious stones, which Pishon brought from the garden of pleasure (paradise) into the middle of Gihon, and Gihon carried them into the Red Sea, and the Red Sea cast them out in that place onto its bank.*

<margin>The bank of the Red Sea teems with gems and precious stones.</margin>
Although these words may appear legendary in their details, it appears from Strabo and Arrian <note>Ancient Greek geographers</note> that the shore in this place teems with rubies, gems, and other precious stones, which provide merchants with the material for great gain and profit. It is also gathered from Rabbi Abenezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a 12th-century biblical commentator</note> that the Egyptians were accustomed to go here frequently to sacrifice to Baal-zephon; commenting on this passage, he says that when Moses had learned the way to Baal-zephon and the sacrifices of the Egyptians that were customarily performed there every year, he sought permission from Pharaoh to go there, so that by instituting sacrifices to the true God in that same place, he might destroy the abominable sacrifices of Baal-zephon, which he also gathers from these words:

<margin>Exodus 5.</margin>

### SYNTAGMA IV. PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. 281 CHAPTER VII

And from all these things demonstrated at length, it is clear that Beelzephon takes its name not from a city or another place, but from an idol worshipped there by the Egyptians. I have undertaken to treat these matters more extensively here, especially for the sake of those who, for I know not what reason, despise these as if they were mere fables of the Rabbis, and who not very prudently quibble with the interpretation of this place made by the Hebrews. It seems that someone either did not understand the books of the Rabbis, or else leveled that charge of Rabbinic falsehood and trifling for the sake of his master, Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a towering scholar of the Renaissance who was often critical of Rabbinic traditions</note>, against the Hebrews. Certainly, I would not think the writings of the Rabbis should be utterly condemned—especially where they do not mock our own faith—and if you set aside the superstitions which they frequently run into, they contain many excellent things. Not unlike treasures hidden under the form of a Silenus <note>A reference to the "Sileni of Alcibiades," a metaphor used by Plato and Erasmus for something that appears ugly or trivial on the outside but contains divine wisdom within</note>, many great things are contained within the fictions and intellectual games they indulge in. But let these things be said in passing; therefore, let us return to the point from which we digressed. Furthermore, what kind of idol that was which the Egyptians worshipped and the Hebrews called Beelzephon is entirely difficult to assert. The Jerusalem Targum <note>An Aramaic translation and expansion of the Hebrew Bible</note> confuses it with Peor or Baal-Peor,

<margin>The Jerusalem Targum written in Syriac characters.</margin>
->"And Pharaoh said to the children of Israel: they are wandering in the wilderness; the idol Peor, which is in the region of the desert, has prevailed over them."<-
<note>original Syriac: "ܘܐܡܪ ܦܪܥܘܢ ܠܒܢܝ ܐܝܣܪܐܝܠ..."</note>

This cannot be said inappropriately, especially if Peor is taken here for Priapus <note>The Roman god of fertility and gardens, often identified by Renaissance scholars with the Moabite god Baal-Peor</note>, as he is a guardian and minor deity of gardens, fields, and woods. The Babylonian Targum asserts that many idols of this kind had been placed there; however, it says that once these were removed and destroyed by divine power, only Baalzephon remained out of all the gods of the Egyptians.

<margin>The Babylonian Targum.</margin>
->"That place, he says, is Tanis between Migdol and the sea, before the idol Zephon, which remains of all the idols of the Egyptians; for this reason the Egyptians say that the idol Beelzephon was chosen above all other idols that remain, and it was not shattered, and they came to worship it."<-
<note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: "הוא אתרא דטניס דביני מגדול..."</note>

Moreover, he deduces that the rest of the idols were scattered by God from that passage in Numbers 33, where it is held that once the firstborn were killed, God also executed vengeance upon their gods. What kind of idols those were, he demonstrates with the following words:

->"The Egyptians, says the Targum, were burying their firstborn, whom the Lord had killed while performing vengeance upon their gods; the molten or cast idols were melted, the idols fashioned from stone, the clay or earthenware idols were broken and crushed; the idols constructed by a certain art of divination and astrological science were made into the likeness of dead beasts or brutes."<-
<margin>Various forms of the Beelzephon idols.</margin>
<note>original Hebrew/Aramaic: "ומצראי מקברין ית דקטל יי..."</note>

From these, only that which is called Baalzephon remained; the rest...

# CHAPTER VII OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAIC TEMPLE

<margin>The Egyptians placed great trust in Beelzephon.</margin>
<margin>Beelzephon was said to have the form of a dog.</margin>
<margin>Jupiter Ammon in Libya. Sminthian Apollo.</margin>
<margin>Mercury, guardian of the ways.</margin>
...either shattered by divine vengeance or taken away by the departing Hebrews by theft (for many of them were made of gold, silver, and other precious materials). This loss was surely the unique cause and the occasion for such great resentment and the continued pursuit by Pharaoh and the rest of the Egyptians against the escaped Hebrews; for he hoped that he would recover both his riches and his idols. He believed this would be achieved through the help of Beelzephon, the only one still remaining, which he knew was stationed at that place which the Hebrews could reach only with difficulty. Or, if they did reach it, they would be forced to turn back, hindered by the hidden power of the idol, and thus caught in those narrow passages—as if in a mountain <term>nassa</term> <note>original: "nassa" - a wicker trap used for catching fish; Kircher uses it here as a metaphor for a geographical dead-end or snare</note>—they would be put to death. Those interpreters err here who say that Beelzephon was a bronze dog deterring the Israelites with its barking; and although the authors of this claim attribute it to the Rabbis, it has not yet happened that I have seen any of the Rabbis who asserted it, though I have sought it with singular zeal. From this it is clear that many things are commonly attributed to the Rabbis of which they never even dreamed. Furthermore, it is likely that the Egyptians placed <term>magical images</term> or idols not only in Pi-hahiroth <note>original: "Phihiroth"</note>, but also in other places in Egypt where there was either easy access into the country or from which the flight of the Israelites was feared. Clear arguments for this are provided by Jupiter Ammon in the Libyan sands near the descent of Egypt; Sminthian Apollo <note>original: "Sminthaeus Apollo" - a title of Apollo often associated with protection against pests or as a guardian of borders</note> among the marshes and the sea at the very entrance from Phoenicia into Egypt, stationed as a guardian of the place; and others of which we shall speak abundantly throughout this work. Moreover, it was the custom of the Egyptians to worship Mercury as the guardian of the roads and governor of the lands under the form of square stones which they call <term>Hermae</term> <note>Boundary markers or statues consisting of a head atop a square pillar</note>. Could that famous Hermanubis <note>A hybrid deity combining the Greek Hermes and the Egyptian Anubis, often depicted with a dog's head</note> of the Egyptians be perhaps that Beelzephon, the tamer of the Northern Typhon <note>original: "Typhonis Borei"</note>, of whom we have spoken until now? Certainly, if the interpreters criticized above take that bronze dog for Hermanubis, they seem to hit the nail on the head. Jonathan <note>Referring to the Targum of Jonathan, an Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible</note>, speaking above of the quadrangular rocks, indicates the not obscure remains of the <term>Hermae</term> having been placed there. But we will suspend this difficulty for now until a greater light shines; I have always judged it more honorable to confess my ignorance in matters not yet explored than to stubbornly defend it with vague conjectures and without a manifest foundation. For I think I have done enough in this place to demonstrate by certain and solid reasons that the idol Beelzephon was constructed by magical art and placed in the said location to restrain the attacks of enemies. Therefore, leaving these things behind, let us turn our pen to other matters.

### SYNTAGMA IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. 283 CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>Where Baalgad was located.</margin>
Baalgad was formerly a city situated at the roots of Mount Hermon, which is a part of Mount Lebanon; of which, besides the Holy Scriptures and other interpreters, <margin>Benjamin.</margin> the Hebrew traveler Benjamin <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler who documented the communities of the Near East.</note> also makes mention in these words:

> *From Laodicea, he says, I came in two days to Baalgad, which is a city in the borders of the land of Hassin; it has a prince for its inhabitants, whom they venerate as a Prophet, and besides him, they recognize no other leader.* <note>original Hebrew: מלאודיקיא באת ימים בבעל גד אשר היא מרזח באפם ארץ חסין ושל יושבי ארץ מכובר מהם כמו נביא ובלעדו לא ידעים שר אחר</note>

In the eleventh chapter of Joshua it is said: *Even from the mount that goeth up to Seir, even unto Baalgad in the valley of Lebanon under mount Hermon.* Where the Chaldean Paraphrast <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note> in place of Baalgad translates it as <term>Gumsher</term>, that is, the plain or field of Gad; whether, therefore, Baalgad is the name of a city or of a field, it certainly derives its name from no other source than from the idol Gad, worshipped in that place. Moreover, Gad among the Hebrews is the same as "Good Fortune," which it can be gathered was <margin>Gad, good fortune.</margin> formerly worshipped in Syria, from that passage in the 30th chapter of Genesis:

<margin>Genesis 30.</margin>
> *And Zilpah, Leah's handmaid, bore Jacob a son; and Leah said: With Gad!* <note>original Hebrew: ותלד זלפה שפחת לאה ליעקב בן ותאמר לאה בגד</note>

That is: *And Zilpah the handmaid of Leah bore a son to Jacob, and Leah said "Begad."* Where the Latin edition <note>The Vulgate.</note> has *happily*; most of the Hebrews, as well as the Greeks, understand "Good Fortune" here. And Leah spoke in this place as if she were giving a good omen for the birth. These words are supported in the Targum <margin>Onkelos.</margin> of Onkelos <margin>Jerusalem Targum.</margin> <term>And Leah said, Gad has come</term> <note>original Aramaic: ואמרה לאה אתא גד</note>: *And Leah said, Gad comes*, that is *fortune*, or as the Jerusalem Targum has it, <term>atba gada</term> <note>original Aramaic: אתא גדא</note>, which amounts to the same thing. The rest of the Rabbis wish Gad to be the same as <term>Mazal Tob</term> <note>Literally "Good Star" or "Good Luck."</note>, that is, good fortune, or a good star, or a good Genius; and they wish it to be the same as the star of Jupiter, which <margin>Gad is the same as Mazal Tob, or the star of Jupiter. Rabbi Ibn Ezra.</margin> they call <term>Cochab Zedek</term> <note>The "Star of Justice/Righteousness," the traditional Hebrew name for Jupiter.</note>. Thus Rabbi Ibn Ezra says in this place:

> *They say, however, that the explanation of the word Gad is the same as Mazal Tob, as it is also in the Arabic language; and they themselves prepare a table for Gad, which they call the star of Jupiter, and they direct it according to the host of heaven.* <note>original Hebrew: ויש אומרים שפירוש גד מזל טוב באשר הוא בלשון ישמעאל ובכמו העורכים לגד שלחן והוא כוכב צדק : והנכון לחיות כמו גדודי שמים</note>

The explanation of Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi, the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator.</note> agrees with this:

<margin>Rashi.</margin>
> *Bagad: its explanation is, Mazal Tob, or good fortune comes; and they prepare a table, judging, etc.* <note>original Hebrew: בגד פירוש בא מזל טוב כמו גד גד שבוגד לא יומת לו העורכים לגד שלחן ואגדה שנולד מהול כמו גד גד אצלנו</note>

Note here that <term>Bagad</term> <note>בגד</note> is to be read separately as <term>Ba, Gad</term> <note>בא , גד - meaning "Gad has come"</note> (the kind of words the Masoretes note as <unclear>read but not written</unclear> <note>original Hebrew: קרי ולא כתיב - a marginal note in the Hebrew Bible indicating a word is written one way but should be read another.</note>, which are written as one but read as two) and it signifies *Mazal Tob*, or what is the same, good fortune. I have seen not once in the houses of the Jews in Germany these words inscribed above the doors; which I understood to mean that they were devoting the protection of the house to a good Genius. These words also signify the same as those words among the Latins, *may it be happy and auspicious*, <margin>What Gad or good fortune may be.</margin> which we use when we undertake a matter of great importance; having explained these things, now no small difficulty arises as to what that "Good Fortune" is, whose help the Syrians formerly implored when about to begin their works. ### SYNT. IV. THE HEBREW PANTHEON. 285 CHAPTER VIII.

...calculating the <term>Mazal</term> <note>Hebrew for a constellation or destiny</note> according to one of the planets; and the Rabbis of blessed memory say in their benediction that this is the Star of Jupiter, which is called thus in the Arabic language; and they "fill a libation for Meni," as if one were to say peace offerings and victims, or a libation of wine to be poured for <term>Meni</term> <note>An ancient deity associated with fate or "numbering"</note>; and this is the star itself which is counted among the seven that they call "the wanderers" [the planets]. And from this practice they used to set tables upon which, having placed idols, they poured libations, as witnessed by the Babylonian Paraphrase <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible</note>, which in this place substitutes "Gad" and "Meni" with:

<margin>The Babylonian Targum.</margin>
->And they arrange tables for their idols, and bowls for their terrifying gods.<-
->*And they arrange tables for their idols, and bowls for their terrifying gods.*<-

<margin>Leah bestows the name Gad upon her son, from the star of fortune.</margin>
Therefore, it should by no means be thought that when **Leah**, having spoken with good omen at the birth of Zilpah's child, said <term>Begad</term> <note>original Hebrew: בגד, literally "in fortune" or "with Gad"</note>, this was merely a lucky exclamation. Rather, it was an invocation of the Deity Gad; she believed that by invoking this divinity—according to the customs and manners of the Gentiles in which she was still entangled—the son would prosper in life. It is likely that, as a sign of her trust in the invoked deity, she even bestowed the name of that deity upon her son; as if she were saying: *Come, good fortune; come, auspicious deity.* Since this is the case, nothing truly remains now except to explain the source from which the worship and invocation of this deity <term>Baalgad</term> <note>Lord of Fortune</note> flowed to the Hebrews. Indeed, since I find this deity to be most ancient and in use among the Hebrews in the earliest times after the Deluge, I certainly do not think it originated from anywhere else but Egypt, which I might not inappropriately call the "nursery" of Hebrew idols. But let all these things be confirmed not just by vague conjecture, but by the authority they deserve.
<margin>Egypt: the nursery of the Gentile gods.</margin>

<margin>The opinion of the Egyptian Astrologers.</margin>
It must be understood that the most ancient Egyptian astrologers thought that the fates of those being born depended greatly upon fortune, or chance, or that "part" which they call the <term>Part of Fortune</term>; and from this they judged <term>concerning fortune</term> <note>original Greek: περὶ τύχης (peri tyches)</note>—concerning, I say, domestic matters, military service, travel, public office, marriage, wealth, nobility, and other things of that kind. <margin>The system of birth horoscopes.</margin> For once the "genethliacal theme" <note>a birth chart or horoscope</note> was established, they calculated from the position of the Sun to that of the Moon through the succeeding signs; they added as many to the ascendant as were in that number, and where those ended, they placed the "Lot of Fortune." They held this Lot as if it were a second Ascendant, and they formed a second chart from it. And just as they sought from the first chart those things pertaining to the person born—namely the body and soul, as internal matters—so in that second chart, whose first seat was the "Lot," they sought fortune, interests, labors, and other external things. This is that reckoning of fate which nature has drawn into one sum, as Manilius says:

<margin>Manilius, Book 3 of the *Astronomica*.</margin>
> *For whatever kind of things, whatever kind of labors,*
> *Whatever works and arts, whatever accidents through all things*
> *Could happen by chance in a human life,*
> *It has embraced them.*

<margin>What are the "Athla" in the birth chart?</margin>
Now, those labors, works, arts, and accidents Manilius calls by the singular name <term>Athla</term> <note>original Greek: Ἄθλα, meaning "contests" or "labors"</note>, so that the first seat—that is, the Lot of Fortune—becomes the first *Athlon*; the second—that is, the Lot of Military Service—becomes the second *Athlon*; the third—namely the Lot of Civic Matters—becomes the third *Athlon*: and so on in order for the rest. ### CHAPTER VIII. 286 THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS' ISIAIC TEMPLE

Regarding the horoscope of the theme, which we have called the second, according to this verse:

> ->Let Fortune hold this place, while the Labors follow<-
> ->In the order of nature as all things are situated.<-
> <note>Kircher is quoting Marcus Manilius, a 1st-century Roman poet and astrologer, specifically his work *Astronomica*.</note>

We, however, assert that the word *Athla* <note>original Greek: Αθλα, meaning "contests" or "labors"</note> was not borrowed from the Greeks, but derived from the Hebrew word *hatal* <note>original: חתל</note>. Now, *hatal* is the same as "to bind," and *machthaloth* <note>original: מחתלות</note> is the same as "ligatures" or "swaddling bands," as if the locations of the Birth System <note>The <term>Genethliacal System</term> refers to the calculation of a person's birth chart</note> must be so united and bound together for the purpose of drawing a judgment that no part can be missing without making the whole undertaking void.

<margin>Scholiast on the 3rd part of the *Tetrabiblos*.</margin>
<margin>What is a Lot?</margin>
<margin>Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*.</margin>
Just as the <term>Dodecatemoria</term> <note>The division of the zodiac into twelve parts or "houses"</note> (from which come the twelve houses or the birth theme) were used, so also in those ancient centuries, it seems, "lots" <note>Latin: *sortes*</note> were in use. The oldest Egyptian mathematicians took specific lots for almost all matters and questions within the positioning of the stars. The Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator or annotator</note> for the third part of the *Tetrabiblos* <note>Ptolemy’s foundational 2nd-century work on astrology</note> testifies: "The Egyptians," he says, "were accustomed to take lots for all headings" <note>original Greek: κεφάλαια (*kephalaia*)</note>, where "headings" refers to the chapters (or the angles, or the titles of the twelve houses, or specifically to things to be sought by the mathematician). This word, according to the testimony of Selden <note>John Selden, a 17th-century polymath and scholar of Near Eastern antiquity</note>, was adopted from the usage of the Rhetoricians. 

However, **Ptolemy** rejects all those *kleroi* <note>original Greek: κλήρους, meaning "lots"</note>—or "lots" or "parts," as some name them—as useless, except only for the "Lot of Fortune" <note>original Greek: κλῆρον τύχης (*klēron tuchēs*)</note>. Relying on the most ancient dogma of the astrologers, he teaches that this lot is to be derived from both nocturnal and diurnal births in the same way we just mentioned; not indeed as some wrongly interpret, by counting from the Sun to the Moon, but by counting from the Moon to the Sun through the following signs. For when the ratio is rightly preserved by numbering from the Sun to the Moon, the Moon stands in relation to the Lot of Fortune as the Sun stands to the Horoscope; and just as the latter is Solar, so the former is Lunar, as Selden well notes. It is the "ascending part," which matches perfectly with the figure of the *Athla* themes of **Manilius**. Likewise, among the ancient Egyptians, the Moon itself was this specific "lot"; and it was called "Good Fortune" <note>original Greek: ἀγαθὴ τύχη (*agathē tuchē*)</note>, which the Hebrews translate as **Mazal Tob** <note>original: מזל טוב, "Good Destiny"</note> and the Jerusalem Targum <note>Aramaic translation and commentary of the Bible</note> translates as **Geda taba** <note>original: גדא טבא, "Good Fortune"</note>. For each of the planets had its own lot, such as:

| Planet | Lot (in English) |
|----------|----------|
| Saturn | Nemesis <note>Retribution/Justice</note> |
| Jupiter | Victory |
| Mars | Boldness |
| Sun | Good Spirit |
| Venus | Love |
| Mercury | Necessity |
| Moon | Good Fortune |

<margin>Hermes the Egyptian in Pico della Mirandola, Book 6, Ch. 18.</margin>
Regarding these, **Hermes the Egyptian** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom and magic</note> is cited in **Pico della Mirandola’s** *Against Astrology*, Book 6, Chapter 18.

<margin>In the past, all things were attributed to Bad or Good Fortune.</margin>
The Egyptian astrologers placed such great value upon this lot, or "good fortune," that they believed all the changes of human life, and all judgment over resources, honors, friendships, and advantages, were within its power. They believed that this "fortune" turns human affairs upside down according to its own will; that it has power over individual men, cities, and kingdoms; and that it overturns friendships—

### SYNTAGMA IV. THE HEBREW PANTHEON. CHAPTER VIII.

...they believe she can overturn whenever it pleases her; and that she can raise up those things that are overturned and lying prostrate, filling them with wealth and a multitude of men, making them most flourishing. For this reason, if anything prosperous, desired, or happy happened from obscure causes—or conversely, if anything turbulent, troublesome, or calamitous occurred—they attributed it entirely to Fortune, whether good or bad. Hence, it is most likely that the Egyptians, when offering legumes to Harpocrates <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian child-god Horus, often depicted with a finger to his lips symbolizing silence.</note> (whom we have explained elsewhere as the God of crops and of other things not yet brought to perfection) and crying out <margin>Invocation of Harpocrates.</margin> "The tongue is fortune, the tongue is a deity," <note>original Greek: γλῶσσα τύχη, γλῶσσα δαίμων; original Latin: *Lingua fortuna, lingua dæmon*</note> as Plutarch records, they were looking to nothing other than these aforementioned presiding powers. Indeed, Vettius Valens of Antioch <margin>Vettius Valens of Antioch.</margin> implies this in manifest words, whom you may see in the works of Selden. Moreover, they used the word "tongue" both to signify that Harpocrates (who suggests silence with his finger) was a God and a son of fortune, and to say that for a man to speak of this was a crime to be expiated by death. Furthermore, they used these words so that they might more easily attract the <margin>The invocation of Isis is understood under the name of Good Fortune.</margin> "multiform Deity"—I mean Isis, the Fortune of the Egyptians and the mother of Harpocrates—as we shall say elsewhere. For since the Egyptians, in all their astrological actions and selections, looked to the "Lunar Horoscope," <note>original Greek: Σεληνιακὸν τὸν ὡροσκόπον</note> or toward "Good Fortune," <note>original Greek: περὶ τὴν ἀγαθὴν τύχην</note> or the "Lot of Fortune." We have said above that this was dedicated by Hermes to the Moon, or Isis. Certainly, it must be judged that those offering to Harpocrates were, through the mediation of the son, invoking Isis—the Lot of Fortune, or Good Fortune, the presiding power over both life and external goods upon their coming into the light. This custom, which the Hebrews had learned in Egypt, they then carried into Assyria and neighboring regions, preserving it and pursuing it with singular worship, as the name **Baal Gad** <note>Hebrew: בעל גד, meaning "Lord of Fortune" or "Lord of Luck."</note> sufficiently demonstrates. However, the Hebrews differ from the Egyptians in this: the Hebrews worshiped and invoked Jupiter under the name of Fortune or "Good Fortune," <note>original Greek: ἀγαθῆς τύχης</note> while the Egyptians invoked the Moon. <margin>The Moon was called Good Fortune by the Egyptians; Jupiter by the Greeks.</margin> After the Greeks, the Latins followed these practices most closely, for they seem to have worshiped no Goddess with greater care than Fortune; as witness the almost infinite inscriptions made to her here in Rome, which you will see in Gruter and in Lipsius’s theater of ancient inscriptions.

<margin>Fortune: Capitoline, Esquiline, Nortia, Praenestine.</margin> Furthermore, it is not our purpose to explain what the Capitoline, Esquiline, Nortia, Praenestine, Primigenia, Blind, Seia, or Rhamnusian Nemesis Fortunes were, or the other mockeries of fortune; therefore, let the eager reader consult Giraldi, who treats them in an entire volume. However, the temples erected in her honor by the Greeks and Romans, as has been said, sufficiently demonstrate that "Good Fortune" and her "Lot" (from which all others were derived as if from a root) were held as a Goddess in the construction of the second birth theme. For it was solemn for them to dedicate monuments "To Good Fortune." <note>original Greek: ΤΗ ΑΓΑΘΗ ΤΥΧΗ</note> Concerning the Romans, Plutarch in his *Roman Questions*, no. 107, <margin>Plutarch in *Roman Questions*.</margin> asks: "Why do the Romans worship Primigenial Fortune?" <note>original Greek: Διατὶ Ρωμαῖοι τύχην σέβονται; Kircher translates the Greek query regarding the origin of Fortune worship in Rome.</note> Regarding the Greeks, the *Alexandrian Chronicle* <margin>*Alexandrian Chronicle*.</margin> records that such worship was very familiar to them, and inscriptions both in Rome and especially at Praeneste "Made to Venus and Primigenial Fortune" bear witness to this. <margin>What is Primigenial Fortune?</margin> By "Primigenial Fortune," nothing else can be understood but the **Lady of Birth**, who describes the measure of happiness for the newly born, as if upon the secret tablets of heaven. And the infant Jupiter, who suckling with Juno in the lap... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "gre-" for *gremio*, "lap."</note>

<header>CHAPTER IX. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE</header>

...once sat in the lap of the Fortune of Praeneste <note>Ancient Palestrina, famous for its temple to Fortuna Primigenia where she was often depicted holding the infants Jupiter and Juno.</note>, and was worshiped most chastely by mothers; this itself seems to reveal enough. From these things it is clear that Baalgad of the Hebrews, or Gad—whether he was Jupiter according to the mind of the Rabbis, or the Queen of Heaven, the Moon, or Isis according to the Egyptians, or as others [take] *Gad Shamayim* <note>original: גד שמים</note> for *Gedud Hashamayim* <note>original: גדוד השמים</note>, that is, the host or celestial army, as Rabbi Abenezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a significant medieval Jewish scholar and astronomer.</note> explains it; certainly it agrees well enough with the theme of fortune explained so far. Philastrius <note>Saint Philastrius of Brescia, a 4th-century bishop who wrote a catalogue of heresies.</note> makes the Queen of Heaven the same as the fortune of heaven: *There is a heresy among the Jews,* he says, *which invokes the Queen, and even the fortune of heaven, whom they also call the "Celestial One" in Africa, and they did not hesitate to offer sacrifices to her.* Not inappropriately; since the Moon—that is, the Queen of Heaven—and her lot [fortune] may be used interchangeably. But we shall treat all these things more extensively when we speak of the ancient Astrology of the Egyptians and its mysteries.

### SYNT. IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER IX.

"Some explain," it is said, "that 'weeping' <note>original: *mebakot* / מבכות; referring to Ezekiel 8:14</note> is a euphemism; that is, they gladden the Thamuz in the month of Thamuz. Others explain that they acted with trickery so that water would come to the eyes of the idol called Thamuz, and they would weep, as if to say he was asking to be worshiped."

*They explain, he says, that the (weeping ones) are recalled to dances and joys, which were celebrated in the month of Thamuz in honor of Thamuz; for in this month they made a festival for this idol, and women were accustomed to come so that they might rejoice: and they explain here that they acted with deceit and fraud, so that by water breaking out from the eyes of the Thamuz idol, it would seem to weep, and by weeping ask for and extort diligent service from its worshipers.*

<margin>Rambam <note>Rabbi Moses ben Maimon (Maimonides), a 12th-century Jewish philosopher.</note> in *The Guide [for the Perplexed]*. The Fable of Thamuz.</margin>

"And in the aforementioned book, a book is mentioned about a man from the prophets of the idols whose name was Thamuz. On the night of his death, all the images from the ends of the earth gathered to the temple in Babylon, to the great golden image which was the image of the Sun. And the image was suspended between heaven and earth, and it fell in the middle of the temple, and all the images were around it, and they began to lament for Thamuz and to tell what happened to him. And this became a constant custom: at the beginning of the first day of the month of Thamuz, they would lament and weep for Thamuz."

### SYNTAGMA IV. THE HEBREW PANTHEON. CHAPTER IX.

...as happens with most gods of the heathens, they are often confused. Furthermore, the death—which they called *disappearance* <note>original Greek: *aphanismon*</note>—and the return to life—which they called *discovery* <note>original Greek: *heuresin*</note>—testify that **Thamuz** and **Adonis** are the same as **Osiris**. These events were celebrated annually by the Egyptians in one and the same month: specifically, the month of **Athyr**. Following the stabilization of the Egyptian calendar <note>The "Year of Nabonassar" was a chronological era used by ancient astronomers; it was later "fixed" to the Julian calendar during the reign of Augustus.</note>, this month fell in the Julian November, as Selden <margin>Selden, in Syntagma 2, *On the Syrian Gods*.</margin> correctly notes. Plutarch relates that the death and return of Osiris were celebrated at that same time, and the ancient Roman Calendar lists the festival of *Discovery* <note>original: *heuresin*</note> in November. This festival, which signifies the finding of **Adonis** or **Osiris**, was spread from Egyptian customs. As you can see, the Egyptian month of *Athyr* is quite far from the Hebrew month of **Thamuz** (which is June), during which the mourning and *lamentation for Thamuz* <note>original Greek: *ōleusis tou Thamuz*</note> was established. However, to understand this discrepancy:

<margin>The nature of the Egyptian vague year.</margin> It must be noted that in the **vague year** of the Egyptians, there was no festival and no month—as only those with a deeper knowledge of Egyptian affairs know—that did not pass through every Julian month and every single day of the year over that great period of 1,460 years <note>The Sothic Cycle, after which the Egyptian "vague" year of 365 days realigns with the solar year.</note>. However, after the year was "fixed" by Augustus, each month retained its festivals in the sequence and season in which they were then being performed. Once the year was fixed, the months and festivals were also fixed.

The Jewish year, however, was not "vague" in this way; it never moved the month of **Thamuz** away from the summer solstice. Therefore, it appears that the same sacred rites and the same celebrations were held by both peoples: by the Egyptians in the vague month of *Athyr* according to their ancestral custom, and by the Jews in the fixed month of **Thamuz**. On all these points, Selden is in full agreement.

<margin>The Festival of Adonis celebrated by the people of Byblos in Phoenicia.</margin> It is no wonder, then, if the Jews—having drawn the names of **Adonis** and **Osiris** from their neighbors—changed the name to **Thamuz** based on the month in which both were celebrated, especially since the solemn ritual was the same in Egypt. For the inhabitants of Alexandria, at the same time the festival of mourning or *Adonism* <note>original Greek: *Adoniasmon*</note> was celebrated among the people of **Byblos** in Phoenicia, would annually perform the proper ceremonies and send a letter. This letter was enclosed in a jar or a vessel made of rushes or papyrus and cast into the sea; it would travel to Byblos of its own accord and announce that "Adonis-Osiris has been found." As soon as the women of Byblos (who were waiting) received this, they would change their groans and lamentations for the lost Adonis into sacred joys. With wonderful gladness, they would spend the remainder of the festival welcoming the God. <margin>Procopius, on Chapter 18.</margin> Procopius mentions this embassy in his commentary on Isaiah, Chapter 18:

> Because Ezekiel said: "and I saw, and behold, there sat women weeping for Thamuz," which is Adonis. Such a custom existed among those living in the city of the youths <note>Alexandria</note>. Taking a clay jar, they put in a letter to the women in Byblos, as if Adonis had been found. Then, having sealed it, they cast it into the sea, performing certain rites over it, and—as those who sent it used to say—it arrived at Byblos of its own accord and refreshed the spirits of all the weeping women there.

<margin>Ceremonies celebrated at the finding of Adonis.</margin> Indeed, in Ezekiel we read these words: *And I saw, and behold, women were sitting there mourning for Thamuz (that is, Adonis)*. Something of this nature was carried out by the custom of that city: they would cast letters into a jar to the women at Byblos, as if <margin>Cyril.</margin> <margin>Lucian.</margin> Adonis had been properly found. Once these letters were sealed and the rites performed, they were lowered into the sea (as the senders say) and were carried spontaneously to Byblos, and by their arrival, they caused the women of the city to cease their mourning. **Cyril** explains the matter in almost the same words. **Lucian** calls that vessel or jar a "papyrus head"...

<sig>Oo 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: head</meta>

<summary>Kircher explains that while the timing of festivals for Thamuz, Adonis, and Osiris differed due to the Egyptian "vague year" vs. the fixed Jewish calendar, the rituals remained identical. He describes a specific Phoenician/Egyptian custom where a letter in a papyrus vessel was sent by sea to announce the god's resurrection.</summary>

### CHAPTER IX. 292 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACI: THE TEMPLE OF ISIS

<margin>A letter arrives by divine means in the space of seven days.</margin>
...the head <note>original Greek: *kephalē*</note>, and he says that it was accustomed to be carried from Egypt to Byblos in seven days, with the sea and wind divinely prepared for the journey. Rabbi David Kimchi calls these <term>reed instruments<note>original Hebrew: *keli gome*</note></term>, or even "reed ships":

<margin>Radak <note>A common acronym for Rabbi David Kimchi (1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian.</note></margin>

<margin>Rabbi Saadias, in his book *On Faith*.</margin>
<margin>Letters enclosed in reed.</margin>
<margin>What are the "Byblian letters"?</margin>
<margin>Osiris and Adonis are the same.</margin>
Rabbi Saadias, in his book *On Faith* <note>Referring to *Emunot ve-De'ot*, written by Saadia Gaon in the 10th century.</note>, calls them "reed baskets." However, Procopius (cited previously) interprets the passage in Isaiah 18—*sending messengers by sea in reed vessels across the surface of the waters*—as referring to the Egyptian custom of sending letters enclosed in reed across the sea to Byblos; here the <term>Septuagint<note>The influential Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note></term> uses the phrase "Byblian letters" <note>original Greek: *epistolas byblinas*</note>. Therefore, the <term>disappearance and discovery<note>original Greek: *aphanismō kai heuresei*</note></term> of Adonis corresponds entirely to the "Search for Osiris," which we discussed at length in the chapter on Osiris. It has been demonstrated more than enough by what we have said regarding Adonis and Thamuz that the Phoenicians, Cypriots, and Hebrews borrowed these ceremonies from the Egyptians. For as we said above, the Egyptian priests, on fixed days of the year, would pretend to have the body of Osiris and an idol buried in hidden parts of the temple. This was kept secret from everyone. On that same day, they would wail for him with the greatest signs of sorrow and enormous lamentation, as if he had been killed by Typhon (whom they called a "boar" because of his cruelty and ferocity). As a sign of mourning, they wandered through the streets and crossroads with shaved heads, beating their breasts. All of these things agree perfectly with what we quoted above from Lucian concerning the mourning and ceremonies performed for Adonis.

<margin>A parallel comparison.</margin>
Therefore, what Osiris (killed by Typhon and mourned by his followers) is to the Egyptians, Adonis (killed by a boar—a name we previously suggested was used for Typhon—mourned by Venus and Proserpina, and called back from the underworld) is to the Phoenicians and Syrians. Furthermore, just as the Egyptians mystically understand the retreat of the Sun through Osiris and his death, so too the Phoenicians understood nothing else by Adonis except that Sun which provides nourishment and the power of germination to all things, according to the verse of Orpheus:

<margin>Orpheus, in the *Hymn to the Sun* and the *Hymn to Adonis*.</margin>
->O wise counselor of many forms, visible nourisher of all,<-
->Maiden and youth, worthy sprout to all, O Adonis,<-
->Extinguished, yet shining again in the beautiful cycles of the seasons.<-

> *You who bring back nourishment to all, whose wisdom is*
> *vast, you who delight in various names, O Adonis,*
> *the author of growth, equally boy and girl,*
> *now dead, and now shining again as the stars glide by.*

### TREATISE IV. THE HEBREW PANTHEON. CHAPTER IX.

<margin>The Syrians call Adonis "Lord."</margin>
From this, the Syrians used to call him Adonis, which is to say "Lord," according to Hesychius: *Adonis is master among the Phoenicians* <note>original Greek: *Αδωνις δεσπότης ὑπὸ Φοινίκων*</note>. Among the Laconians <note>The people of Sparta.</note> he was also called *kyris* and *kyros*, which also means "Lord" <note>original Greek: *κῦρις*</note>, according to the same witness. Ptolemy, writing about the peoples of the East who live under the Northern Trigon <note>An astrological grouping of three zodiac signs; here referring to the northern celestial region.</note>, says they worship Venus, and they call Mars "Adonis," or "Lord," *and they perform certain mysteries for them with lamentations* <note>original Greek: *καὶ μυστήριά τινα μετ᾽ θρήνων ἀποδίδοντες αὐτοῖς*</note>.

The ancients, who believed Adonis was the Sun, imagined that he was struck by a boar—a bristly and rough wild beast—because winter is a rough and bristly season. During winter, the Sun's power gradually fails, a state that is entirely hostile to Venus <note>In this allegorical system, Venus represents the generative, warming power of nature.</note>, since Venus flourishes in the tempering of the air, but recoils from the cold as if from a work hostile to nature.
<margin>Adonis is "Lord" in Syriac and Hebrew. The mystical reason for Adonis.</margin>

<margin>Venus and Proserpina indicate the Sun, existing now in the northern signs, now in the winter signs.</margin>
Therefore, when the Sun stays in the six southern signs, traveling through the zodiac, and the days are shorter and the nights longer, Adonis is then said to dwell in the underworld with Proserpina <note>The queen of the underworld; her Greek name is Persephone.</note>. But when the Northern signs make the days longer, he is then with Venus, through whom all beauty and all fragrance is restored to the fields, according to the words of Orpheus <note>The legendary Greek poet and musician.</note>:

> ->*You who now dwell beneath the earth and the black Tartarus,*<-
> ->*And bring back the fruit-bearing body to the heavens.*<-
> <note>original Latin: *Qui modò sub terris habitas, & tartara nigra / Frugiferumque refers in cælum corpus.*</note>

---

<margin>What the Festival of Adonis around the Summer Solstice means mystically.</margin>
Hence, those who first instituted these funeral dirges <note>original: *nornias*, likely a typo for *naenias* (dirges/songs of mourning).</note> for the festival of Adonis in the month of Thamuz—specifically around the Summer Solstice, when the Sun leaves the Northern parts and travels toward the Southern—intended nothing other than the approach and retreat of the Sun. They mourned its departure as if it were lost, and welcomed its rebirth with joyful omens. But we shall deal with these and similar matters in the following Treatise in their proper place and with thorough attention.

<margin>Osiris, Thamuz, and Adonis are the same in reality.</margin>
Therefore, it is clear from what has been said that Osiris, Adonis, and Thamuz are different in name but entirely the same in reality; their ceremonies, too, flowed from nowhere else but the Egyptian school. Having considered these things rightly, one difficulty remains to be discussed—which no one has touched upon until now—so that we may fully apply everything said so far to those who weep for Thamuz. It is this: why, exactly, are Osiris and Adonis called "Thamuz" by the Hebrews, and from where does that name come? Was it transferred from the month to the idol, or was it transferred from the idol to the month? Let us see what foreign writings reveal to us on this matter.

<margin>The true etymology of Thamuz.</margin>
Abenephius <note>Ahmad ibn 'Ali ibn al-Mukhtar, also known as Ibn Wahshiyya, an author Kircher believed had preserved ancient Egyptian wisdom.</note>, in his book *On Egyptian Servitude*, says that "Thamuz" (which we interpreted above as either a month or an idol) is derived from a certain King of Egypt named Tamusi. He says that this king was the first institutor of the rites and ceremonies that were usually observed in that mournful solemnity of Osiris. He reigned at the time when the children of Israel were staying in Egypt. Since these mournings took place mostly around the Summer Solstice, when the Sun in its summer turning retreats toward the Southern parts, the Hebrews became accustomed to these rites and annual lamentations. Later, they continued to practice them at the same time even while they lived outside of Egypt. From their founder, Tamusi, they called not only the idol but also the month "Thamuz." We subjoin his Arabic words:

تَمُّوزُ <note>Arabic: *Tammūz*</note>

<summary>This page argues that the deities Adonis, Osiris, and Thamuz are all symbolic representations of the Sun's seasonal cycle. It explains the name "Thamuz" as deriving from an Egyptian king named Tamusi, who supposedly established these solar rituals during the Israelite captivity in Egypt.</summary>

### CHAPTER IX. 294 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIACO TEMPLE

<margin>Abenephius <note>A reference to the Arabic author Ibn Wahshiyya, whom Kircher frequently cites for Egyptian lore.</note>.</margin>
At the time when the Children of Israel inhabited the land of Egypt, there was a certain king of Egypt who was a scholar and a philosopher named Thammuzi. He was the first who established the worship of idols and the rituals for those who searched for Osiris with much weeping and wailing. When the Children of Israel mixed with the Egyptians and followed their practices, they returned to their own regions and established these Egyptian gods, performing their worship with weeping and mourning according to the Egyptian custom. They used to call the month in which they wept "Tammuz," after the name of the king, Thammuzi. <note>Translated from the original Arabic text provided in the manuscript.</note>

<margin>King Thamuzi first established the solemnities of the Isiac mourning.</margin>
At that time, he says, when the *Israelites* were staying in the land of *Egypt*, a certain one of the Kings held power in *Egypt* named *Thamuzi*. This King was the first who established the rites and ceremonies usually displayed in that mournful festivity of *Osiris*, which were to be repeated every year. When the *Hebrews* were mixed with the *Egyptians*, they learned their works; and look, having returned to their own region and having been initiated into their sacrifices, they celebrated those rites every year with the same wailing and grief that was customary in *Egypt*. Moreover, they called the month in which these things were usually celebrated *Tammuz*, after their first founder *Thamuzi*. Thus says *Abenephius*. This certainly agrees very well with the Chronology of the Kings of Egypt which we presented in the first Treatise <term>Syntagma</term>; for around the same time that Thamuzi is said to have reigned, I find *Tetmosis* <note>Likely referring to Thutmose.</note>, whom others also call *Tamosis*, from which the great traces of the name Thamuzi clearly appear.

<margin>Tetmosis is the same as Thamuzi, the persecutor of the Israelites.</margin>
Furthermore, *Eusebius* <note>An early Christian historian.</note> records from *Manetho* <note>An ancient Egyptian priest and historian.</note> that this King flourished at the time of the persecution of the children of *Israel*. From this it can be concluded that, driven by excessive zeal for his ancestral Gods and their ceremonies and sacrifices, he moved that cruel persecution against the *Israelites* as if they were despisers of the *Egyptian* idols and rites.

<margin>Philastrius <note>A 4th-century bishop known for his writings on heresies.</note>.</margin>
Indeed, *Philastrius* also seems to allude to this when he says:
> *Tamur* (read *Tamuz*) *was the son of a King of the gentiles, whose image the Judean women used to adore with weeping; and by worshipping the impiety of the gentiles, they did not cease to offer sacrifices to him.*

He adds, as if seeking the name from *Egypt*:
> *For that Pharaoh who presided over the Egyptians at that time under the blessed Moses was called Thamuz, King of the Egyptians.*

<margin>Plato in the Phaedrus. Who is Taut?</margin>
Certainly *Plato* in the *Phaedrus* also mentions a certain *Thamuz* reigning at the time of Mercury Trismegistus, whom he calls *Taut* <note>The Egyptian god Thoth.</note>; all these things, when compared together, seem to fit perfectly with what we have said so far about *Thamuz*. As for what the *Rambam* <note>Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, also known as Maimonides.</note> said—that *Thamuz* was a prophet of idols who, after his death, was mourned by all the images of the earth meeting in Babylonia—it seems to draw its origin from the fact that the *Egyptians* thought all those who had been diligent worshippers of the ancestral Gods in life were honored after death by a public assembly of the Gods. This was thought to take place in Heliopolis or Memphis (which many have called the Egyptian Babylon), where funeral rites were performed with weeping, after which they were led to a blessed life.

<margin>Reconciliation of the different opinions concerning Thamuz.</margin>
And from all these things, it is clear how so many and such diverse opinions brought forward about *Thamuz* and his ceremonies are to be reconciled. For all of them seem to regard the Isiac and Egyptian solemnity and festivity. *Thamuz*, however, does not properly signify Adonis or Osiris, but derived his name from that King who first established the Isiac ceremonies—if we believe Abenephius—named Thamuzi. If these things are properly distinguished, those points which we brought forward a little earlier from Philastrius, the Rambam, the Quran, and others—which are otherwise discordant with historical truth—are easily reconciled.

<summary>Athanasius Kircher attempts to reconcile various historical and religious accounts of Thamuz, concluding that the name refers to an Egyptian king (possibly Thutmose) who founded the mourning rituals of Osiris, which were later adopted by the Israelites and others.</summary>
