## CHAPTER X.

### Apis, or the Golden Calf

<margin>In Exodus 32.</margin>
That the Hebrews once worshiped a Calf or a golden Ox in the desert is clearly evident from that passage in Exodus 32: *But when the people saw that Moses delayed in coming down from the mountain, they gathered against Aaron and said: "Arise, make us gods who shall go before us."* And shortly after: *And he formed it with a casting tool and made for them a molten calf; and the children of Israel said: "These are your gods, O Israel, who led you out of the land of Egypt."* Although the Hebrew word *egel* <note>original: עגל</note> and the Greek *moschos* <note>original: μόσχος</note> mean "Calf," we often find this name *egel* used for *shur* <note>original: שור, meaning "Ox"</note> in Holy Scripture. For instance, in Psalm 105: *They made a calf in Horeb* <note>original: ויעשו עגל בחורב</note>, where for *egel* (calf), *shur* (ox) is understood. Indeed, the metrical paraphraser Apollinarius <note>A 4th-century Christian poet who rewrote the Psalms in Greek verse.</note> demonstrates this sufficiently in this passage when he calls this calf a *keralchea moschon* <note>original Greek: κεραλχέα μόσχον</note>, which means "a calf already possessed of horns."
*And so in gold they fashioned a horned calf.* <note>original Greek: Ε'ν δ' ἄρα χρυσῷ κεραλχέα μόσχον ἔταξαν.</note>

<margin>See Isidore on Hosea, Ch. 13. Athanasius, *Against the Heathen*.</margin>
<margin>What kind of idol the Israelite Calf was.</margin>
I omit here the Chaldean paraphrase of Jonathan <note>The Targum of Jonathan ben Uzziel, an ancient Aramaic translation of the Prophets.</note>, who, commenting on the 13th chapter of Hosea, translates "calves" as *torya* <note>original: תורייא</note>, which means "Oxen." Herodotus also everywhere calls that most famous Ox, whom they call Apis, a *moschos* (calf), as Saint Athanasius testifies. Therefore, "Calf" and "Ox" are often taken to mean the same thing; we thought it necessary to point this out first so that no doubt would hinder the reader in the following pages. With these things understood, there are three main points for us to examine in this chapter: First, what kind of sculpted or molten image was this idol? Second, was this Ox truly the same as the Apis of the Egyptians? Third, how did these rituals of Apis spread from Egypt to the Hebrews?

<margin>Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, Book 3. Optatus of Milevis, Book 3. Lactantius.</margin>
<margin>Whether they worshiped only a Calf's head.</margin>
Regarding the first point, there are those who think the Egyptians did not worship a whole Ox, but only a bovine head. Thus the ancient writer Tertullian, who in his third book *Against the Jews*, says that a "Buffalo head" <note>original: Bubalum caput</note> emerged from the molten gold. Optatus of Milevis agrees with this: *In the times of Moses,* he says, *the people of Israel worshiped the golden head of a calf.* Lactantius, in his work *On True Wisdom*, chapter 10, says: *Having fallen into luxury, they turned their minds to the profane rituals of the Egyptians; for when Moses their leader had ascended the mountain and remained there for forty days, they fashioned the golden head of an Ox, whom they call Apis, which had gone before them as a sign.* Thus the cited authors posit a golden head of a calf, not because the idol was strictly "calf-headed" <note>original Greek: μοσχοκέφαλον (*moschokephalon*)</note>, but in this passage they seem to have spoken according to a Hebrew idiom in which
<margin>2 Kings, Ch. 3. <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Samuel 3:8.</note></margin>
a part is often taken for the whole, as in that passage from 2 Kings, Chapter 3: *Am I a dog's head?* <note>Meaning "Am I a dog?"</note> Additionally, this way of speaking likely drew its origin from that common slander of the Pagans, by which they babbled that the Christians—or more accurately, the Jews—worshiped sometimes the head of an ass, sometimes that of a pig; concerning which, read Apion... <note>Kircher refers to the ancient critic Apion, who spread rumors that the Jews worshiped an ass's head in the Temple.</note>

<summary>Kircher examines the biblical Golden Calf, arguing through linguistic analysis of Hebrew, Greek, and Aramaic that the terms "calf" and "ox" were interchangeable and referred to the Egyptian god Apis. He also addresses early Christian theories suggesting the idol may have been only a head rather than a full animal.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the Golden Calf, moving from the biblical description of the calf as "horned" to historical accounts and polemics regarding donkey and ox worship, ultimately linking the Hebrew idolatry in the desert to the Egyptian worship of Apis and Mnevis.</meta>

### CHAPTER X. 296 THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>Apion according to Josephus.</margin>
<margin>The donkey-headed statue in Jerusalem.</margin>
<margin>The Gnostic deity Sabaoth had the head of a donkey. Epiphanius.</margin>
<margin>Tacitus, *Histories* book 5.</margin>
<margin>A bronze image in the Museum of Torquato Alessandro in Rome.</margin>
We find Apion, as cited by Flavius Josephus, babbling many reckless things about this deity being "donkey-headed" <note>original Greek: ὀνοκέφαλον</note>. Diodorus Siculus also writes of a stone statue found by Antiochus Epiphanes in the inner sanctum of the Temple in Jerusalem, which had a human form, a long beard, and held a book in its hands. Likewise, the Gnostics possessed a book they titled *The Birth of Mary* <note>original Greek: ἡ γέννα Μαρίας</note>, in which they wickedly displayed wonders about Zechariah being killed because of a donkey-like deity he had seen while sacrificing—a story commonly spread by them. Some of them claimed that the one they called Sabaoth <note>A name for God in the Hebrew Bible, which Gnostic sects personified as a lower celestial ruler.</note> among their monstrous deities had the form of a donkey, while others said he had the form of a pig; Epiphanius wrote: "Some say that Sabaoth has the form of a donkey, others that of a pig." <note>original Greek: Φασὶ δὲ, scripsit Epiphanius, ὂν Σαβαὼθ οἱ μὲן ὄνου μορφὴν ἔχειν, οἱ δὲ χוίρου.</note> Tacitus also, speaking of an image that had supposedly dispelled their wandering and thirst by pointing the way, suggests a donkey was kept in the sacred inner sanctum. Thus, this worship of the head of a Donkey, an Ox, or a Pig is seen confusedly throughout various authors. From this we can gather what we hinted at before: that the cited authors took this occasion to label that cast-metal Calf as a buffalo-headed image as well. *In the museum of the illustrious Torquato Alessandro of Rome—a man well-deserving of his reputation in the knowledge of antiquities and the Governor of the Castel Sant'Angelo—there is, among other Egyptian antiquities of which he is a most skilled investigator, a bronze statue. It shows great evidence of this bovine worship performed in the desert; however, since it has not yet been engraved, it seemed more prudent to defer its description to the third volume, where we shall bring forth all his hieroglyphic monuments.*

<margin>The worship of the Golden Calf reflects the worship of Apis.</margin>
<margin>St. Jerome on Hosea, chapter 4.</margin>
Regarding the second point, it is certain that the Hebrews, by this "calf-worship" <note>original Greek: μοχολατρείαν</note>, intended to indicate nothing other than the worship of Apis, which they had seen practiced with such great zeal while they were still staying in Egypt. St. Jerome confirms this assertion of ours in his commentary on the fourth chapter of Hosea: *It seems to me,* he says, *that the people of Israel made for themselves the head of a Calf to worship in the wilderness for this reason: and Jeroboam the son of Nebat fashioned golden calves so that they might preserve in their superstition what they had learned in Egypt—that Apis and Mnevis <note>The two sacred bulls of Egypt; Apis was kept at Memphis and Mnevis at Heliopolis.</note>, who are worshiped under the figure of oxen, were gods.* The testimony we brought forward earlier from Lactantius agrees with this. Furthermore, authors vary on what rituals were used to cast this Calf and by what art.

The Rabbis assert that this "Hebrew Apis" was produced in the desert by Egyptian Magicians using demonic arts; therefore, Rabbi Solomon Iarrhi <note>Commonly known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French rabbi and commentator.</note> calls it "the work of the devil" <note>original Hebrew: מעשה שטן</note> and attributes it to magical deceptions in the following words:

> *When they cast the gold into the fire in the melting pot, or rather into the molds, the Egyptian magicians—the "mixed multitude" <note>original Hebrew: ערב רב (Erev Rav), the group of non-Israelites who left Egypt with the Hebrews.</note> who went up with the children of Israel from Egypt—came and made it by magic arts. And some say that Micah was there, who had been pulled out from the crushed buildings in Egypt, and in his hand was a Name <note>A divine name of power.</note> and a metal plate on which Moses had written "Arise, Ox; Arise, Ox" to make the coffin of Joseph rise up out of the Nile; and he threw it into the furnace, and the calf came out.*

<margin>Arab and Rab magicians.</margin>
*When indeed,* says **Rashi**, *they threw the gold into the fire, into the casting vat, or better into the molds, the magicians Arab and Rab came, who had ascended with the children of Israel out of Egypt, and they made that calf by magical art, saying: "Where is this God, who came out from the midst of the brickwork in which the children of Israel were tasked in Egypt?"*

### SYNTAGMA IV. THE HEBREW PANTHEON. 297 CHAPTER X.

...and there was in his hand the divine name and a metal plate, on which Moses had written these words: <note>original Hebrew: עלי שור עלי שור</note> "Rise up, O ox; rise up, O ox," so that he might cause the coffin of Joseph to rise up from the middle of the Nile. Once these words were spoken, they threw the plate into the middle of the melting pot, and out came the Calf. A little later, he explains himself more clearly:

> It is not said, "These are *our* gods," because it was the <term>Mixed Multitude</term> <note>original Hebrew: ערב רב, *Erev Rav*; a group of non-Israelites who joined the Exodus.</note> who came up from Egypt; they were the ones who gathered against Aaron, and they were the ones who made the calf, and afterwards they led the Israelites astray after it.

Jonathan the Chaldean, the Paraphrast <note>A "paraphrast" is a translator who provides an interpretive explanation; here referring to the author of an Aramaic translation of the Bible known as a Targum.</note>, also points to this deception by the Demon in these words:

<margin>Jonathan the Chaldean Paraphrast.</margin>
> And the people saw, he says, that Moses delayed his descent from the mountain, and the people gathered against Aaron when they saw that the time he had set for them had passed. Then Satan went and led them into error and exalted their proud hearts, and said to him (Aaron): "Rise up, make for us terrifying gods who shall go before us."

The Jerusalem Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible produced in the Land of Israel.</note> agrees with this:

> And it happened when Moses approached the camp and saw the calf and saw them in their festivities, dancing and bowing down before it; and Satan himself was dancing in their midst, leading the choruses before the people.

<margin>Music was used in the casting of the Calf.</margin>
And Moses approaches the camp, and saw the calf and the Israelites with musical instruments in their wicked hands, leaping, dancing, and crawling, bowing themselves before it; and Satan himself was dancing in their midst and leading the dances before the people. From this it is gathered that they also used musical instruments after the manner of the Egyptians; perhaps these were <term>sistra</term> <note>Ancient Egyptian percussion instruments associated with the goddess Isis.</note> and pipes, with which such solemnities were most especially performed in Egypt.

Therefore, that this Golden Calf was made according to the model of Apis <note>The sacred bull of Memphis, worshipped as a god of strength and fertility.</note> is demonstrated more than enough, not only by what has been cited so far from various authors, but also by the ceremonies with which they worshipped it once it was cast. For Apis, according to Herodotus's description, was marked with various symbolic signs and bore various images on his body, which we exhibited above when we dealt with Apis. That similar marks were impressed upon the Golden Calf by Aaron is indicated quite clearly by those words of the Hebrew text:

> And he took it from their hands (namely, the gold) and fashioned it with a graving tool and made it a molten calf; and they said: "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt."

Upon these words, Rabbi Solomon <note>Commonly known as Rashi (1040–1105), a preeminent medieval French rabbi and author of comprehensive commentaries on the Talmud and Tanakh.</note> comments as follows:

> "And he fashioned it with a graving tool": this refers to a sharp craftsman's tool with which they engrave shapes in gold, like a scribe’s pen which carves letters on writing tablets. This is like the phrase "write upon it with a man’s pen" <note>A reference to Isaiah 8:1.</note>. The translation of Onkelos <note>The official Babylonian Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> uses a term for "forgery" or "deception"; it is a craftsman's tool with which they engrave letters in gold, which in the common tongue is called <term>niello</term> <note>original: ניי"ל, *niyel*; a black mixture used as an inlay in engraved metal.</note>, and by its use, seals are forged.

### CHAPTER X. 298 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE

<margin>The Calf was marked with various signs.</margin>
*And he formed, that is, he fashioned that gold with a stylus,* <note>original: "stylo"</note> which is a goldsmith’s tool used to carve and engrave various figures into gold; it is similar to a writer's stylus used to scribe letters on tablets, following the verse: *And write upon it with a man's stylus.* <note>Referencing Isaiah 8:1.</note> This is also what Onkelos <note>A famous 2nd-century convert to Judaism known for his authoritative Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> says: *and he fashioned it with a stylus,* <note>original Aramaic: בחרט (*be-cheret*)</note> that is, with the tool of a craftsman who uses it to complete various engravings in gold, such as animal figures <note>original: "Zoophora"</note> and ribbons <note>original: "Lemniscos," decorative bands often shown on sacrificial animals.</note> (which are called <note>original Hebrew: כנזיל (*kanzil*)</note> in the Gallic tongue), and with which they also engrave signet rings. Therefore, Aaron is said to have marked out that golden Calf of his; however, authors doubt whether he carved the figures directly onto the golden mass or if he first expressed them in a clay model or mold. As far as we have been able to gather from the records of the Oriental interpreters, we believe that after Aaron had collected the earrings, he melted them into a single mass. He then adapted this mass into the figure of a Calf in such a way that the fashioned Calf, when pressed into clay material, provided a model or mold <note>original: "modellam seu formam"</note> from which many calves could subsequently be cast. This was done according to the request of the Hebrews, who demanded not just one single God, but many gods to be made for them, who might precede them like military companies. That this is the case will be clearly evident to those who examine the verse of this passage a little more carefully. Certainly, the Jerusalem Targum and Jonathan Ben Uziel <note>Authors of ancient Aramaic paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible.</note> asserted our opinion in these very words, as follows:

> And he took it from their hands and formed it with a cloth <note>The Aramaic word here can mean a wrap or a tool; Kircher interprets it as part of the casting process.</note> and threw it into a mold, and made it into a molten calf; and they said: "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt."

First, therefore, Aaron fashioned all the figures on the Calf according to the Egyptian custom, perhaps using hieroglyphic marks. Then, by pressing the Calf thus fashioned into prepared material or clay, he cast a matrix or (as it is commonly called) a "model." Once this was done, he finally produced a molten calf <note>original: "Vitulum conflatilem"</note> by the art of metal casting, as the Vulgate edition also testifies. And according to Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator on the Torah.</note> as well: *And he threw it into the midst of the mold, and the calf came out.*

<margin>The Calf was cast from a mold.</margin>
That Aaron made a mold for casting several calves is gathered from this: as soon as the Hebrews saw the successful result of the first casting, they said, *"These are your terrifying gods who brought you out of Egypt,"* denoting in the singular one of many others to be cast. (They perhaps would have cast more had Moses not hindered their wicked daring by his arrival, as Abenezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish Renaissance scholar and biblical commentator.</note> shows). These calves, placed in various locations and borders of the desert according to Egyptian custom, were to be for them like certain <term>Averruncus</term> <note>From the Latin "averruncare" (to ward off); a deity charged with averting evil or disaster.</note> gods. Perhaps the Hebrews were looking back to those most celebrated bulls of the Egyptians, Apis and Mnevis; the latter was dedicated to the Sun and the former to the Moon, and both were worshipped as gods who ward off evil. Certainly, St. Jerome, cited above, indicates quite clearly that Jeroboam <note>The first king of the northern Kingdom of Israel who famously set up golden calves to prevent his subjects from traveling to Jerusalem.</note> also looked back to these when he manufactured two golden calves and placed one in Dan and the other in Bethel to be worshipped. *For,* as the sacred page testifies, *having hidden in Egypt for a long time, he returned to his homeland and, having obtained the kingdom, manufactured two golden calves; mindful of the ancestral deity of the Egyptians, he said: "Behold your gods, O Israel, who led you out of the land of Egypt."*

<margin>The calves of Jeroboam represented the two bulls usually worshipped by the Egyptians.</margin>

<summary>This page discusses the technical process Aaron used to create the Golden Calf, arguing he created a master mold to cast multiple idols modeled after the Egyptian bull-gods Apis and Mnevis.</summary>

### SYNTAGMA IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER X. 299

<margin>Astrological observation.</margin>
There are those who would have it that the Hebrews set up the Calf because there was a "great conjunction" of the two superior planets <note>In traditional astrology, the "superior planets" are Jupiter and Saturn; their meeting or "conjunction" was believed to signal major historical shifts.</note> at the same time the Hebrews were migrating from Egypt. They argue this Calf was placed as a <term>counterpart</term> <note>original Greek: ἀντίστοιχον (*antistoichon*), meaning a corresponding element or equivalent.</note> to the celestial Taurus (the Bull). However, Rabbi Abenezra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Spanish Jewish scholar and astronomer.</note> refutes this opinion with these words:

<margin>Abenezra.</margin>
> The sages, he says, and those skilled in Astrology say that the great conjunction of the two superior planets was in the sign of Taurus; but this is a falsehood, for it was only in the sign of Aquarius. According to astrological reasoning, that sign properly belongs to Israel, and many have tested this secret generation after generation; I also have found it to be so, and behold, they rejoiced in the mid-heaven. <note>original Hebrew: וחכמי המזלות אמרו כי המחברת הגדולה לשני העליונים היתה במזל שור וזה כזב כי לא היתה רק במזל דלי ועל דרך חכמת המזלות הוא מזל ישראל ורבים נסו זה הסוד דור אחר דור גם אני ראיתי ככה והנה שמחו בחצי שמים</note>

Whatever the case may be—whether that Calf was fashioned out of astrological superstition or some other reason—this much is certainly clear to us: it was a perfect image of Apis in every respect. The figures traced upon it by Aaron with a tool show this clearly enough; for it is not easily understood what he would have done with a stylus unless he engraved the marks of Apis distinguished by hieroglyphics, or something of that sort. Furthermore, when the people had already erected the cast Calf, the sacred page says: *And the people sat down to eat and drink, and they rose up to play* <note>Exodus 32:6.</note>; that is, they celebrated the molten deity with song and dances. A little later, in the person of Moses, it is said: *It is not the voice of those shouting for victory, nor the voice of those crying for defeat; but the voice of singers I hear,* or those leading dances, or <term>those leading the wine-revels</term> <note>original Greek: τῶν ἐξαρχόντων οἴνου (*tōn exarchontōn oinou*)</note>, as the Greeks render it—namely, those feasting or "calf-making" <note>Kircher uses the word "vitulantium," a pun on "vitulus" (calf) and "vitulari" (to rejoice/sacrifice).</note>. What else is being related to us by these words except the 
<margin>They emulated the Egyptian solemnities in the song of the Calf.</margin>
dances, games, feasts, and public joys which the Egyptians were accustomed to celebrate for Apis? When the priests led Apis in a solemn procession to Memphis, boys in 그 sacred escort would sing a song in his honor in a group. What else did Moses indicate when he burnt the Calf in fire, ground it into powder, and submerged it in the waters, if not the slaughtering of Apis submerged in the depths of the sacred spring or the Nile? He intended not to imitate this, but to carry it out as a reproach to such idolatry, just as one can see King Josiah did in the Books of Kings.

<margin>Why the Calf was cast from gold.</margin>
Furthermore, that Ox or Calf was golden, which was not without mystery. Indeed, they had learned everything from the Egyptians, who, besides the two live bulls Apis and Mnevis <note>Mnevis was the sacred bull of Heliopolis, associated with the sun god Ra, while Apis was associated with Ptah and Osiris.</note> (whom they nourished in a certain enclosure, as Herodotus testifies and as was said at length in preceding chapters), also worshipped golden images of oxen and calves. They placed these publicly in temples and on temple gates, and wore them on the neck, ears, hands, and belts in place of earrings and bracelets, as will be shown at length in the practical interpretation of the hieroglyphic Obelisks.
<margin>Why golden earrings for the casting of the Calf?</margin>
They were cast from gold because gold was analogous to the Sun, whose image the Calf reflected. For this reason, many of the Rabbis believe that the earrings and bracelets Aaron asked them to give him were remnants from the spoils the Hebrews collected while migrating from Egypt. Among these were various images of sacred animals, of Apis,

### CHAPTER X. 300 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS THE ISIAC TEMPLE

Those who understand these matters should also weigh the incised figures which were commonly carried in honor of Osiris or the Sun, to see if perhaps Aaron formed something similar out of those bracelets—as if from a certain prototype—in the cast Calf. Certainly, he who compares well what we said above with these things will find great arguments for this truth. Furthermore, it was the custom among the Egyptians on that most solemn <margin>The days of the hiding and finding of Osiris.</margin> <note>original Greek: τῷ ἀφανισμῷ καὶ εὑρέσει (*tō aphanismō kai heuresei*)</note> day of the hiding and finding of Osiris, to proclaim it with a herald using a solemn voice, so that the people might be better prepared to celebrate the festivals of the sacred Divinity with devotion. 

Aaron certainly, while proclaiming the tomorrow's solemnity for the already cast Calf and the constructed altars to the Israelites, said: "A festival for Jehovah tomorrow" <note>original Hebrew: חג ליי מחר (*Chag l’Adonai machar*)</note>. He seems to have looked to nothing else but the rites and ceremonies of the followers of Isis; for he knew the character of the superstitious people, to whom nothing could be more pleasing than to do and perform all those things by which they were so greatly affected while they still lived in Egypt. This is also evident from the fact that, in order to please the idolaters more—as <margin>Selden on the Syrian Gods.</margin> <note>Kircher refers to John Selden's influential work on ancient Near Eastern deities.</note> Selden also notes—he wished to attribute the ineffable Name of the best and greatest God, which is proper to Him, to the idol. The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> writes there: "A feast for the Lord" <note>original Greek: ἑορτὴ τῷ κυρίῳ (*heortē tō kyriō*)</note>. 

It is well known, however, that the Tetragrammaton <note>The sacred four-letter name of God, YHWH.</note> was translated by the Greeks according to a very ancient custom sometimes into <note>original Greek: ΠΙΠΙ (*PIPI*). Because the Hebrew letters for YHWH (יהוה) looked like the Greek letters PIPI to those unfamiliar with the script, it was often transcribed this way in early Greek manuscripts.</note>, and sometimes into "Adonai" <note>original Greek: Α'δωναι</note>, which sounds the same in Hebrew; and the Jews read "Adonai" for it by an old institution. Whether indeed the name of Adonis attributed to Osiris was so ancient is doubtful; we certainly judge it to be equally ancient, since "Adonis" is Hebrew in origin. Indeed, Martianus Capella <note>A 5th-century Latin writer who synthesized ancient mythology.</note> shows this sufficiently by calling the Byblian Adon "Osiris." Following him, Ausonius sings thus in his *Myobarbum* to Father Liber <note>Liber was an ancient Roman god of fertility and wine, often identified with Bacchus or Dionysus.</note>:

<margin>Ausonius in *Myobarbus*, epigram 29.</margin>
->Ogygia sings of me as Bacchus,<-
->Egypt thinks me Osiris,<-
->The Arabian race calls me Adoneus.<-

And we have demonstrated extensively above, where we treated the god Thamuz, that Adonis and Osiris shared the same ceremonies and the same sacred rites.

From all these things duly compared among themselves, we finally conclude that the entire process of calf-worship <note>original Greek: μοσχολατρείας (*moscholatreias*)</note> practiced by the Hebrews flowed immediately from the Egyptians. This needs no proof, since the rites used in casting the Calf—the dances, feasts, choruses, insane shouting, the engraving of figures on the Calf made by Aaron, the incantations of the Magicians, and similar things discussed in the preceding pages—demonstrate it more than sufficiently. 

<margin>Martin von Baumgarten in his Travelogue of Arabia.</margin> Martin von Baumgarten writes that there still exists to this day the burial place of the 3,000 men killed by the command of Moses by the sons of Levi after the adoration of the Calf; he also notes that a stone calf was placed in that same cleared spot in memory of the golden one that was burned. He further mentions the nearby water into which Moses scattered the ashes, and finally the round rock against which he shattered the tablets of the law. Moses Gerundensis <note>Also known as Nachmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar.</note> says this vile idolatry so displeased God that there is no vengeance upon the Israelites in which there is not an ounce of the iniquity of the Calf.

<margin>Rambam.</margin> <note>The margin says Rambam (Maimonides), but the text cites Moses Gerundensis; this is a common rabbinic adage regarding the lasting consequences of the Golden Calf.</note> "There is no punishment in Israel in which there is not an ounce of the sin of the Calf."

## CHAPTER XI.

### On the Idolatry of Solomon, and by what means it was first derived to him from Egypt, taking on immense growth among the Hebrews at all times.

<image-desc>A circular institutional stamp appears in the right margin, partially faded and illegible.</image-desc>

<margin>
Idolatry flourished most after the death of Solomon.
</margin>
We have said in the preceding sections by what means that wicked worship of idols, and the other dogmas of foreign servitude which the Hebrews had learned in Egypt, were gradually propagated by successive tradition after the exit from the house of bondage, and subsequently made great progress in the Hebrew Church. Now, however, we must say from where that manifold worship of idols, which crept into the people of God after the time of Solomon, originated. For never did idolatry flourish more among the Hebrews than after the death of Solomon, as is shown more than enough by the introduction of foreign rites and ceremonies, as well as the worship of groves, woods, and forests, and the construction of high places and altars. For this so frequent idolatry, various authors assign various causes; some impute it to the unspeakable 
<margin>
The crimes of Solomon.
</margin>
crimes of Solomon; others to the unpunished license of life, which flourished among the Hebrews at that time by the wicked example of Solomon; others assign other causes, such as insatiable lust and the insane loves for foreign women, by which he was gradually enticed and infatuated. Having been cast headlong from the highest peak of wisdom into the lowest pit of folly, he miserably dragged along with him as many as were held by the desire for a dissolute life. So that all these things may be well understood:

<margin>
Exod. 34.
Ezek. 6.
2 Chron. 21.
Levit. 19.
Hosea 1.
Isaiah 1.

Luxury and lust are called idolatry.

Ephes. 5 v. 5.
Coloss. 3.
</margin>
It must be known that in the language of Holy Scripture, nothing is more frequent than for "fornication" and "idolatry" to be most closely joined in both fact and name. "Do not take a wife," says God, "from their daughters"—meaning the foreigners—"for your sons, lest after they have committed fornication, they make your sons also commit fornication after their gods." And the same is also expressed under the name of "greed," which, as Jerome interprets in the Epistle to the Ephesians, pertains to insatiable lust and luxury: "The fornicator," says the Apostle, "is a greedy man, which is the service of idols." And to the Colossians: "Fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil concupiscence, and greed, which is the service of idols." But in a more significant, though more hidden way of speaking...

### CHAPTER XI. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>Numbers 33.</margin>For the same reason, this matter was signified in Numbers 33: *If you will not kill the inhabitants of the land, those who remain will be like thorns in your eyes and spears in your sides;* <note>original: "clavi in oculis, & lanceæ in lateribus"</note> that is, foreign women who stimulate those lower parts of the body, who prick the loins, and drive one toward shameful acts. <margin>Joshua 23.</margin>And in Joshua 23: *They shall be a pit, and a snare, and a stumbling block at your side, and stakes in your eyes.* There is more than one reason why idolatry is compared to fornication and why both share a common name; some say that Apostasy—in which a human, having abandoned God the Best and Greatest, the true Groom of souls, revolts to a foreign servitude—is like a kind of fornication.

<margin>Theodoret.</margin>Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457 AD), an influential theologian and bishop of the early Christian Church.</note> argues this; and he draws it from that passage in Ezekiel: *You made for yourself masculine images, and committed fornication with them.* Some derive this comparison from the very name of the idols: for since <term>Baal</term> <note>A title meaning "Lord" or "Master" used for various Levantine deities.</note> was the first and most universal name for any idol, as we mentioned previously; <margin>The word Baal is examined.</margin>Baal signifies a "husband" or a "Lord" who subjects a thing to himself and holds it as if yoked. It comes from the same root <note>Hebrew: בַּעַל (*ba‘al*)</note> which means to possess or subjugate something like a husband with a certain burning desire for possession. For this reason, it is usually accepted for the marital act and "to take a wife," and is translated by the interpreter as "to sleep with a wife." Therefore, from its own name, Baal and the idols <term>Baalim</term> <note>The plural form of Baal.</note> signify a husband, a Lord, and a subjugator. The worshippers, however, because they devoted and addicted themselves to these idols so that they might correspond to the name itself, were elegantly said to be subjected to the dominion of a husband like a woman, and as if sexually dominated by the idols, which exercised force and mastery over their followers.

<margin>St. Augustine</margin>
<margin>Rites in the Capitol.</margin>There are those who conclude this connection from certain specific "wedding ceremonies" of which idolatry consisted. St. Augustine, certainly, among other rites of the idols, mentions that certain women used to sit in the <term>Capitol</term> <note>The Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitoline Hill in Rome.</note> who believed they were loved by Jupiter; they were not even terrified by the gaze of the most wrathful Juno. <margin>Strabo.</margin> <margin>On Venus Anaitis.</margin>Strabo, dealing with the idols of the Persians, Medes, and Armenians, writes thus of <term>Anaitis</term> <note>An ancient Iranian goddess associated with fertility and water, often identified with Venus or Aphrodite.</note>: *This,* he says, *is the Venus worshipped in the East as an Armenian idol; the most illustrious of that nation dedicate their virgin daughters to her; and the law is that after they have been defiled at the temple of the God for a long time, they are then given in marriage, with no man disdaining a union with such a woman.* <margin>Herodotus, Book 1.</margin>Herodotus writes something similar regarding Lydian women: *all of them,* he says, *are harlots, and they treat their lovers so blandly that they even provide lodging; and they often give more gifts than they receive; since they supply expenses from their own wealthy resources, they do not accept just anyone, but only those equal to them in dignity.* <margin>Baruch 6:37.</margin>For this reason, these most shameful women subjecting themselves to the Gods are noted in Baruch 6: *Their women set out... and twenty-nine women serve the silver, gold, and wooden Gods; that is, they serve them diligently, like wives to husbands.* To this we may add the opportunities and occasions for unspeakable debaucheries which the most impious priests of the idols provided for the most shameful men; <margin>Josephus, Antiquities Book 18, Chapter 4.</margin>a famous example of this is written by Josephus in Book 18, Chapter 4, and by Hegesippus <note>A 4th-century writer who adapted Josephus’s "Jewish War."</note> in Book 2, Chapter 4. <margin>Paulina is driven to debauchery by marvelous cunning.</margin>They write of Paulina, a woman no less illustrious for her moral integrity than for the nobility of her birth, and moreover opulently beautiful as she was in the very flower of her youth. Decius Mundus, a young man of the equestrian order, had been unable to bend her modesty either by prayer or by the offered price of two hundred thousand drachmas for a single night; a fraud was then devised with the priests of Isis, to whose cult she was vehemently—

### SYNTAGMA IV. PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. 303. CHAPTER XI.

*...Paulina was vehemently devoted <note>The Roman matron Paulina, known for her piety toward the Egyptian gods.</note>, they feign an embassy sent from Anubis, who, being captivated by her beauty, commands that she come to him. Having received the message with a willing heart, and her husband also having been informed that a bed of Anubis was prepared for her, she was led into the temple. There, with the darkness facilitating the ruse, she encountered [Decius] Mundus hiding within, and she yielded to the young man for the whole night, believing she was pleasing the God.* So far, Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 18, Chapter 3. Josephus uses this scandal to explain why the cult of Isis was temporarily banned in Rome.</note> tells the tale. But since these things we have mentioned did not occur in the religion of every idol, another more common reason must be sought that fits the worship of any idol, so that it can be called fornication and impurity. We cannot provide a more certain reason than the one indicated by the Wise Man <note>Referencing the author of the Book of Wisdom in the Deuterocanon/Apocrypha.</note>: <margin>Wisdom 14:12</margin> *The beginning of all fornication is the seeking out of idols: and the invention of them is the corruption of life;* <note>original: "Initium omnis fornicationis est exquisitio idolorum: & adinuentio eorum, corruptio vitæ est"</note> for idols were worshipped with ceremonies that impelled men toward every obscenity and any enormous crime. This occurred by God's permission as a punishment for idolatry, according to that saying of the Apostle: *God gave them up to shameful passions, etc.* <margin>Ambrose</margin> This is where Saint Ambrose explains the matter, and he adds another reason not to be overlooked. <margin>Athanasius</margin> *Because by worshipping God as one who is indifferent—and thus to be neglected—men became more and more dull-witted and were made more ready to admit all manner of evils.* Furthermore, as Athanasius says in his oration against idols <note>Saint Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373 AD) in *Contra Gentes*.</note>: *Idolatry was established by the desire of those who, full of debauchery and disgrace, represent their own fictions. Therefore, the worshippers of idols set before themselves the most shameful life of their own Gods to be imitated.* Athanasius adds beautifully while investigating the origin of idols: *Malice was the precursor and the herald of idolatry, when it magnified only those things which the mind desired and looked upon with pleasure. Feeling pleasure in bodily affections and forgetting divine things, almost all cities abound with every kind of lust because of the monstrosity of morals they see in their own Gods; nor is there anyone in this race of Gods whom you could call chaste.* <margin>The shameful worship of idols.</margin> *In former times, certainly, Phoenician women were prostituted before idols, dedicating their earnings to the Divinities, persuaded that they could propitiate them through harlotry, and that prosperity would arise from it. Men also, having abdicated their sex and no longer bearing to be males, affected the nature of women, as if in this way they would perform a service of honor to the Mother of the Gods <note>Likely referring to Cybele, whose priests, the Galli, castrated themselves.</note>; all live in the most shameful ways and seem to take up a competition of wickedness among themselves; and as that Holy Minister of Christ, Paul, said: Their women changed the natural use.* Thus says the Holy Doctor.

<margin>Why did foreign women strive so zealously to draw others to the worship of idols?</margin> From this, the cause of another not entirely easy question begins to shine through: why was it that such an immense and unrestrained desire came upon foreign women to draw those with whom they associated—the Israelites—toward the religion of their own idols? It was namely this: since they were held completely immersed and blinded by wicked pleasures (of which they considered their very Gods to be the masters and patrons), they believed they would be deprived of these pleasures unless they also subjected the men to whom they were subjugated to their own most impure religion. And hence <margin>1 Kings 11</margin> is the assertion of the Sacred history: *They will most certainly turn away your hearts to follow foreign Gods.* <note>original: "Certissimè auertent corda vestra, vt sequamini Deos alienos." In the Latin Vulgate used by the author, 1 Kings is titled 3 Kings.</note> This happened not only because of the wickedness of the women, but also because of the iniquity of those who, captured by desire and lust for them, established this as their first principle: that they would acknowledge no Divinity except one that promised them impunity and some protection for their depraved life; according to that [canon] of the Eastern [Council] of Elvira <note>The Council of Elvira (Illiberis), held in Spain in the early 4th century, which dealt with issues of idolatry and sexual morality.</note>.

### CHAPTER XI. THE ISIS TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS. 304.

> Where madness drove him, let wanton error lead;
> And let that be permitted, which was merely desired.
<note>original: "Qua furor impulerat, lascivus duceret error, Esset & hoc licitum, quod fuerat libitum." A verse critiquing the surrender of law to personal whim.</note>

<margin>Cyril.</margin>
<margin>The fall of Solomon.</margin>
A woman, therefore, is a deceptive thing, according to the testimony of Cyril <note>St. Cyril of Alexandria, a prominent 5th-century Church Father.</note>, and well-suited to deceiving those once captured in her snares; for *among her other weapons she possesses pleasure, by which the mind is conquered.* Entangled, therefore, in these snares and shackles, Solomon fell into the depths of idolatry. *For King Solomon*, says the sacred text, *loved many foreign women, as well as the daughter of Pharaoh, and women of the Moabites, Ammonites, Edomites, Sidonians, and Hittites, from the nations; concerning which the Lord said to the children of Israel: You shall not go in to them, neither shall they come in to yours; for most certainly they will turn away your hearts to follow their gods. To these, therefore, Solomon was joined with the most burning love.* <note>Referencing 1 Kings 11:1-2.</note>

It is truly a wonder that among these flocks of women, no mention is made of Israelite women. Indeed, Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> and Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrrhus, a 5th-century bishop and theologian.</note> teach in clear words that Solomon had the most beautiful ones. *Raving*, says Josephus, *after women, and immoderate in sexual matters <note>original: "rebus Venereis," literally "matters of Venus."</note>, not content with the women of his own region, he took many of foreign origin: Sidonians, Tyrians, Ammonites, and Edomites.* <margin>300 concubines of Solomon.</margin> However, Suidas <note>The *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia once thought to be written by an author named "Suidas."</note>, under the word *Astarte*, counts them such that he says the foreign wives, together with the Israelite ones, filled the number of those *seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines*. But since no mention of native women is made in the sacred history, the suspicion arises in the mind that he had very few—perhaps almost none—of his own tribe, and perhaps a few more from other tribes; yet he kept a great many of foreign race and religion, so that he might never be affected by any boredom with them. The reason for this must be sought by us a little more deeply.

<margin>Seneca. Why Solomon loved not native but only foreign women.</margin>
The Hebrew race was truly, as they were incredibly prone to lust, so also easily led toward idolatry and given over to adultery, and most greedy for every foreign worship, whether of the soul or the body. And this was the one head and origin of their other vices: a certain natural inconstancy of the soul and mutability of the mind, which is characteristic of unbridled desires—growing weary of what is at home and always hunting for a new pleasure from novelty. *Occupied by new desires*, (says Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the Roman Stoic philosopher.</note>) *we look not at what we have, but what we seek; intent not on what is, but on what we long for; for whatever is at home is trivial.* Hence arose that inclination of the Israelites toward adultery, wearying of what was at home and thirsting for foreign fountains; hence also that lust for foreign women. Since Balaam <note>A prophet in the Book of Numbers who was asked to curse Israel but blessed them instead, later suggesting they be seduced.</note> had well-investigated this Hebrew temperament, he suggested to King Balak that most wicked counsel of throwing foreign women in the path of the wandering people, which John mentions in Revelation chapter 2: *The doctrine of Balaam, who taught Balak to cast a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat and to commit fornication, etc.* The history of this matter is told in Numbers 24 and 25. Nor was there truly only a single Midianite harlot; but as Josephus tells in Book 4, Chapter 6, very many were taken in marriage even by the princes of Israel, and his narrative of this matter is appropriate in this place. *If you seek*, (says Balaam) *to achieve a brief success over them, by this counsel I shall make you masters of your wish: send the most shapely of your daughters, who by their beauty might be able to conquer their minds, dressed and adorned as much as possible, so that [they go] around...*

# SYNTAGMA IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER XI.

<margin>
The method and reason by which the Israelites were drawn to the love of foreign women.
</margin>
...move about the camps and offer themselves readily to the young men seeking their embraces; but when they see them captured by desire, they should suddenly snatch themselves away. And when they are asked to stay, they should not agree unless they have persuaded the men to abandon their ancestral laws and the worship of the God from whom they received them, and instead venerate the gods of the Midianites <note>A nomadic tribe mentioned in the Bible, often depicted as adversaries of the Israelites.</note> and Moabites. The matter was carried out in this way; and now the young men, lured by flatteries and burning with lust, saw the girls preparing to leave. Saddened by the departure of the women, they pleaded with them not to desert them, promising they would stay with them as future wives and mistresses of all their possessions. They affirmed this with an oath and by shedding tears, the better to bend the women to pity. Then the women, once they perceived the men were bound by their intimacy, responded thus: "Since you have grown accustomed to loving us and taking our ambition to heart, if you give us your word of marital goodwill, we will gladly join you as legitimate wives." When the men promised to give their word in any way required, refusing nothing because of their excessive love, the women said: "If you wish to spend your life with us, it is necessary that you worship our gods; for you will persuade us by no other argument that your love is not feigned, unless you worship and adore the same gods as we do. Nor would it be absurd if you choose to worship the specific gods of the land into which you have come; especially since our gods are honored throughout all regions, while no one among you except yourselves deems your God worthy of worship or ceremonies." But the men, blinded by desire and following where they were led, revolted from the religion of their fathers and did everything against the law for the sake of the women. Thus, the impiety of the youth invaded the entire camp, and the ancestral religion was brought into extreme danger; for the youth, having once tasted foreign customs, were carried toward them insatiably. We have described these things more fully from Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian whose works provide much of the extra-biblical detail for this period.</note> so that it might appear how much evil the habit of foreign women brought upon the Hebrews.

<margin>
The Hebrews were wonderfully captivated by external things.
</margin>
Nor was the people only captured by foreign beauty, but also by foreign finery; for this reason, all those ceremonies for marrying a captive wife, which are prescribed in Deuteronomy 21—namely, that she should shave her hair, trim her nails, put aside the garment in which she was captured, and disfigure her face by mourning her father and mother for one month—pertained to this: that if by chance the victor were captured by her beauty, his concupiscence of love might cool or be extinguished once her hair was cut and the ornaments she wore were put aside. This is the most frequent observation of the interpreters on that passage. From this same head—that is, from that inconstancy of the Hebrew temperament—comes that curiosity and zeal among the Israelites for foreign dress, so meticulously imitated from other nations. God rebukes this quite sharply in Zephaniah 1:
<margin>
The worship of [extravagant] clothing is prohibited in the law, and why?
</margin>
> *I will punish all who are clothed*
> *in foreign garments.*
Along with which they simultaneously put on the foreign worship of gods, as the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> expressed it specifically from the Hebrew: *Those who are clothed in alien garments.* And St. Jerome <note>The 4th-century scholar who translated the Bible into the Latin Vulgate.</note> interprets these as those who venerated idols instead of the worship of God; as if the foreignness of garments also brought about a foreignness of religion. Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrrhus (c. 393–458 AD), a bishop and influential theologian.</note> indicated the reason for this matter elegantly and shrewdly: since the law prohibited garments woven of linen and wool in Deuteronomy 22, it is likely that those among the Israelites who came into wealth and flowed with luxuries imitated the clothes of their neighbors, and in place of garments made of linen, they put on ornaments elaborated with purple and artifice; which was against the tradition of the divine law. You see, therefore...

->*Is he so out of his mind and foreign?*<-

<margin>Hebrew men loved foreign women.</margin>
And these foreign pleasures are themselves the acts of harlots, by which the characters of the Hebrews were incredibly captured, softened, and weakened, and were enticed toward every impiety of foreign worship.

<margin>The fall of Solomon.</margin>
With these, therefore (says the Sacred History), Solomon was joined in *most ardent love*, or as the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> has it: *Solomon cleaved to them in loving.* Although this seems to be said in simple speech, there lies hidden that force of most burning love, which the Latin author expressed: *By these snares, the Wise man’s heart, constricted, wasted away; incited by these loves, as his soul grew base, he despised all noble things; finally, in order to please them, he became an <term>Apostate</term> <note>One who renounces their religious faith.</note> by departing from God himself, and did not fear to cling to foreign Gods; for whose sake he also built <term>High Places</term> <note>original: "excelsa"; hilltop shrines for pagan worship.</note>, temples, and altars, decorated them magnificently, and offered incense and libations.* Since these things are so, let us now at last see what those high places and temples were, what the altars and <term>Groves</term> <note>original: "Luci"; sacred clusters of trees used as shrines.</note> were, which the Sacred History records Solomon built for the sake of the women; and who the Gods are that he worshipped, and from where their origin flowed.

# CHAPTER XII.

## Concerning the Temples, High Places, Groves, and Altars built by Solomon.

<margin>Two things complete the act of idolatry.</margin>
There are two things especially that complete the act of idolatry: the internal worship of adoration, and the external honor. The former seems joined with a certain error of the mind, attributing something Divine to a creature. The latter can be offered either out of love, or fear, or some other affection of the mind, without any error of the mind, although this too is illicit. Hence arises the doubt as to what kind of worship was offered by Solomon to idols; was it merely external, or internal as well?

<margin>
Augustine, Book 14 on the City of God, ch. 11.
Rabanus, 4 Kings 23.
Sedulius, 2 Timothy ch. 2.
Galatinus.
Cyril, 7 against Julian.
Gregory, on Job ch. 4, Book 12 of the Moralia, ch. 112.
</margin>
Saint Augustine, Rabanus, Sedulius, Galatinus, and all the Rabbis embrace the first part; they all assert that the most wise Solomon was by no means so foolish as to adore the figments of men, but that, seduced by womanly flatteries, he worshipped them only externally and built temples for them. Cyril and many others hold the second part, as does Gregory in Book 12, Chapter 12 of the *Moralia*: "He who previously had built a temple to God," he says, "overcome by the persistence of lust and even by bad faith, did not fear to build temples to idols, so that the constant petulance of the flesh reached even to the bad faith of the mind." Since, therefore, Solomon worshipped foreign Gods not only with outward ritual, but also with an internal and true act of <term>latria</term> <note>Supreme worship intended for God alone.</note>, the just judgment of God so permitting it. That matter could certainly have held the greatest weight in Solomon’s mind—now ensnared by the most vain superstitions from the persuasion of women—he thought it could contribute much...

### SYNTHESIS IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. 307 CHAPTER XII

<margin>Why Solomon yielded to the women.</margin>...[he reasoned] that for the expansion of his empire, it would be beneficial if he made the Gods of those provinces, under whose protection they were, favorable to himself, and won them over through religious worship. This was surely the main point of persuasion when those Egyptian and Midianite harlots enticed the Israelites to their own religion, as we have previously recounted from Josephus; for among other things, they would say:

<margin>Particular Gods.</margin>
> "Nor would it be absurd, or to be considered a vice, if you should prefer to worship the peculiar Gods of the land into which you have come: especially since ours are honored through all regions, while no one among your people, except yourselves, deems your God worthy of worship or ceremonies; therefore, you must either live according to the custom of the rest, or seek another world where you may lead your life alone according to your own institutions."

<margin>Joshua's Speech.</margin>To this matter, that speech of the leader Joshua to the people in chapter 24 seems to allude:

> "Choose whom you ought especially to serve, whether the Gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell, etc."

<margin>Provincial Gods.</margin>For this reason, they placed individual provinces under the protection of individual Gods; they attributed the mountains to the Gods of the mountains, and the valleys to the Gods of the valleys, by whose protection they promised themselves all things would be prosperous and happy, whether in the mountains or in the valleys; according to that passage:

<margin>3 Kings 20.</margin> <note>original: "3. Reg. 20."; In modern Bibles, this is 1 Kings 20:23.</note>
> "The Gods of the mountains are their Gods; therefore they have overcome us; but it is better that we fight against them in the plains, and we shall overcome them."

But more on these things elsewhere.

<margin>Solomon taught Egyptian rites by Egyptian women.</margin>It could therefore have happened that Solomon was led by the same superstition as the Egyptians, with whom he had frequent dealings—not to mention that he had taken many Egyptian women as his consorts. These women instructed him everywhere in the ancestral rites and ceremonies to be performed for the Gods. It is clear that Solomon, having been instructed in the same art by which the Romans later won over the Gods of foreign provinces—calling them forth into their own city with specific formulas of words and solemn rites <note>This refers to the Roman ritual of *evocatio*, where a besieging army would formally invite the tutelary deity of an enemy city to abandon them and come to Rome instead.</note>—conciliated foreign Gods to himself. The Sacred History seems to reproach King Ahaz for this most vain persuasion in 2 Chronicles 28:

<margin>2 Chronicles ch. 28.</margin>
> "He sacrificed," it says, "victims to the Gods of Damascus who had defeated him, and said: 'The Gods of the kings of Syria help them; I will appease them with sacrifices, and they will help me.'"

When, on the contrary, they were his ruin and the ruin of all Israel. And more clearly in 2 Chronicles 25:14:

<margin>2 Chronicles 25: Amaziah, the impious idolater.</margin>
> "Amaziah, after the slaughter of the Edomites and the bringing back of the Gods of the children of Seir, established them as his own Gods, and adored them, and burned incense to them; for which reason the Lord, angry with Amaziah, sent a prophet to him to say: 'Why have you adored Gods who did not deliver their own people from your hand?'"

It was as if he were reproaching him for the false persuasion that he would make the Gods of those provinces favorable to himself if he worshipped them. The Prophet argued elegantly against this error; and most wisely Rahab, in Joshua 2:11, having already been led to the knowledge of the true God, concluded from the same matter that the true God of the Hebrews presides not only over heaven, but over all the provinces of the earth.

<margin>Solomon received many things from the Egyptian sanctuaries.</margin>
> "The Lord," she said, "our God, He is God in heaven above, and on the earth below."

<margin>Solomon imbued with Egyptian dogmas.</margin>Therefore, to return to our purpose, these things were by no means foreign to the character of Solomon; for he was most curious and a diligent investigator of the rites of neighboring nations, especially the Egyptians, who at that time shone above all others in the whole world for their fame of wisdom and deeper learning. Indeed, the frequent mention of the familiarity he had with Pharaoh Vaphres <note>Pharaoh Apries of the 26th Dynasty, though chronologically mismatched with the historical Solomon, Kircher follows traditional associations.</note>, whose daughter he also took as a wife, as the Sacred Scriptures teach, sufficiently shows this...

### CHAPTER XII. THE ISIAIC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS 308

...he drew many hidden things from the inner sanctuaries <term>adyta: the most private, sacred chambers of a temple</term> of the Egyptians, partly through the reports of the Egyptian women—whom it is likely he joined to himself in marriage as being most wise—and partly through familiar letters from Pharaoh and the Priests. These influences drove him to the aforementioned crimes; indeed, Origen seems to indicate this very thing through a beautiful allegory.
<margin>Origen.</margin>
> "He," said Origen, "while he was most wise and of great merit before God, was nevertheless deceived because he gave himself to many women. I believe that these 'many women' represent many dogmas and the diverse philosophies of many nations. Since Solomon, being most learned and wise, wished to recognize and scrutinize each of these individually, he was unable to keep himself within the rule of divine law."

Similarly, it is said he received the women of the Ammonites, and also of the remaining nations (the Moabites, Egyptians, Sidonians, and Tyrians), and built temples or sacrificed to their idols. Thus Solomon, so that he might be more ardently joined to the women for whom he was dying of love, strove to learn those things which he knew would be pleasing to them. These were the sacred dogmas of the Egyptians or of neighboring nations, which those women had drawn from Egypt itself as if from a perennial fountain of all superstition. As one burning with love, he desired to be one with them; he did not wish to be seen as different through a dissimilarity of customs and the religious rites proper to them. For he knew best how much a mutual likeness in all things serves to foster and increase love. 
<margin>The power of love.</margin>
Hence, in order to keep himself constantly conforming to their actions in all things, he began to erect Shrines, and High Places, and to build Altars—in a word, to do everything to find favor with them. But what sort of Shrines those were, and what sort of High Places and Groves, the time and order of our work now demand that we explain.

---

->Shrines, High Places, Altars, Groves.<-

A **Shrine** <note>original: *Fanum*</note> is so called either from *Faunus*, its first inventor, or from *fando* <note>meaning "speaking"</note>, since the Gods were accustomed to speak and deliver oracles within them. Certainly, in this passage, it is the same as a **High Place** <note>original: *Excelsum*</note>, as is testified by both the Hebrew and Greek texts. The Hebrew uses the word *bamah* <note>original: במה</note>, which Saint Jerome translates as *Fanum* (Shrine); the Greek, however, uses *hypsilon* <note>original: ὕψιλον</note>, which everyone translates as *Excelsum* (High Place). I will subjoin the words of both texts:

->Solomon built a high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, and for Molech, the abomination of<-
->the children of Ammon.<-
<note>original Hebrew: ויבנה שלמה במה לכמוש שקוץ מואב ולמולך שקוץ בני עמון (1 Kings 11:7)</note>

Solomon built a shrine for Chemosh, the idol of Moab, and for Melchom, the idol of the children of Ammon. Where the Hebrew has *bamah*, the Greek reading has *hypsilon*: "And Solomon built a high place <note>original: *hypsilon*</note> for Chemosh the idol of Moab on the mountain that is before Jerusalem, and for Melchom the idol of the children of Ammon." <note>original Greek: Καὶ ᾠκοδόμησε Σαλομὼν ὑψηλόν Χαμὼς εἰδώλῳ Μωὰβ ἐν τῷ ὄρει τῷ πρὸ προσώπου ἱερουσαλήμ, καὶ Μελχὸμ εἰδώλῳ υἱῶν Ἀμμων.</note> Therefore, "Shrine" and "High Place" are taken for the same thing in this context: namely, a high and elevated place where sacrifices were performed to foreign Gods by the nations.
<margin>What a High Place is.</margin>
And although the term "High Place" asserts the loftiness of the location we mentioned, others nonetheless think it was so called because the nations were most frequently accustomed to sacrifice on high mountains and lofty hills—though sometimes also in valleys, as is elegantly noted in that passage of Ezekiel 6:2, where the peo-
<margin>Ezekiel 6:2.</margin>

### SYNT. IV. PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. 309 CH. XII

...the superstition frequently practiced in the high places <note>original: *in excelsis*; these were the 'Bama' or hilltop shrines often condemned in the Old Testament</note> is censured, and sometimes in the valleys:
> *Mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord God; Thus says the Lord God to the mountains, and the hills, and the rocks, and the valleys. Behold, I will bring a sword upon you, and I will destroy your High Places, and I will demolish your images <note>original: *animas vestras*, literally 'your souls,' but used here in the sense of 'sun-images' or 'idols'</note>, and your idols shall be broken together.*

Wherein Jerome indicates that not only by the name of valleys, but also by the name of rocks, one should understand humble places and woody valleys lying between two mountains or two rocks; other more trustworthy Rabbis agree. <margin>Sacrifices in high places.</margin> Nevertheless, superstition was more frequent upon the mountains; hence the so frequent and burning execration by all the Prophets of the mountains and hills, under the persona of a harlot "upon every high and leafy hill." Yet we trace the name of "High Places" not only to mountains, hills, and rooftops, but also to any Basilicas and sacred buildings, which they call lofty and magnificent temples or shrines; although they may also be correctly taken for those places in which there were sublime altars, upon which sacrifices were raised on high and placed. This is especially indicated by the "High Places in Topheth," which was a deep place in the valley of Gehenna; "they built the High Places of Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Ennom." From this it becomes clear that "High Places" and "Shrines" were often used for the thing contained within them—that is, for the altars par excellence <note>original: <term>τὴν κατ’ ἐξοχὴν</term></note>. Indeed, the Latin name for Altar (*Altare*) is derived from altitude; for according to Isidore, an Altar <margin>What is an Altar?</margin> is like a "high altar" <note>original: *alta ara*</note>, although Festus maintains that an *altare* is not the altar of just any gods, but specifically that in which one sacrifices to the celestial gods. For these, consequently, superior and lofty altars were erected, just as for the earthly gods they were built on the ground; for the gods of the underworld, however, sacrifices were made in pits dug in the earth or in caves. Depending on the diversity of places where the Divinities were believed to preside, altars were established either on mountains, in valleys, or by rivers, as was declared at length in the previous Treatise. Vatablus also notes a peculiarity on Ezekiel 20:39: that *Bama* <margin>They chose different places for different gods.</margin> <margin>Vatablus. What is Bama?</margin> is properly a very high altar, which was ascended by steps, such as is perhaps forbidden by God in Exodus 20:26: *Neither shalt thou go up by steps unto mine altar.* And perhaps it was such a temple of Juno as is described by Virgil:

---

-> . . . *rich with gifts and the presence of the Goddess* <-
-> *Whose bronze thresholds rose with steps, and the beams* <- <margin>Virgil.</margin>
-> *were bound with bronze; the hinge creaked on the brazen doors.* <-

---

I certainly understand the "High Place" or "Shrine" in this passage of ours to be a magnificent and royal Altar erected for the worship of the Gods, made only of marble or stone, such as St. Thomas says the Gentiles possessed. <margin>St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica 1.2. q. 102. a. 4. 3.</margin> *The Gentiles,* he says, *constructed great and sublime altars.* For this seems to have been the rite of the Nations: to erect stone and marble altars to their Divinities. Such were the Altars of the Egyptians, which we commonly call Pyramids and Obelisks, which were erected in honor of the Gods both inside and outside the temple <margin>Egyptian Altars were Pyramids.</margin> in public places, full of sacred and divine mysteries, as will be most extensively declared elsewhere. For since Egypt was low-lying and lacked mountains, they invented those high places of the Pyramids <margin>Why the Egyptians used Pyramids.</margin> and Obelisks in place of mountains, which they called by the proper names of "mine-structure" <note>original Greek: <term>μεταλλος</term></note> or "ascent" <note>original Hebrew: <term>מַעֲלָה</term>, *Ma'alah*</note>.

### CHAPTER XII. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIACO TEMPLE 310

...that is, the columns or altars of the Gods; to which one ascended by steps, and they were filled inside and out with every variety of idols, according to that verse:

->*Tawny likenesses of dogs stand upon marble altars.*<-
<note>original: *Marmoreas stant fulua canum simulachra per aras.* Likely a reference to statues of Anubis, the jackal-headed god, placed upon Egyptian altars.</note>

From these things it is clear that this name of "High Places" used by the Hebrews knows no other origin than that which it drew from the Egyptians; who called the Pyramids and Obelisks established around the temples "altars" or "columns of the Gods," as has been said. But lest we seem to insist upon conjecture alone, let us hear Abenephius <note>An Arabic author, often cited by Kircher, believed to preserve ancient Egyptian secrets.</note> showing this in manifest words when he speaks of Obelisks:

<margin>Abenephius.</margin>
->واقاموا الكهنة مصر هذا حجارة مرتفعة بصورة الح مدور ونقبوا بهم هجروفى<-
->الضريرة الاسرار حكمتهم واسموهم مدبحات اللهم.<-

*The Priests of Egypt set up these elevated and high stones in the figure of a cone or a pointed pyramid, and they engraved upon them in symbolic letters the secrets of their wisdom, and they called them the altars of their Gods.* <note>Kircher provides the Arabic text followed by his Latin translation, here rendered into English.</note> Iamblichus agrees with this, saying that Plato drew his knowledge from the "columns of Mercury" <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>—that is, the altars or inscribed pillars erected to him. This refers to the method of the worship of the Gods and of secret Theology, which was practiced around pyramids of this kind, or whose writings were read upon them. It is added that the Poets everywhere call the pyramids of the Egyptians "altars," according to that verse of Lucan dealing with the Egyptian rite:

<margin>Iamblichus. The Columns of Mercury.</margin>
<margin>Lucan.</margin>
->*And vows are fulfilled at the lofty altars of the pyramids.*<-
<note>original: *Votaque pyramidum celsas solvuntur ad aras.*</note>

Since, therefore, a pyramid is like a certain lofty altar erected in honor of the Gods, which also—on account of its most eminent peak—might not poorly be called in the native Egyptian language (as is clear from our Coptic or ancient Egyptian Dictionary) **pistallon** <note>original: *πισταλλον*</note>, that is, "lofty" or a "very high column"; it is likely that the Hebrews, taught by the Egyptians, called the more prominent temples or higher altars <term>Bamma</term> <note>Hebrew: *במה*, Bamah</note> or <term>Rammoth</term> <note>Hebrew: *רמות*, Ramoth</note>, that is, "High Places," or even, as some will have it, "Shrines" from the Greek word <term>phano</term> <note>Greek: *φάνω*, to shine or appear</note>, because they easily appeared high up with their raised peaks.

<margin>Bamma, Rammoth.</margin>
<margin>The mystical reasoning of the Egyptians pleased Solomon.</margin>
For the Hebrews were pleased by all the rites of foreigners, and most especially those of the Egyptians, which they highly esteemed both for their rarity and for the affinity they perceived in them to their own mysteries. And hence we judge that Solomon built altars of this kind with all the greater pleasure, the more he recognized within them the greater mysteries of hidden things; and the Rabbis maintain that under this pretext he constructed the High Places and Altars: for he embraced the Egyptian wisdom then flourishing most greatly, and he was accustomed to freely exchange discourses concerning their affairs, and even more freely did he listen to his Egyptian concubines recounting various things about them. Besides these things, our Pineda <note>Juan de Pineda, a Jesuit scholar who wrote a massive commentary on the life of Solomon.</note> proves with many arguments that he also had frequent correspondence in letters both with Pharaoh and with the Priests themselves. These things therefore having been rightly considered, let us now proceed from altars to groves.

SREATISE IV. THE HEBREW PANTHEON. 311 CHAPTER XII

### *Groves and Woods Consecrated to the Gods*

Nothing is more frequent in sacred history than "Groves," either planted by the impious or cut down by holy Kings; and just as the Prophets attack altars, so they also target groves and leafy trees. Now, we must discuss from where this cult of groves originated.

<margin>Paradise.</margin>
We know that the ancient religion of the first Patriarchs, who worshiped the true God, was practiced in groves and among trees, in places suitable for silence and for being available to God, just as it is written: *Isaac went out to meditate in the field.* <note>Genesis 24:63</note> Paradise itself was nothing other than a certain sacred grove, planted by the hand of God, and handed over to man as the first Priest and guardian of that wooded temple, so that he might "work it and guard it." This word for "working" in Hebrew, <term>עבד</term> <note>Hebrew: *Avad*. This word means both "to work" and "to worship" or "to serve." Kircher is highlighting that Adam's gardening was a form of religious service.</note>, demonstrates this sufficiently; for it properly signifies "to work by serving and administering divine matters." Furthermore, in this grove, God specifically willed the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil to be sacred to Himself—it was to be left entirely untouched, to be looked upon with contemplation of the mysteries contained within it. Moreover, we read that Abraham also planted a grove in Beersheba, and there he called upon the name of the eternal God:

<margin>Genesis 21.</margin>
->ויטע אשל בבארשבע ויקרא שם בשם יי אל עולם:<-
<note>original Hebrew: *Wayyitta eshel bi-V’er Sheva wa-yiqra sham be-shem Adonai El Olam.*</note>
*And he planted a grove in Beersheba, and invoked there the name of the God of the world.* Or as the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> says, <term>Θεὸς αἰώνιος</term> <note>original Greek: *Theos aiōnios*, meaning "Eternal God."</note>, where Onkelos the Chaldean Paraphraser <note>Author of the Targum Onkelos, an influential Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> writes:

<margin>Onkelos.</margin>
->ונציב נציבא בבארשבע וצלי תמן בשמא דיי אלהא עלמא:<-
<note>original Aramaic: *U-netsiv netsiva bi-V’er Sheva u-tsalli tamman bi-shma de-Adonai Elaha Alma.*</note>
*And he planted a plantation in Beersheba, and prayed there in the name of the Lord, the Eternal God.* The Jerusalem Targum <note>Another Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> however, says: <margin>Jerusalem Targum.</margin> Abraham planted a garden full of the best fruits and received travelers with hospitality, to whom he supplied all necessary things for free. He demanded nothing as a price, except that they acknowledge the Creator of the world and venerate and fear the Ruler of heaven and earth, whose gift alone was whatever they had eaten or drunk. Thus, he dismissed them after they had been instructed in the true religion and converted to the practices of a better life. I will cite the words of the Targum:

<margin>The Jerusalem Targum written in Syriac characters from the Vatican Bible.</margin>
> And he established a paradise in Beersheba and prepared food and drink within it.
> And to those who ate and drank, they would offer a gift to him from whom they ate
> and from whom they drank. But he did not wish to receive anything from them, but
> said to them: Pray before your Father who is in heaven, from whose [hand] you have eaten
> and drunk. And they did not move from their places until they confessed the name of the Lord.

*The Targum says,* Abraham established a paradise in Beersheba, and placed food and drink in the middle of it (that is, he prepared a feast). The guests who had eaten and drunk offered him gifts because they had eaten and drunk, but our father Abraham did not want to accept anything from them. Instead, he said to them: "Pray to your Father who is in heaven, from whose hands you have eaten and drunk." And they did not move from their places until...

...since he had taken them to dwell with him on the path of eternity and had instructed them in the knowledge of the true God; and he confessed there, and prayed in the name of the eternal God. <margin>Cajetan.</margin>
Cajetan <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a prominent Italian Dominican theologian and philosopher.</note> also says in clear words that this grove was like a temple and oratory both for Abraham and for others who worshiped the true God.

<margin>Genesis 35 and Joshua 24.</margin>
Abraham was followed by his son Jacob, who is also read to have consecrated an oak to the most high God in Genesis 35. And in Joshua 24, Joshua took a very large stone and placed it under the oak which was in the sanctuary of the Lord. Here you see that an oak, or a grove of oaks, was sacred to God.

<margin>Judges 6.</margin>
Similarly, it appears that a religious oak or grove of oaks was that under which the Angel of the Lord appeared to Gideon in Judges 6, which is gathered from the altar that was in the same place; for it is added: *He took everything under the oak, and offered it to him,* etc. There was also a use for a grove and a certain religious tree at a tomb, which it was not permitted to violate, as is clear from Genesis 35, where Deborah is buried under an oak, and in 1 Kings 31 <note>Commonly known today as 1 Samuel 31.</note>.

<margin>Genesis 35. 1 Kings 31.</margin>
<margin>Judges 9.</margin>
The inhabitants of Jabesh Gilead bury the bones of Saul and his sons in the grove of Jabesh; we also read in Judges 9 that a grove of oaks served for the inauguration of princes. *They appointed Abimelech King next to the oak which was in Shechem.* It is clear from these words, therefore, that the ancient Fathers entered forests and groves to practice the cult and veneration of the Divine Power before they had temples, and that they built altars there. The Rabbis give the reason that places removed from the company of men, such as forests and groves are, are more suitable for divine apparitions,

<margin>Why the ancients sought out deserts for the sake of devotion.</margin>
according to that saying: *I will lead him into the wilderness, and I will speak to his heart.* <note>Hosea 2:14</note> Hence we read that Moses did not enjoy the conversation of God except in the solitude of Mount Sinai; the sacred history of the Kings also shows that Elijah saw God in the desert. For this same reason, those in the "Law of Grace" <note>A theological term for the Christian era.</note> striving for the height of Christian perfection followed Christ and sought out hermits’ cells and solitudes to devote themselves to divine contemplations more easily and without any impediment.

<margin>The Devil is the Ape of God.</margin>
But antiquity, deluded by the Demon—the "Ape of God"—transferred all these things to the most vain superstition of idols, occupying mountains, hills, valleys, torrents, groves, and leafy, shaded trees, according to that passage in Isaiah:

<margin>Isaiah ch. 57.</margin>
