### SYNTHESIS IV. PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER XII.

...[to those who were wandering in error] (they sacrificed boys), it was a foreign servitude for those who sacrificed their own sons to their Gods; and they did this in valleys, in a place where there were rocks, and under branches. Moreover, this word <term>sa’iph<note>Original Hebrew: סעיף (sa'iph), which can mean a branch of a tree or a cleft/fissure in a rock.</note></term> is explained in two ways: thus, their machinations were either in a branch or in a "tooth" of a cliff (for just as a tooth relates to a rock, so a branch relates to a tree), or in a rocky and branchy place [in parts of the valleys]. This was because as soon as they found a smooth stone, beautiful in appearance among the stones of the valleys, they suddenly began to worship it, according to what our Rabbis say of such things: "My portion is the shape of a smooth stone." Thus says Rabbi David <note>Likely Rabbi David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a renowned medieval Jewish commentator and grammarian.</note>. In forests, therefore—in shady, rocky, and branchy places—superstition established its ancient temples. 

<margin>Pliny, Book 12, Chapter 1.</margin>Pliny also mentions this: "These were once the temples of the Deities; and by ancient rite, even now the simple country-folk dedicate an outstanding tree to a God, and they do not consecrate images shining with gold and ivory any more than they do groves and woods; and in them, we adore the silences themselves."

Certainly the Egyptians also consecrated groves to the Gods; that memorable grove of Ammon in the desert of Libya was consecrated in his honor, of which we spoke above in the chapter on Ammon. We also asserted above that there was a reedy grove in which Baal-Zephon <note>Original: Beelsephon. A location mentioned in the Book of Exodus, which Kircher identifies here as an Egyptian sacred site.</note> was established by the Egyptians; and other groves and leafy places in various locations and cities of Egypt, such as Heliopolis, Canopus, and Sais—about which you may read Herodotus, Athenaeus, and Pausanias—testify sufficiently to this. Since the worship of all these flourished long before Solomon, it is certain that the Hebrews and Greeks received it from the Egyptians, just as they did everything else; from these, indeed, this type of worship was derived to other nations and pervaded the whole world everywhere. Regarding the Germans, Tacitus writes specifically: <margin>Tacitus, Book 1, *On the Customs of the Germans*.</margin> *They consecrate groves and woods, and they call by the names of Gods that secret thing which they see only through reverence.* To these were added images of the Gods, that is, statues made of rough logs and unpolished oak. As Lucan describes in the siege of Marseille:

<margin>Lucan.</margin>
> *There was a grove never violated through a long age,*
> *A horror of its own dwells in the trees; then much water*
> *Falls from black springs, and the mixed images of the Gods*
> *Lack art, standing out as formless shapes from hewn trunks.*
> *The very decay and the pallor from the rotting wood*
> *Strikes them with awe.*

<margin>Why groves were not to be cut.</margin>Although there is no doubt that later various forms of the Gods were also sculpted from wood and marble, and cast from bronze and metals, and thus added to the altars of the groves. Furthermore, it was a sacrilege to cut or desecrate a sacred grove, and therefore many are mentioned by the poets as "uncut" <note>Original: *incædui*, a Latin legal and religious term for a grove where it was forbidden to fell trees.</note>, according to that passage in the *Aeneid*:

> *In the middle of the city was a grove, most joyful with shade;*
> *Here Sidonian Dido was founding a vast temple to Juno.*

<margin>Servius on Virgil.</margin>Where Servius <note>Maurus Servius Honoratus, a 4th-century grammarian famous for his commentary on the works of Virgil.</note> also observes that wherever Virgil places a grove, a consecration is also placed. And I know not what presence of a Divine Power <note>Original: *Numen*, the spiritual force or presiding spirit of a place.</note> those deluded people perceived from that shady depth, as he used to say.

### CHAPTER XII. 314 THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIACO TEMPLE

->*A grove lay beneath the Aventine, dark with the shade of the holm-oak,*<-
->*At the sight of which you might say, "A Divinity dwells within."*<-
<note>original: "Lucus Aventino suberat niger ilicis umbra, Quo possis viso dicere, Numen inest." These lines are from the Roman poet Ovid’s *Fasti*, describing the atmosphere of a sacred grove.</note>

<margin>St. Jerome on Hosea, Chapter 4.</margin>
And under the pretext of worshipping a Divinity, they introduced banquets, dances, and the most impure ceremonies of every kind, as we have already often stated. All of these things prove that Solomon either established shrines and altars in sacred groves, or certainly planted them according to a profane rite. But this was primarily because groves and forests served the indecencies and works of darkness of the idols; for they sought out the shade, as St. Jerome <note>A 4th-century scholar and priest known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> testifies:
> *Seeking the shade,* he says, *they deserted the truth; and furthermore, because that ancient and sensual religion had overturned the austerity of the one true religion; for among the shadows and darkness, they indulged in impure pleasures.*

<margin>The grove served for impurities.</margin>
Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Jewish scripture.</note> indicated this very thing regarding this matter:
> *There is no grove within its boundaries [the Temple], because the law forbade it for many reasons; first, because a true temple does not require pleasant scenery, but rather strict purity. Furthermore, the thickets of the woods are convenient for evildoers, who seek safety and opportunities for ambush from within their hiding places.*

If, in these groves, that ancient superstition concerning lamps, as well as veils and other gifts with which the most superstitious women were accustomed to adorn the trees and forests, placed its furnishings, how frequently did lamps burn there? How great was the abundance and care given to the little houses or other coverings? How great was the wealth of gifts under the most opulent King [Solomon]? Regarding the first point, the name itself reminds us: it is called a <term>lucus<note>The author is referencing the famous Latin etymological joke "lucus a non lucendo," suggesting a grove is called "lucus" (light/shining) because it is actually dark (lacks light).</note></term> because it lacks light of its own, and therefore shines only when lamps are hung within it. Regarding the second point, this is seen in 2 Kings 23, when Josiah destroyed the little houses of the <term>effeminate ones<note>Refers to the "qedeshiym," or male cult prostitutes, mentioned in the Hebrew Bible.</note></term>, for whom the women <margin>Complutensian Bible.</margin> wove, as it were, little houses for the grove, as the Complutensian <note>The Complutensian Polyglot Bible, the first printed polyglot version of the entire Bible, produced in Spain in the early 16th century.</note> editions read:
> *You destroyed the house of the initiated, which was in the house of the Lord, where the women wove robes for the grove there.*

<margin>Arnobius.</margin>
And perhaps Arnobius <note>An early Christian apologist of the 4th century.</note> speaks of these things, whether they be little houses or coverings for the trees, in his fifth book where he speaks of the slain Acdestis <note>Agdistis, a deity of Greek, Roman, and Anatolian mythology, often associated with Cybele and Attis.</note>.
<margin><unclear>... ... ...</unclear></margin>
> *What of the fleeces of wool,* he says, *with which you bind the trees and wrap the trunk? Is that not a repetition of those wools with which the Mother of the Gods covered her dying son, thinking she could bring some warmth back to his freezing limbs?*

And indeed, that fable of Acdestis is a foul and obscene thing, just like the acts that the effeminate ones performed or endured under these little houses at the trunks of the trees. From this, Arnobius adds:
> *What of those adorned with crowns of violets and wreathed with the branches of the tree? Does that not indicate how the mother first breathed upon him with the first flowers as a miserable sign and testimony of his fortune?*

<margin>Branches of trees were adorned with gifts.</margin>
Regarding the third point—that is, the gifts and <term>anathemata<note>Votive offerings or objects dedicated to a divinity and hung in a sacred space.</note></term> suspended from the branches of the grove—it is a well-known matter, of which Arnobius speaks in Book 1:
> *I used to worship (oh, the blindness!) until recently images and ribbons on ancient trees...*

<margin>Which trees were consecrated for groves.</margin>
Finally, if you ask what kind of groves these were, or from what trees they were planted—whether from olives, other fruit-bearing trees, or wild ones—the previously cited Philo says that the groves consisted of both fruit-bearing and wild trees. For among the idolatrous Hebrews, these trees were in use and held in high value, according to that passage in Hosea:
> *Under the oak, and the poplar, and the terebinth; because its shade is good.*

But let these brief remarks on the Groves suffice; now let us turn our pen to describing the Gods who were worshipped in such places and groves.

# CHAPTER XIII.

->*Astarte, the Goddess of the Sidonians.*<-

<margin>Astoreth, Astaroth, and Astarte are the same.</margin>
It is abundantly clear from the context of sacred history that Solomon not only planted groves, but also built and worshiped at shrines and altars, and these were by no means empty, but decorated with various images of idols. "And when he was now old," it says, "his heart was turned away by women so that he followed strange gods; nor was his heart right with the Lord his God; but Solomon worshiped Astarte, the goddess of the Sidonians, and Chemosh, the god of the Moabites, and Moloch, the idol of the Ammonites." And a little later: "Then Solomon built a shrine for Chemosh, the idol of Moab, on the mountain which is opposite Jerusalem, and for Moloch, the idol of the children of Ammon; and in this manner he did for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods." <note>These passages are from 1 Kings 11:4-8.</note>

<margin>Who was Astarte?</margin>
Let us now discuss who these listed gods were and from where they originated. First, regarding Astarte, Astaroth, or as others prefer, Astoreth, various opinions from different authors arise. Some argue about the name, others about the substance. Some maintain that Astarte is the same as Astaroth, and they say the name is a generic term for all goddesses, as was the opinion of Augustine in his 16th question on Judges. He seems to gather this primarily from 1 Samuel 31 <note>In the original Latin text, this is cited as 1 Kings 31, following the Vulgate numbering where 1 and 2 Samuel are titled 1 and 2 Kings.</note>: "When they hung the arms of Saul in the temple of Astaroth," and 1 Samuel 7, when Samuel commands that Baalim and Astaroth be removed from the midst of the people—whom the people confessed they had worshiped—where the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> read it as a plural name: "They served the Baalim and the Astartes," as the cited Augustine elegantly observes and explains in the mentioned passage. Furthermore, Peter Crinitus <note>Pietro Crinito (1475–1507), an Italian humanist scholar.</note> in Book 14 of *On Honest Discipline*, chapter 8, asserts that she is the same as the one named Adagartes; however, I find that Giraldus <note>Lilio Gregorio Giraldi (1479–1552), a Renaissance mythologist.</note> expresses doubt on this point.

Regarding the origin of the word, <margin>Arias Montanus.</margin> Montanus <note>Benito Arias Montano (1527–1598), a Spanish orientalist and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible.</note> must now be cited; he considers it to be a word of Hebrew origin. Others derive it from Hebrew in a different way: for the same word in Deuteronomy 7 is used for "flocks of sheep"; therefore, they want Astarte to be so named as if she were a sheep-like image. Thus Rabbi David Kimchi <note>Known as Radak (1160–1235), a medieval Hebrew grammarian and biblical commentator.</note> says:

->"And the Rabbis say that the Astaroth idols were made in the likeness of sheep."<-
<note>original Hebrew: ואומרים ר״ שהצלמים עשתרות עשוים בצורת צאן</note>

<margin>Radak.</margin>
*Astaroth,* he says, *according to the Rabbis, are images made in the likeness of sheep.* Others strive to derive it more curiously from <margin>Various derivations of the word Astaroth.</margin> **Ash** <note>Hebrew: עש</note>, which they interpret as "Arcturus" or the "Wagon" <note>The constellation known as the Big Dipper.</note>, and **Tor** <note>Hebrew: תור</note>, which signifies "order," as if she were one of the circling stars; and since it is spoken of in the plural, it would signify the twelve signs of the Zodiac. But this, while excessively curious, is less solid and more uncertain. Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist.</note> believes the name was made from a star and that she is "Lucifer" <note>The Morning Star, or the planet Venus.</note>. This much is certain: the word is foreign and belongs to the nation where her worship flourished. For just as they adopted the religion and foreign rites, so indeed should it be believed that the Hebrews favored the foreign name itself, which was common among the nations. And if we must proceed by conjectures, we could not badly derive Astaroth from the Arabic or Punic **Alzaharet** <note>original: الزهره, referring to the planet Venus</note>, or better yet from the Egyptian word **Tifurot** <margin>What **Tifurot** means in Egyptian.</margin> <note>original Coptic: Ϯcρωτ</note>, which our Coptic-Arabic Treasury <note>Reference to Kircher's own lexicographical work on the Coptic language.</note> interprets as Venus. Now, **Tifurot** does not differ much from Astaroth. From this, I conclude that Astaroth...

# SYNTAGMA IV. THE HEBREW PANTHEON. CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>What Asheroth properly is.</margin>
...it is clear; namely, that *Asheroth*, which was called **Asherah** <note>original Hebrew: אשרה</note> both from the grove in which it was worshipped and from the oak leaves with which it was adorned, has provided material for many errors. For it was characteristic of the pagan nations to derive the names of their gods from the groves, cities, mountains, and caves where the deities were worshipped. 
<margin>Gods were named after places.</margin>
For example, Jupiter was called **Endendros** <note>original Greek: ἐνδενδρος, meaning "within the tree"</note> by the Rhodians, as well as Diana of the Woods <note>original: "Nemorensis Diana"</note>, and **Dendrites** <note>original Greek: δενδρίτης, meaning "of the tree"</note> Bacchus; the Goddess Albunea, and six hundred others of this sort, which may be seen treated at length in the works of Giraldus <note>Lilio Gregorio Giraldi (1479–1552), a Renaissance scholar who wrote extensively on classical mythology.</note>.

<margin>Radak.</margin>
However, it is clear from Rabbi David Kimchi <note>A famous medieval Jewish grammarian and commentator, often referred to by the acronym Radak.</note> that in this place **Asherah** [אשרה] does not signify a grove, but the idol itself. Under the root **Ashar** [אשר], he writes that every tree that is worshipped is called an **Asherah** [אשרה]. His words are as follows:

->**Asher and Asherah: it is said that every tree worshipped in foreign service <note>A common Rabbinic term for idolatry.</note> is so called.**<-

<margin>Ben Gerson. R. Salomon. An oak idol of Asherah.</margin>
*Every tree that is worshipped with foreign service is barbarously called* **Asherah**. Levi Ben Gerson <note>Also known as Gersonides (1288–1344), a medieval philosopher.</note> and Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval commentator.</note> support this; speaking of the idolatry of King Ahab in 1 Kings 21, they say that by the word **Asherah**—whether meaning a grove, an oak, or an oak idol to which worship was offered—this is what is understood. Furthermore, in Judges 6, Gideon destroyed the altar of Baal and cut down the **Asherah** <note>original Hebrew: האשרה</note> which was *upon* the altar; for I translate the Hebrew **alav** <note>עליו</note> as "upon it," not "beside it." This is how the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> seem to have translated it, for they have **ep’ autō** <note>ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ</note>, meaning "upon the altar." Moreover, in 2 Kings <note>The original text cites "4. Reg." following the Vulgate numbering, where 1 & 2 Kings are called 3 & 4 Kings.</note>, Josiah is read to have destroyed the houses of the male prostitutes <note>original: "scortatorum," referring to ritual prostitution.</note> which were next to the house of the Lord, where women wove hangings for Asherah. Upon this passage, Rabbi David Kimchi comments on these words:

<margin>Radak on 2 Kings.</margin>
**He destroyed the houses of the consecrated ones:** <note>original: ויתץ את בתי הקדשים. Here referring to ritual prostitutes.</note> *And he cut down the houses of the prostitutes and the effeminate.*

**The houses of the consecrated ones are explained as being for the idol; the context teaches that women wove "houses" there for the Asherah. But the Asherah that Manasseh made in the house of the Lord—he made houses there for the women to weave curtains in honor of the Asherah. These curtains were "houses" for the Asherah, meaning they were constructed in her honor as separate dwellings. It is likely that these curtains were hung around the Asherah, and it served as the Asherah's house and place. The explanation is that the women sitting there were carefully attending to and looking after the Asherah.**

<margin>Superstitions of women in the groves.</margin>
These words certainly cannot refer to a mere image of a deity unless someone were to say that Manasseh planted a grove in the temple itself, built houses, and extended curtains around the grove—which would be a foolish thing to assert. It is more likely that this idol of Asherah was wooden and made of oak. 
<margin>The Idol of Asherah.</margin>
Hence, perhaps, it is designated under the names of "grove" or "oak" to mock the false divinity. For it was burned by King Josiah, and its ashes were scattered over the graves of the common people, as recorded in 2 Kings 23:6. Therefore, the wooden images dedicated to Astarte were called Ascherim and Ascheroth...

The author supports this by citing prominent Jewish commentators like Radak and Rashi, and by analyzing biblical accounts of the destruction of these idols.</summary>

# CHAPTER XIII. THE ISIAIC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS
<sig>3</sig>

<margin>Selden, Syntagma 2, fol. 147.</margin>
...or more often called groves, as I perceive; this was done so that the name would both allude to the place and, by that very word, reproach the materials of such an unworthy divinity with an insult; as Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English jurist and scholar of Oriental antiquities.</note> also rightly observes. We, however, shall indicate other reasons for this naming below.

<margin>St. Augustine: Juno is called Astarte.</margin>
St. Augustine, in his 16th question on the Book of Judges, thinks that Juno is Astarte; he is followed by the Interlinear Gloss <note>A standard medieval commentary on the Bible.</note> of Nicholas of Lyra, Abulensis <note>Alfonso Tostado, a Spanish bishop and prolific commentator.</note>, and Dionysius. Those who say she is the same as the Moon include Masius <note>Andreas Masius (1514–1573), a Flemish humanist and Syriac scholar.</note> and Lucian in *The Syrian Goddess*. Augustine proves the cited passage by considering Baal to be the name of Jupiter, whom they called "Lord" by that name in the Punic or Arabic language. From this, they understand **Baalsamen** <note>original: "Baalsamen"; from Hebrew *Ba'al Shamayim*</note> to mean "Lord of Heaven"; for among them, the heavens are called **Samen** <note>original: "Samen"; referring to *Shamayim*</note>. However, "Baalsamen" appears to be a corruption; for among the Arabs, one does not find *Baalsamen*, but **Baalsamai** <note>original Arabic: بعلسماي, *Ba'al-samai*</note>. Since Juno was both the sister and wife of Jupiter, and since **Baalim** and **Astaroth** are so frequently joined in Scripture, we must understand them to have been Jupiter and Juno.

<margin>Cicero, Book 3 of *On the Nature of the Gods*.</margin>
Besides Suidas, Cicero also asserts that Astarte is Venus; for here, among the four Venuses, he also counts Astarte. His words are: *“The first Venus was born from the foam of the sea, from whom and Mercury we have received the second Cupid; the third was born of Jupiter and Dione, who married Vulcan, but the son born of her and Mars is called Anteros <note>The god of requited or "counter" love.</note>; the fourth is the Syrian one, conceived in Tyre, who is called Astarte, and is said to have married Adonis.”* <margin>Nicetas in Oration 15 of Gregory of Nazianzus. Cedrenus in the *Compendium of History*. Eusebius.</margin> Not a few later writers seem to have followed this same point, such as Nicetas and Cedrenus where he treats Solomon. Eusebius agrees with this in Book 1, Chapter 7 of *The Preparation for the Gospel*, which concerns Phoenician Theology; he makes Astarte the mother of Love and Cupid by Saturn, which is Venus. <margin>Theophylact.</margin> It is also clear from his Commentary on Hosea 4 that Theophylact confuses Astarte with Venus, where he writes about her under these words: *“A people without understanding shall be beaten”* <note>Hosea 4:14.</note>:
<margin>Astarte and Venus are the same.</margin>
> He brings these things forth concerning the two tribes, namely the Kingdom of Judah, since they were also thought to have the knowledge of God, as those who reigned in Jerusalem, the city of God; they were sacrificing to the idol of Astarte, or Venus. For they named her a harlot; indeed, her image stood naked, breathing out fornication and abomination by its very sight or gaze. Solomon erected the image of Astarte to please his wife.

Thus says Theophylact; these points fit Solomon’s undertaking quite aptly, for the rites of Venus seem much more suited to Solomon's unrestrained lust and most foul idolatry than any others. This is especially true since the Israelite women also loved Venus’s lover, Adonis—as was said in the chapter on Adonis, where we also identified him with Thammuz—lamenting for him in Ezekiel 8. And just as Astarte was the particular Goddess of the Phoenicians or Syrians, so too was Adonis familiarly worshipped by the Assyrians with the highest veneration in ancient times, as Macrobius witnesses in *Saturnalia*, Book 2, Chapter 21.

<margin>Astarte is confused with the Moon.</margin>
Finally, the greatest part of authors confuse Astarte with the Moon, and they say she is the same one whom the Phoenicians call **Baaltim**; Varro calls her **Jana** or **Covella**; the Arabs call her **Alilat** <note>original Arabic: اليلات, *al-Lāt*</note>; the Syrians **Mulitha** <note>original Syriac: ܡܘܠܝܕܬܐ, *Mūlīthā*</note>; the Hebrews **Lilith** <note>original Hebrew: לִילִית</note>; the Chaldeans **Ammes** <note>original Chaldean/Aramaic: אמתּא, *Ammetha* or *Amma*, meaning "Mother"</note>; the Greeks distinguish her as the **Syrian Goddess** and **Io**, and by other similar names. As for us, in such a great diversity of sentences and opinions...

### TREATISE IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER XIII.

...setting aside this diversity of opinions so that we may establish something certain, we state that **Astarte** is nothing other than that most celebrated **Isis** of the Egyptians, whom Plutarch not undeservedly calls *polyonymous* <note>original: "πολυώνυμον"; meaning "of many names"</note>, as she is represented by the names of all the goddesses mentioned.

<margin>Aelian.</margin>
<margin>A cow was offered to Heavenly Venus.</margin>
And first, that **Heavenly Venus** was indeed worshipped in Egypt, and that she is the same as Isis, Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a 3rd-century Roman author and teacher of rhetoric.</note> testifies in the following words: *In Egypt,* he says, *in a village called Schussa—not a large one, to be sure, but certainly elegant—which was counted in the Hermopolitan Nome (that is, the Prefecture of Venus <note>The symbol ♀ represents the planet and goddess Venus.</note>), it was customary for Venus to be worshipped with great religious devotion and sanctity. They called her Urania, which means "Heavenly Venus," and they also venerated a cow for this reason: because it was thought to have an affinity and suitability with the Goddess herself.* However, a cow was offered to no one except Isis; therefore, the point stands as proven.

<margin>Nephthe is the same as Venus Urania.</margin>
<margin>She is also called Athôr, and the month takes its name from her. Epiphanius, Strabo. Momemphitic Venus.</margin>
<margin>In the Book of Tobit, she is called Baal; also called Belthis and Aphrodite.</margin>
<margin>Beltis is Juno, just as Baal is Jupiter.</margin>
<margin>Astarte is the Moon.</margin>
I find in Plutarch that this **Heavenly Venus** was also called **Nephthe** <note>Nephthys</note> by the Egyptians, whom he says was born in the fifth place and worshipped alongside Typhon. However, Hesychius says this Venus is called *Apho* <note>original: "Ἀφὼ"; a reference to the goddess Hathor</note> by the Egyptians, from which comes the month **Athyr**, which falls roughly in our November, as we have shown in our *Prodromus Coptus*. Epiphanius mentions this in Book 3 of *Against Heresies*: *Some,* he says, *interpret Tithyrambo as Hecate; others worship Senephthus*—you should rather read Nephthys—*others offer sacrifices to Thermuthis, and others to Isis.* Strabo, in Book 17, calls this Nephthe the "Momemphitic Venus," named after the Nome or Prefecture in which she was worshipped. *For this Goddess,* he says, *they nourished a sacred cow, just as the people of Memphis kept the Apis bull and those of Heliopolis kept the Mnevis bull, whom they raised as gods.* You see, therefore, that the aforementioned goddesses—Urania, Nephthe, and Momemphitica—are nothing other than Isis, which the worship of the cow (specific to Isis) demonstrates more than sufficiently. Certainly, she is the same one who is called the goddess **Baal** in the history of Tobit, who was worshipped with a cow; for so it is written in chapter 1, verse 5: *They sacrificed to the Baal, to the heifer* <note>original Greek: "Ἔθυον τῇ Βαὰλ τῇ δαμάλει"</note>; that is, they performed sacred rites to the "Baal" (feminine), meaning the heifer or cow. This is also found in another place, namely 1 Kings 19, where Baal is read in the feminine gender: *They did not bow the knee to Baal* <note>original Greek: "Οὐκ ἔκαμψαν γόνατα τῇ Βαὰλ"</note>. I truly believe that in those places "Baal" is taken for **Baaltis**. For *Baalis* was the same as the *Baaltis* of the Phoenicians, whom Megasthenes (quoted in Eusebius) calls *Beelida Beltin*. Furthermore, Hesychius says: *Belthes is Juno or Venus* <note>original: "Βεήλθης ἡ Ἥρα ἢ Ἀφροδίτη"</note>. Since the Phoenicians sacrificed a heifer to her, it is likely that she is the same as the Egyptian Venus, or Isis, or the **Astarte** of the Assyrians. For just as **Baal** is Jupiter, so **Baalis** or **Belthis** is Juno or Venus. Parallel to these are **Adonis** or **Thammuz** and **Venus** or **Astaroth** (the former being the *Beel* of the Assyrians, the latter their *Belthis*), to whom correspond **Osiris** and **Isis**, the Jupiter and Juno (or Venus) of the Egyptians. Again, just as *Baalsamim* <note>original Hebrew: בעל שמים, "Lord of Heaven"</note> is the Olympian Jupiter, so *Baaleth samaim* <note>original Hebrew: בעלת שמים, "Lady of Heaven"</note> is the Olympian Juno—namely, the Mistress of Heaven or the **Queen**. This is what the Seventy Interpreters <note>The translators of the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament.</note> call her in Jeremiah chapters 7 and 44, a name that properly belongs to Isis, Astarte, Juno, or Venus, as can be seen from various monuments of ancient inscriptions in the works of Janus Gruterus <note>A Dutch philologist known for his massive collection of Roman inscriptions.</note>. Since the **Moon** is properly denoted by the "Queen of Heaven," it follows from this that Venus, Juno, Isis, and Astarte are also commonly called the Moon, as will be clear from what follows. # THE ISIACTEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>
CHAPTER XXI.

Herodian.
</margin>
Herodian <note>A 3rd-century Greek historian of the Roman Empire.</note> discusses the statue of his "African Heavenly Urania" brought to Rome by Elagabalus <note>Kircher refers to him as "Pseudo-Antoninus."</note> in his fifth book. He says: *They say that Dido the Phoenician established it when she built the ancient city of Carthage by means of the cut ox-hide; the Libyans call her Urania [Heavenly], but the Phoenicians call her Astroarche [Star-Ruler], intending her to be the Moon.* <note>original Greek: "Φασὶ δὲ αυτὸν Διδὼ τὴν Φοίνισσαν ἱδρύσασθαι, ὅτε δὴ τὴν ἀρχαίαν Καρχηδόνα πόλιν ἔκτιζε βύρσα κατ' ἐπιμήθη· Λίβυες μὲν οὖν αὐτὴν οὐρανίαν καλοῦσι· Φοίνικες δ' Ἀστροάρχην ὀνομάζουσι· Σελήνην εἶναι θέλοντες."</note> **That is to say:** They say that Dido the Phoenician placed it there when she built ancient Carthage from a dissected hide; the Africans call her Urania; but the Phoenicians assert she is Astroarche and the Moon.

<margin>Astroarche and Astarte are the same.</margin>
He used the name *Astroarche* as a coined term to designate Astarte, as if he were calling her "Queen of the Stars," or, as Apuleius does, "Mother of the Stars," the Moon. Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar of the 1st century BCE.</note> shows that Juno and the Moon are the same when the Priests, "calling out" <note>The Latin "calantes" refers to the ritual of the Calends, the first day of the month.</note> the nones of the months on the Capitoline in the Calabra Court, would proclaim: *In five days I call upon you, new Juno.* Or as others read it, *couella*, which means "heavenly."

<margin>"Conum" meant heaven to the ancients.</margin>
For *couum* was the same as *coelum* [heaven] in ancient times, according to Sextus Pompeius. Virgil also shows that Juno is the same as the Moon in this verse:

<margin>Virgil.</margin>
->*But I, who walk as Queen of the Gods,*<-
->*Both sister and wife of Jupiter.*<-
<note>original: "Ast ego quæ Diuûm incedo Regina Iouisq́; Et soror & coniunx." from the Aeneid, Book I.</note>

<margin>All goddesses are resolved into the Moon.</margin>
In this context, mythologists understand Jupiter to be the Sun and Juno to be the Moon. Furthermore, Juno is called "Lucina," either because she was the presiding goddess of light—in which sense the idol **Asher** <note>Hebrew: אשר; likely referring to a sacred pole or goddess related to Astarte.</note>, of which we spoke above, can be understood, and thus she is conflated with Diana—or because she surveys all things with her light, and thus can be understood as the Moon insofar as she is the "illuminator of the air." There are some who also take her to be the same as Vesta or the Earth, and thus Juno would be the same as Isis, whom Plutarch indicates is sometimes the Moon, sometimes the Earth, and sometimes Nephthys. In a word,

<margin>The many names of Isis or the Moon.</margin>
the names of Minerva, Juno, Venus, and the Moon are so confused when you look at the Asiatic gods, that whoever calls her Minerva-Belisama, Juno-Belisama, Venus, the Moon, or Isis-Astarte, has always said the same thing. Now, as to who that Heavenly Venus or "Urania" is—whom the Assyrians call Mylitta, the Arabs Alilat, the Persians Mitra (as Herodotus writes in the *Thalia*), or whom the Hebrews call **Lilith** <note>Hebrew: לילית; a night-spirit or goddess.</note>—Mor Isaac, the Syrian Bishop, mentions Mylitta or "Molutho" in his *Syriac Cosmography*. There he says she is the same as the star of Venus, which the Syrians call Astaruth, as we have shown above. He says she is called *Mialdotho* <note>Syriac: ܡܘܠܕܬܐ</note>, that is, "she who causes to give birth" or "she who labors"; or she acts as a midwife, or is called *Ialedotho* <note>Syriac: ܡܚܒܠܢܝܬܳܐ</note> because she herself gives birth to all things, or acts as the mother of all. I will add his Syriac words here:

<margin>Mor Isaac the Syrian in the Syriac Cosmography.</margin>
->Astaruth is one of the seven shining stars that are called wanderers,<-
->or movers; and she is also called the Mother and the Midwife.<-
->܀<-

*Astaruth,* he says, *is one star of the seven wanderers, or planets, which is also called the mother and the midwife, because she is like the mother of all, the producer of all things, the nurturer and preserver of everything in the world.* Thus says Mor
<margin>Eileithyia.</margin>
Isaac. We believe that Mylitta is the same as Eileithyia <note>The Greek goddess of childbirth.</note>; but
<margin>Hecate Prothyraea.</margin>

# SYNTAGMA IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>
Pausanias.
The statue of Ilithyia "On Her Knees."
</margin>
...they sacrificed and sang hymns; and for the same reason in the land of Attica they secretly <note>original Greek: "ἐλάθρα" (elathra)</note> placed her among the Genetyllides <note>original Greek: "γενετυλίδας," goddesses who presided over birth and generation</note>, goddesses who were thought to oversee the process of birth; and for this reason Venus was also called Genetyllis. Thus, she is the same as the Mylitta of the Assyrians, whom the historian Diodorus also identifies as the daughter of Juno. Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer.</note> mentions her in his *Description of Greece*, where he says that a temple of Ilithyia <note>The Greek goddess of midwifery and childbirth.</note> stood in the forum, and that the people of Tegea possessed a statue of her which was historically called "On Her Knees" <note>original Greek: "ἢ γόνασις" (hē gonasis)</note>. This name suggested she was kneeling, just as women are accustomed to do when giving birth. The statue was covered from head to foot with a very thin cloth; one of its hands was stretched out straight, while the other held a lighted torch. This was either because the pains of birth are likened to the heat of fire, or rather because she was believed to bring the newborn into the light. If she were present and favorable, she protected both the mother and the small child; but if she remained adverse, she struck both with a heavy misfortune. Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine monk and scholar.</note> refers to her in his book *On the Operation of Daemons*.

<margin>
A female-formed demon.
</margin>
For indeed, he says: "I have heard from many: you might call all the goddesses of the childbed a female-formed demon." <note>original Greek: "Θηλόμορφון καὶ γὰר, πολλῶν κατεπάסας ἔχω· Θηλόμορφון πάסας ἓן λέχοις θεᾶς."</note> That is to say: *I have heard from many that a demon in female form appears to all women in childbirth.*

<margin>
Empusa, Gello, Lucina, Lamia.
</margin>
From these accounts, it appears that Ilithyia is the same as the **Empusa**, **Gello**, **Lucina**, and **Lamia** <note>Various female monsters or goddesses from classical folklore associated with stealing children or haunting mothers.</note>. Concerning these, one may read Hesychius and the playwright Aristophanes, along with the commentator on his play *The Frogs*. See also Plutarch in his book *On Divine Matters* and his philosophical works <note>original Latin: "ἐκ τῶν φιλοσοφίας."</note>.

What is the Lilith of the Hebrews?

It will also become clear from what we are about to say that the **Lilith** of the Hebrews, or **Hecate**, or the nocturnal demon, corresponds to the aforementioned Juno. Among the Hebrews, Lilith <note>original Hebrew: לִילִית</note> is the same as the Lamia. It is said that there are four mothers of demons: Lilith, Naamah, Ogereth, and Machalath. It is further said that Lilith is particularly hostile to women in childbirth. In the *Alphabet of Ben Sira*, in the fifth question that Nebuchadnezzar asked him, it is written: 'Why do children die when they are eight days old?' They told him: 'Because Lilith kills them.' ... I do not believe in these things, but it is a common custom among us Ashkenazim to draw a circle around the walls of the room where the woman in labor lies, using charcoal or soot, and we write on every wall: 'Adam and Eve, Lilith get out,' and on the door of the room from the inside we write the names of these three angels: Senoy, Sansenoy, and Semangelof, just as Lilith promised them at the time those angels intended to drown her in the sea.

</margin>

# SYNTHESIS IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER XII.

...signifies a "Night-Witch," and they say that she departed from Adam because she did not want to be inferior to him. Fleeing and going toward the shore of the sea, three Angels encountered her and persuaded her to return to her husband. However, being in no way willing to consent to this request of theirs, Lilith promised that every time she saw their three names in a room where Adam's little children were staying, she would not do any harm in that place. But if those names were not present, she would—provided she was able—kill as many as she could find along with her company. With this condition, they let her go; and their names are these:

->SANOI, SANSANOI, SAMNAGALAPH.<-

And then they write in the said room the three-letter name of God, <term>Shadai</term> <note>original: <term>שדי</term></note>, which means "Almighty." I say, therefore, that while they claim these three aforementioned names belong to Angels, it is stated otherwise in the "secrets of my Uncle" <note>Kircher is quoting an Italian source here, likely referring to a specific kabbalistic or familial tradition shared with him</note>. Namely, that these three names are spoken in the Egyptian language: *Sanoi* signifies in their idiom the "first branch of Divinity"; the second name, *Sansanoi*, the "second branch of Divinity"; the third, *Samnagalaph*, signifies the "third branch of Divinity." Then they join to them the three-letter name <term>Rapha</term> <note>original: <term>רפא</term>, meaning "to heal," also the root of the name of the angel Raphael</note>. Thus says Raphael.

<margin>Explanation of foreign names</margin>
These ceremonies certainly bear an Egyptian character; they have led us to the opinion that those three names signify nothing other than those three Geniuses <note>In this context, "Geniuses" refers to guardian spirits or divine entities</note> and principal presiding deities of the Universe, whom the Egyptians call Osiris, Isis, and Horus. By Lilith, however, one should understand that perverse Typhon <note>Typhon was the Greek name for Set, the Egyptian god of chaos and storms</note>, whom Plutarch describes as an obscure power, suited for vexing and harming, and therefore accustomed to being appeased by supplications. I find that our opinion is supported by no weak reasons when I examine Plutarch more carefully. <margin>Osiris.</margin> For what else is Osiris to the Egyptians but that first divinity holding the governance of all things? <margin>Isis.</margin> His consort, Isis, is surely the second divinity—as the Egyptians speak—acting as the passive principle of all things. <margin>Horus. Lilith, Typhon.</margin> From these two is produced Horus, who represents this entire mundane house, as Plutarch says, and is the third divinity. To these three, Typhon—that nocturnal and obscure demon—is perpetually opposed. For besides the fact that he is said to have killed Osiris, he is also recorded to have snatched away the son, Horus, through constant treachery and submerged him; yet Isis restored him to life and immortality, as we have recounted elsewhere from the writings of Plutarch. <margin>Women in labor appeased Typhon</margin> And for this reason, Typhon was greatly feared by women in childbirth in Egypt. As Plutarch testifies, they strove to appease him as a hostile demon in various ways and ceremonies, and to ward him off with amulets. We shall speak of these things extensively in another place. It is most likely that the Hebrews received this custom from them, since both the three names of the Geniuses cited above are Egyptian in origin, and the ceremonies and superstitious methods of acting are proper to the Egyptians, indicating an underlying Egyptian influence.

<margin>Nephte, the wife of Typhon.</margin>
It should be added that Nephte <note>Nephthys</note>, the Egyptian Venus, whom we previously identified with Astaroth and Lilith, is called the wife of Typhon according to Plutarch. In the vast variety of names and different versions of these myths, it was not difficult to confuse her with Typhon. But let us return to Lilith, who is also celebrated by the Arabs and called <term>Alilath</term> <note>original: <term>הלילת</term></note> from <term>Lail</term> <note>original: <term>ליל</term></note>, which...

# OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: THE TEMPLE OF ISIS

<margin>Alilath, Mistress of the Night.</margin>
<margin>Alitta of the Arabs.</margin>
<margin>Alilath is the same as Hecate.</margin>
He says that the ancients, among other false gods, served one whom they called *Alilath*, and they claimed she was the Moon; they called her *Alilath* because she is the Mistress and Queen of the night. **Herodotus** agrees with this in his *Thalia* <note>Book 3 of Herodotus's Histories</note>, where he asserts that the Arabs worshipped a goddess by the name of *Alitta*; I believe the reading should be *Alilath*. He says: "The Assyrians call Aphrodite *Mylitta*, the Arabs *Alilath* <note>original Greek: Ἀλίλατ</note>, and the Persians *Mitra*." **Herodotus** differs here from **Aben Sihal** in that the latter interprets her as the Moon, while the former sees her as Venus; however, in such an equivalence of names, this discrepancy is pardonable. Therefore, the *Alilath* of the Arabs and the *Lilith* of the Hebrews are understood to be the same deity as *Hecate* or *Proserpina* <note>Goddesses of the underworld and night</note>, as the etymology of the name sufficiently demonstrates, since both names are derived from "night." This is contrary to the derivation by **Selden** <note>John Selden, a contemporary English polymath and author of "On the Syrian Gods"</note>; for he, in order to more easily connect *Alilath* to *Mylitta*, derives the former from *Valad* <note>Arabic: ولاد</note>, which means "to give birth." Whatever the case may be—whether *Mylitta* comes from *Valad*, or *Alilath* from *Lail* <note>night</note>—it will be clear from what has been said that all the names reviewed so far—*Ilithya*, *Mylitta*, *Alilath*, *Lilith*—are the same goddess, whether you call her Venus, the Moon, Hecate, or by any other name.

<margin>Astarte is distinguished by the names of all the gods.</margin>
<margin>Why they are called Astaroth.</margin>
<margin>What is Asera?</margin>
From all these points so extensively proven, we finally infer that the much-celebrated *Astarte* of the Sidonians is nothing other than that Great Mother of the gods, whom the Egyptians call *Isis*, the inhabitants of Argos call *Io*, the Greeks *Cybele*, and **Lucian** calls the *Syrian Goddess*, while others call her by different names. She is surely the one who provided the cradle and the seeds for all things from moisture <note>The ancient idea that life originates from a primordial watery element</note>, the universal Cause and Nature, who taught mortals the beginning of all good things. She is truly one being indicated by diverse names because of the diversity of effects she exerts in different parts of the world. Thus, from the power she exerts in the Moon, she is called the Moon; from her effect on generation, Venus; from her effect in the air, Juno; from her effect on the earth, Vesta, Tellus, Hecate, Proserpina, Lamia, Lucina, Lilith, Alilath, Mulitha, Ilithya, and Mitra (which signifies "mother" in Persian and is called *Amma* by the Assyrians). Furthermore, she is called *Astaroth* because sacrifices were made to her from the flocks of sheep and goats; for <term>Ashtaroth</term> <note>original: <term>עשתרות</term></note> signifies "flocks," and we have already stated in the chapter on the sacrifices of the gods that such animals were both offered in sacrifice to Isis in Egypt and most religiously worshipped. **Lylius Gyraldus** shows this at length in his 12th *Syntagma* under the word "Isis." Truly, she is called <term>Asera</term> <note>original: <term>אשרה</term> (Asherah)</note> from oak leaves, or from the oak tree itself, under which they were accustomed to worship *Astaroth*; for <term>Asera</term> also signifies an oak, as we showed above from **Rabbi David Kimchi** <note>A famous medieval Jewish grammarian and biblical commentator</note>. Without doubt, they drew this ceremony from Egypt; for in the explanation of the Obelisks, we shall prove from **Apollodorus** and **Apollonius** that the sacred statues of Osiris and Isis were adorned with oak leaves and flowers during the time of the *Comasiae* <note>Festivals involving the carrying of statues</note>. Moreover, that *Astaroth*—whom we have called now Venus, now the Moon—is the Great Mother of the gods, **Ptolemy the Egyptian** testifies in these words:

This **Syrian Goddess**, or **Astaroth**—whether you look at the rituals or the images of both—is certainly our "Mother of the Gods," whether you call her **Isis** with the Egyptians or **Cybele** with the Greeks. This is indicated by the scepters, drums, thunderbolts, and tower-bearing cities, the lions yoked to the reins, and even the name **Amma** itself, which according to Hesychius means "mother" in the Syrian tongue. The method of performing her rituals also indicates this; see Apuleius, book 8, where he discusses the <term>Metagyrtes</term> <note>begging priests of the goddess Cybele</note> who go through the streets and towns clashing cymbals, rattles, and sistrums, carrying around the Syrian Goddess or Isis to compel people to give alms to the Mother of the Gods. <margin>Astaroth is shown with bovine horns.</margin> Furthermore, the bovine horns which were assigned to the Assyrian Venus-Astaroth provide no small evidence that she was the same as **Io** or **Isis**. <margin>Comparison of Isis with Rhea.</margin>
This is also a very strong argument by which we may prove **Astarte** was the same as **Isis**: for what Belus and Rhea <note>Rhea was a Greek Titaness, here identified with Babylonian deities</note> were to the Babylonians, or **Osiris** and **Isis** to the Egyptians, so were **Adonis** and **Astarte** to the Assyrians and Sidonians. Again, just as the Egyptians lamented and bewailed **Osiris** during certain annual solemnities, raving through the crossroads; so too the Assyrians lamented their **Thammuz**, or **Adonis**, whose consort was that Astaroth-Venus of whom we just spoke, with not dissimilar ceremonies. However, since we have discussed such things amply in the preceding pages, I have judged it superfluous to say more here. It only remains now for us to say something about the idol of Astarte, which was fashioned differently according to the diversity of her names. <margin>Theophylact. Image of Astarte. Suidas. Theophilus. Kimchi. Elias Thisbi.</margin> Theophylact, cited earlier, depicts her as naked. But Suidas and Theophilus describe her in the form of a star. David Kimchi, and after him Marinus of Brescia, suspect she was in the form of a sheep because of the similarity in the meaning of the words for "herds" and "flocks" <note>the Hebrew name 'Ashtarot' is also a word for the increase of the flock</note>. And (as Elias says), the idol took its name from the city of **Astaroth** because the craftsmen found in that city were skilled in making or carving that idol. <margin>Forster in his lexicon.</margin> Johann Forster thinks this was an idol of the **Many-Breasted Venus**, who was held and worshipped as the nurse of all things because of her fertility; and thus she is conflated with the **Mylitta** of the Assyrians and with the "Breasted Isis" of the Egyptians.

I believe she was worshipped according to the superstitious sacred laws of each region, and consequently her idol was adapted to those—

...desired. For those who worshipped her as **Venus** depicted her entirely naked, as Theophylact <note>Theophylact of Ohrid, an 11th-century biblical exegete</note> rightly notes; this was not difficult, but rather quite pleasant, for a people prone to every luxury. It is probable that the images which Solomon arranged to be made were of this kind. However, those who considered **Astarte** to be the **Moon** depicted her with those symbols by which either the Egyptians described **Isis**, or the Greeks described **Cybele** and **Diana**, or Lucian described the **Syrian Goddess**. From this, it is also likely that her insignias were drums, sistra <note>an ancient Egyptian percussion instrument associated with Isis</note>, pipes, sheep, a horned lion, or a tower-crowned head <note>a "mural crown," representing city walls, typically worn by Cybele</note>, and similar things that are commonly attributed to the Great Mother. Symbols of this kind are still seen to this day carved into the stone at Pennes near Marseille, as will be shown elsewhere.

But since all these things rest upon mere conjectures, I have preferred to let them remain untouched rather than to rashly affirm uncertain things about them. It is enough for us to have demonstrated here that all worship of **Astarte** first flowed from the Egyptians. Therefore, let us proceed to other matters.

# CHAPTER XIV.
## *Chemosh, the Idol of the Moabites.*

<margin>
Some confuse **Chemosh** with **Peor**.
</margin>
Among those idols which sacred history records **Solomon** to have worshipped, **Chemosh** occupies the second place. For Solomon worshipped **Astarte**, the Goddess of the Sidonians, and **Chemosh**, the God of the Moabites, etc. We must now investigate the nature of this deity. St. Jerome, at the beginning of Isaiah 15, maintains that **Chemosh** is the same as **Beelphegor** <note>Baal-Peor</note> and **Priapus** <note>a Greek fertility god</note>; Selden <note>John Selden, a famous 17th-century orientalist</note> was also of this opinion. Both avoided giving the reasons for this assertion. Others, followers of Jerome, confuse **Chemosh** with **Beelphegor** for the reason that **Chemosh** was an idol of the Moabites just as **Peor** was. I would also willingly embrace their opinion if they could show us that the Moabites worshipped only a single image; but since this is false—as the sacred scriptures themselves testify, making mention of Moabite idols in various places—this opinion does not please me, unless it be reconciled by the reasoning we provide below. Better is the opinion of those who derive this name from the Greek <term>κῶμος</term> <note>original: kōmos; meaning a village festival or a riotous procession</note>, which is the name for a festive drinking party and gluttonous revelry. From such revelry, one easily falls into that deep sleep which the Greeks call <term>κῶμα</term> <note>original: kōma; meaning a lethargic slumber or trance</note>, to which are joined lewdness, luxury, wickedness, **Venus**, **Bacchus**, and the impulses of Venus and Bacchus: insolence, dancing, singing, and all shameful revels. Certainly, Arias Montanus <note>a 16th-century Spanish orientalist</note>, in his Greek-Latin Dictionary, explained the word <term>κῶμος</term> <note>kōmos</note> quite well as the God presiding over nocturnal revelries and dances; perhaps following Aristophanes, who calls <term>κῶμον</term> <note>kōmon</note> youthful impudence and a feast of intemperance.

<margin>
**Chemosh**, the God of revelry.
</margin>
<margin>
**Chemosh** is the same as **Bacchus**.
</margin>
From these points, it is gathered that the said authors indicate nothing else by this word <term>κῶμος</term> <note>kōmos</note> than **Bacchus**, the God of drunkenness and intoxication. The Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> touched upon the shameful and drunken religion of his nocturnal revelries in Romans 13, when he says:
> Not in reveling <note>original: "commessationibus"</note> and drunkenness, not in chambering...

# SYNTHESIS IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS.
## CHAPTER XIV.

...couches and impurities. That this **Chemosh** is the same as **Bacchus**, I am led to believe by many arguments. And first, indeed, by the etymology of the word **Chemosh**, which is derived from the root *KMS* <note>original Hebrew: כמש</note>, signifying "to hide" or "to conceal," as if you were to say "the concealed God." For they sacrificed to **Bacchus** at night and in secret, accompanied by the immense madness and shouts of the revelers, especially the women. From this, those ceremonies of the Bacchic religion were called **Nyctelia** <note>from the Greek word for "night"</note>, because they were performed at night; and for that very reason, Bacchus was called **Nyctelius**. **Plutarch** mentions this in his treatise on the inscription at Delphi, where he briefly summarizes the orgies of the "Night-Bacchus" and indicates almost exactly what is described more extensively and in detail by others: <margin>Dithyrambs.</margin> they sing **Dithyrambs** <note>wild, passionate hymns</note> to Bacchus, songs full of emotional stirrings and changes, joined with wanderings and running about in various errors; they depict and imagine him in manifold forms, varied figures, and appearances; <margin>Bacchic Ceremonies.</margin> they attribute to him permitted jokes, petulance, fury, and instability, invoking **Bacchus** as **Evius** <note>a ritual name for Bacchus/Dionysus</note>, running and dwelling among women in the mountains with insane honors. Finally, in the orgies of Bacchus, they carry a chest full of that fruit, the plucking of which Bacchus made sterile, as **Clement** <note>Clement of Alexandria, an early Christian author who wrote against pagan practices</note> describes in his work *Against the Heathen*. When I examined these things a little more carefully, I finally recognized, through various comparisons of the aforementioned matters with those we treated in the previous Synthesis, that: <margin>Chemosh is the same as Osiris, the Egyptian Dionysus.</margin> **Chemosh** signifies nothing else to the Hebrews than **Osiris** or **Dionysus**, that Egyptian **Bacchus**, whom authors everywhere entitle with various names, making him identical to Bacchus. He was called **Chemosh**, however, either as has been said from the Hebrew word *KMS* <note>original: כמש</note> which signifies "hidden," or from the solemnity and pomp of the **Comasiaria** <note>processions or revels</note> which they performed annually in honor of the Egyptian Dionysus. For solemnities of this kind were named from the Greek word *kome* <note>original: ἀπὸ τῆς κώμης</note>, meaning from the "villages" and "crossroads" through which the **revelers** <note>original: κωμάζοντες</note> wandered with the greatest mental dissolution and insanity. <margin>The Pomp of the Revelers.</margin> From this also the verb "to revel" <note>original: κωμάζειν</note> arose, which is usually applied to those who behave petulantly. In the same way, the Egyptians were accustomed to behave with thyrsi <note>staffs topped with pinecones</note> and sistra <note>rattles</note>, dressed in linen robes and with shaved heads, carrying around that covered chest; these matters were treated copiously in the previous Synthesis, and therefore we refer the reader who desires to know them more clearly to that place. 

That lust and every kind of impurity were ordinarily joined to festivities of this kind is clear from those shameful crimes of the **Ithyphalli** and **Pammylia** <note>festivals involving the display of phallic symbols</note>—scarcely to be called "sacred"—which we mentioned a little earlier, and which the Egyptians celebrated annually in honor of the phallus, or if you prefer, the Egyptian **Dionysus**. But since all these things flee from the light, they are surely worthy of **Chemosh**, who by his very name warns that they must be hidden and consigned only to the darkness of night. Thus, as has often been said, since the Hebrews were extremely prone to every kind of such dissolution and shameful rites, nothing was easier for them than to learn such a licentious cult of the Gods, either from the Egyptians while they were still mixed with them in Egypt, or from the **Moabite** harlots in the desert who openly practiced Egyptian servitude in all things, <margin>Numbers 21, 22, 24; Judges 11:24. Chemosh is a very ancient false god.</margin> and then to transmit it, once propagated, to their descendants. (For it is clear from the **Book of Numbers** that the worship of **Chemosh** was most ancient). This worship, which was then fading in the Church of God, **Solomon** finally recalled from the underworld; for worship of this kind...

<meta>catchword: ...kind (modi)</meta>

<summary>Athanasius Kircher identifies the Moabite god Chemosh with Bacchus and Osiris, arguing that the name derives from a Hebrew root meaning "to hide," reflecting the secret, nocturnal, and often licentious nature of his rituals. He suggests the Israelites adopted these "shameful" Egyptian and Moabite practices during their time in the desert before Solomon later revived them.</summary>

CAP. XV 328 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS THE ISIAIC TEMPLE

<margin>Chemosh is confounded with Pluto.</margin>
A deity of this sensuous kind, filled with luxury, lasciviousness, and revelry, could not be better suited than to a man devoted to women and the pleasures of the flesh, such as we read Solomon to have been. It is no wonder, then, if through Egyptian and Moabite women and concubines, he brought that cult from Egypt, which would be primarily pleasing and delightful both to the concubines and to himself—such as was that Bacchic fury and insanity, continually foaming with luxury and banqueting. Furthermore, those who confuse **Chemosh** (so called from his "hiding" <note>original: "ab occultatione," referring to the Hebrew root *KMS*</note>) with **Pluto** <note>the Roman god of the underworld</note> are not to be rebuked, since Pluto, Dis, Osiris, Dionysus, and Serapis are everywhere confused with one another, as has been said. Nor are those to be blamed who wish Chemosh to be the same as **Beelphegor** <note>Baal-Peor</note>, provided they understand it with this moderation: that Beelphegor is the same as **Priapus** <note>the Greco-Roman god of fertility</note> or the phallus of **Osiris** worshipped with divine honor by the Egyptians, a cult which we read the Moabites especially professed. You see, therefore, by what reasoning the diverse opinions of various scholars are to be reconciled; but let these things said about Chemosh suffice.

# CHAPTER XV.

## *Moloch, the Idol of the Ammonites.*

<margin>4 Kings 17 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 17.</note></margin>
<margin>The Etymology of Moloch.</margin>
<margin>Leviticus 18:21.</margin>
<margin>Rabbi Shlomo, Abenezra, Kimchi, Ben Gershon.</margin>
**Moloch** or **Melchom**, the idol of the Ammonites (which the Sepharvites call sometimes **Adramelech**, sometimes **Anamelech**, according to the scripture: *They burned their sons in the fire of Anamelech and Adramelech, the gods of Sepharvaim*), obtains no less a diversity of etymology than of names. Some derive it from the Hebrew *Melek* <note>original: מלך</note>, which signifies "to reign." Others derive it from *Holikh* <note>original: הוליך</note>, which is derived from the verb *Yalakh* <note>original: ילך</note>, that is, "to walk"; in the causative form <note>the Hebrew *Hiphil*</note>, this means "he caused to walk, proceed, go, or pass through." For *Holikh* in the present participle <note>original: "in Benoni" מוליך</note> signifies one who promotes a transition or "passing through," such as Moloch showed himself to be <note>referring to the ritual of "passing children through the fire"</note>. Both etymologies suit Moloch. For it is clear he was called "King" from the translation of the **Septuagint** <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note>, who for Moloch in Leviticus 18:21 translate *Archonta* <note>original: ἄρχοντα, meaning "Prince" or "Ruler"</note>: *Of your seed you shall not give to serve the Prince* (understand here the idol Moloch). They do the same in Leviticus 20, although elsewhere they use the name "Moloch" itself properly. It is indeed very frequent, both in the Latin Vulgate and in the Septuagint, that proper names are interpreted as common nouns. Those, however, who derive the name from *Holikh* find strong arguments for their opinion; see these among the Rabbis Shlomo, Abenezra, Kimchi, and Ben Gershon in the fourth book of Kings, chapter 21. but these things are easy to understand.

<margin>Who and what Moloch was.</margin>
The greater difficulty is: who was this god Moloch? What kind of idol was it? And from where did such bloody customs of sacrifice take their origin? The greatest part of authors suppose him to be **Saturn**, because Saturn is everywhere said to be appeased by human victims, just as Moloch was by the sons of the Hebrews, according to the Psalm: *They immolated their sons and their daughters to demons, whom they sacrificed to the carvings of Canaan.* Where, by "demons," all the interpreters in this place understand to a man the idol Moloch, and Anamelech or Adramelech, the idols of Sepharvaim. It was performed, however...

### SYNTAGMA IV. PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER XV.

...this kind of sacrifice in the valley of **Tophet**, belonging to the sons of **Hinnom**, according to that passage in the 4th Book of Kings, chapter 23: <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 23:10.</note> *He defiled Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Ennom, so that no one might consecrate his son or daughter through the fire to Moloch.* Indeed, those who conflate **Moloch** with **Saturn** <note>The Roman god associated with time, agriculture, and in some traditions, the devouring of his own children.</note> are led by a twofold conjecture. The first of these is from the sacrifice of children, as has been said, by which he was worshipped by parents, and from the use of fire; the second is from the name of "King" itself, which is everywhere attributed to Saturn. 
<margin>Diodorus Siculus, Book 6, Chapter 15.</margin>
For **Diodorus** also says that Saturn, the son of Heaven, was made King, and so forth. 
<margin>Eusebius.</margin>
**Eusebius** <note>A 4th-century Christian historian.</note> likewise makes him the King of Phoenicia, the brother of Astarte, etc. They confirm the first conjecture by the custom of the Phoenicians and Carthaginians, 
<margin>Infants were offered to Saturn.</margin>
whom **Plato** records in his *Dialogue on Laws* to have consecrated infants as victims to Saturn, choosing the most excellent and dressing them in royal ornaments. 
<margin>Plato.</margin>
*For our laws,* he says, *do not permit the sacrificing of human victims; but among the Carthaginians, it is considered just and holy, so much so that some of them sacrifice their sons to Saturn.* And 
<margin>Plutarch.</margin>
**Plutarch**, in his *Sayings of the Emperors*, writes that **Gelon the Tyrant**, having defeated the Carthaginians in war, settled a peace on the condition that they would never again immolate their children to Saturn in the future. But it is not a burden to explain and confirm this matter 
<margin>Tertullian.</margin>
using the very words of **Tertullian** in his *Apology*, chapter 9: *Infants,* he says, *were publicly sacrificed to Saturn in Africa until the Proconsulate of Tiberius, who exposed those same priests on the very trees of their temple that shaded them, as votive crosses for their crimes; as witnessed by the soldiers of our own country, who performed that duty for the Proconsul. But even now this criminal deed persists in secret. It is not only you Christians who are despised; no crime is ever eradicated forever, nor does any God change his ways. Since Saturn did not spare his own children, he continued by not sparing those of others, whom indeed their own parents offered, and willingly gave up, even caressing the infants so that they would not be sacrificed while weeping.* Regarding this matter, **Pammelius** <note>Jacques de Pamele, a 16th-century theologian.</note> has written many learned annotations from Justin, Lactantius, Augustine, and other writers of secular history.

<margin>The method of immolating children.</margin>
As for what pertains to rites of this kind, I find authors holding various opinions. Most of the Hebrews write that the children were not burned or slaughtered, but having built two pyres, they were merely led through the middle of them, and in this manner were as if "purified" <note>original: "februatos," referring to the Roman Februa purification rituals.</note>, with the priests of Moloch managing the affair. <margin>Moloch is an Egyptian name.</margin>
And since the Egyptian Mars in the ancient Egyptian or Coptic language is called **Moloch**, as is clear from the Coptic (or Egyptian) Dictionary translated by me from Arabic into Latin; in which the planet Mars is called **Moloch** in Egyptian; it is quite clear that the **Moloch** of the Hebrews, the **Mithras** of the Persians, and **Typhon** the Egyptian demon were one and the same deity. For just as they used to appease each of these with human victims as a hostile deity, according to Plutarch, so they were also accustomed to appease Moloch for the same reason, as has been said.

<margin>The form of Moloch, Anamelech, and Adramelech as a mule or horse.</margin>
Since these things are so, it remains only for us to describe what the idol **Moloch** was like. ### SYNT[AGMA] IV. THE HEBREW PANTHEON. CHAPTER XV

<note>original: "שהיו כל בתי ע"ז בירושלם המולך היה חוץ לירושלם..." This is a quote from the medieval Jewish commentator Rabbi David Kimchi, also known as Radak.</note>
Because all the houses of foreign worship were within Jerusalem, but the Moloch was outside Jerusalem. It was made as a hollow bronze statue, placed within seven partitions. For anyone who offered fine flour, they would open one of these for him; for a turtle-dove or a young pigeon, they opened two; for a lamb, they opened three; for a ram, they opened four; for a calf, they opened five; for an ox, they opened six; and for anyone who offered his own son, they opened all seven. Its face was the face of a calf, and its hands were spread out upon the ground, as if opening its hands to receive something from its companion. They would heat it with fire, and the priests would take the child and place him within the hands of Moloch, and the child’s soul would depart.

<margin>Description of Tophet.</margin>
*That is to say: There was a place there where they made their sons pass through to Moloch. This place was called Tophet, and they say it was named so from the beating of drums <note>The Hebrew word "Toph" means a drum or tambourine.</note> and the dances they performed at the time of sacrifice to drown out the wailing and weeping of the infants; this was done lest the father, perhaps moved by the pitiable voice of his son, might snatch the boy or girl from the hands of those offering them, or be turned away from such sacred rites by the blood-curdling cries. Furthermore, this place was a valley belonging to a man whose name was Hinnom, and it was called the Valley of Hinnom, or the Son of Hinnom, because it belonged to the sons of Hinnom or one of them. This place was later defiled, as if to say: it became a place into which all corpses, carcasses, and whatever is unclean were cast, so that no memory of such an unspeakable sacrifice and the lethal immolation of children might remain for posterity. Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explain the work of Moloch and say that although all the shrines of foreign service were within the city of Jerusalem, Moloch alone had his shrines—or rather, his caves—outside the city.* <margin>Sacrifices to Moloch were performed outside the city.</margin> *The image of Moloch was hollow, containing seven chambers or rather receptacles within. The first they opened for the offering of fine flour; the second for turtledoves or pigeons; the third for a sheep or lamb; the fourth for a ram or goats; the fifth for a calf; the sixth for a bull. For him who wished to offer his son, the seventh chamber was opened. Finally, the face of this idol was like the face of a calf. Its hands were held out flat and extended to receive something from those standing by, and meanwhile they danced while the boys were burned by the fire kindled inside the idol, beating drums so that the boy's wailing would not be heard.* 

And thus far **Kimchi** <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a prominent medieval rabbi and grammarian.</note>; whose description of the statue and the manner of the ceremonies to be performed for Moloch matches the <term>Mithraic rites</term><gloss>the ancient Persian mysteries of the god Mithras</gloss> so closely that, with few exceptions, you will find everything to be the same. Do not be troubled by the fact that we previously identified Mithras with Osiris and the Sun; for we do not do this except insofar as we denote one and the same substantial thing throughout all the names of the various deities that are commonly confused by authors. We make a distinction only in their "formalities"—to speak with the <term>Scholastics</term><gloss>medieval theologians and philosophers who used precise logical categories</gloss>—or rather in certain formal aspects, which are the different properties and powers shining forth in the Sun, or Osiris. The same must also be said of Mithras, Typhon, and Moloch; they denote nothing other than that vehement power of Osiris, or the Sun, which is harmful to the lower world. Or rather, they represent that divinity which, through a harsh and immoderate heat, brings about a <term>disharmony</term><gloss>original Latin: "discrasium," referring to an imbalance of physical humors or elements</gloss> in things, such as we showed the Typhonic and Mithraic power to induce just a moment ago. <margin>How Moloch is to be understood as the same as Osiris.</margin> It is no wonder, therefore, if they sought to appease this Demon of the Sun with such precious victims. I have decided to place the image of Moloch here, according to the description of **Rabbi David Kimchi**, so that the reader may more easily compare its seven gates with the Mithraic mysteries.

And this is the figure of Moloch, which Radak <note>Rabbi David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish scholar</note> described for us as being quite consistent with the Mithraic and Egyptian rites. It is, moreover, so similar to a brick kiln that regarding the passage in Zephaniah chapter 1, verse 5, "they swear by their King," that is, in Hebrew <term>במולכם</term> (*be-malkam*), "by your Moloch"; the Masoretes <note>Scholars who standardized the Hebrew Bible</note> interpreted <term>מלכם</term> (*malkam*) as a "brick furnace." <margin>The origin of the Moloch sacrifices.</margin>
<margin>Saturn, King of Phoenicia, sacrifices his son.</margin>
<margin>Porphyry.</margin>
<margin>The pagans contaminated the histories of Holy Scripture with strange fables.</margin>
Therefore, these matters having been duly demonstrated, it now remains for us to show—which is our principal goal—whence this deadly method of sacrificing drew its origin. There are some who derive the origin of this fatal sacrifice from Abraham, when by God's command he had resolved to sacrifice his son; others from Jephthah sacrificing his daughter. The former group takes the reasoning for their assertion from Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> in Eusebius’ *Preparation for the Gospel*, books 1 and 4. For he claims that Saturn—whom the Phoenicians called *Israel* and was a most ancient King of Phoenicia—in order to free his kingdom from the extreme danger of an imminent war and to have the gods above propitious, sacrificed his "only-begotten" <term>μονογενῆ</term> (*monogenē*) son, whom he had fathered by Anobret, upon an altar built for the purpose, dressed in royal finery and pride. He claims that posterity later followed this example. That Porphyry is speaking here of Abraham is evident from this: that the "only-begotten," that is, that unique son, is called by Porphyry and Philo *Ieoud*; and in Genesis 22, Isaac is called <term>בנך את יחידך</term> (*bin-cha et yechide-cha*), namely "your son, your only one," where in *Iehid* we read almost the entirety of *Iehoud*. It is likely, therefore, that the pagans drew from there if not all, then at least some part of their superstitions. Even if, as can be seen in most of the monuments of profane writers, they corrupted and defiled the sacred history in a pitiable manner with their false narrations. For they confused Moses with God, and the Patriarchs with inextricable error; they snatched up sacred words and things for the impious works of the Magi, and from things divinely performed and recorded in the holy books, they formed profane deities; [they formed] new, ridiculous, and wicked—

### SYNT. IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CAP. XV.

they established these abominable cults. But we shall treat of these and similar matters more copiously elsewhere. We therefore consider it plausible that their opinion—those who feel that the rites of Moloch were derived from the sacrifice of Abraham and Isaac—is reasonable; for I would not easily deny that the Egyptians took many things from the Hebrews, especially since I show this in another place with many arguments. Yet, I consider much more probable and certain the view of those who derive all such detestable ceremonies from Egypt and Persia; let us explain the reasoning behind this.

<margin>The origin of the Moloch superstition from Egypt.</margin>
After the death of Misraim <note>The biblical name for the progenitor of the Egyptians, whom Kircher identifies here with Osiris.</note>, or Osiris, when a famine and a high cost of grain—brought about by the sterility of the fields—afflicted all of Egypt in a foul manner, it happened that the Egyptians, pressed by this dire evil, suddenly fled to the Oracle to learn what should be done in this public calamity. The oracle responded that the evil would cease if they promised to sacrifice a man to Osiris every year around the time of the Nile’s inundation. No sooner said than done. Once the sacrilegious sacrifice was performed, the Nile, through its fertile overflow, soon delivered the land from all sterility and made it so productive that it easily compensated for all the poverty of the sterile years with a single harvest. Hence it arose that every year sacrifices of this kind were performed with the greatest solemnity; however, this custom was abolished by later Kings, which subsequently gave rise to the immolation of animals. But let us hear Abenephius <note>An Arabic author frequently cited by Kircher, likely referring to Ibn Wahshiyya, whose works mixed history with occultism.</note> discussing this in the following words in Arabic:

<margin>Abenephius. When the famine in Egypt was dispelled.</margin>
In those days there was a severe famine in all of Egypt, and many were dying of hunger. Their priests asked their god about this misery, and he answered them: "The famine shall not cease unless you sacrifice a man to the great God of Fire every year at the time of the flood of the river called the Nile." When they did according to the word of their god, the famine ceased in all of Egypt. This was the penalty, and from this began the sacrifice of people in the land of Egypt. <note>original: "في تلك الايام كان جوعا شديدا..."</note>

> In those times, he says, a huge famine grew strong in the land of Egypt, so that many of the Egyptians were killed by hunger. Their priests, anxious about this public calamity, consulted their gods, and they responded that the high price of grain would not cease before they had sacrificed a man to the great God of Fire every year, and that around the inundation of the Nile. When they did according to the precept of the gods, the famine ceased in the whole land of Egypt, and from then on the custom of sacrificing men arose.

Apollodorus <note>A Greek scholar and mythographer.</note> relates that this famine occurred in the time of Busiris (whom we have handed down from Diodorus as having lived in the time of Menes, the first King of the Egyptians, and having succeeded him). His words fit perfectly with the words of Abenephius, for he says in Book 2 of *On the Origin of the Gods*:

Hercules traveled through Libya and Egypt; Busiris, son of Poseidon and Lysianassa, daughter of Epaphus, reigned there. This man, warned by a certain oracle, used to sacrifice strangers at the altar of Zeus; for for nine years a lack of crops had gripped Egypt. But Thrasius, a seer who had come from Cyprus and was skilled in his art, said that the barrenness would cease if they slaughtered a foreign man to Zeus every year. Busiris, having first slaughtered that very seer, then slaughtered the strangers who arrived. <note>original: "Ἡρακλῆς δὲ Λιβύην καὶ Αἴγυπτον ἐξῄει..."</note>

<margin>Busiris, the first sacrificer of men.</margin>

In the midst of this, Thrasius, skilled in prophecy, arrived from Cyprus and announced that this high cost of grain would cease if a foreign man [was sacrificed] every year
