### CHAPTER XV 336 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACI: THE ISIAC TEMPLE

<margin>
Busiris is the same as Typhon.
</margin>
...for nine years they had sacrificed to Jupiter <note>Kircher uses the Roman name Jupiter for the Egyptian deity Amun or perhaps a personified sky-god in this context.</note>; then Busiris, having first sacrificed that very Seer who suggested the rite, proceeded to slaughter all guests who arrived thereafter. Who, furthermore, this Busiris was, remains a matter of doubt. Diodorus, placing him among the first Kings of Egypt, identifies him as the founder of Thebes; Apollodorus calls him the son of Neptune and Libya; Agathon of Samos asserts he was the son of Aganippe and that he exercised a tyranny in Egypt. Truly, if I diligently examine everything I find written about this Busiris among various authors, I judge that by him none other is understood than the Egyptian Mars, namely Typhon or Mithras <note>Typhon was the Egyptian god of chaos and storms; Mithras was the Persian sun god. Kircher frequently synchronizes gods from different cultures.</note>. You will find him frequently confused with Menas, Minos, Osiris, Epaphus, and Apis, as has been said elsewhere; for he is described by all as <term>syngchyton</term> <note>original: "σύγχυτον", meaning "confused," "mixed," or "jumbled together."</note>. Regarding these matters, the reader may, if he pleases, consult what we have written in the first treatise of this section, on the 16th Dynasty of the Kings of Egypt. For, as Eratosthenes also rightly feels, it is probable that there was never any King by this name, but that they bestowed the name of such cruelty upon Typhon.

<margin>
Red-haired men were sacrificed to Typhon, and why?
</margin>
The tomb of Osiris was a place where red-haired men, according to Plutarch, were killed because Typhon, the slayer of Osiris, had been of that color; later, red oxen were used, from which the name of Busiris was fashioned—as if you were to say "Oxen to be consecrated to Osiris" and "the altars of Busiris." Virgil also makes mention of this:

<margin>
Athanasius.

### SYNT. IV. PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. 337 CH. XV.

...insofar as they are confirmed by the authority and reckoning of the most trustworthy writers. It suffices for us to have shown by their tradition that the origin of the sacrifices performed to Moloch emanated from nowhere else but Egypt. For we have already sufficiently indicated that he is the same as the Egyptian Mars, whom authors also call Typhon and Mithras <note>Kircher equates the Canaanite Moloch with the Egyptian chaos-god Typhon and the Persian sun-god Mithras, viewing them all as manifestations of the same destructive principle.</note>, and likewise that the sacrifices for each were the same. The neighboring nations show that from these, as if from the most ancient of deities, all remaining superstitious methods of sacrificing sprouted; these nations, following the example of the Egyptians, are said to have appeased the gods everywhere with human victims. 

Hence, the Cypriots, in the month of Aphrodisius <note>The month dedicated to Aphrodite.</note>, slaughtered a man to Agraulus, the son of Cecrops. In Chios, they slew a dismembered man for Dionysius Homalius <note>A "raw-eating" or "cruel" aspect of Dionysus.</note>; the same was done at Tenedos. The Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note> themselves sacrificed to Mars with human blood. The Curetes and Cretans used to sacrifice boys to Saturn. From this, as Lampridius testifies, the Emperor Commodus polluted the Mithraic rites with actual homicide <note>The Emperor Commodus was said to have actually killed someone during a ritual that was usually only symbolic.</note>. The Druids of the Gauls also appeased the gods Esus and Teutates with human gore. The story of Agamemnon and Iphigenia is well known. As Silius Italicus writes in his fourth book:

<margin>Various customs of sacrificing humans flourished among the nations.</margin>
<margin>Silius Italicus</margin>
> It was the custom among the peoples whom the foreigner Dido established, 
> To seek pardon from the gods through slaughter, and to place young sons 
> Upon the flaming altars—unspeakable to tell. 
> The urn brought back the wretched tribute annually.
<note>original: "Mos fuit in populis..." This passage refers to the Carthaginians, descendants of Dido, who were infamous in Roman literature for sacrificing their children to Ba'al/Saturn.</note>

Indeed, Ludovicus Vives <note>A Spanish humanist and scholar (1493–1540).</note> testifies that in modern times such nefarious customs still flourish in many places of the world. <margin>Ludovicus Vives in Indian History.</margin> "At the time we were publishing these things," he says, "an island was found by our sailors, which they call Carolena <note>Likely referring to territories in the Americas named in honor of Emperor Charles V (Carolus).</note> after the name of the Prince; in it statues of the gods are frequently seen which those nations worship, made of bronze, hollow inside, with hands joined and outstretched, in which they place infants and boys whom they sacrifice to those gods; and there they are cruelly <unclear>burned</unclear> by a fire kindled within the hollow images, the <unclear>bronze</unclear> glowing with excessive heat." <margin>Aloysius Froes.</margin> Aloysius Froes <note>Luis Frois (1532–1597), a Portuguese Jesuit missionary to Japan.</note> relates similar things in his Japanese letters concerning a certain valley into which countless men were cast headlong every year to be sacrificed in honor of Zaca and Amida <note>Zaca refers to Shakyamuni (the historical Buddha) and Amida to Amitābha Buddha. Kircher interprets Buddhist practices through the lens of Western "idolatry."</note>.

> So great a weight of evil could religion persuade [men to do],
> Which has so often given birth to every kind of unspeakable crime.
<note>original: "Tantum relligio potuit suadere malorum..." A famous line from Lucretius' "De Rerum Natura" regarding the sacrifice of Iphigenia.</note>

And let these things suffice concerning Moloch.

<margin>CHAPTER XVI.</margin>

# CHAPTER XVI.

->Concerning the Gods of the Syrians, Philistines, and Arabs,<-

->WHO ARE<-

->Dagon, Derceto, Atergatis, Cabar, and the Asian Venus.<-

->§. I.<-

->Dagon, the God of the Azotians.<-

<margin>Ralbag.</margin>
<margin>The Etymology of Dagon.</margin>
Dagon, the divinity of the Philistines or Azotians <note>Azotus is the Greco-Roman name for the city of Ashdod, one of the five major Philistine cities.</note>, though largely unknown to secular writers, was celebrated in sacred history. This is shown by the frequent disputes among interpreters regarding the nature of this deity, all of which I shall strive to reconcile by divine grace. First, however, we must investigate the form of Dagon's idol. I find that most Rabbis differ in assigning a shape to this divinity. Ralbag—that is, Rabbi Levi Ben Gerson <note>A 14th-century philosopher and biblical commentator also known as Gersonides.</note>—attributes a human figure to him. He claims the god was called Dagon either from fish scales <note>original: "piscium squamis"</note>, which his clothing resembled, or from grain, which in Hebrew is *dagan* <term>דגן (Dagan): the Hebrew word for grain or corn</term>, because the invention of grain was ascribed to him. We shall see later that Philo of Byblos <note>A historian who claimed Dagon was a god of agriculture equivalent to the Greek Cronus.</note> held this same opinion. The words of Ralbag are:

> *And behold, the Philistines brought the Ark of the God of Israel into their house of alien service <note>A common Jewish term for a temple of idolatry.</note> which belonged to them; in it was an image in the form of a human being, which they called Dagon.*

Ralbag gathers this from the fact that Dagon’s hands were found cut off, as the sacred scriptures relate:

> *And when the people of Ashdod rose early the next morning, behold, Dagon had fallen on his face to the ground before the Ark of the Lord; and the head of Dagon and both the palms of his hands were cut off on the threshold; only the Dagon <note>The Hebrew text here says "only Dagon was left to him," which commentators often interpret as the trunk or the fish-part of the idol.</note> remained upon it.*

From this, the "palms of the hands" are properly attributed to a human. Indeed, Ralbag could have gathered this much more truly from the description by the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, in which mention is made not only of the hands but also of the feet being cut off, and only the shoulder remaining, all of which are missing in the Hebrew text. I cite the words of the Seventy:

<margin>The 70 Interpreters.</margin>
> *And it happened when the people of Ashdod rose early the next day, and behold, Dagon had fallen upon his face...* <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἐγένετο ὡς ὤρθριασαν τῇ ἐπαύριον οἱ Ἀζώτιοι, καὶ ἰδὲ, Δαγὼν πεπτωκὼς ἐπὶ πρόσωπον</note>

TREATISE IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. 339 CHAPTER XVI.

...her face before the ark of God, and the head of Dagon, and both the soles of her feet were cut off upon the front of the thresholds, and both the wrists of her hands were fallen upon the porch; only the back of Dagon was left. <note>original Greek: "σώπον αὐτῆ... πλὴν ὁ ῥάχις Δαγὼν ὑπελείφθη." This is a citation from the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament (1 Samuel 5:4). Interestingly, the Greek uses feminine pronouns for the idol here.</note>

> *And it happened, when the citizens of Azotus <note>The ancient Philistine city of Ashdod.</note> rose early the next morning, behold, Dagon lay fallen on his face before the ark of God, and the head of Dagon and both the soles of his feet were cut off upon the front of the thresholds, and both the joints of his hands lay upon the threshold. Truly, only the shoulder of Dagon was left, etc.* Based on this description by the *Seventy Interpreters* [the Septuagint], following *Ralbag*, there have been those who concluded that the statue of *Dagon* was that of a man. However, we shall see shortly how these details can be harmoniously adapted to the opinion to be introduced below.

<margin>What was the idol of Dagon like?</margin>
Rassi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, better known as Rashi (1040–1105), the preeminent medieval French commentator.</note>, whom they also call Rabbi Solomon Jarchi, in his commentary on this passage, is of the opinion that Dagon was in the shape of a fish, for the reason that the name itself signifies nothing other than "fish" <note>In Hebrew, *dag* (דג) means fish.</note>. Yet this opinion cannot hold unless perhaps he understands here an anthropomorphic fish <note>original: "ἀνθρωπόμορφον," meaning human-shaped.</note> endowed with hands and feet, as is apparent from the sacred words cited above. Therefore, Radak—or Rabbi David Kimchi <note>A 12th-13th century grammarian and biblical commentator.</note>—has the best insight compared to the others. <margin>Dagon fish-shaped <note>original: "ἰχθυόμορφος."</note></margin> He asserts that the statue of Dagon was neither precisely a man nor precisely a fish, but was a human statue in the form of a fish, fused from the figures of both. Those Rabbis of more refined intellect follow his view. I have thought it necessary to provide Radak’s words:

: אמרו כי דגון מחבורו ולמטה חיה צורת דג לפיכך נקרא דגון ומטבורו ולמעלה צורת אדם כמו שאומר ושתי כפות ידיו כרותות אל המפתן ואו פירושו רק דגון נשאר עליו צורת דג נשאר עליו וי"ת לחות גופיה דגון אשתאר עלוהי :

<margin>Radak.</margin>
*That is: They say that Dagon was composed from the figure of a fish in his lower part, from which he also takes his name; but from the navel toward the upper part, he retained the figure and likeness of a man, according to the text: "the two palms of his hands were cut off upon the threshold." Regarding the phrase,* "only Dagon was left in him," *they explain it thus:* "only the figure of a fish was left in him"; *and Jonathan <note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary.</note> explains it as: "only the body of Dagon remained upon him."* These are the words of Radak. In this description, he not only excellently reconciles the opinions of the Rabbis cited shortly before, but also writes in a manner most consistent with secular history, as we shall see in the following; in which we shall show that the idols of the Goddesses Derceto and Atergatis, who are ancient deities of the Assyrians, were constructed in a similar form.

Lucian.</margin>
Lucian also observed that this was a half-wild girl, stating: <note>original Greek: "Ἡμίσεια μὲν γυνὴ τὸ δὲ ὁπόσον ἐκ μηρῶν εἰς ἄκρους πόδας, ἰχθύος ἀποτάνει."</note> *She was half woman, but from the thighs down to the tips of her feet, she ended in a fish.* Diodorus agrees with this in the second book of his *Library*, where he discusses her statue consecrated in Ascalon: <note>original Greek: "τὸ μὲν πρόσωπον ἔχει γυναικὸς τὸ δὲ σῶμα πᾶν ἰχθύος."</note> *She has the face of a woman,* he says, *but the rest of her entire body is fish-shaped.* He says that Derceto had a woman’s face, but the rest of her body was shaped like a fish. Furthermore, Ctesias, as cited by Strabo, teaches that this Derceto was the same as Atargatis in these words:
<margin>Ctesias. Derceto is the same as Atargatis.</margin>
*He says that there were many changes of names even among the ancients, as when he says Atargatis was called Athara, whom Ctesias called Derceto.* Pliny also mentions the Syrian goddess Derceto or Atargatis in the fifth book of his *Natural History*, as we have learned through the favor of Hermolaus <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493) was a Venetian scholar known for his corrections to the text of Pliny the Elder.</note> in chapter 23: *Bambyce, which is called by another name, Hierapolis, but called Magog by the Syrians; there the prodigious Atargatis (called Derceto by the Greeks) is worshipped.* Furthermore, the name itself clearly reveals that Atargatis is the same as Derceto and Dagon; for the word *Adargatis* is a corrupted form of the same thing as <term>Adir-daga<gloss>אדיר דגא; meaning "magnificent fish" or "mighty fish" in a mix of Hebrew and Aramaic roots</gloss></term>, which signifies a magnificent or powerful fish. The Babylonians proclaimed
<margin>What is Adardaga and from where does it come?</margin>
Dagon or Derceto to be such a creature, just as the people of Sepharvaim honored their own Moloch with the splendid title of <term>Adramelech<gloss>אדרמלך; "Magnificent King"</gloss></term>, that is, a powerful or magnificent King. From these things, it clearly appears that Dagon, Derceto, and Atargatis were the same deity, differing only in name, and we shall show a little later in the following pages that she was none other than the Maritime Venus <note>Venus as a goddess of the sea, often associated with the myth of her birth from the sea foam.</note>. Nor does it stand in the way that Sacred History makes the deity masculine; for this was done for a twofold reason: both because the names of goddesses were never in common use among the Hebrews, and also because among idolaters we see the sex of the gods confused everywhere;
<margin>The Gentiles confused the sex of the Gods.

The Figure of Dagon.</margin>
just as we have already shown in various places regarding a male and female Venus, regarding Juno and the Moon, and similar instances. But let us return to the image of Dagon; that it was a mixture of human and marine forms, like that of Derceto or Atargatis, is sufficiently proven by those things which we have produced both from Holy Scripture and from various authors. However, his body was marine, but his face was human, as were his hands and feet; for Sacred Scripture expressly says that when he fell before the Ark of the Covenant, his hands were cut off or broken off, and nothing remained except "Dagon," or the trunk of the fish. Moreover, it is gathered from the version of the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> that feet were attached to the tail; thus, I believe the figure of Dagon, Derceto, or Atargatis was none other than what we exhibit on the following page.

These things having been thus duly demonstrated, let us now inquire why Dagon, Derceto, or Adardaga was worshipped by the Assyrians under the form of a fish.

<margin>Diodorus Siculus.</margin>
Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian from the 1st century BCE.</note> writes that near the city of Ascalon there was a famous temple of the goddess whom the Syrians called Derceto; this goddess is said to have had a woman’s face, but the rest of her body had the shape of a fish. Her daughter, Semiramis, was raised by doves, which birds are therefore held sacred by the Syrians. Diodorus adds in the same place: *Venus, having once met Derceto, cast upon her a love for a certain youth who was sacrificing to her; when the goddess had a daughter by him, affected by shame for her error, she removed the youth from her presence and exposed the daughter in a deserted and rocky place where huge flocks of doves nested; these doves nourished the girl. Derceto, however, driven by shame and grief, threw herself into a lake*

...she cast herself [into a lake], and was changed into a fish; for which reason, he says, the Syrians abstain from fish and established a temple on the shore of the pond. They worshipped the idol of Derceto with the face of a beautiful woman, but the rest of her parts were those of a fish.

<margin>Nigidius.</margin>
Nigidius <note>Publius Nigidius Figulus (98–45 BCE) was a Roman scholar and Pythagorean philosopher.</note> in his commentaries on the *Phænomena* of Aratus relates another fable to us: namely, that fish in the Euphrates river rolled an egg of marvelous size onto the land, and a dove, having animated it by sitting upon it, <margin>Origin of the worship of doves and fish in Syria.</margin> hatched that Syrian Goddess who is called Venus. For this reason, the fish, having been granted divinity <note>original Latin: *apotheosi affectos*</note>, began to be held in the highest veneration by the Syrians; and the worship of the Fish-shaped Virgin was established from that time. Manilius, in the fourth book of his *Astronomy*, and Hyginus, in his *Astronomicon*, seem to assign a truer cause for this Syrian <term>ichthyolatry|fish-worship</term>.

<margin>Manilius.</margin>
> Indeed, because the Cytherean <note>original: "Cytherea," a common epithet for Venus, named after her island of Cythera.</note> transformed herself into a fish,
> When, submerged, she fled into the Babylonian waves;
> And when Typhon, the serpent-footed one, brought forth his winged claws,
> She entwined her own fires with the scaly fish.

And in the same book, a little later:

> The Euphrates was given to the fish, where the fish-lover
> Venus, when she fled Typhon, settled beneath the waves.

<margin>Diogenetus of Erythrae.</margin>
<margin>Origin of the story about abstaining from fish.</margin>
Ovid also touched upon this fable in his *Fasti*, and Hyginus mentions it twice where he deals with fish. In the first place, he says: Diogenetus of Erythrae <note>An ancient historian who wrote about the history of the East.</note> says that at a certain time Venus came with her son Cupid to the river Euphrates in Syria, and in that same place the giant Typhon <note>A monstrous giant in Greek mythology who challenged the gods.</note> suddenly appeared. Venus, however, threw herself into the river with her son, and there they changed their appearance into the form of fish; by doing this, they were freed from danger. Therefore, afterwards the Syrians who live closest to those places ceased eating fish, because they fear to catch them, lest for a similar reason they might [offend] the protection of the gods...

### CHAPTER XVI. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>
The fable had its origin from the Egyptians.
</margin>
...they might seem to challenge it. But if all these things are discussed more carefully, it will become clearly evident that this entire cult of Venus, Derceto, or Dagon did not flow from anywhere else but from the Egyptians. For Herodotus and Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus (1st century BCE) was a Greek historian; Herodotus (5th century BCE) is often called the Father of History.</note> teach us that in certain Egyptian Nomes <note>administrative districts of ancient Egypt</note>, fish were sacred—namely the Lepidotus, the Phagrus, the Oxyrhynchus, and the Eel. The Phagrus was sacred because it is said to have devoured the private parts <note>original Latin: *pudendum*</note> of Osiris; others, such as Hyginus in the fourth book of his *Astronomy*, say that Isis or Venus transformed herself into the shapes of such fish while fleeing from Typhon <note>the monstrous enemy of the gods in Greek/Egyptian mythology</note>. We have cited the poems just a little before this. Hegesias, cited in Hyginus, indicates that the fish was also sacred to the Egyptians because it saved Isis while she was searching for Osiris, when he treats the "Southern Fish" <note>the constellation Piscis Austrinus</note>: <margin>Hyginus.</margin> <margin>Isis saved by a fish.</margin> *This fish,* he says, *is seen to receive water in its mouth from the sign of Aquarius; it is thought to have once saved Isis when she was in distress, for which benefit he placed the image of the fish and its sons among the stars.* <margin>Fish are held as household gods.</margin> Therefore, many Syrians do not eat fish, and they worship gilded images of them as their household gods <note>original Latin: *Diis penatibus*</note>.

<margin>
Dagon, meaning grain.
</margin>
Moreover, the greatest proof that the cult of Dagon flowed from the Egyptian Osiris and Isis is that Philo of Byblos <note>a grammarian and historian (c. 64–141 CE)</note> says Dagon was the son of Heaven, and was so named from the Hebrew root *Dagan* (דגן), which signifies "grain," because he was the inventor of grain. And therefore, in Greek, he also calls him: *Siton Dagon*, he says, *which is to say, the Provider of Grain* <note>original Greek: Σιτὼν Δαγὼν, ὃς ἐστὶ Σιτὼν</note>. He was also held to be the discoverer of the plow; <margin>Jupiter the Plowman.</margin> and for that reason, he was called *Zeus Arotrios*, as if he were Jupiter the President of Agriculture. Who does not know that Osiris and Isis were the inventors of grain, and were the first to teach the method of cultivating fields among men? Was not <margin>Isis, Ceres.</margin> Isis for that reason called *the giver of grain* <note>original Greek: δῶτις σῖτον</note>, or *Sito*—that is, Ceres—by the Syracusans? Certainly Polemo in his *Banquet of the Sophists* (Book 3), Phornutus, Apollodorus, and other mythologists mention her.

<margin>
Why he is shown in the form of a fish.
</margin>
But the question is asked: why did the Syrians worship her depicted in the form of a fish-man <note>original Greek: ἰχθυανθέρωπος</note>, when we commonly find her distinguished by a spiked crown or bovine horns, and equipped with a sistrum <note>a sacred rattle used in Egyptian ritual</note> in one hand and a bucket in the other? To solve this,

<margin>
Diodorus.
</margin>
it must be noted that the ancient Kings and Queens of the Egyptians had this custom (according to Diodorus) that when returning from war, or from a ritual circuit of the world, they walked dressed in various animal garments, such as the skins of a bull, a lion, an asp, or other monsters—either to inspire terror and admiration among their subjects, or for some other mystical reason and purpose. Various hieroglyphics of this kind show that this custom first flowed from Osiris and Isis, under which you may see Osiris or Isis everywhere, terrible with the tail of a dog, a lion, a cat, a hawk, or most especially an asp or a Nile eel, as will be clearly shown in the following pages. Moreover, the Egyptians say, according to Diodorus, that Osiris and Isis often appeared to men in this form and taught various things necessary to the human race, especially the sciences, as we have shown <margin>What kind of monster was Oannes?</margin> already in many places. All these things seem to have been clearly suggested to us by Berosus <note>a Babylonian priest and historian (3rd century BCE)</note>, Apollodorus, and his Polyhistor, regarding that monster which they call Oannes; they say this animal was two-headed, a fish in its other parts, from whose tail feet similar to human ones grew out; they also attribute to it a human voice; from...

->SYNT. IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS, CHAPTER XVI.<-

...and they say that, having emerged from the Erythraean Sea <note>The "Red Sea" in antiquity often referred to the Indian Ocean or Persian Gulf as well as the modern Red Sea.</note>, he reached Babylonia (understand this as the Babylon of Egypt, namely Memphis or Heliopolis). When the sun set, he returned into the sea, repeating this custom daily like an exchange <note>Greek: *amoibē* (ἀμοίβην)</note>. From him, men learned all kinds of arts, letters, agriculture, the consecration of temples, architecture, and political laws, as well as everything that pertains to civilized life.

<margin>Osiris, appearing to men in various forms, taught various things.</margin>
For it was said in the preceding pages that Osiris devoted himself to astrology in the mountains near the Red Sea, and afterwards entered nearby cities clothed in a lion’s or fish’s skin. By teaching others, he made public those things which he had learned in private; and it is likely that the history, or more truly the fable, of Oannes <note>A mythical half-fish, half-human teacher in Babylonian mythology.</note> originated from this.

Moreover, his statue was preserved until the time of Berosus <note>A Babylonian priest and historian of the 3rd century BCE.</note>, that is, until the beginnings of the Greek Monarchy. We have chosen to transcribe here the words of Berosus, borrowed from Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654), an English polymath and scholar of ancient religions.</note>:

<margin>Berosus from Selden.</margin>
> "The rest of the body was that of a fish, but under the head another head had grown beneath the fish's head, and feet similarly human had grown out from the tail of the fish, and he had the voice of a man. His image is still preserved even now." <note>original Greek: Τὸ μὲν ἄλλο σῶμα ἔχειν ἰχθύος, ὑπὸ δὲ τὴν κεφαλὴν παραπεφυκυῖαν ἄλλην κεφαλὴν ὑποκάτω τῆς τοῦ ἰχθύος κεφαλῆς, καὶ πόδας ὁμοίως ἀνθρώπου παραπεφυκότας δὲ ἐκ τῆς οὐρᾶς τοῦ ἰχθύος, εἶτα δὲ αὐτοῦ φωνὴν ἀνθρώπου. Τῆν δὲ εἰκόνα αὐτοῦ ἔτι καὶ αὐτοῦ νῦν φυλάσσεσθαι.</note>

<margin>Description of Oannes’s form.</margin>
That is: *The rest of the body was indeed that of a fish, the head two-formed, and feet similar to a man's grown from the tail of the fish; his voice was human, and his image is preserved even to this day,* etc. Furthermore, Selden says that Apollodorus, citing the same Berosus, recounts that four creatures called <term>Annedoti</term> <note>A term for the semi-divine fish-teachers; the word suggests something "repulsive" or "unclean" in certain contexts, though here used as a title.</note> appeared from the Red Sea according to the various changes of the ages, each of whom was half-man and half-fish.

<margin>4. Oannes or Annedoti.</margin>
But in the time of King Edorach of the Chaldeans—who, if the Chaldeans are to be believed, lived several centuries after the Flood—he noted that another monster of similar shape emerged, whose name was <term>Odakon</term> <note>original: Ωδάκων</note>, in which name the clear traces of Dagon <note>The Philistine and West Semitic fish-god.</note> appear. According to Selden, Abydenus mentions a second of these Annedoti and attributes the form of a "half-demon" <note>Greek: *himidaimonos* (ἡμιδαίμονος)</note> to him; mention of these is hardly made elsewhere.

<margin>"Ō" is the same as Oannes.</margin>
Whether <term>Ō</term> <note>original: Ωω</note>, whom Helladius of Byzantium mentions, was the same as the Oannes of Berosus is uncertain; but considering all the circumstances of the report made about him, it is probable that he was. For the cited author relates that he rose from the Red Sea with a human head, hands, and feet, while the rest of his limbs resembled a fish; and that he demonstrated letters and the science of the stars. All these are almost the very same details as Berosus’s history of Oannes. Therefore, Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a leading scholar of the Renaissance.</note> perceives the name of Oannes to have been corrupted into "Ō" due to the shorthand writing of scribes. Helladius adds:

<margin>Helladius.</margin>
> "Being entirely a man, he appeared to be a fish because he was clothed in a whale-like skin." <note>original Greek: Ἄνθρωπον δὶ ὄντα τὰ πάντα ἰχθύου δόξαι σωτήρα ἡφίετο κητώδη δορὰν.</note>

That he was entirely a man, but resembled a fish because he was dressed in a whale-like skin. In this description, he quite cleverly alludes to the ancient habit of the Kings of Egypt indicated above, which, since it was mostly fashioned from the skins of beasts, could easily have given occasion for a "multiform" <note>Greek: *polymorphia* (πολυμορφίας)</note> fable of this kind.

<margin>Why did the Syrians abstain from fish?</margin>
Furthermore, as to why we read that the Syrians abstained from eating fish, I think it happened for two main reasons: the first of which is that I find they did it in veneration of Rhea, whom I conflate with Io or Isis. For the Syrians were taught such worship and ceremonies, as well as various other things, by Io or Isis when she traveled through Syria seeking Epaphus; and therefore, in memory of the benefits conferred, [they abstained from] the fish into which, while Typhon was pursuing...

->THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAIC TEMPLE<-

<margin>CHAPTER XVI.</margin>
<margin>Athenaeus.</margin>
...they say she was transformed by Typhon, they abstained from [fish]. Athenaeus relates this somewhat differently; *It was a solemn custom*, he says, *for the Syrians to abstain from fish in veneration of Rhea, who was indeed no other Goddess than Isis, who chiefly rules over the rains; for <term>ῥέω</term> <note>original: "rheo"; Greek for "to flow"</note> is the same as to flow; for they thought the nature of things consisted primarily of water and air, and they worshipped fish in place of water, and the dove in place of air.* So says Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the 'Deipnosophistae'.</note>.

<margin>In the Oxyrhynchite Nome they worshipped a fish, which other Nomes detested.</margin>
But there is another cause: that in all things they studied to imitate the Egyptians, who were celebrated for wisdom and religion. Among the Egyptians, some worshipped a fish with the highest cult as a Goddess, especially in the prefecture or "Nome" of Oxyrhynchus <note>A city in Upper Egypt famous for its archaeological finds; its name means "city of the sharp-snouted fish".</note>; others worshipped it as an adversarial power and the marine offspring of Typhon. This hateful and ill-omened animal they did not so much worship as appease, just as they were accustomed to do with the Crocodile for the same reason. For these reasons, both parties abstained from fish: the latter because it was an evil and accursed thing, the former out of the veneration due to a Deity. But regarding this abstinence, consult Plutarch, Book 8 of the *Table Talk*, Question 8.

<margin>The benefits of Osiris and Isis to the human race.</margin>
And so the Syrians, hearing various things about Osiris and Isis—how he, for instance, traveled the whole world, how he subjugated Ethiopia, India, and other most remote parts of the globe, and finally, having returned to Egypt, enriched it with most salutary laws and the benefits of his inventions, and was at last taken up to govern the heavens; and how she, in her husband's absence, studying the utility of mankind, discovered various things useful for human life, and by her skill in the medical art freed men from infirmity; how she also often appears in dreams to those who invoke her, suggesting various remedies to those suffering from infirmities and diseases. Furthermore, since Osiris was raised in Nysa, a city of Arabia Felix <note>Literal translation: "Happy Arabia"; the fertile southern part of the Arabian Peninsula.</note>—from which he was later called Dionysus—near the Erythraean Sea, he taught men various things, planted vineyards, and tamed wild beasts with tools and weapons, using their skins for clothing. Behold, for these and similar reasons, that fable of Oannes later arose: namely, that a man or two-headed, fish-shaped animal emerged from the Erythraean Sea and taught men various things. Because of these benefits, they later adorned him with divine worship, constructing a <term>ἰχθυομόρφῳ</term> <note>original: "ichthyomorpho"; Greek for "fish-shaped"</note> idol in his honor, and also abstaining from fish, either because they understood the parts of Osiris were devoured by fish, or for other reasons indicated above.

<margin>Various fables emerged from the deeds of Osiris.</margin>
It is no wonder, therefore, if from the various actions and deeds of the Egyptian Gods, related differently by different people, there also arose various cults, various ceremonies, and—what is most important—from monstrous fictions of this kind, monstrous idols also emerged, such as we show above Dagon, Derceto, Atargatis, and Oannes to have been. This is especially true since it was a solemn custom among the Egyptians to combine any animal with a human form in the composition of their idols, as Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher who wrote extensively on Egyptian religion.</note> relates.

<margin>The ambiguity of the names of the Gods and Goddesses confused in Osiris and Isis.</margin>
And from this comes that nearly infinite diversity of idols which the Egyptians and the neighboring nations, their disciples, introduced. This diversity proceeded from nothing other than that <term>πολυωνυμία</term> <note>original: "polyonymia"; Greek for "having many names"</note> by which they titled their Gods, confounding the names of all the Gods in the one Osiris, and the names of all the Goddesses in Isis.

Since these things are so, no one should wonder that Dagon, Derceto, Atargatis, Astarte, Mylitta, and other monsters of names are everywhere confused among authors. For they denoted one Goddess, namely the "Syrian Goddess," whom the Egyptians call Isis; for whether they call her Venus, the Moon, or the Earth...

### SYNT. IV. THE HEBREW PANTHEON. CHAPTER XVI.

<margin>Where does the diversity of images come from?</margin>
<margin>Osiris as the Sun and Isis as the Moon signify diverse powers through such images.</margin>
<margin>The symbolic dress of idols.</margin>
<margin>What Adad is, and his image.</margin>
<margin>The image of Atergatis.</margin>
Whether you speak of Nephtys, Juno, Minerva; or Dagon, Derceto, and Astarte, you will always be speaking of one thing: namely, the Moon, manifold in her power. And from this source, the diversity of images has also arisen, causing various disputes among authors and the greatest confusion in explaining histories. Thus, many authors have established Astarte and Derceto as different deities based on the diversity of their idols; for the latter [Derceto] possessed a fish-shaped statue, while the former [Astarte], as Lucian—an investigator of the sacred rites of both—reports: *The one in the Holy City is entirely a woman* <note>original Greek: "Ἡ δ' ἐν τῇ ἱερῇ πόλει πᾶσα γυνή"</note>, representing a woman completely; yet they are found to be different not so much in essence as in power. In a word: just as the <term>polyonomy</term> <note>The practice of giving many names to a single deity.</note> of Osiris indicates nothing else but the various powers and perfections in the Sun; so the polyonomy of Isis denotes nothing other than the manifold powers and perfections in the Moon. Because of the power by which she moves the force of generation, she is called Venus; because of the power enclosed in the earth, she is called Astarte, Isis, Ceres, or Proserpina; because of the dominion she holds over moisture, she is called Dagon, Derceto, Nephtys, Thetis, and so on for the rest. From this, they also expressed this power through various images. They shadowed forth the power of the Moon on the lands with a crowned head of grain, a cornucopia, a bull's face, and other symbols expressed in the idol; the power of the Moon in the waters by a bucket, fish, and other aquatic creatures; and finally, other perfections of the Moon with other similar symbols. Thus the Assyrians attributed the power over all things to Adad, the name of the God whom Macrobius <note>A Roman provincial who wrote the 'Saturnalia', a source for much solar and lunar mythology.</note> understands as the Sun, and to Atergatis, by which they denoted the Moon or the Earth, the consort of Adad. Therefore they formed the image of Adad with rays pointing downward, by which they showed that the power of heaven resides in the rays of the Sun which are sent down to the earth. But the image of Atergatis, with rays turned upwards, showed that whatever the earth produces is born by the force of the rays sent from above; beneath the same image are the forms of lions, indicating the earth for the same reason that the Phrygians fashioned the Mother of the Gods <note>The goddess Cybele, often depicted with lions.</note>. Indeed, Nigidius also identifies Ceres herself with Atergatis in his commentary on the *Phaenomena* of Aratus. But since we have treated these and similar matters more copiously in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>Kircher's 1650 work 'Obeliscus Pamphilius', interpreting the hieroglyphs on the obelisk in Rome's Piazza Navona.</note>, and have interpreted each point at length, we shall refrain from discussing them further here. One thing remains to be investigated: namely, who is that famous Venus, celebrated throughout all Asia, whom authors are now accustomed to celebrate under the titles of Anaitis, Aphacitis, Cabar, and similar names.

Eusebius explicitly calls the temple of Venus which Constantine the Great destroyed on Mount Lebanon the temple of Aphacitis; with this Macrobius agrees, who [describes] the temple also...

### CHAPTER XVI. 346 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAK TEMPLE

<margin>Macrobius on the shrine of Venus Anaitis.</margin>
Macrobius also mentions the famous shrine of Venus Architis on Mount Lebanon (a name I believe is corrupted and should have the name "Aphacitis" substituted for it); I will add his words: 
> There will be no doubt that Adonis is also the Sun, if one examines the religion of the Assyrians, among whom the greatest veneration of Venus Architis and Adonis once flourished, which the Phoenicians now hold. <note>Macrobius was a 5th-century Roman official and writer; Kircher is citing his *Saturnalia*, which sought to prove all gods were aspects of the Sun.</note>

And a little later: <margin>The Statue of Venus Anaitis.</margin>
> *The image of this Goddess on Mount Lebanon is fashioned with a veiled head, a sad appearance, holding her face within her cloak with her left hand; tears are believed to flow in the sight of those looking on.* 

From this description, surely nothing else is indicated to us but that Thamuz <note>Tammuz</note>, or Adonis, or Adad, or Osiris, whom we previously mentioned when discussing Thamuz, was fashioned with a weeping appearance, and whom the Egyptians (and the Assyrians taught by them) were accustomed to bewail. <margin>Venus Aphacitis.</margin> And Venus Aphacitis, the spouse of Adonis, or Isis the wife of Osiris, whom we also called Astarte above; with whom we previously identified Dagon, Derceto, and Atargatis. <margin>Dagon, the fish of sorrow.</margin> For Saint Jerome calls Dagon the "fish of sorrow" for no other reason than because of the frequent lamentations that were offered to him in his sacred rites. <margin>Artemidorus.</margin> Moreover, Artemidorus makes Dagon, Derceto, or Atargatis the same as Astarte or Venus Aphacitis, because the same ceremonies belonged to both: both had sacred fish and doves, and both were worshiped by abstaining from eating fish. For he says in Book 1, Chapter 9 of his *Interpretation of Dreams*: *All Syrians eat fish, except for some who worship Astarte.*

<margin>Venus Anaitis. Strabo.</margin>
Furthermore, Strabo writes about Venus Anaitis (so called by the Persians) in Book 12, dealing with the city of Zela, once famous and sacred. 
> *In it,* he says, *is the temple of Anaitis, who is worshiped by the Armenians; in this place, sacred rites were celebrated with the greatest holiness, and oaths regarding the most important matters were made here.*

The same Strabo, in Book 15, dealing with Cappadocia, says: 
> *These sacred rites are performed in the shrines of Anaitis and Amanus, for their shrines are there, and the Statue of Amanus is led in a procession.*

And Strabo himself writes that he saw these things. <margin>The rites of Anaitis are called Saca.</margin> Indeed, the sacred rites of this Goddess Anaitis were called "Saca," and the festival day "Saca," because on that day King Cyrus had conquered the Sacae. Others write, moreover, that the ancients dedicated girls from the more prominent families to this Goddess to serve as prostitutes; these were later given to men as if they were sacred, and husbands received them joyfully. <margin>Hermolaus.</margin> We will deal with these matters more fully in the following pages. Hermolaus, following Pausanias in his *Description of Laconia*, reports that the Cappadocians and those who dwell near the Black Sea are in doubt, because there is an image of this Goddess also among the Lydians, which is the <term>Sanctuary of Artemis Anaitis</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀρτέμιδι ἱερὸν Ἀναιτίδι</note>. But if we examine her sacred rites a little more carefully, and that golden statue which they called <term>holosphyraton</term> <note>A technical term meaning a statue made of solid metal, hammered into shape rather than cast hollow.</note> placed in her temple, we conclude that she is surely the same as that common Venus of Asia, differing only in name and worshipers. But I leave all these things for you to compare among themselves, lest I be too long in a matter that is quite clear.

<margin>Who is the goddess Cabar?</margin>
Furthermore, who that "Cabar" might have been—mention of whom is made in the books of the Arabs and Saracens—presents a slightly greater difficulty. To solve this:

<margin>Before the arrival of Muhammad, the Nations worshiped Kabar.</margin>
It must be noted that before the arrival of the impure Muhammad, most Saracens and Ishmaelites (whom they also call Arabs) were pagans and devoted to the wicked worship of idols. Among other gods, they worshiped Cabar <note>original Arabic: **كبير**, meaning "The Great" or "The Great One." In pre-Islamic Arabia, this often referred to the goddess Al-Uzza.</note>, whom they interpret as either Venus or the Morning Star <note>original: "Luciferum"</note>; he mentions...

### SYNT[AGMA] IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER XVI. 347

<margin>Euthymius Zygabenus.</margin>
Euthymius Zygabenus <note>A 12th-century Byzantine monk and theologian known for his work *Panoplia Dogmatica*.</note> says in Part 2, title 24: *“The Saracens <note>A medieval term for Arabs.</note> until the times of the Emperor Heraclius worshiped idols, adoring both Lucifer <note>The morning star, Venus.</note> and Venus, whom in their own language they call Chamar (read "Cabar" in place of the corrupted word), which signifies 'Great.'”* The Catechism of the Saracens also shows that when Saracens were brought back to the true law, they were accustomed to abjure all the Gods they had learned from the Gentiles; among the rest, special mention is made of Lucifer or Venus, whom they called *Cabar*. I will subjoin the words of the renunciation: <margin>The Muslims are accustomed to abjuring "Cabari."</margin> "I anathematize those who worship the morning star, Lucifer and Venus, whom in the language of the Arabs they call Chabar, that is, 'Great.'" <note>Original Greek: Ἀναθεματίζω τὸν τῷ ἑωϊνῷ προσκυνοῦντας ἀστρῷ τῷ Ἑωσφόρῳ, καὶ τῇ Ἀφροδίτῃ, ἣν καὶ τῇ Ἀράβων γλώσσῃ Χαβὰρ ὀνομάζουσι, τουτέστι μεγάλω.</note> Even children know that Lucifer and Venus are one and the same star. Cedrenus <note>George Kedrenos, an 11th-century Byzantine historian.</note> mentions this Saracen Goddess, and among other arguments by which he proves that the Muslims still worshiped false powers, he brings forward this one: that they worshiped the Venus or Lucifer of the Greeks with divine honors. His words are:

<margin>Cedrenus.</margin>
> *For of old they were idolaters, worshiping the one called Aphrodite by the Greeks—that is, "Pleasure"—and they mythologized about her star, Lucifer, in the dawn. Therefore, naming it "Kebar" in their own foul-sounding tongue, which means 'Great,' they have continued until now to call Venus a God. Lest we seem to some to be speaking falsely, let us explain their great mystery. The wording of their foul and most profane prayer is as follows: 'Alla, Alla, and Kybar, Alla.' Now "Alla, Alla" is interpreted as 'God, God,' and the "and" [wa] as 'Greater.' And "Kybar" means 'Great,' namely the Moon and Venus. Thus it means: 'God, God is greater and the great one'; thus Venus is God, and this is made clear by the addition of the far-shining 'Alla.' All these things they speak in a hidden way through the character of their own language.* <note>Kircher provides a lengthy Greek passage from Cedrenus and then his own Latin translation below it.</note>

<margin>The words of the invocation of Cabar.</margin>
*For since ancient times, led astray by false superstition, they worshiped the Venus of the Greeks (that is, "Pleasure") with divine honors, and they fabled that her star was Lucifer, which they also called "Kubar" from its greatness in their clumsy language; to this very day they attribute the name of God to Venus. Lest we seem to anyone to be inventing this, we shall explain their great mystery; the words of their obscene and most profane prayer are these:* <margin>The invocation of Cabar.</margin> اللہ اللہ وکبر اللہ [*Allah Allah wa Kubar Allah*]. *If you interpret "Allah Allah," it is 'God, God'; "wa Kubar," that is 'Great,' or the Moon and Venus, 'God'; so it goes: 'God, God, greater and great,' namely Venus the God. And this "Allah" added at the end indicates that they pronounce all these things hidden by the property of their own speech.* Thus far Cedrenus. In this recitation, I find that some things crept in due to Cedrenus's ignorance of the Arabic language, which I have thought should be corrected before we proceed further. The first is that he calls Venus "Kubar," contrary to the common pronunciation of the Arabs, who pronounce these Arabic words thus: اللہ اللہ وکبر اللہ *Allah Allah wa Kabar Allah*; it is not, therefore, *Kubar*, but *Kabar* <note>كبر - k-b-r, the root for "great" or "large."</note>, which properly signifies "Great," by which that Power is named. Truly, he is to be forgiven for this, as one who did not understand the pronunciation of the Arabs. The other error does not deserve excuse: that he understands the comparative <note>i.e., "greater"</note> through the particle **و** <note>the Arabic letter 'wa', meaning 'and'</note> or the copulative; for he asserts this word is the same as "Greater," just as "Kubar" is the same as "Great"; as if it were said: "God, God, and Greater, Kubar, Great Venus." Certainly even children know that **و** [wa] in the Arabic language serves only the function of a conjunction, nor does it possess any other meaning by itself outside of a sentence. Whence much...

THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

## CHAPTER XVI.

Constantine Porphyrogenitus <note>A 10th-century Byzantine Emperor and author.</note> speaks more appropriately regarding this Arabian deity in his book *On Administering the Roman Empire*, chapter 14, where he deals with the genealogy of Muhammad, writing as follows:

<margin>Constantine Porphyrogenitus</margin>

> "They also worship the star of Venus, which they call Chabar, and they cry out in their prayer thus: *Alla oua Chabar*, which means, 'God is Venus'; for they call God *Alla*, and they use *oua* in place of the conjunction 'and,' and they call the star *Chabar*. And so they say: *Alla oua Chabar*." <note>Original Greek: Προσκύνουσι δὲ καὶ εἰς τὸ τῆς Ἀφροδίτης ἄστρον, ὃ καλοῦσι Χαβὰρ, καὶ ἀναφωνοῦσιν ἐν τῇ προσευχῇ αὐτῶν οὕτως· Ἀλλὰ οὐὰ Χαβὰρ, ὅ ἐστιν, ὁ Θεὸς ἡ Ἀφροδίτη· Τὸν γὰρ Θεὸν Ἀλλὰ προσονομάζουσι, Τὸ δὲ οὐὰ ἀντὶ τοῦ καὶ συνδέσμου τιθέασι· καὶ τὸ Χαβὰρ καλοῦσι τὸ ἄστρον. καὶ λέγουσιν οὕτως. Ἀλλὰ οὐὰ Χαβὰρ.</note>

> *He says, "They adore the star of Venus also, which they call Cabar, and while praying they exclaim thus: Allah va Kabar, that is, God is Venus; for they call God Allah, but they place Va for the conjunction 'And'; Cabar denotes the star; thus they say:* الله وكبر <note>Arabic: Allah wa-kbar</note> *Allah va Kabar. However, it is written* كبر <note>Kabar</note> *in the masculine gender, not the feminine* كبيرة <note>Kabirat</note>, *because they have no distinction of sex among the Gods, just as we said the rest of the Easterners did. This is not unlike the star of Venus, which is everywhere called by both sexes—Lucifer, Hesperus, and Venus—among astronomers. With these things established, let us now discuss who this Goddess was."*

<margin>
Bacchus and Urania: the Gods of the Arabs.
<br/>
Herodotus.
<br/>
The sex of the Gods.
</margin>
Certainly, we read that the Gods of the ancient Arabs were only Bacchus and Urania <note>The personification of the Heavens</note>, whom we called *Alilath* above, according to the testimony of Herodotus and Celsus (as quoted by Origen). Since *Cabar* is considered one among the other deities of the Arabs or Saracens, it is necessary that *Cabar*, *Alilath*, and *Urania-Venus* are the same entity. Herodotus, speaking of the Urania of the Persians, clearly indicates that she is the same Goddess of the Assyrians and Arabs, because the Persians learned the entire cult of Urania from them: *“They learned to sacrifice to Urania from both the Assyrians and the Arabs.”* <note>Original Greek: Ἐπιμεμαθήκασι τῇ Οὐρανίῃ θύειν παρά τε Ἀσσυρίων μαθόντες, καὶ Ἀραβίων.</note> But it is also helpful here to remember the sex of the Gods. For that Urania was also called both Uranus and Jupiter by the ancients. He is called *Uranus* by Arrian, but *Jupiter* by Strabo; yet both write that only two deities were worshiped by them, and they name the other one Dionysus or Bacchus. As for the fact that Stephanus confuses *Uranius* with *Oboda*, he should not be thought to have done so as if he were establishing a different deity from Bacchus, but only one different in name.

<margin>Uranius is the Sun, and Cabar is the Moon.</margin>
Since that *Uranius* of the Arabs is nothing other than the Sun, certainly *Urania* or *Kabar* will be nothing other than the Moon. The former is everywhere called among the Arabs بعل سما <note>Ba'al Sama</note>, that is, *Lord of Heaven*; the latter is called بعلة سما <note>Ba'alath Sama</note>, or commonly *Belisama*, *Lady of Heaven*. The former, because of his power and magnitude, is called كبر <note>Kabar</note>, that is, *Great*; the latter, for the same reason, is called كبيرة <note>Kabiret</note>, the *Great [Female]*. Therefore, these two great luminaries were those first deities of the ancient Arabs, of whom we spoke shortly before.

<margin>Why was Cabar called Venus?</margin>
Regarding the fact that some assert *Cabar* to be Venus, I believe this happened because Venus and the Moon, due to the similarity of the effects they produce, are everywhere taken for one and the same. On this matter, an ancient Greek writer is a brilliant witness:

<margin>Philochorus.</margin>
This is Philochorus <note>An Athenian historian and mythographer of the 3rd century BCE.</note>, who affirms that Venus and the Moon are the same; and that men perform sacrifices to her in women's clothing, and women in men's, because she is estimated to be both male and female. Rambam <note>Moses Maimonides, the 12th-century Jewish philosopher.</note> also mentions this in *The Guide for the Perplexed*.

<margin>Rambam, Book 3, Chapter 38.</margin>
> "You will find it in the ninth book of the *Mofat* [Laws] where it commands that a man should wear the colored garment of a woman [when standing before the star of Venus]..." <note>Original Hebrew: תמצאהו בספר ט' מפט יצוה שילבש האיש בגד אשה צבוע. Maimonides is discussing the forbidden "Sabian" rites of cross-dressing during planetary worship.</note>

<margin>The Unknown God.</margin>
Furthermore, as to why **Cabar** <note>A reference to Al-Uzza, "The Great One."</note> (Venus) and **Dysares** <note>Dushara, a chief deity of the Nabataeans, often represented by a stone block.</note> (Mercury) were worshipped under the form of this kind of quadrangular stone, I find no other cause for this matter except the custom of the **Egyptians**. <margin>The cause of Muhammad’s flight.</margin>
> And Muhammad rose in the night after the New Moon fleeing from **Mecca** because of those who were infidels before, and they tasted the penalty of their business, and for them a penalty full of pain, because their Apostles came to them with contracts <note>Kircher uses "contractibus" here to translate the Arabic 'clear signs' or 'proofs'.</note>, and they said, "Shall men direct us?" and they were infidels, and they turned their backs, and they despised his law, plotting against his life, and for that reason he was forced to flee.

From this flight, all the followers of Muhammad today calculate their years, and they call them <term>The Year of the Flight</term> <note>original: "سنة الهجرة" (Senathil hegira-thi)</note>, or <term>The Chronology of the Flight</term> <note>original: "تاريخ الهجرة" (Tarichil hegirathi)</note>—a most auspicious law indeed, which begins from a flight, and for fleeing scoundrels! But I would consider this a pure lie; for <term>Hegirath</term> <note>original: "هجرة"</note> is the name of the **Hagarene** people and the region 
<margin>Hegirath named not from "flight," but from Hagar.</margin>
to which Mecca is also assigned. Therefore, that era is not the "era of flight," but the "Hagarene era"; however, since the Arabs themselves interpret it as "flight," let it indeed be a flight, and let all the followers of Muhammad flee where and as much as they please. We, however, shall assert that antiquity is safe from their lies; we know that the word in its original sense is derived from the **Hagarenes**, not from a flight. Therefore, the worship of the **Moon** along with the **Lunar era** did not proceed from the followers of Muhammad, nor from the flight of a wicked impostor, but from the Hagarenes or **Ishmaelites**, who were much older than Muhammad. This will be easily gathered by anyone who reads that the ornaments of this sickle-shaped Moon were the symbols of the nation for the ancient Kings of the Ishmaelites and their camels.

### OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: THE TEMPLE OF ISIS

<margin>
CHAPTER XVI.

Friday is this solemn day for the Mohammedans.

...as if it were their own; indeed, the Arabs call the sixth day, which is called the day of Venus [Friday], *Yaum al-Jum’ah* <note>original: "يوم الجمعة" (ium algiumah)</note>, which signifies a gathering <note>original: "συνάξιν" (synaxin)</note>, an assembly <note>original: "ἐκκλησίαν" (ekklesian)</note>, a sermon, a discourse, or a meeting. This is the day they hold in the same regard as we hold the Lord's Day [Sunday] and the Jews hold the Sabbath. I say that this Friday and its solemnity flowed from no other source than the Hagarenes <note>The descendants of Hagar; a common historical term for the Arabs.</note>, as is clear from the fact that no mention of the celebration of this day is found in the Mohammedan law <note>The Quran.</note>. Therefore, the Mohammedans adopted it from the most ancient rite of the Saracens. For the Saracens, according to the testimony of Politiano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), an Italian humanist scholar.</note>, once celebrated the sixth day as sacred to the Supreme Goddess, imitating the Egyptians, as will be discussed in its proper place. They did this primarily because the dominion of Venus falls on the first hour of that day, and the dominion of the Moon falls on the last hour. That this is true is clear from the arrangement of the planets occurring during the hours of that day. Since a natural day contains 24 hours, it is necessary that if on the Sabbath [Saturday] the first hour is ruled by Saturn (from whom the day of Saturn is named), then on the following day, the first hour is ruled by the planet following in reverse order, skipping two: namely the Sun, from which the day of the Sun [Sunday] is named. Similarly, on the next day the Moon rules, whence the day of the Moon [Monday], and so on through the rest until Friday, on which the first hour falls to Venus, the second to Mercury, and so on through the others until the twenty-fourth hour, which the Moon will occupy, as appears in the example placed here:

Friday, therefore, seems to have been established by the Hagarenes for a mystical reason: so that in it **Cabar** (or that Venus the "Dawn-bringer" <note>original: "Ἑωσφόρος" (Heosphoros)</note>) would inaugurate the first hour, while the Moon (or **Alilath**, the celestial Urania) would close the day by occupying the last hour; the former as the president of the day, the latter of the night. And although these were once distinct planets among the Eastern astronomers, they were gradually confused by their successors, creating such confusion that they everywhere took Venus and the Moon for one and the same Goddess. Furthermore, another cause of this confusion could be that the ancient Arab astronomers, according to Hyparchus <note>Hipparchus of Nicaea, the ancient Greek astronomer.</note>, also called Venus the "Moon." Was it perhaps because those lynx-eyed <note>A metaphor for being sharp-sighted, referring to the mythical Lynceus.</note> astrologers once detected Venus mimicking the crescent phases of the Moon? Certainly, we showed above in our introduction that many things were once known that we now gaze upon with great wonder as if they were new and recently invented. For why could the ancient Arabs not have discovered the phenomena of Venus increasing and decreasing, putting on the face of the Moon—which were only first discovered in this century with the aid of the telescope—since they combined an ingenuity of mind for observing the stars with continuous vigils, and enjoyed pure air, subject to no hazy obstructions? SYNT. IV. PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. 353 CHAPTER XVII.

We will not dwell further on these conjectures, leaving everyone free to believe what they wish. From all that has been so extensively demonstrated thus far, gather this one point: that "Cabar" <note>original: "Cabar"; likely referring to the Arabic "Al-Kabar" or "Al-Uzza," meaning "The Great."</note> of the Arabs is nothing other than the common Asiatic Venus, the celestial Urania, whom the Egyptians call Isis, the Babylonians Dagon, Derceto, or Atargatis, the Phoenicians Astarte, and whom the Greeks call now the Moon, now Hecate, Lucina, Diana, Proserpina; the Arabs also call her by another name, *Alilath* <note>Al-Lat</note>. In reality, she is the same deity, with the diversity of names merely denoting a diversity of effects. This is treated more fully in my *Egyptian Mystagogy* of the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, where we have explored the mystical meanings of these names more profoundly. Now, to other matters.

# CHAPTER XVII.

### *The Colony of Babylonian Gods brought by Shalmaneser into Samaria.*

Shalmaneser, King of the Assyrians, when he had finally brought Samaria into his power along with its inhabitants—after it had been exhausted by that long three-year siege—and lest the stubbornness of that intractable people cause him any further trouble, he instituted an exchange of colonies. He sent the Samaritans, as if they were treacherous men, away into the cities of the Medes. In their place, he summoned men from Babylon, from Cutha (from which the Samaritans were later also called <term>Cutheans</term>), from Avva, from Hamath, and from Sepharvaim, and gave them the Samaritan cities and the entire region to inhabit. 

When this was done, as the Holy Scripture says, each nation made its own gods and placed them in the temples of the high places which the Samaritans had made; each nation did so in the cities where they lived. The men of Babylon made *Succoth Benoth*; the men of Cuth made *Nergal*; the men of Hamath made *Ashima*; the Avvites made *Nibhaz* and *Tartak*; and those of Sepharvaim burned their children in 
<margin>The Babylonians as imitators of the Egyptians.</margin>
fire to *Adrammelech* and *Anammelech*, the gods of Sepharvaim. Thus, according to the diversity of nations and cities, the Babylonians established various gods in Samaria. In this, they were imitating the Egyptians, who, according to the diversity of their <term>Nomes</term> <note>Nomes were the administrative districts of ancient Egypt, each with its own local patron deity.</note> or cities, also worshiped different deities, as was shown in the preceding pages. From these examples, the Hebrews were later instructed and received these <term>Toparchs</term> <note>Guardian deities of a specific place or "topos."</note> as gods into their own cities as well. 
<margin>Jeremiah c. 2. v. 28.</margin>
Jeremiah seems to reproach them for this madness when he says: 
> *Where are your gods that you made for yourself? Let them arise and deliver you in the time of your affliction; for according to the number of your cities were your gods, O Judah.* <note>original: "Vbi sunt Dij tui, quos fecisti tibi? surgant & liberent te in tempore afflictionis tuæ; secundùm numerum quippè ciuitatum tuarum erant Dij tui Iuda."</note>

For as <note>Kircher refers to the medieval Jewish commentators Rashi and Radak.</note> Rashi and Radak rightly observe on this passage: 
> *In each and every city, there was one god.*

<margin>
The Devil is the Ape of God.

Just as we read everywhere that the Hebrews suffered various calamities whenever they neglected the worship of the true God, so too did the Devil—the <term>Ape of God<note>original Latin: *Diabolus Dei Simia*. This was a common theological concept suggesting that the Devil mimics God’s actions to lead people into superstition or idolatry.</note></term>—inflict various miseries upon the Gentiles whenever they grew lax in their idol worship. He did this so that, being convinced they were dealing with an angry Deity, he might bind them even more tightly to the false worship of gods. To appease these spirits, there was nothing so monstrous, nothing so impious or cruel, that they would not undertake it. For the sake of reconciling with them, they spared no honor, no reputation, no wealth, nor even their own children (whom they loved most dearly, as we saw in the discussion of the sacrifices to <term>Moloch<note>An ancient deity associated with child sacrifice.</note></term>). But having noted these things in passing, let us now return to those colonies of gods brought from Babylon to Samaria. It is clear from the passage of sacred history cited above that each nation built its own idols in Samaria. The time has come to explain what kind of idols these were, beginning with Succoth Benoth.

## CHAPTER XVIII.

->Succoth Benoth, the Idol of the Babylonians.<-

<margin>
Succoth Benoth.
</margin>
<margin>
What is Succoth Benoth?
</margin>
The proper meaning of Succoth Benoth is a matter of dispute among authors. Some, including <term>Selden<note>John Selden, a 17th-century scholar of ancient Near Eastern religions.</note></term>, believe that Succoth Benoth refers not so much to a specific God or Goddess, but rather to the temple itself and the sacred rites and ceremonies performed there. They argue that Succoth Benoth was nothing other than the temple of <term>Mylitta<note>The Babylonian name for Venus.</note></term>, also known as the Celestial Venus or Urania. In this temple, girls wearing wreaths sat in individual spaces separated by ropes, waiting for guests. Once a man had properly invoked the "Venus Mylitta" and paid a small amount of money (which was considered sacred to the Goddess), he would lead the girl away from the temple to have relations with her.
<margin>
A shameful custom.
</margin>
No woman was allowed to leave until someone had chosen her for these Venus-like acts according to the ritual. Consequently, it often happened that some women—especially those who were unattractive or unfortunate—would wait for two or even three years. According to the law of their country, it was mandatory for all women to sit there once in their lives and have relations with strangers. However, the wealthier women would arrive in covered, arched carriages, leaving a large crowd of servants behind them, and take their place in front of the temple. These assertions are grounded in the accounts collected from Herodotus and Strabo.
<margin>
What kind of idol Succoth Benoth was.
</margin>
However, it is so certain that Succoth Benoth was a physical idol that I believe anyone who thinks otherwise contradicts the truth of sacred history itself, since the Holy Scripture indicates in plain words that it was a graven image:

> <note>original Hebrew: "And every nation made gods of their own, and put them in the houses of the high places which the Samaritans had made, every nation in their cities wherein they dwelt. And the men of Babylon made Succoth Benoth." (2 Kings 17:29-30)</note>

# SYNOPSIS IV. THE HEBREW PANTHEON. CHAPTER XVIII.

"And every nation," he says, "fashioned its own god, and they placed them in the shrines of the high places which the Samaritans had built; every nation in their own cities in which they lived. The men of Babylon, however, made **Succoth Benoth**, etc." In this passage, **Succoth Benoth** can by no means be understood as a "shrine" or "tent," since the idols are said to have been made and then *placed inside* the shrines themselves—unless one were to argue that a shrine was placed inside a shrine, which I would call the claim of a fool rather than a wise man. Nor can the term refer to ceremonies, since the verb "to fashion" or "to make" hardly fits such a meaning. It remains, therefore, that **Succoth Benoth** was an idol. Furthermore, the only difficulty lies in determining which idol it was. <term>Selden<note>John Selden (1584–1654) was an English polymath and scholar of ancient Near Eastern religions, famous for his work *De Diis Syris* (On the Syrian Gods).</note></term> too rigidly dismisses the opinion of the Hebrews in this matter, who assert it was the figure of a **Hen**. I, however, am so far from rejecting that view that I support it, as they say, <term>with hands and feet<note>original Latin: *manibus, pedibusque*. An idiom meaning "wholeheartedly" or "with all one's might."</note></term>; for that interpretation is most consistent with the teachings not only of the Arabs and Assyrians, but also of the Egyptians. But before we demonstrate this, I shall first cite the opinions of the Rabbis here. **Radak**, commenting on this passage, speaks as follows:

<margin>
The idol Succoth Benoth is a Hen with her chicks.
</margin>

<margin>
Radak:
</margin>
<note>Radak is the acronym for Rabbi David Kimhi, a medieval Jewish biblical commentator and grammarian.</note> [**Succoth Benoth**] This was the name of the idol that they worshipped in their land. We see that the idol of the Babylonians in the time of King Nebuchadnezzar was, according to the Scripture, **Bel**, as the text says: *Bel bows down, Nebo stoops* [Isaiah 46:1]. But in the days of the King of the Assyrians, their idol was **Succoth Benoth**. Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, say that **Succoth Benoth** was a **Hen**—that is to say, they worshipped an idol in the likeness of a hen, and its name was Succoth Benoth. And just as they call a cock *Sekvi* <note>original Hebrew: שכוי (*Sekhvi*), a word for rooster or heart/intellect found in Job 38:36.</note>, so they called the hen *Succoth*, and *Benoth* (daughters) refers to her chicks.

> [**Succoth Benoth**,] this was the name of the idol which they worshipped in their land; we see that the idol of the Babylonians, in the time of King Nebuchadnezzar, according to the scripture, was **Bel**; but in the time of the King of the Assyrians, they had an idol by the name of **Succoth Benoth**. Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, say that **Succoth Benoth** was a **Hen**; as if to say, they worshipped an image of a **Hen** under the name **Succoth Benoth**. For just as they call the Cock *Succui* <note>original Hebrew: *Sekhvi*</note>, that is, "the one who covers/observes," so they called the Hens *Succoth*, as if they were "brooders" and "coverers," and they explained *Benoth* as her "daughters," or her chicks, whom they are accustomed to cherish and cover with their wings. **Rashi** agrees with this in the same place:

From this description by the Rabbis, I conclude that **Succoth Benoth** was nothing other than an image of the **Celestial Venus** (whom we have previously called **Alitta** among the Arabs, and **Mylitta** and **Ilythia** among the Syrians) fashioned in the form of a Hen with her chicks. To make this clear:

It must be noted that the ancient astrologers of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Arabs—through frequent inspection and long observation of the celestial bodies—discovered that part of the Zodiac which the ancients marked with the title of **Taurus** to be, among the other <term>twelve signs<note>original Greek: δωδεκάμορια (*dodekamoria*), referring to the twelve 30-degree divisions of the zodiac.</note></term>, the most vital. For in this sign, the Sun being positioned, it fills all things with vital heat and moisture; in this sign, the earth, clothed in a green garment, presents itself as if in a theater to be viewed by mortals.

### CHAPTER XVIII. 356 THE ISIAIC TEMPLE OF OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS

<margin>Why the ancients held the sign of Taurus in such high regard.</margin>
...it provides a certain [influence], where trees spreading with luxuriant branches show a hint of internal fertility; indeed, birds and all other animals, stirred by the itch of Venus, contemplate prolific mating. In this sign, the ancients believed something lay hidden beyond the usual conditions of nature, so much so that they called it nothing less than the "House of the Gods." Specifically, they called it the House of the Exalted Moon, because it fell most heavily under the dominion of the Moon; and the proper House of Venus, because all lower things seemed to swell with fertile moisture when the Sun was positioned within it.

<margin>What the Pleiades signified.</margin>
Since the sign of Taurus shines everywhere with stars of extraordinary beauty, I find that those seven—which modern astronomers call the Pleiades, or <term>Succulae<note>Literally "Little Pigs," a traditional Latin name for the Pleiades, though many ancient authors debated whether the name came from the word for "swine" or "moisture."</note></term>, or Piglets—were called by the name of the **Hen** by the ancients. This was partly because they resembled a Hen with her chicks, and partly because Venus, the <term>Mistress of the House<note>original Greek: *Οἰκοδέσποινα* (Oikodespoina)</note></term> of this <term>dodecatemory<note>A 30-degree division of the Zodiac, i.e., one of the twelve signs.</note></term>, seems to imitate a hen in fostering and sustaining lower creatures with fertile moisture and heat.

<margin>The Celestial Hen.</margin>
For the hen is an animal that is quite lustful, fertile, and <term>loving of its offspring<note>original Greek: *φιλόστοργον* (philostorgon)</note></term>; these qualities especially suit Venus, specifically the one we have called <term>Ilithyia<note>original Greek: *ἰληθεῖαν*. The goddess of childbirth.</note></term> or **Mylitta** on account of her role in birthing. For this very reason, the Hebrews not inappropriately judged that this constellation should be called עיש (*Ash*), which is to say, "from gathering." For just as a hen fosters her gathered chicks, so Venus **Succoth Benoth** is the gatherer and fosterer of all things in the world. Hence, this constellation is aptly called by the Hebrews the "consistency of the age."

<margin>The Pleiades are called the consistency of the age.</margin>
Among all the constellations, this one is held as the most renowned in the Sacred Scriptures, as in Job chapters 9 and 38, and likewise in Amos 5. In these places, mention is made everywhere of the Pleiades and Orion under the names עיש (*Asch*), or כימה (*Cima*), and כסיל (*Kesil*). Regarding these, the Rabbi <term>Rashi<note>Kircher writes "Rassi," referring to the famous medieval commentator Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki.</note></term> comments on Amos 5 as follows:

<margin>Explanation of the names.</margin>
> "[He who] makes the Pleiades and Orion." Job mentions these stars, he says, because in them is the consistency of fruits or yields in their proper seasons; and these preserve the world and its laws by the contrary qualities in which they excel. Job does not mention the Sun and the Moon, even though in them lies the consistency of the age, because they rule the entire year, whereas those constellations are rulers of recognized seasons within the year, and are necessary to the world and its laws. Our Rabbis of blessed memory say that the Pleiades (or **Succoth Benoth**) is a cold constellation and acts as a sort of "binding" for the fruits; whereas Orion (or *Kesil*) is a warm constellation, bringing them to maturity. They also say that the constellation of the Pleiades is the final part, or the tail, of **Aries**. To this latter point, **Rabbi Ibn Ezra** agrees:

Ash, he says, is a constellation consisting of seven stars in the sign that is called Taurus in the Arabic language. And in Amos chapter 5:

<margin>The stars of the Pleiades show the shape of a Hen with chicks.</margin>
->Ash and the stars in the sign of Taurus; its form is a hen with her chicks.<-

“Ash,” he says, “are seven stars in the sign of Taurus, whose shape is like a hen with her chicks.” He seems to have gathered this assertion from the Arabs, who call this constellation of the Pleiades sometimes <note>original Arabic: الثريא</note> *Al-Thurayya* (the Abundant), sometimes <note>original Arabic: الدجاجة</note> *Al-Dajajah* (the Hen), but most frequently <note>original Arabic: بنات النعش</note> *Banat Na'sh*, which means “the daughters of the bier” <note>Kircher translates this as "daughters of sustenance" to link it to his theory of Succoth Benoth, though it traditionally refers to the stars of the Big Dipper</note>; with this word they allude very closely to the name Succoth Benoth. But let us hear Alhaghi Ben Joseph <note>likely referring to the astronomer Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf ibn Matar</note>, who says thus in his *Arabic Astronomy*:

<margin>Alshagi Ben Ioseph.</margin>
->The sign of Taurus; in it is the house of Venus, mistress of the blood, and from ten days within it the Pleiades or the Daughters of the Bier arise; it is good therein for sea travel and sowing, and for carrying out every work of agriculture.<-
<note>original Arabic: برجا الثور فيه بيت الزهرة سلطانة الدم والعشرة ايام منه تطلع الثريا اوبنات نعش ويصلح فيه ركوب البحر وزروع</note>

<margin>The Pleiades contribute to agriculture.</margin>
Regarding the sign of Taurus: the house of Venus is within it; it rules over the blood (namely, that which is moist and warm), and from ten days after this point, *Altaria* <note>a variant of Al-Thurayya</note> or *Benath Algnasch* arises. It is good in that sign to complete maritime journeys, to sow, to practice every work of agriculture, and work suitable for Venus. Therefore, one may call this Succoth Benoth, or *Benat Algnasch*, or by another name, the Celestial Venus. Aelian, in particular, testifies with these words that she was once held in great veneration by the Egyptians: *They used to worship this Venus Urania religiously and most holily in a village called Shusa—not a large one, to be sure, but certainly elegant—which was counted in the Hermopolitan Nome, that is, the Prefecture.* For the same reason, they venerated the Cow or the Bull, both because of the celestial house of Taurus over which she presides, and because of the affinity and suitability which this animal is thought to have with the Goddess herself.

<margin>The lustfulness of cattle.</margin>
For an animal of this kind is incited toward Venus with such great force that when the female hears the lowing of the male, she is most vehemently inflamed for mating. For the same reason, I find that roosters and hens were sacred to the Egyptians.

<margin>Hens were offered to Osiris and Isis.</margin>
For Plutarch testifies that roosters and hens were customarily offered to Osiris and Isis (or the Sun and Moon), to Aesculapius, Hermanubis, Mercury, Harpocrates, and the other deities—especially to Ceres, whom we identify with Isis, because Ceres is called that "Celestial Venus" who presides over fruits and grain. That Succoth Benoth, or the constellation of the Pleiades, is that celestial hen has been made clear from what preceded; indeed, Plutarch indicates this in manifest words when he says:

<margin>Plutarch.</margin>
> Truly, at the time when the Egyptians perform their sacred rites, many similar things are done at the same time among the Greeks. For at Athens, the women observing the Thesmophoria <note>A festival in honor of Demeter/Ceres</note> fast while sitting on the ground; and the Boeotians move the Megara of Achæa, and they call that festival a troublesome one, doubtless because Ceres is in grief on account of the descent of her daughter Proserpina into the underworld.

These things take place in the month of sowing, around the rising of the <term>Vergiliae</term> or Pleiades (which we have said are Succoth Benoth). The Egyptians call this month Athyr (as they also call Isis), the Athenians call it Pyanepsion, and the Boeotians call it Damatrius, that is, the Month of Ceres.

<margin>Why the greatest solemnities were held in the month of Athyr.</margin>
From this it is clear that any more notable solemnities were performed by the Egyptians and Greeks in the month of Athyr, corresponding to the rising of the Pleiades, for no other reason than that they looked upon this region of the sky—or the <term>dodecatemory<note>A 30-degree division of the Zodiac, i.e., one of the twelve signs.</note></term> of Taurus in which Venus, or that Celestial Hen, fixed her seat—as more divine than the others, and more favorable, as it were, to the human race. I conclude finally from all—
