<meta>This page continues the argument from page 357, where Kircher linked the biblical "Succoth Benoth" (tents of daughters) to the constellation of the Pleiades—traditionally called "the Hen and her Chicks" in various cultures—and the goddess Venus as a symbol of fertility.</meta>

### EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAIC TEMPLE ###

<margin>
CHAPTER
XVIII.

The idol of Succoth Benoth: a hen with her chicks.
</margin>
From all these points brought forward, it is clear that Succoth Benoth was an idol of a hen with her chicks, under which the Babylonians worshipped Venus, as the Rabbis have rightly observed. I speak of that Venus who is the nurturer of all earthly things, the same whom the Arabs call *Alilath*, the Syrians call *Mulitho* or *Melitta*—that is, the "Generatress"—and the Greeks call *Latona* <note>The mother of Apollo and Artemis</note>, the protector of those in childbirth. (Indeed, Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric</note> teaches that hens were sacred to her for this reason.) <margin>Why the Gods were shown in various forms.</margin> She is also the one the Egyptians call Isis, or the star *Sothis* <note>Sirius</note>, the god of crops; or finally, she whom Lucian <note>A 2nd-century Syrian satirist</note> calls Juno or the Syrian Goddess. She was depicted in the form of a hen with chicks to indicate the fertility of this Venus, just as they depicted her in the form of a fish to hint at her power over the waters and humors of the body. <margin>Lucian.</margin> Lucian points out this varied imagery in his work *On the Syrian Goddess*, where he says:

> *Juno, however, if you look more closely, by no means displays the form of just one species; for generally speaking, one would truly call her Juno, yet she also possesses something of Minerva, Venus, the Moon, Rhea, Nemesis, and the Fates. In one hand she holds a scepter, and in the other a distaff; she wears rays upon her head, and a tower, and she has the girdle <note>The "cestus," a magical belt that inspired desire</note> with which they adorn only the Heavenly Venus. On the outside she is surrounded by gold and very precious gemstones.*

<margin>The Assyrians expressed Astarte in various ways.</margin> Thus, the Assyrians depicted their Astarte—or Juno, or the Syrian Goddess—in various ways to point toward her variety of effects. Some portrayed her in the form of a half-fish, like Dagon or Derceto; others in the form of a dove, or a hen with chicks like Succoth Benoth; and others in different ways, yet she was always "many-formed" <note>original Greek: πολύμορφος (polymorphos)</note>, just as Lucian writes the Syrian Goddess was fashioned.

But perhaps we are dwelling on these points more frequently than is necessary. Therefore, let us return to our purpose. The Hebrews assert, not without reason, <margin>The nature of the Succoth Benoth idol.</margin> that the idol of Succoth Benoth was in the shape of a hen with chicks; for this symbol suits Venus more than any other. Furthermore, this opinion was by no means fabricated by the Hebrews (as Selden <note>John Selden, a 17th-century polymath who wrote on Syrian gods</note> suggests), but was drawn from the deepest mysteries of pagan astrology. Just as the frequent and continuous contemplation of the stars provided the occasion for all idolatrous superstition, so too this <term>zodiacal sign</term> <note>original Greek: δωδεκαμόριον (dodekamorion)</note> of Taurus ♉, and the fertile nature of the stars occurring within it, could easily have provided the observers of superstition with the occasion to represent Venus under the form of a hen and chicks.

Certainly, some very ancient coins of the Mamertines and the Selenuntines <note>Peoples of ancient Sicily</note> show the truth of this matter in various places. On one side of these coins, there appears a cock or a hen with a <gloss>leaf of the selenion</gloss> <note>Possibly wild celery or a plant sacred to the moon/Venus</note> sacred to Venus; on the other side is the image of a Bull held by its horn. These clearly seem to refer to nothing other than the mysteries mentioned.

On a certain coin of the people of Tyana, a cock is also seen in an upright position as if letting out a crow, which has a grain of wheat above its crest and a star behind its back; in front is the inscription: TIANO. On the other side is the helmeted head of Mars. It is to be believed, therefore, that the cock was so depicted on such a coin because it is the bird of Mars and specifically sacred to him; the grain is a symbol of fertility from agriculture. As for the star, which is likewise seen on several other coins of neighboring peoples, some think it refers to the fact that Greater Greece <note>Magna Graecia, the Greek-settled areas of Southern Italy</note> was previously called Hesperia <note>The Land of the Evening Star</note>.

<summary>Kircher identifies the idol Succoth Benoth as a hen with chicks, symbolizing the fertility of Venus and the constellation of the Pleiades. He supports this by citing ancient authors like Lucian and examining Numismatic evidence where solar, agricultural, and avian symbols overlap.</summary>

<margin>Why the constellation of the Pleiades is confused with Aries. Why Venus is depicted riding Aries. Why the Pleiades, Hyades, and Vergiliae are commonly confused.</margin>
Furthermore, regarding the fact that Hebrew authors confuse the constellation of the Pleiades with the tail of Aries, I would think this happened because of the proximity of the Pleiades to the tail of Aries, as the figure shows. And from this I also judge it to have happened that the ancient Mythologists depicted Venus riding upon Aries, either due to the obvious closeness of Aries to the Venusian star-cluster of the Pleiades, or because at the end of Aries, Venus immediately begins to exert her power. We see the Pleiades, the Hyades, and the <term>Vergiliae</term> <note>The Latin name for the Pleiades, derived from *ver*, meaning Spring</note> commonly confused, either because of the clusters of stars of which each of the three said constellations consists, or because their rising, which happens at nearly the same time, provides similar effects and operations in the lower world. It is not surprising, therefore, if authors understand the Pleiades, Hyades, and Vergiliae to be one and the same constellation.

Therefore, this cluster of stars—whether they were of the Pleiades, the Hyades, or the Vergiliae—was worshipped with divine honor by the ancient Astrologers of the Chaldeans for the reasons stated, under the figure which follows.

### CHAPTER XVIII. THE ISIAIC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS ###

<margin>
The wicked custom of Babylonian women.
</margin>
Until now, we have spoken of the form and figure of **Succoth Benoth**; now it is time for us to discuss, at an equal pace, the ceremonies and rites usually performed for it. According to the law of their country, it was common to all Babylonian women—as we also related above—that once in their lives, after having duly invoked **Venus Mylitta**, or **Succoth Benoth**, they would sit in a sacred precinct, separated by paths marked with cords and wearing crowns, to have intercourse with strangers. For more on these and similar matters, <margin>Herodotus. Strabo.</margin> consult **Herodotus**, Book 1, and **Strabo**, Book 16, from whom we have drawn the information we presented. That passage of Jeremiah, in the epistle attached to Baruch <note>Referring to the Letter of Jeremiah found in the deuterocanonical Book of Baruch, Chapter 6</note>, also hints at these ceremonies where he attacks the harlots of the Babylonians; he speaks in this manner:

> The women also with cords about them, sitting in the ways, burn bran for incense. And if any of them, drawn by some passer-by, lies with him, she reproaches her neighbor, that she was not thought as worthy as herself, nor her cord broken. <note>original Greek: Αἱ δὲ γυναῖκες περιθέμεναι σχοινία ἐν ταῖς ὁδοῖς ἥκαθῶντο θυμιῶσαι τὰ πίτυρα...</note>

*The women, he says, sit in the ways surrounded by cords to burn bran; and if any of them should sleep with any stranger who has drawn her away from her path, she would taunt her neighbor because she was by no means affected by a similar <margin>What are the cords?</margin> honor, nor was her cord broken.* Regarding what <term>girding with cords</term> <note>original: Περιθέμεναι σχοινία</note> meant, Selden <note>John Selden, a 17th-century English polymath and scholar of Syrian deities</note> confesses he does not know. We say that by <term>cords</term> <note>original: σχοινία</note> nothing else is understood but the rush-cords which they twisted for the purpose of constructing curtains or tents. For <term>cord</term> <note>original: σχοινίον</note> signifies nothing other than a rope twisted from sedge or marsh-rushes. That they wove these mats or curtains in <margin>See the chapter on Astaroth.</margin> honor of **Astaroth**, or the **Assyrian Venus**, was indicated extensively above; and **Herodotus** shows this sufficiently when he calls the entrances that were stretched with rush-cords toward the sitting woman or harlot, <term>passageways stretched with cords</term> <note>original: διέξοδος σχοινοτενέες</note>—that is, entrances covered on all sides with rushes. These are also called by the Rabbis <term>Battei Kedeshim</term> <note>original: בתי קדשים</note>, that is, "houses of the consecrated ones" (or harlots), which were destroyed by Josiah in the Fourth Book of Kings <note>Known as 2 Kings 23:7 in modern Bibles</note>. For when, as was said above, harlots of this kind sat in the sacred precinct of **Succoth Benoth**, or **Mylitta**, waiting for the arrival of guests, they [constructed] their booths or tents...

### CHAPTER XVIII. THE HEBREW PANTHEON ###

They covered [the booths] with willow and reeds, both to avoid the discomfort of the sun and air and to carry out the Venusian ceremonies with newcomers. From this practice arose the Athenian term <term>perischoinizein</term> <note>original: περισχοινίζειν; literally "to rope off"</note>, a word they used when they kept the profane away from sacred trials by using stretched-out reed curtains; so says Pollux in Book 8, and Demosthenes <margin>Pollux. Demosthenes.</margin> uses the term <term>perischoinismos</term> <note>original: τῷ περισχοινισμῷ</note> for one who is excluded from the <term>perischoinismenos</term> <note>original: περισχοινισμένῳ; "roped-off"</note> forum, as Harpocration noted. In the temple of Venus—otherwise known as Mylitta or Succoth Benoth—the girls who sat there were imitating that "Venus of the Booths," whose specific role is to devote herself to the generation of offspring, just as those women were doing. For the sacred rites had to conform, and the ceremonies of the mysteries had to be analogous to the actions of the Deity they worshipped; this is a point well worth noting. Hence, <margin>Offerings which were made to Succoth Benoth.</margin> the offerings were also made to conform to Succoth Benoth, or Venus, that "Celestial Hen," since they offered her bran, flour, salted cakes <note>original: molas falsas; a traditional sacrificial mixture of toasted grain and salt</note>, libations, and sacrificial cakes, which they knew were pleasing to hens. For it is clear from the passage cited just before that harlots <term>burn bran as incense</term> <note>original: τα πίτυρα θυμιῶσιν</note>, which is to say, they were accustomed to offering bran. It is likely, however, that these cakes were marked with the figure of the idol Succoth Benoth—namely, a hen with her chicks. But I shall pull back my pen, lest I cause the reader nausea by the tedious repetition of these things already so often emphasized. I say only this: whoever compares these findings well with what preceded will see that Succoth Benoth is entirely the same as that Venus common to all the peoples of Asia. Whether you call her Alilath with the Arabs, Mylitha with the Syrians, Astarte with the Phoenicians and Sidonians, Dagon or Derceto with the people of Ashdod and the Assyrians, Succoth Benoth with the Babylonians, or finally by any other names, you are saying nothing other than that she is the "Great Mother of the Gods," manifold in her power. But let us leave these things and proceed to others.

# CHAPTER XIX.
->Concerning Nergal and the other Idols of the Samaritans.<-

<margin>Why the Samaritans were held in hatred by the Hebrews.</margin>
There are many causes and reasons why the Hebrews pursued the Samaritans with such great hatred, some of which are recorded in the second Book of Ezra <note>referring to the Book of Nehemiah</note> and in Josephus’ *Antiquities of the Jews*. Among others, the reasons were that the Samaritans obstructed the building of the walls of Jerusalem in various ways and laid traps for Nehemiah. Abraham ibn Ezra <margin>R. Abenezra.</margin> <note>A celebrated 12th-century Jewish polymath and biblical commentator</note> mentions the rest in these words:

> "What did Ezra, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Joshua the son of Jozadak do? They gathered the entire congregation into the Temple of the Lord, and they brought three hundred priests, and three hundred shofars <note>original: שופרות (*shofrot*); ritual rams' horns</note>, and three hundred Torah scrolls in their hands. They declared that no man of Israel shall ever eat the bread of a Cuthean. From this they said: 'Whoever eats the flesh of a Cuthean, it is as if he ate the flesh of a pig.' No Cuthean may ever convert, and they have no portion in the resurrection of the dead, as it is said: *'It is not for you and us to build the house of our God'*—not in this world, and not in the world to come. Furthermore, they shall have no portion or inheritance in Jerusalem."

*What did Ezra and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Joshua the son of Jozadak do? They gathered the whole congregation into the house of the Lord, and they caused three hundred priests and three hundred boys to come; moreover, three hundred trumpets and three hundred books of the law were in their hands. ### CHAPTER XIX. 364 THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS THE ISIAC TEMPLE ###

...with the Cuthites <note>Samaritans</note>, whom Ezra and Nehemiah had driven away from the house of the Lord; and he <note>Sanballat</note> asked Alexander <note>Alexander the Great</note> for permission for the priests of his own lineage to build a temple on Mount Gerizim. Once this was done, Israel was divided into two parts: one part of the people followed Simeon the Just and his disciple Antigonus, and their congregation, according to what they had received from Ezra and the Prophets; the other part, however, followed Sanballat and his sons-in-law. They offered burnt offerings and sacrifices outside the house of God, and they devised ordinances from their own hearts, as well as idols of the nations. In that house, the son-in-law of Sanballat, Manasseh (the son of Joshua, son of Jehozadak the high priest), performed the sacrificial duties. At that time, Sadok and Boethus <note>traditional founders of the Sadducees and Boethusians</note>, disciples of Antigonus, became the leaders, and this was the beginning of the heresy; for in the time of Antigonus their master, they had gone to the temple of Gerizim and became its leaders.

<margin>Rabbi Abraham in the Kabbalah and the Book of Juchasin (Genealogies).</margin>
These words so closely agree with the words of Rabbi Abraham in the *Kabbalah* and the *Book of Juchasin* <note>A famous 16th-century Jewish history book by Abraham Zacuto</note> that they seem to have been entirely transcribed by Seduna. It is established from the reproaches fashioned by the Jews that the Samaritans were devoted to idolatry above all other nations. For besides the common idols brought into Samaria from Babylonia, 

<margin>Nergal, an idol of the Samaritans.</margin>
we read that they also worshipped Nergal with a singular cult. However, what sort of idol this was remains unknown to Latin authors; 

<margin>Selden.</margin>
we must therefore seek some knowledge of this from others. Selden <note>John Selden, a 17th-century polymath and expert on ancient religions</note> thinks that Nergal is derived from the Hebrew *Ner Gal* <note>original: נר גל</note>, which signifies "lamp" and "rotation," and was nothing other than a perpetual fire religiously preserved by the Cuthites. 

<margin>Nergal was not a Vestal fire, but a carved image.</margin>
Truly, this seems to contradict the words of Holy Scripture, which asserts that Nergal was a carved deity <note>original: *Numen sculptile*</note> fashioned by the Cuthites, just like the other idols. There are some who believe Nergal was an image in the form of a dove. For the Talmudic Rabbis relate, in the treatise *Chullin*, section 1, that an idol in the likeness of a dove was found on the peak of Mount Gerizim, wherefore they <note>the Samaritans</note> were judged entirely as "people of the land" <term>people of the land: a term often implying religious ignorance or paganism</term>; the words are:

<margin>Talmudic Rabbis, tractate 1, Chullin, section 1.</margin>
> In the time of Rabbi Meir, an image was found on Mount Gerizim in the shape of a dove, and from then on they were judged entirely as the people of the land. <note>original Hebrew: בזמן ר' מאיר נמצא צלם בהר גריזים דמותו דמות יונה ומכאן ואילך נדונים לגמרי כגויי הארץ</note>

<margin>Rabbi Azarias.</margin>
<margin>Jeremiah chapter 25.</margin>
Rabbi Azarias <note>Azariah dei Rossi</note> also mentions this dove in chapter 21 of *Imre Binah* <note>The Words of Understanding</note>, saying it was the banner of Semiramis <note>A legendary Queen of Assyria</note>, and later of the Assyrians; hence Jeremiah chapter 25 says: *Their land has been made a desolation because of the wrath of the dove.* <note>Kircher follows a specific interpretation of the Hebrew word 'yonah,' which can mean both 'oppressor' and 'dove'</note>. 

<margin>Diodorus Siculus.</margin>
Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian</note> reports in his third book the occasion for choosing this banner: that birds, especially doves, nourished the newborn Semiramis; whence, says Diodorus, 

<margin>From where the name was given to Semiramis.</margin>
the name Semiramis was given to her from the chirping and peeping of birds. This is not improbably deduced by that Rabbi from *Zamir* <note>original: זמיר</note>, or in Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> *Zimra* <note>original: זמרא</note>, by swapping the letter *Zain* for *Samekh* due to their similar sound, as if she were called *Zamiris* instead of *Semiramis*. He says, moreover, that certain peoples so honored the memory of Semiramis that they entirely abstained from eating doves; all of which agrees with what we reported above concerning Derceto and Dagon, the idols of the Assyrians. Finally, he concludes that the Samaritans, who originated from the Assyrians, erected and worshipped the idol of a dove on Mount Gerizim in honor and memory of Semiramis.

<margin>Gedelias.</margin>
Others, such as Gedelias <note>Gedaliah ibn Yahya</note>, wish this to be the idol that Jacob brought from Assyria and buried under a terebinth tree near the city of Shechem (Genesis 35). Whatever the case may be, it is certain that the Samaritans worshipped the dove just as the other Assyrians...

### SYNT. IV. HEBREW PANTHEON. CHAPTER XIX. ###

...worshipped. Whether this was the same idol as Nergal, someone might rightly doubt; some of the Rabbis, as has been said, are of that opinion. We, however, believe it to be different and distinct from the others; indeed, we assert that the Samaritans worshipped Derceto, or Atargatis, or Semiramis through the image of a dove. See the reasons for this provided above in the appropriate place. <margin>Nergal had the likeness of a rooster.</margin> I find, however, that Nergal was an idol in the form of a rooster <note>Latin: *gallus gallinaceus*</note>, under which the Persians—from whom the Cuthites originated—formerly worshipped the Sun or fire. The authorities of many writers move me to believe this; for Seduna, the Patriarch of Gaza, in the previously cited account written in Samaritan letters, writes that Nergal had the likeness of a rooster; I shall provide his Samaritan words:

<margin>Seduna.</margin>
->Because our fathers abandoned the Law of the Lord and were serving the abomination of the rooster, which is called "Nergal" in the Samaritan tongue.<-

->*Ki Abinu sabakim, & thorath Adonai ve haiu gnobedim tagnauuat tharnigol, sche neemar belschcon somroni Nergal.*<-
>That is: *Because our fathers left the law of God, and served the idol Nergal in the likeness of a rooster—for in the Samaritan language a rooster is called Nergal—therefore, and so forth, as follows.*

<margin>Baal Aruch.</margin>
These words are supported by the *Baal Aruch* <note>The *Arukh*, a famous 11th-century dictionary of Talmudic and Midrashic Hebrew by Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome</note>, who asserts that Nergal is the same as <term>Tharnigol</term> <note>Hebrew: תרנגול</note>, which means "rooster" to the Hebrews; his words are:
->Nergal, in the fourth chapter of the commentary called <term>Arba Mithoth</term> <note>The "Four Deaths," a section of the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin</note>, in the third distinction titled *bannoded bismo*, they made Nergal in his name, and from this comes the *Tharnigol*, that is, the rooster.<-

The Syrian Onomasticon <note>A dictionary of names</note> used by the Maronites explains this more distinctly:
<margin>Syriac Onomasticon.</margin>
->And the men of Cuth worshipped Nergal. Now this Nergal was an image in the form and likeness of a rooster.<-

All of this is confirmed by Rashi <note>Solomon ben Isaac, the preeminent medieval French rabbi</note>, in his commentary on the 17th chapter of the 4th book of Kings <note>2 Kings 17 in modern Bibles</note>, where he says:
<margin>Rashi.</margin>
->Succoth Benoth was the form of a hen with her chicks, and Nergal was a rooster.<-

<margin>Guido Fabricius.</margin>
<margin>Nergal is a Samaritan word.</margin>
Guido Fabricius <note>A 16th-century French scholar and linguist</note> agrees with these points in his Syro-Chaldaic Dictionary under the word *Nergal*. Therefore, Nergal is a Samaritan word, and it means the same thing as *Tharnigol*, namely, a rooster; this is sufficiently demonstrated by the slight difference between <term>Nergal</term> and <term>Tharnigol</term>.

<margin>Nergal was an idol of fire or the Sun in the figure of a rooster.</margin>
With these things presupposed, I conclude that Nergal, which the sacred history records the Cuthites made for themselves, was nothing other than an idol of fire or the Sun, worshipped under the figure of a rooster, which corresponds <term>analogously</term> <note>Kircher uses the Greek *ἀναλόגως*</note> to the properties of fire and the Sun. For since the Cuthites were Persians by origin, and the Persians worshipped the Sun and fire under various animals representing them, it is probable that the Cuthites, when migrating into Samaria, subsequently retained these types of idolatrous rites.

<margin>The Persians worshipped roosters.</margin>
That the Persians worshipped the Sun and fire has been proven most extensively above. It remains for us to prove that roosters were held in the highest honor among the Persians...

<summary>This page identifies the Samaritan idol Nergal as a rooster, linking its worship to Persian solar and fire cults. Kircher supports this by citing various Jewish, Samaritan, and Syriac authorities to show the linguistic and symbolic connection between the name Nergal and the rooster.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the rooster as a sacred animal among the Persians and Samaritans. The previous page established that the idol Nergal was represented as a rooster. Here, the author provides classical Greek and Roman evidence to support the Persian origins of this symbolism and its connection to the gods Mars and Mithras.</meta>

### THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS ###

<margin>CHAPTER XIX.</margin>
...held in honor. And first indeed Aristophanes—an author of the highest authority—shows in *The Birds* that the rooster was held in such honor by posterity, starting from the time of Alexander the Great, because the rooster once "ruled over the Persians" and was sacred to Mars. He uses these words:

> <margin>Aristophanes.</margin> ->*A bird of our own Persian race,*<-
> ->*Who is said to be the most solemn ruler everywhere,*<-
> ->*The chick of Mars.*<-
> <note>original Greek: Ὄρνις ἀφ' ἡμῶν τοῦ γένους τοῦ Περσικοῦ / Ὅσπερ λέγετ' δυνάστης ὢν πανταχοῦ / Ἄρεως Νεοττός.</note>

<margin>The Scholiast.</margin> Regarding this passage, the Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator or annotator of classical texts</note> says: *He is certainly speaking of the rooster. For he is called a Mede [a Persian]; and the "chick of Mars" because he is brave and warlike.*

<margin>Roosters were first brought out of Persia.</margin>
It contributes no small amount to the promotion of this cult that Persia is said to have been the first to produce roosters, and from there they were carried into other regions of the world. The words of Athenaeus are: <margin>Athenaeus.</margin> *Menodotus of Samos, in his book on the things seen in the temple of the Samian Juno, says: "There are peacocks there sacred to Juno, first born and raised in Samos, and from there taken and carried into other regions, just as roosters were brought from Persia, and those birds called Meleagrides [guinea-fowl] from Aetolia; thus the rooster is widely known as the 'Persian bird'.* <margin>Hesychius. Suidas.</margin> Hesychius says: *The Persian bird is the rooster.* Suidas also calls it the Persian bird: *The rooster is the Persian bird because of the crest on its helmet, and because everything costly used by the King was called 'Persian'.* <margin>Persian soldiers named Roosters.</margin> For this reason, the soldiers of the Persians were called "Roosters" by the Carians because of the crests <note>The plumes or "cones" on top of the helmet</note> with which they had their helmets adorned. For that same reason, Artaxerxes honored the man from Caria (who was believed to have wounded Cyrus with a spear) with this reward: that he should carry a golden rooster fixed upon a spear at the head of the battle line. <margin>Plutarch.</margin> The author of this is Plutarch in his *Life of Artaxerxes*.

Therefore, for many reasons, the rooster was sacred to the Persians, and most especially to Mars. In the preceding sections, we have conflated Mars with <term>Mithras</term> <note>The Persian god of the Sun and light</note> and, following Plutarch, we have shown a certain warlike or resisting power shining forth in the Sun. Indeed, the rooster is a "Mime of Mars"; this is sufficiently demonstrated by his high-mindedness, strength, boldness, pugnacity, his "helmet" [crest], his spurs, his circumspection and vigilance, and in addition to all this, his extreme lustfulness and lewdness, and other properties that belong to Mars. It is no wonder, therefore, if the Persians expressed the Sun—whom they understand through Mithras (that is, that glowing stone)—under the form of a rooster, while expressing Venus through a hen with her chicks.

How great the friendship and sympathy is between Mars and Venus, there is no one who does not know. How great the lustfulness of each is, the mythologists sufficiently show by attributing to Mars the most lustful animals—the rooster and the horse—and to Venus the hen and the ram (upon which Venus rides), as well as sparrows pulling her chariot, doves, and similar animals of Venus. For these are symbols, or a kind of <term>hieroglyph</term> <note>In this context, a symbolic representation of a divine concept</note> of the passion with which they indicate both Venus and Mars burn.

<summary>This page explores the symbolic link between the rooster and the Persian culture, identifying it as the "Persian bird" sacred to Mars and Mithras. Kircher argues that the rooster's physical traits—like its crest and spurs—represent the warlike and solar qualities of these deities.</summary>

368 THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

## CHAPTER XX.

->*Asima, Nibhaz, Tarthac, Anamelech, Adramelech.*<-

<margin>Radak</margin>
Concerning Asima, the deity of the people of Hamath, the Rabbis <note>The term "Rabbis" here refers to medieval Jewish commentators who analyzed the biblical text.</note> hold various opinions; some derive it from **אשם**, which signifies a "guilt offering" <note>Hebrew: *asham*</note>, and take it to refer to any kind of livestock; thus Radak <note>Rabbi David Kimhi (1160–1235), a famous grammarian and biblical commentator.</note>:
->**אשימה אימרא במה דתימא באיל האשם :**<-
*The word Asima is as if the sacrifice or offering for sin were completed in the livestock,*

<margin>R. Elias</margin>
R. Elias the German <note>Elia Levita (1469–1549), a Hebrew philologist whose dictionary was titled *Tishbi*.</note> in *Tishbi*, thinks that Asima is an Ape:
->**ואומר אני שיותר נכון לאמר שהוא כלשון עשו את אשימה שהוא חקוף וכן נקרא בלעז טמיא :**<-
<margin>Asima signifies a goat.</margin>
*I say, however, he says, that it is more correct to say that Asima comes from that passage in 2 Kings 17, "They made for themselves Asima"; for in that place Asima signifies an Ape; just as it is also called "Simia" in Italian.* Others, however, more truly interpret Asima as a male or female goat; as if it were called an image of a goat without wool; so says the *Baal Aruch* <note>A dictionary of the Talmud and Midrash compiled by Nathan ben Jehiel in the 11th century.</note>, under the word **אשימה**:
<margin>Baal Aruch</margin>
->**אשימא בפר' ד' מיתות נמסרו לב"ד בגמ' הנודר בשמו ואנשי חמת עשו אשימא ומאי ניהו ברחא קרחא פי' ברחא תייש קרחא שאין לו צמר והוא בקרח ולכן נקרא אשימא שהוא שמם מצמר :**<-

# FOURTH SYNTAGMA: THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER XX.

<margin>Samaritan reading.</margin>
In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.
: The earth and the heavens.

<note>original: "Beqameth veeth berefchit bara Elohim & fchamaim veeth haretz." This is the first verse of Genesis transcribed from the Samaritan Hebrew script.</note>

->*In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.*<-

And this is the reading in the Vatican Samaritan-Hebrew Pentateuch, which differs in no way at all from the common Hebrew reading; nor does it differ in the vernacular language of the Samaritans, which reads as follows:

In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.
: The earth.

<note>original: "Beqama dtalmaz elhaa iath fchomih viath araah." This is the Samaritan Aramaic translation, or Targum, of Genesis 1:1.</note>

->*In the beginning God created, etc.*<-

When I had seen these things, I noticed that all these claims—that the Samaritans had substituted the name of their idol for God—were either fabricated out of that ancient and irreconcilable hatred of the Jews toward the Samaritans, or at least that such a reading was used in copies written by idolaters before they received the pure law of the Hebrews. For since the Jews knew the Samaritans were worshippers of Asima—that is, the goat, a most foul-smelling animal—and it was established among them that they had inserted the names of their idols into the sacred page in place of the name of the true God; they thought no greater slander could be brought against them than if they thrust upon them this most foul reading of the creation of the world performed by a goat. Truly, we did not want to pass over these matters for the sake of interest; therefore, let us return to our purpose.

We say, therefore, that **Asima** was an idol of the Hamathites <note>The people of Hamath, a city in Syria.</note> depicted in the form of a goat; no one should doubt that this method of representing a deity originated from the Egyptians, since the highest solemnities exhibited annually in the city of Mendes testify that the Egyptians, especially the Mendesians, always held the goat in the highest honor. <margin>Herodotus, Book 2.</margin> Herodotus also calls the Goat and Pan by a single Egyptian word, *Mendes*, from which those famous "Goat-worshippers" <note>Greek: Τραγολάται (*Tragolatai*).</note> of Mendes arose. <margin>Diodorus.</margin> Diodorus Siculus, providing the reason for this goat-worship, says:

> *The Egyptians deified the Goat, just as the Greeks did Priapus, clearly on account of that part of the body from which the birth of all things comes; not only the Egyptians, but many others perform sacred rites to the genitals. And from this the Egyptians, as Horus <note>Kircher refers to Horapollo, an author on hieroglyphs.</note> testifies, when painting a Goat, signify a fertile phallus in a hieroglyphic manner <note>Greek: hieroglyphicῶς</note>; for a goat copulates seven days after its birth, and although it produces a weak and sterile seed, it nevertheless copulates sooner than other animals.*

Certainly, in the hieroglyphics, nothing is more frequent than a goat's head, or one placed upon a staff or an altar, as follows.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting the head of a goat with curved horns, facing right. The head is placed on a rectangular pedestal or altar. On the side of the pedestal, the word "MENDES" is printed. The illustration is surrounded by a double-line rectangular frame.</image-desc>

<margin>Consult the Bembine Tablet and the Flaminian and Lateran Obelisks.</margin>

Truly, what these things signify you will find in our practical interpretation of the hieroglyphics, where we explain them most extensively. The Samaritans or Hamathites followed the Egyptians in this place, worshipping the phallus of Osiris under the image of a goat; for we read that they adored the idol of Asima set up on high. <margin>The goat is worshipped by various nations.</margin> The Greeks also are said to have held Pan, rough with his goat-like legs, in the place of the Supreme Deity, for no other reason than to express the fertility of nature by that symbol. For the same reason, a Goat is to Bacchus at every altar

->Sacrificed, and the ancient plays enter upon the stage.<-
<note>A quote from Virgil's *Georgics*, referring to the origin of theater in Dionysian goat-sacrifices.</note>

<summary>Kircher argues that the Jewish claim of Samaritans replacing "God" with "Asima" (a goat) in Genesis is a sectarian slander, as evidenced by Vatican manuscripts. He then identifies Asima as a goat-god derived from the Egyptian Mendes/Pan, symbolizing natural fertility and the generative power.</summary>

# THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<page-num>370</page-num>

<margin>CHAPTER XX.</margin>
The image of Venus *Pandemos*, <note>original: "πανδήμου," meaning "of all the people," referring to the "Common" or "Vulgar" Venus associated with physical desire</note> that is, the so-called "Vulgar" Venus, is also made of bronze and sits upon a goat; this was a work of the sculptor Scopas, according to Pausanias in the second book of his *Eliaca*. As for why she sits upon a goat, he leaves the reader to guess. To me, the reason seems immediately obvious: the goat is the animal most prone to lust. The pagans placed their *Pandemos* Venus in charge of this animal, as we stated in the preceding pages. <margin>Plutarch.</margin> Hence, Plutarch, in his *Great Parallels*, calls her *epitragia*, <note>original: "ἐπιτראγια," meaning "upon the goat"</note> that is, the Venus "named from a goat." From these details, we conclude that Asima was the same as the Mendes of the Egyptians, the Pan of the Greeks, and the Baal-peor of the Hebrews—one and the same deity, designated by different names by various nations. Therefore, let these remarks on Asima suffice.

<margin>Nibhaz.</margin>
The fourth image that the Samaritans placed in their shrines was called Nibhaz, of which sacred history <note>2 Kings 17:30–31</note> speaks thus:

> *And the men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth; and the men of Cuth made Nergal; and the men of Hamath made Asima; and the Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak.*

What kind of image this Nibhaz might have been is difficult to determine from Latin and Greek authors; nonetheless, traces of this deity are not lacking in the books of the Eastern peoples. By pressing forward with these sources and searching sagaciously, we have finally "scented out" and discovered what it was: namely, an idol in the form of a dog, which was that Egyptian Anubis. And first, indeed, <margin>Rashi.</margin> Rashi <note>A famous 11th-century French rabbi and commentator</note> indicates in clear words that Nibhaz was in the shape of a dog: *Nibhaz*, he says, *possessed a canine form.* <note>original Hebrew: נבחן דמות כלב</note> And <margin>Radak.</margin> Radak <note>David Kimhi, a 12th-13th century Hebrew grammarian and philosopher</note> explains himself a little more fully in this passage:

> *Nibhaz is written at the end with the letter Zain, although there are some books that write it with a Nun; but those books are in error, for it should only be written with a Zain. Furthermore, Nibhaz signifies nothing other than a dog; and Nibhaz is a compound name from "nibbah" and "haz." "Nibbah" means "to bark"—specifically referring to one who cannot bark (alluding to the idol)—while "haz" in this context signifies the face of a dog with its teeth remarkably bared in anger.*

The Rabbi is alluding sarcastically to the image of a dog that is unable to bark, according to that passage in Isaiah 56: <margin>Isaiah 56.</margin>

> *They are dumb dogs, unable to bark.* <note>original Hebrew: כלבים אלמים לא יוכלו לנבוח</note>

This also refers to that toothed mouth with which they frequently depicted him—just as with the previous idol, Asima, which they also mockingly called a goat without wool or hair; for the Jews were accustomed to thrust all these descriptions upon the nations as an insult to their idolatry. <margin>Nibhaz signifies a dog.</margin> Therefore, Nibhaz is derived from *nibah*, which is to say, it signifies a "barker" or dog; *haz* is a name fashioned from the shape of the teeth that rabid dogs display. However, other Eastern writers—regardless of what Radak says—correctly write it with a *Nun* at the end, such as the Syrians and Arabs: *Nibhon*.

<summary>Kircher identifies the Samaritan idol Nibhaz as the Egyptian dog-god Anubis, using etymological analysis of Hebrew and Rabbinic texts to link the name to the act of barking and the baring of teeth.</summary>

# SYNT. IV. PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. 371 CHAPTER XX.

<margin>Herodotus. Virgil.</margin>
Nibhaz; both of which are derived from the terms <insert>ܢܒܚܐ</insert> <note>Syriac for "barking"</note> and <insert>נבח</insert> <note>Hebrew: "nebach"</note>, which signifies "to bark," indicating a dog—as if you were to say "the barkers." Therefore, the Avvites worshipped a dog, following the example of the Egyptians, for whom nothing was more sacred than the dog. They delicately nourished this animal as the guardian and protector of Egypt, calling him Anubis in their native language, according to the testimony of Herodotus. Virgil also mentions him among the other gods of the Egyptians:

> Monsters of gods of every kind, and barking Anubis. <note>From Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book VIII, line 698.</note>

<margin>Clement of Alexandria.</margin>
They used to carry this god around the crossroads and streets of the city with public solemnity during the festivals of the *Comasiae*, <note>A Greek term for revelries or processions in honor of gods.</note> as Clement of Alexandria records in the fifth book of his *Stromata*. However, concerning this <term>Cynolatria</term> <note>dog-worship, from the Greek "kyon" (dog) and "latreia" (worship)</note> of the Egyptians, and its causes and reasons, we shall treat it everywhere throughout this *Oedipus*; thus, we do not wish to be more long-winded here. It suffices for us to have shown here that Nibhaz was an idol in the form of a dog, worshipped by the Avvites after the custom of the Egyptians. For the Avvites worshipped the dog for no other reason than that they understood the Egyptian "Cynopolites" <note>Residents of the "City of Dogs" in Egypt</note> ascribed all their prosperity to dog-worship; it is likely they turned their minds to this type of beast-worship to achieve the same prosperity.

<margin>Thartak.</margin>
Furthermore, what the other deity, Thartak, might have been—which the aforementioned Avvites are also said to have worshipped—is difficult to assert. The Rabbis say it was in the figure of an ass; thus Rashi and Radak <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki and Rabbi David Kimhi, famous medieval Jewish commentators.</note> in the cited place:

<margin>Rashi & Radak.</margin>
-> פירשו ר' בי תרתק צורת החמור : <-
<gloss>They interpreted Tartak as the form of an ass.</gloss>

<margin>Plutarch.</margin>
They interpret, he says, that Thartak was in the figure of an ass. I find in Plutarch's book *On Isis and Osiris* that the Egyptians, among other nations, represented Typhon <note>The Egyptian god Set, associated with chaos and the desert.</note> under the figure of an ass, and contended to appease him as a sinister deity. They also worship the dog, or Anubis, among other reasons and causes, because he was the companion of Isis in her search for the body of Osiris (which had been torn apart by Typhon), and he betrayed the machinations of Typhon and pointed out the body of Osiris. Hence, they believed him to be a good and fortunate deity, while the ass (or Typhon in the form of an ass) was a sinister deity to be driven away by the dog. Do not manifest traces of this matter lie hidden in the idols of the Avvites, Nibhaz and Thartak, the former of which we have shown refers to a dog, and the latter to an ass? Certainly, since the Avvites were neighbors to Egypt, it is probable that just as they learned other rites and ceremonies, so they learned to observe these <term>αντίστοιχα</term> <note>Greek for "counterparts" or "correlates"</note> deities—namely, Anubis and Typhon—under the figures of a dog and an ass. However, since nothing remains to us concerning idols of this kind except conjectures (if you exclude the cited authorities), I have thought it superfluous to dwell on these any longer, especially since our purpose is to bring forward nothing in this work of ours except what is established by the testimonies of trustworthy authors.

<margin>Anamelech and Adramelech, idols of the Sepharvaim.</margin>
It remains, finally, that we investigate what Anamelech and Adramelech, the idols of the Sepharvaim, properly were. Sacred Scripture seems to confuse them with Moloch when it says: *the Sepharvaim burnt their children in the fire to Anamelech and Adramelech.* All Christian [writers] follow the sacred history...

### CHAPTER XX. 372 OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS THE ISIAC TEMPLE

<margin>The Interpreters of Rashi:</margin>But the Rabbis say in this place that the idol Adramelech was in the form of a mule, while Anamelech was in the form of a horse. Thus Rashi says in the cited passage:

->Adramelech had the form of a mule, Anamelech the form of a horse.<-
<note>original Hebrew: אדרמלך דמות פרד ענמלך דמות סוס</note>

*Adramelech, he says, had the form of a mule, Anamelech of a horse.* Radak <note>Rabbi David Kimhi, a 12th-13th century grammarian and biblical commentator.</note> asserts in this place that Adramelech was so named because he is magnificent in carrying burdens for his master and is supremely useful; just as Anamelech is called so because he is useful to his lord in war:

<margin>Radak.</margin>->Adramelech is a mule and is so called because he is magnificent for his master in his burdens—meaning he carries for his lord all his loads; Anamelech is this horse because he answers his master in battle.<-
<note>original Hebrew: אדרמלך הוא פרד ונקרא כן דאדר ליה למריה בטעוניה... ענמלך זה הסוס דעני ליה למריה בקרבא. Radak is using a play on words: "Adir" (magnificent/mighty) for Adramelech and "Anah" (to answer/obey) for Anamelech.</note>

*Adramelech, he says, is a mule, and is so called because he is magnificent to his master in his burdens—that is, because he carries all his loads for his master; while Anamelech is a horse, and is so called because he obeys his lord the King in war.* These things are also handed down by the *Baal Aruch* <note>The author of the Arukh, a famous 11th-century dictionary of the Talmud.</note>. However, the Jerusalem Targum <note>An ancient Aramaic translation and expansion of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, cited by Radak and the *Baal Aruch*, says that Adramelech and Anamelech were fashioned in the likeness of a peacock and a pheasant; I will bring forward its words:

<margin>The Jerusalem Targum.</margin>->Adramelech and Anamelech are these: a peacock and a pheasant. And the peacock is what is called in the foreign tongue "pavon," and it is known that it is a pheasant.<-
<note>original Hebrew: אדרמלך וענמלך זה טווס ופסיוני... The "foreign tongue" refers to Latin/Romance "pavo."</note>

*Adramelech and Anamelech are those in the likeness of a peacock and a pheasant, which in the Latin language are called "pavo," and it is known that the latter is a pheasant.*

Certainly, in such a great variety of opinions and discrepancy among the Rabbis, although it is difficult to determine anything certain about the figure of Adramelech and Anamelech, we shall nevertheless attempt to explain the matter, that we might bring some light to these things insofar as we can achieve through probable conjectures. If the writings of the most ancient Rabbis still survived—those whose names are cited everywhere in the Talmudic tractate *Avodah Zarah* <note>Literally "Foreign Worship," the section of the Talmud dealing with idolatry.</note>—little or rather no account would be taken of certain books which today, in the scarcity of better ones, are held in high esteem by us. But now, since nothing is left to us of their writings regarding this subject except the desire for them, we are forced to relieve our poverty with certain poorly connected fragments of the moderns.

<margin>Anamelech and Adramelech are the same as Moloch.</margin>Therefore, I suppose that Anamelech and Adramelech are entirely the same Deity as Moloch, as the Sacred Scripture itself testifies (as we have demonstrated in the preceding pages), even if this one differs in form from others. For it was characteristic of the nations to represent one and the same Deity—for example, the Sun and the Moon—with different figures in different regions, as we have declared at length in the preceding chapters. Thus, the image of Moloch near Jerusalem in the **Valley of Hinnom** was different from his image among the people of Sepharvaim. I have thought it necessary to mention this first, lest anyone conclude a diversity of Deities from the diversity of their idols.

<margin>Anamelech in the form of a horse. Horses sacred to Mars. Justin.</margin>Since we have demonstrated in the preceding pages that Moloch is none other than the Egyptian Mars or the Persian Mithras, we assert along with the Rabbis that Anamelech was in the form of a horse. I read in Justin, Book 1, that horses were sacred to Mars among the Persians, and that a horse was sacrificed to him as a pleasing and fitting victim; *For the Persians, he says, [worshipped] the Sun*

He argues that despite these different forms, they are both manifestations of the god Moloch, whom he identifies with the Egyptian Mars and the Persian Mithras.</summary>

### SECTION IV. THE HEBREW PANTHEON CHAPTER XX.

<margin>Xenophon in the Cyropaedia.</margin>
...they believe in one God, and they say that horses are sacred to Him. Xenophon, in the eighth book of the *Cyropaedia* <note>original Greek: Παιδ. · ἵπποι ἄγουσι θῦμα τῷ Ηλίῳ; "horses lead the sacrifice to the Sun."</note>. And so Philostratus, in book 1 of the *Life of Apollonius*, writes in these words that the King of the Persians, when performing a divine rite, sacrificed a white horse to the Sun:

<margin>Philostratus.</margin>
> He was about to sacrifice a white horse of the very best Nisaean <note>The Nisaean plain in ancient Persia was famous for producing the finest and largest horses in antiquity, often reserved for royalty and sacred rites.</note> breed to the Sun at its setting, having decorated it with cheek-pieces, as if for a procession. <note>original Greek: Λεκόν δὲ ἄρα ἵππον τῷ σφόδρα Νισαῖῳ κατὰ δύσιν ἔμελλε τῷ ἡλίῳ φαλάροις κοσμήσας, ὥσπερ εἰς πομπὴν.</note>

And in this matter, the rhetorician Himerius plays quite gracefully:

<margin>Himerius.</margin>
> In his valedictory speech, he says: to my colt, a leader-colt, sacred and proud; which the people of the Nisaean city drive for the Sun God. Of these, I, having decorated a colt with the bits of song, and having mixed it all with the Graces, have made an offering. As to some God, I have dedicated my great first-fruits. <note>original Greek: Ἐν προπεμπτηρίῳ λόγῳ, αἰτ, τῷ ἐμῷ πώλῳ, ἐξάρχῳ πώλῳ ἱερῷ, καὶ ἀγέρωχῳ· οὕς ἡλίῳ Θεῷ Νισαῖοι πόλις πολέουσιν. τούτων ἐγὼ ὃν πῶλον ψαλίοις κοσμήσας μελῶν, καὶ χάριτων μίξας ὅλον ποιῆσαι ἀνάθεῖν. ὡς θεῷ τινι τ' ἐμὰς μεγάλας ἀπαρχὰς φέρων ἀνέθηκα.</note>

Ovid provides a quite clever reason for this practice in book 1 of the *Fasti* with these verses:

<margin>Ovid.</margin>
->The Persian placates Hyperion <note>A name for the Sun god.</note> girt with rays with a horse,<-
->Lest a slow victim be given to the swift God.<-

<margin>Herodotus.</margin>
Herodotus, at the end of book 1, offers the same reason why the Massagetae <note>A nomadic confederation of Central Asia.</note> sacrificed horses to the Sun, whom they worshipped above all:
> Of the gods, they worship only the Sun, to whom they sacrifice horses. The law of the sacrifice is that to the swiftest of all the gods, the swiftest of all mortal things is offered. <note>original Greek: Θεῶν δὲ μοῦνον ἥλιον σέβονται τῷ θῦουσι ἵππους. Νόμῳ δὲ ἐστὶ ἡ θυσίης τῷ Θεῶν τῷ ταχίστῳ πάντων τῶν θνητῶν τὸ τάχιστον δατίον.</note>

Indeed, they worship the Sun as the only and unique God, to whom they immolate horses; the law of this sacrifice was that the swiftest of all animals should be dedicated to the swiftest of all the Gods. Moreover, it was shown above in the chapter on Mithras that the Persians worshipped the Sun under the name of Mithras; and Strabo in book 15 clearly hands this down:

<margin>Strabo, Suidas, Hesychius.</margin>
> They honor, he says, the Sun, whom they call Mithras. <note>original Greek: Τιμῶσι, αἰτ, τὸν ἥλιον, ὃν καλοῦσι Μίθραν.</note> And Suidas: The Persians consider Mithras to be the Sun. <note>original Greek: Μίθραν νομίζουσι Πέρσαι εἶναι τὸν ἥλιον.</note> And Hesychius: Mithras is the Sun among the Persians; etc. Mithras is the first God among the Persians. <note>original Greek: Μίθρας ὁ ἥλιος παρὰ Πέρσαις· &c, Μίθης ὁ πρῶτος ἐν Πέρσαις Θεός.</note>

Mithras is the Sun to the Persians; Mithras is the first God among the Persians.

<margin>Mithras is the same as the "Horse-Mars" of the Persians. Tertullian.</margin>
Moreover, that Mithras is the same as the "Horse-Mars" <note>term: Mars Hippios (the Equestrian Mars)</note> of the Persians is more than sufficiently demonstrated both by what we previously handed down regarding Moloch, and by the "soldiers of Mithras" whom Tertullian asserts were initiated in the cave or grotto of Mithras. He says the same in the book *On the Prescription against Heretics*:
> He [the devil] also baptizes some, certainly his believers and faithful; he promises the expiation of sins through a washing; and thus he still initiates for Mithras; he signs his soldiers there on their foreheads; he also celebrates the offering of bread, and introduces an image of the resurrection, and redeems a crown under the sword.

But whoever desires to know more about the initiation of the Mithraic soldier and the various levels of torment that he had to undergo, should consult, besides the cited Tertullian, Nonnius on Gregory Nazianzen, and others whom we have already cited in various places.

Therefore, since the Persians worshipped the Sun, or Mithras, under the form of horses—as those who, by their natural gifts, most fully express the virtues of the Sun, or in which Mars would take the greatest delight as things most similar to himself—it is probable that the Sepharvaim, who had already migrated from the borders of Persia into Samaria by the command of Shalmaneser, preserved their ancestral religion and introduced Adramelech (this horse-idol, I say) among the other idols discussed so far into the shrines and high places. From them, the superstitious Jews subsequently learned this horse-worship <note>term: hippolatry (ἱππολατρεία)</note> and propagated it far and wide; however, King Josiah later abolished this impious superstition, as the sacred history of 2 Kings 23 relates.

<summary>This page argues that the idol Adramelech was a horse-god, identifying it with the Persian solar deity Mithras. Kircher uses classical sources to explain that horses were sacrificed to the Sun because their speed matched the Sun's movement, a practice eventually adopted by the Jews before being suppressed by King Josiah.</summary>

### CHAPTER XX. 374 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE

<margin>Radak</margin>
*He also removed the horses that the Kings of Judah had dedicated to the Sun at the entrance to the Temple of the Lord, near the chamber of Nathan-melech the Eunuch, which was in the precincts; and he burned the chariots of the Sun with fire.* <note>This is a translation of 2 Kings 23:11, describing the reforms of King Josiah.</note> As for the ceremonies used by the Judean Sun-worshippers—or "Heliognostai" <note>Greek for "those who know or worship the Sun."</note>—Radak <note>Rabbi David Kimhi (c. 1160–1235), a famous medieval Jewish biblical commentator.</note> explains in this passage:

->And they worshipped the sun, and they placed horses there that were prepared for this service; they would ride them and go out to meet the sun in the morning when it rose. <note>original Hebrew: והיו עובדים לשמש ונתנו שם סוסים שהיו מוכנים לזאת העבודה שהיו רוכבים עליהם והולכים לקראת השמש בבקר בזרחו</note><-

*For those who worshipped the Sun, horses were prepared in that place, destined solely for this service; they would mount these in the morning, riding toward the Sun as if to salute it, and to appease it with animals pleasing to it. Thus say Radak and the Rabbis.*

<margin>Where the custom of attributing chariots and horses to the Sun originated.</margin>
There are those who, in this passage, attribute the sun’s chariots and horses not to the Persians or other nations, but to the "rapture" of the Prophet Elijah <note>Referring to Elijah being taken to heaven in a chariot of fire in 2 Kings 2:11.</note>. This is the opinion of John, Bishop of Jerusalem; for in Greek, *Helius* is the name for the Sun, which sounds like *Helias* (Elijah), as Sedulius <note>Coelius Sedulius, a 5th-century Christian poet.</note> shows when he sings:

<margin>Sedulius.</margin>
> *How well the shining path of the watery sky*
> *Suits Elijah, shining in merit and in name;*
> *He was worthy of this aid, since in the Achaean <note>Greek</note> tongue*
> *Only one letter is changed by an accent, and it is "the Sun."* <note>original Latin: Quàm benè fluminei prælucens semita cæli / Conuenit Eliæ, meritòque & nomine fulgens, / Hâc ope dignus erat, quoniam sermonis Achiui / Vna per accentum mutetur litera, Sol est.</note>

Hearing from the Israelites (who were rumored to possess divine writings) that Elijah was carried to the heavens by a chariot of fire and horses of fire—or perhaps seeing this very scene depicted on a wall—the Greeks believed (deceived by the similarity of the name for the Sun) that a transit through the heavens was being described. Thus, a miracle performed by God was transformed into a fictional argument for human folly. This is the view of Angelomus, an ancient author of keen judgment regarding the hidden places of Holy Scripture in his *Miscellanies on the Books of Kings*. Indeed, this opinion seems so probable to me that I am quite convinced the myth of Phaethon <note>The son of Helios who attempted to drive the solar chariot and crashed.</note> had no other origin than this sacred history. But we shall discuss these matters more precisely elsewhere.

Furthermore, as to why the people of Sepharvaim expressed the idol Adramelech in the image of a mule, I have little to say, unless perhaps the Rabbis were looking to the custom of the Elians. Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer.</note> records that, in the opinion of others, they were accustomed to carve the Moon riding on a mule. <margin>Pausanias.</margin> *On the base of the throne of Olympian Zeus,* he says, *other images of the Gods are expressed, as well as the Moon on a horse, as it seems to me; yet others say she is carried by a mule, not a horse.* Certainly, Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note> confirms the opinion of Pausanias in clear words: <margin>Festus.</margin> *The mule,* he says, *is used for the vehicle of the Moon because she is as sterile as a mule; or because, just as a mule is created not from its own kind but from a horse, so she shines not by her own brightness but by the Sun's.* Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>, in his commentary on Hesiod, also records that the mule was sacred to the Moon. <margin>Proclus.</margin>

<margin>Adramelech was in the form of a peacock.</margin>
Nevertheless, having carefully considered everything, I lean more toward the opinion of the Jerusalem Paraphrast <note>The Targum, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, who asserts that Adramelech was in the form of a peacock, or some other beautiful bird, such as a pheasant or a guinea fowl. I am moved not only by the etymology but also by the highest honor paid at all times by the Persians and other nations to this bird,

### TREATISE IV. THE PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER XX.

<margin>The peacock is sacred to Juno.</margin>
...clothed. For the peacock is a bird of such beauty that it is not without reason that it rejoices in the name of Adramelech, which signifies a "Magnificent King." <note>The name Adramelech is derived from the Hebrew *Adar* (magnificent) and *Melech* (king).</note> It follows that, due to its rare qualities of spirit and body, it was not without cause that it was dedicated to the supreme Goddess and Mother of the Gods, obtaining the title of "Juno’s bird." We have previously shown from the writings of Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the *Deipnosophistae*.</note> that the first colonies of peacocks, guinea fowls, and roosters were brought out of Persia; these established their seats in various regions, but most notably in Samos, where they began to be held sacred to Juno. Indeed, they were held in such high honor there that, according to Pierius <note>Pierio Valeriano (1477–1558), a famous Renaissance author on hieroglyphics and symbols.</note>, the people understood the Goddess Juno herself through the single <term>hieroglyphic</term> <note>Kircher uses this term broadly to mean a sacred symbol or visual metaphor.</note> of the peacock. Various coins found here and there demonstrate the truth of this matter. On a coin of Julia Pia Felix <note>Julia Domna, wife of Emperor Septimius Severus.</note>, there is a sign of Juno with a spear and a <term>patera</term> <note>A shallow ceramic or metal libation bowl used in ritual offerings.</note>, with a peacock placed nearby, bearing the inscription *Pauonem* <note>original: "Pauonem" (Peacock), notably in the accusative case.</note> in the accusative case, which is a rare occurrence. On the coins of Faustina <note>Likely Faustina the Elder or Younger, Roman Empresses.</note>, there is likewise an idol with a lance and a patera, with a peacock at its feet; the inscription reads: TO JUNO LUCINA. <note>original Latin: "IVNONI LVCINÆ." Juno Lucina was the goddess who presided over childbirth, "bringing children into the light."</note> Furthermore, they imagine this bird belongs to Juno and follows her chariot because Juno is considered the same as the Moon; for the Moon, having received her brightness from the Sun, gladdens all lower things with her charming and beautiful appearance, of which the peacock's feathers—expressing a likeness to the moon—were a symbol.

<margin>Athenaeus.</margin>
Athenaeus relates that for the same reason, the peacock was held in honor by the Persians, because by its manifold brightness and variety of colors, it exactly reflected the image of the Sun, whom they worshipped as their one and only God. Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–180 AD), a Syrian-Greek satirist and rhetorician.</note> describes this sympathy of the peacock for the Sun, and other gifts of its nature, most elegantly in these words:

<margin>Lucian.</margin>
> At the beginning of Spring, he says, the peacock approaches some meadow, just as the flowers are coming forth—flowers that are not only more lovely, but, so to speak, more florid, and more liquid in their colors and dye. He himself also extends his feathers, showing them to the Sun and lifting his tail, spreading it out all around himself. He offers for inspection his own flowers and that "Spring of feathers," as if the meadow itself were provoking him to a contest and rivalry of this kind. For he turns himself about and wheels around, as if in a certain procession of his own beauty, appearing even more admirable in the splendor of the Sun as the colors vary, passing gradually from one shade into another, and repeatedly taking on a new appearance of beauty. This happens especially in the circles <note>The "eyes" of the peacock tail.</note> which he has at the ends of his feathers, each of which is surrounded by something like a rainbow. For what just before appeared bronze-like is seen as golden when he leans slightly; and again, what appeared blue toward the Sun, if it is moved into the shade, appears green; thus it varies according to the change of light.

<margin>The Egyptians called the peacock "Argos."</margin>
<margin>Pierius.</margin>
Thus far Lucian. Beholding this wonderful change of colors, the later Egyptians were so amazed that, according to Pierius, they took the peacock—which they called "Argos" <note>Referring to Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed giant of Greek myth whose eyes were placed in the peacock's tail by Juno.</note>—to be a hieroglyphic for night and day. Signifying Night, he says, they figured the peacock with its tail raised in a circle; for when they interpreted the peacock as Argos, distinguished by so many lights (eyes), they understood it as "all-seeing." This seems to refer to nothing other than the sky at night, and they professed that its name was given from its splendor and swiftness (for *Argos* signifies both). Since the rays of the stars do not twinkle and shine more brightly at any other time than at night, a place was given for this fiction, so that through the "eyed" tail of that bird, Night itself might be signified in a mystical and hieroglyphic sense. But if they wished to suggest Day...

### CHAPTER XXI.
->Concerning Nisroch, Rimmon, Nebo, and Sesach.<-

**I** find hardly anyone who relates what kind of deity Nisroch of the Assyrians was; however, the words of sacred history clearly show that it was a deity and an idol:

<margin>2 Kings ch. 19, last verse.</margin>
And it came to pass, as he was worshiping in the house of Nisroch his god: <note>original Hebrew: ויהי הוא משתחוה בבית נסרוך אלהיו</note>

*And Sennacherib the King of the Assyrians departed,* it says, *and dwelt in Nineveh; and it came to pass, as he was worshiping in the temple of Nisroch his God, etc.* Where the Chaldean paraphrase <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> holds, instead of *his God*, *his idol*:

And it was when he was worshiping in the temple of Nisroch his idol: <note>original Aramaic: והוה הוא סגיד בבית נסרוך פתכריה</note>

*And it happened when he was worshiping in the temple of Nisroch his idol.* As far, therefore, as I am able to understand from the *Meturgamim* <note>The "Translators" or commentators of the Aramaic Targums.</note> of the Hebrews, I find that Nisroch was nothing else but a plank from the Ark of Noah, which was always held in the highest veneration in Assyria. <note>Kircher is likely deriving "Nisroch" from the Hebrew word *neser*, meaning a plank or board.</note> However, whether they simply worshiped the Plank, or whether they worshiped it fashioned into the form of some image—either that of Janus or the image of Saturn, by which names I read in Berosus <note>Berosus was a 3rd-century BCE Babylonian priest and historian whose works survive only in fragments cited by others.</note> that Noah was called by posterity—is open to debate; traces of both types of worship are found everywhere among authors. In order that these things may be properly understood:

<margin>Noah most famous among the Easterners.</margin>
It should be noted that, because of his extreme antiquity, Noah is still today most famous among the peoples of the East for the preservation of human safety—so much so that the Scythians <note>An ancient nomadic people of Central Asia.</note> of old, as Berosus testifies, were accustomed to call Noah the father of all gods, major and minor, the Author of the human race, both Chaos and the seed of the world; while they called Thytea "Aretia" <note>From the Hebrew *eretz*, meaning earth.</note>, that is, the earth, in which Chaos placed the seed, and from which all came forth as if from the earth.

<margin>The place where the Ark of Noah rested.</margin>
Now indeed, that the remains of the Ark and the certain traces of its resting place are still held in the highest veneration is testified to, besides Nicephorus, by the Emperor Heraclius, <note>Byzantine Emperor (r. 610–641 CE).</note> whom the Arab Elmacinus <note>Al-Makin, a 13th-century Christian Arab historian.</note> relates in book 1, near the end of chapter 1, to have wished to see this so famous mountain, moved by the renown of the place. For when he had overcome the Persians in neighboring Armenia in battle, he departed from there to the town of Themanim <term>Thamaneen, meaning "Eighty"</term> <note>Traditional site near Mount Judi; the name refers to the eighty people believed by some traditions to have been on the Ark.</note> which Noah himself with his family was believed to have both founded and inhabited after exiting the ark; and having climbed the highest mountain, he diligently investigated the site of the location and the remains. His Arabic words are:

*When Heraclius the Caesar defeated the King of the Persians, he entered and passed over the very high mountain named Al-Judi; when he heard many things about it, he himself sought to see it and climbed it to view the place. When he descended from the mountain, he came to the place named Themanim, which is the city of the sons of Noah, and he saw everything with his own eyes.* <note>original Arabic: فلما غلب هرکليس قيصر ملك الفرس ودخل مجتازاً للجبل العالي جدا اسمه الجودي فلما يسمع منه كثيرين يطلب نفسه لنظره وصعد عليه لنظر الموضع فلما ينزل من الجبل جا الى الموضع اسمه ثمانين التي هى مدينة بني نوح وكل شي نظر بعينيه</note>

### SYNTAGMA IV. THE HEBREW PANTHEON. 377
### CHAPTER XXI.

When the Emperor Heraclius, having defeated the King of Persia, was crossing that very high mountain in Armenia named *Gurdi* <note>Mount Judi, often identified in Eastern traditions as the landing site of the Ark rather than the modern Mount Ararat.</note>, about which he had heard so much, he was seized by a desire to survey it himself. He therefore ascended to see its entire situation, and as he was descending from the mountain, he also came to that place which they call *Temanin* <note>From the Arabic "Thamanin," meaning "eight," referring to the eight survivors of the Flood.</note>. This is the city which Noah is said to have built with his sons after the Flood; the Emperor wished to survey all these things with his own eyes. This is according to Elmacinus <note>George Elmacin, a 13th-century Coptic Christian historian.</note>, where you should understand that by Mount *Gurdi*, no other is meant than Mount Ararat; for the Chaldean *Targum* of Onkelos <note>An ancient Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note> calls it so in Genesis, chapter 8.

<margin>Chaldean Targum</margin>
And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, upon the mountains of Kordu. <note>original Aramaic: ונחת תיבותא בירחא שביעאה בשבעת עשרא יומא לירחא על טורי קרדו</note>

*And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, upon the mountains of Kordu.* Strabo also recognizes the *Gordiaean* mountains between Armenia and Mesopotamia; indeed, even today the tradition of the *Cordaeans* <note>The Kurds.</note> living there—now infamous for robberies—is very common in Persian travelogues. The *Nubian Geography* <note>The "Tabula Rogeriana" by the medieval Arab geographer al-Idrisi.</note> also mentions *Temanim* and Mount *Gurdi*, which lies adjacent to it; I include its words:

<margin>Strabo.</margin>

<margin>Nubian or Arabic Geography, p. 3, climate 4.</margin>
From Mosul to the city of Beld is twenty-one miles, whether you go by land or by the Tigris river; from Beld to the island of Aben Amar is sixty-nine miles. This is connected to Mount Temanim and Masurin, and Qilsabur; all of these are in the mountain range from which comes Mount Algudi <note>Al-Judi</note>, which reaches to Amid on the side of the frontier fortresses. This Mount Temanim is the very Judi upon which the Ark of Noah (peace be upon him) came to rest. <note>original Arabic: من الموصل الى مدينة بلد احد وعشرون ميلا ان شيت في البر وان شيت في الدجلة من بلد الى جزيرة ابن عمر تسعة وستون ميلا وهي متصلة بجبل يمنين وماسورين وقلسابور جميعها في الجبل الذي منه جبل الجودي المتصل بامد من جهة الثغور وجبل يمنين هو الجودي الذي استقرت عليه السفينة نوح عليه السلام</note>

*From Mosul to the city of Beld is 21 miles, whether you wish to go through the desert, or on the river Digla itself (that is, the Tigris); from Beld to the island of Aben Amar is 69 miles. This is joined with Mount Temanim and Masurin, and Kilfabur, both are on that mountain from which is Mount Algudi (understand this as Gurdi), which reaches to Amid from the direction of the citadels. This Mount Temanim or Themanim is the Gordian mountain itself, in which the Ark of Noah rested; peace be upon him.* And that place *Themanim* seems to be the one which Berosus <note>A Babylonian priest and historian from the 3rd century BCE.</note> calls sometimes *Myriada*, and sometimes *Merinacha*—that is, the place of egress, or the descent of *Noah*. From all the perplexity I encountered in this passage, I was rescued by Jonathan Uzielides <note>Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, an Aramaic translation of the Torah.</note>, the Chaldean Interpreter (*Meturgeman*), who in his paraphrase of Genesis chapter 8 explains the difficulty of the whole matter in express words.

<margin>Jonathan Uzielides.</margin>
And the ark rested in the seventh month, which is the month of Nisan, on the seventeenth day of the month, upon the mountain of Kardon; the name of one mountain is Kardania, and the name of the other mountain is Armenia, and there they built the city of Armenia in the land of Merinacka. <note>original Aramaic: ונחת תיבותא בירא שביעאה הוא ירחא דניסן בשבעעשרי יומין לירחא על טורא דקרדון שום טורא חד קרדניא ושום טורא חד ארמניא ותמן מתבניא קרתא דארמנייא בארעה מרינחא</note>

*And it rested, he says, the ark in the seventh month (that is the month of Nisan), on the seventeenth day of the Month, upon mount Kardon.* Now, there is the name of one mountain of the *Gordenes*, and the name of a mountain in *Armenia*, and there they built a city of *Armenia* in the land of *Merinacka*. Furthermore, *Merinacka* is a corrupted word, meaning the same as *Morid Noah* <note>Hebrew: מוריד נח</note>, which is to say, the "Descent of Noah," which Berosus, cited above, also calls the "Egress of Noah." This also explains *Moriadam*, a word which the translator of Berosus mistakenly calls "the field of the eviscerated men"; whereas *Mori Adam* intended to indicate nothing else but *Morid Adam* <note>Hebrew: מוריד אדם</note>, that is, the "Descent of the sons of Adam," or the "Descent of Man"; because from the descent of *Noah*, a single man, the entire human race was resuscitated.

### 378 THE ISIACO TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>CHAPTER XXI.</margin>
<margin>Eastern peoples worshipped Noah and the remains of the ark.</margin>
Since, therefore, Noah—as the "seed of the world"—was worshipped at all times with divine honors as a certain Deity under the names of Osiris, Saturn, or Janus by various nations (as we also demonstrated in the first *Syntagma* <note>The first major section of Kircher's *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*.</note>); and since he placed the remains of that prodigious vessel, by which he preserved the world, upon the Gordyaean mountains <note>The Judi Dagh or Ararat range.</note>, or the Ararat of Armenia, which was one of the provinces of the Assyrians; there is no doubt that the neighboring nations worshipped not only Noah himself, but also the remains of that wonderful house with divine honors, even to the point of extreme superstition. Indeed, the narrative of Berosus <note>Berossus was a 3rd-century BCE Babylonian priest. Kircher is likely quoting a version popular in the Renaissance attributed to Annius of Viterbo.</note> makes me believe this entirely, for he reports that the neighboring tribes were accustomed to scrape off the **bitumen** <note term="bitumen">A naturally occurring petroleum-based pitch or tar used to waterproof the Ark.</note> from it to use as an amulet. I shall provide his words:

<margin>Berosus.</margin>
> *There was one among the Giants,* he says, *who was more reverent toward the Gods and more prudent than all the others of the upright men in Syria; his name was Noah, with his three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and their wives Titea the Great, Pandora, Noela, and Noegla.* <note>These names for the wives are not found in the Bible but come from the "Pseudo-Berosus" traditions.</note> *Fearing the calamity which he had foreseen from the stars, in the seventy-eighth year before the inundation, he began to build a ship covered like an ark. Thus, in the seventy-eighth year from the beginning of the ship, the Ocean unexpectedly overflowed, and all the Mediterranean seas and the rivers and springs bubbling up from the depths inundated above all the mountains, with most impetuous and supernatural rains falling from the sky for many days. Thus the entire human race was suffocated by the waters, except for Noah with his family, who were saved by the ship; for, lifted by the waters, it rested on the summit of the Gordyaean mountain, of which a certain part is still said to exist, and men take bitumen from it, which they use especially for expiation.* <note>In this context, "expiation" refers to ritual purification or protection from evil.</note>

Haython, himself a native of Armenia (whatever those who claim he was from Cilicia may say), confirms that in his own time—namely 1300 years after Christ—the remains of the ark were still seen on the mountain.

<margin>Haython.</margin>
> *In Armenia,* he says, *there is a mountain higher than any in the whole world, which is commonly called Ararat; and on the summit of that mountain, Noah’s ark first settled after the flood. Although, because of the abundance of snow which is always found on that mountain both in winter and summer, no one is able to climb it, something black always appears on its summit, which men say is the ark of Noah.*

I have heard more than once from the Armenians themselves about the superstitions regarding the pieces of the ark and the bitumen collected around the neck of the highest peak by neighboring tribes who visit the mountain at certain times of the year to ward off diseases and misfortunes. The Armenian Annals also record that a small piece of this ark was divinely brought by an Angel to Saint Syrianus <note>Likely St. Jacob (Hagop) of Nisibis, who is traditionally associated with seeking a piece of the Ark.</note>; as I have heard many times from Father Petro Copo, an Armenian very familiar to me and my master in the Armenian language. Indeed, the most trustworthy traveler Benjamin <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler.</note> teaches that a shrine was built by a Caliph in later times for the sake of religion from the very timbers of the ark; his words are:

<margin>Benjamin.</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: מטם שני ימים לגזירה בן עמר והוא בתוך נהר חדקל לרגלי הרי אררט מהלך ד' מילין למקום שנחה שם תבת נח אבל עמר בן אלכטאב לקח את התיבה מעל הראש ההרים ועשה אותה כנסת לישמעאלים ובקרוב התיבה כנסת עזרא הסופר עד היום הזה וביום באים יהודים להתפלל שם וגו'</note>
