### SYNTAGMA IV. PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER XXI.

[...he took] it from the summit of the twin mountain, and built a temple from it for the Ishmaelites <note>A common historical term for Muslims.</note>, specifically for their religious use; near which is also the Synagogue of Ezra the Scribe, where Jews gather for prayer on holidays. If these things Benjamin <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler.</note> reports are true, they certainly should not be understood as the entire Ark being removed for the use of the Church <note>Meaning for the construction of religious buildings.</note>; but rather regarding parts found here and there, decayed by the passage of time, or scattered by the force of winds and rains from the summit to the lower part of the mountain.

<margin>Nisroch was an Ark made from the wood of Noah's Ark.</margin>
Thus, to return to our path, since all nations have always greatly worshipped relics of this kind; I conclude from all this that the deity **Nisroch**, whom we showed from Sacred Scripture was worshipped by Sennacherib, was nothing other than either an idol or a small chest or "little boat" made from the remains of Noah’s Ark. Under this form, the neighboring Assyrians or Babylonians worshipped **Saturn** or **Janus**—whom they called **Nisroch** in their own language—not unlike how the Egyptians worshipped that Ark in which they fabulously claim **Osiris** was thrown by **Typhon** <note>The myth of Osiris and Set.</note>; I mean that secret Ark, fertile with sacred mysteries, about which you may consult Apuleius in Book 11 of the *Metamorphoses*. The example of the Hebrews could have greatly stabilized the worship of the Noachic Ark in the minds of the Assyrians. The Hebrews attributed all prosperity to the worship and veneration of the **Ark of the Covenant**, adoring it as God Himself manifesting within it; this is clearly shown by the words of the people of Beth-Shemesh <note>original: "Betsamitarum"</note>, whom we read cried out in terror before the presence of the Deity after that formidable slaughter of seventy thousand men who looked irreverently upon it:

> *Who will be able to stand in the sight of the Lord, this holy God? And to whom shall he go up from us?*

These words clearly show that the people of Beth-Shemesh revered the Ark itself as some sort of Deity; which the Rabbis also assert in this place. By this example, therefore, the Assyrians also constructed an Ark in which—just as the Hebrews stored the **Tables of the Law**, the **Manna**, the **Rod of Aaron**, and similar sacred <term>lipsana</term> <note>A Greek-derived term for holy relics or physical remains.</note> to recall God’s benefits and the conditions of the sworn covenant—so too it is very probable that the Assyrians (who had received many traditions concerning Noah and his Ark, and always saw the present remains on the nearby mountain before them) attempted something similar from pieces joined together from Noah’s Ark. This they called **Nesroch**, that is, the "Deity of the Ark" (For נסרא *Nesra*, or נסר *Neser* in Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> means nothing other than a plank from Noah's Ark), and they worshipped it as a God. But lest anyone think I assert these things without foundation or reasons, I will produce as a witness of this matter that most famous treatise which the Jews call <term>אגדת חלק</term> *Agadat Helek* <note>The "Legendary portion of Chelek," referring to a famous chapter in the Talmudic tractate Sanhedrin.</note>, in which the author, speaking of the idolatry of Assyria, mentions **Nisroch** among other things in these words:

<note>original Hebrew: וסגיד סנחריב בית נסרוך אלהיה וחיה נסרוך טעותא נסר מתיבותא של נח עבדוהו אנשי אשור כאלחיה</note>
*And Sennacherib worshipped in the house of Nesroch his God; and this Nesroch was an idol made from a plank of Noah’s Ark, which the men of Assyria venerated as their God.* 

If perhaps anyone trusts these words less, let him hear the more common Rabbis—Rabbi Solomon Jarchi <note>Also known as Rashi.</note> and David Kimchi—confirming these statements, where Kimchi says in his commentaries on 2 Kings 19 <note>original: "19. l. 4. Regum." In the Vulgate, 2 Kings is titled 4 Kings.</note>:

### CHAPTER XXI. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

->The House of Nisroch is a plank from the Ark of Noah:<-

<margin>Rabbis Solomon, Jarchi, David</margin>
This means: *Beth Nisroch, from a plank of the Ark of Noah.* <note>Kircher is citing the Rabbinic tradition (Rashi and Kimchi) which connects the name of the Assyrian god Nisroch to the Hebrew word 'Nesher' or 'Neserr,' meaning a plank or board.</note> I do not cite the other source, as it confirms the matter with the exact same words. Moreover, it is said in the sacred text that Sennacherib worshipped in the house of Nisroch his god:

->And it came to pass, as he was worshipping in the house of Nisroch his god:<-

*And he worshipped in the house of Nisroch his god, that is, the Ark of Noah:* Now, the Chaldean Paraphrast <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and exposition of the Hebrew Bible.</note> suggests that this Ark was treated like a certain idol when he says:

->And he worshipped in the house of Nisahkh, his idol:<-

<margin>The Chaldean Paraphrast.</margin>
*And he worshipped in the house of Nisroch his idol.* <note>The Aramaic word 'ta’ut' used here literally means 'error' or 'wandering,' a common Jewish term for an idol.</note> Therefore, Nisroch was nothing else but an idol or a chest constructed from the wood of the Noachic Ark, under which form they honored their Saturn or Bel, who we have stated above was Noah.

<margin>Rimmon.</margin>
The sacred history of the Kings also teaches us that Rimmon was a deity among the Syrians; however, as to what kind of deity it was, there is deep silence from everyone. Some think it was Venus, because *Rimmonim*—that is, *pomegranates*—are read to have been sacred to her. <margin>Selden.</margin> John Selden says that Rimmon was the same deity that the Phoenicians call *Elioan*, <margin>Hesychius.</margin> and Hesychius calls *rhamas*, which is to say, *the highest God* <note>Original Greek: ῥαμὰς ... ὕψιστον Θεὸν</note>. <margin>Rimmon is the same as Pomona.</margin> It is more likely that Rimmon was the same deity that the ancients called Pomona, namely, the goddess presiding over orchard-fruits and produce. For the priest of Pomona <note>Latin: Flamen Pomonalis.</note> mentioned in the works of Festus sufficiently shows that this goddess was worshipped with the highest veneration by the nations. The etymology of the word greatly supports the truth of this conjecture; for just as the goddess of flowers, Flora, comes from "flowers"; and the goddess of the earth, Tellus, from "earth"; and the goddess <note>While traditionally a male god, Kircher classifies Dagon here among nature-deities with a feminine grammatical association in his comparison.</note> of fish and the sea, Dagon, comes from "fish"; and their goddess Astaroth from *Asherah*, that is, from "woods and groves"; and other deities of the nations about which we spoke previously—all obtained their names either from the things over which they preside, or from the effects they work upon the matter they oversee; thus Rimmon also, no differently than Pomona, seems to have its name from the fruit <note>Latin: pomum, connecting to the Hebrew 'Rimmon' for pomegranate.</note>. But let it suffice to have only suggested these things.

<margin>Nebo.</margin>
Furthermore, among other deities of the Babylonians, Nebo also occurs, according to that passage of Isaiah 46:1: *Bel is bowed down, Nebo is broken; their idols were upon the beasts and the cattle, your heavy burdens even unto weariness.* Yet what kind of idol this was, is difficult to assert.

<margin>The Seventy Interpreters.</margin>
<margin>St. Jerome.</margin>
The Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translate it in this place as Dagon: *Bel has fallen, Dagon is shattered* <note>Original Greek: Επεσε Βὴλ, συνετρίבה Δαγὼν</note>. St. Jerome, in his commentary on this passage, considers Nebo to be an idol through which they practiced divinations and sought oracles. His words are: *Babylon has fallen, Nebo is broken.* The Greeks call Bel *Belos*, and the Latins call him *Saturn*; whose religious devotion was so great among the ancients that they sacrificed to him not only human victims of captives and ignoble mortals, but even their own children. Nebo, however, is that same idol which is interpreted as "divination" and "prophecy," which Jerome indicates fell silent throughout the whole world after the truth of the Gospel arrived; or according to the Seventy it is *Dagon* <note>Original Greek: Δαγὼν</note>, which however is not found in the Hebrew. It is the idol of Ashkelon, Gaza, and the remaining cities of the Philistines. And from the specific he passes to the general: *their idols were made for beasts and cattle*; not because the idols of the nations were exposed as prey for beasts and cattle, but because...

From this it is clear that for some in this passage, Nebo is concluded to be none other than Chemosh, whom we have shown above to be Bacchus; let them see for themselves on what foundation they base this. To us, indeed, it is more probable that Nebo and Bel were nothing else than any kind of portable idols, transported by the labor of cattle as their worshippers migrated from place to place. This was done in such a way that all those idols through which they practiced divinations, or which they used in place of oracles—such as the <term>Teraphim</term> <note>Household idols or figurines used for divination, often mentioned in the Old Testament.</note>, <term>Ob</term> <note>A medium or a "familiar spirit," often associated with necromancy.</note>, <term>Yiddeoni</term> <note>Translated here as "Ieduah," meaning a "knowing one" or a wizard's spirit.</note>, the table of great fortune, and similar instruments of the magical art—were called "Nebo" from divination and prophecy; while other images were called by the common name "Bel" or "Baal," as we showed in the chapter on the Baalim of the Hebrews.
<margin>Nebo signifies any kind of portable images.</margin>
The truth of this opinion is indicated not only by the text of sacred history, which, in order to mock the worshippers of such idols, aptly alludes to transport by saying that the beasts themselves groaned, bowed down under the weight of the gods. But also St. Jerome, in the cited passage, along with the commentators on this place, asserts in manifest words that those idols were multiform and fashioned from gold and silver, where they describe the ceremonies performed for such gods no less learnedly than with great wit.
<margin>St. Jerome</margin>
Moreover, what the Table of Great Fortune was, we have said in the chapter on Baal-Gad; it seemed appropriate to explain briefly what <term>Ob</term> and <term>Yiddeoni</term> were. Moses deals with *Ob* and *Yiddeoni* in Leviticus chapter 20, where the Sacred Scripture asserts that every soul turning aside to magicians and soothsayers must be cut off.

### CHAPTER XXI. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>
Moses of Coucy in *The Commandments*, neg. 38.
Rambam in *Yachazik* ch. 6.
Paul Riccius on *The Commandments*, neg. 36.
Ralbag.
</margin>
Most translate this as a Python or a Magician; however, from Rabbi Moses of Coucy <note>A 13th-century French rabbi, author of the *Sefer Mitzvot Gadol*.</note>, Rambam <note>Maimonides (1135–1204), the preeminent Jewish philosopher and legal scholar.</note>, and Paul Riccius <note>A 16th-century Jewish convert to Christianity and physician to Emperor Maximilian I.</note>, I gather that the **Ob** <note>Hebrew: אוב; often translated as "medium" or "familiar spirit."</note> was nothing other than a Spirit or Demon. This spirit gave responses from the "unclean parts" of the body—parts which cannot be decently named—and sometimes from the head or armpits. It spoke in a low voice, either through a Soothsayer or as if the deceased were speaking from the depths of the Earth, such that it could not be heard clearly but was perceived only in the mind of the one consulting it; so says Ralbag <note>Gersonides (1288–1344), a philosopher and commentator.</note> in his commentary on the 28th chapter of 1 Samuel.

> The Rabbis of blessed memory say that the meaning of the *Ob* is one who raises the dead; he himself does not hear a word, but he sees the image of the dead. The one inquiring, however, does not see the image, but hears words according to his thoughts regarding his question, etc.
<note>original Hebrew: "ארזל סענין האוב הוא שהמעלה את המת הוא בלתי שומע דבר רואה תמונת המת הוא ושואל לא יראה התמונה ההיא אבל ישמע דברים מח לפי מחשבתו על שאלתו וגו'"</note>

> *The Rabbis of blessed memory say,* Kircher continues, *that the Ob or Python was a phenomenon that caused the dead to rise; the medium, without hearing a word, saw the image of the deceased; the one asking the Python, however, did not see the image or shadow of the dead, yet heard the words which he had conceived in his mind regarding his inquiry. Thus for Saul, the likeness of the deceased Samuel was represented by a woman, from whose private parts the Ob spoke. The woman, whether she be called a Pythoness or, as the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translate it,* <gloss>a woman who speaks from the belly</gloss> <note>original Greek: "γυναῖκα ἐγγαστρίμυθον" (engastrimythos), the origin of the word "ventriloquist."</note>, *is called by the Scripture* <gloss>a woman possessing an Ob</gloss>, <note>original Hebrew: "אשת בעלת אוב" (Eshet Ba'alat Ob)</note> that is,

<margin>Ob, a ventriloquist spirit.</margin>
A woman having an **Ob**. Therefore, the **Ob** itself is this ventriloquist spirit; the Pythoness herself, or the Soothsayer, is called by this name: *Baal* or *Baalath Ob* <note>"Master" or "Mistress of the Spirit."</note>. While they were being initiated, they held in their hands a <gloss>myrtle wand</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: "שרביט של הדס" (Sharvit shel Hadas)</note> and were purified with smoke, as Rambam testifies in the cited place. Furthermore, Rabbi Abraham Ben David <note>A 12th-century critic of Maimonides.</note> records that the location for such rituals was the grave of the deceased.

<margin>St. Jerome</margin>
This shameful and ridiculous religion of the ventriloquist Python-spirit originated from nowhere else but Egypt. To the Egyptians, a filthy demon often gave responses through the private parts of the human body, most especially through the rear with a burst of noise. We have already recorded in *Syntagma 2*, in the chapters on Egyptian superstitions, that this sound from the belly was worshipped by them with divine honors. St. Jerome also records this in his commentary on the 56th chapter of Isaiah, as do others whom we cited in the said *Syntagma*. To gain greater prestige for these most foul oracles, the unclean Devil would involve superstitious minds more easily by often granting an infallible result to the questions asked. But let these things suffice regarding those unspeakable rites. Let us now pass to the *Iedeonim*.

<margin>The Iideonim is a Soothsayer.</margin>
They say, therefore, that the *Iideonim* <note>Hebrew: ידעוני; usually translated as "wizard" or "familiar spirit."</note> is a Soothsayer who, by placing the bone of a living creature called the <gloss>Iedoa</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: "ידעוני" (Yedua)</note> into his mouth, would teach of future things and resolve inquiries. Regarding that animal, they write that this *Iadoa* <note>Likely referring to the "Vegetable Lamb of Tartary," a legendary zoophyte thought to be part plant and part animal.</note> had a human form in every part, but was tied to a cord of a certain root and remained fixed there alive from its first birth, until those who dared not approach closer due to its innate ferocity killed it with arrows. However, it is more likely that *Iideonim* is derived from the word <gloss>to know</gloss> <note>original Hebrew: "ידע" (Yada)</note>; that is, he knew. It is the same as a Soothsayer who consults on a matter with a certain mental purpose. They expected the dead to make them more certain of the things they asked about through dreams while they spent the night next to tombs. With the help of the Pythonesses, they even consulted the summoned spirits of the dead, as is said of Samuel; which Rambam confirms...

<margin>Jonathan the Chaldean</margin>
> Who dwell in houses built from the dust of graves, and stay with the corpses of men, and eat the flesh of swine.
<note>original Aramaic: "דיתבן בבתיא דבנָן מעפר קבריא ועם פגרי בני אנשׁא דירין דאכלין בשר חזיִרא"</note>

*Who dwell in houses, which are built from the dust of graves, and stay with the corpses of the sons of men, and eat swine's flesh.* With these words, the Paraphrast <note>The author of the Targum.</note> primarily refers to the customs of the Egyptians, from whom the Hebrews had drawn all their own practices, as has already been said often. It was solemn for them to enter those shrines—their subterranean caves where they used to bury the bodies of the dead—to seek responses; as we shall show in detail in the place where we treat the mummies of the Egyptians. Indeed, Radak <note>Rabbi David Kimhi (1160–1235), a prominent medieval rabbi and grammarian.</note> reveals the reason why they stayed in such places to consult oracles:

<margin>Radak</margin>
> Sitting in graves to consult the dead; they stay in ruins at night so that demons might appear to them, for they believe that harmful spirits appear in ruins to those who believe in them.
<note>original Hebrew: "היוֹשְׁבִים בקברים לדרוֹשׁ אל המֵתים בחורבות ילינוֹ בלילה שׁיראוּ להם שׁדים לדעתם כי המזיקים נראים בחורבות למאמינים"</note>

*Sitting in graves, that they may consult the dead; they stay in solitudes and in the night, so that demons might appear to them and they might know them: since those nocturnal demons tend to appear to those who believe in them (that is, their worshipers) nowhere more easily than in solitudes and dark places.* But let us return to our subject. There were, therefore, various instruments or idols through which the ancients performed their divinations, with the Devil giving responses through them. These were called **Nebo**, which is to say, prophecy or divination, from the effect they produced. Of this sort were the Teraphim, the Isiac statues, the Ob, the Ieduah, Beelphegor; the Fortune’s Counting-Board, the table of the Sun and Moon, and similar things, which will be treated specifically elsewhere. And these are those idols of Nebo which they carried with them wherever they went, transported in chariots; through these they prophesied, and finally, they held these in the place of Gods. Moreover, there were various forms of this kind: some of infants, others of serpents or other beasts, many of a man, an infant, or a maiden, through whose obscene parts the demon spoke, as we have shown in the preceding pages.

<margin>Sesach</margin>
Furthermore, having explained these things—perhaps more extensively than was proper as the occasion arose—order now requires that we also say something about **Sesach** <note>Sheshach, mentioned in Jeremiah 25:26 and 51:41; generally understood as a cryptogram for "Babel."</note>. This name is found in two places in Jeremiah, namely chapters 25 and 51. Truly, I do not see by what reasoning many count Sesach among the deities of the Babylonians; since it cannot be shown from the cited passages of Jeremiah, nor are other reasons available by which it could be effectively proven. John Selden <note>1584–1654, an English jurist and scholar of ancient Near Eastern religions.</note>, moved by I know not what conjecture, attempts to prove this from the *Sacca*, a Babylonian festival dedicated to the deity Sesach. He brings as a witness of this— <margin>Selden</margin>

EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE
384

<margin>CHAPTER XXII.</margin>
Athenaeus, in his *Deipnosophistae* <note>A 3rd-century Greek work titled "The Banquet of the Learned."</note>, Book 14, quotes Berosus <note>A Babylonian priest and historian from the 3rd century BCE.</note>: "Berosus," he says, "in the first book of the *Babyloniaca*, states that on the sixteenth day of the month of Loos, a festival called Sacea is celebrated in Babylon for five days. During these days, it is the custom for masters to be ruled by their servants; one of the servants leads the household, dressed in a robe similar to a king’s, and he is called the *Zoganes*." <note>original Greek: "Βήρωσός, inquit ille, ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ Βαβυλωνιακῶν, τῷ λώῳ μηνὶ ἐκκαιδεκάτῃ φησί, ἄγεσθαι ἑορτὴν Σακέαν προσαγορευομένην ἐν Βαβυλῶνι ἐπὶ ἡμέρας πέντε, ἐν αἷς ἔθος εἶναι ἄρχεσθαι τοὺς δεσπότας ὑπὸ τῶν οἰκετῶν, ἀφηγεῖσθαί τε τῆς οἰκίας ἕνα, αὐτὸν ἐνδεδυκότα στολὴν ὁμοίαν τῇ βασιλικῇ, ὃν καὶ καλεῖσθαι ζωγάνην."</note> Ctesias <note>A Greek physician and historian of Persia.</note> also mentions this festival in the second book of his *Persica*.

*Berosus, in the first book of the Babylonian Histories, reports that on the sixteenth day of the month of Loos, the festival called Sacean is celebrated in Babylon for five days; during these, it is the custom for masters to obey the command of servants, and for one of them to preside over the family, clothed in royal attire, and he is named the Zoganes.*

<margin>Ctesias.</margin>
*Ctesias* also records the festival in the second book of the *Persian Histories*. Truly, from all these accounts, only this one thing is proven: that the Babylonians celebrated a festival by the name of Sacean. However, whether this festival takes its name from *Sesach*, or was dedicated to the honor of a deity named *Sesach* (as the cited author contends), this cannot be demonstrated by any reasoning from the passage of Berosus provided, saving the judgment of others. We therefore, relying on a better foundation, assert that *Sesach* is not 
<margin>Sesach signifies Babylonia and its King.</margin>
so much a specific deity, but rather a name devised by the Prophet through the *Atbash* method of the *Themura* Cabala <note>A system of Hebrew mysticism involving the substitution of letters.</note>, by which they mystically designated Babylonia and its King. For *Sesach* is written as ששך [S-Sh-K], and *Babel* as בבל [B-B-L]; by reversing the order of the letters starting from *Tav* (ת) <note>This is the Atbash cipher: the first letter is replaced by the last, the second by the second-to-last, etc. Thus, Beth (ב, the 2nd letter) becomes Shin (ש, the 21st/2nd from end), and Lamed (ל, the 12th) becomes Kaph (כ, the 11th).</note>, if you take *Shin* (ש) twice for *Beth* (ב), and *Kaph* (כ) for *Lamed* (ל), *Babel* becomes *Sesach*. Indeed, these things are commonly known even to schoolboys. Therefore, the devised name *Sesach* 
<margin>Concerning the Atbash Alphabet, see the Cabala of the Hebrews.</margin>
signifies nothing other than *Babel*. Thus, in this place, almost all the Rabbis explain it: "Its interpretation is that it is Babel through *Atbash*." <note>original Hebrew: "פֵּירוּשֵׁהוּ שֶׁהוּא בָּבֶל בָּא"ת בָּ"שׁ"</note> Moreover, Jonathan <note>Referring to the Targum Jonathan, an ancient Aramaic translation.</note>, in the cited passages of Jeremiah, translates *Sesach* in no other way than as *Babel*. The Prophet, therefore (as most of the Hebrews believe), lest he provoke the King of Babylon against himself, skillfully transformed the name *Babel* into *Sesach* by changing the letters; for it is said: *And Sesach shall drink after them—namely, the cup of the wrath of God.* <note>Jeremiah 25:26.</note> Nor is there a need for many authorities sought from elsewhere, since the Holy Scripture itself, to which we refer the reader, easily resolves the entire difficulty. Nor does the festival of the "Sacean days" (τῷ Σακαίων ἡμερῶν) do anything to establish the divinity of *Sesach*, since that festival was found to have been instituted in honor of the Babylonian and Persian Venus (whom we called Anaitis above) long before the time of Jeremiah, on account of a victory of the Persians and Babylonians (who are frequently confused by authors) over the *Sacae*—a Scythian people living within the Imaus mountains—as we 
<margin>Strabo, Photius, Iamblichus, Hesychius.</margin>
have also shown elsewhere. On these matters, consult Strabo, Book 11; Photius in the *Myriobiblon*, codex 72; Iamblichus the Syrian in his erotic tales of *Rhodanes and Sinonis*; and Hesychius, who also calls this festival a "Scythian feast" for the stated reason. And let these things said about *Sesach* suffice.

### TREATISE IV. PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. CHAPTER XXII.

<margin>Acts of the Apostles 7 v. 43.</margin>
...seventh [chapter], where St. Stephen reproaches the Jews for the idolatry of their ancestors with these words: *“And you took up the tabernacle of Moloch, and the star of your god Remphan, the figures which you made to worship them.”* Where the Syriac version has *Rephon* for *Remphan*:

->But you carried the tabernacle of Malcum <note>A name for Moloch used in the Syriac Bible.</note> and the star of the god Rephon, the images which you made that you might worship them; I will move you beyond Babylon.<-
<note>original Syriac: "ܐܠܐ ܫܩܠܬܘܢ ܡܫܟܢܗ ܕܡܠܟܘܡ ܘܟܘܟܒܐ ܕܐܠܗܐ ܕܪܦܢ ܕܡܝܬܐ ܕܥܒܕܬܘܢ ܕܬܗܘܘܢ ܣܓܕܝܢ ܠܗܘܢ ܐܫܢܝܟܘܢ ܠܗܠ ܡܢ ܒܒܠ܀"</note>

*“Rather, you carried the canopy of Melchum, and the star of your god Rephon, the images you made to worship them; I will move you beyond Babylon.”*

Who then was this Rephan? The opinions of interpreters regarding this passage vary; some interpret it as Venus, or the star which astronomers call Lucifer <note>The "Light-Bringer," or the Morning Star.</note>; others as Jupiter; there are also those who think Rephan is one of the fixed constellations. We, leaving aside all these conjectures, shall offer something more certain.

<margin>The word Rephan is Coptic; it signifies Saturn.</margin>
We say, therefore, that the word *Rephan* is Egyptian or Coptic, and that in the said language it signifies nothing other than Saturn, as is clearly established from our Coptic-Arabic-Latin *Onomasticon* <note>A dictionary or collection of names and technical terms published by Kircher.</note>, where Saturn is called *Rephan*, evidently on account of his gigantic size. I will here add the names of the Planets, as they are called by the Egyptians, excerpted from our said *Onomasticon*.

And you carried the canopies of Moloch, and the star of your God Repham you worship, which you yourselves made, etc.*

Therefore, it is not *Rompha* or *Rempham*, but *Rephan* is the proper name of Saturn in this place. I wonder at one thing: why in the Hebrew text of Amos 5, last verse, is it not read as *Rephan*, but as *Ciun* <note>original Hebrew: "כיון"</note>, when nevertheless in the cited passages both the Vulgate and the Septuagint, along with others recently mentioned, everywhere translate it as *Rephan*. I will provide the words of the Prophet here:

<margin>Amos 5, last verse.</margin>
## And you carried the tabernacle of your king and Ciun your images, the star of your gods, which you made for yourselves. <note>original Hebrew: "ונשאתם את סכות מלככם ואת כיון צלמיכם כוכב אלהיכם אשר עשיתם לכם׃"</note>

Which literally sound like this: *And you carried the tabernacles of your King, and the Ciun of your idols, the star of your God which you made for yourselves.* This seems to differ greatly from the Latin Vulgate version; for in this place the Vulgate has it thus:

<margin>Vulgate reading.</margin>
*And you carried the tabernacle for your Moloch, and the image of your idols, the star of your God Rempham.* To which another Greek reading agrees, which has *rompha* in place of *Ciun*. <margin>Jonathan the Chaldean.</margin>
## And you carried the tabernacles of the house of your priests, Ciun your image, the star your idol, which you made for yourselves. <note>original Aramaic: "ונטלתון ית סיכות בית כמיסיות כיון צלמיכם כוכב טעותכון די עברתון לבון׃"</note>

*And you carried together the tabernacles of your priests, and Ciun your image, the star your idol, which you made for yourselves.* And from all these things it is clear that *Ciun* and *Rephan* are taken for the same thing in this place. <margin>Rephan and Ciun are taken for the same thing.</margin> However, whether these two are different names for one idol, or whether it is the same name differing only by the corruption it suffered from various transcriptions, is doubtful. I find authors for both opinions. The Rabbis posit a different name from *Rephan*, <margin>Ciun, the cakes.</margin> and they say that *Ciun* <note>original Hebrew: "כיון"</note> here is the same as *Ceuauim* <note>original Hebrew: "כונים"</note>, that is, honeyed cakes, which were offered to the Queen of Heaven or Venus, whom we previously called *Succoth Benoth* <note>A deity or ritual site mentioned in 2 Kings 17:30, traditionally associated with "booths for daughters" or Venus.</note>. So Radak <note>Rabbi David Kimhi, a medieval Jewish commentator.</note> reports from others:

<margin>Radak.</margin>
## And you carried the tabernacle of your king, another name for a star that was made into an idol in his name, and he called it "king" because they thought him to be a king over them; or it was a great star in the host of heaven, which is— <note>original Hebrew: "ונשאתם את סכות מלככם אחר על כוכב שנעשה ע"ז על שמו וקורא אותו מלך לפי שהם חושבים אותו למלך עליהם או שהיה כוכב גדול בצבא השמים שהוא"</note>

### SYNTAGMA IV. THE HEBREW PANTHEON. CHAPTER XXII.

He who is like a king over his army; and "the Chiun of your images," some explain Chiun as being like "making cakes" <note>original Hebrew: *kavanim*</note>, and we have already explained in the book of Jeremiah that these are types of food prepared for worship, and for this reason they are called *kavanim*.

*And you took up the tabernacles of your King* <note>original Hebrew: מלככם (*malkekem*)</note>. *This is said of the star or idol whose name is Moloch; and they call him King, either because they think he is the King ruling over them, or because he is a great star in the host of heaven, in which he stands out over his army like a Leader, King, or Emperor. [And Chiun your image.] There are those who explain it as if "making cakes"* <note>original Hebrew: כוונים (*kavanim*)</note>, *that is, honey cakes; and we have already explained in the book of Jeremiah that Cauanim are certain types of food prepared for an Idol, and therefore they are called Cauanim. But we do not support this opinion. The explanation added a little later by the cited Radak* <note>Rabbi David Kimhi, a celebrated 12th-century Hebrew grammarian and scholar</note> *is better:*

<margin>Radak.</margin>
We explain that Chiun is the star of Saturn, and so it is called in the language of the Ishmaelites <note>The "Ishmaelite" language refers to Arabic</note> and Persia, *Kiwan*.

<margin>R. Abenezra.</margin>
*We explain that Chiun is the same as the star of Saturn, and thus Saturn is called in the Ishmaelite language (Arabic) and in Persian, Ceuan. Rabbi Abenezra* <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a renowned 12th-century biblical commentator and astronomer</note> *says it is the name of Saturn, composed from the Arabic and Persian languages. Whatever it may be, no one can deny that in the Persian name Saturn is called* כיואן *Ceuan, unless they have perhaps not read the Persian books, which commonly call him by this name; however, I do not remember ever finding this name in the monuments of the Arabs. From this, some think that Ceuan and Rephan are entirely the same name, which the Persians received from the Egyptians, corrupting it by changing the 'R' to a 'C' in the manner of those with a lisp; so Johannes Drusius* <note>A prominent 16th-century Dutch Protestant scholar of Hebrew</note> *boldly asserts.* <margin>Drusius.</margin> *(He thus reads* כיון *as Chiun). It would be, he says, Cheuan, unless a straying hand had preferred to write Rephan* <note>original Greek: Ῥεφὰν</note>, *'e' for 'k,' or perhaps the Interpreters themselves read* ריון *[Rion] instead of* כיון *[Kiun]. He would have done better to say it would have been Rhiphan, unless a straying hand preferred to write* כיון *Ceuan; for we have shown before that Rephan is the genuine name of Saturn among the Egyptians, while Ceuan is the name corrupted by the neighboring Persians. This opinion has found other supporters as well, and it would not displease me, if the authority of this venerable Translator did not deter me from such an assertion, and if better solutions did not remain by which we might reconcile these difficulties.*

<margin>Chiun signifies Saturn, and Hercules, and is the same as Rephan.</margin>
We say, therefore, that Chiun did not creep into the sacred writings by error, as Drusius and his followers claim; rather, it was placed in this location by the Prophet by design as the name of an idol, which the Egyptians used to call sometimes Saturn, sometimes Hercules, confusedly—a name very well known to the Hebrews. For Chiun, or in Coptic <term>Ⲋⲓⲕⲱⲛ</term> <note>Kircher identifies this with the Coptic/Greek word for "image" or "icon"</note>, is the same as image, figure, or idol, by which name they called the statue of Saturn or Hercules interchangeably, "by way of excellence" <note>original Greek: τὴν ἐξοχὴν</note>. They called it Saturn insofar as he is one of the seven planets, but because of the intensity of the effects he produces, they called him Rephan, as if you were to say the "strength of a giant." Therefore, they called the idol of Saturn "Chiun" or "Chon," and the star "Rephan." Furthermore, the Egyptian Hercules, whom Herodotus counts among the eight gods of the Egyptians, was called Chon or Chiun in Egyptian, as shown by the *Great Etymologicum* <note>A 12th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Greek language</note> in these words:

<margin>Great Etymologicum</margin>
> "The Chones are a people of Italy. They say that in the Heracleion, according to the dialect of the Egyptians, Hercules is called Chon, through whom Italy was named, and from him the people were called Chones."

*Chones, a people of Italy, say Hercules was called Chon according to the Egyptian dialect, and from his subjugation of Italy, they were called Italians. They were afterwards called Chones.*

### CHAPTER XXII 388 ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>Antiochus Zenophenes.</margin>
All of these things are confirmed by Antiochus Zenophenes <note>A lost Greek historian cited by later Renaissance scholars like Gyraldus</note> in Lilius Gyraldus, *Syntagma X*. He says, "Chon is the name for Hercules in the language of the Egyptians, *who together with Osiris liberated Italy from tyranny; and it is handed down that Italy was called 'Chone' in ancient times after this Egyptian Hercules Chon*." Petrus Leo Castella briefly narrates the history in his booklet *On the Aborigines and the Janigenae* <note>Referring to the mythical early inhabitants of Italy and the descendants of Janus</note>. *And so this Osiris, after the death of Sicanus, was summoned by the Italians—specifically by the twelve, six, and one protectors of the people—and arrived in Italy, where Novelty and Virtue always rule. He conquered all the giants, and if he spared any, he led them in triumph, having gained control over all Italy, accompanied by Hercules Chon, after whom the last peoples in Italy were called Chones, who were finally driven out by the Sabines.* I find in Hesychius <note>A 5th-century Greek grammarian and lexicographer</note> that this Hercules was also called *Gignon*:
<margin>Petrus Leo Castella.</margin>

<margin>Hesychius.</margin>
*Gignon*, he says, *or by some Gigon, Patacus, Epipatecus, Trapezius; some consider him the Egyptian Hercules.*
<note>original Greek: Γιγνῶν, οἱ δὲ Γηγῶν, Πάταικος, Ἐπιπάταικος, Τραπεζικός, οἱ δὲ Αἰγυπτίων Ἡρακλέα νομίζουסי.</note>

*Gignon*, or by some *Gigon*, *Patacus*, *Epipatecus*, *Trapezius*, some call him the Egyptian Hercules. This word does not differ from *Rephan* if you look at the meaning; for both indicate the powers of that Divinity, since it is evident from what has been said that both *Rephan* and *Chon* signify a Giant. We conclude, therefore, that *Rephan* and *Chiun* (or *Chon*) in the cited passages of Holy Scripture are nothing other than the image of Saturn, worshipped either under the figure of a star or because of a star inserted into the forehead of the idol; and different names were attributed to the same entity. For we proved in the third *Syntagma* of this work that Saturn (whom we showed to be Rephan) and Hercules (whom we showed to be Chon) are everywhere confused with Osiris. But these things will be discussed better in the following sections. Therefore, leaving Rephan behind, let us proceed to *Marcolis*.

<margin>Marcolis is the same as Mercury.</margin>
*Marcolis* <note>original Hebrew: מרקוליס</note> is the same to the Hebrews as Mercury is to the Latins; so I gather from that Hebrew proverb: *Casting a stone at Marcolis* <note>original Hebrew: זורק אבן למרקוליס</note>, that is, at Mercury; concerning which Rabbi Elias the German <note>Elijah Levita, a 16th-century Hebrew scholar and philologist</note> says thus in his work *The Tishbi*:

<margin>R. Elias.</margin>
> *Markolis is the name of an idol, and they say that by throwing stones (into a heap) its worship is performed; they also say that this is the name of the one who was worshipped in Rome under the name Mercury.*
<note>original Hebrew: זורק אבן למרקוליס שם ע"ז שכך היתה עבודתה ויש אומרים שהוא שם אלה שעבדו לו ברומא ונקרא מרקוריא :</note>

So says Rabbi Elias concerning the stated parable. Indeed, this proverb flowed from no other source than that parable of Solomon in Chapter 26, verse 8.
<margin>An explanation of the passage in Proverbs Ch. 26 v. 8.</margin>
*As he who casts a stone into the heap of Mercury, so is he who gives honor to a fool.* Where the Hebrew truth has "in a heap" <note>original Hebrew: במרגמה (*be-margemah*)</note>; from which word the ancients perhaps formed "Mercury"; although the Greek interpreters, Jonathan, and most of the moderns understand it to mean a "sling" there. However, there is such great difficulty among authors in explaining this passage, and such a variety and disagreement of opinions, that it can scarcely be discerned what someone ought to believe.

We, in order to bring some light to this passage, say that this parable is by no means to be understood as the throw of a sling (as the authors cited above feel), nor of a stone wrapped in purple <note>original Hebrew: בארגמן (*be-argaman*)</note> as the Rabbi says; nor of a tomb or a dismal place where the bodies of the condemned were overwhelmed with stones; nor of counting-stones or arithmetic pebbles, as Saint Thomas says; but of the stones which are in honor of *Marcolis* or Mercury...
<margin>St. Thomas, Summa Theologica 2. 2. question 63, article 3, in the body of the text.</margin>

[The previous page ended with a discussion of the name Mercury...] stones were thrown into a heap of stones piled up for the said Deity. Therefore, the wisest of mortals <note>Referring to Solomon, the traditional author of Proverbs</note> meant that he who honors a fool does the same as if he were increasing the aforementioned heap of Mercury by throwing a stone. Benefits are conferred on both the fool and the heap—to the latter by the addition of a stone, to the former by honor; yet neither repays with a grateful soul, the fool no more than the heap of stones; neither acknowledges the benefit bestowed as sufficient.

<margin>Bede.</margin>

<margin>Statues of Mercury: double, solitary, and social.</margin>
<margin>Cicero. Turnebus.</margin>
<margin>Pollux. Lucian. Suidas. Hesychius.</margin>
<margin>Thucydides. Herodotus. Macrobius.</margin>
<margin>Clement of Alexandria. Plutarch. Aemilius Probus. Why is Mercury depicted with three heads?</margin>
Truly, so that these rites of Mercury, and their origin, rituals, and ceremonies may be more deeply understood, it must be known that famous statues of Mercury existed among almost all nations. Some were solitary, in which he alone stood on a base; some were social, in whose single base Pallas <note>Athena</note> was joined with him—which were called *Hermathenae*; or Hercules—which were called *Heraclae*. These were characteristic of Gymnasiums, as is clear from Cicero's letters to Atticus, and Turnebus, book 7, *Adversaria*, final chapter. *Solitary* ones, says Bertius, were more frequent, not only on tombs, but on the posts of beds, indicating Mercury as the guardian of sleep, to whom therefore the last or third <term>cyathus</term> <note>A cup or measure used in drinking bouts; the original Latin term refers to a specific ladle-sized measure</note> was sacred in banquets, as witnessed by Pollux, book 6, chapter 15, and Lucian, book 3, *Dialogues of the Gods*. These sculptures indeed are called <term>hermenes</term> <note>original Greek: ἑρμῆνες</note> by Suidas, and <term>hermaia</term> <note>original Greek: ἕρμαια</note> by Hesychius; they are placed not only in shrines but also in the vestibules of private houses, in a quadrangular shape, and are for the most part made of stone. So says Thucydides in book 6 of the *Peloponnesian War*. Concerning others, see Herodotus, book 2, and Macrobius, chapter 19 of the *Saturnalia*. The Egyptians, and after them the Greeks and Romans who were taught about godlings of this sort, fashioned them with a human form only as far as the chest, or with only the head and neck, while the rest were simple trunks. Concerning these, consult Clement of Alexandria in his *Exhortation*, and Arnobius, book 6 *Against the Nations*, Plutarch in his lives of *Alcibiades* and *Nicias*, Aemilius Probus, Thucydides, and others. I know that sometimes Mercury was accustomed to be painted with three heads, whence the adage <term>trikaros Hermes</term> <note>original Greek: Τρίκαρος Ἑρμῆς - "Three-headed Mercury"</note>—a three-headed Mercury—is used for men who are either extremely undecided about what they should undertake, or are very crafty. I believe the cause for this is that he was held to be the same Deity of trade, speech, and travel; the writer of adages <note>Erasmus</note> thinks that each head had an inscription indicating where this way led, and where that one went.

<margin>Why Mercury was painted only as far as the head.</margin>
Furthermore, the most common material was stone, more rarely wood; but it had to be a specific wood, according to the saying: *A Mercury is not made from just any wood*. As has been said, they formed these into a statue where, if you except the head, all the rest would be trunks. Did they form them thus so that it might be understood that the God is entirely Mind? Certainly the verses of Empedocles found in Tzetzes, book 3, *Chiliads*, history 464, hint at this.

<margin>Empedocles.</margin>
-> For indeed, limbs are not joined to a mortal head, <-
-> Nor indeed do two branches spring from the shoulders, <-
-> No feet, no swift knees, nor shaggy private parts, <-
-> But <-
-> A holy and ineffable Mind alone he was, <-
-> Sweeping through the whole world with swift thoughts. <-

->*But only the sacred and immense mind exists,*<-
->*Which moves the whole world more swiftly with its cares.*<-

<margin>Mercuries of the ways.</margin> Such, then, were the little Herms <note>original: "Hermulæ"</note>. For this reason, Mercury is introduced by Xenocrates in the 4th book of the *Greek Anthology* in an epigram, complaining that although men confess him to be a swift-footed runner and a vigorous wrestler with his hands, they nevertheless fashion him *without feet* <note>original: "ἄποδα"</note> and *with mutilated hands* <note>original: "κολοβὸν χεῖρας"</note>. And these features are common to all Herms. However, certain things were peculiar to those called "Viales" <note>Mercuries of the Ways or Roads</note>, which were sacred to Mercury; from whom also all statues of men, according to Tzetzes <note>Joannes Tzetzes, a 12th-century Byzantine poet and grammarian</note>, were called "Herms"; perhaps because Mercury was a distinguished sculptor, as Jupiter relates in Martianus Capella's first book *On the Marriage of Philology* <note>A famous 5th-century allegorical work</note>.

<margin>Martianus Capella.</margin> These roadside Herms were also square, made of wood or stone, displaying the face of Mercury at the top, and bearing inscriptions of the roads on the flat lower part, as Ulpian clearly testifies in his commentaries <note>original: "scholijs"</note> on Demosthenes' oration *Against Leptines*.

<margin>Ulpian.</margin> "Square wood or stones having the face of Hermes above, and on the flat part below, the inscriptions" <note>original: "Ξύλα, ἢ λῖθοι τετράγωνοι τὰς ἔχοντες ὄψιν Ἑρμοῦ ἐπάνω, κάτω δὲ ἐν τῷ πλάνῳ τὰ ἐπιγράμματα"</note>—namely, those indicating the roads; see on these matters Phornutus <note>Cornutus, a Stoic philosopher</note> and Lylius, Synthesis 9.

<margin>Heaps of stones were added to the roadside Herms by travelers.</margin> To these Herms, therefore, travelers used to add heaps of stones in honor of Mercury. Tzetzes teaches in his *Chiliads* (Book 12, History 429) that the name for these heaps was the same as the name for the stones themselves.

<margin>Tzetzes.</margin>
->Hermes: both the entire statue, and the heap of stones.<-
-><note>original Greek: "Ἑρμοῦ, καὶ σύμπας ἀνδριάς, καὶ ὁ σωρὸς τῶν λίθων"</note><-

<margin>These heaps were adjacent to the statues themselves.</margin> From this, two difficulties now arise. The first is whether those heaps were piled up adjacent to the statue itself, such that only the top of the statue projected out; this is what Alciatus <note>Andrea Alciatus, famous for his book of Emblems in the 16th century</note> seems to have thought in *Emblem 8* with these verses:

> *In the crossroads is a mound of stones, above which*
> *A truncated image of the God stands out as far as the chest.*
> *It is the tomb of Mercury; traveler, hang*
> *Garlands for the God, who shows you the right path.*

<margin>Hugh of Saint-Cher.</margin> Hugh of Saint-Cher <note>A 13th-century Dominican cardinal and biblical scholar</note> compares those Herms to the wooden crosses which pilgrims proceeding to holy places erect today, standing out among the piles of stones placed by those passing by; the French call them *Montjoies*. But the difference is that our pilgrims do not heap up stones in honor of the cross, but rather so that those following may take a sign of the journey from there; and they are indices of only one journey. The Herms were indices of various paths and were established in honor of Mercury.

<margin>The Odyssey. Hesychius.</margin> On this depends the solution to the second doubt: whether "Mercury’s heap" is to be understood as any pile of stones whatsoever, even one collected without religious purpose. This is the opinion of all those who, citing the *Odyssey* (Book 16), Strabo (Book 16), Hesychius, and the author of the *Etymologicum Magnum* as witnesses, prove that a *Mercurial hill* <note>original: "Ἑρμαῖον λόφον"</note>, or Mercurial heap, is nothing other than a pile of stones. Truly, if you read these three accurately, you will find that they provide a double meaning: one broad, which looks to any piles of stones whatever; the other specific...

...a certain and proper [account] of those superstitious rites. This is easily proven from Hebrew, Greek, and the Latin writers. For even the *Baal Aruch* <note>The *Aruch* is a famous 11th-century Talmudic dictionary by Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome</note> clearly indicates this with these very words:

It remains certain, therefore, that the "Hermian mounds" were nothing other than Mercurial heaps of stones, piled up at public roads and crossroads to demonstrate the path to travelers; these passing travelers increased the mounds by the frequent throwing of stones in honor of Mercury. For Mercury—that is, Hermes—was the overseer of the ways, and called "the wayfarer" <note>original: "ἐνόδιος" (Enodios)</note>. # THE ISIAIC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS 392

### CHAPTER XXII.

<margin>
The custom of heaping stones at roadside Herms, and where it began.
</margin>
It is certain that this custom was taken from Mercury himself, though it is uncertain from which of his deeds it arose. There are those who argue it comes from his habit of clearing stones from the roads to make them more convenient, removing the rocks and arranging them into a single heap at the side of the path; at the same time, this served to reassure travelers that they were on the correct path or the Royal Road. This is the view of <margin>Favorinus.</margin> Favorinus, page 218, at the end. <margin>Didymus.</margin> Didymus, in his commentary on the *Odyssey*, book 1, recites a fable on this matter from Antislides: *They say that when Mercury was about to undergo the vote of the gods in the assembly of the High Ones—for he was then accused by Juno for the murder of Argus—the crowd of gods, to please Jupiter, acquitted Mercury. However, according to the unique rite of the celestial court, they heaped all the voting stones* <note>original: "calculos". In ancient courts, jurors cast pebbles to vote; a white pebble signaled acquittal.</note> *at his feet by throwing them; by which act they showed that they were performing that cursed slaughter to please Juno.* From this event, such a custom became common among men in honor of Mercury. But on these matters, see more extensively Phurnutus, Lactantius book 1, chapter 20, and others cited shortly before.

We say that this entire method of erecting stones flowed primarily from the Egyptians, and from their Hermes or Mercury, to other nations. For Diodorus and Strabo teach that he was the first of mortals to teach Geometry <note>The Greek word "Geometry" literally means "earth-measurement."</note> and show the method of placing boundaries. Because all of Egypt was covered with mud from the annual flooding of the Nile, the greatest contentions and lawsuits arose among the Egyptians regarding the distribution of fields and estates; they say that Mercury first taught the method of the land-measuring art, and established boundaries, which were nothing other than certain oblong and square stones used to distinguish one man's field from another's. All of this we shall prove, God willing, in the following sections from various authors. Hence, the Egyptians, moved by such a great benefit and in memory of the favor provided, worshipped him as the guardian of the earth and boundaries and as a protective deity <note>original: "Numen auerruncum", a deity that wards off evil or disputes.</note>. They did this sometimes by making a heap of stones, sometimes by fitting a round stone in the likeness of a head at the top, and sometimes by placing a square, triangular, or pyramidal rock rising up into a head and shoulders. From them, the Hebrews and other nations later learned and practiced this. But because material for speaking on these things will be provided most copiously in many places in this work, I refrain from saying more now, lest I cause boredom in the reader by frequently repeating the same things. The figures of the Herms occurring here and there among authors follow:

SYNTAGMA IV. PANTHEON OF THE HEBREWS. 393 CHAPTER XXIII.

## C H A P T E R XXIII.

->*Concerning the inner shrines and caves of the Hebrews, and of other Eastern peoples.*<-

<margin>Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, Book 1.</margin>
That nothing was once more famous than the **inner shrines** <note>original: "adytis". From the Greek *adyton*, meaning "not to be entered"; the most sacred, restricted part of a temple.</note> of the Egyptians is sufficiently shown by the journeys undertaken by so many distinguished Philosophers to visit them. Indeed, Pythagoras was carried away by such a great desire for them—as Clement testifies—that he did not even refuse circumcision, so that he might become a participant in the mysteries usually handed down within them.

<note>original Greek: Ὁ Πυθαγόρας ἐπετιμήθη... Pythagoras was honored so that, having descended into the inner shrines, he might learn the mystical philosophy from the Egyptians.</note>

<margin>Inner shrines of the Egyptians:</margin>
<margin>Arnobius.</margin>
<margin>Eusebius.</margin>
Moreover, these inner shrines were certain solitary, subterranean places, removed from all human company, filled with a diverse variety of monstrous idols. Under these <term>hieroglyphic symbols</term> <note>Kircher viewed hieroglyphs as symbolic vessels for secret divine truths rather than a phonetic writing system.</note>, the method of worshipping the Gods and the precepts of other clandestine arts were taught, according to that saying of Arnobius: *Pythagoras, he says, was a Magician; he perfected all those things by secret arts, taking the names of powerful Angels and remote disciplines from the inner shrines of the Egyptians.* Eusebius mentions these in Book 2 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*:

<note>original Greek: Καὶ μὴν ἄδυτα Αἰγυπτίων... Truly the inner shrines of the Egyptians and the necromancies of the Tyrrhenians are darkness and images of monsters, and these divinations are truly the sophistries of the godless and faithless, and the portents of an insane mind.</note>

*Certainly, the inner shrines of the Egyptians and the necromancy of the Tyrrhenians are condemned by darkness; they are entirely the mad frauds of faithless men, and the mockeries of pure error.*

<margin>Justin.</margin>
<margin>Ezekiel.</margin>
And Justin, in *Questions to the Orthodox*: *At that time, hieroglyphic science was held in high esteem among the Egyptians, which was taught in the inner shrines only to the most select, not to common men, etc.* In these places, therefore, by attracting Demons into the idols through various ceremonies, adjurations, and <term>suffumigations</term> <note>The ritual burning of incense, herbs, or other materials to produce smoke, believed to attract or repel spirits.</note> composed of various types of spices, herbs, and juices, and finally through hymns and magic songs, they would receive answers when consulting about avoiding evils and attaining goods. By acting according to these responses, they believed they would possess eternal happiness. Thus the Hebrews and their neighboring nations—the Assyrians, Babylonians, and Persians—when they recognized that the Egyptians were being exalted with success because of this secret worship of the Gods, they persuaded themselves that they could reach the same intended goal through similar means, aspiring to a similar fortune. Therefore, having fashioned all kinds of monstrous Gods, they chose inner shrines, or certain hidden and dark retreats, to worship them. What kind of retreats these were, what idols were shadowed within, and what the rites of the priests were, Ezekiel shows us beautifully in Chapter 8, where it is held thus:

> *And he brought me to the door of the court; and I looked, and behold, a hole in the wall. And he said to me: Son of man, dig in the wall; and when I had dug in the wall, a door appeared. And he said to me: Go in, and see the wicked abominations that these men are doing here. And I went in and saw, and behold, every likeness of creeping things and animals, an abomination, and all the idols of the house of Israel were depicted on the wall all around. And seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel, and Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan, stood in the midst of them, standing before the pictures; and each man had a censer in his hand, and a cloud of vapor rose from the incense.*

If we can clearly understand these arts and institutions, it will be by no means difficult—by making a comparison of individual things among themselves—to bring to light various matters relating to the antiquities and mysteries of the Egyptians that have been unknown to us until now; may God prosper our efforts.

# CHAPTER II. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

...rites and superstitions in the religion of the most recent nations, shining forth as if in a certain mirror. Thus, when I recognized these things, a great desire immediately seized my mind to establish a comparison between these and the religion of the ancients. This was done by collecting the idols, rites, and ceremonies usually performed by various nations from all over, gathered from Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, and French letters (of which I had a great abundance here in Rome, supplied from the archives of the Society of Jesus in the Supreme Curia). I hoped that from this kind of collation, no small light would be shed upon my labors in the matter of hieroglyphs; for I did not think it would be difficult to investigate whence they flowed based on the similarity and analogy of rites, ceremonies, and images. For these reasons, therefore, I have embraced this subject—which might otherwise seem to be outside my scope—and for the sake of better method and to avoid confusion, we have thought it should be divided into three classes, as it were. The first part contains the idolatry and sects of the Chinese, Japanese, and Tartars; the second, those of the Indians and Africans; and the third, the rites and ceremonies of the Americans in the worship of their Gods.

<margin>The three sects among the Chinese: The Literati, Shakya, and Laozi.</margin>
Three books of the Chinese, therefore, enumerate the sects of the world; for thus they call their own Kingdom along with the neighboring adjacent places, as they know of no others.

The first is the sect of the Literati <note>The Confucian scholars</note>; the second is called Sciequia <note>Shakyamuni, or Buddhism</note>; the third they call Laucu <note>Laozi, the founder of Taoism</note>. All the Chinese, and the remaining neighboring peoples who use Chinese characters—such as the Japanese, Koreans, Tonkinese, and Cochinchinese, of whom we shall speak later—profess one of these three. And these three sects correspond almost exactly in all respects to the three kinds of men of which the Kingdom of the Egyptians once consisted: namely, the wise priests, the Hierogrammatists <term>Hierogrammatists: sacred scribes who dealt with hieroglyphs</term> or hieroglyphic writers, and the common people. <margin>The sect of the Literati.</margin> The sect of the Literati is proper to the Chinese and the most ancient in this kingdom; it governs the Republic, abounds in many books, and is praised above the others. They acknowledge Confucius as the author or Prince of philosophers, just as the Egyptians did their famous Thoyt <note>Thoth</note>, whom the Greeks call Hermes Trismegistus <term>Hermes Trismegistus: "Thrice-Great Hermes," a legendary figure associated with the invention of writing and magic.</term>. Regarding this, Trigault <note>Nicolas Trigault (1577–1628), a Jesuit missionary to China</note> says in *The Christian Expedition to China*: "Hence they assert that the duty of sacrificing to the King of Heaven and of worshiping him belongs only to the King. They also claim another duty for themselves; for they promise to draw down rain from a dry sky, or to restrain excessive rains, and they claim to be able to avert other private or public misfortunes. And these are roughly the three main points of the pagan sects; but human vanity does not rest even in these, for as the centuries have passed, individual sources have been diverted into so many twists and turns by the masters of deceit, <margin>The greatest multitude of idols among the Chinese.</margin> that they seem scarcely able to be counted. The almost incredible multitude of idols itself shows this sufficiently; they expose these for worship not only in temples, which often reach several thousand [idols], but also in almost every private home in a place designated for that purpose. In the marketplace, in the streets, on ships, and in public palaces, this one abomination presents itself to view almost everywhere. In this, they seem to have imitated the Egyptians, who were infamous for the all-encompassing variety of their idols.

<margin>It is proven by three arguments that the Chinese derived their idol worship from the Egyptians. The first argument.</margin> There are such certain and evident signs of this matter that, if nothing else, three in particular seem able to prove it. The first is that, no differently than the Egyptians and Greeks, they believe certain [deities] preside [over specific domains]; they build mystical temples for them; and they are accustomed to either appease them when angry or attract their favor through various rites and ceremonies in the Egyptian manner.

<margin>The second argument.</margin> The second argument that the Chinese religion was borrowed from the Egyptians is so manifest that it cannot be doubted; it is that to this day, temples are found there dedicated to Mars, Venus, Fortune, Peace, the Oreads <note>mountain nymphs</note>, and other gods common to the Greeks and Egyptians. I could show this through many diverse Portuguese and Spanish annual reports; but a representation of all of them will be the *Ichnographia* <note>a ground plan or map</note> of the metropolitan city of Nanchang <note>original: "Nenchienfis"</note> in China, no less elegantly than accurately printed on Chinese silk by our Fathers and sent from China to Rome in years past. In this map, besides other superb buildings and massive fortifications, individual temples of the gods are seen, each assigned to specific places. You may see in this map shrines dedicated to Mars, Fortune, Peace, the Oreads and Nymphs, the Genius of the air, of birds, of the sea, of rivers, the protector of the city, the Sea Dragon, Jupiter, Atlas, and other Greek and Egyptian gods. Since I perceived this with the greatest admiration, I could not omit adding it here—extracted with the utmost fidelity—to further demonstrate the affinity of the Chinese religion with the Egyptian and Greek ones.

### CHAPTER III. 402 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS THE ISIAIC TEMPLE

And indeed, these things agree so well with the Greeks and Egyptians that their entire system of idolatry seems to have migrated into China.

<margin>The third argument.</margin>
The third argument is that, besides the written characters—in which they very closely imitate the hieroglyphics of the Egyptians, as we shall show in the second part of *Oedipus*—they possess almost the same rites and ceremonies as the Egyptians. We know that the Egyptians always honored pyramidal shapes with a certain divine respect; traces of this worship remain in China to this day. For the pyramids—which the Chinese call *Chines* <note>original French: "Chines." This likely refers to specific shrines or spirit-houses described by early missionaries.</note>—are held in such honor and veneration that no one dares to undertake any task unless they have first appeased them with specific rituals. As a witness to this matter, I bring forward Pierre Jarric, who, in Book 5 of his *History of the Indies* <note>Pierre du Jarric (1566–1617) was a Jesuit historian who compiled accounts of missions in the East.</note> published in French, mentions them in Chapter 51 with these words: *Besides these wooden idols, there are others which they call "Chines," made in the form of ornate pyramids, inside of which there is a certain species of white ants <note>likely termites</note> which do not show themselves outside, but have their little dwellings within, though no one knows what they feed upon. They destroy the structures where they are placed, which are built in the shape of an Oratory. The Pagans are greatly amazed by this. For they have a great fear of these "Chines"; so much so that when they buy a slave, they first bring him before one of these pyramids with an offering of wine and other things, and consign him to it, as if into its hands, praying to the idol that if the slave runs away, it will cause snakes, lizards, and tigers to kill and devour him. This the poor slaves fear so much that even though they are mistreated by their masters, they almost never dare to leave or abandon them.* From this it is clearly evident that the Chinese took all these things from the Egyptians, Persians, and others, whom we have often indicated in preceding sections—and will demonstrate throughout what follows—to have worshipped a stone or a pointed rock shaped into a cone or pyramid in place of a Deity.

Furthermore, just as the Egyptians enclosed Demons in statues to give oracular responses and dedicated certain temples to them, so do the Chinese; regarding whom, listen to the aforementioned Jarric speaking in the same passage: *Similarly, in each Kingdom, there is a place dedicated to the Devil, where they go to make the most solemn sacrifices to him on a small island. They call the idol Camassono <note>A local deity or spirit, possibly a transcription of a regional name</note>; and those who pass by there greatly dread this idol, and for fear that it will sink their ships, they offer to it—when they are across from the island—either rice (which they throw into the sea), or oil, or other things they carry.* Regarding their Oracles, Nicolas Trigault <note>A famous Jesuit missionary to China who edited Matteo Ricci's journals</note> explains in Book 1, Chapter 8 of *On the Christian Expedition among the Chinese*: *Some consult the Demons themselves and "familiar spirits," as they call them—of which there are not a few among the Chinese—and it is commonly believed that these matters involve more divine power than demonic fraud. But in the end, they lead everyone into deception. Their Oracles are received through the voices of infants, or even of beasts; they reveal past and distant things in their usual way, so as to make the falsehood by which they predict the future seem not unlike the truth.* Furthermore, we read that all these things were common to our own ancient Pagans. There is one thing, however, that can be said to be unique to the Chinese: the custom in choosing a site for building private and public houses, or for burying corpses. They compare that site with the head, tail, and feet of various Dragons, which they fabulously claim live buried under our soil; from these dragons they believe comes all adverse and prosperous fortune, not only for families, but for cities, provinces, and the whole Kingdom...

# SYNTAGMA V. THE EGYPTIAN APE. CHAPTER III.

...believe [all things] depend. And for this reason, many of the leading men occupy themselves in this supposedly hidden science, and are summoned from afar when necessary—especially when certain public towers, structures, or machines are built for the purpose of summoning good fortune and driving away public misfortunes. For just as Astrologers measure the fates of regions from an inspection of the stars, so these **Geologists** <note>Kircher uses "Geologists" to mean practitioners of Feng Shui or geomancy—those who read the "omens" of the earth's layout.</note> measure them from the situation of mountains, rivers, and fields. And truly, you might say that nothing more absurd could be found. For they dream that the health, wealth, honors, and entire fortune of a family depend on a door being turned toward this or that side, or a window usually being opened in this or that direction, or because a roof in the region is somewhat higher, and other similar trifles. The villages are full, the taverns are full, and the marketplaces are full of these Astrologers, Geomancers, Soothsayers, Interpreters of dreams, and—to put it in one word—impostors. Thus far Trigault <note>Nicolas Trigault (1577–1628), a Jesuit missionary to China whose writings Kircher relied upon heavily.</note>. Who does not see here another face of Egypt, where all things were managed by auguries and omens? Time would fail me if I wished to recount all these things here. Therefore, whoever desires to know more of this kind should consult the cited authors; we judge it sufficient to have demonstrated, from these few examples brought forward, a truly great affinity to the mysteries of the Egyptians. Having left these matters behind, let us turn ourselves to the Japanese.

## C A P V T III.

### The idolatry of the Japanese and Tartars as a parallel to the Egyptian.

<margin>Two sects of the Japanese: one denying, the other asserting the immortality of the soul.</margin>
Since the Japanese received the entire system of their idolatrous religion from the Chinese, there is no less a variety and difference of sects among them than among the Chinese; these can, however, be reduced primarily to two heads. The first is of those who deny another life, and believe that neither reward nor punishment is destined for good or evil works; rather, they lead a life that is entirely **Epicurean** <note>Kircher uses "Epicurean" in the classical sense to mean those who believe the soul dies with the body and that pleasure or tranquility is the highest good.</note>. This sect is called **Xenxus** <note>Likely a reference to Zen Buddhism, specifically the "Soto" or "Rinzai" schools as interpreted by early missionaries.</note>. The **Bonzes** <note>A term used by early travelers for Buddhist monks.</note>, the ministers of this sect, together with their followers, worship certain idols which they call **Chamis** <note>Kami, the spirits or deities of Shinto, which were often syncretized with Buddhism.</note>. To these they erect quite proud and sumptuous temples; by these they swear in grave matters that present themselves, or when homage must be paid to the King. They supplicate them with offerings of various things, both to avoid harms and unfortunate outcomes and to impel victory against enemies; in a word, so that they may enjoy present happiness, which is the sole aim of this sect. 

Others, who follow the immortality of the soul and another life, approach more closely to the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed in the transmigration of souls.</note> in their rites and ceremonies. They worship an idol by the name of **Amida**, about whom they spread a thousand fables; since these have nothing to do with our purpose, I gladly omit them. I will say this one thing: they attribute so much to this idol that they believe nothing else is required for their salvation except the frequent repetition of these words: *Namu, Amida, Buth*, that is, *Blessed Amida, save us* <note>original: "Namu, Amida, Buth" (Namu Amida Butsu). Kircher translates the phrase into Latin as "Felix Amida, salva nos."</note>. They repeat these words repeatedly; they carry their rosaries, or crowns made of prayer-beads, which the Japanese have in common with Christians, and they are almost always depicted in the hands of the idols, as you see here in the joined image, which represents the image of Amida.

They believe that saying these five words with devotion—*Namu, Mio, Foren, Qui, Quio* <note>The Daimoku: "Namu Myoho Renge Kyo," meaning "Devotion to the Mystic Law of the Lotus Sutra."</note>—is sufficient to attain blessedness, even though no one has yet understood the true power of said words.

The disciples of this Shaka were **Kobo Daishi** <note>original: "Cambadagi," the founder of Shingon Buddhism.</note> and **Kakuban** <note>original: "Cacubao," a prominent monk of the Shingon school.</note>, both of whom the Japanese honor with divine worship because of their excellence. Kobo Daishi seems to have been more truly a demon than a man, if faith is to be placed in the reports; he was the first to teach the rites of worshipping the Demon, as well as the method of binding a Demon into anyone's body through certain incantations of words, and he demonstrated similar things peculiar to demons.

Following this sect is the one they call **Yamabushi** <note>original: "Iamabugi," meaning "one who lies in the mountains."</note>, which means "soldier of the mountains." These men most closely emulate the rites of the Egyptians in conjuring spirits and Genii into statues. They are devoted to divinations of every kind; they love solitude and rugged mountains, and therefore are rarely seen in cultivated and inhabited places. Of them, Guzmán says:

<margin>Guzmán, Book 5, Chapter 7.</margin>

Those who belong to this sect are called **Yamabushi**, which means "soldiers of the Sierra," because most of them live in very rugged mountains and are rarely seen in town. ### SYNTHESIS V. THE EGYPTIAN APE. 407 CHAPTER III.

...since these things are not our primary purpose, let us turn our pen to those matters that pertain to our subject.

<margin>The Egyptians worshipped God sitting upon a Lotus flower.</margin>
We know from **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on Egyptian mysteries.</note> and **Clement of Alexandria** <note>A Christian theologian (c. 150–215 AD) who described Egyptian religious customs.</note> that the Egyptians mystically depicted God sitting upon a lotus flower. The **Gnostics** <note>An early mystical religious movement that blended various philosophies.</note> later followed this sacred method of painting, representing **Harpocrates** <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Horus-the-Child, often shown sitting on a lotus and representing silence.</note> equipped with various symbols on that same lotus flower. It seems that this custom penetrated not only into Persia and India, but even into the furthest Orient—namely, Japan. <margin>The Japanese depict Amida sitting upon a Rose flower.</margin> They depict their famous deity **Amida** (also called by the name **Fombum**) sitting upon a flower or a rose, or a water-lily, shining with a great splendor of rays. When the Reverend Father Assistant of Portugal shared an image of this with me, I wished to include it here.

<margin>The Fombum of the Zen sect among the Japanese.</margin>
They call this the sect of the **Ienxii** <note>Kircher's Latinized term for the Zen sect.</note>, who speak of this Fombum in a far different way than the sect of the **Xodoxii** <note>The Jōdo or "Pure Land" sect of Buddhism.</note> mentioned shortly before. For they say he is an invisible substance, separate from any composition of the elements, existing before every creature, the source of all good things. Hence they mystically paint him above a water-lily flower—more truly a lotus—to obscurely suggest his hidden virtues and perfections, which are also indicated by the robes in which he is seen wrapped. All these things are confirmed by the Portuguese letters sent from Japan to Europe in the year 1565, in one of which **Luis Froës** <note>Luís Fróis (1532–1597), a famous Portuguese Jesuit missionary in Japan.</note> writes as follows in Portuguese about this Amida: <margin>Luis Froës in the Histories of Japan.</margin>

> [ <note>original Portuguese: "Os seus mosteiros..."</note> Their monasteries are very sumptuous and have great incomes. The monks cannot have women under penalty of death. Amida is placed in their temples on an altar in the middle of the sanctuary. The statue is made of **shion** <note>Likely referring to a precious wood or a specific gilded finish.</note> much like the "Pagodas" of India, naked from the waist up, sitting like a woman with pierced ears and a brilliance of rays surrounding him, seated upon a very beautiful wooden rose that encircles him. ] And in another place: [ In the first question, he proposed that the **Zen** practitioners held there to be an invisible being separate from the nature of the four elements, which they called by another name **Fonrai** like **Mogui** <note>Terms possibly referring to the "Original Nature" or "Nothingness" (Mu) in Zen philosophy.</note>. The attributes that the learned gave to this invisible being were as follows: namely, that before this world, the heavens, and the earth were created, **Fombum** always was and never had a beginning, nor would have an end, and that all things were created by him. His being was within the earth, in the heavens, and outside of them, as he is not limited to a finite place. In the government and preservation of all things, he suffered no movement; nor did he have color or any visible quality by which he could be seen by bodily eyes. Whatever men and all creatures possessed, existed in this Fombum in a more eminent degree of perfection, for he is the perennial source of all good. ]

From these accounts, it is clear that the more prudent men, following the guidance of the light of nature, feel very differently about their gods than the more unrefined commoners. For while the common folk assert (among many fictions) that Amida was an exceptional man, the more learned—following the example of the Egyptians—twist the fables commonly believed about him into mystical meanings.

<margin>The Japanese worship the Sun and Moon.</margin>
Furthermore, they also worship the Sun and Moon, following the example of the Egyptians and other Eastern peoples, as is evident from the Portuguese letter: [ Most of them believe in ancient men, who (according to what I have gathered) were men... ]
