### CHAPTER III. THE ISIAC TEMPLE OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS 408

...men, who lived as philosophers; many of these worship the Sun, and others the moon. <note>original Portuguese: "mes, que viuerao como philosophos; muitos destes adorao o Sol, e outros à lua"</note>] This is confirmed by a certain letter from our Holy Father Francis Xavier, dated November 5, 1549, and sent to the College of Goa, where you will find many other details regarding the superstitions of these people. If you compare the parades or festivities which they hold annually for their Gods with the Egyptian parades and solemnities usually performed every year, you will find them to be entirely the same, with few exceptions. You will see in them—just as in the Egyptian *Komasios* <note>A term for festive processions or revelries, often associated with the display of idols</note> according to the testimony of Clement—monstrous statues of the Gods carried about in various parades with the ridiculous gestures of the **Bonzes** <note>A term used by early European explorers and missionaries to describe Buddhist monks</note>; about which Luís Fróis writes thus in a certain letter:

<margin>Various rites of the Bonzes.</margin>

> [It is a very ancient custom of Mount Hiei <note>original: "Fiyenoiyama"</note> that every year the Bonzes hold a most sumptuous festival there for this idol, with all the Bonzes descending from above in arms, carrying on their backs seven very large chairs, which are kept in seven temples. When this festival of Sakamoto is finished, another is immediately held in the Capital <note>original: "Micào," referring to Miyako or Kyoto</note> for another idol or **Kami** <note>A Shinto deity or spirit</note> called Gion <note>original: "Guion"</note>. This is the most solemn festival in all Japan, in which it seems the Devil wished to counterfeit the feast of Corpus Christi, because there all the districts perform dances, games, and masquerades, carrying the idols in their hands. These are followed by eight or ten hand-lanterns at their sides, wrapped in thin veils, with the name of their Pagoda written on them and lit candles inside, and so forth.] <note>original Portuguese: "He costume antiquissimo de Fiyenoiyama..." Kircher provides this lengthy quote to show how Japanese processions mirrored European Catholic ones, which he interpreted as a demonic imitation or a survival of ancient Egyptian "pomp."</note>

Who does not see the Isiac <note>Relating to the Egyptian goddess Isis</note> parade described here?

After the procession is finished, they enter their temples, in which—just as in the inner sanctuaries of the Egyptians—one may see an innumerable crowd of Gods of every form. Many of these are deformed with the heads of oxen, dogs, and other animals, presenting a formidable spectacle to those who look upon them; others are depicted with many arms, looking more like monsters than Gods. The second volume of *Various Navigations and Travels* written in Italian mentions this Japanese idolatry on page 51:

<margin>Various Japanese idols.</margin>

> *In this Island, and in others nearby, all their idols are made differently; for some have the heads of Oxen, others of Pigs, others of dogs and Goats, and of various other manners. There are some that have one head and two faces, others three heads—namely, one in the proper place and the other two above each shoulder. Others have four hands, some ten, and others a hundred; those who have the most are held to have the most power, and to those they show the greatest reverence. When the Christians ask them why they make their Idols so diverse, they answer: "Thus our Fathers and Predecessors left them to us."* <note>original Italian: "In questa Isola, & in altre vicine..." Kircher is quoting from the collection of travels compiled by Giovanni Battista Ramusio.</note>

These words seem to be taken word-for-word from Marco Polo the Venetian; for in Book 3, Chapter 6, where he speaks of the Island of **Zipangu** <note>original: "Zipangri," the name for Japan used by Marco Polo</note>, which is the same as Japan, he writes thus:

> [The men of Zipangu worship various idols, some of which have the head of an ox, some the head of a pig, and some the head of a dog, and of other various animals. There are some that have four hands, others twenty, and others a hundred; and the more hands it has, the greater its power is thought to be. There are others, again, which have four faces on one head, and others three heads—one upon the neck, and two others upon each shoulder. And when the inhabitants are asked from where they have this tradition, they are accustomed to answer that they imitate their Fathers in this, and ought to believe nothing other than what they received from them.] <note>original Latin: "Colunt viri Zipangrij varia idola..."</note>

### THE POLYMORPHIC EGYPTIAN APE 409. CHAPTER III.

It has certainly been shown in various places in the preceding pages that the Egyptians represented **Osiris** (or the Sun) with the head of a bull; **Anubis** (or Mercury) with a dog’s head; **Pan** with a goat's; and finally **Ammon** with a ram's. Virgil <note>The Roman poet Publius Vergilius Maro</note> also teaches us that the image of **Serapis** <note>A Graeco-Egyptian god of the underworld and fertility</note> and **Diana** was three-headed:

<margin>Virgil.</margin>
->*And threefold Hecate, the three faces of the Virgin Diana.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Tergeminamque Hecaten, tria Virginis ora Dianæ." From the Aeneid, IV.511.</note>

<margin>Why Janus is four-faced.</margin>
<margin>What the hundred-handed Briareus signifies.</margin>
Frequent mention is also made among the mythologists of the four-faced **Janus**, as well as the hundred-handed **Briareus**. By these figures, the ancients truly intended nothing other than the manifold effects of the Sun. Indeed, the four-faced Janus was typically fashioned in many places for this reason: because the beginnings and ends, the entrances and exits of all things were dedicated to him. Furthermore, the temples erected to him were made in a square shape, so that through those four faces he might indicate the four parts of the year, which the Greeks and Latins called the **Hours** <note>original Latin: "Horas"; here referring to the seasons</note> in common parlance. Moreover, the hundred-handed Briareus is said to be the same as the Sun, which is why Homer called the Sun <term>hekatoncheira</term> <note>original Greek: ἑκατόγχειρα, meaning "hundred-handed"</note>. Since the meanings of these figures are interpreted as a kind of hieroglyph, it is not out of place to explain them here. The interpreters of Hesiod <note>An early Greek poet</note> hand down the tradition that **Springtime** is represented by Briareus, because of the abundance of herbs, flowers, and foliage which it so fluently provides. By **Gyges**, however, they mean **Winter**, who is also hundred-handed because of the many things he has long ago collected and heaped up, which he soon distributes for various uses and accommodates to his needs. Truly, that the Sun is "hundred-handed" to Homer is due to its many and innumerable duties, which are more obvious and well-known than is necessary to recount here. Since these things are so: have the Japanese not looked toward this same variety of transformations in their idols? Certainly, Luis de Guzman asserts this in his *History of Japan*, book 5, chapter 9, where he relates that the Japanese are accustomed to venerate with the highest honor a certain three-headed statue, <term>triprosopon</term> <note>original Greek: τριπρόσωπον, meaning "three-faced"</note>, by which he says the Japanese mean nothing else than the various perfections of that Deity. I subjoin his Spanish words:

> On one altar of this temple there was a very large idol, covered in gold, with three heads and more than forty arms and hands; they say that by this they understand the many perfections of their God. Beside this idol there were another one thousand five hundred, also gilded, arranged in nine orders in the manner of choirs of angels, and each was the height of a man.

Who does not see here that the Devil has emulated the superstitions of the ancients mixed with Christian mysteries? We have displayed just above one of these images which we happened to see here in Rome.

Furthermore, the Japanese have not only emulated the <term>polymorphia</term> <note>original Greek: πολυμορφίαν, meaning "multiformity" or "diversity of shapes"</note> of the Egyptians in the fashioning of their Gods, but following the Egyptian custom, they have also adored living beasts, such as fish, chickens, deer, wolves, dogs, and oxen, as Luis Fróis testifies in the letter already often cited, following the account of Marco Polo the Venetian. [The first is a lagoon a musket-shot in length and width, and the fish are so many they are beyond counting—they go about, they are beyond counting— <note>The translator notes a repetition in the original Portuguese: "andaõ tem conto andaõ tem conto andaõ"</note> swimming one on top of the other; and because it is dedicated to the **Pagoda** <note>Used here to refer to the temple or the deity therein</note>, no person dares to take any fish from it, believing that if they take them they will become lepers. The **Bonzes** <note>Buddhist monks</note> do not eat fish, because they hold it in their law to be most gra-

<margin>Doctrines of the Cochinchinese.</margin>
Before I put an end to this chapter, I came across a certain report written in Italian, which Christoforo Borri <note>An Italian Jesuit missionary (1583–1632) who provided one of the first detailed European accounts of Vietnam</note> had made not long ago regarding the affairs of Cochinchina <note>A historical region encompassing parts of modern-day central and southern Vietnam</note>. Many things occurred in that report which are truly relevant to our subject; because they can contribute much to confirming what has been said, I decided they should be added. For besides the dogmas which they hold in common with the Chinese and Japanese, they also hold others proper and particular to that people, by which they most closely approach the doctrine of the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, known here for their belief in the "transmigration of souls" or reincarnation</note>.

### SYNTHESIS V. THE EGYPTIAN APE. CHAPTER III. 411

...believe. They believe in the immortality of the soul, <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>original: "μετεμψύχωσιν"; the transmigration of the soul into different bodies</note>, <term>palingenesia</term> <note>original: "παλιγγενεσίαν"; rebirth or the cycle of regeneration</note>, the Soul of the World, and other concepts proper to Platonic and Pythagorean philosophy. Furthermore, they believe the World was a kind of egg, from whose shell the firmament was formed, from the white the ethereal space, and finally the earth consisted of the yolk. They also assert that the machine of the World is nothing other than a certain great animal or man; they profess that its head is the sky; its eyes, the stars; its hair, the trees, plants, and herbs; and its bones, the metals—similar things to what the aforementioned philosophers asserted regarding that great animal and the <term>megacosmos</term> <note>original: "megacosmo"; the "great world" or universe as a reflection of the human "microcosm"</note>. But let us hear the words of the Author himself.

<margin>Christophorus Borrus <note>Cristoforo Borri (1583–1632), a Jesuit missionary to Cochinchina (modern-day Vietnam)</note>.</margin>
[ This Philosopher <note>Referring to the local religious figures described by Borri</note> gave knowledge of the structure of the World through two metaphors: one was that the World was born from an egg, which then expanded in such a way that from its shell the heavens were stretched out, from the white the air was formed and the waters and fire were scattered, and from the red [yolk] the earth and all other terrestrial things were formed. He took the other metaphor from the body of a certain very great man called by them **Bancò** <note>This is Pangu, the primordial giant of Chinese mythology</note>, whom we would call the <term>Microcosmos</term> <note>The human being as a "little world"</note>; saying that from this tallest giant man, this machine of the World had issued, his skull extending into the heavens, his two eyes into the Sun and Moon, his flesh into the earth, his bones into the mountains, his hair into herbs and trees, and his belly into the sea; and in such a way, minutely adapting all the members and composition of the human body to the structure and ornament of this world through various operations, he goes on to say that from the lice of this giant all other men had been formed, who then dispersed throughout the world. ] Again, along with other neighboring nations, they assert that the deceased require food and drink, wherefore splendid banquets are prepared for them daily. *Thirdly, that the souls of the deceased have need of physical sustenance and maintenance; wherefore at certain times during the year according to their custom, sons make for their deceased fathers, husbands for their wives, and friends for other friends, splendid and lavish banquets, waiting a long time for the invited deceased to arrive and sit at the table to eat.*

<margin>Errors of the Tartars <note>The Mongols</note>.</margin>
The Tartars are in the same error; **Marco Polo of Venice** <note>original: "Paulus Marcus Venetus"</note> says: "They worship as God a certain Divinity fashioned by them, whom they call **Natagai**, and they think him the God of the earth, and they appease him with flocks of cattle. They hold this Divinity in the highest honor, nor is there anyone who has not dedicated an image to him in his house. And since they believe the Divinity Natagai has a wife and children, they also place small images in the place of a wife and sons next to their own household gods <note>original: "penates"</note>, placing the statue of the wife on the left, and the images of the sons before the face of the idol. They show great reverence to these idols, especially when they go to lunch or dinner; then, even before they themselves eat, they smear the mouths of the images with the fat of cooked meat, and placing a part of the lunch or dinner outside the house in their honor, they believe they are fed from this. But let us return to the **Cochinchinese** <note>The people of modern Vietnam</note>; it is their custom to revere Kings illustrious for sanctity of life with divine honors, dedicating innumerable idols to them: in the solemnity of the **Apotheosis** <note>The process of a human becoming a god</note> itself, they imitate the Egyptians in every respect. The manner of the Apotheosis follows.

### CHAPTER IV. 412 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAIC TEMPLE

...they prepare the destined structure with no less expense; once it is placed on the aforementioned Altar, the Onsai <note>Kircher refers here to the "Bonzes," or Buddhist monks, whom he calls "Onsai"</note> dressed in white garments, consecrate it with various ceremonies and sacrifices, offering a great number of living cattle, oxen, and other animals. When these rites have been duly performed, they burn that entire mass along with its furnishings, reserving for themselves only the body of the deceased. Feigning to bury it, they secretly and cunningly move it through twelve other burial sites, from one to another. They do this so that the superstitious common people may always remain doubtful and uncertain about the place of burial; consequently, from this uncertainty, devotion and veneration toward this new idol <note>Here "idol" refers to the deceased person being deified</note> increase all the more. Meanwhile, in all those places where they suspect the bones might be hidden or could be found, they perform the rites and sacrifices owed to the other gods.

But let us hear the words of Borri: <note>original Italian: "Finiti questi giorni posero fuoco à tutta quella machina, abbrugiando & il palazzo, & il tempio con tutti gli addobbi & apparati, solo conseruando l'arca con il cadauero, quale fu poi sepelito & transifugato per dodici sepolture da vna in vn'altra segretamente & di nascosto, acciò restando il popolo dubioso sempre in qual luogo fusse lasciato, con l'incertezza maggiormente crescesse la veneratione del nouo idolo, adorandolo in tutti quelli luoghi, nelli quali potessero pensare, che si ritrouasse quell'essa."</note> "Once these days were finished, they set fire to that whole machine, burning both the palace and the temple with all the decorations and furnishings, only preserving the chest with the corpse. This was then buried and moved through twelve tombs, from one to another, secretly and in hiding, so that the people, always remaining in doubt as to which place it was left, would increase their veneration of the new idol all the more due to the uncertainty, worshipping it in all those places where they might think it was found." Thus says Borri.

In this, they certainly imitate the Egyptians, who, instructed by Isis, acquired divinity for their Osiris by a similar ruse. Regarding Isis, Plutarch says: <margin>Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*</margin> "When she had found all the scattered parts of Osiris except the genitals, desiring that the tomb of her husband remain unknown but that he be held in honor by all Egyptians and individuals, she fashioned each of those parts from spices and wax into the shape of a man similar to her husband. Then, calling together the priests, she gave to each an image of Osiris, asserting that his body had been entrusted to them alone, and adjuring them never to divulge to the public that they had the tomb of Osiris, but to worship him as a God kept in secret. From this practice, even now, every priest testifies that Osiris is buried in his possession." And so on for the rest of the account. This was an invention of the cunning demon, which was very effective in ensnaring the minds of the superstitious in the false worship of the Gods. But let these remarks on the Japanese suffice.

# C H A P T E R IV.

->*On the Indian and African Idolatry Parallel to the Egyptian.*<-

<margin>The Indians worship the Sun and fire.</margin>
India is divided into various provinces and has various adjacent islands, all of which use nearly the same ceremonies in the worship of the Gods. For besides countless other particular gods, they primarily worship the Sun and fire; for the latter, they establish various feasts and solemnities throughout the course of the year. In all these, they agree so much with the Egyptians and Persians that almost nothing appears in their sacred rites that they do not seem to have taken from them.

<margin>They venerate the idols of the Egyptians and Greeks.</margin>
<margin>They worship Apis in the form of a Cow.</margin>
Furthermore, those who have traveled through those regions testify that the images of the Greeks and Egyptians are still found there and are worshipped with the highest veneration. Above all others, the cult of <term>Apis</term> <note>The sacred bull of ancient Egypt, regarded as an intermediary between humans and the gods</note> thrives in the form of a Cow or a horned Ox...

### SYNT. V. THE EGYPTIAN IMITATION. CHAPTER IV. 413

...is flourishing, whom you may find in all temples, porticoes, and ways. 
<margin>Louis Sachin of Avignon.</margin>
Louis Sachin, a merchant of Avignon, reported to me that in the Kingdom of the Mughals <note>original: "Regno Mogorum," referring to the Mughal Empire in India</note>, in that place where it borders Bengal, on the public and Royal road stands a massive Ox, in whose eye cavities two very large Carbuncles or Rubies are set, making the idol radiate in a wondrous manner. He also reported that no one begins their journey without first appeasing this Bovine idol with certain sacrifices. Marco Polo of Venice <note>original: "Paulus Marcus Venetus"</note> supports these statements; 
<margin>Marco Polo of Venice.</margin>
for he relates that most of the islands near Bengal are imbued with this wicked worship of the Ox; I will add his words: *The inhabitants of the Kingdom of Var <note>original: "Var," likely referring to Ma'bar on the Coromandel Coast</note> are all idolaters, and many of them adore the ox as a holy thing, nor do they kill any; however, when some ox dies, they anoint their houses with its fat.* And concerning the city of Mylapore <note>original: "Meliapore," a site in modern Chennai associated with the Apostle St. Thomas</note>, chapter 28: *When those who adore oxen go forth to war, they carry with them the hair of a wild ox and tie it to the manes of their horses, with which they attack; the infantry, however, tie those hairs to their shields and their own hair, believing themselves safe in war from all danger; for they assert the wild ox is of great holiness.* And chapter 30 of the same book: *The people of Laos <note>original: "Laënses"</note> adore oxen, and with great reverence anoint themselves with an ointment made from crushed bovine bones.* That traces of the Greek gods, besides the Egyptian ones, also exist is clear from the letters of Father Juan Lopez of the Society of Jesus, Procurator of India and the Philippine Islands, with whom I discussed these matters in person later here in Rome: 
<margin>Juan Lopez of the Society of Jesus.</margin>
<margin>The idolatry of the Philippines rivals the idolatry of the Egyptians and Greeks.</margin>
[The sect of the Filipinos, he says, is the same idolatry as that of the Romans and Greeks; they still adore Jupiter and other Gods. They have the names of these Gods, but in their own language. For example, Jupiter is called *Maglente*, which means "vibrating lightning," derived from *lente*, which means lightning, and *mag*, which signifies "to vibrate" <note>This refers to the Tagalog word for lightning, "kidlat," though Lopez's etymology is specific to his era's linguistic understanding</note>. Atlas is called **TOMCON LANGIT**, that is, Pillar of Heaven; *Langit* means Heaven and *Tomcon* means Pillar. And so with the rest: they also have their own Elysian Fields <note>The ancient Greek conception of the afterlife for the blessed</note>, which they call *Calangdan*, that is, the setting of the Sun.] Which is a clear sign that the idolatry of the Egyptians and Greeks reached even to the farthest East. Indeed, Philostratus <note>A Greek sophist of the Roman imperial period</note> shows this even more clearly in the *Life of Apollonius*:

<margin>Philostratus in the Life of Apollonius, book 3, chapter 3.</margin>
> They say they encountered statues of the gods. If they were Indian or Egyptian, it would be no wonder. But they found the most ancient of those among the Greeks: statues of Athena Polias, and of the Delian Apollo, and of Dionysus, and the Amyclean Apollo, and as many others as are so ancient. These Indians had established these and thought it pleasing to live in the Greek manner. They say they inhabit the middle of India, and make the mound of this hill the navel. From it they celebrate a fire, which they say they draw from the sun's rays; and to this they sing a hymn once a day at noon. <note>original Greek: "Θεῶν δ' ἀγάλμασιν ἐντυχεῖν φάσιν..."</note>

[Apollonius reports that he saw many statues of the Gods there, and was not surprised to see images of Indian or Egyptian Gods; but he was stunned to see statues of those who are considered the most ancient among the Greeks, such as Athena Polias, and the Delian Apollo, furthermore Dionysus, and the Amyclean Apollo, and others of this sort; for the Indians set up a statue for each of these and sacrifice to them according to Greek ritual; they say they dwell in the middle of India, and that mound is like a navel, and from it they take sacred fire, which they boast they received from the rays of the Sun, and in memory of that event they continually chant a hymn until noon.]

### CHAPTER IV. 414 OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS THE ISIAC TEMPLE

<margin>The Brahmins follow the dogmas of Pythagoras.</margin>
It is well established from the Indian history of Maffei <note>Giovanni Pietro Maffei (1533–1603), a Jesuit historian who wrote extensively about the Portuguese missions in the East.</note> and others that the Brahmins and Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers," a term used by ancient Greeks for Indian ascetics.</note> lived—as they once did and still do to this day—according to the Pythagorean life. Damis, the companion of Apollonius, also discusses them at length in the works of Philostratus. They profess the dogmas of Pythagoras; their chief study is in divination; they sleep on the ground and live only on herbs; they adore the Sun and, with the greatest zeal, tend to a fire sparked by the sun's rays. They appease this fire with various rituals and prayers. They grow their hair long, wear a Mitre <note>original: "Mythram," likely referring to a turban or head-covering.</note> and carry Pagodas <note>original: "Pagodes," here used to mean small portable idols or statuettes.</note> or Isiac statues; they walk with bare feet, are clothed in linen garments, and support themselves with a staff—all of which are certainly characteristic of the Egyptian priests of the Sun.

<margin>Niccolò de' Conti.</margin>
Niccolò de' Conti, the Venetian, also mentions these things in the book he wrote concerning his journey to the Indies:
> Throughout all India they adore idols (that is, Pagodas), for which they build churches not unlike those of Egypt, full of images of every form painted within. On the days of their solemnities, they adorn them with flowers and branches. The idols are made of gold, silver, stone, or ivory, some of which are sixty feet in height. The manner in which they sacrifice to them is very varied among them, because some wash themselves with clear water before they enter the temple, once in the morning and another time at vespers. Others make sacrifice to their idols with aloe wood or other similar scents. <note>Translated from the Italian quote of Niccolò de' Conti, a 15th-century explorer.</note>

From these accounts, the manifest traces of Egyptian customs and rituals are clearly seen.

<margin>The Indians worship a Demon.</margin>
There is no shortage of those among the Indians who—following the example of certain Egyptians who worshipped Typhon <note>the chaotic "evil" deity of Egyptian myth</note> as a malignant demon with most solemn rites—themselves adore the Devil, the enemy of the human race, and appease him with various sacrifices. Ludovico di Varthema describes this kind of worship and the ceremonies usually performed for it in Book 2 of his *Travels in India*, chapter 2. I will subjoin his words:

<margin>Ludovico di Varthema.</margin>
> The King of Calicut <note>modern Kozhikode, India</note> is a pagan and adores the Devil in the manner you shall hear. They confess that one God created the heaven and the earth and all the world, and is the first cause in all things. They say that if He wished to judge you and me, and a third and a fourth, He would have no pleasure in being Lord, but that He has sent this world to do justice; to him who does well, He does well, and to him who does evil, He does evil. They call him the Deumo <note>likely a corruption of "Deva" or a local spirit interpreted as a demon.</note>, and they call God "Tamerani" <note>likely "Tamburan," a title for a lord or deity in Malayalam.</note>. This Deumo the King of Calicut keeps in his chapel in this manner: His chapel is two paces wide on each side and four paces high, with a wooden door all carved with devils in relief. In the middle of this chapel there is a Devil made of metal, who sits in a chair also made of metal. The said Devil wears a crown made in the fashion of the Papal Kingdom with three crowns <note>original: "Regno Papale," referring to the triple-tiered papal tiara.</note>, and he also has four crowns <note>The text says "corone" (crowns) again, though some versions of Varthema's text suggest horns.</note> and four teeth with a very large open mouth, with an ugly nose and most terrible eyes that look cruelly; his hands are curved like a hook and his feet like those of a cock, so that to see him is a very frightening thing. Around the said chapel the paintings are all she-devils, and on every side of it there is a Satanas <note>Satan</note> placed sitting in a chair, which is placed in a flame of fire, in which is a great quantity of souls half a finger and a finger of the hand long. The said Satanas with his right hand holds a soul in his mouth, eating— <note>The text ends mid-sentence as a catchword for the next page.</note>

<margin>The Indians worship fire as a sacred animal.</margin>
But above all else, they worship fire as a sacred animal; to this they sacrifice their children, and into this they throw themselves to be burned, showing their veneration toward it by this act. Indeed, they learned this cult from no other source than the Persians and their neighbors the Chaldeans; they maintained it themselves, as was said above, in several small shrines as a perpetual flame, and they consulted it like an oracle concerning future events. Benjamin <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century Jewish traveler.</note> mentions this in his travelogue with these words:

<margin>The Persians worshiped fire.</margin>
<margin>The same people threw themselves alive into the fire.</margin>
Before the altar of the sacred buildings is a huge pit, in which a massive fire burns through continuous ages; they call this "divinity." Through it they lead their children, and they cast their dead entirely into it. The Rabbi <note>referring again to Benjamin of Tudela</note> continues and records the astonishing devotion of this foolish nation: that those who affect a reputation for holiness cast themselves alive into this fire, and with the great applause of the onlookers, they endure a voluntary death. This reminds me of that wanderer in Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata, a 2nd-century satirist who wrote about the public self-immolation of the philosopher Peregrinus Proteus.</note>, who, in order to provide a spectacle for others, inflicted tortures upon himself by spontaneously burning himself at the Olympic assembly, at least so that he might acquire fame for his name:

They all rejoice for him and say to him: "Happy are you and well it is for you." And when the day of his vow arrives, they make him a great feast, and he rides—if he is wealthy—

By such a lying enchantment, performed by these Magical Priests, the people are so convinced that they claim nothing like it happens anywhere else in the world. <margin>Idolatry of the Africans.</margin>
Africa is divided into three parts: the Southern, the Torrid (or Ethiopia), and the Northern. The Ethiopians, and all those who inhabit the Torrid Zone, are steeped in various religions everywhere. For obelisks, columns, and pyramids still stand in various places. They hold gods in common with the Egyptians, such as Dionysus, Ammon, Hercules, Apollo, Mercury, and others. ### CHAPTER V.

->**On the Religion of the Americans as Parallel to the Egyptian.**<-

**I**t should seem a wonder to no one, considering that almost all of Asia became infected over time by that insane idolatry of the Egyptians; for, due to the continuity of kingdoms and lands, and the mutual trade of neighboring nations, it was by no means difficult to spread it. But that Egyptian rites crept even into the New World, separated by an almost infinite distance of lands and ocean, seems to exceed all wonder.

It clearly appears that that ancient enemy of the human race <note>the Devil</note>, who once oppressed Egypt and the rest of Asia with his untamed tyranny, having been driven out by the light of the most holy Gospel, has fixed his seat in these furthest corners of the world. He has corrupted these people with the same devices with which he corrupted the ancients; indeed, there is no type of superstition used by the ancients that is not found among them. Like the Egyptians, they adore water, earth, flowers, herbs, birds of every kind, all domestic items, or whatever finally falls to their use in any way. Like the Persians, they worship fire; like all Eastern peoples, they worship the Sun, Moon, and Stars; in their fables and various inventions about the Gods and the origin of all things, they come very close to the Greeks, as those things we have gathered for this purpose from various Spanish, French, and Italian authors sufficiently demonstrate.

In the island of Hispaniola <note>modern Haiti and the Dominican Republic</note>, the natives were found to worship nothing other than the lights of heaven when the Spaniards first discovered the said island. But, when many of the Spaniards lived in closer companionship among them and the languages of both sides were mixed, they discovered that various ceremonies and various rites were observed among them. They are as follows.

<margin>Idolatry of the inhabitants of Hispaniola.</margin>
Out of woven cotton <note>original: "Gossypio"</note> stuffed on the inside, they form images in the appearance of seated figures, which imitate the nocturnal spirits <note>original: "Lemures"</note> in the way our painters fix them to walls. These idols they call <term>Cemes</term> <note>These are the 'Zemis' of the Taíno people.</note>, which are very similar to those the Chinese call *Chamis*. The smaller of these, resembling infant demons, they tie to their foreheads when they are about to engage in hand-to-hand combat with enemies. From these they believe they obtain rain, if rain is lacking, or sunshine, if they need the sun; for they think the *Cemes* are the messengers of Him whom they confess to be the only one, without lack, almighty, and invisible. Each petty king <note>original: "Regulus," likely referring to a Cacique</note> has his own *Cemen* whom he worships; to the eternal Divinity...

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE ISIAC TEMPLE
# PAGE 418

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>These two names, *Iocauuna Guamanaocon*, were bestowed by their ancestors. They say that the Divinity itself has a mother, who is called by these five names: namely, *Atabeira*, *Mamona*, *Guacarapita*, *Liella*, and *Guimazoa*. Now, listen to what they believe regarding the origin of man on earth. There is a region on the Island <note>Hispaniola, modern-day Haiti and the Dominican Republic</note> named *Caunana*, where they babble that the human race came forth from two caves of a certain mountain. They declare that the greater part of men came out from the wider mouth of the cave, and the lesser part from the narrower one. The rock from which the caves open they call *Cauta*. The larger cave they name *Cazibaxagua*, and the smaller one *Amiauna*. 

Before men were permitted to go out from there, they say simply that the mouths of the cave were accustomed to be guarded every night by a man named *Machochaël*. When this *Machochaël* had gone a bit too far from the cave out of a desire to see the world, he was caught by the Sun—whose sight he was least able to endure—and is said to have been changed into stone. They tell similar fables about several others who, having proceeded so far from the cave at night out of a desire for fishing that they could not return before sunrise (whom it was not permitted to look upon), were transformed into fig trees. 

They say, moreover, that a certain chief named *Vaguoniona* sent one of his attendants out of the cave to fish; they say he was changed into a philomela <note>original: "philomelam"; a nightingale</note> for the same reason—because the Sun came upon him before he could retreat. From this, every year at that same time when he was turned into the little bird, he is said to complain of his fate with his song at night and implore the help of his master *Vaguoniona*. 

But *Vaguoniona*, out of longing for his attendant whom he loved ardently, led out only the women with the little children whom they were nursing, leaving the men behind in the cave. It is said that he left the women on one of the islands of that region, which is called *Mathmino*, but took the infants away with him. These poor little ones, overcome by hunger on the bank of a certain river, crying out *toa, toa*—that is, "mama, mama"—are said to have been turned into frogs. They say that is why that voice has remained in frogs during the springtime. Thus, they devise the story that in those caves from which men were scattered throughout Hispaniola, only the men remained without women. 

They relate furthermore that *Vaguoniona* himself, wandering through various places and never changed by special grace, descended to a beautiful woman whom he saw at the bottom of the sea; they say he received from her certain marble pebbles, which they call *Cibas*, and certain yellow tablets made of orichalcum <note>original: "aurichalco"; a gold-copper alloy often called 'guanín' by the Taíno</note>, which they call *Guaninos*. These ornaments are held as sacred among their Kings even to this day. 

They relate that those men, whom we said were left in the caves without women, went out at night to wash themselves at the pools of rainwater. On one of these nights, they saw from afar certain animals resembling women, crawling through the trees like columns of ants. They attempted to seize these women, but they slipped away like slippery eels. They took counsel; and on the advice of an Elder, they sought out any among them who were scabby or leprous, who might have rough and calloused hands, so that they might more easily hold them once caught. These men they call *Caracaracolos*. They went out to hunt, and out of the many they caught, they kept only four. They attempted to use them as women, but found they lacked a female nature. Calling the Elders again to consult on what should be done, they decided that the woodpecker bird should be let in, to dig out a hole between their thighs with its sharp beak.

### SYNTAGMA V. THE EGYPTIAN MONKEY. 419 CHAPTER V.

...they [were]; while the "Caracaracols" themselves <note>original: "Caracaracolibus"; a term referring to men with scabby or rough skin in Taíno mythology</note>, men with calloused skin, held the women, a woodpecker was brought forth to open their sex <note>original: "sexum aperit"; referring to the myth where woodpeckers carved female anatomy into sexless beings</note>. From this, the islands obtained the women they desired, and from them, offspring were subsequently procreated.

Let no one now marvel that Greece filled so many volumes describing the Myrmidons—as if the Myrmidons were procreated from ants. These and many other stories of this kind are suggested by the wiser men from their platforms and pulpits to the simple, wondering crowd with a calm and serene expression, and they are recited as sacred truth.

<margin>The myth of the origin of the sea among the inhabitants of Hispaniola.</margin>
But regarding the origin of the sea, I shall add another story not unlike the Talmudic fables. There was once on the Island a powerful man named Iaia, who buried his only son—who was shedding his human form—within a gourd <term>gourd: original "cucurbita", a large hollowed-out fruit used by the Taíno as a vessel or container</term> in place of a tomb. After a few months had passed, this Iaia, impatient with grief over the death of his son, returned to the gourd. When he had opened it, massive whales and great sea-monsters came forth; for this reason, he declared to certain neighbors that the sea was enclosed within that gourd. 

Moved by this rumor, four young brothers, born from the same birth (though their mother perished in the delivery), approached the gourd in the hope of catching fish. They took it in their hands, but when Iaia arrived—who frequently visited to see the enclosed bones of his beloved son—the youths were terrified. Caught in the suspicion of sacrilege and theft, and watching Iaia closely so they might flee more quickly, they let the gourd slip from their hands. Crushed by its excessive weight, it broke; the sea poured out through its cracks, the valleys were filled, and that vast plain, which used to occupy that whole region of islands as dry land, was submerged. Only the mountains, on account of their height, escaped that inundation, and these now constitute the islands that one may see today.

They say then that these brothers, out of fear of Iaia, wandered for so long through various places that they almost perished from hunger. While seeking bread, they knocked at a baker's house; the baker is said to have spat upon one of them so sharply that a very swollen dropsy <note>original: "intercus"; a swelling or fluid under the skin</note> soon arose therefrom. But by the council of the brothers, the ulcer was opened with a sharp stone; from it, they say a woman was born, whom all those brothers used in turn, and they say they fathered sons and daughters by her. 

Mark another more pleasant thing. There exists a cave named *Iauanaboina* in the domain of a certain petty king <term>petty king: original "Regulus", referring to a Cacique or local tribal leader</term> who is called *Machinnech*. They worship and venerate this cave more religiously than the Greeks once did Corinth, or Cyrrha and Nysa; it is decorated with a thousand kinds of pictures. In the entrance of this cave, they have two sculpted *Cemes* <term>Cemes: also known as Zemis; physical objects or carvings believed to house ancestral spirits or deities</term>, one of whom they call *Binthaibellem* and the other *Marohum*. When asked why they worshiped the cave with such great piety, they answered gravely and sensibly: because the Sun and the Moon came forth from there to provide light to the world. 

Their augurs, whom they call *Boitios* <term>Boitios: shamans or medicine men of the Taíno people</term>, imbue them with these superstitions. These same men are also physicians, who devise a thousand frauds for the common people who are ignorant of things. Because they hold exceptional authority, they force the people to believe that they speak with those *Cemes* and predict the future. And if anyone laboring under adverse health recovers, they persuade him that he achieved this by the gift of the *Ceme*. These *Boitios* bind themselves to fasting and purification when they take charge of some high-ranking person; they devour an intoxicating herb <note>likely tobacco or cohoba, a hallucinogenic snuff</note>, which, when they have taken it in powdered form, drives them into a frenzy like Maenads <note>original: "Mænades"; female followers of Bacchus known for their ecstatic, wild behavior</note>, and they murmur that they have heard many things from the *Cemes*. They enter the infirmary with a bone or a small stone hidden in their mouth, or a small piece of flesh; they cast everyone out from the semi-circle except for one or two whom the sick man himself chooses...

The Boitius <note>original: "Boitius"; a term for a Taíno shaman or medicine man</note> circles the nobleman three or four times, contorting his face, lips, and nostrils with foul gestures; he blows upon the forehead, the temples, and the neck, inhaling the air from the sick man; after this, he claims to have drained the disease from the sufferer's veins. Then, rubbing the sick man's shoulders, thighs, and legs, he draws his joined hands down to the feet, and thus with hands clasped, he runs to the open door and shakes out his open hands, persuading the man that he has put the disease to flight and that he will shortly be healthy. But approaching him from behind, like a magician, he pulls a small piece of meat out of his mouth and cries out to the sick man, saying: "Behold what you had eaten beyond necessity; you shall be well, since I have removed it from you." If, however, he intends to deceive the sick man more gravely, he persuades him that a Cemi <note>original: "Cemen"; an ancestral spirit or deity of the Taíno, often represented by an idol</note> is angry with him, because he either did not build him a house, or did not worship him with enough devotion, or did not dedicate a field to him. If it happens that the sick man dies, his relatives compel the dead man through sorcery to confess whether he died by fate or by the negligence of the Boitius—because he did not fast completely, or did not provide a medicine suitable for the sick man. If he died by the fault of the Boitius-physician, they take vengeance upon the Boitius. And let these things concerning their fables, which we have translated from Spanish sources, suffice; now let us return to the Cemes.

<margin>Peter Martyr, Decade 1, Book 9 of the New World.</margin>

According to the testimony of Peter Martyr <note>Peter Martyr d'Anghiera (1457–1526), a primary chronicler of the early Spanish explorations</note>, they have spirits whom they worship; some construct wooden ones, warned by nighttime shadows among the trees; others, if they have received oracles from within the rocks, carve them from marble. Others are worshiped among roots, found among *Ages* <note>a type of edible root or sweet potato</note>; they believe these Cemes have care over them, not unlike Ceres <note>the Roman goddess of agriculture</note> or Proserpina among the Greeks, so that their bread may grow together. They believe others preside over waters and forests, just as antiquity thought the Dryads, Hamadryads, Satyrs, Pan-gods, or Nereids <note>various Greek nature spirits of trees, woods, and sea</note> had care of the springs, forests, and the sea, and assigned their own gods to each thing so that each might protect its own kind; in the same way, these islanders believe their invoked Cemes listen to their desires. Therefore, when the petty kings consult the Cemi regarding the outcome of a war, the harvest, or their health, the Boitius enters the house dedicated to the Cemi. There, having inhaled through his nostrils *Cohobba* <term>Cohobba: a hallucinogenic snuff used by the Taíno, typically made from the seeds of the Anadenanthera peregrina tree</term> (for so they call the intoxicating herb by which the Boitios are immediately turned into a frenzy), he dreams that he sees the house moved with the roof turned toward the foundations and people walking with their tracks reversed. As soon as the madness ceases, he embraces his knees with his head lowered between his arms. Having remained in this stunned state for a short while, he raises his head as if sleepy, and lifting his eyes to heaven, first mutters certain confused things to himself. Then the primary courtiers standing by (for no one from the common people is admitted to those sacred rites) give thanks with raised voices that he has now returned to them from his conversation with the Cemes, and they inquire what he has seen. He, opening his mouth, raves that the Cemi spoke to him at that time, and like one possessed, he predicts either victory or destruction if they join battle with enemies, or famine or abundance, plague or health, and whatever comes into his mouth. Who does not see here the traces of the Pythonic spirit <note>referring to the Pythia, the priestess of the Oracle of Delphi</note>, Apollonian frenzy, and the ecstasy of the ancient Magi? Certainly, in the second part of *Oedipus*, I shall relate these men with similar rituals most closely to the Hieromants <note>priests of sacred mysteries</note> of the Egyptians, the Magi of the Persians, and the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers," a term used for Indian ascetics</note> of the Indians, God willing.

Kircher draws direct parallels between these Caribbean practices and the religious ecstasies of ancient Greek, Egyptian, and Persian priests.</summary>

### SYNTAGMA V. THE EGYPTIAN APE. 421 CHAPTER V.

...with God's help, we shall show. Now let us turn to the remaining things which the Americans have in common with the Egyptians.

<margin>The idols of the Americans.</margin>
And first, they held mysteries in the construction of their idols that were not unlike the mysteries of the Egyptians. The Egyptians fashioned idols from every kind of material—wood, stone, and metal—joined together, as has been said elsewhere regarding the idol of Serapis <note>Serapis was a Graeco-Egyptian deity; Kircher frequently uses him as a primary example of Egyptian syncretism.</note>, and we shall explain the mysteries of this kind of construction in the following part. In a similar manner, the Americans in many places to this day still worship certain statues as Gods, fashioned from every kind of their own seeds and kneaded with the blood of human hearts; they strive to appease their Deities with a ritual of sacrifice that is not dissimilar. This is established from the account of Hernán Cortés <note>original: "Franciscus Cortesius"</note>, which he gives concerning the Mexican city of Tenochtitlan <note>original: "Themistiana"; a common early modern Latinization of Tenochtitlan.</note> in these words:

<margin>Hernán Cortés.</margin>
> *The idols they worshiped were certain statues the size of a man or larger, made of a paste of all the seeds that they have and eat, which they kneaded with the blood of human hearts; and of this material were their Gods. They kept them seated in certain chairs like episcopal thrones, with a small shield on one arm and a sword in the other; and the places where they kept them were certain towers of this sort.*

<margin>America: they build temples in the manner of Pyramids.</margin>
Furthermore, following the example of the Egyptians, they build certain mystical temples in the manner of pyramids, in which they worship their idols according to their accustomed ceremonies. The aforementioned Cortés describes such structures in the following words:
> *They build a structure like a square tower, one hundred and fifty paces or a little more in length, and one hundred and fifteen or one hundred and twenty in width. This structure begins entirely solid, and is as high as two man-heights. The material is entirely solid, made of lime and stone; and here, on three sides, they provide steps. They ascend in this manner until they reach one hundred and twenty or one hundred and thirty steps. At the top, there remains a reasonably sized small plaza, and in the middle of it, two other towers begin from within, which rise ten or twelve man-heights high, and at the summit there are windows. In these high towers, they keep their idols very well arranged and adorned; and the entire room where they had their principal God was also well-finished and ordered (the name of which varied according to the provinces). For the principal God of the great city of Mexico was called Huitzilopochtli <note>original: "Horchilocos"; Kircher’s phonetic rendering of the Nahuatl name.</note>, and in another city, which was called Cholula <note>original: "Chuennila"</note>, it was Quetzalcoatl <note>original: "Quecadqueal"</note>. In this room where the idol stood, no one was permitted to enter except their High Priest. And every time they had some necessity—such as for rain, or that it stop raining when it rains too much, or if they were besieged by their enemies, or for other needs—they perform sacrifices to them.*

<margin>The manner of sacrifice among the Americans.</margin>
Thus far Cortés. Moreover, the manner of sacrificing was that which follows. A man who offers himself voluntarily to be sacrificed is led through all the crossroads and streets of the city with the greatest festivity and in the appearance of a triumph. When this solemnity is completed, he is presented to be killed before the idol, which is at the corner of the said tower. With hymns and dances renewed, a minor priest <term>sacrificulus</term> <note>A term for a priest who performs small or specific sacrificial rites.</note> opens the chest of the victim crosswise with a certain stone razor. Having extracted the heart, while it is still warm and bubbling with the heat of the blood, he first anoints the mouth of the idol; afterward, having cast a portion of the flowing blood toward the Sun, or by night toward the Moon, he anoints the mouths of the other idols, and also the cornice <term>coronidem</term> of the door of the Temple. Finally, he reduces the burnt heart to ash, the dust of the remains...

### CHAPTER V. 422 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS THE ISIAC TEMPLE

...acting as a substitute for remains, which they similarly do with the ashes of the whole body. However, so that the reader might more easily compare pyramidal masses of this kind with those of the Egyptians, it seemed appropriate to place here their construction, which we have taken from Cortés <note>Hernán Cortés (1485–1547), the Spanish Conquistador whose letters described Aztec society to Europe.</note>.

->Figure of the Temple of the American Deity Horebolisos.<- <note>The name "Horebolisos" appears to be Kircher’s idiosyncratic Latinization or a corruption of a Nahuatl deity name, possibly related to Huitzilopochtli.</note>

<margin>The Americans worship the Sun and Moon.</margin>
Furthermore, in other parts of America they also worship the Sun and the Moon; in others, the Stars and the portents of Meteors; in some, Lions and other similar fierce animals, of which things they keep images and statues in their Temples; so indeed, that their temples are not unlike the temples of the Egyptians, in which every variety of monster was seen in the place of Gods. Thus, from this chapter it may well appear that the inventor of such monstrous religion was the same: namely, the Devil, the father of monsters.

<margin>... p. 43. ... p. 253</margin>
We have said in the preceding pages that the phallus, or human genitals, was always held in the highest veneration among the Egyptians and other Oriental nations. Certainly, the previously cited Cortés reports that the Americans participated in the same cult; for they worship the male member in the Province of Pánuco <note>A region in Mexico; early Spanish accounts frequently highlighted (and often exaggerated) "idolatrous" sexual imagery to justify colonization.</note>. They venerate it placed in temples together with images expressing all acts of lust; which things were introduced by the Devil for this reason: so that no pagan sacred rites, then as now, might be conducted without shameful acts of debauchery.

<margin>The Americans worship the Devil.</margin>
Finally, there is no lack of those who worship the Devil himself, feeding him with human hearts and venerating him with other detestable rites. So says Cortés: *It is a very well-known thing that those people used to see the Devil in those figures that they made,* <note>original Italian: "E coſa molto notoria, che quelle genti vedeano il Diavolo in quelle figure, che eſsi faceuano"</note>

### SYNTHESIS V. THE EGYPTIAN APE. CHAPTER V.

...and that they hold to their idols, and that the Devil would place himself inside those idols, and from there he spoke with them, and commanded them that they should sacrifice, and give to them the hearts of men, because they [the idols] ate nothing else. For this purpose they were very diligent in sacrificing men, giving them the hearts and the blood; he [the Devil] also commanded them many other things, which they did punctually, just as he told them. These are the most devout people, and the most observant of their religion, of all the nations that God has created, so much so that they themselves voluntarily offered to be sacrificed, thinking that in this way they would save their souls. They even drew blood from their own tongues, and from their ears, and from their thighs, and from their arms, to sacrifice it and offer it to their idols. They have many shrines <note>original: "eremitonj," referring to small hermitages or roadside shrines.</note> outside and along the roads, where they go to shed their blood and offer it to the idols. *These things according to Cortés.* <note>Hernán Cortés (1485–1547), the Spanish explorer whose accounts of the Aztec Empire were primary sources for European scholars like Kircher.</note>

From these accounts it clearly appears that the demon has always been so thirsty for human blood that he never permitted any sacred rite to be celebrated by the Gentiles without it. For instance, to **Moloch** <note>A Canaanite deity associated with child sacrifice.</note>, the parents’ own children were offered, as they were also to **Saturn**; to **Mars**, soldiers were offered; and without human blood, the **Mithraic** <note>Refers to the mysteries of Mithras, a Roman mystery religion.</note> rites were never completed. Furthermore, we have seen such cursed rites still flourishing in many regions; it seems that the most thirsty Devil can quench his thirst by no other thing except the drink of human blood, and truly can remove his hunger by no other thing except the feeding upon human hearts. But let these things suffice concerning the idol **Horchilouos**. <note>Kircher's Latinization of Huitzilopochtli, the Aztec god of war and the sun.</note>

<margin>The Mexican Idol.</margin>
Furthermore, there is celebrated in the Mexican Province another certain idol, or rather a demon, fashioned with various heads of animals as if they were certain hieroglyphic figures. This idol was not appeased except by human blood. In their own language, they called him the **Lord of the Year**, which both those hieroglyphic symbols and the mystical numbers sufficiently show. For once he was appeased by this worship and the customary sacrifices, they promised themselves a great abundance of things. The image of this statue exists in a certain Mexican book in the Vatican Library; the head is like a bushel measure <note>original: "instar Modij," referring to a Roman unit of dry volume, suggesting a cylindrical shape.</note>, with radiant eyes, donkey ears, and a nose and mouth with teeth, deformed in a foul manner. It holds vessels pertaining to sacrifice in both hands; on the rest of the idol's body, various heads of different animals are seen carved everywhere, by which they were accustomed to represent the months and the Zodiac. It has the feet of an elephant; the rest, modesty forbidding, I have not thought should be spoken of. But, lest anything should seem lacking for the adornment of this work, I have decided that its figure ought to be placed here.

Many things would have to be said by me in this place concerning the mystical images of this idol, the interpretation of which I have received from our Mexican Fathers <note>Jesuit missionaries stationed in colonial Mexico who sent reports and codices back to Rome.</note>; but since we have reserved those for another place, I have judged it superfluous to dwell on them here any longer. Let it suffice for now to have demonstrated in this place the affinity of American idolatry to that of the Egyptians, which was our sole aim.

### EPILOGUE.

Having thus demonstrated the affinity between the idolatry of various nations and the idolatry of the Egyptians—which we have shown throughout this work to be the source and fountainhead of all others—it will certainly not be difficult for a wise **Oedipus** <note>Kircher often uses "Oedipus" as a metaphor for the scholar—specifically himself—capable of solving the "riddles" of ancient mysteries.</note> to reveal through this method many things pertaining to **Isiac** <note>Related to the goddess Isis or the religious systems derived from Egypt.</note> antiquities that were previously unknown to us. Consequently, this method will bring much light to the investigation of the science of **hieroglyphics** <note>term: hieroglyphicorum. Kircher viewed hieroglyphics not just as writing, but as a symbolic language of divine and demonic mysteries.</note>. 

For since the Egyptians practiced those arts taught to them by the **Devil**, and these mentioned nations learned from the same Master, it is so likely that they shared the same rules and used the same rites and ceremonies in the worship of their gods that I consider it a sin to doubt it any further. This being the case, I hope no one thinks we have wandered off course in this matter; indeed, far from being irrelevant, I am convinced that nothing will bring more authority to our work than this study of the idolatry of remote nations. This will be understood by anyone who carefully compares this section with those that follow.

### TREATISE II.

# THE PRINTER
## TO THE READER.

If you set aside the punctuation marks, which were done wrongly through the negligence of the corrector, very few typographical errors are found in a work so vast and varied that could escape your diligence, Reader, or delay your reading. I would like you to credit this to a most expert man, very well-versed in various languages, Zacharias Dominicus of Kronenfeld, my <term>typotheta: a typesetter or compositor</term>. In the following table of errors, the first number signifies the page, the second the line of the page. I do not add more, because those that remain are insignificant.

Note, Reader, on page 48, line 31, those words of Diodorus Siculus (seventeen hundred thousand) contain a manifest error. For if the notable towns of Egypt were 18,000, how could there be only 170,000 people? The Greek text has *seven million* <note>original: "ἑπτακοσίας μυριάδας" — seven hundred myriads</note> (seven hundred myriads, or seven million); or as Laurentius Rhodomanus translates it, (seventy hundred thousand). Even if these equal only 7,000,000, they still make too small a number, in my judgment, to fill so many towns.

### Admonition to Hebrew and Arabic Readers.

As for the errors <term>sphalmata: slips or mistakes</term> that occur in the Hebrew and Arabic, readers skilled in these languages will easily correct them; especially since in Hebrew nothing happens more easily than taking *Kaph* for *Beth*, *Daleth* for *Resh*, *Tav* for *Chet*, *Chet* or *Tav* for *He*, *Vav* for *Yod*, final *Mem* for *Samekh*, final *Vav* for *Nun*, and vice versa. In Arabic, *Ra* for *Zay*, *Ha* for *Kha* or *Jim*, or *Kha* for *Ha* or *Jim*, just as *Ba* for *Ta* and *Nun* are easily interchanged; so also nothing is easier than to commit similar errors. The same must be thought of the shapes of similar letters, as if *Fa* for *Qaf*, *Waw* for *Ra* or *Qaf*, and vice versa. However, the skilled reader will correct these by himself with no difficulty. And so we wanted first to advise the skilled reader of these things, so that if he finds the stumbling blocks of similar errors, he may kindly excuse them.

### Decorative Marbled Endpaper

->Decorative Motif<-

This page features a full-page <term>marbled paper pattern</term> <note>A decorative technique where colors are floated on a liquid bath, combed into patterns, and then transferred to a sheet of paper.</note>. The specific design shown is known as a <term>nonpareil pattern</term> <note>A French term meaning "matchless" or "without equal." It is a classic marbling style characterized by fine, rhythmic, fan-like or scalloped rows.</note>. 

This style, sometimes called a peacock or feathered design, was a staple of the bookbinder's craft in the 17th and 18th centuries. These sheets were typically used as <term>endpapers</term>—the protective leaves pasted to the inside of the book's covers. Beyond their beauty, these complex patterns helped to hide the glue and structural cords of the binding, while also making any wear or staining less visible over centuries of use. 

The image shows dense, undulating swirls that create a sense of movement across the page. At the bottom center, there is a small blank area where the pigment did not take, likely due to a bubble or a fold in the paper during the original marbling process.

<summary>This page displays a nonpareil marbled paper design, a decorative element used in traditional bookbinding to provide an elegant finish to the interior covers. It represents the artistic craftsmanship involved in historical book production.</summary>

<keywords>marbled paper, nonpareil pattern, bookbinding, decorative arts, endpaper, peacock style, 18th-century binding</keywords>
